You can also say "au commissariat" for "at/to the police station" (common in France).
target_language_example: On va au poste de police pour déposer une plainte.
native_language_example: We’re going to the police station to file a report.

meaning: on the first floor (France: the level above the ground floor).
additional_notes: Used to say where something/someone is located or where to carry/take something. In France and many French-speaking places, "le rez-de-chaussée" is the ground floor, so "le premier étage" is one floor up (what Americans often call the second floor). Often used with verbs like "monter" (go up), "descendre" (go down), "porter" (carry), and "se situer" (to be located).
target_language_example: La salle de réunion est au premier étage, juste à gauche de l’ascenseur.
native_language_example: The meeting room is on the first floor, just to the left of the elevator.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens in spring in general (a recurring season). You can use it at the start of a sentence to set the time: « Au printemps, … ». Similar patterns: « en été » (in summer), « en automne » (in autumn), « en hiver » (in winter).
target_language_example: Au printemps, il commence souvent à faire plus chaud.
native_language_example: In spring, it often starts to get warmer.

additional_notes: Used to say something should happen earlier, before another action or event. Common with verbs like demander (to ask), prévenir (to warn), téléphoner (to call), or discuter/parler de (to discuss). It’s a fairly formal way to say "avant" / "d’abord".
target_language_example: Merci de me prévenir au préalable si vous êtes en retard.
native_language_example: Please let me know beforehand if you’re going to be late.

meaning: at the restaurant; to the restaurant.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le". With a verb of location (être, manger, travailler), it often means "at the restaurant"; with a verb of movement (aller), it can mean "to the restaurant". Used for a general place rather than a specific named restaurant (otherwise you might use "dans ce restaurant" or name it).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au restaurant à 19 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the restaurant at 7 p.m.

additional_notes: A common time + place phrase. **Au** = **à + le** (“at the”). Often used with **aller** (“to go”): *aller au restaurant* = “to go to a restaurant / go out to eat.” In questions with **aller** in the past, you may see agreement in **allé/allée/allés/allées** depending on who went (male/female, singular/plural), e.g. *Êtes-vous allée… ?* (to one woman), *Êtes-vous allées… ?* (to several women).
target_language_example: On est allés au restaurant hier soir.
native_language_example: We went to a restaurant last night.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like dire or faire: dire au revoir à quelqu’un = to say goodbye to someone. The à introduces the person/people you’re saying goodbye to (au revoir à Lydia, au revoir à tout le monde). Often shortened to just au revoir when the person is obvious.
target_language_example: On doit partir : dis au revoir à tes amis.
native_language_example: We have to leave: say goodbye to your friends.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located on the building’s street-level floor (the level you enter from outside). In French, the ground floor is the "rez-de-chaussée" (the next level up is the "premier étage"), which can differ from US English where the "first floor" is usually street level.
target_language_example: Les toilettes sont au rez-de-chaussée, juste à gauche de l’entrée.
native_language_example: The bathrooms are on the ground floor, just to the left of the entrance.

meaning: on the ground; on the floor.
additional_notes: Literally “to the ground” (à + le = au, sol = ground). Common with verbs like tomber (to fall) or être (to be): tomber au sol = “fall to the ground.” In some contexts (e.g., aviation/military), it means “ground” as opposed to “in the air”: unité au sol = “ground unit,” remettre au sol = “bring/put back on the ground” (e.g., land). Often similar to par terre in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Après l’explosion, tout le monde s’est retrouvé au sol.
native_language_example: After the explosion, everyone ended up on the ground.

meaning: at the top/summit of the mountain.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le" (at the). "Sommet" means the highest point (summit/peak). Used to say something is located at, or someone arrives/spends time at, the mountain’s highest point. You can swap in another place: "au sommet de la colline" (at the top of the hill).
target_language_example: On s'est retrouvés au sommet de la montagne pour admirer le lever du soleil.
native_language_example: We met at the top of the mountain to watch the sunrise.

meaning: in the basement; downstairs (in the basement).
additional_notes: "Sous-sol" means "basement." "Au" is the contraction of "à + le" and often means "in/at the." Use "au sous-sol" to say something or someone is located in the basement of a building.
target_language_example: La buanderie est au sous-sol.
native_language_example: The laundry room is in the basement.

meaning: at the supermarket; to the supermarket.
additional_notes: "Au" = "à + le". Use it with places (being there or going there): Je suis au supermarché (I’m at the supermarket) / Je vais au supermarché (I’m going to the supermarket). For a feminine place you’d use "à la" (e.g., à la boulangerie).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au supermarché à 18 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the supermarket at 6 p.m.?

meaning: seriously (in « prendre … au sérieux » = “to take … seriously”).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with the verb « prendre »: « prendre quelqu’un/quelque chose au sérieux » (to take someone/something seriously). Very often appears in the negative: « ne pas prendre … au sérieux » (not to take … seriously).
target_language_example: Il faut prendre ce problème au sérieux.
native_language_example: We need to take this problem seriously.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "jouer" (to play): "jouer au tennis" = to play tennis. You can also use it after adjectives to talk about ability: "bon/mauvais/médiocre au tennis" = good/bad/average at tennis.
target_language_example: Je ne joue pas souvent au tennis, mais je suis assez bon au tennis.
native_language_example: I don’t play tennis often, but I’m pretty good at tennis.

meaning: to the theater; at the theater.
additional_notes: "Au" is the contraction of "à + le" and is used with masculine singular places. With verbs of movement (aller, aller/venir), it often means "to the theater" (destination): « Je vais au théâtre. » With location/context, it can mean "at the theater": « Il y avait trop de monde au théâtre. » Note the past participle agreement in « aller » with "être": « ma femme et moi sommes allés » (mixed or all men) vs « sommes allées » (all women).
target_language_example: On se retrouve au théâtre à 19 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the theater at 7 p.m.

meaning: to the zoo / at the zoo.
additional_notes: "Au" is the contraction of "à + le". Use "au zoo" after verbs like aller (to go), être (to be), venir (to come), and emmener (to take/bring someone). The meaning can be "to the zoo" (direction) or "at the zoo" (location), depending on the verb and context.
target_language_example: On se retrouve au zoo à 14 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the zoo at 2 p.m.

meaning: no doubt; no question about it.
additional_notes: Used to say there is zero uncertainty. Often appears with negatives like « Je n’ai aucun doute » (I have no doubt) or in fixed expressions like « (ne) faire aucun doute » / « (ne) laisser aucun doute » meaning “to leave no doubt.” « Là-dessus » means “about that / on that point.”
target_language_example: Il n’y a aucun doute : elle viendra ce soir.
native_language_example: There’s no doubt: she’ll come tonight.

meaning: 'will it have...?' / 'will he have...?' (formal question form).
additional_notes: This is the future tense of *avoir* (il/elle/on **aura**) used in an inverted question: **aura-t-il ... ?** The **-t-** is added for pronunciation when a verb ending in a vowel is followed by **il/elle/on** (e.g., *aura-t-il*, *aura-t-elle*). Often used when asking about consequences or effects: *Quel effet cela aura-t-il ?*
target_language_example: Cette décision aura-t-elle des conséquences ?
native_language_example: Will this decision have consequences?

additional_notes: Future form of « avoir lieu » (literally “to have place”), used for scheduled or planned events (meetings, conferences, parties, competitions). It agrees with the subject: « l’événement aura lieu… ». Often followed by a time and/or place: « demain », « dimanche prochain », « à Tokyo », etc.
target_language_example: Le concert aura lieu samedi à 20 h.
native_language_example: The concert will take place on Saturday at 8 p.m.

meaning: "should have" (regret about what you did or didn’t do).
additional_notes: This is the conditional form of devoir (“to have to / should”): j’aurais dû = “I should have…”. It’s typically followed by an infinitive (often a past infinitive idea in English): j’aurais dû te le dire (“I should have told you”). With negation: je n’aurais pas dû… (“I shouldn’t have…”). Also used with other persons: tu aurais dû, il/elle aurait dû, nous aurions dû, etc.
target_language_example: J’aurais dû écouter ton conseil.
native_language_example: I should have listened to your advice.

additional_notes: "Aurais pu" is the conditional perfect of "pouvoir" (to be able to). It often expresses a missed possibility, regret, or reproach: "Tu aurais pu appeler" = "You could have called" (implying you didn’t). It can also describe an unreal/hypothetical past: "tout ce que j’aurais pu espérer" = "all I could have hoped for." In speech you often hear contractions like "T’aurais pu…" for "Tu aurais pu…".
target_language_example: J’aurais pu te prévenir, mais j’ai oublié.
native_language_example: I could have warned you, but I forgot.

additional_notes: Form of « devoir » in the conditional perfect (e.g., il/elle/on aurait dû + infinitive). Used to express regret, criticism, or that something was expected but didn’t happen: « On aurait dû partir plus tôt. » It can also express that something was supposed to happen: « Ça aurait dû le tuer. »
target_language_example: J'aurais dû te prévenir avant de venir.
native_language_example: I should have warned you before coming.

meaning: "could have" (would have been able to), for something possible in the past.
additional_notes: This is the conditional perfect: avoir in the conditional (aurait) + past participle of pouvoir (pu). It’s used to talk about a past possibility that didn’t happen, or to say something almost happened: Elle aurait pu y rester = She could have stayed/ended up there (but didn’t). Often used for regrets, warnings, or near-misses (e.g., Il aurait pu se briser le cou = He could have broken his neck).
target_language_example: On aurait pu se perdre sans ton aide.
native_language_example: We could have gotten lost without your help.

meaning: could have been / might have been.
additional_notes: Past conditional: "aurait" (would have) + "pu" (been able to) + "être" (to be). Used to talk about an unreal past possibility—often to say a situation was possible but didn’t happen, or to express a near miss ("It could have been worse/you").
target_language_example: L'accident aurait pu être très grave.
native_language_example: The accident could have been very serious.

additional_notes: Used to compare: **aussi bien … que …** = “as well … as …” (Je parle aussi bien français que Tom.). With **tout aussi bien**, it often means “might as well / just as well” to suggest an option is equally acceptable (Tu pourrais tout aussi bien rester ici.). It can sound dismissive or sarcastic depending on context.
target_language_example: S'il pleut, on peut aussi bien rester à la maison.
native_language_example: If it rains, we might as well stay at home.

meaning: as well as; just as well as.
additional_notes: Used for comparisons. (1) To say two things/people are included equally: « les adultes aussi bien que les enfants » = “adults as well as children.” (2) To say someone does something at the same level as someone else: « Elle skie aussi bien que son frère » = “She skis as well as her brother.” Often intensified with « tout » (tout aussi bien que = “just as well as”) or softened with « presque » (presque aussi bien que = “almost as well as”).
target_language_example: Il cuisine tout aussi bien que sa sœur.
native_language_example: He cooks just as well as his sister.

additional_notes: Used to compare height or size. Pattern: aussi + adjective (grand/grande) + que + noun/pronoun. With a negative, it becomes “not as … as”: pas aussi grand que…. You can also add approximations like presque / à peu près (“almost / about”) before aussi.
target_language_example: Cette table est aussi grande que celle-là.
native_language_example: This table is as big as that one.

additional_notes: Used to compare equality: aussi + adjective (here grande) + que + noun/pronoun. It agrees with the person/thing described (grand/grande/grands/grandes). For other adjectives, replace grande: aussi petit(e) que, aussi important(e) que, etc.
target_language_example: Ma chambre est aussi grande que la tienne.
native_language_example: My room is as big as yours.

additional_notes: Used to say something should happen at the earliest time you can manage. Common after verbs like faire, commencer, quitter, répondre. Often abbreviated as “ASAP” in English, but in French you usually say the full phrase.
target_language_example: Appelez-moi aussi tôt que possible.
native_language_example: Call me as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Used to compare speeds or how quickly two actions happen: aussi + adverb (vite) + que + the reference (a person, thing, or clause). It can mean equality ("as fast as") and often implies a limit with pouvoir: « aussi vite que je peux / que tu le peux » = "as fast as I/you can."
target_language_example: On va avancer aussi vite que possible.
native_language_example: We’ll move forward as fast as possible.

additional_notes: Used to say you will do something with maximum speed. It can stand alone as an instruction/request (“As quickly as possible.”). Often used after a verb: courir/venir/se préparer/répondre aussi vite que possible. You can also hear "le plus vite possible" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Envoyez-moi les documents aussi vite que possible, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please send me the documents as quickly as possible.

meaning: "as far as I know" (to the best of my knowledge).
additional_notes: Used to qualify what you’re saying and show you’re not 100% certain. It can stand alone as a short answer (“Autant que je sache.”), appear at the start (“Autant que je sache, oui.”), or be inserted in the middle with commas (“Il est, autant que je sache, un ami fiable.”). The negative form is common: “Pas autant que je sache.” = “Not that I know of.”
target_language_example: Autant que je sache, le magasin est encore ouvert.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the store is still open.

additional_notes: Used to express something surrounding/encircling something (a belt around the waist, a rope around a beam) or moving in a circle/orbit around something (the Moon around the Earth). It’s the feminine form: autour du (masc. singular), autour des (plural).
target_language_example: Il y a un parc autour de la gare.
native_language_example: There is a park around the train station.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or position around something masculine singular: autour du lac (= around the lake). With feminine singular, use "autour de la"; with a vowel sound, "autour de l'"; with plural, "autour des". Also common in set phrases like "autour du monde" (= around the world).
target_language_example: On s'est promenés autour du parc.
native_language_example: We went for a walk around the park.

additional_notes: Used to say people are gathered/sitting/dancing in a circle near a fire. Common with verbs like s’asseoir (to sit), être assis (to be sitting), danser (to dance).
target_language_example: Le soir, on raconte des histoires autour du feu.
native_language_example: In the evening, we tell stories around the fire.

additional_notes: Used to describe people gathered in a circle around a campfire, often for relaxing, singing, talking, or dancing. "Autour de" + noun = "around" something; "feu de camp" means "campfire."
target_language_example: On raconte des histoires autour du feu de camp.
native_language_example: We tell stories around the campfire.

meaning: at cards; playing cards (as a game).
additional_notes: Used after the verb jouer to mean “to play cards” (jouer aux cartes). The preposition à + les becomes aux. It refers to card games in general (e.g., poker, belote), not necessarily “at the cards” in a literal location sense.
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on joue souvent aux cartes.
native_language_example: After dinner, we often play cards.

meaning: to/at video games (i.e., playing video games).
additional_notes: Used most often after the verb "jouer" (to play): "jouer à" + a game/sport. "Aux" is the contraction of "à + les" (plural), so "jouer aux jeux vidéo" = "to play video games." For one video game, you can say "jouer à un jeu vidéo".
target_language_example: Le week-end, je joue aux jeux vidéo avec mes amis.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I play video games with my friends.

meaning: to the toilet/bathroom; to use the restroom.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (aller, entrer, se rendre) to say you’re going to the bathroom. Very common and neutral; in many contexts it means “to use the restroom.” You can also say "Je vais aux toilettes" on its own to excuse yourself.
target_language_example: Pardon, je vais aux toilettes.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to the bathroom.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the game of chess in general (“In chess, …”) and after verbs like **jouer à**: **jouer aux échecs** = “to play chess.” **Aux** is the contraction of **à + les**. **Échecs** (plural) means “chess” here; don’t confuse it with English “checks.”
target_language_example: Aux échecs, il faut souvent penser plusieurs coups à l’avance.
native_language_example: In chess, you often have to think several moves ahead.

additional_notes: Used with a subject (often "j'": "j'avais dit") in the plus-que-parfait to talk about something you said earlier than another past moment. Very common in phrases like "Je te l’avais dit" (= "I told you so / I told you").
target_language_example: Je t’avais dit de venir plus tôt.
native_language_example: I had told you to come earlier.

meaning: 'you had said that' / 'you had told (me) that' (past perfect).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said earlier, before another past moment. It’s the plus-que-parfait of dire: avoir (avais) + past participle (dit) + que + clause. Often appears with an object pronoun: je t’avais dit que… (I had told you that…), tu m’avais dit que… (you had told me that…).
target_language_example: Tu m’avais dit que tu viendrais plus tôt.
native_language_example: You had told me that you would come earlier.

meaning: '(I) had told (you) that it…' / '(I) had said that it…'.
additional_notes: This is a common pattern in the plus-que-parfait: **j’avais dit que + [clause]**. It refers to something you said earlier (before another past moment), often to remind someone you were right: **Je te l’avais dit !** (“I told you so!”). In the examples, **ça** means “it/that” and is followed by a verb in the conditional/future-in-the-past (e.g., *ça allait…*, *ça arriverait*, *ça marcherait*).
target_language_example: Je t’avais dit que ça fonctionnerait.
native_language_example: I had told you that it would work.

additional_notes: This is the imperfect of *avoir* + past participle (*vu*) in a negative sentence: **(je) n’avais jamais vu…** = “I had never seen…”. In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: **j’avais jamais vu…**. You may also see **j’en avais jamais vu** (“I’d never seen any/of them”), where **en** refers back to something previously mentioned (a quantity or a type of thing).
target_language_example: Je n’avais jamais vu un film aussi long.
native_language_example: I had never seen a movie that long.

additional_notes: From **avoir raison** = “to be right.” **avais** is the imperfect past of *avoir* (e.g., *tu avais raison* = “you were right”; *j'avais raison* = “I was right”). Used to say someone’s opinion/guess turned out correct. Note: it doesn’t literally mean “had reason” in English.
target_language_example: Tu avais raison : il allait pleuvoir.
native_language_example: You were right: it was going to rain.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something someone had already said before another past moment. It’s formed with the imperfect of avoir (avait) + past participle (dit). Often appears with pronouns: « On m’avait dit… » = “I had been told…”, « Elle me l’avait dit » = “She had told me (it).”
target_language_example: Je croyais qu’il avait dit la vérité.
native_language_example: I thought he had told the truth.

additional_notes: Used with a singular subject (il/elle/on, or a singular noun) to talk about something that happened before another past event (plus-que-parfait). Very common in the passive voice: "avait été" + past participle = "had been" + past participle (e.g., "La porte avait été ouverte" = "The door had been opened"). For plurals, you’ll often see "avaient été".
target_language_example: Je croyais qu’il avait été informé.
native_language_example: I thought he had been informed.

additional_notes: This is the imperfect of avoir (avait) used with subject–verb inversion to ask a question: "avait-il… ?" = "had he…?" / "did he have…?" It’s relatively formal/written compared with just using intonation ("Il avait… ?"). The hyphen links the verb and the pronoun (il). Often appears with negatives: "N’avait-il pas… ?" = "Didn’t he have…?"
target_language_example: Avait-il déjà une idée en tête ?
native_language_example: Did he already have an idea in mind?

additional_notes: Imperfect past of « avoir besoin de » (“to need”). Use « avoir besoin de + noun/pronoun » to say someone needs something: « J’ai besoin de toi » (I need you). In the past: « Il/Elle avait besoin de… » (He/She needed…). Often implies necessity or dependence (e.g., help, money, something specific).
target_language_example: Elle avait besoin de repos après le voyage.
native_language_example: She needed rest after the trip.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of avoir: il/elle/on avait = “he/she/one had” or “was having/used to have.” Use "avait des + plural noun" to describe possession or something present/visible (e.g., des larmes, des numéros, des caméras, des tatouages). With body issues you often hear "avoir des + noun" (e.g., avoir des ampoules = to have blisters).
target_language_example: Quand il était jeune, il avait des cheveux très longs.
native_language_example: When he was young, he had very long hair.

additional_notes: From the expression "avoir le mal du pays" = "to be homesick" (literally "to have the pain/sickness of one’s country/home"). It’s commonly used with the imperfect (avait) to describe an ongoing feeling in the past.
target_language_example: Pendant les premières semaines à l’étranger, j'avais le mal du pays.
native_language_example: During the first weeks abroad, I was homesick.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of "avoir peur de" (to be afraid of). Use "de" + noun/pronoun (avoir peur de Marie, de son ombre) or "de" + infinitive (avoir peur de faire une erreur, de mourir). In the present: "a peur de"; in the passé composé: "a eu peur de".
target_language_example: J'avais peur de parler en public.
native_language_example: I was afraid to speak in public.

additional_notes: From the expression « avoir raison » = “to be right.” « avait » is the imperfect past (“was/used to be”), used to talk about a past situation or opinion. It does not mean “had a reason.” Often used with a person: « Tu avais raison » / « Il avait raison ».
target_language_example: Tu avais raison : le train est déjà parti.
native_language_example: You were right: the train has already left.

additional_notes: “Avait” is the imperfect past tense of *avoir* (to have). It’s commonly used for descriptions and background information in the past (e.g., someone’s traits, possessions, or what they were wearing). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun with *un* (for feminine, you’d use *avait une*).
target_language_example: Quand j'étais petit, j'avais un chien.
native_language_example: When I was little, I had a dog.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of avoir ("to have") for il/elle/on: "avait" = "was having / had" in an ongoing, descriptive past. Used to describe possession or characteristics in the past. "Une" is the feminine form of "a/an" and is used before a feminine noun (une voix, une torche, une peau).
target_language_example: Quand j’étais petit, j’avais une peur bleue des chiens, et mon frère avait une grande patience avec moi.
native_language_example: When I was little, I was terribly afraid of dogs, and my brother had a lot of patience with me.

additional_notes: Used to express that one action happens earlier than another. It is followed by an infinitive verb (avant de + infinitive). If the verb that follows starts with a vowel sound, it becomes "avant d’" (e.g., avant d’arriver).
target_language_example: Lave-toi les mains avant de manger.
native_language_example: Wash your hands before eating.

additional_notes: Used to say an action should happen earlier than the moment of leaving. Often follows advice or instructions (e.g., do X avant de partir). Can refer to leaving a place now or departing for a trip.
target_language_example: Appelle-moi avant de partir, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Call me before you leave, please.

avant la tombée de la nuit

target_language_multi_word_term: avant la tombée de la nuit
additional_notes: Used to set a deadline meaning “before it gets dark” (before dusk/nightfall). Common with future plans, instructions, or safety reminders (e.g., return/arrive before dark).
target_language_example: On doit finir la randonnée avant la tombée de la nuit.
native_language_example: We have to finish the hike before night falls.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/thing is accompanied by, has, or uses unspecified plural items: "avec des jouets" (with some toys), "avec des couverts" (using cutlery). It can also mean "together with" or "against" depending on context: "se battre avec des filles" (fight with/against girls). "des" is the plural of the indefinite article ("some" / "any").
target_language_example: Je suis venu avec des amis.
native_language_example: I came with some friends.

additional_notes: Means being together/in her company, or doing something jointly with a female person already mentioned. Very common after verbs like aller/sortir (go out with her; sometimes “date her” in context), être ami(e) (be friends with her), parler/s’entretenir (talk with her), and after questions like “Que fais-tu avec elle ?” (“What are you doing with her?”).
target_language_example: Je veux parler avec elle après le cours.
native_language_example: I want to talk with her after class.

meaning: 'with them' (referring to a group of males or mixed gender).
additional_notes: Uses the stressed pronoun "eux" (not "les") after a preposition like "avec". Refers to a group (they/them) that is masculine or mixed; for an all-female group, use "avec elles". Often contrasts groups: "avec nous" vs "avec eux".
target_language_example: Tu peux venir avec eux si tu veux.
native_language_example: You can come with them if you want.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like attendre (to wait/expect) to show you’re really looking forward to something. Common pattern: attendre [something] avec impatience / attendre avec impatience de + infinitive.
target_language_example: J’attends avec impatience les vacances.
native_language_example: I’m looking forward to the vacation.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is together with a specific masculine noun: avec le chien, avec le garçon. If the noun starts with a vowel or silent h, le becomes l’ (avec l’ami). For feminine singular, use avec la; for plural, avec les.
target_language_example: Je suis avec le professeur.
native_language_example: I’m with the teacher.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “with the …”. It can express accompaniment (venir avec les amis), a relationship/connection (un lien avec les amis), comparison (comparer … avec les leurs), or something being associated/affected (un problème avec les freins). In set phrases: « Avec les compliments de… » = “With compliments from…”.
target_language_example: Je suis venu avec les enfants.
native_language_example: I came with the children.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together/spending time with children (your kids or other children), or doing something in their presence: rester avec les enfants (stay with the children), aller avec les enfants (go with the children), jouer/parler avec les enfants (play/talk with the children). "Les" is the plural definite article (“the”). Note: French "enfants" means “children,” not specifically “infants.”
target_language_example: Je reste à la maison avec les enfants ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm staying home with the children tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with a male person (“lui” = him). Often answers “avec qui ?” (with whom?). In negatives, it’s common to shorten to “Pas avec lui.” = “Not with him.”
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas venir avec lui.
native_language_example: I don't want to come with him.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together/doing something in your sister’s company. In "Tom sort avec ma sœur", "sortir avec" often means "to date" (be in a relationship) rather than just "go out".
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec ma sœur ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with my sister tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is together with you (physically or as company): « Elle est avec moi. » It can also mean doing something together (« travailler avec moi ») or how someone behaves toward you (« gentils avec moi » = “nice to me”). In some contexts, « Tu es avec moi ? » can mean “Are you with me?” (following/agreeing).
target_language_example: Tu veux venir avec moi au marché ?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with me to the market?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is accompanying you/your group (coming with you) or staying together with you. Often appears after verbs like venir (to come), aller (to go), rester (to stay), travailler (to work).
target_language_example: Tu viens avec nous au cinéma ?
native_language_example: Are you coming with us to the movie theater?

additional_notes: Used to say you are accompanied by someone (go/come/do something with someone): « aller avec quelqu’un ». With « être avec quelqu’un », it can also mean being in a romantic relationship with someone ("she’s seeing someone"). Often followed by « d’autre » to mean “someone else”: « avec quelqu’un d’autre ».
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec quelqu’un ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with someone tonight.

meaning: "with whom?" / "who ... with?" (asking which person someone is with).
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask about the person someone is talking to, going with, competing with, etc. In French the preposition stays in front: "Avec qui... ?" (not "Qui... avec ?"). In phrases like "sortir avec", it can mean “to go out with / date.”
target_language_example: Avec qui tu vas au cinéma ce soir ?
native_language_example: Who are you going to the movies with tonight?

additional_notes: Used when the noun after it is feminine singular: avec sa langue (his/her tongue), avec sa classe (his/her class), avec sa main droite (his/her right hand). For a masculine singular noun, use "avec son"; for plural, "avec ses". It can also appear in "rompre avec sa ..." (“to break up with his/her ...”).
target_language_example: Il est venu avec sa sœur.
native_language_example: He came with his sister.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "avec" (with) + the possessive determiner "ses" before a plural noun: "ses talons", "ses clients". "Ses" means "his/her/their" depending on context, and it agrees with what is owned (plural), not with the owner’s gender.
target_language_example: Elle est venue avec ses amis.
native_language_example: She came with her friends.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together/spending time with their friends. "Ses" agrees with the person who has the friends (his or her), not with the friends themselves. Common with verbs like être, partir, discuter, boire, regarder, jouer, prendre un café.
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec ses amis ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with his/her friends tonight.

meaning: "with his" / "with her" / "with its" (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: “Son” is a possessive adjective used with masculine singular nouns (son livre, son bébé) and can mean “his,” “her,” or “its” depending on context. Use “avec son” to say someone is with their masculine-singular thing/person, or to talk about using something as a tool (e.g., with his brush). For feminine singular nouns, use “avec sa”; for plural, “avec ses.”
target_language_example: Il est venu avec son frère.
native_language_example: He came with his brother.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together/accompanied by their brother. It can describe doing an activity together (jouer avec son frère), coming with him (venir avec son frère), sharing something with him (partager… avec son frère), or being compared/confused with him (confondre… avec son frère). Note: it refers to a male person’s brother; for a female person, you’d usually say « avec son frère » as well (frère is masculine), but the possessor is shown by context or by using « son/sa » for the person being talked about.
target_language_example: Il est parti en vacances avec son frère.
native_language_example: He went on vacation with his brother.

meaning: “with your” (talking to one person; followed by a plural noun).
additional_notes: Used with the informal singular subject “tu” to refer to things that belong to the person you’re speaking to: “avec tes voisins” = “with your neighbors.” It’s common in complaints/insults: “avec tes …” can mean “with your stupid/dirty …,” depending on context and the adjective that follows. For feminine plural it becomes “avec tes …” as well; for singular: “avec ton” (masc.) / “avec ta” (fem.).
target_language_example: Arrête avec tes excuses !
native_language_example: Stop with your excuses!

additional_notes: Used to say someone is with you or accompanies you, or that you do something together with the person you’re speaking to. Uses informal "toi" (to a friend, child, etc.); the formal/plural version is "avec vous".
target_language_example: Tu veux venir avec moi ? Je dois parler avec toi.
native_language_example: Do you want to come with me? I need to talk with you.

additional_notes: Used after an adjective or verb to say how someone behaves toward all people in general (not just one person). Common with être gentil(le), aimable, poli(e), parler avec, etc.
target_language_example: Il parle avec tout le monde à la fête.
native_language_example: He talks with everyone at the party.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something using an object/tool: « avec un bâton » = “with a stick.” « un » changes depending on the noun’s gender/number (avec une…, avec des…).
target_language_example: On peut ouvrir la boîte avec un couteau.
native_language_example: You can open the box with a knife.

additional_notes: Used to say what tool/instrument you use to do an action. Often follows the verb (e.g., couper, manger). You can swap the noun: avec une fourchette (with a fork), avec une cuillère (with a spoon).
target_language_example: Ouvre le paquet avec un couteau, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Open the package with a knife, please.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is accompanied by or contains an object/feature. “Une” is the feminine form of “a/an,” so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., une douche, une bombe).
target_language_example: Je voudrais un café avec une pâtisserie, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a coffee with a pastry, please.

additional_notes: "Avez-vous" is "avoir" (to have) in the present tense (vous = you, formal or plural) with subject–verb inversion used to ask a question in a formal/neutral style. Often followed by a past participle to form the passé composé question: "Avez-vous + participé / fini / écrit… ?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous un stylo ?
native_language_example: Do you have a pen?

additional_notes: Inversion form used to ask a question with the verb acheter (to buy) in the passé composé: avez (have) + acheté (bought). Used with “vous” for one person formally or for multiple people. In everyday speech, French often uses “Vous avez acheté… ?” (rising intonation) instead.
target_language_example: Avez-vous acheté du pain ?
native_language_example: Did you buy any bread?

additional_notes: Formal question form (inversion) using the verb apprendre (past participle: appris) with avoir. It can mean (1) 'have you learned' a skill/fact (e.g., a language, a number) or (2) 'did you hear/learn (find out)' some news or information. In informal speech you’ll often hear: « Vous avez appris… ? » or « Qu’est-ce que vous avez appris ? ».
target_language_example: Avez-vous appris la nouvelle aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Did you hear the news today?

additional_notes: A polite/formal question using inversion: "avez-vous" + past participle "apprécié" (passé composé of apprécier). Used to ask for feedback about an experience, visit, meal, gift, etc. More informal: "Vous avez apprécié… ?" or "Ça vous a plu ?".
target_language_example: Avez-vous apprécié le dîner ?
native_language_example: Did you enjoy the dinner?

meaning: "did you say?" / "have you said?" (formal "you"), used to ask what someone said.
additional_notes: This is the inversion form of the passé composé: "avez" (have) + "vous" (you) + "dit" (said). It’s used in questions, often to confirm or clarify what someone said: "Avez-vous dit oui ?" (Did you say yes?) and in set phrases like "Qu’avez-vous dit ?" (What did you say?) and "Pardon, qu’avez-vous dit ?" (Sorry, what did you say?). With an object: "Que lui avez-vous dit ?" (What did you say to him/her?) and "Pourquoi lui avez-vous dit cela ?" (Why did you tell him/her that?).
target_language_example: Pardon, avez-vous dit quinze ou cinquante ?
native_language_example: Sorry, did you say fifteen or fifty?

additional_notes: "Avez-vous" is the formal/polite inversion for "have you" (to a person or group). "Déjà" can mean either (1) "already" (something has happened earlier than expected or by now) or (2) "ever" in questions about life experience. In casual speech, you’ll often hear "Vous avez déjà… ?" (same meaning, less formal).
target_language_example: Avez-vous déjà visité Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever visited Paris?

meaning: "Have you ever eaten…?" or "Have you eaten already?" (formal).
additional_notes: This is a polite/formal question using inversion: "avez-vous" = "have you". With "déjà", it can mean either (1) asking about life experience ("Have you ever…?": Avez-vous déjà mangé des huîtres ?) or (2) asking if something has happened yet/already ("Have you eaten already?": Avez-vous déjà mangé votre souper ?). You can use it by itself: "Avez-vous déjà mangé ?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous déjà mangé ici ?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten here?

additional_notes: "Avez-vous" is the formal/polite inversion form of "have you" (more common in writing or formal speech). "déjà" means "already" and, with questions like this, often corresponds to English "ever" (asking about past experience). Used to ask if someone has seen something before, or rhetorically to express surprise: "Have you ever seen anything like that?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous déjà vu un film aussi drôle ?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a movie that funny?

additional_notes: Formal question using inversion (avez-vous). "déjà" means "ever/already" depending on context; here it’s usually "ever" in an experience question. Follow with a singular masculine noun; change it to "une" for feminine nouns (Avez-vous déjà vu une baleine ?), and to "des" for plural (Avez-vous déjà vu des tigres ?). In everyday speech, people often say: "Vous avez déjà vu un… ?" or "Est-ce que vous avez déjà vu un… ?".
target_language_example: Avez-vous déjà vu un château comme celui-ci ?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a castle like this?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s past experiences. It’s the formal/inverted question form with vous. "déjà" = "ever/already"; "été" is the past participle of être (to be). Often followed by an adjective (amoureux), a past participle (licencié), or a situation/state (pris dans un accident). Agreement: "été" stays the same, but adjectives/past participles after it can agree (e.g., traitée for a woman).
target_language_example: Avez-vous déjà été à Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Paris?

additional_notes: This is the verb "entendre" (to hear) in the passé composé: "avez" + "entendu", used with inversion to form a question in a more formal style. It can mean hearing a sound/news (Avez-vous entendu la nouvelle… ?) or sometimes "Did you hear/understand me?" (M'avez-vous entendu ?). In everyday speech, you’ll often hear: "Vous avez entendu … ?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous entendu ce que le professeur a dit ?
native_language_example: Did you hear what the teacher said?

additional_notes: This is the formal, inverted question form of the passé composé of *avoir*: **vous avez eu** (“you had/you got”) → **avez-vous eu… ?**. It’s used to ask about something in the past, often meaning **had/received** (e.g., *des nouvelles* = news), **had/drank/eaten** (e.g., coffee), or **got/obtained** (e.g., a phone number, an item). In everyday speech, people often say **Vous avez eu… ?** instead of inversion.
target_language_example: Avez-vous eu le temps de lire mon message ?
native_language_example: Did you have time to read my message?

additional_notes: A polite/formal question in the past tense (passé composé) using inversion: « avez-vous… ? ». It’s often used in medical, administrative, or police-style questions to ask whether something happened/was experienced before now. It’s usually followed by a plural noun with « des » (e.g., « des nausées ») or a plural event/experience (« des rapports sexuels »).
target_language_example: Avez-vous eu des douleurs ces derniers jours ?
native_language_example: Have you had any pain in the last few days?

meaning: "have you done" / "did you do" (formal or polite question).
additional_notes: Inversion of verb + subject used to ask a question in a formal/polite way. Built from "avoir" (avez) + "vous" + past participle "fait" (from "faire"). Used to ask whether someone has done something (e.g., chores, homework) or what they did to someone: "Que lui avez-vous fait ?" = "What did you do to him/her?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous fait la réservation ?
native_language_example: Have you made the reservation?

meaning: "have you done that?" / "did you do that?"
additional_notes: Formal/inverted question using "vous" (polite or plural): "avez-vous" = "have you" and "fait" is the past participle of "faire" (to do/make). Used to ask whether someone has done something; you can add details like "pour moi" (for me), "toute seule" (all by yourself), "combien de fois" (how many times), "pourquoi" (why). In everyday spoken French, you more often hear: "Vous avez fait ça ?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous fait cela exprès ?
native_language_example: Did you do that on purpose?

additional_notes:
Used to ask if someone is done with an activity or task. This is the polite/formal question form with inversion ("avez-vous"), common in writing and formal speech. You can follow it with:
- "de" + infinitive: « Avez-vous fini de lire ? » (finished reading?)
- a noun: « Avez-vous fini votre repas ? » (finished your meal?)
You may also see « En avez-vous fini avec… ? » meaning “Are you done with …?” where « en » refers back to what you’re doing/using.
target_language_example: Avez-vous fini de remplir le formulaire ?
native_language_example: Have you finished filling out the form?

additional_notes: Uses subject–verb inversion (avez-vous) to form a formal question. With a question, "jamais" usually means "ever" (not "never"). In everyday speech, you’ll often hear: "Vous avez déjà… ?" or "Est-ce que vous avez déjà… ?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous jamais visité Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever visited Paris?

additional_notes: Uses inversion (verb–subject order) for a more formal style: « Avez-vous… ? ». In questions, « jamais » often means “ever” (not “never”). Common alternatives are « Avez-vous déjà mangé… ? » (“Have you eaten … before?”) or « Est-ce que vous avez déjà/jamais mangé… ? ».
target_language_example: Avez-vous jamais mangé des escargots ?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten snails?

additional_notes: Formal question using inversion (avez-vous…). Used with a past participle after être to ask about someone’s past experience/state. In questions, "jamais" often means "ever" (not "never"). With être, the past participle agrees with the subject (e.g., été mariés / mariées; été seul / seule / seuls / seules).
target_language_example: Avez-vous jamais été à Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Paris?

additional_notes: Formal question using inversion (avez-vous…). Used with a past participle after être to ask about someone’s past experience/state. In questions, "jamais" often means "ever" (not "never"). With être, the past participle agrees with the subject (e.g., été mariés / mariées; été seul / seule / seuls / seules).
target_language_example: Avez-vous jamais été à Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Paris?

additional_notes: "Avez-vous" is the formal (vous) way to ask a question using inversion. "lu" is the past participle of "lire" (to read), used with "avoir" in the passé composé. It can be followed by a noun (Avez-vous lu les instructions ?) or used with a direct object pronoun: "L’avez-vous lu ?" = "Have you read it?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous lu ce message ?
native_language_example: Have you read this message?

meaning: formal/inverted question form of «vous avez mis»: “did you put / did you place” or “how long did you take (to do something)” (with «mettre»).
additional_notes: «Avez-vous mis… ?» is the formal question form (inversion) of «Vous avez mis… ?». With a direct object (keys, sunscreen, etc.), «mettre» means “to put/place”: «Où avez-vous mis… ?» = “Where did you put…?”. With «combien de temps… pour + infinitive», it means “to take (time)”: «Combien de temps avez-vous mis pour… ?» = “How long did you take to…?”. Past participle agrees only with a preceding direct object pronoun (e.g., «les»).
target_language_example: Avez-vous mis du sucre dans le café ?
native_language_example: Did you put sugar in the coffee?

additional_notes: Used to ask how/where/how many someone has obtained or received. It’s the passé composé of obtenir: avoir (avez) + past participle obtenu. The word order is the formal inversion used in questions (avez-vous…?). In everyday speech, you often hear: « Vous avez obtenu… ? »
target_language_example: Avez-vous obtenu une réponse de l’administration ?
native_language_example: Have you gotten an answer from the administration?

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of « parler » used with inversion (« avez-vous… ? ») to ask a question in a formal or written style. It’s often followed by a preposition: « parler à quelqu’un » (to speak to someone) or « parler avec quelqu’un » (to talk with someone). With « depuis », it means “since then / since (that time)”: « Avez-vous parlé depuis ? » = “Have you spoken since then?”
target_language_example: Avez-vous parlé à votre professeur après le cours ?
native_language_example: Did you speak to your teacher after class?

additional_notes: "Avez-vous" is the formal/inverted way to ask a question with "vous" (you). "Perdu" is the past participle of "perdre" (to lose), so the phrase is in the passé composé: "Have you lost …?" It’s used both for physically misplacing something (un cahier) and for losing something in a broader sense (du poids = weight; connaissance = consciousness).
target_language_example: Avez-vous perdu votre téléphone ?
native_language_example: Have you lost your phone?

additional_notes: This is the verb "prendre" in the passé composé ("vous avez pris") with inversion to form a formal question. It’s used both literally (taking something) and in common expressions like: "prendre du poids" (to gain weight), "prendre note" (to take note), "prendre part" (to take part), "prendre un petit-déjeuner" (to have breakfast).
target_language_example: Avez-vous pris vos clés avant de partir ?
native_language_example: Did you take your keys before leaving?

additional_notes: Formal/inverted question using the verb pouvoir (to be able to) in the passé composé: "avez" (have) + "pu" (been able). Used to ask whether someone managed to do something, get something, or had the opportunity/possibility to do it. Often followed by an infinitive ("avez-vous pu aider ?") or by a verb like "obtenir"; can imply success/possibility rather than permission.
target_language_example: Avez-vous pu trouver une place pour vous garer ?
native_language_example: Were you able to find a place to park?

additional_notes: Formal inversion question using **vous** (often used with strangers, in interviews, with customers). Used to ask whether someone observed something: **avez-vous remarqué + noun** (Avez-vous remarqué sa robe ?) or **avez-vous remarqué que + clause** (Avez-vous remarqué que votre sac avait disparu ?). In everyday speech, you’ll also hear **Vous avez remarqué… ?**
target_language_example: Avez-vous remarqué que la porte était ouverte ?
native_language_example: Did you notice that the door was open?

additional_notes: This is the formal question form (inversion) of *vous avez rencontré* in the passé composé of **rencontrer**. It’s used to ask whether someone has met someone (or encountered something) in the past. In everyday speech, French often uses *Vous avez rencontré … ?* instead of inversion.
target_language_example: Avez-vous déjà rencontré notre nouvelle prof ?
native_language_example: Have you met our new teacher yet?

additional_notes: Uses inversion (verb + “-vous”) for a polite/formal question in the passé composé. Often followed by a direct object: « Avez-vous reçu + noun ? ». In everyday speech you’ll also hear: « Est-ce que vous avez reçu… ? » or « Vous avez reçu… ? ».
target_language_example: Avez-vous reçu mon e-mail ?
native_language_example: Have you received my email?

additional_notes: Uses inversion (verb + hyphen + subject) to ask a question with "vous". It’s the passé composé of "trouver" (avez + trouvé), often used to ask whether someone has found something or what they thought of something (e.g., "Avez-vous trouvé ça utile ?" = "Did you find that useful?").
target_language_example: Avez-vous trouvé votre chemin jusqu’ici ?
native_language_example: Did you manage to find your way here?

additional_notes: Inversion question form of "vous avez vu" (you have seen). Used to ask if someone has seen a person/thing, or has noticed/witnessed something: "Avez-vous vu Tom ?" / "Avez-vous vu ce qu’il a fait ?" In casual speech you’ll often hear "Vous avez vu… ?" or "Est-ce que vous avez vu… ?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous vu mon sac quelque part ?
native_language_example: Have you seen my bag anywhere?

additional_notes: A polite/formal question using inversion: "avez-vous" = "have you". Add a masculine singular noun after "le" (e.g., le collier, le spectacle). For feminine nouns, use "avez-vous vu la…?" and for plural, "avez-vous vu les…?". In everyday speech, people often say "Vous avez vu le…?".
target_language_example: Avez-vous vu le train pour Lyon ?
native_language_example: Have you seen the train to Lyon?

additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of the passé composé of être (vous avez été). Used to ask politely or to more than one person what someone’s state/experience was. It’s often followed by an adjective or a past participle used like an adjective, which agrees with the person/people you’re talking to (e.g., blessée/blessés; amoureuse/amoureuses).
target_language_example: Avez-vous été satisfait de votre séjour ?
native_language_example: Were you satisfied with your stay?

additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of the passé composé of être (vous avez été). Used to ask politely or to more than one person what someone’s state/experience was. It’s often followed by an adjective or a past participle used like an adjective, which agrees with the person/people you’re talking to (e.g., blessée/blessés; amoureuse/amoureuses).
target_language_example: Avez-vous été satisfait de votre séjour ?
native_language_example: Were you satisfied with your stay?

additional_notes: "Avez dit" is the passé composé of **dire** with **vous** (2nd person plural or polite singular). It’s often used with object pronouns placed before the verb: **Vous l’avez dit** (“You said it / You told him/her”), **Vous leur avez dit ?** (“Did you tell them?”). With a negative, **ne...pas** surrounds the auxiliary: **Vous ne l’avez dit à personne ?** (“You didn’t tell anyone?”). Note: sentence 1 should be **Je vous l’ai dit** (“I told you”)—not *Je vous l’avez dit*.
target_language_example: Pourquoi ne me l’avez-vous pas dit plus tôt ?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me earlier?

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of "avoir" for "vous" (formal singular or plural): "vous avez" + past participle "eu". It’s used to talk about having/experiencing something in the past: "vous avez eu des problèmes" (you’ve had problems). Depending on context, it can translate as either "you have had" or "you had."
target_language_example: Vous avez eu raison de m’appeler.
native_language_example: You were right to call me.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *faire* with *avoir*: *vous avez fait* + object (*vous l’avez fait* = “you did it”). Used with **vous** for one person politely/formally or for multiple people. In questions you may see *Avez-vous fait… ?* (“Did you do…?”) or emphasis with *C’est vous qui avez fait… ?* (“Was it you who did…?”).
target_language_example: Pourquoi avez-vous fait ça ?
native_language_example: Why did you do that?

additional_notes: Passé composé of **trouver** with **vous**: **vous avez trouvé**. Often used in questions like **Comment vous l’avez trouvé ?** (“What did you think of it?/How did you find it?”) and **Où est-ce que vous l’avez trouvé ?** (“Where did you find it?”). **l’** is an object pronoun meaning “it/him/her,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Vous avez trouvé mes clés ?
native_language_example: Did you find my keys?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has seen something/someone. It’s the passé composé of voir (to see): vous + avez (have) + vu (seen). Often appears in questions like « Vous l’avez vu ? » (Have you seen him/it?) or with « en »: « Vous en avez vu ? » (Have you seen any/some of them?).
target_language_example: Vous avez vu mes clés ?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys?

additional_notes: "Avez été" is the passé composé of "être" with "vous" (formal singular or plural). It’s used to talk about a past state or condition. With verbs/adjectives that use "être" in the passé composé, the past participle often agrees with the subject in gender and number (e.g., "vous avez été blessé" (m. sg.), "blessée" (f. sg.), "blessés" (m. pl.), "blessées" (f. pl.)).
target_language_example: Vous avez été très patients pendant l’attente.
native_language_example: You were very patient during the wait.

additional_notes: "Avez-vous" is "avoir" (to have) in the present tense (vous = you, formal or plural) with subject–verb inversion used to ask a question in a formal/neutral style. Often followed by a past participle to form the passé composé question: "Avez-vous + participé / fini / écrit… ?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous un stylo ?
native_language_example: Do you have a pen?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone needs. It’s the inversion form of the verb phrase « avoir besoin (de) » (“to need”). Pattern: « Avez-vous besoin de + noun ? » (Avez-vous besoin du téléphone ?) or « Avez-vous besoin que + [subject] + verb (subjunctive) ? » (Avez-vous besoin que je vous aide ?).
target_language_example: Avez-vous besoin d’aide ?
native_language_example: Do you need help?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone politely/formally if they need something. It’s the inversion form of « vous avez besoin de… ? ». It is followed by a noun (« …de fruits ») or an infinitive verb (« …de boire »).
target_language_example: Avez-vous besoin d’aide ?
native_language_example: Do you need help?

additional_notes: Polite/inverted question used in formal situations (doctor’s office, pharmacy, customer service). It’s followed by a noun, often an uncountable one: de la fièvre (fever), de la monnaie (change), de la toux (a cough). You’ll also see variations depending on the noun: "Avez-vous du..." (masc.), "Avez-vous des..." (plural), and "Avez-vous un/une..." for a single countable item.
target_language_example: Bonjour, avez-vous de la crème solaire ?
native_language_example: Hello, do you have (any) sunscreen?

meaning: "Do you have any …?" (formal; asking about plural items).
additional_notes: Uses subject–verb inversion (avez-vous) for a polite/formal question. Followed by "des" + a plural noun (or things thought of in the plural). Often translates as "any" in English: "Avez-vous des menus en anglais ?" → "Do you have any English menus?"
target_language_example: Avez-vous des chambres disponibles ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you have any rooms available tonight?

avez-vous la moindre idée de qui

target_language_multi_word_term: avez-vous la moindre idée de qui
meaning: “Do you have the slightest idea who…?”
additional_notes: A polite/formal ("vous") question used to express that you think the other person probably doesn’t know. It’s often followed by a verb phrase: « …de qui + verb » (e.g., « …de qui vient ce message ? ») or « …de qui il/elle est » (“who he/she is”). You can make it less formal by switching to « as-tu » (singular informal).
target_language_example: Avez-vous la moindre idée de qui a envoyé ce message ?
native_language_example: Do you have the slightest idea who sent this message?

additional_notes: This is the formal question form (inversion) of *vous avez quelque chose ?* It’s used to ask if someone has an item or option: *Avez-vous quelque chose contre… ?* (for/against a problem, e.g., a headache), *Avez-vous quelque chose sans… ?* (without), *Avez-vous quelque chose à + infinitive ?* (something to do/use). In some idioms it means “to have something on your conscience” (to feel guilty) or “to have something in mind.”
target_language_example: Bonjour, avez-vous quelque chose de plus chaud à boire ?
native_language_example: Hello, do you have something warmer to drink?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask if someone has anything to add, declare, show, or say. It’s the inversion question form of « vous avez… ? », so it’s common in formal situations (e.g., at customs: « Avez-vous quelque chose à déclarer ? »). Followed by an infinitive verb (ajouter, dire, montrer, déclarer, etc.).
target_language_example: Avez-vous quelque chose à signaler ?
native_language_example: Do you have something to report?

meaning: “Do you have a…?” (formal/polite, for one masculine item).
additional_notes: This is the formal inversion question form of « vous avez ». Use it in polite situations (shops, hotels, officials). « un » is used for a singular masculine noun (un passeport, un parapluie). For feminine nouns, use « avez-vous une… ? » (une réservation). For plural, « avez-vous des… ? ».
target_language_example: Bonjour, avez-vous un plan de la ville ?
native_language_example: Hello, do you have a city map?

additional_notes: Used to ask a question with inversion (verb + -vous). It’s followed by a feminine singular noun: Avez-vous une boutique… ? For masculine singular, use « avez-vous un… ? »; for plural, « avez-vous des… ? ». Common in shops, restaurants, and formal situations.
target_language_example: Avez-vous une table pour deux ?
native_language_example: Do you have a table for two?

additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase «avoir besoin (de)» = “to need.” «Vous avez besoin de + noun» (Vous avez besoin de temps.) and «Vous en avez besoin» uses «en» to replace «de + something» (“You need some/it/of that”). In questions/negatives, you often see «de» become «de» (not «des») and «rien»: «Vous n’avez besoin de rien ?» = “You don’t need anything?”
target_language_example: Vous avez besoin d’aide ?
native_language_example: Do you need help?

avez besoin de quoi que ce soit

target_language_multi_word_term: avez besoin de quoi que ce soit
additional_notes: Used after "si" (if) to offer help: « Si vous avez besoin de quoi que ce soit… ». The full verb phrase is « avoir besoin de + noun » (= to need). « quoi que ce soit » means “anything at all” and is common in polite, reassuring offers (calls, emails, asking for help).
target_language_example: Si vous avez besoin de quoi que ce soit, je suis là.
native_language_example: If you need anything, I’m here.

additional_notes: "Avez" is the "vous" form of "avoir" (to have). "Des" means "some" (plural, indefinite). Very common in statements and in "si" (if) clauses: "Si vous avez des..." = "If you have any..." You’ll often see "en" with it to mean "some of it/them": "Vous en avez" = "You have some (of them)."
target_language_example: Si vous avez des questions, demandez-moi.
native_language_example: If you have any questions, ask me.

additional_notes: Form of the verb *avoir* (to have): *vous avez* + a feminine singular noun (*une réservation, une réaction, une copie*). Often used in questions, especially with *en* meaning “one/some of it”: *Vous en avez une copie ?* = “Do you have a copy (of it)?” Note: in *en avoir une paire*, it’s part of an idiom meaning “to have guts,” but *avez une* itself is just the literal “you have a.”
target_language_example: Vous avez une réservation au nom de Martin ?
native_language_example: Do you have a reservation under the name Martin?

additional_notes: This is the past infinitive: avoir + past participle (fait). It’s used to talk about an action completed before another action, often after another verb or expression (e.g., sembler, nier, admettre, merci de, pourquoi). Example idea: Il nie avoir fait ça = “He denies having done that.”
target_language_example: Je regrette d'avoir fait cette erreur.
native_language_example: I regret having made this mistake.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a state that happened *before* another action/time, often after another verb (e.g., *sembler* “to seem”, *devoir* “must/probably”, *penser* “to think”). Pattern: **[verb] + avoir été + adjective/noun** → “to have been + adjective/noun.” Example: *Elle semble avoir été heureuse* = “She seems to have been happy.”
target_language_example: Il doit avoir été fatigué après le voyage.
native_language_example: He must have been tired after the trip.

additional_notes: "Avoir" means "to have". "Des" is an indefinite article meaning "some" used before a plural noun (des détails, des choses, des chatons). In many contexts, English may drop "some" and just say "have" (e.g., "avoir des détails" = "have details" / "have some details").
target_language_example: J'aimerais avoir des informations, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like to have some information, please.

meaning: "to have something to" (followed by an infinitive); often "to have something to do with / to be related to".
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: avoir quelque chose à + verb (e.g., "avoir quelque chose à dire" = to have something to say, "avoir quelque chose à montrer" = to have something to show). Very common in the expressions "avoir quelque chose à voir avec" and "avoir quelque chose à faire avec" meaning something is connected/related to something else. Negative form: "n'avoir rien à + infinitive" (to have nothing to...).
target_language_example: Cette décision a quelque chose à voir avec la sécurité.
native_language_example: This decision has something to do with safety.

meaning: "to have a" (to possess or to have/experience something).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: avoir un + noun (un rendez-vous, un effet, un avis, un passe-temps, un sens, un but, un chien). For feminine nouns, use "avoir une" (ex. avoir une idée). It can mean owning something (have a dog) or having/experiencing something more abstract (have an opinion, have meaning, have a goal).
target_language_example: J’aimerais avoir un moment pour te parler.
native_language_example: I’d like to have a moment to talk to you.

meaning: to have a baby; to be expecting a baby (pregnant).
additional_notes: Common way to say someone is going to have a baby. With "va" (near future), it often means "is going to have a baby" and can imply either being pregnant now or that the birth is coming. Also used in the past: "Elle a eu un bébé" = "She had a baby."
target_language_example: Ils vont avoir un bébé en juin.
native_language_example: They’re going to have a baby in June.

meaning: 'to have a' / 'to get a' (a thing, a seat/table, a connection, a talk, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun: avoir une + noun. Depending on context it can mean possession ("have") or request/obtain ("get/can we have...")—common in travel/restaurant situations: "Puis-je avoir une correspondance ?" (a connection), "Pourrions-nous avoir une table ?" (a table), "Pouvons-nous avoir une fourchette ?" (a fork). Also used for events/actions: "avoir une discussion/une conversation" (to have a discussion/conversation), and for abstract nouns: "avoir une raison" (to have a reason).
target_language_example: Est-ce que je peux avoir une minute, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can I have a minute, please?

meaning: "do we have...?" / "have we...?" (formal inverted question form of "nous avons").
additional_notes: Used in formal or written French to ask a question with inversion: verb (avons) + subject (nous). In everyday speech, people often say "Est-ce que nous avons… ?" or simply "On a… ?". With an object pronoun, it can appear as "En avons-nous… ?" (= "Do we have any?/Do we have the means for it?").
target_language_example: Avons-nous besoin d'un rendez-vous ?
native_language_example: Do we need an appointment?

meaning: 'we did' / 'we have done' (past tense of faire).
additional_notes: Used with the subject nous in the passé composé: nous + avons (present of avoir) + fait (past participle of faire). It can mean “we did” or “we have done,” depending on context. Common with expressions like faire un rêve (to have a dream) and in phrases like Nous l'avons fait. (“We did it.”).
target_language_example: Nous avons fait nos devoirs hier soir.
native_language_example: We did our homework last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of parler for nous: avoir (avons) + past participle (parlé). Often used with "en" to mean "talked about it/that": « Nous en avons parlé » = « We talked about it. »
target_language_example: On en a déjà parlé, mais nous n'avons rien décidé.
native_language_example: We already talked about it, but we didn’t decide anything.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *trouver* with *nous*: **nous avons trouvé** + object. Often used with an object pronoun: **nous l’avons trouvé** = “we found it / we’ve found it.”
target_language_example: On a enfin une solution : nous avons trouvé un moyen de partir.
native_language_example: We finally have a solution: we found a way to leave.

meaning: "do we have...?" / "have we...?" (formal inverted question form of "nous avons").
additional_notes: Used in formal or written French to ask a question with inversion: verb (avons) + subject (nous). In everyday speech, people often say "Est-ce que nous avons… ?" or simply "On a… ?". With an object pronoun, it can appear as "En avons-nous… ?" (= "Do we have any?/Do we have the means for it?").
target_language_example: Avons-nous besoin d'un rendez-vous ?
native_language_example: Do we need an appointment?

additional_notes: Used before a noun: beaucoup de + noun (e.g., beaucoup de travail). It works with countable and uncountable nouns. 'De' usually stays the same (no agreement), and after a negation you often use 'pas beaucoup de' (not many/not much).
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup de monde ici.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people here.

meaning: a lot of luck; very lucky.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has been lucky (often about a situation or outcome). Common pattern: avoir beaucoup de chance = “to be very lucky.” You can also say Tu as beaucoup de chance / Vous avez beaucoup de chance (“You’re very lucky”).
target_language_example: On a eu beaucoup de chance avec la météo aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: We were very lucky with the weather today.

meaning: a lot of things; many things.
additional_notes: Used to talk generally about a large number of things (events, objects, facts, activities). Often follows verbs like faire (do), acheter (buy), révéler (reveal), se passer (happen): « Il s’est passé beaucoup de choses. » It can also appear in « avoir beaucoup de choses en commun » (“to have a lot in common”).
target_language_example: J'ai encore beaucoup de choses à faire aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I still have a lot of things to do today.

meaning: a lot of things have changed.
additional_notes: Common phrase to talk about how life, a situation, or a place is different now than before. Often followed by a time expression like « ces dernières années » (in recent years) or « depuis… » (since…). « Beaucoup de choses » = “a lot of things”; « ont changé » is the past tense (passé composé) of « changer » = “to change.”
target_language_example: Depuis la pandémie, beaucoup de choses ont changé dans notre façon de travailler.
native_language_example: Since the pandemic, a lot of things have changed in the way we work.

additional_notes: Used to say there are many tasks or items to do/see/discuss/etc. It is usually followed by an infinitive verb (voir, faire, discuter, rattraper): « beaucoup de choses à + infinitive ». You can add « encore » to mean “still a lot of things to …”.
target_language_example: J’ai beaucoup de choses à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to do today.

meaning: a lot of things to do.
additional_notes: Used to say you have many tasks/errands or a busy schedule. Often used with avoir (“to have”): « J’ai beaucoup de choses à faire. » It can also be used with il y a (“there is/are”): « Il y a beaucoup de choses à faire. » You can add timing words like encore (“still”) or today: « J’ai encore beaucoup de choses à faire aujourd’hui. »
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas sortir ce soir : j’ai beaucoup de choses à faire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out tonight: I have a lot of things to do.

meaning: many people; a lot of people.
additional_notes: Common way to talk about a large number of people in general. Often used as the subject at the start of a sentence: « Beaucoup de gens + verb » (e.g., Beaucoup de gens pensent que…). « Beaucoup » can also modify a specific group: « beaucoup de mes amis » (many of my friends).
target_language_example: Beaucoup de gens veulent apprendre le français.
native_language_example: Many people want to learn French.

meaning: a lot of books; many books.
additional_notes: “Beaucoup de” means “a lot of / many” and is followed by a noun: beaucoup de livres, beaucoup de temps, beaucoup de gens. In negative sentences, it often becomes “pas beaucoup de” (“not many”): Je n’ai pas beaucoup de livres.
target_language_example: J’ai beaucoup de livres à la maison.
native_language_example: I have a lot of books at home.

meaning: a lot of people; lots of people.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of people in general (a crowd), not “many worlds.” Often used with quantities: « Il y a beaucoup de monde » (It’s crowded / There are lots of people). You can also use it as the subject: « Beaucoup de monde est venu » (Many people came).
target_language_example: Il y avait beaucoup de monde au marché ce matin.
native_language_example: There were lots of people at the market this morning.

meaning: many people; a lot of people.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of people in general. Often followed by a verb: « Beaucoup de personnes + verbe ». You can also say « beaucoup de gens » (more common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Beaucoup de personnes pensent que c'est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: Many people think it's a good idea.

additional_notes: "Beaucoup de" means "many/a lot of". "Beaucoup de questions" is used to say there are many questions, or that someone is asking many questions. Common with verbs like "poser" (to ask): "poser beaucoup de questions" = "to ask a lot of questions". You can add a topic with "à propos de" or "au sujet de" (about): "beaucoup de questions au sujet de…".
target_language_example: J’ai encore beaucoup de questions sur ce projet.
native_language_example: I still have a lot of questions about this project.

meaning: a lot of time; much time.
additional_notes: Used to say something takes a long time, or that someone spends a long time doing something. Often follows verbs like prendre (to take) or passer (to spend): « prendre beaucoup de temps », « passer beaucoup de temps à + infinitive », « passer beaucoup de temps avec/ensemble/devant… ».
target_language_example: Je n’ai pas beaucoup de temps, je dois partir.
native_language_example: I don’t have much time; I have to leave.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to say someone spends (or wastes) a lot of time doing something: « passer / consacrer / perdre beaucoup de temps à + infinitif ». Often implies the activity takes longer than expected or is not very productive (especially with « perdre »).
target_language_example: On passe beaucoup de temps à attendre ici.
native_language_example: We spend a lot of time waiting here.

meaning: a lot of work; lots of work.
additional_notes:
Used to say there is a large amount of work to do. Often used with:
- "C’est beaucoup de travail" = “It’s a lot of work.”
- "Il y a beaucoup de travail" = “There’s a lot of work (to do).”
- "J’ai/On a encore beaucoup de travail" = “I/We still have a lot of work.”
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas sortir ce soir : j’ai beaucoup de travail.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out tonight: I have a lot of work.

meaning: a lot of work to do.
additional_notes: Used to say there’s a large amount of work that still needs to be done. Very common with "il y a..." (there is/are...) or "avoir..." (to have...). You can swap the subject: "J’ai / Nous avons / On a..."
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas sortir ce soir : j’ai beaucoup de travail à faire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out tonight: I have a lot of work to do.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir" (to have): "avoir beaucoup en commun" = to share many interests/traits/experiences. It can refer to people (friends, couples, coworkers) or even things (two ideas/products can have things in common). Often appears with "nous", "toi et moi", "vous deux", etc.
target_language_example: On a vraiment beaucoup en commun, c’est drôle !
native_language_example: We really have a lot in common—it’s funny!

additional_notes: Used to strongly compare improvement (health, quality, situation, etc.). Often follows a verb like "être" (C'est beaucoup mieux), "se sentir" (Je me sens beaucoup mieux), or "sonner" (Ça sonne beaucoup mieux). It can also mean "deserves better" / "could do better" depending on context (Il mérite beaucoup mieux; Tu pourrais faire beaucoup mieux).
target_language_example: Après une bonne nuit de sommeil, je me sens beaucoup mieux.
native_language_example: After a good night’s sleep, I feel much better.

additional_notes: Used to intensify a comparison with plus: beaucoup plus + adjective/adverb (beaucoup plus simple = much simpler), or beaucoup plus de + noun (beaucoup plus de temps = much more time). Common in comparisons: beaucoup plus ... que (much more ... than).
target_language_example: Ce film est beaucoup plus intéressant que le premier.
native_language_example: This movie is much more interesting than the first one.

additional_notes: Used to say someone still needs to learn many things (often implying they’re not very experienced yet). Common patterns: “J’ai beaucoup à apprendre” (I have a lot to learn) and “Tu as encore beaucoup à apprendre” (You still have a lot to learn).
target_language_example: On débute tous un jour : j’ai encore beaucoup à apprendre.
native_language_example: We all start someday: I still have a lot to learn.

additional_notes: Used to say you have many tasks/things to take care of. Often with forms of "avoir" (j’ai / tu as / il y a) or "rester" (il reste...) to mean there’s still a lot left to do.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j’ai beaucoup à faire ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have a lot to do tonight.

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s eyes. It’s the plural form: beau → beaux (masculine plural) + yeux (eyes). You often hear it with a possessive: tes beaux yeux / vos beaux yeux, and intensifiers like si / tellement. Note: in the expression « pour les beaux yeux de quelqu’un », it means “just to please someone / for no real reason,” not literally about eyes.
target_language_example: Je pourrais te regarder toute la journée : tu as de beaux yeux.
native_language_example: I could look at you all day: you have beautiful eyes.

additional_notes: Usually means your son’s wife (your daughter-in-law), especially in phrases like « la belle-fille de quelqu’un ». It can also mean a stepdaughter (your spouse’s daughter). Even though it looks like « belle » (pretty) + « fille » (girl), it does not mean “pretty girl.”
target_language_example: Ma belle-fille vient dîner dimanche.
native_language_example: My daughter-in-law is coming for dinner on Sunday.

additional_notes: Means an attractive/pretty woman. You’ll most often see it with an article (une belle femme = “a beautiful woman”, la belle femme = “the beautiful woman”) or as an exclamation (Quelle belle femme ! = “What a beautiful woman!”).
target_language_example: C'est une belle femme, mais surtout une personne très gentille.
native_language_example: She's a beautiful woman, but above all a very kind person.
