It’s commonly followed by other pronouns too (e.g., **le lui**, **le leur**) and then a verb: *C’est moi qui le lui ai demandé* (“I’m the one who asked him/her for it”).
target_language_example: C’est moi qui le fais, ne t’inquiète pas.
native_language_example: I’m the one doing it—don’t worry.

meaning: "I'm the one who ... (did it/have done it) to/for him/her."
additional_notes: This is an emphasis structure (a cleft sentence): **c’est moi qui + verb** = “I’m the one who…”. **lui** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him/to her,” and **ai** is the auxiliary **avoir** for the passé composé (e.g., *j’ai appris / j’ai fait / j’ai proposé*). After **c’est moi qui**, French uses the verb as if it were with **je**: *c’est moi qui ai…* (not *c’est moi qui a…*).
target_language_example: C'est moi qui lui ai envoyé le message.
native_language_example: I'm the one who sent him/her the message.

meaning: “It was me who…” / “I’m the one who…” (emphasis: I did it to you).
additional_notes: This is an emphatic structure: **C’est moi qui + verb** to stress that *you* are the person responsible (often to admit, claim credit, or take blame). **t’** is the shortened form of **te** (“to you” / “you”), placed before the auxiliary **ai** in the past tense: *t’ai + past participle* (e.g., **t’ai trouvé(e)** = “found you”). The past participle may agree with the person found/seen/etc. when the direct object pronoun (**t’**) comes before the verb (e.g., *trouvée* to a woman).
target_language_example: C’est moi qui t’ai appelé ce matin.
native_language_example: I’m the one who called you this morning.

meaning: "it’s my" (introducing something that belongs to me, masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or point out something as yours: "C’est mon + [masculine singular noun]". It can mean ownership (mon bar, mon magasin, mon livre) or a relationship (mon petit-fils). For feminine nouns, use "c’est ma"; for plural, "ce sont mes". You may also hear "c’est mon" before some feminine nouns starting with a vowel or silent h (e.g., "c’est mon amie") because "ma" becomes "mon" to avoid two vowels.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, c’est mon sac.
native_language_example: Excuse me, that’s my bag.

additional_notes: Used to identify something as belonging to, or shared by, “us” (a group including the speaker). It often introduces a noun: « C’est notre chambre. » Note: « notre » is used with singular nouns (masculine or feminine). With plural nouns, use « ce sont nos … » or « c’est nos … » (informal): « Ce sont nos amis. »
target_language_example: C'est notre première fois à Paris.
native_language_example: It's our first time in Paris.

additional_notes: Used to show or confirm the direction to go. Often said while pointing or leading someone: "Venez, c’est par là." The "là" refers to a place/direction, and "par" suggests going via/along that way.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, la sortie ? — Oui, c’est par là.
native_language_example: Excuse me, the exit? — Yes, it’s that way.

additional_notes: Used to show strong approval or that something suits you well. Often said as a polite, upbeat response (e.g., after getting information, receiving something, or agreeing on a plan). You can add details with pour + person/thing: “C’est parfait pour nous/toi.”
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 18 h ? — Oui, c’est parfait !
native_language_example: Shall we meet at 6 p.m.? — Yes, that’s perfect!

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French. It drops the “ne” from the standard negation: “Ce n’est pas…” → “C’est pas…”. Use it in casual conversation; in formal writing or careful speech, prefer “ce n’est pas”. It can also introduce corrections/nuance (e.g., “C’est pas que…” = “It’s not that…”).
target_language_example: T’inquiète, c’est pas grave.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s not serious / it’s not a big deal.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about a statement: "It’s maybe..." In speech it often introduces a guess or possibility (about a person, situation, explanation, etc.). It can be followed by a noun/adjective clause: "C’est peut-être notre chance" (It might be our chance), "C’est peut-être mieux ainsi" (Maybe it’s better this way). In informal spoken French you may hear "C’est peut-être pas..." meaning "Maybe it’s not..." (more formal: "Ce n’est peut-être pas...").
target_language_example: C'est peut-être trop tard pour l'appeler.
native_language_example: Maybe it’s too late to call him/her.

additional_notes: Used to compare: **C’est plus + adjective** = “It’s more + adjective / -er” (C’est plus simple = “It’s simpler”). Often followed by **que** to say “than” (C’est plus dur qu’on croit = “It’s harder than you think”). You can also use it alone as an answer: *—C’est important ? —Oui, c’est plus important.*
target_language_example: Avec un plan, c’est plus facile.
native_language_example: With a plan, it’s easier.

additional_notes: Used to say something can be done or might be true. Often said on its own as a brief reply (“C’est possible.” = “It’s possible.”). You can add emphasis with “bien sûr” (of course) or uncertainty with tone/context.
target_language_example: Tu peux venir demain ? — Oui, c’est possible.
native_language_example: Can you come tomorrow? — Yes, it’s possible.

additional_notes: Used to say what something is intended for, often followed by an infinitive to give the goal: « C'est pour + infinitif » = “It’s to / in order to …”. You can also use it with a noun: « C'est pour toi » = “It’s for you.”
target_language_example: C'est pour te protéger.
native_language_example: It's to protect you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the consequence or explanation that follows from what was just said. Very common in spoken and written French. Often refers back to a previous idea: *Cela* = "that" (the thing mentioned), *pour cela* = "for that reason".
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas de réseau ; c'est pour cela que je ne réponds pas.
native_language_example: I have no signal; that's why I'm not replying.

additional_notes: Used when giving something to someone or saying something is intended for them. You can also use it in emphatic sentences like "C'est pour toi que je le fais" ("I'm doing it for you"). Variations: "c'est pour moi" (for me), "c'est pour vous" (for you, formal/plural).
target_language_example: Tiens, j'ai un petit cadeau : c'est pour toi.
native_language_example: Here, I have a small gift: it’s for you.

additional_notes: Used to give (or ask about) the reason for something. Very common before "que" + a clause: "C'est pour ça que..." (= "That's why..."). It can also be used alone: "C'est pour ça ?" (= "Is that why?").
target_language_example: Il pleuvait, et c'est pour ça qu'on est restés à la maison.
native_language_example: It was raining, and that's why we stayed home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the cause or explanation for something. It’s often followed by a clause (subject + verb): « C’est pour ça qu’il est parti. » In careful writing you may see « c’est pourquoi » (more formal). The final « qu’ » is the shortened form of « que » before a vowel sound (e.g., « qu’il », « qu’on », « qu’elle »).
target_language_example: J'étais fatigué, c'est pour ça qu'on est rentrés tôt.
native_language_example: I was tired, that's why we went home early.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for a situation about him, followed by an adjective or place (e.g., ici, en ville, si riche). With a past action, French usually uses the similar pattern "c'est pour ça qu'il est venu" (“that’s why he came”). You can change "il" to another subject: "c'est pour ça que je suis…", "c'est pour ça qu'elle est…"
target_language_example: C'est pour ça qu'il est si fatigué.
native_language_example: That's why he's so tired.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason or explanation for something. "C'est pour ça" = "that's why / that's the reason" and "qu'on" introduces what follows (often "we" in casual speech). "On" can mean "we" (very common in spoken French) or "people/they" in a general sense, depending on context.
target_language_example: C'est pour ça qu'on arrive en avance.
native_language_example: That's why we’re arriving early.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the consequence or explanation of something just mentioned. It’s followed by a full clause (subject + verb): « C’est pour ça que je suis là. » You can also hear « C’est pour ça » on its own meaning “That’s why / That’s the reason.”
target_language_example: Je n’ai plus de batterie, c’est pour ça que je ne réponds pas.
native_language_example: My battery is dead, that’s why I’m not replying.

additional_notes: Used to explain your reason for doing something. It introduces the cause, and is usually followed by a verb (e.g., "C'est pour ça que je viens" = "That's why I come"). You can also hear the shorter form "C'est pour ça que…" without "je" if the subject changes.
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, c'est pour ça que je me couche tôt.
native_language_example: I'm tired, that's why I go to bed early.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the reason for what someone (tu) is doing. Often followed by a verb: « C’est pour ça que tu pars ? » = “Is that why you’re leaving?” In statements it explains a cause: « C’est pour ça que tu viens avec moi. » = “That’s why you’re coming with me.”
target_language_example: C'est pour ça que tu es en retard ?
native_language_example: Is that why you're late?

c'est pour ça que tu es

target_language_multi_word_term: c'est pour ça que tu es
meaning: "is that why you are…" / "that’s why you are…"
additional_notes: Used to give or ask for the reason for someone’s situation/state. It’s often followed by an adjective (fatigué), a place (ici), or a past participle with être (parti/partie, venu, revenu). In questions, it suggests “So that’s the reason…?”
target_language_example: C'est pour ça que tu es fatigué ?
native_language_example: Is that why you're tired?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s identity, often when pointing someone out or asking about a person already mentioned. Common in casual speech; in more formal French you can say “Qui est-ce ?” or “Qui est-ce que c’est ?”. Often followed by a noun phrase: “C’est qui, ce monsieur ?”.
target_language_example: C’est qui, le monsieur près de la porte ?
native_language_example: Who’s that man near the door?

meaning: Informal way to ask “what is it?” / “what’s …?”
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French to ask for an explanation or clarification: “C’est quoi le plan ?” (“What’s the plan?”), “C’est quoi le rapport ?” (“What’s the connection?”). In more formal or careful French, you often hear “Qu’est-ce que c’est ?” or “Quel est … ?” instead.
target_language_example: C’est quoi ce truc ?
native_language_example: What is this thing?

meaning: “What’s this …?” / “What is this …?” (often: “What the heck is this …?”).
additional_notes: Very common spoken/casual way to question or react to something, often showing surprise, confusion, or annoyance. It’s usually followed by a noun: « C’est quoi, ce bruit ? » You can also say « C’est quoi, ça ? » (= “What’s that?”). More neutral/formal: « Qu’est-ce que c’est, ce … ? » or « Qu’est-ce que c’est que ce … ? »
target_language_example: C’est quoi, ce bruit ?
native_language_example: What’s that noise?

additional_notes: Used in spoken French to question or react to something you see/hear: “C’est quoi, cette + noun ?” The comma reflects a pause in speech. “cette” is the feminine form of “this,” so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., cette histoire, cette lumière). For a masculine noun you’d say: “C’est quoi, ce … ?” (e.g., C’est quoi, ce bruit ?).
target_language_example: C'est quoi, cette odeur ?
native_language_example: What’s that smell?

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French and informal writing. Used to ask for an explanation or the meaning of something: « C’est quoi le deal ? » = “What’s the deal?” In more formal French, you can say « Quel est le … ? » (e.g., « Quel est le sujet ? »).
target_language_example: C’est quoi le problème ?
native_language_example: What’s the problem?

additional_notes: Common spoken phrase used when something starts again (often with a sigh or a joking tone). You’ll often hear "C’est reparti !" by itself, or "C’est reparti pour un tour" = “here we go again (for another round).” Literally it’s like “it’s started up again,” but it’s used idiomatically.
target_language_example: On a enfin fini, et cinq minutes après, c’est reparti !
native_language_example: We finally finished, and five minutes later, here we go again!

meaning: “It’s his/her …” (referring to a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify something as belonging to him/her: c’est = ce + est (“it is/that’s”), sa = “his/her” before a feminine singular noun (sa voiture, sa spécialité). For a masculine singular noun, use “c’est son …” (c’est son livre).
target_language_example: C'est sa voiture, pas la mienne.
native_language_example: It’s his/her car, not mine.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or adverb to intensify it: "C'est si + adjectif" (It’s so + adjective) or "C'est si + adverbe" (It’s so + adverb). Often expresses surprise or emphasis, and can be used in questions: "Tu crois que c'est si facile ?" = “Do you think it’s that easy?”
target_language_example: C'est si beau ici !
native_language_example: It’s so beautiful here!

meaning: 'it's his / her / its' (referring to something that belongs to someone).
additional_notes: Used to identify ownership: "C'est" = "it is/that's", and "son" is a possessive meaning "his/her/its". Important: "son" is chosen because the thing owned is masculine singular (e.g., son plan, son style). For a feminine singular noun, you usually use "sa" (sa voiture), and for plural, "ses" (ses amis). "Son" can mean "his" OR "her"—French chooses based on the noun’s gender, not the owner’s gender. Also, don’t confuse French "son" with English "son" (child).
target_language_example: C'est son idée, pas la mienne.
native_language_example: It's his/her idea, not mine.

additional_notes: A very common, informal way to express enthusiasm or approval. You can say it alone as a reaction (C'est super !) or follow it with "de + infinitive" to mean "It’s great to..." (C'est super de te revoir.) and with "pour" to mean "That’s great for..." (C'est super pour toi.).
target_language_example: C'est super de passer du temps avec vous.
native_language_example: It's great to spend time with you.

additional_notes: Used to point out or identify something that belongs to “you” (informal singular). Structure: c’est (= it is) + ta (= your, feminine singular). Use **ta** before a feminine singular noun (e.g., ta chance, ta réponse). Before a masculine noun you’d use **ton** (c’est ton ami).
target_language_example: C'est ta décision.
native_language_example: It’s your decision.

additional_notes: Used to identify or emphasize the person being talked about. Very common in sentences like "C'est toi que..." (It’s you that/who...) and "C'est toi qui..." (You’re the one who...), where "toi" is stressed for contrast or focus.
target_language_example: Non, ce n'est pas moi : c'est toi !
native_language_example: No, it’s not me: it’s you!

additional_notes: This is a cleft sentence used to strongly emphasize the person “toi” (“you”): **C’est toi que je + verb** (e.g., cherche/choisis/regarde). It often contrasts with other possibilities (“not someone else”). Note: **toi** (stressed pronoun) is used after **c’est**, not **tu**.
target_language_example: C’est toi que je veux aider.
native_language_example: It’s you I want to help.

meaning: "It’s you who…" / "You’re the one who…" (emphasis on 'you').
additional_notes: Used to strongly identify or blame/praise the person who did something. It’s part of the emphatic structure "c’est + stressed pronoun (toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux/elles) + qui + verb". The verb after "qui" agrees with the subject implied (usually "tu" with "toi": "C’est toi qui as…", "C’est toi qui fais…").
target_language_example: C’est toi qui as oublié les clés.
native_language_example: You’re the one who forgot the keys.

meaning: “it’s you who (did/has done) …” (emphasizing that you are the one).
additional_notes: Used to put strong emphasis on the person (toi) who did the action—often to blame, accuse, confirm, or highlight responsibility. It’s a cleft sentence: « C’est + person + qui + verb ». Here « as » is the 2nd-person singular of avoir in the passé composé, so it’s followed by a past participle: « C’est toi qui as dit / fait / mis… ». In neutral speech you can also say « Tu as… », but « C’est toi qui as… » is more emphatic.
target_language_example: C’est toi qui as cassé le verre ?
native_language_example: Was it you who broke the glass?

meaning: "It’s you who (did it)" / "You’re the one who (did it)" (emphasis).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that *you* are the person who did the action. Structure: **c’est + stressed pronoun (toi) + qui + verb**. Here **l’** is an object pronoun meaning “it/him/her,” and **as** is the present of *avoir* used to form the **passé composé** (e.g., *tu l’as fait(e), tu l’as trouvé(e)*). The past participle changes depending on the verb: *fait(e)*, *garé(e)*, *trouvé(e)*, *voulu*, *écrit(e)*.
target_language_example: C’est toi qui l’as cassé ?
native_language_example: Was it you who broke it?

meaning: "It was you who … to me" / "You’re the one who … to me" (emphasis).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that *you* (toi) are the person who did the action. It’s a common French emphasis pattern: **C’est + person + qui + verb**. Here **m’as** is the start of **tu m’as …** (“you have … me”), so it’s followed by a past participle (appelé, dit, donné, etc.).
target_language_example: C'est toi qui m'as aidé hier.
native_language_example: It was you who helped me yesterday.

meaning: 'it's your' (addressing one person; masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to the person you’re talking to. "Ton" is the masculine singular possessive (e.g., ton cousin, ton avenir) and is also used before a vowel or silent h even with feminine nouns (e.g., ton amie). For feminine nouns starting with a consonant, use "c'est ta"; for plural, "c'est tes".
target_language_example: C'est ton choix.
native_language_example: It's your choice.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens every time ("always"), or that something remains true/possible (often like "still"). Common set phrase: « C’est toujours ça » = “That’s something (at least)” / “Better than nothing.”
target_language_example: C'est toujours mieux que rien.
native_language_example: It's still better than nothing.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm or emphasize an adjective or description: *C’est tout à fait différent* (“It’s completely different”), *C’est tout à fait normal* (“That’s perfectly normal”). Often interchangeable with *c’est complètement / c’est absolument*, but *tout à fait* can also mean “quite” depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: C’est tout à fait possible de le faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: It’s absolutely possible to do it today.

meaning: "that’s all that…" / "it’s all that…" (used before a relative clause).
additional_notes:
Used to say something is the only thing that matters/is needed/is interesting, etc. It’s followed by a relative word depending on what comes next: 
- "c’est tout ce qui…" (subject: “that… which…”) 
- "c’est tout ce que…" (direct object: “that… which…”) 
- "c’est tout ce dont…" (with "de": “that… which… about/of”) 
- "c’est tout ce à quoi…" (with "à": “that… which… to/that… about”).
target_language_example: C’est tout ce que je sais.
native_language_example: That’s all I know.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the only thing involved, needed, remembered, etc. "Dont" replaces something introduced by "de" after the verb/adjective: e.g., "avoir besoin de" → "C'est tout ce dont j'ai besoin" ("That's all I need"), "se souvenir de" → "C'est tout ce dont je me souviens" ("That's all I remember"). Often followed by a verb phrase.
target_language_example: C'est tout ce dont j'ai envie aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: That's all I feel like today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the only thing needed, wanted, known, possible, etc. It’s followed by a clause. "ce que" becomes "qu'" before a vowel sound: "C'est tout ce qu'il faut" (= C'est tout ce que il faut).
target_language_example: C'est tout ce qu'on doit faire aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: That's all we have to do today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the only thing someone did/said/took/deserves/can do, or the only thing that remains. "Il" can mean "he" (a person) or "it" (an impersonal subject like "what remains"). It’s typically followed by a verb: "C’est tout ce qu’il a dit" (that’s all he said), "C’est tout ce qu’il reste" (that’s all that remains).
target_language_example: C’est tout ce qu’il me reste.
native_language_example: That’s all I have left.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the only thing available/known/needed. The structure is: c’est + tout + ce qu’ + on + verb. "On" often means "we" in everyday French, but it can also mean "people" or "someone" (a general subject). It’s normally followed by a verb: "C’est tout ce qu’on sait" (That’s all we know), "C’est tout ce qu’on demande" (That’s all we ask).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : c’est tout ce qu’on peut faire pour l’instant.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: that’s all we can do for now.

meaning: "That's all we have" / "that's all we've got."
additional_notes: Used to say there isn’t anything else available (often as an answer to a question or to point out limitations). Very common in spoken French; you can also hear it with a follow-up like « comme X » (“as far as X goes”), e.g. « C’est tout ce qu’on a comme tailles. »
target_language_example: Désolé, c’est tout ce qu’on a en stock.
native_language_example: Sorry, that's all we have in stock.

additional_notes: Used to say there is nothing more to add, do, say, or know. It’s often followed by a verb clause: « C’est tout ce que je vais dire » (That’s all I’m going to say), « C’est tout ce que tu as à savoir » (That’s all you have to know). In speech, « tu as » is often shortened to « t’as ».
target_language_example: C'est tout ce que je peux faire pour toi.
native_language_example: That's all I can do for you.

additional_notes: Used to say you have nothing more to give/show/say/offer. Often followed by extra detail: "...maintenant" (right now), "...sur moi" (on me), or an infinitive like "à dire" (to say) / "à offrir" (to offer). Can sound apologetic or final ("Sorry, that’s all I have").
target_language_example: Je peux te donner dix euros, mais c'est tout ce que j'ai.
native_language_example: I can give you ten euros, but that’s all I have.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re limited to only that action/thing. You usually complete it with a verb: *C’est tout ce que je sais/veux/peux faire/possède* (“That’s all I know/want/can do/own”). In speech you’ll often hear the contracted form *c’est tout c’que je …*.
target_language_example: Désolé, c’est tout ce que je peux faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, that’s all I can do today.

c'est tout ce que je peux

target_language_multi_word_term: c'est tout ce que je peux
additional_notes: Used to set a limit on what you’re able or willing to do. It’s usually followed by an infinitive (dire, faire, offrir, promettre) or used with pronouns like te/t’ (to you, informal) and vous (to you, formal or plural): « C’est tout ce que je peux te dire » / « … vous dire ». Often implies “I can’t do more than this.”
target_language_example: Désolé, c'est tout ce que je peux faire pour l'instant.
native_language_example: Sorry, that’s all I can do for now.

c'est tout ce que je voulais

target_language_multi_word_term: c'est tout ce que je voulais
additional_notes: Used to say you’re satisfied because you’ve gotten the information/answer/thing you were looking for. Often followed by an infinitive like entendre (to hear), savoir (to know), dire (to say): “C’est tout ce que je voulais savoir.” Literally “It’s all that I wanted,” but in English you usually say “That’s all I wanted (to know/hear/say).”
target_language_example: Merci, c'est tout ce que je voulais savoir.
native_language_example: Thanks, that’s all I wanted to know.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the only thing someone does/says/gets, often with a surprised, disappointed, or critical tone. It’s typically followed by a verb: « C’est tout ce que tu obtiens » (That’s all you get), « C’est tout ce que tu trouves à dire ? » (Is that all you can think of to say?). « ce que » = “what/that which”.
target_language_example: C'est tout ce que tu peux faire ?
native_language_example: Is that all you can do?

c'est tout ce que vous avez

target_language_multi_word_term: c'est tout ce que vous avez
meaning: "Is that all you have?" / "That's all you have."
additional_notes: Literally “it’s all that you have.” Used to say something is the only thing available, or (often as a question) to challenge someone: “Is that all you’ve got (against me / to say / to do)?” Common patterns: « C’est tout ce que vous avez à + infinitive » (to say, to do, to know). « vous » is the formal/plural “you.”
target_language_example: C'est tout ce que vous avez à proposer ?
native_language_example: Is that all you have to propose?

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the only thing that matters or the only thing remaining. Often followed by a verb like importe (matters) or reste (is left). Can refer to different people by changing the pronoun later in the sentence: c’est tout ce qui me/lui/nous reste.
target_language_example: C’est tout ce qui compte pour moi.
native_language_example: That’s all that matters to me.

additional_notes: Used to describe something with emphasis: C’est (= it is/that’s) + très (= very) + an adjective/adverb (e.g., bien, doux, intelligent). Often followed by an adjective (très bon, très joli) or by an adverb + past participle (très bien fait).
target_language_example: C'est très important pour moi.
native_language_example: It’s very important to me.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone or react politely when they say or do something nice. Often followed by **de + infinitive** to say what is kind: *C’est très gentil de m’aider.* You can also say **C’est très gentil à vous** (more formal, addressing someone as *vous*).
target_language_example: C’est très gentil de votre part, merci !
native_language_example: That’s very kind of you, thank you!

meaning: "it's a / it's an" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something/someone: c'est un + noun/adjective + noun. Use **c'est une** before a feminine singular noun. For plural, use **ce sont des** (more formal) or often **c'est des** (informal).
target_language_example: C'est un bon restaurant.
native_language_example: It’s a good restaurant.

meaning: "It’s a beautiful/nice …" (said before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to compliment something: **C’est un beau + noun** (masculine singular), like *C’est un beau cadeau* (“It’s a nice gift”). Before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or silent h, French usually changes **beau** to **bel**: *C’est un bel appartement.* For feminine nouns, use **une belle**: *C’est une belle journée.*
target_language_example: C'est un beau quartier, très calme.
native_language_example: It’s a nice neighborhood, very quiet.

meaning: "It's a good ..." (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something is good, followed by a noun: "C'est un bon + nom". "Bon" agrees with the noun (masc. sing.). With a feminine noun, use "C'est une bonne ..." (e.g., "C'est une bonne idée").
target_language_example: C'est un bon plan.
native_language_example: It's a good plan.

meaning: "it's a great / big ..." (before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used in the pattern **c'est un grand + noun** to emphasize importance, intensity, or size: **un grand honneur** (a great honor), **un grand moment** (a big moment), **un grand pas** (a big step), **un grand garçon** (a big boy / grown-up boy). In French, **grand** often means “big/important” (or “tall”), not necessarily “grand” in the English sense.
target_language_example: C'est un grand plaisir de vous aider.
native_language_example: It's a great pleasure to help you.

additional_notes: Used with **c’est** to identify or describe someone as a man, often followed by an adjective or extra information: **C’est un homme bon.** You can also use it in more general statements: **C’est un homme comme les autres** (“He’s a man like any other”).
target_language_example: C'est un homme très gentil.
native_language_example: He’s a very kind man.

additional_notes: Used in formal or polite situations to show respect and gratitude (meeting someone, working with someone, receiving an award or invitation). Often followed by "de" + infinitive: "C’est un honneur de vous rencontrer." You can also add a title/name: "C’est un honneur, Monsieur."
target_language_example: C’est un honneur de faire votre connaissance.
native_language_example: It’s an honor to meet you.

additional_notes: A very formal, polite phrase used with **vous** (the formal/plural “you”), usually followed by an infinitive: **C’est un honneur de vous + infinitive** (avoir ici, connaître, recevoir, servir, rencontrer, etc.). Often used in speeches, ceremonies, professional settings, or when showing respect.
target_language_example: C’est un honneur de vous rencontrer en personne.
native_language_example: It’s an honor to meet you in person.

meaning: "It's a game." / "This is a game." (often: "Are you kidding?" / "Do you think this is a joke?")
additional_notes: Literal meaning is that something is a game. In questions like « Tu crois que c’est un jeu ? », it’s often rhetorical and means the speaker thinks the situation is serious and shouldn’t be treated lightly. You can also hear the stronger version « Ce n’est pas un jeu ! » (“This is no game / This is no joke!”).
target_language_example: Tu crois que c’est un jeu ? On n’a pas le temps !
native_language_example: Do you think this is a game? We don’t have time!

meaning: "It's a bit…" / "It's kind of…" (to soften what you say).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective or phrase to mean something is slightly too much/not quite right, often as a polite or gentle criticism: C'est un peu grand (It’s a bit big), C'est un peu fort (That’s a bit much/strong), C'est un peu juste (It’s a bit tight/just barely enough). In speech it can also be followed by a pause: C'est un peu… grand.
target_language_example: C'est un peu cher pour moi.
native_language_example: It's a bit expensive for me.

meaning: "It's a bit…" / "It's kind of…" (to soften what you say).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective or phrase to mean something is slightly too much/not quite right, often as a polite or gentle criticism: C'est un peu grand (It’s a bit big), C'est un peu fort (That’s a bit much/strong), C'est un peu juste (It’s a bit tight/just barely enough). In speech it can also be followed by a pause: C'est un peu… grand.
target_language_example: C'est un peu cher pour moi.
native_language_example: It's a bit expensive for me.

additional_notes: Used as a polite, friendly way to say you’re happy to do something or to meet/see/work with someone. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., te rencontrer, travailler avec vous). Common in professional contexts. Note: you’ll often hear it with an object pronoun (te/ vous): « C’est un plaisir de te voir / de vous voir ».
target_language_example: C'est un plaisir de vous aider aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: It’s a pleasure to help you today.

additional_notes: Used as a polite, fairly formal phrase with **vous**. It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb: **C’est un plaisir de vous + accueillir / connaître / recevoir / avoir parmi nous**. You can switch to **te** for informal situations: *C’est un plaisir de te…*.
target_language_example: C’est un plaisir de vous rencontrer.
native_language_example: It’s a pleasure to meet you.

meaning: "it's a" / "that is a" (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something: c'est (= ce + est, “it/that is”) + une (“a/an” for feminine singular nouns). Common in definitions and introductions. For masculine nouns, use "c'est un".
target_language_example: C'est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: It's a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to describe something with a feminine noun: c’est une belle + noun (e.g., femme, idée, maison, matinée, soirée, ville). The adjective agrees in gender/number: belle (feminine singular), bel (masculine singular before a vowel sound: C’est un bel appartement), beau (masculine singular: C’est un beau jour), belles (feminine plural: Ce sont de belles idées). Often paired with "une" because the noun is feminine.
target_language_example: C’est une belle journée pour se promener.
native_language_example: It’s a beautiful day for a walk.

additional_notes: This is usually an incomplete phrase that needs a feminine noun after it: "C’est une bonne idée" (a good idea), "C’est une bonne nouvelle" (good news). "Bonne" agrees with a feminine noun (compare: "C’est un bon …" before a masculine noun). Note: "une bonne" can also mean “a maid/servant” in older usage, but learners most often meet it as "une bonne + noun".
target_language_example: C’est une bonne idée de partir tôt.
native_language_example: It’s a good idea to leave early.

meaning: 'it's a good thing' / 'that's a good thing'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is positive or beneficial. Often followed by a short tag question to ask for agreement, like “n’est-ce pas ?” or “non ?”. You can also embed it in a longer sentence: “Je pense que c’est une bonne chose.”
target_language_example: Pour ta santé, c'est une bonne chose de marcher tous les jours.
native_language_example: For your health, it's a good thing to walk every day.

additional_notes: Used to say you think something is a good plan or suggestion. Often refers to something just mentioned; you can add "ça" at the end ("C'est une bonne idée, ça") for emphasis. In questions ("Tu penses vraiment que...") it can express doubt: "Do you really think it's a good idea?"
target_language_example: Je pense que c'est une bonne idée de partir tôt.
native_language_example: I think it's a good idea to leave early.

additional_notes: Used to point out that something is an idea or suggestion. Very common with an adjective: « C’est une idée brillante / intéressante. » You can also add ownership: « C’est une idée à moi » = “It’s my idea.” (Note: « Voilà une idée ! » is also common for “That’s an idea!”).
target_language_example: C'est une idée, mais je ne suis pas sûr que ça marche.
native_language_example: It’s an idea, but I’m not sure it will work.

meaning: 'it's a matter of' / 'it's a question of'.
additional_notes: Used to say something depends on, or comes down to, a particular factor (often abstract): point de vue (point of view), principe(s) (principle(s)), respect, survie (survival), volonté (willpower). Often implies importance or that it’s non-negotiable (especially with « une question de principe »).
target_language_example: Pour moi, c'est une question de confiance.
native_language_example: For me, it's a matter of trust.

additional_notes: Used to identify or confirm that something belongs to the person you’re speaking to (one person, polite/formal). It’s often used in questions: « C’est votre signature ? » = “Is this your signature?” (Addressing more than one person: « C’est votre » can also mean “it’s your (plural) …”.)
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, c’est votre sac ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is this your bag?

additional_notes: Used to put emphasis on "vous" (you, formal or plural) as the person responsible for an action. It’s very common for clarifying or accusing: « C’est vous qui avez fait ça ? » = “Was it you who did that?” In sentences like « C’est vous qui commandez », it can also mean “You’re the one in charge.”
target_language_example: C’est vous qui avez appelé la police ?
native_language_example: Were you the one who called the police?

meaning: 'It’s you who have…' (emphatic: you are the one who…).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that *you* (vous) are the person who did something. It’s the pattern **c’est + [person] + qui + verb**. With *vous*, the verb here is **avez** (from *avoir*) and is often followed by a past participle: **C’est vous qui avez + fait/commencé/écrit…**. You can swap the person: *C’est moi qui ai…*, *C’est lui/elle qui a…*, *C’est nous qui avons…*.
target_language_example: C’est vous qui avez oublié vos clés.
native_language_example: You’re the one who forgot your keys.

additional_notes: Used to confirm that something is true or correct. You can use it as a full sentence (C’est vrai.) or before a clause (C’est vrai que… = “It’s true that…”).
target_language_example: C’est vrai, je suis en retard.
native_language_example: That’s true, I’m late.

meaning: “it’s really” / “it’s truly” (used to emphasize an opinion).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective or noun phrase to add strong emphasis: “C’est vraiment + adjectif/nom” (e.g., C’est vraiment parfait / la fin du monde). Depending on tone, it can be sincere or sarcastic (“Yeah, right, it’s really…”).
target_language_example: C'est vraiment incroyable !
native_language_example: It’s really incredible!

meaning: "it’s to (someone)" / "it’s up to (someone)" (used to point out who is concerned).
additional_notes: Often used in a cleft sentence to emphasize the person you’re talking to or about: « C’est à elle que… » = “It’s (to) her that…”. With a question word it can introduce what something is about or who something is directed to: « C’est à quel sujet ? » = “What is it about?” The exact meaning depends on what follows (a person, a thing, a subject, etc.).
target_language_example: C’est à toi de choisir.
native_language_example: It’s up to you to choose.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something and to place responsibility/blame on someone or something. It’s often followed by a noun or pronoun: c’est à cause de l’argent (money), de toi (you), de lui/elle (him/her), de nous (us), de vous (you). In questions, it can suggest blame: C’est à cause de moi ? = “Is it my fault?”
target_language_example: C’est à cause du trafic que je suis en retard.
native_language_example: It’s because of traffic that I’m late.

meaning: 'he’s the one you need to / should (do it) with' (emphasizing him).
additional_notes: This is a cleft sentence used to stress the person after "à" (the indirect object). Pattern: "C’est à + person + qu’il faut + infinitive" = “That person is the one you need to/should + verb.” Often used for giving the right contact person: "C’est à lui qu’il faut demander" = “You need to ask him (not someone else).” You can replace "lui" with "elle", "eux", "elles", a name, etc.
target_language_example: C’est à lui qu’il faut envoyer le formulaire.
native_language_example: He’s the one you need to send the form to.

additional_notes: Literally “it’s to me.” Often used with **que** to emphasize the person: **C’est à moi qu’il parle ?** = “Is he talking to me?” / “Is it me he’s talking to?” On its own, **Maintenant, c’est à moi** commonly means “Now it’s my turn.”
target_language_example: C'est à moi que tu demandes ça ?
native_language_example: Are you asking me that?

meaning: "it's up to me to" / "it's my turn/responsibility to" (to do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say that you are the one who should do something (your responsibility, role, or turn). You can swap the pronoun: c'est à toi de… (you), c'est à lui/elle de… (him/her), c'est à nous de… (us), etc.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, c'est à moi de payer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s up to me to pay.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you (the speaker) are the person being addressed—often because you’re surprised, offended, or clarifying who someone is speaking to. Pattern: « C’est à moi que tu + verb ? » (e.g., parles, dis ça, demandes ça). Literally it’s like “It’s to me that you…”, but in natural English it’s usually “Are you … me?” / “Are you …ing me?”.
target_language_example: C’est à moi que tu parles ?
native_language_example: Are you talking to me?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic or subject of what you’re talking about. Often followed by a person, thing, or event: C’est à propos de + noun/pronoun. Neutral register.
target_language_example: C’est à propos de notre rendez-vous.
native_language_example: It’s about our appointment.

meaning: “it’s you” / “to you” (used to emphasize who is concerned, asked, etc.).
additional_notes: Often appears in the emphatic pattern **C’est à toi que…** to stress that *you* are the person being addressed: **C’est à toi que je demande** = “You’re the one I’m asking.” On its own, **C’est à toi** can also mean “It’s yours” or “It’s your turn,” depending on context.
target_language_example: C’est à toi que je parle, pas à lui.
native_language_example: It’s you I’m talking to, not him.

meaning: "it’s up to you to" / "it’s your turn to".
additional_notes: Used to put responsibility on the person you’re talking to (toi = you, informal singular). It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « C’est à toi de + infinitif ». For a formal/plural "you," use « c’est à vous de ».
target_language_example: C’est à toi de commencer.
native_language_example: It’s your turn to start.

meaning: "So this is …?" / "Is this what … is?" (often rhetorical).
additional_notes: Used to react to a situation by naming it with a noun (la justice, la vraie vie, la raison, etc.), often to express doubt, disappointment, or irony. The comma highlights a pause: « C’est ça, la justice ? » ≈ “So that’s justice?”
target_language_example: C'est ça, la vraie vie ?
native_language_example: So this is real life?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a specific thing is the one you mean, often before a verb phrase: « C'est ça que je veux » = “That’s what I want.” It’s basically « c’est ça » (“that’s it/that’s the one”) + « que » introducing what follows. In everyday speech you may also hear « c’est ça que… » shortened to « c’est ça, … » depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: C'est ça que j'essayais d'expliquer.
native_language_example: That's what I was trying to explain.

meaning: “Is that what you…?” / “So that’s what you…?” (introduces a question or confirmation about what someone did/wants/was looking for).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French to point to a specific thing/action and ask for confirmation. Usually followed by a verb phrase: « C’est ça que tu cherchais ? » (Were you looking for that?), « C’est ça que tu veux faire ? » (Is that what you want to do?). Often said with a questioning intonation; can sound slightly surprised or accusatory depending on tone.
target_language_example: C’est ça que tu voulais me dire ?
native_language_example: Is that what you wanted to tell me?

meaning: "Is that what you want?" / "Is that what you mean?"
additional_notes: Used to confirm what the other person wants, means, or is asking for. Often said with a questioning tone (C'est ça que tu veux ?) and can sound a bit challenging or impatient depending on intonation (especially with "hein ?"). In speech, it’s often shortened to "C’est ça que tu veux ?" or even "C’est ça que tu veux, toi ?" for emphasis.
target_language_example: D’accord… c’est ça que tu veux que je fasse ?
native_language_example: Okay… is that what you want me to do?

additional_notes: Contraction of « ce » + « était » (imperfect past of « être »). Used to talk about how something was in the past, to describe a past situation (with an adjective or a noun), or to refer back to something previously mentioned: « C'était comment ? » = “How was it?”; « C'était ma décision » = “That was my decision.”
target_language_example: C'était vraiment sympa.
native_language_example: It was really nice.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. Structure: C’était il y a + duration (cinq mois / huit ans / longtemps). In speech you may also hear: « C’était il y a longtemps » or « C’était il y a deux ans ».
target_language_example: C’était il y a deux semaines, je crois.
native_language_example: That was two weeks ago, I think.

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify something in the past. It’s made of **c’** (= *ce*, “it/that”), **était** (“was”), and **la** (“the” for feminine singular nouns). Often followed by a noun phrase: *c’était la belle époque* (“it was the good old days”), *c’était la chose à faire* (“it was the thing to do”).
target_language_example: C'était la première fois que je venais ici.
native_language_example: It was the first time I came here.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something in the past. "C'était" is the imperfect of "c'est" (it is/that is), often used for background description or to say what something/someone was. "Le" is "the" for masculine singular nouns, and it’s also used before masculine superlatives and ordinals: "le mieux" (the best), "le plus facile" (the easiest), "le troisième" (the third).
target_language_example: C'était le bon choix.
native_language_example: It was the right choice.

meaning: 'it was my' (talking about something in the past).
additional_notes: "C'était" is the imperfect past of "c'est" (= it is/that is), used to describe or identify something in the past: "It was...". "Mon" means "my" before a masculine singular noun (mon but, mon devoir) and also before a feminine noun starting with a vowel sound (mon idée, mon intention). For a regular feminine noun, use "c'était ma..."; for plural, "c'était mes...".
target_language_example: C'était mon premier jour au travail.
native_language_example: It was my first day at work.

additional_notes: Conversational way to ask for a reminder or clarification about something previously mentioned, often when you’ve forgotten a detail (a name, the point/idea, etc.). You can add “déjà ?” to emphasize “again”/“already” (as in “What was it again?”).
target_language_example: Attends, c'était quoi l'adresse, déjà ?
native_language_example: Wait, what was the address again?

additional_notes: Used to say something was pleasant/enjoyable, often at the end of a conversation or meeting. It’s in the past tense (c’était = “it was”). Follow it with an infinitive verb: c’était sympa de + parler / discuter / vous rencontrer. Common polite variation: « C’était sympa de votre part » = “That was nice of you.”
target_language_example: C'était sympa de passer nous voir.
native_language_example: It was nice of you to stop by and see us.

additional_notes: Used to describe how something was in the past: c'était (= ce + était, “it was”) + très (“very”) + an adjective (agréable, impressionnant, gentil, etc.). Common when giving feedback about an experience. The adjective agrees with what you’re describing (e.g., C’était très gentil de ta part = “That was very kind of you”).
target_language_example: Le concert ? C'était très bien !
native_language_example: The concert? It was really good!

additional_notes: Past description with être (“to be”): c’ (ce) + était (was) + un (a). Use it to identify or describe someone/something in the past, usually followed by a noun (often with an adjective): « C’était un brave homme. » It can refer to a person (“he was a…”) or a thing/event (“it was a…”), depending on context.
target_language_example: C’était un moment important pour moi.
native_language_example: It was an important moment for me.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (c'était = "it was") to describe what something was (its nature/identification) in the past. Often used to explain that something happened unintentionally. Can also appear in reported speech: "Ils ont dit que c'était un accident."
target_language_example: Désolé, c'était un accident.
native_language_example: Sorry, it was an accident.

meaning: "it/he was a good…" (introduces a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something in the past. It’s short for "ce était" → "c’était" (= "it was" / "that was"). "un bon" must be followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., "un bon chien", "un bon début"). For a feminine noun, use "c’était une bonne…" (e.g., "une bonne idée").
target_language_example: C’était un bon professeur.
native_language_example: He was a good teacher.

meaning: 'it was a' (talking about a feminine noun).
additional_notes: "C'était" is the imperfect of "c'est" and is used to describe, explain, or give background about something in the past. "Une" is the feminine form of "a/an", so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., "une expérience", "une soirée", "une époque"). For a masculine noun, you’d say "c’était un".
target_language_example: C'était une bonne idée.
native_language_example: It was a good idea.

meaning: “How are you?” / “Are you OK?”; also “I’m OK / it’s going OK.”
additional_notes: Very common everyday expression. As a question ("Ça va ?") it’s a casual way to ask how someone is; with a name or title it can be friendly or polite: "Ça va, monsieur ?". As an answer ("Ça va.") it means you’re fine/OK (sometimes just “not bad”). The negative form "Ça va pas" means “I’m not OK / it’s not going well,” and "Ça va pas !" can also mean “That’s not OK!/That’s not right!” depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: — Ça va ? — Ça va, merci. Et toi ?
native_language_example: — How are you? — I’m fine, thanks. And you?

additional_notes: From the verb *cacher* = “to hide.” Used when you suspect someone isn’t telling the whole truth. In sentence 1, *Il nous cache quelque chose* means “He’s hiding something from us.” In sentence 2, *Ça cache quelque chose* means “There’s something fishy / there must be something behind this.”
target_language_example: Elle sourit, mais je pense qu’elle cache quelque chose.
native_language_example: She’s smiling, but I think she’s hiding something.

meaning: the calm before the storm; a quiet period before trouble.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used when things seem peaceful now, but you expect problems, conflict, or intense activity soon. Often used with the definite article: « C’est le calme avant la tempête. » It can also be said alone as a comment: « Le calme avant la tempête. »
target_language_example: Tout est silencieux au bureau aujourd’hui : c’est le calme avant la tempête.
native_language_example: Everything is quiet at the office today; it’s the calm before the storm.

meaning: "Calm down" / "Relax" (said to one person you address as tu).
additional_notes: Imperative of the reflexive verb se calmer. It’s a direct request telling someone to stop getting upset or excited. The hyphen links the verb and the object pronoun: calme + toi. (Formal version: « Calmez-vous. »)
target_language_example: Calme-toi, on va trouver une solution.
native_language_example: Calm down, we’re going to find a solution.

meaning: "Calm down" / "settle down" (spoken to one or more people).
additional_notes: Imperative form of "se calmer" with "vous" (addressing several people, or one person in a formal/polite way). Often used as a direct request or command, sometimes to stop arguing or panicking. You can soften it with "un peu" (a bit) or "s'il vous plaît".
target_language_example: Calmez-vous, s'il vous plaît, on va trouver une solution.
native_language_example: Calm down, please—we're going to find a solution.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the other students who are in your class at school/university. Often used with possessives: mes/tes/ses/nos/vos camarades de classe. You can also say "Nous sommes camarades de classe" = "We’re classmates."
target_language_example: Je vais travailler avec mes camarades de classe sur ce projet.
native_language_example: I’m going to work with my classmates on this project.

additional_notes: A medical term meaning a cancer located in the lung(s). Often used with articles like "un cancer du poumon" (a lung cancer) or "le cancer du poumon" (lung cancer as a disease in general). "Du" = "de + le" (of the), so it literally means "cancer of the lung".
target_language_example: Mon oncle a eu un cancer du poumon il y a dix ans.
native_language_example: My uncle had lung cancer ten years ago.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb: « être capable de + infinitive » to say someone has the ability (skills, strength, courage) to do something. « Capable de » can also be followed by a noun to mean “capable of” in a general sense.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas capable de finir ce travail aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I’m not able to finish this work today.

meaning: free rein; full permission to act as you want.
additional_notes: Often used with avoir/donner: « avoir carte blanche » (to have free rein) or « donner carte blanche (à quelqu’un) » (to give someone full authority). It means you’re trusted to decide, with few or no restrictions.
target_language_example: Le chef m’a donné carte blanche pour organiser l’événement.
native_language_example: My boss gave me free rein to organize the event.

additional_notes: Plural of « carte de crédit ». Common in shops/restaurants when asking or stating whether credit cards are accepted: « Vous acceptez les cartes de crédit ? » / « Nous prenons/acceptons les cartes de crédit. »
target_language_example: Désolé, je n’ai pas de liquide : est-ce que vous acceptez les cartes de crédit ?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have cash—do you accept credit cards?

meaning: broke the window (have broken the window).
additional_notes: Uses the past participle of *casser* (“to break”) with *avoir* in the passé composé: *j’ai cassé la fenêtre* (“I broke the window”). *Casser* is used for breaking something (accidentally or on purpose).
target_language_example: J’ai cassé la fenêtre en jouant au foot.
native_language_example: I broke the window while playing soccer.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the noun phrase **la cause de + noun** to name what produces an effect: *la cause de la mort*, *la cause de son retard*. Often followed by **de + noun** (or **de + infinitive** in some contexts). Don’t confuse with **à cause de** (“because of”), which introduces a reason in a full sentence.
target_language_example: La cause de l'accident n'est pas encore connue.
native_language_example: The cause of the accident is not known yet.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific sound/noise in the situation or just mentioned. With "-là" ("ce bruit-là"), it means "that noise" and adds emphasis or points to a particular one. Often used in complaints or commands: "Cessez ce bruit !" (Stop that noise!).
target_language_example: Tu entends ce bruit ?
native_language_example: Do you hear that noise?

additional_notes: “Ce” means “this/that” (masculine singular) and is used before a masculine noun like “bâtiment” (building). It can refer to a building nearby (“this”) or one already identified in the conversation (“that”). Before a vowel or silent h, use “cet” (e.g., “cet immeuble”).
target_language_example: On se retrouve devant ce bâtiment à 18 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet in front of this building at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: "Ce" is a demonstrative adjective meaning “this/that.” It agrees with masculine singular nouns, so it’s used with "chien" (a masculine noun). In speech, "ce" can refer to a dog that’s nearby (“this dog”) or one already known/mentioned (“that dog”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ce chien est très gentil avec les enfants.
native_language_example: This dog is very gentle with children.

additional_notes: Used to describe a specific dog. Structure: "ce" + masculine singular noun (chien) + "est" (is). What follows can be an adjective ("blanc", "vieux"), a noun/adjective label, or a possession: "le vôtre" (yours), or "à moi / à toi" (mine / yours). In exclamations you can put "comme" at the start: "Comme ce chien est vieux !" = "How old this dog is!"
target_language_example: Ce chien est très gentil.
native_language_example: This dog is very nice.

additional_notes: "Ce" is a demonstrative adjective meaning "this/that". Use "ce film" for a masculine singular noun starting with a consonant sound (film). It refers to a specific movie already known from context. For a feminine noun use "cette" (ex: cette série). For a masculine noun starting with a vowel sound use "cet" (ex: cet acteur).
target_language_example: J'aime beaucoup ce film, je l'ai déjà vu deux fois.
native_language_example: I really like this movie; I've already seen it twice.

additional_notes: Use it to describe a movie you’re talking about. It’s built from ce (“this”), film (“movie/film”), and est (“is”). Often followed by an adjective like ennuyeux (boring), merveilleux (wonderful), passionnant (exciting), intéressant (interesting), etc.
target_language_example: Ce film est vraiment drôle.
native_language_example: This movie is really funny.

meaning: “that son of a bitch” (very vulgar insult).
additional_notes: Very offensive and aggressive. Literally means “that son of a whore,” used like English “that son of a bitch” to insult someone (often a man, but it can be used for anyone). "Ce" here means “that/this,” pointing to the person being talked about. Avoid using it in polite or everyday situations.
target_language_example: Je déteste ce fils de pute, il a tout détruit.
native_language_example: I hate that son of a bitch; he destroyed everything.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective ce (= this/that) + garçon (= boy) to point out a specific boy. Often translated as “this boy” when near or in focus, and “that boy” when farther away or already mentioned. Before a feminine noun, use cette (cette fille).
target_language_example: Ce garçon parle très vite.
native_language_example: That boy speaks very fast.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to refer to a type/category of thing (often with a slightly judgmental or emphatic tone depending on context). It agrees with the noun only in the demonstrative: singular is common (“ce genre de + noun”), and plural can be “ces genres de + noun(s)”. Often followed by a plural noun: “ce genre de trucs / réponses”.
target_language_example: Je n’aime pas ce genre de musique.
native_language_example: I don’t like this kind of music.

meaning: 'this kind of thing' / 'that sort of thing'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to an example or category of actions/events without naming something specific. Often follows verbs like faire (to do) or arriver (to happen). You can also use it to generalize: Ce genre de chose arrive rarement. It can sound mildly disapproving depending on context (e.g., Faire ce genre de chose...).
target_language_example: Je n'aime pas ce genre de chose.
native_language_example: I don't like that kind of thing.

additional_notes: Used to refer in a general way to a type of situation, behavior, or event, often something already mentioned or understood from context. It can be neutral or slightly dismissive depending on tone. You can also say: "ce genre de truc" (more casual) or "ce genre de situation" (more specific).
target_language_example: Je n'aime pas ce genre de choses.
native_language_example: I don't like that kind of thing.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific type of behavior (often disapproving) that’s obvious from context or was just mentioned. You can change the demonstrative: "ce" (this/that), "ce genre de" (this kind of), "ce genre d’" before a vowel sound like in "attitude". Often appears in questions like "Tu comprends ce genre d’attitude ?" meaning “Do you understand/accept that kind of behavior?”
target_language_example: Je n’aime pas ce genre d’attitude au travail.
native_language_example: I don’t like that kind of attitude at work.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "ce" ("this/that") + the noun "jeu" ("game"). It points to a specific game that’s known from context. Before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or silent h, use "cet" (e.g., "cet exercice"). Feminine: "cette" (e.g., "cette partie").
target_language_example: J'adore ce jeu, mais je ne sais pas y jouer.
native_language_example: I love this game, but I don't know how to play it.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective "ce" + noun to point out a specific person (often meaning either "this" or "that" depending on context). "Ce" is used before a masculine singular noun starting with a consonant; before a vowel or silent h, it becomes "cet" (e.g., "cet homme").
target_language_example: Ce jeune homme cherche son téléphone.
native_language_example: This young man is looking for his phone.

meaning: "that day" (a specific day in the past or in a story).
additional_notes: Used to point to a particular day already known from context (often something important happened). It’s common in storytelling and memories. You can also use it alone for emphasis: « Ce jour-là. »
target_language_example: Je me souviens encore de ce jour-là.
native_language_example: I still remember that day.

additional_notes: "Ce" is a demonstrative adjective meaning “this/that” before a masculine singular noun. So "ce livre" refers to a specific book (often one you’re holding, pointing to, or already talking about).
target_language_example: J'ai acheté ce livre hier.
native_language_example: I bought this book yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to describe a specific book you’re pointing out or talking about. It’s the start of a sentence, followed by an adjective or description (e.g., destiné, divisé, difficile, vieux). You can also use it with comparisons: « Ce livre est plus … que … ».
target_language_example: Ce livre est très intéressant, mais un peu long.
native_language_example: This book is very interesting, but a bit long.

additional_notes: "Ce" (masculine singular) points to a specific store. In speech, it can mean either “this” (nearby/just mentioned) or “that” depending on context; for extra clarity you can say "ce magasin-ci" (this one) or "ce magasin-là" (that one).
target_language_example: J'aime bien ce magasin, on y trouve de tout.
native_language_example: I like this store; you can find everything there.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the morning of today (something that happened earlier today). Often placed at the end of the sentence: « Je me suis levé(e) à sept heures ce matin. »
target_language_example: Je suis allé au marché ce matin.
native_language_example: I went to the market this morning.

additional_notes: Common in spoken French. "Mec" is informal (like “guy”/“dude”) and can sound a bit blunt depending on tone and context. Often used to point out or talk about a specific man: "Ce mec-là ?" = “That guy?”
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas ce mec, mais il a l'air sympa.
native_language_example: I don’t know this guy, but he seems nice.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the current month (the month we are in now). Often placed at the end of the sentence to set the time frame; it can also be used at the start for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je suis très occupé ce mois-ci.
native_language_example: I’m very busy this month.

additional_notes:
Often used with a preposition:
- « à ce moment(-là) » = “at that moment / then” (refers to a specific point in time, often in a story).
- « en ce moment » = “right now / at the moment” (what’s happening currently).
« moment » is masculine, so it’s « ce moment » (not *cette*).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas parler en ce moment.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific word in context (a word you just said, a word written somewhere, or a word being discussed). "Ce" is a demonstrative determiner meaning "this/that"; with masculine singular nouns like "mot" it becomes "ce" (or "cet" before a vowel sound).
target_language_example: Comment s’écrit ce mot ?
native_language_example: How do you spell this word?

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative determiner "ce" (masculine singular) to point to a specific medicine being talked about or shown. Often used in health contexts with verbs like "prendre" (to take) and with instructions like "entre les repas" (between meals). In formal/medical contexts you may see it with "ordonnance" (prescription).
target_language_example: Ce médicament est très efficace, mais il peut avoir des effets secondaires.
native_language_example: This medication is very effective, but it can have side effects.

additional_notes: "Ce" is a demonstrative adjective meaning "this/that". "Ce pays" points to a specific country understood from context (the country you’re talking about, the one you’re in, or one you just mentioned). The exact sense can be "this" or "that" depending on the situation; to be more explicit you can use "ce pays-ci" (this country) and "ce pays-là" (that country).
target_language_example: J'aime vivre dans ce pays.
native_language_example: I like living in this country.

additional_notes: "Ce" means "this" (or sometimes "that") and is used before a masculine singular noun like "problème". Use "ce problème" when referring to a specific problem already known or mentioned. Common verbs with it include: signaler ce problème (report this problem), avoir ce problème (have this problem), traiter/résoudre ce problème (deal with/solve this problem).
target_language_example: On doit régler ce problème tout de suite.
native_language_example: We need to fix this problem right away.

meaning: 'this project' (a specific project being talked about).
additional_notes: Used to point to a particular project already known from the context (or just mentioned). Often appears as the subject or object of a sentence (e.g., "Ce projet a échoué", "Que pensez-vous de ce projet ?"). It agrees with the masculine noun "projet" (singular).
target_language_example: Nous devons terminer ce projet avant vendredi.
native_language_example: We have to finish this project before Friday.

additional_notes: "Rapport" means a report (e.g., school/work/military/police). "Ce" is the masculine singular demonstrative meaning "this/that"; it becomes "cet" before a vowel sound (e.g., "cet article"). In conversation, "ce rapport" typically refers to a specific report already known in context.
target_language_example: Tu peux m'envoyer ce rapport avant midi ?
native_language_example: Can you send me this report before noon?

additional_notes: "Ce" is a demonstrative adjective meaning "this/that" used with a masculine singular noun. Which one you mean depends on context (nearby = "this", more distant or previously mentioned = "that"). It becomes "cet" before a vowel sound (e.g., "cet hôtel"). Feminine: "cette"; plural: "ces".
target_language_example: J'aime bien ce restaurant : on y mange très bien.
native_language_example: I really like this restaurant: you eat very well there.

additional_notes: Use **ce/ cet/ cette + noun + est** to describe something with an adjective or a phrase. Here, **ce restaurant** = “this restaurant” (masculine singular), and **est** = “is”. You’ll typically add an adjective (e.g., *cher, nul*) or a description (e.g., *réputé pour…*).
target_language_example: Ce restaurant est vraiment bon.
native_language_example: This restaurant is really good.

additional_notes: "Ce" is the masculine singular demonstrative adjective meaning "this" (or "that" depending on context). "Sac" means "bag" (e.g., a shopping bag, backpack, or sack). Use "ce sac" when pointing to or referring to a specific bag nearby or already identified. For a feminine noun, use "cette" (e.g., "cette valise").
target_language_example: Je vais mettre les courses dans ce sac.
native_language_example: I’m going to put the groceries in this bag.

meaning: that evening / that night (on that particular day).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific evening already known from context (often a past event). It’s "ce soir" (this evening) + "-là" meaning "that" (not "this"). Can also appear after prepositions: "de ce soir-là" = "from that evening."
target_language_example: Je me souviens encore de ce soir-là.
native_language_example: I still remember that evening.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific topic being discussed or mentioned. Often follows prepositions like « de » (discuter de ce sujet, parler de ce sujet).
target_language_example: On va éviter ce sujet pour l’instant.
native_language_example: We’re going to avoid this topic for now.

additional_notes: "Ce" means "this/that" (masculine singular) and is used before a noun: *ce livre, ce musée*. *Tableau* can also mean a "chart/table" (e.g., *un tableau de chiffres*), but in everyday conversation it very often means a painting or artwork you look at (especially in a museum or gallery).
target_language_example: J'adore ce tableau : les couleurs sont magnifiques.
native_language_example: I love this painting; the colors are beautiful.

additional_notes: "Ce" is a demonstrative meaning "this" (masculine singular), used with a noun: "ce travail" = the specific work/job you’re talking about. "Travail" can mean work in general, a task/assignment, or a job (employment), depending on context (e.g., "Ce travail payait bien" = "That job paid well"). Note: "travail" looks like English "travel" but it means "work" (false cognate).
target_language_example: Je n’aime pas ce travail, mais il paie bien.
native_language_example: I don’t like this job, but it pays well.

meaning: "this thing" (a vague way to refer to something).
additional_notes: Used when you don’t know, don’t remember, or don’t want to name the object/idea/activity. Often sounds casual and can be negative or dismissive depending on tone (e.g., “Arrête ce truc.” = “Stop that thing/that stuff.”). Also common in questions like “C’est quoi, ce truc ?” / “Qu’est-ce que c’est que ce truc ?” (“What is this thing?”).
target_language_example: C'est quoi, ce truc ?
native_language_example: What is this thing?

additional_notes: In everyday French, "type" often means "guy" or "man" and can sound a bit casual or sometimes slightly dismissive depending on tone and context. You’ll also hear it used with a negative feeling (e.g., someone creepy or annoying) or neutral/positive ("J’adore ce type"). It’s not the same as English "type" = "kind/sort" (that meaning exists too: "ce type de problème" = "this type of problem"). For a more neutral/polite option, say "cet homme" (this man).
target_language_example: Je n'aime pas ce type, il est bizarre.
native_language_example: I don't like that guy, he's weird.

meaning: “this guy is…” / “that guy is…” (talking about a man).
additional_notes: "Ce type" is an informal way to mean “this guy/that guy” (often like “some guy”). It can sound a bit dismissive depending on tone. Use "cet homme" (more neutral) or "ce monsieur" (polite) if needed. Note: French "type" is a common false friend—here it means a person, not a “type/category.”
target_language_example: Ce type est vraiment sympa.
native_language_example: This guy is really nice.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the coming/next weekend relative to now. Often used when making plans or asking about availability. You can also hear/spell it as "ce weekend"; it’s a common borrowed term.
target_language_example: On se voit ce week-end ?
native_language_example: Are we seeing each other this weekend?

meaning: "what" / "that which" (when it means "of which" or "about which").
additional_notes: Used to refer to a thing introduced by "de" (dont = de + which/what). Common after verbs and expressions that take "de", e.g. parler de (talk about), avoir besoin de (need), se souvenir de (remember), être fier de (be proud of). It often translates as “what … about” or “what … of.”
target_language_example: Voilà ce dont j'ai besoin.
native_language_example: That's what I need.

additional_notes: Built with **ce dont** because **avoir besoin de** requires **de**: *J’ai besoin de quelque chose* → *ce dont j’ai besoin* (“what I need”). It can refer to a thing, help, information, etc. You can change the subject/tense: *ce dont tu as besoin* (what you need), *ce dont j’aurai besoin* (what I’ll need).
target_language_example: Je vais acheter ce dont j’ai besoin pour le dîner.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy what I need for dinner.

additional_notes: Used to say something is exactly what you needed. Built with "ce dont" (= "what/that which" + "de"), used with verbs that take "de" like "avoir besoin de" (to need). In other tenses you change "j'avais" (imparfait) to match: "ce dont j'ai besoin" (what I need), "ce dont j'aurai besoin" (what I will need). Often emphasized with words like "juste" (just), "pile" (exactly).
target_language_example: Merci, c'est exactement ce dont j'avais besoin !
native_language_example: Thanks, that's exactly what I needed!

meaning: what we need / what is needed.
additional_notes: Uses the relative pronoun "dont" with the expression "avoir besoin de" (to need). "Ce dont on a besoin" refers to the thing(s) that are necessary. "On" here is general and often means "we" or "people in general."
target_language_example: Voilà ce dont on a besoin pour commencer.
native_language_example: That’s what we need to get started.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the thing(s) someone needs. It’s built from **ce dont** (“what/that which … of/that …”) + **tu as besoin** (“you need”). Often used after verbs like *dire* (to tell), *savoir* (to know), *prendre* (to take): *Dis-moi ce dont tu as besoin* (“Tell me what you need”), *Prends ce dont tu as besoin* (“Take what you need”).
target_language_example: Je peux t’aider à trouver ce dont tu as besoin.
native_language_example: I can help you find what you need.

additional_notes: Uses **ce dont** to mean “what/that which” with the verb **avoir besoin de** (“to need”). **dont** replaces something introduced by **de**: *avoir besoin de quelque chose* → *ce dont vous avez besoin*. Often follows verbs like *dire, savoir, prendre*: *Dites-moi / Je sais / Prenez ce dont vous avez besoin*.
target_language_example: Je peux vous aider à trouver ce dont vous avez besoin.
native_language_example: I can help you find what you need.

additional_notes: "Ce" means "it/that" and "fut" is the passé simple form of *être* ("to be") for "il/elle". You’ll mostly see *ce fut* in books, stories, news writing, or very formal speech to narrate completed past events. In everyday conversation, French usually uses *c’était* or *ça a été* instead.
target_language_example: Ce fut une journée difficile, mais on a réussi.
native_language_example: It was a difficult day, but we managed.

additional_notes: Uses the passé simple of être (fut) with ce to state what something/someone was in the past. Common in writing, books, speeches, or formal style; in everyday conversation you usually say "c'était un/une".
target_language_example: Ce fut un moment inoubliable.
native_language_example: It was an unforgettable moment.

additional_notes: A very polite way to say you enjoyed doing something (meeting someone, working with someone, serving someone). "Ce fut" is a formal/literary past tense (passé simple) of "c'est"; in everyday conversation you’ll more often hear "Ça a été un plaisir de..." or "C’était un plaisir de...". Often used as a closing line in emails, customer service, or formal conversations.
target_language_example: Ce fut un plaisir de vous aider aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: It was a pleasure to help you today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something in the past, especially in writing, storytelling, news, or formal speech. In everyday conversation, French usually prefers *c’était une...* or *ça a été une...*. It must be followed by a feminine singular noun (*une catastrophe, une expérience, une fête, une période*).
target_language_example: Ce fut une journée inoubliable.
native_language_example: It was an unforgettable day.

meaning: "it/this" + "not" (the start of a French negation, before a vowel).
additional_notes: "Ce n'" is the shortened form of "ce ne" (ne → n' before a vowel or silent h). You’ll most often see it in negatives like: "Ce n’est pas…" (It’s not…), "Ce n’est plus…" (It’s no longer…), "Ce n’est toujours pas…" (It still isn’t…). The negation is completed by a second word such as "pas", "plus", "jamais", etc.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas possible.
native_language_example: It's not possible.

meaning: “it is not / this is not” (start of a negative sentence with être).
additional_notes: Used with negation: ce n’est pas… (“it’s not…”), ce n’est plus… (“it’s no longer…”), ce n’est toujours pas… (“it’s still not…”), ce n’est personne (“it’s nobody”), ce n’est rien (“it’s nothing”), ce n’est plus que… (“it’s nothing more than…”). Often followed by an adjective, noun, or pronoun.
target_language_example: Désolé, ce n’est pas possible aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s not possible today.

additional_notes: Used to negate "c'est" ("it is/this is") with the French negation "ne ... pas" around the verb "être". Before a vowel or silent h, "ne" becomes "n'": "Ce n'est pas...". Common for saying something is not true, not correct, not yours, not normal, etc.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas mon problème.
native_language_example: It's not my problem.

additional_notes: Used to say that a statement, assumption, or situation is not true or does not apply. Often follows phrases like "j’espère que…" (I hope…), "peut-être que…" (maybe…), or "sauf que…" (except that…). It refers back to something already mentioned ("le cas" = the situation/case).
target_language_example: Tu crois qu’il est déjà parti, mais ce n’est pas le cas.
native_language_example: You think he already left, but that’s not the case.

meaning: "it’s only / it’s just" (used to downplay or minimize).
additional_notes: Used before a noun (ce n’est qu’un/une + noun) to say something is “nothing more than” that thing. It often reassures, minimizes importance, or contrasts with what someone implied. In speech you may also hear: « C’est qu’un… » (less formal).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, ce n’est qu’une erreur.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s just a mistake.

additional_notes: Used to downplay or minimize something, often meaning “nothing more than a…”. Very common pattern: “Ce n’est qu’un(e) + noun” (feminine: “Ce n’est qu’une…”). You can also use other forms: “Ce n’est que + noun/phrase” (e.g., “Ce n’est que le début.”).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : ce n'est qu'un test.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s just a test.

additional_notes: Used to minimize or downplay something. It’s the negative form of “c’est” + “ne…que” (meaning “only/just”): “ce n’est qu’une + noun (f.)”. For masculine nouns, use “ce n’est qu’un …” (e.g., “Ce n’est qu’un détail.”).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : ce n'est qu'une erreur.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s just a mistake.

additional_notes: Uses the restrictive pattern "ne … que" (= “only”). It downplays or limits what something is: "Ce n’est que de l’eau" = “It’s just water.” Note that there’s no "pas" here ("ne … que" is not the same as "ne … pas"). You can also use it with abstract nouns: "Ce n’est que le début" (“It’s only the beginning”), or to soften a statement: "Ce n’est que mon opinion" (“It’s just my opinion”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, ce n’est que du bruit.
