With *fille*, *une grande fille* often means “a grown-up girl / big girl.”
target_language_example: Paris est une grande ville.
native_language_example: Paris is a big city.

additional_notes: Used to identify something as a language: “[X] est une langue …” (“[X] is a … language”), often followed by an adjective (difficile, sympathique) or a category/origin (slave, berbère). The verb is present tense of être (“to be”).
target_language_example: Le français est une langue très utile.
native_language_example: French is a very useful language.

meaning: “is a person” (used to describe someone or define a job).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives to describe someone (e.g., "est une personne bizarre/bavarde") or with "qui..." to define what someone does ("Un fleuriste est une personne qui..."). Often interchangeable with "il/elle est + adjectif" when describing someone, but "être une personne + adjectif" can sound a bit more general.
target_language_example: Ma sœur est une personne très gentille.
native_language_example: My sister is a very kind person.

additional_notes: Used to say that an activity isn’t worth doing because it doesn’t bring enough benefit. It often follows an infinitive (e.g., “Regarder la télévision est une perte de temps.”). You can also use it with something: “Twitter est une perte de temps.”
target_language_example: Pour moi, faire la queue ici est une perte de temps.
native_language_example: For me, waiting in line here is a waste of time.

additional_notes: Used with a singular feminine noun to identify a place: [Place] + est une ville + adjective (calme, tranquille) or + de + country/region (“une ville de Russie” = a city in Russia). For plural, use “sont des villes.” For masculine nouns like “village,” use “est un …”.
target_language_example: Lyon est une ville très agréable.
native_language_example: Lyon is a very pleasant city.

additional_notes: Passé composé of venir with the auxiliary être. It can mean a person came/has come (e.g., « Tom est venu tôt. ») or in set phrases like « Le temps est venu de… » = “the time has come to…”. With être, the past participle agrees in gender/number: elle est venue, ils sont venus, elles sont venues.
target_language_example: Le moment est venu de partir.
native_language_example: The time has come to leave.

meaning: "came to see me" / "came to visit me."
additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern **venir + infinitive**: **venir voir** = “to come (and) see/visit.” Here it’s in the **passé composé** with **être**: **il/elle est venu(e)**. The past participle agrees with the subject (venu, venue, venus, venues). In a negative sentence you normally say: **Personne n’est venu me voir** (“Nobody came to see me”).
target_language_example: Elle est venue me voir après le travail.
native_language_example: She came to see me after work.

additional_notes: Passé composé of venir for a feminine singular subject (elle / ma sœur / la police, etc.). It describes someone (or something) coming/arriving, or coming to do something: « Elle est venue me voir » = “She came to see me.” It can also be used more figuratively with time: « Ton heure est venue » = “Your time has come.” Note: « venue » is a false friend with English “venue” (place).
target_language_example: Elle est venue à la maison hier soir.
native_language_example: She came to the house last night.

additional_notes: Used with singular subjects to say something contains nothing or has no people/space left (e.g., a can, box, jar, park). For batteries, it means the battery is dead/has no charge. Feminine form: "est vide" also (same spelling/pronunciation), e.g., "La boîte est vide."
target_language_example: Le frigo est vide.
native_language_example: The fridge is empty.

meaning: "is your" (used to ask/confirm who someone is to you).
additional_notes: Made of **est** = “is” (from *être*) + **votre** = “your” (formal singular or plural “your”). Common in questions like **Qui est votre… ?** (“Who is your…?”) or **X est votre… ?** (“Is X your…?”).
target_language_example: Qui est votre professeur ?
native_language_example: Who is your teacher?

additional_notes: Used to say that a statement/fact is true. Often appears after “que” in longer sentences (e.g., “Je crois que … est vrai”). For emphasis you can also say “C’est vrai !” (“That’s true!”).
target_language_example: Ce que tu dis est vrai.
native_language_example: What you're saying is true.

additional_notes: Used with être (“to be”) to emphasize that something is genuinely the case: *C’est vraiment…* = “It’s really…” It often comes before an adjective (*est vraiment très beau*) or a noun phrase (*est vraiment une fille…*).
target_language_example: Ce restaurant est vraiment excellent.
native_language_example: This restaurant is really excellent.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is within a building/space (indoors) or within an area (e.g., inland: « à l'intérieur des terres »). Often answers “Where is … ?” → « Il/Elle est à l’intérieur. »
target_language_example: Le chat est à l’intérieur parce qu’il fait froid dehors.
native_language_example: The cat is inside because it’s cold outside.

additional_notes: Used with être to say someone is at home (physically at their house). For questions, keep the same structure and raise intonation or add a question mark: « Il est à la maison ? ». You can change the subject and the verb form: « je suis / tu es / il est / elle est / on est / nous sommes / vous êtes / ils sont / elles sont à la maison ».
target_language_example: Ma sœur est à la maison ce soir.
native_language_example: My sister is at home tonight.

additional_notes: Used to express possession/ownership: *X est à moi* = “X is mine.” Often contrasts with *c’est mon/ma/mes* (“it’s my...”), which is used directly before a noun (e.g., *c’est mon sac*). Here, *à moi* emphasizes who the owner is and can sound insistent (e.g., “It’s mine!”).
target_language_example: Ce livre est à moi, pas à toi.
native_language_example: That book is mine, not yours.

additional_notes: Used to show ownership/possession with être + à + stressed pronoun: « C’est à moi / à toi / à lui / à elle / à nous / à vous / à eux / à elles ». With plural: « sont à toi ». For formal or plural “you,” use « est à vous ».
target_language_example: Ce livre est à toi.
native_language_example: This book is yours.

meaning: "and it's / and that's" (used to introduce or emphasize what comes next).
additional_notes: Made of et (“and”) + c’est (“it is/that is”). Often used to link to a conclusion, explanation, or the key point in a sentence: « Et c’est ce que… », « Et c’est comme ça que… », « Et c’est à cause de… ». In speech it can add emphasis or a slightly insistent tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Et c’est pour ça que je pars.
native_language_example: And that’s why I’m leaving.

meaning: and there is / and there are; and also (there’s…).
additional_notes: Used to add another thing to a list, description, or situation: “and there’s…” / “and then there’s…”. It can introduce an extra example (“Et il y a ça aussi.”), a person/thing (“Et il y a moi…”), or a point (“Et il y a pire.” = “and it can be worse / and there’s worse”). The verb is always singular (il y a) even when referring to plural things.
target_language_example: On a du pain, du fromage, et il y a des fruits aussi.
native_language_example: We have bread, cheese, and there’s fruit too.

meaning: "and I" (in the past), introducing a reflexive verb in the passé composé.
additional_notes: Used to link two past actions with "et" (and). "Je me suis" is the passé composé form used with many reflexive verbs (verbs with "se"), e.g. "je me suis habillé(e)" (I got dressed), "je me suis séché(e)" (I dried myself), "je me suis foulé..." (I sprained...). The past participle may agree with the subject in some cases (e.g. "je me suis retrouvé(e)").
target_language_example: Je suis rentré chez moi et je me suis couché tôt.
native_language_example: I came home and went to bed early.

meaning: "and I (to you)" / "and I will (to you)" (introduces what I do/say to you).
additional_notes: Used to link to the next action: « et » = “and”, « je » = “I”, « te » = “to you” (informal singular object pronoun). It’s very common before a verb: « et je te promets… » (and I promise you…), « et je te rendrai… » (and I’ll make you…). With threats it often sounds like “and I’ll … you”. For formal “you,” use « et je vous … ».
target_language_example: D’accord, et je te rappelle ce soir.
native_language_example: Okay, and I’ll call you back tonight.

meaning: “and the” (plural); also “and what about the …?” in questions.
additional_notes: Most often it simply links two plural noun phrases: « X et les Y ». At the start of a question (« Et les … ? »), it can mean “What about …?” or “And the …?” (bringing up something not yet answered). « les » is the plural “the.”
target_language_example: Et les billets, tu les as achetés ?
native_language_example: And the tickets—did you buy them?

meaning: “and me” / “and I” (adding yourself to a subject or object).
additional_notes: Used to include yourself with someone else: “X et moi …” = “X and I …” as the subject (often followed by a plural verb: « Mon frère et moi avons… »). It can also appear in object-like phrases such as « ma famille et moi » (“my family and me”). In formal French, « et moi » is preferred over « et je » after a noun/pronoun.
target_language_example: Paul et moi, nous habitons à Lyon.
native_language_example: Paul and I live in Lyon.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize yourself, often to contrast with someone else or to complain/protest: “And me—what am I supposed to do?” It’s common in spoken French, and the repetition (moi + je) adds emphasis.
target_language_example: Et moi, je fais comment pour rentrer chez moi ?
native_language_example: And me—how am I supposed to get home?

meaning: “and I, we…” (spoken way to say “X and I…” as the subject).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French: after a subject like “Tom et moi”, speakers often add “on” (meaning “we”) before the verb: “Tom et moi, on + verbe”. It emphasizes the group and sounds natural in conversation, but in more formal writing you’d usually say “Tom et moi, nous + verbe” (or simply “Tom et moi + verbe” without repeating the subject).
target_language_example: Ma sœur et moi, on part à huit heures.
native_language_example: My sister and I are leaving at eight o’clock.

meaning: 'and I, we’re…' (meaning 'X and I are…' in casual speech).
additional_notes: Common spoken pattern with left-dislocation for emphasis: “X et moi, on…” = “X and I, we…”. Here “on” is used instead of “nous” and the verb is in 3rd person singular (on est). In more formal/written French you’d usually say “X et moi, nous sommes…”.
target_language_example: Ma sœur et moi, on est fatigués ce soir.
native_language_example: My sister and I are tired tonight.

additional_notes: Used to bring the focus back to yourself—often to complain, defend yourself, or ask what you should do next. It’s followed by a full question (e.g., "Et moi, qu’est-ce que je peux faire ?"). Similar in tone to "What about me?" or "And what am I supposed to do?".
target_language_example: Et moi, qu’est-ce que je suis censé faire maintenant ?
native_language_example: And what am I supposed to do now?

meaning: “and I have” (as part of “X et moi avons…” = “X and I have…”).
additional_notes: Used in a compound subject with another person/name: “Tom et moi avons…” means “Tom and I have…”. French uses the stressed pronoun “moi” (not “je”) after “et”. The verb is plural (avons) because the subject is two people. Often you’ll see the full pattern: “Lui/Elle/Tom/Mes amis et moi avons …”.
target_language_example: Ma sœur et moi avons réservé une table.
native_language_example: My sister and I booked a table.

meaning: “and I are” (used after a name/noun: “X and I are …”).
additional_notes: This appears in patterns like “Tom et moi sommes …” to make a subject with two people. French uses **moi** (not *je*) after **et**: “Paul et moi…”. The verb is **sommes** (1st person plural, “we are”), and adjectives/past participles agree in plural (e.g., “ma femme et moi sommes **allées** …” if the group is feminine/mixed with a feminine speaker).
target_language_example: Mes parents et moi sommes contents de te voir.
native_language_example: My parents and I are happy to see you.

meaning: “and I went” (past tense, with a male or mixed-gender “we”).
additional_notes: Used when the subject is “X et moi” (= “X and I”), so the verb is conjugated like **nous**: **nous sommes allés** (passé composé of *aller* uses **être**). **Allés** agrees with the group: use **allées** if the group is all female (e.g., *Ma sœur et moi sommes allées...*). Often you’ll see the full pattern: **[Name/person] et moi sommes allés + place/verb**.
target_language_example: Mes amis et moi sommes allés au restaurant après le travail.
native_language_example: My friends and I went to the restaurant after work.

et moi sommes dans la même classe

target_language_multi_word_term: et moi sommes dans la même classe
meaning: “and I are in the same class.”
additional_notes: Used after naming another person (e.g., « Marie et moi… ») to say you and that person are in the same class. « et moi » (“and me/I”) is part of the subject, so the verb is plural: « sommes » (we are).
target_language_example: Paul et moi sommes dans la même classe.
native_language_example: Paul and I are in the same class.

et moi sommes du même âge

target_language_multi_word_term: et moi sommes du même âge
additional_notes: Used to say you and someone else have the same age. Because the subject is “X et moi” (“X and I”), the verb is in the 1st person plural: *nous sommes* → *sommes*. The person comes before *et moi* (e.g., *Elle et moi…*, *Toi et moi…*).
target_language_example: Mon frère et moi sommes du même âge.
native_language_example: My brother and I are the same age.

additional_notes: Used when you list yourself with someone else as the subject (X et moi). Even though it uses “moi,” the meaning is “X and I.” The verb is in the plural: “étions” is the imperfect (past) form of être for “nous,” often used for background description in the past.
target_language_example: Ma sœur et moi étions fatigués après le voyage.
native_language_example: My sister and I were tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Often used to continue a story or add an extra point. It can introduce the next event in time (“and then…”) or add a new element (“and also / besides”). In speech it can work like a soft transition (“and then, anyway…”).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un café, et puis je rentre à la maison.
native_language_example: I’m going to have a coffee, and then I’m going home.

meaning: "So/and what…?" (used to introduce a follow-up question).
additional_notes:
Often used at the start of a question to continue a conversation or ask for the next detail, similar to “So what did…?” / “And what does…?”. It’s usually followed by:
- **qu’est-ce que + subject + verb**: *Et qu’est-ce que tu fais ici ?* (“So what are you doing here?”)
- **qu’est-ce qui + verb**: *Et qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?* (“So what happened?”)
It’s neutral in tone; not slang.
target_language_example: Et qu'est-ce que tu veux dire par là ?
native_language_example: So what do you mean by that?

additional_notes: Used in conversation to ask for the next detail: “And/so what did she say/do/want…?” It’s the start of the longer structure “Et qu’est-ce que + subject + verb… ?”. In writing you may also see the full form “et qu’est-ce que …”. You can omit “et” if you’re not continuing a story: “Qu’est-ce qu’elle a dit ?”.
target_language_example: Et qu'est-ce qu'il a répondu ?
native_language_example: So what did he reply?

additional_notes: Used to ask a follow-up question, often after someone has said something: “And/so what does he…?”, “And/so what happens…?”, “And/so what did he say…?” The **il** is often a “dummy” subject (especially in **qu’est-ce qu’il se passe ?** = “what’s happening?”) and doesn’t always refer to a specific “he.” In casual speech you may hear **et qu’est-ce qu’y…**.
target_language_example: Et qu'est-ce qu'il veut exactement ?
native_language_example: So what exactly does he want?

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a question to continue the conversation or react to what was just said, often to ask for more information: « Et qu’est-ce que tu as vu ? » (“And what did you see?”). Depending on tone, it can sound neutral, surprised, or a bit impatient (like “So what are you going to do?”).
target_language_example: D'accord, et qu'est-ce que tu veux faire maintenant ?
native_language_example: Okay, so what do you want to do now?

meaning: "And what did that do / lead to / bring?" (asking about the result or point).
additional_notes:
Used to start a follow-up question, often after someone mentions an action or event. The exact meaning depends on the verb that follows: 
- « Et qu'est-ce que ça a donné ? » = What was the outcome?
- « Et qu'est-ce que ça m'apporte ? » = What’s in it for me?/What do I get out of it?
- « Et qu'est-ce que ça peut faire ? » = What difference does it make?/So what?
Common in spoken French; it can sound skeptical or challenging depending on tone.
target_language_example: Tu as tout essayé ? Et qu'est-ce que ça a changé ?
native_language_example: You tried everything? And what did that change?

additional_notes: An informal, often humorous command used to hurry people up or demand immediate action (similar to “chop-chop!”). Often said on its own as an impatient prompt, or after naming what you want done (e.g., an order, a task, bringing food). Not literally about jumping; it’s an idiomatic way to say “right now!”
target_language_example: Allez, on se dépêche : et que ça saute !
native_language_example: Come on, hurry up—get moving!

meaning: "what if he/it…?" (introduces a hypothetical idea or worry).
additional_notes: Used to ask about a possibility, make a suggestion, or express concern. It’s often followed by a verb in the imperfect to imagine a scenario: « Et s’il venait ? » (“What if he came?”). Literally it’s “and if he…”, but in English it’s usually translated as “what if…”.
target_language_example: Et s'il pleuvait demain ?
native_language_example: What if it rained tomorrow?

meaning: "What if he/it doesn’t…?" / "What if there isn’t/aren’t…?"
additional_notes: Used to introduce a worried or hypothetical question. It’s built from **et si** (“what if”) + **il** (“he/it”) + **n’y… pas** (negation with **y**, referring to a place/there). The verb changes depending on what follows: *Et s’il n’y arrive pas ?* (doesn’t manage), *Et s’il n’y en a pas ?* (there aren’t any), *Et s’il n’y est pas ?* (isn’t there).
target_language_example: Et s'il n'y a plus de batterie ?
native_language_example: What if there’s no battery left?

meaning: “and what if he doesn’t…?” / “and if he doesn’t…?”
additional_notes: Used to raise a concern or possibility about a negative outcome. It introduces a conditional question: et + si (“and if”) + il (“he”) → s’il, followed by the negative ne (usually with pas/jamais/plus, etc.): “Et s’il ne vient pas ?” = “What if he doesn’t come?”
target_language_example: Et s'il ne répond pas ?
native_language_example: What if he doesn’t answer?

additional_notes: Used to add “his/her friends” as an extra subject along with someone already mentioned (e.g., “Elle et ses amis…” = “She and her friends…”). Note: “ses” is a possessive meaning “his/her/their” and is used here because “amis” is plural; the owner is understood from context.
target_language_example: Paul et ses amis vont au cinéma ce soir.
native_language_example: Paul and his friends are going to the movies tonight.

meaning: 'what if it were…?' (introduces a hypothetical possibility).
additional_notes: Used to imagine an alternative or to question a situation: “What if that wasn’t the case?”, “What if it was true?”, etc. Very often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (vrai, trop tard, toi, lui). In speech it can sound like a suggestion, doubt, or worry. Uses the imperfect (c'était) for “were/was” in hypothetical questions.
target_language_example: Et si c'était une erreur ?
native_language_example: What if it were a mistake?

meaning: "What if I..." (to suggest or imagine a possibility).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical idea, proposal, or concern about what might happen if you do something. Often followed by a verb in the imperfect or present, depending on context: « Et si je courais ? » (proposal) / « Et si je refuse ? » (worry/question).
target_language_example: Et si je prenais le train au lieu de conduire ?
native_language_example: What if I took the train instead of driving?

additional_notes: Used to propose an idea or option, often gently or spontaneously. It’s usually followed by the imperfect tense in French (e.g., « Et si on partait ? ») even though it refers to a possible action now or soon.
target_language_example: Et si on allait boire un café ?
native_language_example: What if we went to get a coffee?

meaning: “and you?” (asking the question back, to one person informally).
additional_notes: Used after you answer or comment, to ask the other person the same thing: « Je vais bien, et toi ? » It uses « toi » (singular informal “you”), so it’s for someone you address with « tu ». For a formal/plural version, say « et vous ? ». In other contexts, « et toi » can also simply mean “and you” (adding the person to a statement).
target_language_example: Moi, ça va bien—et toi ?
native_language_example: I’m doing well—and you?

additional_notes: Used in conversation to turn the question back to the other person. "Et toi" means "and you" (informal singular), and "qu'est-ce que" introduces a question like "what did you do / what do you have / what are you becoming (how’s it going) / what are you going to do / what do you want". Often followed by "tu" and a verb; in casual speech you may hear "t'as" instead of "tu as".
target_language_example: J'ai fini tôt. Et toi, qu'est-ce que tu fais ce soir ?
native_language_example: I finished early. And you, what are you doing tonight?

meaning: "and you?" / "what about you?" (often to turn the question back to someone).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to shift focus to the other person, often after you’ve been talking about someone else or after answering a question. "Et toi" is very common; adding "tu" sets up the verb that follows and can sound a bit more insistent or challenging depending on tone (e.g., "Et toi, tu m'aimes ?").
target_language_example: Moi, j’ai fini. Et toi, tu as déjà commencé ?
native_language_example: I’m done. And you, have you started already?

additional_notes: Used to add that something involves all people in a group. It can appear in the middle of a sentence, or at the beginning ("Et tout le monde…") to emphasize what happens to everyone or what everyone knows/does.
target_language_example: On part à 8 h, et tout le monde doit être à l'heure.
native_language_example: We’re leaving at 8, and everyone has to be on time.

additional_notes: Used to add information about the person you’re speaking to, often after another clause: "…, et tu es …". It can also start a question meaning "And are you…?". "Tu es" is the singular informal "you are" (to one person you address as "tu").
target_language_example: Tu dis que tu ne peux pas venir, et tu es sûr(e) ?
native_language_example: You say you can’t come—are you sure?

additional_notes: Used as an instruction in the imperative (vous form), often by security staff or police during a check. It’s frequently paired with other commands like « Enlevez/Retirez/Ôtez votre manteau… ». Singular informal would be « et vide tes poches »; polite singular is still « videz vos poches ».
target_language_example: Avant de passer au contrôle de sécurité, enlevez votre ceinture et videz vos poches.
native_language_example: Before going through security, take off your belt and empty your pockets.

additional_notes: Used with the verb « avoir » (to have): « j’ai eu de la chance » = “I was lucky.” « eu » is the past participle, so it’s most often seen in the past tense (passé composé): « avoir eu de la chance ». You can add details with « avec… », « pour… », etc.: « On a eu de la chance avec lui » = “We were lucky with him / He worked out well for us.”
target_language_example: On a eu de la chance : il n’y avait pas de bouchons.
native_language_example: We were lucky: there was no traffic.

additional_notes: Used in the passé composé with avoir: j’ai eu / tu as eu / il a eu / nous avons eu / etc. + des + plural noun. It often translates as “had” or sometimes “got/experienced” depending on the noun (e.g., avoir des vertiges = to feel dizzy). Note: “eu” doesn’t agree with the subject (it stays eu) unless there’s a preceding direct object (advanced).
target_language_example: J’ai eu des problèmes avec ma voiture.
native_language_example: I had some problems with my car.

additional_notes: Used with « avoir » to talk about an event occurring: « a eu lieu » (it took place), « n’a pas eu lieu » (it didn’t happen). Often found in formal or neutral contexts (events, meetings, incidents). In questions: « Quand cela a-t-il eu lieu ? » = “When did that happen?”
target_language_example: La réunion a eu lieu hier soir.
native_language_example: The meeting took place last night.

additional_notes: Used with « avoir » in the past (passé composé): « j’ai eu un… / il a eu un… ». In questions with « déjà », it often means “have you ever had…?”. The noun after « un » tells what was had or experienced (e.g., « un animal », « un malaise »).
target_language_example: J’ai eu un problème avec ma carte.
native_language_example: I had a problem with my card.

additional_notes: Used with the verb « avoir » (to have) to talk about an accident in the past: « j’ai eu un accident » (I had an accident), « tu as eu un accident ? » (Did you have an accident?). It can refer to a car accident or another kind of accident; add « grave » to mean a serious accident (« un accident grave »).
target_language_example: Ça va ? J’ai appris que tu as eu un accident.
native_language_example: Are you okay? I heard you had an accident.

additional_notes: This is the past participle phrase used with the verb "avoir" in the passé composé: "avoir un accident de voiture" = "to have a car accident." It agrees with the subject only through the auxiliary (j'ai eu, elle a eu, nous avons eu, etc.). You can also say "un accident" or "un accident de la route" depending on context.
target_language_example: Heureusement, elle a eu un accident de voiture sans gravité.
native_language_example: Luckily, she had a minor car accident.

additional_notes: Used in the passé composé: *avoir* → *j’ai / tu as / il a…* + *eu* + a noun with an article. *Eu* does not change for gender/number here (it stays *eu*). You’ll see it before many feminine nouns: *eu une idée, eu une amende, eu une relation*, etc.
target_language_example: J’ai eu une bonne nouvelle ce matin.
native_language_example: I had some good news this morning.

additional_notes: Used right before a relative pronoun like **que** or **qui**: **exactement ce que…** = “exactly what…”, **exactement ce qui…** = “exactly what… (as the subject)”. Common for emphasizing that something is the precise thing needed or the precise action to do: **J’ai exactement ce qu’il faut** (“I have exactly what’s needed”), **Faites exactement ce que je vous dis** (“Do exactly what I tell you”).
target_language_example: C’est exactement ce que je cherchais.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I was looking for.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is precise or matches perfectly. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb): « exactement ce que je dois faire », « exactement ce que je pensais ». It can also be used as a short reply/fragment to mean “exactly what I thought/wanted.”
target_language_example: Je vais te dire exactement ce que tu dois faire.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you exactly what you have to do.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or state the precise details of an event. Often follows verbs like "savoir" (to know) or "dire" (to say/tell): "Je sais exactement ce qui s'est passé" / "Dis-moi exactement ce qui s'est passé." Here, "ce qui" means “what (that)” and "s'est passé" is the past tense of "se passer" (“to happen,” “to take place”).
target_language_example: Explique-moi exactement ce qui s'est passé hier soir.
native_language_example: Explain to me exactly what happened last night.

meaning: "Excuse me, I…" (polite way to start an apology or make a request).
additional_notes: Used to politely get someone’s attention before explaining what you need or why you’re interrupting/leaving. "Excusez-moi" is the formal/polite form (to a stranger, in public, or in customer service). It’s often followed by "je + verb" (je dois…, je suis…, je vous ai…).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je dois y aller.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have to go.

meaning: “Excuse me, could you…?” (polite way to ask someone to do something).
additional_notes: Very formal/polite: use it to get someone’s attention and make a request (asking for directions, help, information, or asking someone to repeat). "Excusez-moi" is the polite “excuse me,” and "pourriez-vous" is the conditional form of "pouvoir" (“could you”). Often followed by an infinitive (pourriez-vous répéter) or by "me dire" / "me montrer".
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, pourriez-vous m’aider à trouver cette adresse ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you help me find this address?

additional_notes: This is the inverted (more formal) question form of « il existe » (“there is/there exists”). It’s used to ask whether something exists or is available: « Existe-t-il une solution ? » = “Is there a solution?” You’ll often see it followed by a noun phrase (un moyen, une option, une version…).
target_language_example: Existe-t-il une autre façon de faire ?
native_language_example: Is there another way to do it?

additional_notes: Used as a noun phrase in expressions like « la face cachée de X » (the side you can’t see). With cards or objects, « (mettre/poser) … face cachée » means placing it with the front/visible side against the surface (face down). You may also see it set off by commas: « la carte, face cachée, sur la table ».
target_language_example: Il a retourné la feuille pour montrer sa face cachée.
native_language_example: He flipped the sheet over to show its hidden side.

additional_notes: Used to describe that something is easy to do: facile à + infinitive (facile à utiliser, facile à comprendre). It also appears in the set phrase “Facile à dire” (“Easier said than done”). Feminine: facile; plural: faciles.
target_language_example: Ce logiciel est facile à apprendre.
native_language_example: This software is easy to learn.

meaning: to do what (…); to do the thing that (…).
additional_notes: Used before a clause with a verb to mean “do what … does/said/wants,” etc. Often followed by a subject + verb: « faire ce que je veux » (do what I want), « faire ce que Mary dit » (do what Mary says). In commands/polite requests, it can sound like “please do what we asked.”
target_language_example: Je vais faire ce que tu m’as dit.
native_language_example: I’m going to do what you told me.

meaning: to do whatever you want (to do).
additional_notes: Uses the formal/plural "vous". Often follows verbs like "pouvoir" (can) or "avoir le droit de" (have the right to) to give permission or freedom of choice. "Ce que" here means "what/that which" (the thing that you want).
target_language_example: Ici, vous pouvez faire ce que vous voulez.
native_language_example: Here, you can do whatever you want.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase used to refer to a specific action (“this”). It often follows another verb (e.g., devoir, pouvoir, laisser, forcer). In the causative construction, it can appear as “faire + [person] + faire ceci” = “to make/have someone do this.”
target_language_example: Tu peux faire ceci maintenant ?
native_language_example: Can you do this now?

meaning: to do that; to do it.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to an action already mentioned or understood from context. "Cela" is a neutral/standard way to say "that" (often interchangeable with "ça" in speech: "faire ça"). Often appears after modal verbs like "pouvoir", "devoir", "vouloir" (e.g., "devoir faire cela" = "have to do that").
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas faire cela aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I can’t do that today.

additional_notes: Used to say you trust a person or can rely on them. It’s often followed by a person or pronoun: faire confiance à Tom / faire confiance à quelqu’un / faire confiance à lui/elle. The negative is common: ne faire confiance à personne = to trust nobody.
target_language_example: Je te fais confiance, mais sois prudent.
native_language_example: I trust you, but be careful.

meaning: to get a haircut; to have your hair cut.
additional_notes: Uses the pattern (se) faire + infinitive to mean “have something done (by someone else).” Most often you’ll hear it reflexively: « Je dois me faire couper les cheveux » (“I need to get my hair cut”). You can add details like style/length: « courts », « juste les pointes », etc.
target_language_example: Je vais me faire couper les cheveux demain matin.
native_language_example: I’m going to get my hair cut tomorrow morning.

meaning: to do something else; what else can/should I do?
additional_notes: Used mostly in questions with que/qu’est-ce que/qu’aurais-je… to ask about another option: « Que faire d’autre ? » = “What else can I do?” Here « d’autre » means “else/other (thing)”. Very close in meaning to « faire autre chose » (often more common).
target_language_example: On a fini plus tôt—tu veux faire quelque chose d’autre ?
native_language_example: We finished early—do you want to do something else?

additional_notes: Often used with an indirect object pronoun: « faire du mal à quelqu’un » = to hurt someone / to harm someone (e.g., « Je ne vais pas te faire de mal. »). It also appears in fixed reassuring phrases like « Ça ne peut pas faire de mal » / « Ça ne fait pas de mal » meaning “It can’t hurt” (often: it won’t do any harm to try). In « faire de mal » without « du », you’ll commonly see it in negative or general statements (e.g., « ne peut (pas) faire de mal »).
target_language_example: Ne lui fais pas de mal, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Don’t hurt him, please.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to talk about doing/making things in general: faire des tests (do tests), faire des efforts (make efforts), faire des fautes (make mistakes), faire des compromis (make compromises). With an adjective before the noun, you often use de instead of des: faire de grands efforts. In the negative, des often becomes de: ne pas faire de fautes.
target_language_example: On doit faire des efforts pour réduire les déchets.
native_language_example: We have to make efforts to reduce waste.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for buying what you need, especially food and household items. Often used with "aller" in the near future: "Je vais faire des courses." You can add details like where or what: "faire des courses au supermarché", "faire des courses pour la fête".
target_language_example: Je vais faire des courses après le travail.
native_language_example: I'm going to do the grocery shopping after work.

additional_notes: A common, neutral way to say you’re going shopping, especially for everyday purchases (clothes, groceries, small items). Often used with verbs of going: « aller faire des emplettes », « partir faire des emplettes ».
target_language_example: Je vais faire des emplettes cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I'm going shopping this afternoon.

meaning: 'to do' / 'to go (and) do' an activity (often a sport or leisure activity).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (du = de + le) to mean you do that activity as a general thing: faire du sport, faire du ski, faire du camping, faire du lèche-vitrines. For feminine nouns, you typically use faire de la (faire de la natation), and for plural nouns faire des (faire des courses). It can also appear in ongoing-action structures like être en train de faire du…
target_language_example: On va faire du vélo après le travail.
native_language_example: We’re going to go cycling after work.

additional_notes: Common, everyday way to talk about shopping as an activity. You can say "faire du shopping" in general, or specify what you’re buying: "faire du shopping pour des vêtements" (to shop for clothes). Very close to English usage, since "shopping" is borrowed in French.
target_language_example: On va faire du shopping cet après-midi ?
native_language_example: Are we going shopping this afternoon?

meaning: to ride a bike; to go cycling.
additional_notes: Used with "faire" + "du" + a sport/leisure activity. It often means the ability to ride a bike ("savoir faire du vélo") or asking if someone can ride ("Savez-vous faire du vélo ?").
target_language_example: Le week-end, on fait du vélo dans le parc.
native_language_example: On weekends, we go cycling in the park.

meaning: to make sure that; to ensure that; to arrange for (something to happen).
additional_notes: Used when you take action to cause a result. Very often followed by **que + subjunctive**: *Fais en sorte que tout se passe bien.* It can also mean “to manage to” in context: *On peut faire en sorte que ça marche* (“We can make it work”). Slightly formal but common.
target_language_example: Je vais faire en sorte que tu reçoives les informations à temps.
native_language_example: I’ll make sure you receive the information on time.

meaning: Very vulgar: “to tell someone to fuck off / go fuck themselves.”
additional_notes: Most often used as **(aller) se faire foutre** (“go get fucked”), an extremely insulting way to dismiss someone. Common in the imperative (**Va te faire foutre !** / plural **Allez vous faire foutre !**) or with **qu’…** to express “let them go fuck themselves” (**Qu’ils aillent se faire foutre !**). Avoid in polite situations; it’s stronger than *va-t’en* or even *va te faire voir*.
target_language_example: Si ça ne te plaît pas, va te faire foutre.
native_language_example: If you don’t like it, fuck off.

meaning: to tell the difference between; to distinguish between.
additional_notes: Used when comparing two (or more) things and deciding which is which. Very common with people, similar-looking objects, or abstract ideas (e.g., le bien et le mal). Often used with pouvoir/savoir: « Je ne peux pas / je ne sais pas faire la différence entre… ».
target_language_example: Je n’arrive pas à faire la différence entre ces deux couleurs.
native_language_example: I can’t tell the difference between these two colors.

additional_notes: Used to encourage someone (sometimes teasingly or reproachfully) to improve their effort or performance. Commonly said with "tu peux" (“you can”) or as an imperative: "Fais mieux que ça !"
target_language_example: Je sais que tu es fatigué, mais tu peux faire mieux que ça.
native_language_example: I know you’re tired, but you can do better than that.

meaning: to do something; to take action.
additional_notes: Very common and flexible. With "faire", French often uses one verb where English might choose "do" or "make" depending on context. Often used to ask someone to act (e.g., "Tu peux faire quelque chose ?" = "Can you do something about it?").
target_language_example: On doit faire quelque chose pour l'aider.
native_language_example: We have to do something to help him.

additional_notes: Used when “quelque chose” is followed by an adjective describing it: faire quelque chose de bien/chouette/intéressant (“do something good/cool/interesting”). The “de” links “something” to the adjective.
target_language_example: On pourrait faire quelque chose d'utile ce week-end.
native_language_example: We could do something useful this weekend.

meaning: to do something for (someone/something); to take action to help.
additional_notes: Used when you want to help someone or improve a situation: faire quelque chose pour Tom (do something for Tom), faire quelque chose pour mon bras (do something about my arm). Often appears in offers of help: Puis-je faire quelque chose pour vous aider ? = “Can I do anything to help you?”
target_language_example: Je vais faire quelque chose pour régler ce problème.
native_language_example: I’m going to do something to fix this problem.

additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to do you a favor/help you. The verb "faire" changes with the subject and tense (peux-tu faire…, tu dois faire…, tu vas faire…, voudriez-vous faire…). You can swap "moi" for other people: "pour toi" (for you), "pour lui/elle" (for him/her), "pour nous" (for us).
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu pourrais faire quelque chose pour moi, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you do something for me, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask what action to take. Often comes at the end of a question in spoken French: « Je dois faire quoi ? » (= « Qu’est-ce que je dois faire ? »). Common with « avec ça » (what to do with this), « maintenant » (now), or « être censé » (to be supposed to).
target_language_example: On est censés faire quoi, maintenant ?
native_language_example: What are we supposed to do now?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is no action possible or no action taken, especially in negative contexts (e.g., with ne…pas/jamais/personne/rien) or after expressions like trop…pour: « Ils avaient trop peur pour faire quoi que ce soit. » It has a strong sense of “anything whatsoever.”
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas faire quoi que ce soit sans ton aide.
native_language_example: I can’t do anything without your help.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone (informal singular “tu”) to complete their schoolwork. The verb “faire” (to do/make) + “tes devoirs” (your homework). In commands you’ll often see “Fais tes devoirs !” (Do your homework!). It can also appear in the causative structure “faire faire” (have someone else do it): “Fais faire tes devoirs par ta mère !” = “Have your mom do your homework!”
target_language_example: Tu peux sortir après avoir fait tes devoirs.
native_language_example: You can go out after doing your homework.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to express performing an action or producing something: faire un choix (make a choice), faire un détour (take/make a detour), faire un boulot (do a job). In many cases English uses different verbs (make/take/do), but French often uses faire.
target_language_example: On peut faire un arrêt ici ?
native_language_example: Can we make a stop here?

meaning: to go for a drive; to take a drive (around).
additional_notes: Used for driving around for pleasure or to get out for a bit, not for a specific destination. Often used with "aller" (aller faire un tour en voiture) to suggest an outing, including as a proposal/question: "Si on allait… ?".
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on peut faire un tour en voiture pour se détendre.
native_language_example: After dinner, we can go for a drive to relax.

meaning: to make/do a (something) (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Common pattern: faire + un/une + noun to express an action in French. In your examples: faire une offre (make an offer), faire une remise (give a discount), faire une remarque (make a comment/remark), faire une bêtise (do something stupid / make a big mistake). The exact meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Je peux vous faire une suggestion.
native_language_example: I can make you a suggestion.

meaning: to do such a thing (often: something shocking/unacceptable).
additional_notes: Used when reacting with surprise, disapproval, or disbelief about an action. Common in questions like « Comment as-tu pu… ? » (How could you…?) and « Qui a pu… ? » (Who could have…?). « Une chose pareille » means “such a thing / something like that.”
target_language_example: Je n'arrive pas à croire qu'il ait fait une chose pareille.
native_language_example: I can’t believe he did such a thing.

meaning: to take a break; to pause.
additional_notes: Used when you want to stop an activity for a short rest (work, studying, driving, etc.). Very common with verbs like vouloir (want), pouvoir (can), devoir (should/must), and avoir besoin de (need).
target_language_example: On peut faire une pause de cinq minutes ?
native_language_example: Can we take a five-minute break?

meaning: to go for a walk; to take a stroll.
additional_notes: Used for a leisure walk (often outside). Very common with "aller" (aller faire une promenade = go for a walk). You can add where you’ll walk with "dans" or "le long de" (e.g., dans la campagne, le long du fleuve).
target_language_example: Après le dîner, on va faire une promenade dans le parc.
native_language_example: After dinner, we're going to go for a walk in the park.

additional_notes: Used to react to or question an action seen as surprising, shocking, or hard to understand. "Une telle" means "such a" (often with emphasis). You can swap in other nouns: "faire une telle erreur" (make such a mistake).
target_language_example: Je n’arrive pas à croire qu’il ait fait une telle chose.
native_language_example: I can’t believe he did such a thing.

additional_notes: Common, everyday way to refer back to an action already mentioned or understood from context. It can take different shades of meaning depending on context (do it, do this/that, handle that). Often used with timing or manner: « faire ça maintenant » (do that now), « faire ça bien » (do it properly), « faire ça tout de suite » (do it right away).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas faire ça aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I can’t do that today.

additional_notes: Imperative of faire (“to do/make”) + direct object pronoun le (“it”). Used to tell one person you address as tu to do something. With a hyphen in the imperative: Fais-le ! (You can also add adverbs: Fais-le correctement. Fais-le tout simplement.)
target_language_example: Tu hésites ? Fais-le maintenant.
native_language_example: Are you hesitating? Do it now.

additional_notes: Imperative of faire ("to do/make") + indirect object pronoun moi ("to me"). Common in requests: fais-moi savoir ("let me know"), fais-moi connaître ("tell me/let me know"), fais-moi une faveur ("do me a favor"), fais-moi une offre ("make me an offer"). Often said as Fais-moi... or with politeness: S'il te plaît / je te prie.
target_language_example: Fais-moi savoir quand tu arrives.
native_language_example: Let me know when you arrive.

additional_notes: An informal/neutral command using the tu form: fais (from faire) + moi (me). Used to reassure someone or ask them to rely on you. For a more formal/polite version, say: « Faites-moi confiance. ». Note: « confiance » looks like English “confidence,” but here it usually means “trust.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, fais-moi confiance.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, trust me.

meaning: "do you...?" / "are you doing...?" (question form of *faire* with *tu*).
additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of *tu fais* (“you do/you’re doing”). It’s used in more formal or written questions: *Que fais-tu ?* (“What are you doing?”). In everyday speech, French often uses *Tu fais quoi ?* or *Qu’est-ce que tu fais ?* instead. It can also mean “do you…?” in expressions like *faire confiance* (“to trust”): *Me fais-tu confiance ?* (“Do you trust me?”).
target_language_example: Pourquoi fais-tu ça ?
native_language_example: Why are you doing that?

additional_notes: Informal singular imperative of « faire attention ». Used to warn someone or tell them to be cautious; can stand alone (“Fais attention !”) or be followed by « en + -ant » (Fais attention en traversant…), « où » (Fais attention où…), or a situation (sur la route, la prochaine fois).
target_language_example: Fais attention, c’est glissant ici.
native_language_example: Be careful, it’s slippery here.

additional_notes: Imperative ("you" singular) of *faire attention à*. Used to warn someone or tell them to be cautious. Followed by (1) a noun/pronoun: *Fais attention à lui*, (2) *ce que* + clause: *Fais attention à ce que tu fais*, or (3) *à* + infinitive, often negative: *Fais attention à ne pas te couper*.
target_language_example: Fais attention à la marche en descendant.
native_language_example: Watch your step when going down.

additional_notes: Used to give an instruction in the tu form (imperative of faire). It’s typically followed by a clause like "fais ce que je te dis" (do what I tell you) or "fais ce que tu veux" (do what you want). For vous, use "faites ce que".
target_language_example: Fais ce que tu veux, mais sois prudent.
native_language_example: Do what you want, but be careful.

fais ce que je te dis

target_language_multi_word_term: fais ce que je te dis
additional_notes: A firm command using the imperative of **faire** (“fais” = “do”). **ce que** means “what/that which,” and **je te dis** means “I’m telling you” (literally “I tell you”). Often used when someone wants immediate obedience; tone can be strict or angry depending on context.
target_language_example: Calme-toi et fais ce que je te dis.
native_language_example: Calm down and do what I tell you.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to do whatever they think is right/necessary, followed by another verb: « Fais ce que tu dois faire / ce que tu estimes juste / ce que tu juges bon. » In the past tense, it’s « Tu as fait ce que tu devais faire » (not *fais*).
target_language_example: Fais ce que tu peux, et on verra demain.
native_language_example: Do what you can, and we’ll see tomorrow.

additional_notes: Imperative of *faire* + *ce que tu veux* (“what you want”). Used to give permission (“go ahead”) or to show indifference/resignation (“whatever, do as you like”). Often followed by an object: *Fais ce que tu veux de moi* (“Do what you want with me”) or with the pronoun *en* referring to “it/that”: *Tu en fais ce que tu veux* (“You can do whatever you want with it”).
target_language_example: J’ai fini mon travail : fais ce que tu veux maintenant.
native_language_example: I’m done with my work: do what you want now.

additional_notes: Informal imperative of « faire gaffe ». Used to warn someone or tell them to pay attention (to danger, a mistake, or how they speak). Often followed by « à + noun » (Fais gaffe à la marche !).
target_language_example: Fais gaffe en traversant la rue !
native_language_example: Watch out when crossing the street!

meaning: “don’t …” (informal negative command; short for “ne fais pas”).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: the “ne” is dropped in negative commands ("Fais pas ça" = "Ne fais pas ça"). You often see it in fixed expressions like "(Ne) t’en fais pas" / "T’en fais pas" meaning “Don’t worry.”
target_language_example: Fais pas ça, c’est dangereux.
native_language_example: Don’t do that, it’s dangerous.

additional_notes: Informal spoken negative imperative of *faire* (“to do/make”). In careful/written French you usually say **ne fais pas ça**; in speech, **ne** is often dropped: **fais pas ça**. Often used to stop someone, protest, or beg (“Please, don’t do that”).
target_language_example: Fais pas ça, tu vas te blesser.
native_language_example: Don’t do that—you’re going to hurt yourself.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French as a shortened, informal question (often in: « Je fais quoi ? »). Used when you’re unsure what to do next or what someone expects you to do. More formal: « Qu’est-ce que je fais ? » or « Que dois-je faire ? »
target_language_example: Bon, j’ai fini le dossier… je fais quoi maintenant ?
native_language_example: Okay, I’ve finished the file… what do I do now?

meaning: “does he do / is he doing” (question form of *il fait*).
additional_notes: Used in questions with subject–verb inversion: *il fait* → *fait-il ?* It’s the verb *faire* (“to do/make”), so the meaning depends on context (doing something, making something, or “what is he doing?”). Written with a hyphen in inversion.
target_language_example: Pourquoi fait-il ça ?
native_language_example: Why is he doing that?

additional_notes: Used in the pattern « [subject] fait ce qu’ + pronoun + verb » to mean “does what (someone) …” or “does whatever (someone) …”. Very common with « veut »: « Il fait ce qu’il veut » = “He does what he wants.” The « qu’ » is just « que » shortened before a vowel (e.g., « qu’il », « qu’elle », « qu’on »).
target_language_example: Je fais ce qu'il faut pour finir à temps.
native_language_example: I do what it takes to finish on time.

meaning: (has/have) done what needed to be done; did the right thing.
additional_notes: Used to say someone took the necessary/proper action in a situation. Often implies responsibility or reassurance ("we did what we had to do"). Can be used on its own ("On a fait ce qu'il fallait") or followed by an infinitive for emphasis ("ce qu'il fallait faire").
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : on a fait ce qu'il fallait.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we did what needed to be done.

fait combien de temps que vous êtes

target_language_multi_word_term: fait combien de temps que vous êtes
meaning: "How long has it been since you…?" / "How long have you…?" (talking about time since an event).
additional_notes: Used in the common structure « Ça/Cela fait combien de temps que + subject + verb (often in the past) ». Here « vous êtes arrivé(e)(s) » is passé composé with être, so « arrivé » agrees with the person(s): arrivé (m. sg.), arrivée (f. sg.), arrivés (m./mixed pl.), arrivées (f. pl.). Often equivalent to « Depuis combien de temps… ? » in meaning.
target_language_example: Ça fait combien de temps que vous êtes ici ?
native_language_example: How long have you been here?

meaning: to get your hair cut (have someone cut your hair).
additional_notes: Uses the causative structure "se faire + infinitive" to mean you arrange for a service to be done to you. With haircuts it’s almost always "se faire couper les cheveux" (not *couper mes cheveux* in this context). Common in past tense: "Je me suis fait couper les cheveux" = “I got my hair cut.” You can add where/when: "chez le coiffeur" (at the hairdresser’s), "hier" (yesterday).
target_language_example: Je me suis fait couper les cheveux chez le coiffeur ce matin.
native_language_example: I got my hair cut at the hairdresser’s this morning.

additional_notes: This is the verb phrase **faire de son mieux** (“to do one’s best”) conjugated in the present tense: **il/elle fait de son mieux**. The possessive changes with the subject: **je fais de mon mieux**, **tu fais de ton mieux**, **nous faisons de notre mieux**, **vous faites de votre mieux**, **ils/elles font de leur mieux**. It’s often followed by **pour + infinitive** (e.g., *faire de son mieux pour aider*).
target_language_example: Je fais de mon mieux pour parler français.
native_language_example: I’m doing my best to speak French.

additional_notes: From the verb **faire** + **des** (= “some”). It’s used with plural nouns to talk about doing or making things in general: **faire des plans** (make plans), **faire des biscuits / des crêpes** (make cookies / crêpes), **faire des efforts** (make an effort), **faire des sacrifices** (make sacrifices), **faire des compliments** (give compliments). With **Il a fait des...**, it’s past (“he made/did some…”).
target_language_example: Elle fait des progrès en français.
native_language_example: She is making progress in French.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **faire des progrès** = “to make progress.” It’s commonly used with **en + subject/skill** (e.g., *faire des progrès en anglais*) or with an adjective like *rapides*, *remarquables*. Tense changes with the subject (e.g., *je fais*, *tu fais*, *il/elle fait*, *nous faisons*, *vous faites*, *ils/elles font*; past: *a fait*, *ont fait*).
target_language_example: Tu as fait des progrès en français depuis le début de l’année.
native_language_example: You’ve made progress in French since the beginning of the year.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *faire* + the partitive article *du* (="some") to talk about doing an activity, making/causing something, or having a common set expression. Examples: *faire du ski* (to go skiing), *faire du bruit* (to make noise), *se faire du souci* (to worry), *faire du mieux qu’on peut* (to do the best one can), *faire du bon boulot* (to do good work). The exact translation depends on the noun after *du*.
target_language_example: Je fais du sport trois fois par semaine.
native_language_example: I work out / do sports three times a week.

additional_notes: Used with a subject (often Ça) + faire du bien + indirect object pronoun to say something is beneficial or pleasant for someone: «Ça me fait du bien» (It does me good / It feels good). You can change the pronoun (me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur) and tense: «Ça t’a fait du bien ?» (Did it do you good?).
target_language_example: Après une longue journée, une douche chaude me fait du bien.
native_language_example: After a long day, a hot shower does me good.

meaning: (has) done a good job; (has) done good work.
additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s work. It’s the past tense with avoir: "j’ai fait du bon boulot" (I did a good job), "tu as fait…", "il/elle a fait…", "nous avons fait…", "vous avez fait…", "ils/elles ont fait…". In speech you’ll also hear the present: "Tu fais du bon boulot" (You’re doing a good job).
target_language_example: Bravo, tu as fait du bon boulot sur ce projet !
native_language_example: Well done, you did a good job on this project!

meaning: (has) done good work; did a good job.
additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s performance or the quality of what they did. Often appears as "Tu as fait du bon travail" (you did a good job) or "Vous avez fait du bon travail" (you did a good job—formal/plural). With a name/subject: "Il/Tom fait du bon travail" = he/Tom does good work. Note: agreement happens on "toutes" when addressing a group of women ("Vous avez toutes fait...").
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide : tu as fait du bon travail.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help: you did a good job.

meaning: "gives you the creeps" / "makes your blood run cold."
additional_notes: Common idiom used with an object pronoun: « Ça me fait froid dans le dos » (It gives me the creeps). Can refer to something scary, disturbing, or unsettling. Often used with « ça » (that/it), or a person/thing as the subject (e.g., « Il/Elle me fait froid dans le dos »).
target_language_example: L'idée de rester seul dans cette maison la nuit me fait froid dans le dos.
native_language_example: The idea of staying alone in that house at night gives me the creeps.

additional_notes: Past tense of « faire le bon choix » (“to make the right choice”). Used to say someone chose correctly; often appears with « j’ai/tu as/on a fait le bon choix ». You can also say « faire le bon choix » in general statements: « Il faut faire le bon choix. »
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : tu as fait le bon choix.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you made the right choice.

additional_notes: Used with a person as the indirect object (me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur): « Ça me fait mal » = “It hurts (me).” In questions about pain: « Qu’est-ce qui vous fait mal ? » (“What hurts?”) or « Quelle dent/jambe vous fait mal ? » (“Which tooth/leg hurts?”). Past: « Ça vous a fait mal ? » = “Did it hurt?”
target_language_example: Ça me fait mal au dos.
native_language_example: My back hurts.

additional_notes: Used with "de": "faire partie de" = to be part of something (a group, a whole, an experience). Very common in the fixed expression "Ça fait partie de…" meaning “That’s part of … / It comes with …” (often to say something is normal or expected).
target_language_example: Je fais partie de l’équipe.
native_language_example: I’m part of the team.

additional_notes: Used with a singular subject (il/elle/on, a thing, a person) to say it is included in a larger whole or group. It’s the verb phrase "faire partie de" (to be part of). Commonly followed by a noun or group: "faire partie de la famille", "faire partie d’une équipe". With a plural subject, use "font partie de".
target_language_example: Elle fait partie de mon équipe.
native_language_example: She is part of my team.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is included in a group, organization, set, or whole. It’s the 3rd-person singular present of "faire partie de" (to be part of). You’ll also see changes like "font partie de" (they are part of) and forms with "de la / de l’ / des" depending on the noun: "fait partie du club" (of the club), "fait partie de la famille" (of the family), "fait partie des membres" (of the members).
target_language_example: Cette rue fait partie du centre-ville.
native_language_example: This street is part of the city center.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "faire peur (à quelqu’un)" = “to scare someone.” It agrees with the subject (fait / font / faisait / a fait, etc.). The person who is scared is often introduced with an indirect object: "Ça me fait peur" (It scares me), "Les chiens nous ont fait peur" (The dogs scared us).
target_language_example: Ce film me fait peur, alors je préfère regarder une comédie.
native_language_example: This movie scares me, so I’d rather watch a comedy.

additional_notes:
Used with **faire** in the past (passé composé): *il a fait… / ils ont fait…* = “he/they did…”. Often implies something unspecified.
- **faire quelque chose à quelqu’un**: “do something to someone” (can suggest harming them): *Il t’a fait quelque chose ?*
- **mal faire quelque chose**: “do something badly / do something wrong.”
- **en faire quelque chose**: “make something of it” (turn something into something meaningful/useful): *partant de rien, en fait quelque chose*.
target_language_example: Je crois qu’on a fait quelque chose de travers.
native_language_example: I think we did something wrong.

meaning: "(is/are/did) do what?" → "what is/are (someone) doing?" / "what did (someone) do?"
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French as a casual question using *faire* + *quoi*. The tense changes with context: **il/elle fait quoi ?** = “what is he/she doing?”, **tu as fait quoi ?** = “what did you do?”. With **ça te fait quoi ?**, it means “how does that make you feel?” (literally “what does that do to you?”). Often sounds a bit blunt depending on tone.
target_language_example: Tu fais quoi ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are you doing tonight?

meaning: 'came all this way to' / 'went to all this trouble to'.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone traveled a long distance or made a big effort, often with surprise, frustration, or to highlight the importance of the goal. It’s commonly used with the passé composé: « J’ai fait tout ce chemin pour… » (I came all this way to…).
target_language_example: J’ai fait tout ce chemin pour te dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I came all this way to tell you the truth.

additional_notes: Used with the verb faire to talk about doing or making something: "faire un gâteau" (make a cake), "faire un voyage" (take/make a trip). "fait" can be the past participle in the passé composé (j’ai fait un…) or the 3rd-person singular present (il/elle fait un…).
target_language_example: J’ai fait un choix difficile.
native_language_example: I made a difficult choice.

additional_notes: From **faire un rêve** (“to have a dream”). Very common in the **past tense**: **J’ai fait un rêve** = “I had a dream.” You can also use the verb **rêver**: **J’ai rêvé** = “I dreamed.” Literally it’s “made a dream,” but the natural meaning is “had a dream.”
target_language_example: J’ai fait un rêve étrange cette nuit.
native_language_example: I had a strange dream last night.

additional_notes: This is the present tense form of *faire* with *une* (he/she/it: *il/elle fait une…*). It’s commonly used in medical/health expressions: *faire une allergie* (to have/get an allergic reaction), *faire une overdose* (to overdose), *faire une crise* (to have an attack/episode), etc. It does not translate literally as “makes a.”
target_language_example: Elle fait une réaction allergique aux noix.
native_language_example: She has an allergic reaction to nuts.

meaning: '(has) done a good deed' (done something kind/helpful).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "faire" + "une bonne action" to say someone did something morally good or helpful. It’s commonly used in the passé composé: "a fait une bonne action" (he/she did a good deed), "j’ai fait une bonne action" (I did a good deed).
target_language_example: J’ai fait une bonne action en aidant ma voisine à porter ses courses.
native_language_example: I did a good deed by helping my neighbor carry her groceries.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "faire une erreur" (to make a mistake). It changes with subject and tense: je fais / j’ai fait, il fait / il a fait, vous faites / vous avez fait. Often used to point out an error: "Je pense que vous avez fait une erreur."
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai fait une erreur dans le numéro de téléphone.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a mistake in the phone number.

additional_notes: From **faire** (to do/make). **fait** is the 3rd person singular present: *il/elle/on fait ça* = “he/she/one does that.” Used to refer to an action that’s understood from context. You can change the subject: *je fais ça* (I do that), *tu fais ça* (you do that), etc.
target_language_example: Pourquoi est-ce qu'il fait ça ?
native_language_example: Why does he do that?

additional_notes: Imperative (command) with **vous** form of *faire* (“to do/make”) + the direct object pronoun **le** (“it/him”), joined with a hyphen. Often means **“do it”** (e.g., *Faites-le sans attendre.*). With an infinitive, it can be the causative *faire*: **faites-le + infinitive** = “make him/it + verb” (e.g., *Faites-le parler* = “Make him talk”).
target_language_example: Si tu es prêt, faites-le maintenant.
native_language_example: If you’re ready, do it now.

additional_notes: From the polite command form of *faire* (“faites”) + *moi* (“me”). It’s often followed by an infinitive or set phrases: **faites-moi connaître** = “let me know”, **faites-moi part de…** = “tell me / share… with me”, **faites-moi voir** = “show me”. You can also add **s’il vous plaît** for extra politeness.
target_language_example: Faites-moi savoir quand vous arrivez, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please let me know when you arrive.

additional_notes: This is the verb "faire" (vous form: "faites") with inversion "-vous" to form a question in formal/polite French: "Faites-vous… ?" = "Do you…?" It can also appear with pronouns: "Comment le faites-vous ?" (How do you do it?) and with a reflexive verb: "Où vous faites-vous coiffer ?" (Where do you get your hair done?). In a command, "Faites-vous plaisir" means "Treat yourself" (literally "Make yourself pleasure").
target_language_example: Que faites-vous ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are you doing tonight?

additional_notes: Imperative (vous form) of « faire attention ». Often followed by « à » + noun or clause: « Faites attention à la voiture » (Watch out for the car) or « Faites attention à ce que vous dites » (Be careful what you say). Used both as a warning and as advice to be mindful.
target_language_example: Faites attention en traversant la rue.
native_language_example: Be careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: Polite/plural command (vous form) used to warn someone to avoid a bad outcome. Pattern: « Faites attention à ne pas + infinitive » (e.g., « … ne pas tomber »). For one person you know well: « Fais attention à ne pas … ».
target_language_example: Faites attention à ne pas oublier votre passeport.
native_language_example: Be careful not to forget your passport.

additional_notes: Imperative using "vous" (polite singular or plural). It can sound genuinely permissive ("you’re free to choose") or, depending on tone/context, dismissive/annoyed ("fine, do whatever you want"). Often used with objects too: "Faites ce que vous voulez de X" = "Do whatever you want with X" (including people, in a figurative sense).
target_language_example: Si ça te convient, tant mieux; sinon, faites ce que vous voulez.
native_language_example: If it suits you, great; if not, do what you want.

additional_notes: A polite, welcoming phrase said to guests to tell them to feel comfortable and act naturally. Grammatically it’s the imperative of "faire" + "comme" + "chez vous" (using "vous" either for several people or for one person politely).
target_language_example: Entrez, posez vos affaires et faites comme chez vous.
native_language_example: Come in, put your things down, and make yourself at home.

additional_notes: Fixed expression said by a dealer or announcer in gambling contexts (casino, roulette, etc.) to invite players to bet. It uses the formal/plural command form (faites = “do/make” to you all / to a customer). Not used much outside betting contexts.
target_language_example: Au casino, le croupier a dit : « Faites vos jeux ! »
native_language_example: At the casino, the dealer said, “Place your bets!”

meaning: 'made for each other' (a perfect match, especially as a couple).
additional_notes: Used with **être**: *Ils/Nous/On/Vous êtes faits l'un pour l'autre.* It agrees with the people involved: **faits** (masc. plural or mixed group), **faites** (fem. plural). You can also change **l'un** to **l'une** if the person referred to is female: *Ils sont faits l'un pour l'autre* / *Elles sont faites l'une pour l'autre*. Common in romantic contexts, but can also describe a great pairing in general.
target_language_example: Je pense que vous êtes faits l'un pour l'autre.
native_language_example: I think you’re made for each other.

additional_notes: From the verb "falloir" ("il faut" = "it’s necessary"). Very often used as "il faut faire + infinitive" (e.g., "Il faut faire vite" = "We/you have to do it quickly"). It can also change with an indirect object pronoun: "Il me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur faut faire..." = "I/you/he/we/you/they need to do...". Dropping "il" ("Faut faire...") is common in casual spoken French.
target_language_example: Faut faire attention en traversant la rue.
native_language_example: You have to be careful when crossing the street.

meaning: We have to go / We’ve got to get going.
additional_notes: Short for "(il) faut y aller". "Il faut" expresses necessity (“it’s necessary / you have to”), and "y aller" means “to go there / to go (to it).” Very common when it’s time to leave or when you must go do something. "Y" can refer to a place (there) or to an activity you need to go to (e.g., an appointment).
target_language_example: Bon, faut y aller, sinon on va être en retard.
native_language_example: Alright, we’ve got to go, otherwise we’ll be late.

additional_notes: Usually appears as **il faut être + adjective/noun** (“you/one must be…”) or with an object pronoun: **il me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur faut être…** (“I/you/he… must be…”). Often expresses necessity or advice: *Il faut être prudent* = “You have to be careful.”
target_language_example: Pour ce travail, il faut être patient.
native_language_example: For this job, you need to be patient.

meaning: need to be more (…); have to be more (…).
additional_notes: Used in the common structure « Il me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur faut + infinitive » to express necessity: « Il te faut être davantage patient » = “You need to be more patient.” « davantage » means “more” (often a bit more formal than « plus »). Adjectives agree with the person: « organisé/organisée », « patient/patiente », etc. Note: « davantage » looks like “advantage” but it doesn’t mean that.
target_language_example: Il te faut être davantage prudent si tu conduis la nuit.
native_language_example: You need to be more careful if you drive at night.

additional_notes: This is the question form (inversion) of "il faut" ("it’s necessary / we need"). It’s often used in real questions (e.g., asking what’s needed) and also in rhetorical questions expressing doubt or surprise ("Faut-il…?" = "Do we really have to…?").
target_language_example: Faut-il réserver à l’avance ?
native_language_example: Do we need to book in advance?

meaning: "we have to / we need to" (short for "il faut qu’on").
additional_notes: Very common spoken shortcut meaning that something is necessary. It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive: « faut qu’on parte », « faut qu’on puisse… ». « on » often means “we” in everyday French. In more careful speech/writing, you’ll often see « il faut qu’on… ».
target_language_example: Faut qu’on y aille maintenant.
native_language_example: We have to go now.

additional_notes: Very common spoken shortcut for « il faut que … » (from the verb « falloir », “to be necessary”). It’s followed by the subjunctive: « Faut que je parte. » = “I have to leave.” You may also hear « y faut que … » in casual speech.
target_language_example: Faut que je rentre avant huit heures.
native_language_example: I have to get home before eight o’clock.

meaning: “it has to be” / “it must be” (introduces a requirement).
additional_notes: Short for “il faut que ce soit…”. Very common in spoken French (“faut que…”). It’s followed by the subjunctive: “que ce soit” (from “être”). Used to say something is necessary/required.
target_language_example: Faut que ce soit prêt avant midi.
native_language_example: It has to be ready before noon.

meaning: “I have to go (to…)” / “I need to go (to…).”
additional_notes: Informal spoken version of **« Il faut que j’aille… »** (“It’s necessary that I go…”). It expresses an obligation/need and is followed by **j’aille** (subjunctive of *aller*) plus a place (**au boulot, en cours, à l’hôpital**) or an action (**voir ma mère, boire une bière**). Often used to mean you should leave or you have something you must do.
target_language_example: Désolé, faut que j’aille, je suis en retard.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go—I’m late.

meaning: “I have to go / I need to go (there).”
additional_notes: Short for “(il) faut que j’y aille,” from the impersonal expression “il faut que…” + subjunctive (“j’aille”). “y” means “there” or “to it/that place,” referring to somewhere already mentioned or understood. Often used to excuse yourself: “Bon, faut que j’y aille.”
target_language_example: Désolé, faut que j’y aille maintenant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now.

meaning: "I have to / I need to" (informal for "il faut que je").
additional_notes: Very common spoken shortcut of "il faut que je" to express necessity/obligation. It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive: "Faut que je parte", "Faut que je fasse…". In writing or more formal speech, prefer "Il faut que je…".
target_language_example: Désolé, faut que je file maintenant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now.

meaning: "I have to / I need to" (followed by a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Short, informal spoken version of « il faut que je me… ». It’s used to say something is necessary/urgent. It’s typically followed by a reflexive verb in the present (je me + verb): « Faut que je me repose » (I need to rest), « Faut que je me dépêche » (I have to hurry). In more careful speech/writing, use « Il faut que je me… ».
target_language_example: Faut que je me dépêche, je suis en retard.
native_language_example: I have to hurry, I'm late.

additional_notes: Common in speech as a shortened form of “Il faut que je retourne…”. Uses the verb “falloir” (il faut que…) to express necessity (“have to / need to”), followed by “je retourne” (“I go back”). Often used with places or activities: au travail/au boulot, bosser.
target_language_example: Faut que je retourne au bureau, on m’attend.
native_language_example: I have to go back to the office; they’re waiting for me.

meaning: “I need to talk to you / I have to talk to you.”
additional_notes: Short for **(Il) faut que je te parle**. Uses **falloir** (“to be necessary”) in the common pattern **il faut que + [subject] + verb (subjunctive)**. In conversation, dropping **il** (**faut que…**) is very common and informal. Often used to introduce an important or serious topic; you can add **de + noun/pronoun**: *Faut que je te parle de ça / d’un truc.*
target_language_example: Faut que je te parle après le cours.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you after class.

meaning: "I have to / I need to (…you…)" (introduces what you must do to someone).
additional_notes: Spoken, informal shortening of « il faut que je vous… » (= “I have to/need to …”). It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive: « faut que je vous parle » (…that I talk to you), « faut que je vous voie » (…that I see you). « vous » is the formal/plural “you” object pronoun (“to you / you”).
target_language_example: Faut que je vous explique quelque chose.
native_language_example: I need to explain something to you.

additional_notes: Short, spoken form of "il faut que tu". It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "Faut que tu comprennes", "Faut que tu signes"). Common for giving strong advice, instructions, or saying something is necessary.
target_language_example: Faut que tu fasses attention en traversant la rue.
native_language_example: You have to be careful when crossing the street.

meaning: "you have to be" / "you need to be" (it’s necessary that you be…).
additional_notes: Informal spoken form of « il faut que tu sois… » (the « il » is dropped). It’s used to say something is necessary/required. The verb after « faut que » is in the subjunctive: « tu sois » (from « être », to be). Often followed by an adjective or noun: « plus organisé(e) », « prêt », « un héros ».
target_language_example: Faut que tu sois à l’heure demain.
native_language_example: You need to be on time tomorrow.

meaning: "You need to be more..." / "You have to be more..."
additional_notes: Shortened from "Il faut que..." ("it’s necessary that..."). It introduces a requirement or strong advice and is followed by the subjunctive: "vous soyez" + an adjective (e.g., "plus organisé(e)(s)"). The adjective agrees with who you’re talking to: "organisé" (one man), "organisée" (one woman), "organisés" (group/mixed or men), "organisées" (group of women). Common in spoken French; "Il faut que" is a bit more neutral/formal.
target_language_example: Faut que vous soyez plus patients avec les enfants.
native_language_example: You need to be more patient with the kids.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **falloir** (almost always as **il faut…**). With an indirect object pronoun, it means someone needs something: **Il lui faut un manteau** = “He needs a coat” (literally: “To him, a coat is necessary”). Common patterns: **Il faut un + noun** (“You need a/an…”) and **Il me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur faut un/une + noun** (“I/you/he… need a/an…”).
target_language_example: Il nous faut une carte pour entrer.
native_language_example: We need a ticket/card to get in.

meaning: a way of; a way to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a method/means (“une façon de + infinitive” = “a way to + verb”) or someone’s manner/style (“une façon de + verb/noun” = “a way of …”). Often preceded by an article or quantity: « la/une seule/une autre façon de… ».
