additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy went back to his place (home). With "rentrer" you often specify how/when: "à six heures" (at six), "trois heures après" (three hours later), "à pied" (on foot). Past tense uses "être": "il est rentré" (feminine: "elle est rentrée").
target_language_example: Après le travail, il est rentré chez lui en métro.
native_language_example: After work, he went home by subway.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *rester* with *être*: *il est resté*. Used for staying in a place (*il est resté au Japon / chez moi / dehors*) and also for remaining in a state or position (*il est resté couché, debout, muet, fidèle à...*). The feminine form is *elle est restée* (often with an extra -e), and in plural: *ils sont restés / elles sont restées* (agreement in writing).
target_language_example: Il est resté à la maison toute la journée.
native_language_example: He stayed at home all day.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *revenir* with **être**: *il est revenu* (he came back). The feminine form is *elle est revenue*. Often followed by a place with **à/chez/ici** (*il est revenu chez lui*), or by an origin with **de** (*il est revenu de France*).
target_language_example: Il est revenu trop tard pour le dîner.
native_language_example: He came back too late for dinner.

meaning: "it's time" (to do something / for something to happen).
additional_notes: Used to say that the appropriate moment has arrived, often as a prompt or suggestion. Common patterns: (1) il est temps de + infinitive: Il est temps de partir. (2) il est temps pour + person + de + infinitive: Il est temps pour moi de rentrer. (3) il est temps que + subjunctive: Il est temps qu'on parte / que les choses changent.
target_language_example: Il est temps de faire une pause.
native_language_example: It’s time to take a break.

additional_notes: Used to say that the right moment has arrived to do an action. It is followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., partir, voter, dire, découvrir).
target_language_example: Il est temps de partir, on est en retard.
native_language_example: It's time to leave; we're late.

meaning: "it’s time (that)…" (often with a sense of “it’s about time”).
additional_notes: Used to say something should happen now, often after waiting or delaying. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive: « Il est temps que je parte / tu te lèves / les choses changent ».
target_language_example: Il est temps que nous commencions le cours.
native_language_example: It’s time we started the class.

meaning: "it’s time for you to…" / "it’s about time you…"
additional_notes: Used to say something should happen now (often with a sense of urgency or that it’s overdue). It is typically followed by the subjunctive: « Il est temps que tu partes. »
target_language_example: Il est temps que tu te reposes.
native_language_example: It’s time for you to rest.

meaning: 'he fell' (or, in 'tomber malade', 'he got sick / fell ill').
additional_notes: Passé composé of *tomber* uses **être**: *il est tombé*. It can be literal (physically falling: *dans la rivière*) or part of common expressions like **tomber malade** = “to fall ill / get sick.” (Feminine: *elle est tombée*; plural: *ils sont tombés*, *elles sont tombées*.)
target_language_example: Il est tombé et il s'est fait mal au genou.
native_language_example: He fell and hurt his knee.

additional_notes: Used to describe a habitual or constant situation. With a person, it often comes before an adjective (Il est toujours ponctuel = He’s always punctual) or before a place/time expression (Il est toujours à l’hôpital = He’s still/always at the hospital). In patterns like « Il est toujours + adjective + de + infinitive » (Il est toujours bon de…), « il » is impersonal and means “it” (“It’s always good to…”).
target_language_example: Il est toujours important de vérifier l’adresse.
native_language_example: It’s always important to check the address.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to say someone is excessively something. Very often followed by an infinitive with « pour »: « Il est trop + adjectif + pour + verbe » (e.g., “too big to run fast”). In everyday spoken French, « trop » is also often used informally to mean “really/so” (e.g., « Il est trop malin ! » = “He’s so smart!”), depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Il est trop fatigué pour sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: He’s too tired to go out tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say something shouldn’t happen yet because it’s still early. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., aller, dormir, boire). You can also negate the idea: « Il n’est pas trop tôt pour… » = “It’s not too early to…”.
target_language_example: Il est trop tôt pour décider.
native_language_example: It’s too early to decide.

meaning: 'he is very…' (used to intensify an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective (or an adverb + adjective) to describe a man or boy: « Il est très connu / intelligent / sympa. » If you’re talking about a woman, use « elle est très ». For plural: « ils/elles sont très ». It can also be used more generally with the impersonal « il » in other contexts, but in these examples it refers to a person.
target_language_example: Il est très fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: He is very tired today.

additional_notes: Uses être as the auxiliary in the passé composé: venir → il est venu (masc.), elle est venue (fem.), ils sont venus, elles sont venues. Often followed by an infinitive to express purpose: il est venu te voir / me rencontrer (“he came to see you / meet me”). Can also mean “he came by/visited” a place or person.
target_language_example: Il est venu te voir ce matin.
native_language_example: He came to see you this morning.

meaning: he came to see me; he came to visit me.
additional_notes: Common way to say someone came to see/visit you. Built with "venir" in the passé composé ("il est venu" = he came) + an infinitive ("voir" = to see). The pronoun goes before the infinitive: "me voir" = to see me. You can change the subject and tense: "Elle est venue me voir" (She came to see me), "Il vient me voir" (He’s coming to see me).
target_language_example: Il est venu me voir après le travail.
native_language_example: He came to see me after work.

meaning: “he/it is at/in” (location); also “he/it is to…” (e.g., to blame / yours).
additional_notes: This is the pattern **être + à** with **il** (“he/it”). Most commonly it gives a location: *Il est à Paris* (“He’s in Paris”). With certain expressions, **à** introduces a role or relationship: **il est à blâmer** (“he is to blame”) and **il est à vous** (“it’s yours / it belongs to you”). The exact English translation depends on what follows **à**.
target_language_example: Il est à la maison aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: He’s at home today.

additional_notes: Literally "he was doing/making" (imperfect of faire), but very often used with impersonal il to describe background conditions: weather (Il faisait froid / chaud / beau) and time-of-day (Il faisait déjà nuit). It can also appear in questions about someone’s actions: Qu’est-ce qu’il faisait ? (= What was he doing?). Note: in phrases like « il faisait partie de… », it’s the verb phrase « faire partie de » = “to be part of.”
target_language_example: Il faisait beau quand on est sortis.
native_language_example: It was nice out when we went out.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal "il" with "faire" to talk about the weather. "Il faisait..." is in the imperfect tense, often used for background descriptions in the past (e.g., what the weather was like). You can swap in other weather adjectives: "il faisait chaud" (it was hot), "il faisait beau" (the weather was nice).
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé à la gare, il faisait très froid.
native_language_example: When I arrived at the station, it was very cold.

additional_notes: "Il" can mean "he" (a person) or the impersonal "it". With verbs/expressions like "faire en sorte (que)..." (make sure that...), "faire pousser" (grow), or "faire pipi" (pee), it usually means "he does/makes". With weather/temperature, "il fait" means "it is" (e.g., "Il fait chaud" = "It’s hot"). Many fixed expressions use "faire" (e.g., "Il fait feu de tout bois" = he uses every means available / makes do with whatever he has).
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, il fait froid, alors je mets un manteau.
native_language_example: Today it’s cold, so I’m wearing a coat.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal weather expression "il fait + adjective" (literally “it makes/does + adjective”). You can add a place with "à" (Il fait froid à Boston.) or use "quand" to mean “when it’s cold.”
target_language_example: Ferme la fenêtre : il fait froid dans l’appartement.
native_language_example: Close the window: it’s cold in the apartment.

additional_notes: Imperfect of "il faut" (to be necessary). Used to talk about a necessity or obligation in the past, often in a general/ongoing way. Very commonly followed by "que" + subjunctive: "Il fallait que je parte" = "I had to leave" (literally: "it was necessary that I leave"). In casual speech, "Il fallait pas" means "You/I shouldn’t have" or "It wasn’t necessary."
target_language_example: Il fallait que je rentre tôt, alors je suis parti.
native_language_example: I had to get home early, so I left.

meaning: "I had to" / "I needed to" (it was necessary for me to...).
additional_notes: From the verb "falloir" (impersonal: "il faut"). "Il fallait" is the imperfect, often used to talk about a necessity/obligation in the past. It is followed by "que" + the subjunctive: "il fallait que je parle / que je voie". In English, this is usually translated more naturally as "I had to..." rather than "it was necessary that I...".
target_language_example: Il fallait que je finisse ce travail avant ce soir.
native_language_example: I had to finish this work before tonight.

meaning: "you must / you need to"; "it’s necessary to".
additional_notes: Impersonal expression with the verb *falloir* to talk about necessity or obligation. Most common pattern: **il faut + infinitive** (Il faut partir = We have to leave). It can also be **il faut + noun** (Il faut du temps = It takes time / You need time). With an indirect object it becomes **il me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur faut** = “I/you/he… need” (Il me faut un stylo = I need a pen).
target_language_example: Il faut réserver à l’avance.
native_language_example: You need to book in advance.

additional_notes: Built with the impersonal expression **il faut** + infinitive. It means “it’s necessary to…,” and often translates as “you have to…” or “we need to…,” depending on context. It’s commonly followed by a place/direction (**aller à… / par là / ici**) or by another infinitive idea like **aller le/la chercher** (“go get him/her/it”).
target_language_example: Il est tard : il faut aller à la maison.
native_language_example: It’s late: we have to go home.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression: it doesn’t refer to a specific “he.” Used to say something is necessary/required. Common pattern: « il faut + infinitive » (here, « faire »), often followed by what needs doing: « Il faut faire vite » (We have to be quick). Can also take a direct object: « Il faut faire quelque chose » (Something must be done).
target_language_example: Il faut faire attention quand on traverse la rue.
native_language_example: You have to be careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: "Il faut" is an impersonal way to say something is necessary/required. "La" is a direct object pronoun meaning "her" or "it" for a feminine singular person/thing previously mentioned (e.g., la table → il faut la réparer; Mélanie → il faut la croire). This pattern is usually followed by an infinitive: il faut la + verb (inf.).
target_language_example: La voiture est en panne : il faut la faire réparer.
native_language_example: The car is broken down: we have to get it repaired.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to express necessity/obligation in an impersonal way: il faut + direct object pronoun (le = him/it) + infinitive. The pronoun comes before the infinitive: « Il faut le laver » = “We have to wash it/him.” (le can refer to a masculine person or thing; for a feminine one you’d use « il faut la ».)
target_language_example: Il faut le réparer avant demain.
native_language_example: We have to fix it before tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the impersonal expression **il faut** (“it’s necessary”) followed by a **reflexive verb** starting with **se**: *il faut se comprendre* (“we/you have to understand each other”), *il faut se dire* (“you have to tell yourself”). The subject is general (people in general, we, you, one) and depends on context.
target_language_example: Il faut se calmer avant de parler.
native_language_example: You have to calm down before speaking.

meaning: we/you have to go; we/you need to leave.
additional_notes: Used to say it’s necessary to leave or get going. "Il faut" is an impersonal way to mean "it’s necessary" (often said as "we/you have to" in English). "Y" refers to the place/activity you’re going to, so in this phrase it usually just means "go/leave" without naming the destination. Often used as a prompt, sometimes urgently: "Vite, il faut y aller !"
target_language_example: On est en retard, il faut y aller !
native_language_example: We’re late—we have to go!

meaning: "you have to be" / "one must be" (it’s necessary to be).
additional_notes: Impersonal expression ("il" doesn’t refer to a person). Used to express necessity or a requirement. Commonly followed by an adjective (Il faut être prudents.), a noun phrase (Il faut être médecin pour faire ça.), or a complement like "à + infinitive" (Il faut être deux pour porter ça.). Can be general advice/rules or what’s needed for something to work.
target_language_example: Pour réussir, il faut être patient.
native_language_example: To succeed, you have to be patient.

meaning: "he has to / it’s necessary that he" (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity, obligation, or something required about “he” (il). The verb after "qu'il" is normally in the subjunctive: "il faut qu'il parle" (he must speak). Can also mean “it’s important that he… / he needs to…” depending on context.
target_language_example: Il faut qu'il vienne demain.
native_language_example: He has to come tomorrow.

meaning: "we have to / we need to" (literally: "it’s necessary that we...").
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation for a group including the speaker. It is followed by the subjunctive in French: il faut qu’on + verb (ex: qu’on aille, qu’on appelle, qu’on discute). "Qu’on" is the contraction of "que" + "on" (here, "on" often means "we" in everyday French).
target_language_example: Il faut qu’on parte maintenant.
native_language_example: We have to leave now.

meaning: "We need to talk" / "We have to talk."
additional_notes: Literally "it’s necessary that we talk." Very common to introduce an important (sometimes serious) conversation. After "il faut que", French uses the subjunctive: "qu’on parle". Often followed by "de + [topic]" (il faut qu’on parle de ça) or "en privé" (in private).
target_language_example: Il faut qu'on parle après le dîner.
native_language_example: We need to talk after dinner.

meaning: “we need to / we have to … (each other / ourselves)” (before a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Literally “it’s necessary that we…”. Very common way to say “we must/need to” before a verb in the subjunctive: il faut qu’on se parle (we need to talk), …qu’on se voie (we need to see each other), …qu’on se sépare (we need to separate). “On” often means “we” in everyday French. “Se” changes meaning depending on the verb (each other vs. ourselves).
target_language_example: Il faut qu’on se dépêche, on est en retard.
native_language_example: We need to hurry, we’re late.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity, obligation, or something that needs to happen. It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., il faut que j’y arrive, il faut que tout le monde se calme). Often translates as “I have to… / we need to…” depending on context.
target_language_example: Il faut que tu partes maintenant.
native_language_example: You have to leave now.

meaning: “it has to be / it must be” (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation about a person/thing/state: il faut + que + [subjunctive]. Here, "ce soit" is the subjunctive of "c’est" (from "être"). Often followed by an adjective or noun: "Il faut que ce soit prêt" (It has to be ready), "Il faut que ce soit moi" (It has to be me).
target_language_example: Il faut que ce soit maintenant.
native_language_example: It has to be now.

meaning: "I have to / I need to" (introduces what I must do).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation. It’s the start of the pattern "Il faut que + subject + verb"; after "que", the verb is typically in the subjunctive (e.g., "j’appelle", "j’essaie"). The "j'" is just the shortened form of "je" before a vowel or silent h.
target_language_example: Il faut que j'y aille maintenant.
native_language_example: I have to go now.

meaning: "I have to go" / "I need to go".
additional_notes: Built from the impersonal expression "il faut" (it’s necessary) + "que" + the subjunctive of "aller" ("j’aille" = I go). Used to say you must go somewhere or go do something (work, study, see someone). Often followed by a place ("au lycée", "à l’hôpital") or an infinitive ("bosser", "travailler").
target_language_example: Désolé, il faut que j’aille maintenant.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now.

meaning: "I have to go" / "I need to go" (I must leave).
additional_notes: Used to say you have an obligation/need to leave. Built from: "il faut" (it’s necessary) + "que" + subjunctive "j’aille" (that I go). "y" means “there/to it” and often just refers to leaving in general. Common with softeners like "écoute(z)", "OK ?", "je crois que...".
target_language_example: Désolé, il faut que j'y aille : j'ai un rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go: I have an appointment.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity/obligation. It’s built on the impersonal expression "il faut" + "que" + a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., je commence, je prenne, je regarde). Often translates as “I have to / I need to,” or sometimes “I must.”
target_language_example: Il faut que je parte maintenant.
native_language_example: I have to leave now.

meaning: "I have to" / "I need to" (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal expression "il faut" (it is necessary) + "que" + subjunctive: "je fasse" (from "faire"). It expresses necessity/obligation (from strong need to a requirement). Often followed by what you must do: "Il faut que je fasse + [noun/verb phrase]". Question form: "Qu'est-ce qu'il faut que je fasse ?" = "What do I have to do?".
target_language_example: Il faut que je fasse mes devoirs avant ce soir.
native_language_example: I have to do my homework before tonight.

meaning: "I have to / I need to (do it)."
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation. After "il faut que", French uses the subjunctive (e.g., "il faut que je le fasse"). "le" is an object pronoun meaning "it" or "him" (depending on context) and comes before the verb.
target_language_example: Il faut que je le fasse aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I have to do it today.

meaning: "I have to… / I need to…" (before a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity/obligation. It introduces a clause with the subject “je” and a reflexive verb starting with m’ (m’habiller, m’informer, m’occuper, m’y faire). Grammar note: after « il faut que », French typically uses the subjunctive (e.g., « Il faut que je m’habille »). The m’ is short for « me » and changes to m’ before a vowel or silent h.
target_language_example: Il faut que je m'excuse.
native_language_example: I have to apologize.

meaning: "I have to / I need to (myself)…" (starting a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary: **il faut que + subject + verb** (usually in the **subjunctive**). Here, **je me** shows the next verb is **reflexive** (an action you do to yourself): *je me cache* (I hide), *je me coiffe* (I do my hair), *je me tire* (I get out of here / I leave—informal).
target_language_example: Il faut que je me dépêche.
native_language_example: I have to hurry.

meaning: I need to know / I must know.
additional_notes: Built with the impersonal expression "il faut que" (“it’s necessary that…”), followed by the subjunctive: "je sache" (from "savoir", to know). Used to insist that knowing something is necessary or essential: "Il faut que je sache la vérité" (“I have to know the truth”).
target_language_example: Il faut que je sache si tu viens demain.
native_language_example: I need to know if you’re coming tomorrow.

meaning: "I need to be / I have to be" (it’s necessary that I be).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation about yourself. It’s the pattern: il faut que + subject + verb in the subjunctive; here sois is the subjunctive of être (to be). Often translates as “I have to be…” or “I need to be…”, depending on context.
target_language_example: Il faut que je sois prêt avant 8 heures.
native_language_example: I need to be ready before 8 o’clock.

meaning: "I have to / I need to (tell/ask/see you...)"
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you must do involving the person you’re talking to ("te" = "to you"). After "il faut que", French normally uses the subjunctive: "Il faut que je te parle" (not *"je te parle" in a simple statement sense). Common with verbs like parler, demander, dire, voir, rappeler, quitter.
target_language_example: Il faut que je te parle deux minutes.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you for two minutes.

il faut que je te dise

target_language_multi_word_term: il faut que je te dise
meaning: “I have to tell you” / “I need to tell you.”
additional_notes: Used to introduce something important or necessary to say. Built on the impersonal expression “il faut que …” (“it’s necessary that …”), which is followed by the subjunctive (here: “je te dise”). Often followed by “quelque chose” or what you need to say.
target_language_example: Il faut que je te dise la vérité.
native_language_example: I have to tell you the truth.

il faut que je te parle

target_language_multi_word_term: il faut que je te parle
meaning: I need to talk to you / I have to talk to you.
additional_notes: Common way to introduce an important or urgent conversation. Literally “it’s necessary that I talk to you,” using the expression il faut que + subjunctive (je parle). Often followed by de + topic (de ça, d’un truc) or en privé (“in private”). Can sound serious depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Il faut que je te parle ce soir, c’est important.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you tonight; it’s important.

meaning: "I need to find" / "I have to find".
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal expression "il faut que" ("it’s necessary that") + a subject + a verb in the subjunctive: "je trouve". It expresses necessity/obligation: you must find something, often a solution, a place to live, people to hang out with, etc.
target_language_example: Il faut que je trouve mon passeport avant de partir.
native_language_example: I need to find my passport before leaving.

meaning: "I have to / I need to (…you…)" (introduces what you must do).
additional_notes: Used with a verb after it: « Il faut que je vous + verbe » (e.g., dise, montre, parle). Grammatically, « il faut que » is followed by the subjunctive in French, even though English usually just uses “I have to / I need to.” « vous » is the formal/plural “you” (to you).
target_language_example: Il faut que je vous explique un truc.
native_language_example: I need to explain something to you.

meaning: "we need to / we have to" (it’s necessary that we…).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation. After "il faut que", French uses the subjunctive: "nous commencions", "nous parlions", "nous partions", etc. Often translates as "we have to" or "we must" in English.
target_language_example: Il faut que nous fassions attention.
native_language_example: We have to be careful.

meaning: "you have to" / "you need to" / "you must" (followed by a verb in the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation directed at “you.” After « il faut que tu », French uses the subjunctive (e.g., « tu comprennes », « tu rentres », « tu voies »). In speech, it’s often shortened to « faut que tu… ».
target_language_example: Il faut que tu fasses attention en traversant la rue.
native_language_example: You have to be careful when crossing the street.

meaning: you have to / you need to (do).
additional_notes: Built from "il faut que" + subjunctive: it expresses necessity/requirement. Because of "il faut que", the next verb is in the subjunctive: "tu fasses" (from "faire"). Often used to give strong advice, instructions, or say something is required.
target_language_example: Il faut que tu fasses attention en traversant la rue.
native_language_example: You have to be careful when crossing the street.

meaning: "you have to / you need to" (to do it/to him).
additional_notes: Used with the impersonal expression "il faut que" to express necessity/obligation. It is followed by the subjunctive: "Il faut que tu le voies" (not *tu le vois*). "le" is an object pronoun placed before the verb; it can mean "it" or "him" depending on context.
target_language_example: Il faut que tu le finisses aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You have to finish it today.

meaning: 'you have to be' / 'you need to be'.
additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary or required. It comes from the impersonal expression « il faut que + subjunctive » (“it’s necessary that…”). « sois » is the subjunctive form of « être » for « tu ». The adjective after it often agrees with the person (e.g., « agressif/agressive », « patient/patiente », « prudent/prudente »).
target_language_example: Il faut que tu sois à l’heure demain.
native_language_example: You have to be on time tomorrow.

meaning: 'you need to / you have to' (followed by a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity/obligation directed at "you" (tu). It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "tu te lèves", "tu te reposes"). The "te" is a reflexive pronoun, used with reflexive verbs where the action is done to yourself (se lever = to get up, se calmer = to calm down).
target_language_example: Il faut que tu te dépêches, on est en retard.
native_language_example: You need to hurry up; we’re late.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation. After « il faut que », French uses the subjunctive: « que vous compreniez / laissiez / parliez / sachiez / travailliez / voyiez ». « vous » can mean either 'you' (formal singular) or 'you all' (plural).
target_language_example: Il faut que vous soyez à l’heure demain.
native_language_example: You need to be on time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation. Literally “it’s necessary that you be…”, and it is followed by the subjunctive: vous soyez (from être). What follows is often an adjective or a phrase describing how you should be: patient(s)/patiente(s), prudent(e), là pour…, etc. Adjectives agree with who “vous” refers to (singular/plural, masculine/feminine).
target_language_example: Il faut que vous soyez prêts à partir à huit heures.
native_language_example: You have to be ready to leave at eight o’clock.

il faut que vous soyez plus

target_language_multi_word_term: il faut que vous soyez plus
meaning: "You need to be more…" / "You must be more…"
additional_notes: Used to tell someone that a change is necessary. It’s built with the impersonal expression « il faut que » + the subjunctive: « vous soyez » (from « être »). After « plus », you add an adjective: « plus organisé(e)(s) », « plus patient(e)(s) », etc. The adjective agrees with the person/people you’re addressing (masc./fem., singular/plural).
target_language_example: Il faut que vous soyez plus prudent(s) sur la route.
native_language_example: You need to be more careful on the road.

additional_notes: A formal/literary past tense mainly used in written French (stories, history). In everyday speech, you usually use "il a été" (completed past: he was/has been) or "il était" (ongoing past: he was).
target_language_example: Il fut très heureux d'apprendre la nouvelle.
native_language_example: He was very happy to hear the news.

meaning: “he has it / he did it” (il + l’ + a).
additional_notes: Very common structure: **il** (he) + **l’** (short for *le* or *la*, meaning “it/him/her”) + **a** (has, from *avoir*). Used with the **passé composé**: *Il l’a trouvé* = “He found it.” If followed by a past participle like **été**, it can mean “he was/has been”: *Il l’a été* = “He was (that).”
target_language_example: Il l’a déjà vu.
native_language_example: He’s already seen it.

additional_notes: Very common past tense using the passé composé: il + l’ (short for "le" or "la" = "it") + a fait ("has done/did"). The l’ refers to something already mentioned or understood from context. Often followed by a reason or purpose: "Il l’a fait pour toi" (He did it for you), or with emphasis like "exprès" (on purpose) and "lui-même" (himself).
target_language_example: Il l'a fait hier soir, mais il ne veut pas en parler.
native_language_example: He did it last night, but he doesn’t want to talk about it.

meaning: “he has them” / “he ___ them” (with a verb in the passé composé).
additional_notes:
Used when the direct object pronoun **les** (“them”) comes **before** the auxiliary **a** (from *avoir*) in the **passé composé**: *Il les a + past participle*.

When **les** is a **direct object** placed before the verb, the **past participle often agrees** in gender/number with what “les” refers to: *Il les a battues* (them = feminine plural), *Il les a tirés* (them = masculine plural).
target_language_example: Il les a vues hier.
native_language_example: He saw them yesterday.

meaning: 'he ... to him/her' (with a past action: 'he has/he did ... to him/her').
additional_notes: Used with the indirect object pronoun **lui** (= “to him” or “to her”). In the passé composé, **lui** comes before the auxiliary **a**: **il lui a + past participle** (e.g., *il lui a montré…* = “he showed him/her…”). In some expressions it can mean “it was … for him/her” (e.g., *il lui a été difficile…* = “it was difficult for him/her…”).
target_language_example: Il lui a téléphoné hier soir.
native_language_example: He called him/her last night.

additional_notes: "Il" = he. "Lui" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him" or "to her" (same form for both). "A donné" is the past tense (passé composé) of "donner" (to give). Used when someone gives something to another person: Il lui a donné le livre = He gave the book to him/her.
target_language_example: Il lui a donné les clés après le dîner.
native_language_example: He gave him/her the keys after dinner.

meaning: 'he has' or 'he (did) to me' (he + me + has).
additional_notes: Very common start of a sentence in the past tense: **il** = he, **m'** = to me / me (before a vowel sound), **a** = has (present of *avoir*). Used with a past participle to form the **passé composé**: *Il m'a dit* (He told me), *Il m'a invitée* (He invited me). With **être** verbs like *amener* in these examples, the past participle can agree with a female direct object: *Il m'a amenée* (if the speaker is a woman).
target_language_example: Il m'a envoyé un message hier soir.
native_language_example: He sent me a message last night.

meaning: "he asked me to" / "he told me to".
additional_notes: Used to report what a man asked or instructed you to do. Structure: subject + a demandé à + person + de + infinitive (e.g., Il m’a demandé de venir). For a woman: Elle m’a demandé de…; for plural: Ils/Elles m’ont demandé de…. In French, you use the infinitive after de (venir, donner, etc.).
target_language_example: Il m'a demandé de t'appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: He asked me to call you tonight.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *dire* (to say/tell): *il* (he) + *m’* (to me) + *a dit* (has said/told). Often followed by **de + infinitive** (*Il m’a dit de partir.*) or **que + clause** (*Il m’a dit qu’il venait.*). You can swap the subject and pronoun: *elle m’a dit* (she told me), *il t’a dit* (he told you).
target_language_example: Il m'a dit qu'il était occupé.
native_language_example: He told me he was busy.

additional_notes:
Often used with **faire** in two common patterns:
1) **Il m’a fait + infinitive** = “He made/caused me to …” (sometimes “got me to …” or “forced me to …,” depending on context): *Il m’a fait penser…* / *Il m’a fait promettre…*
2) **Il m’a fait + noun** = “He did (something) to me”: *Il m’a fait la même chose* (“He did the same thing to me”).
**m’** is short for **me** before a vowel (a + fait).
target_language_example: Il m'a fait rire.
native_language_example: He made me laugh.

additional_notes: A simple present-tense sentence: « il » = he, « mange » = eats, « souvent » = often, « du poisson » = (some) fish. « du » is the partitive article for an unspecified amount of a mass noun (like “some” in English). You can add a meal after it: « au dîner / au souper » (at dinner/supper) or « pour dîner / pour le souper » (for dinner/supper).
target_language_example: Il mange souvent du poisson le vendredi.
native_language_example: He often eats fish on Fridays.

meaning: "to me" after an impersonal "il" (as in il me reste… = “I have … left”).
additional_notes: Used in impersonal expressions like: il me reste + [noun/infinitive] (“I still have … left / there is … left for me”). Here, "il" doesn’t mean “he”; it’s a dummy subject like English “it/there.” The pronoun "me" comes before the verb: il me reste, il me faut, il me semble, etc.
target_language_example: Il me reste deux euros.
native_language_example: I have two euros left.

additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary for you. It literally means “it is necessary to me,” and is often followed by an infinitive (il me faut partir = I have to leave) or a noun (il me faut du temps = I need time). You can swap the indirect object pronoun: il te faut (you need), il lui faut (he/she needs), il nous faut (we need), etc.
target_language_example: Il me faut dormir un peu avant de partir.
native_language_example: I need to sleep a little before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary for you. It literally means “it is necessary to me,” and is often followed by an infinitive (il me faut partir = I have to leave) or a noun (il me faut du temps = I need time). You can swap the indirect object pronoun: il te faut (you need), il lui faut (he/she needs), il nous faut (we need), etc.
target_language_example: Il me faut dormir un peu avant de partir.
native_language_example: I need to sleep a little before leaving.

meaning: "I need (some)" / "I must have (some)" (followed by a plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to express a necessity or requirement: literally “it is necessary to me.” Common in speech and writing. Use **des** before a plural noun meaning “some” (des détails, des outils). For one thing, use **il me faut un/une…**; for an unspecified amount with an uncountable noun, use **il me faut du/de la/de l’…**.
target_language_example: Il me faut des informations avant de décider.
native_language_example: I need some information before deciding.

meaning: "I need some" / "I require (some)" (with a masculine or uncountable noun).
additional_notes: Uses the expression « il faut » (“it’s necessary”) + an indirect object pronoun: « il me faut… » = “I need…”. « du » is the partitive article, used for an unspecified amount of something (often an uncountable or “mass” noun), e.g. « du dentifrice » (some toothpaste), « du temps » (some time). With other nouns you’ll switch the partitive: « de la » (feminine), « de l’ » (before vowel sound), « des » (plural). You can also add an infinitive clause: « Il me faut du temps pour + infinitif » = “I need time to…”.
target_language_example: Il me faut du courage pour lui parler.
native_language_example: I need some courage to talk to him.

additional_notes: "Il me faut" is a common way to say you need something (often in a more formal or firm way than "j’ai besoin de"). It literally means “it is necessary for me.” The thing needed comes after it: "il me faut un/une + noun" (e.g., "il me faut une carte"). You can also change the person: "il te faut..." (you need), "il lui faut..." (he/she needs), "il nous faut..." (we need), etc.
target_language_example: Pour m’inscrire, il me faut un passeport.
native_language_example: To register, I need a passport.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something: literally “it is necessary to me.” The word after "une" must be a feminine noun (une adresse, une signature). For a masculine noun, use "il me faut un...". Often sounds a bit more formal/insistent than "j’ai besoin d’une...".
target_language_example: Il me faut une minute pour finir.
native_language_example: I need a minute to finish.

additional_notes: Used to say what remains for you (time, things to do, pages, money, etc.). The verb is **rester** (“to remain”), and **me** indicates it’s remaining *for me*. It’s often followed by a quantity: **Il me reste trois pages (à lire)**, **Il me reste combien de temps ?** You can add **encore** (“still”) for emphasis: **Il me reste encore...**.
target_language_example: Il me reste dix minutes avant de partir.
native_language_example: I have ten minutes left before leaving.

meaning: “it seems to me that…” / “I think (that)…” (not completely certain).
additional_notes: Used to give your personal impression or opinion, often with some uncertainty (like “I feel like…” or “I think…”). It’s commonly followed by the indicative: « Il me semble que tu as raison. » You can also use it without « que »: « Il me semble que oui / non. »
target_language_example: Il me semble que le train est en retard.
native_language_example: I think the train is late.

additional_notes: Basic negation with the verb être (“to be”): **il + ne + est + pas**. In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: **Il est pas…**. **Il** can mean “he” (a person) or “it” (a thing/idea), depending on context. Often followed by an adjective (**Il n’est pas normal**), an adverb (**Il n’est pas loin**), or a prepositional phrase (**Il n’est pas à toi**).
target_language_example: Il n’est pas disponible aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: He/It isn’t available today.

meaning: start of a negation with “y” (“there isn’t/aren’t…”, “he doesn’t… (about it)”).
additional_notes: “Il n’y…” is most commonly the beginning of the negative form of **il y a** (“there is/there are”): **il n’y a pas de…** (“there isn’t/aren’t any…”), **il n’y aura pas…** (“there won’t be…”), **il n’y avait…** (“there wasn’t/weren’t…”). It can also appear with other verbs that use **y** to mean “there” or “about it,” e.g. **il n’y connaît rien** (“he doesn’t know anything about it”). Often followed by **en** in expressions like **il n’y en a pas** (“there aren’t any”).
target_language_example: Il n’y a pas de place ici.
native_language_example: There isn’t any space here.

meaning: "there isn't/aren't" (negative form of "il y a" = "there is/are").
additional_notes: Usually completed with a negative word like **pas** (not) or **plus** (no longer): **il n'y a pas...** = "there isn't/aren't...", **il n'y a plus...** = "there is/are no more...". With **que** it often means "only": **Il n'y a pas que lui** = "It’s not only him"; **Il n'y a plus que nous** = "There’s only us left".
target_language_example: Il n'y a plus de café.
native_language_example: There’s no more coffee.

additional_notes: Negative form of **il y a** (“there is/there are”). Used to say something doesn’t exist or isn’t available: **Il n’y a pas de…** (“There is no/There aren’t any…”). Often appears in set patterns like **Il n’y a pas longtemps** (“not long ago”), **Il n’y a pas mieux** (“there’s nothing better”), and with **que**: **Il n’y a pas que…** (“it’s not only…”).
target_language_example: Il n’y a pas de place ici.
native_language_example: There isn’t any room here.

meaning: "there is no / there are no" (there isn’t any).
additional_notes: Negative form of "il y a" (there is/there are), used to say something doesn’t exist or isn’t present. It’s followed by a noun; with plural nouns it still uses "de" (not "des"): "Il n’y a pas de fenêtres". If the noun starts with a vowel or silent h, "de" becomes "d’": "Il n’y a pas d’eau".
target_language_example: Désolé, il n’y a pas de place ici.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s no space here.

additional_notes: Used to express limitation or exclusivity (“only”). Often followed by a noun (Il n’y a que des enfants), a pronoun (Il n’y a que lui), or a relative clause with "qui" (Il n’y a que lui qui sache = only he knows). With people you can list: Il n’y a que toi et moi (only you and me). Note the verb agreement in the relative clause: Il n’y a que toi qui comptes (because "toi" = you, so "tu comptes").
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, il n’y a que nous ici.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s only us here.

meaning: It’s only us / there’s only us.
additional_notes: Built on the common structure « il n’y a que … » = « there is only … / nothing but … ». « Nous » is the stressed pronoun here (like « only us », not « we »). You can add place/time/number: « Il n’y a que nous ici » (only us here), « Il n’y a que nous deux » (only the two of us).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il n’y a que nous dans la salle.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s only us in the room.

additional_notes: Built from "il y a" (there is/there are) + the negation "ne ... rien" (nothing). It can be followed by extra details, e.g. "il n'y a rien de mieux" (there’s nothing better) or a place: "il n'y a rien dehors" (there’s nothing outside). In casual speech, "ne" is often dropped: "il y a rien".
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il n’y a rien à craindre.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there’s nothing to be afraid of.

meaning: "there is nothing (…)", used before an adjective (often in comparisons).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to say that nothing has that quality: « Il n'y a rien de bien » (“There’s nothing good”). Very common in comparisons like « Il n'y a rien de mieux/meilleur » (“There’s nothing better”). It’s often followed by a complement: « Il n'y a rien de mieux que ça » (“There’s nothing better than that”).
target_language_example: Il n'y a rien de plus simple.
native_language_example: There’s nothing simpler.

meaning: "he/it doesn’t…" (start of a negation with il + ne…).
additional_notes: Used to begin French negative structures with the subject il (“he/it”). It’s usually completed by a second negative word: ne…pas (not), ne…plus (no longer / no more), ne…jamais (never), ne…rien (nothing), etc. In writing and careful speech, ne is often kept; in casual speech it’s often dropped ("il revient pas"), but learners should know the full form. Also note ne…que means “only” (e.g., "Il ne vient ici que…" = "He only comes here…").
target_language_example: Il ne mange pas de viande.
native_language_example: He doesn’t eat meat.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression with *falloir* ("to be necessary"). It gives a general rule or strong advice (not aimed at a specific person), followed by an infinitive: *Il ne faut jamais + infinitif* (e.g., *Il ne faut jamais abandonner*).
target_language_example: Il ne faut jamais parler au conducteur pendant qu’il conduit.
native_language_example: You must never talk to the driver while he’s driving.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression based on « il faut » (= “it is necessary”). With « ne … pas », it becomes a negative rule or advice: “one must not / you shouldn’t.” Often used for general instructions, warnings, or prohibitions (not about a specific person). You can add an infinitive after it: « Il ne faut pas + verbe » (e.g., parler, y aller).
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas oublier ton passeport.
native_language_example: You mustn’t forget your passport.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *falloir* to express a strong prohibition or warning. It’s followed by the subjunctive: *Il ne faut pas que tu oublies* (“You mustn’t forget”). Often used to say something should not happen.
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas que tu arrives en retard.
native_language_example: You mustn’t arrive late.

additional_notes: Negative form of the verb pouvoir ("can/to be able to"): il + ne ... pas + peut. Depending on context, il can mean a specific "he" or an impersonal "it" (as in "Il ne peut pas y avoir..." = "There can't be..."). In speech, ne is often dropped: "il peut pas".
target_language_example: Il ne peut pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: He can't come tonight.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of pouvoir (pouvait), often describing an ongoing inability or repeated situation in the past ("he couldn’t sleep", "he couldn’t walk any farther"). It’s followed by an infinitive: il ne pouvait pas + verb (dormir, ouvrir, marcher, etc.).
target_language_example: Il ne pouvait pas venir ce soir-là.
native_language_example: He couldn’t come that evening.

additional_notes: "Il" is the subject pronoun (he/it). "Nous" is an object pronoun meaning "us" and is placed before the verb in French: "Il nous aide" = "He helps us." Depending on the verb, "nous" can mean "us" as a direct object (he sees us) or indirect object (he talks to us). In expressions like "Il nous tarde de...", French literally says "It is long for us to..." but the natural translation is "We can't wait to..." / "We're looking forward to...".
target_language_example: Il nous appelle ce soir.
native_language_example: He’s calling us tonight.

meaning: “he … us” (past tense), or in “il nous a fallu…”: “it took us / we needed …”.
additional_notes: Very common pattern in the passé composé with avoir: il (he) + nous (to us / us) + a (has) + past participle → “He [verb] us” (e.g., il nous a aidés = he helped us). With the verb falloir, French uses an impersonal subject il: il nous a fallu + time/thing + infinitive = “it took us … to … / we needed … to …”.
target_language_example: Il nous a fallu deux heures pour arriver.
native_language_example: It took us two hours to get there.

meaning: we need / we have to (it is necessary for us).
additional_notes: From the impersonal verb « falloir » (only used as « il faut » + infinitive or noun). « Il nous faut + infinitive » = “we have to + verb” (Il nous faut décider…). « Il nous faut + noun/pronoun » = “we need + noun” (Il nous faut encore du temps / Il nous faut les arrêter). « Nous » can change: il me faut (I need), il lui faut (he/she needs), il leur faut (they need).
target_language_example: Il nous faut partir tout de suite.
native_language_example: We need to leave right away.

meaning: “we need to” (used before a reflexive verb: “we need to [do something] ourselves/to ourselves”).
additional_notes: This is the start of the structure **Il nous faut + infinitive** = “We need to / We have to…”. Here, the next verb is reflexive, so you add **nous** again as the reflexive pronoun: **Il nous faut nous + verb** (e.g., *il nous faut nous dépêcher*). In everyday speech, people often say **On doit…** or **Il faut qu’on…** instead.
target_language_example: Il nous faut nous dépêcher si on veut arriver à l’heure.
native_language_example: We need to hurry if we want to arrive on time.

meaning: we need / we have to (it is necessary for us).
additional_notes: From the impersonal verb « falloir » (only used as « il faut » + infinitive or noun). « Il nous faut + infinitive » = “we have to + verb” (Il nous faut décider…). « Il nous faut + noun/pronoun » = “we need + noun” (Il nous faut encore du temps / Il nous faut les arrêter). « Nous » can change: il me faut (I need), il lui faut (he/she needs), il leur faut (they need).
target_language_example: Il nous faut partir tout de suite.
native_language_example: We need to leave right away.

additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary: literally “it takes to us (some) …”, meaning “we need some …”. It’s followed by a plural noun: Il nous faut des + noun (e.g., des héros). In the negative, you’ll often see: Il ne nous faut pas de + noun.
target_language_example: Il nous faut des chaises pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: We need some chairs for everyone.

additional_notes: Built on the verb phrase « il faut » (impersonal: “it is necessary”). « Il nous faut un + noun » means “we need a + noun.” The object pronoun changes with who needs it: « il me faut… » (I need…), « il te faut… » (you need…), « il lui faut… » (he/she needs…), « il leur faut… » (they need…).
target_language_example: Pour ce travail, il nous faut un ordinateur.
native_language_example: For this job, we need a computer.

meaning: "it is not necessary that" / "you don’t need to…"
additional_notes: Used to say something is not required. It is commonly followed by the subjunctive (e.g., que tu sois, que vous soyez). It can reassure someone or remove an obligation: “You don’t have to…”.
target_language_example: Il n’est pas nécessaire que tu viennes demain.
native_language_example: You don’t need to come tomorrow.

meaning: “there is/are” (negative or in fixed patterns like “il n’y a pas…”, “il n’y a que…”)
additional_notes:
From the verb phrase “il y a” = “there is/there are.” Most often used as:
- “il n’y a pas de…” = “there is/are no …”
- “il n’y a pas + noun” can also mean “there isn’t/aren’t any …”
- “il n’y a que …” = “there is/are only …” (restriction)
- “quand il n’y a personne” = “when there is nobody.” Note: after “pas”, French often uses “de/d’” instead of “des” (e.g., “pas d’orange”).
target_language_example: Désolé, il n’y a plus de café.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s no more coffee.

meaning: "there is no / there are no" (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Used with a noun that starts with a vowel sound; it’s the shortened form of “il n’y a pas de”. Use it to say something doesn’t exist or isn’t present. Example pattern: “Il n’y a pas d’ + noun” (Il n’y a pas d’eau, d’air, d’orange).
target_language_example: Il n’y a pas d’eau ici.
native_language_example: There’s no water here.

additional_notes: Used to report information you heard (a rumor or something not confirmed), often without saying who told you. Common in conversation; can introduce either bad or good news. Similar to “on dit que…” (“they say that…”).
target_language_example: Il paraît que le train est en retard.
native_language_example: Apparently the train is late.

additional_notes: From the verb *parler* (to speak/to talk). Use **il parle + [language]** to say what he speaks (e.g., *il parle français / il parle le français*). Use **il parle trop vite / il parle bien anglais** to comment on how he speaks. In questions like *De quoi est-ce qu'il parle ?*, it means “What is he talking about?”
target_language_example: Il parle très bien français.
native_language_example: He speaks French very well.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about ability, permission, or possibility: il peut venir (he can come). In questions like « Où est-ce qu’il peut être ? », it often means 'where could he be?' (possibility/guess).
target_language_example: Il peut rester ici ce soir.
native_language_example: He can stay here tonight.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal subject il (“it”) with the verb pleuvoir (“to rain”). Commonly used with time expressions like depuis (“since/for”) to say how long it has been raining: Il pleut depuis hier = “It’s been raining since yesterday.”
target_language_example: Il pleut encore, prends un parapluie.
native_language_example: It’s still raining—take an umbrella.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of pleuvoir (“to rain”) to describe ongoing/background weather in the past, often setting the scene or describing a repeated situation (e.g., “It was raining when…”, “It used to rain every day”). The “il” is an impersonal “it” (not a real subject).
target_language_example: Quand je suis sorti, il pleuvait encore.
native_language_example: When I went out, it was still raining.

meaning: "he" + "s'" (= "se"), used with pronominal/reflexive verbs (often 'himself' or just part of the verb).
additional_notes: “S’” is the shortened form of “se” used before a vowel or silent h: il se → il s’ (il s’habille, il s’approche). It appears with reflexive actions (he dresses himself), reciprocal actions, and many pronominal verbs where “se/s’” is just required in French and isn’t always translated literally (il s’y connaît = he knows about it).
target_language_example: Il s'est levé tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: He got up early this morning.

meaning: “it’s about…” / “it’s a question of…” / “it is…” (used to identify what or who is being talked about).
additional_notes: Often used with **de**: **Il s’agit de + noun** = “It’s about / it’s a matter of + noun” (Il s’agit d’argent = “It’s about money”). With a person, it commonly appears in **(de) qui il s’agit**: **Je sais de qui il s’agit** = “I know who it is / who you mean.” This expression is impersonal (it doesn’t refer to a specific “he”).
target_language_example: De quoi s’agit-il exactement ?
native_language_example: What exactly is it about?

meaning: 'it's about' / 'it's a matter of' / 'this is' (used to introduce what something is).
additional_notes: Used mainly in more formal or neutral contexts to specify the subject or nature of something: Il s'agit de + noun (or de + infinitive). It doesn’t mean “it acts” in the normal sense of agir; think of it as “the point is / we’re talking about…”. Often used to clarify: « Il s'agit d'autre chose » = “It’s something else.”
target_language_example: De quoi parle ce document ? Il s'agit d'un contrat.
native_language_example: What is this document about? It's a contract.

meaning: 'it’s about…' / 'it’s a matter of…' / 'this is…' (introducing what or who something is about).
additional_notes: Impersonal, fairly formal phrase used to identify or specify the topic/subject. Often followed by a noun/pronoun (Il s’agit de mon fils. = This is my son.) or by an infinitive (Il s’agit de comprendre. = The point is to understand.). Usually used in explanations, presentations, or official contexts rather than casual speech.
target_language_example: De quoi s’agit-il ? Il s’agit d’une erreur.
native_language_example: What is it about? It’s a mistake.

meaning: “he … it/from it” (se + en), used with certain verbs.
additional_notes: “S’en” is the combination of the reflexive pronoun (se → s’, “himself”) + en (“of it / from it,” often replacing “de ça / de…”). It appears in many fixed verb patterns, so you translate the whole verb, not word-by-word. Common ones from your examples: s’en sortir = to manage / get through; s’en prendre à quelqu’un = to take it out on someone / attack someone; s’en occuper = to take care of it; s’en souvenir = to remember it.
target_language_example: Il s'en sortira malgré les difficultés.
native_language_example: He’ll get through it despite the difficulties.

meaning: 'he has' (used with reflexive/pronominal verbs in the past: “he …ed himself/got …”).
additional_notes: This is the start of a reflexive verb in the passé composé: il + se → s’ + être (s’est). It’s followed by a past participle: il s’est excusé (he apologized), il s’est évanoui (he fainted), il s’est disputé (he argued), il s’est moqué (he made fun), il s’est occupé de… (he took care of…). In English you often don’t translate the “se” literally; it just marks the verb as pronominal.
target_language_example: Il s'est levé tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: He got up early this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the verb "se passer" (= to happen), used impersonally with "il" as a dummy subject: "Il s'est passé quelque chose" (Something happened), "Il s'est passé beaucoup de choses" (A lot happened). Often followed by "quelque chose", "des choses", "des trucs" (more informal), etc.
target_language_example: Il s'est passé quelque chose d'étrange hier soir.
native_language_example: Something strange happened last night.

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to say an event occurred (often implying it was important, unexpected, or unclear). Uses the impersonal subject "il" + the verb "se passer" in the past (passé composé). It can be followed by details: "ici" (here), "d'autre" (something else), or "entre nous / entre vous" (something happened between us/you—often suggesting a personal, romantic, or tense situation).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas tout expliquer, mais il s'est passé quelque chose hier soir.
native_language_example: I can’t explain everything, but something happened last night.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French. It uses the verb phrase **se passer** (“to happen”) in the past tense (**il s’est passé…**) with **quoi** at the end. More neutral/formal versions: **Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?** or **Que s’est-il passé ?**. You can add details after it: **Il s’est passé quoi entre vous ?** (“What happened between you two?”).
target_language_example: Il s’est passé quoi pendant la réunion ?
native_language_example: What happened during the meeting?

additional_notes: Present tense of **savoir** (il sait). Used for knowing a fact, having information, or knowing how to do something. (For knowing a person/place, French often uses **connaître** instead.) Often followed by a question word: *il sait où/qui/ce que...*
target_language_example: Il sait que tu es ici.
native_language_example: He knows that you are here.

additional_notes: Used before a verb to show the subject (il = he) is doing the action to himself or that the verb is reflexive: il se lave (he washes himself), il se dépêche (he hurries). The pronoun se can also be part of a pronominal verb where English often doesn’t use “himself” (e.g., il se rend à… = he goes to…). In negatives, it becomes: il ne se … pas.
target_language_example: Il se prépare pour l’école.
native_language_example: He’s getting ready for school.

additional_notes: This is the passé simple (literary past) of "il se met à". It’s common in written stories, narration, and more formal/literary style. It’s followed by an infinitive: "il se mit à + infinitive" (e.g., "il se mit à pleuvoir" = it started to rain). In everyday speech, you’ll usually see/hear "il s’est mis à" (passé composé) instead.
target_language_example: En entendant la nouvelle, il se mit à pleurer.
native_language_example: On hearing the news, he began to cry.

additional_notes: Past simple (literary/storytelling tense) of "il se met à pleuvoir". Used to describe a sudden beginning of rain, often with time adverbs like "soudain" (suddenly), "tout à coup" (all of a sudden), or "à peine" (hardly). In everyday speech, you’ll more often hear: "il s’est mis à pleuvoir" (it started to rain).
target_language_example: Tout à coup, il se mit à pleuvoir et nous avons couru nous abriter.
native_language_example: All of a sudden, it started to rain and we ran to take shelter.

additional_notes: Used to say that events are happening (often unexpected, strange, or serious). Very common with an indefinite subject like "Il se passe quelque chose…" (Something is happening…) or in a question: "Il se passe quoi ?" (What’s going on?). Here, "il" is an impersonal/dummy subject (it doesn’t refer to a person), and "se passer" means “to happen,” not “to pass.”
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce qu’il se passe ici ?
native_language_example: What’s going on here?

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal "il" (it) with "se passer" (to happen). Often used when you suspect something is happening, sometimes something unusual or important. You can add a place with "ici / à la maison / entre vous".
target_language_example: Je pense qu'il se passe quelque chose dans le bureau.
native_language_example: I think something is going on in the office.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French. Literally “what is happening,” using se passer (“to happen”). You can add a place: « Il se passe quoi ici ? » (“What’s happening here?”). In a conditional question it can mean “what happens if…”: « Si je lis pas ça, il se passe quoi ? » (“If I don’t read that, what happens?”). More standard/written: « Que se passe-t-il ? »
target_language_example: Hé, il se passe quoi dehors ?
native_language_example: Hey, what’s going on outside?

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It is followed by the subjunctive (e.g., « il se peut que je sois… », « il se peut qu’il vienne… »). Often interchangeable with « il est possible que », though « il se peut que » is very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Il se peut que nous soyons en retard à cause du trafic.
native_language_example: We might be late because of traffic.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It’s followed by the subjunctive (e.g., *il se peut que je sois / que je doive*). Common in polite, careful speech; in casual French you’ll also hear *peut-être que je…* or *je peux… / je pourrais…* depending on meaning.
target_language_example: Il se peut que je ne puisse pas venir demain.
native_language_example: I might not be able to come tomorrow.

meaning: 'it’s possible that you…' / 'you may…' (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. After "il se peut que", French uses the subjunctive mood (e.g., "vous ayez", "vous fassiez", "vous restiez"). Often translates as "it may be that you…" or simply "you might…" in English.
target_language_example: Il se peut que vous soyez en retard à cause du trafic.
native_language_example: You might be late because of traffic.

meaning: "it might be that" / "it could be that" (expresses possibility).
additional_notes: Used to say something is possible but not certain. It’s fairly formal/neutral, and it is normally followed by the subjunctive: « Il se pourrait que ce soit… », « …que tu aies… », « …que vous soyez… ».
target_language_example: Il se pourrait que le train ait du retard.
native_language_example: The train might be late.

meaning: "he was standing" / "he was positioned" (was staying in a certain posture or place).
additional_notes: Imperfect of the verb "se tenir" (reflexive). Used to describe someone’s posture or where they were located for a period of time. It’s often followed by details like "debout" (standing up), "contre" (against), or a place/distance: "à quelques mètres de moi" (a few meters from me).
target_language_example: Il se tenait près de la porte et attendait en silence.
native_language_example: He was standing near the door and waiting in silence.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a fact (often unexpected or relevant to the situation), similar to “it so happens that…”. It’s followed by a clause with que: « Il se trouve que + [subject] + [verb] ». It can also be used as a short reply: « Il se trouve que oui/non » (“It turns out yes/no”).
target_language_example: Il se trouve que j’ai déjà réservé une table.
native_language_example: It turns out I already booked a table.

additional_notes: Used to express an impression or something that appears true (often with some uncertainty). It can be personal ("Il semble heureux" = "He seems happy") or impersonal with "il semble que + subjunctive" ("Il semble que ça ait cours..." = "It seems that it's common..."). With negation and infinitives, you often see: "Il semble ne pas..." / "Il semble ne rien...".
target_language_example: Il semble que le train soit en retard.
native_language_example: It seems that the train is late.

additional_notes: Used to express an impression or conclusion based on what you see/know, not full certainty. Often followed by the subjunctive in more formal French (e.g., « Il semble que Jeanne ait… »), but in everyday speech you may hear the indicative (« Il semble que Jeanne a… »). Can also be shortened to « Il semble que oui/non » (“it seems so/not”).
target_language_example: Il semble que le train ait du retard.
native_language_example: It seems that the train is delayed.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a future state/identity/quality: *Il sera là* (he’ll be there), *Il sera un bon mari* (he’ll be a good husband). With negation, standard French is *Il ne sera pas…* (often spoken as *Il sera pas…*). Also appears in impersonal/passive-style phrases like *Il sera exigé de vous…* = “You will be required to…”.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il sera prêt demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’ll be ready tomorrow.

meaning: "you just need to" / "all you have to do is".
additional_notes: Used to say that something is enough to achieve a result, often implying it’s easy or requires only that one action. Structure: il suffit de + infinitive (Il suffit d’appeler). Can also be followed by "pour" + infinitive to state the purpose: Il suffit d’appuyer ici pour commencer.
target_language_example: Pour ouvrir la porte, il suffit de tourner la clé.
native_language_example: To open the door, you just have to turn the key.

additional_notes: Contraction of "il te a" → "il t'a" before a vowel sound. Common in the passé composé: "il t'a parlé" = "he spoke to you" / "he has spoken to you"; "il t'a fait quelque chose ?" = "did he do something to you?" The meaning depends on the past participle that follows (parlé, posé, fait, etc.).
target_language_example: Il t'a envoyé un message hier soir.
native_language_example: He sent you a message last night.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *dire*: **il a dit** = “he said/told”. **t'** is short for **te** (“to you”). Often used in questions with rising intonation: **Il t'a dit ?** = “Did he tell you?” You can add what was said with **que...** (“that...”) or ask for details: **Il t'a dit quoi ?** (“What did he tell you?”).
target_language_example: Il t'a dit quand il arrive ?
native_language_example: Did he tell you when he’s arriving?

additional_notes: "Il" can mean "he" or "it" (and sometimes an impersonal "it" in set phrases). "Te" is an object pronoun meaning "to you" (informal singular). Common in expressions like "il te faut…" (you need…) and "il te reste…" (you have … left / … is left for you), and with verbs like "parler à" → "il te parle" (he’s talking to you).
target_language_example: Il te manque deux euros.
native_language_example: You’re missing two euros / You need two more euros.

additional_notes: Impersonal structure with the verb *falloir*: **il faut** + indirect object (**te**) + infinitive. It expresses necessity/requirement and is a bit more emphatic than *tu dois* in some contexts. Often followed by an infinitive: *Il te faut partir*, *Il te faut étudier*.
target_language_example: Il te faut dormir un peu si tu veux être en forme demain.
native_language_example: You need to sleep a bit if you want to be in shape tomorrow.

additional_notes: Impersonal structure with the verb *falloir*: **il faut** + indirect object (**te**) + infinitive. It expresses necessity/requirement and is a bit more emphatic than *tu dois* in some contexts. Often followed by an infinitive: *Il te faut partir*, *Il te faut étudier*.
target_language_example: Il te faut dormir un peu si tu veux être en forme demain.
native_language_example: You need to sleep a bit if you want to be in shape tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that something is pleasing to someone (with the verb "plaire" = "to please"). It often refers to a thing, idea, name, etc.: « Il te plaît, ce nom ? » = “Do you like that name?” Don’t confuse with « s’il te plaît » (with s’), which means “please” (as in a polite request).
target_language_example: Ce cadeau, il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Do you like this gift?

additional_notes: "Il" = "he" and "travaille" is the present tense of "travailler" (to work). Use it to talk about someone's job, where they work ("Il travaille dans un hôpital"), what field they work in ("dans le domaine de..."), or how much they work ("du matin au soir" = all day; "à peine" = barely/hardly).
target_language_example: Il travaille aujourd'hui, donc il ne peut pas venir.
native_language_example: He's working today, so he can't come.

additional_notes: From the verb *aller* (“to go”): *il va* = “he goes/ he’s going.” Very often it’s used for the **near future** (*futur proche*): **il va + infinitive** (“he’s going to + verb”): *Il va vomir* (“He’s going to throw up”), *Il va vous recevoir* (“He’s going to see/receive you”). With *manquer*: *Il va me manquer* = “I’m going to miss him / He’s going to be missed by me.” In the fixed phrase **il va y avoir**, it’s impersonal and means “there is going to be”: *Il va y avoir une enquête* (“There’s going to be an investigation”).
target_language_example: Attention, il va tomber !
native_language_example: Watch out, he’s going to fall!

meaning: "he/it is going to do/make"; also "the weather is going to be" (talking about weather).
additional_notes: This is the futur proche: aller (il va) + infinitive (faire) to talk about something that’s going to happen soon. "Il" can mean "he" (about a person) or an impersonal "it" (especially with weather: "Il va faire quel temps ?" = "What’s the weather going to be like?"). In questions you’ll often see: "Il va faire quoi ?" (What’s he going to do?) and "Il va faire quel temps ?" (What will the weather be like?).
target_language_example: Demain, il va faire beau, alors on va sortir.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, it’s going to be nice out, so we’re going to go out.

meaning: "we're going to have to" / "it will be necessary to" (soon).
additional_notes: Impersonal expression using the near future of falloir ("to be necessary"). It means that something must be done, often implying obligation or necessity. Common patterns: il va falloir + infinitive (Il va falloir attendre.) and il va falloir que + subjunctive (Il va falloir que tu viennes.).
target_language_example: Il va falloir partir maintenant.
native_language_example: We’re going to have to leave now.

meaning: “(someone) will have to …” / “it’s going to be necessary to …”.
additional_notes: Impersonal expression of necessity: “il” doesn’t refer to a person (it’s like “it” in “it’s necessary”). Very common to say something must be done soon or in the near future. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive: il va falloir que je parle / que tu acceptes / qu’on fasse, etc. Often used when the situation leaves no real choice.
target_language_example: Il va falloir que nous partions tôt demain.
native_language_example: We’ll have to leave early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to predict upcoming rain. Very common with a time marker like "demain" (tomorrow), "ce soir" (tonight), or "dans la soirée" (later in the evening). "Il" here is an impersonal subject (it doesn’t refer to a person).
target_language_example: Prends un parapluie : il va pleuvoir.
native_language_example: Take an umbrella: it’s going to rain.

meaning: "something is going to happen" (it’s about to happen).
additional_notes: From the near future: "aller" (va) + "se passer" (to happen). It’s often used with "quelque chose" to suggest an event is coming soon, sometimes with a feeling of worry or anticipation: "Il va se passer quelque chose (de grave)." You’ll also hear it in questions: "Il va se passer quoi ?" = "What’s going to happen?"
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il ne va rien se passer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: nothing is going to happen.

meaning: “there is/are going to be” (there will be).
additional_notes: Very common way to say something will happen/exist soon. Built from "il va" (it is going to) + "y avoir" (to be/there to be). The thing that will exist comes after: "Il va y avoir + noun". Often used with quantities: "beaucoup de…", "des…", "de l’…".
target_language_example: Il va y avoir un problème si on arrive en retard.
native_language_example: There’s going to be a problem if we arrive late.

additional_notes: An impersonal expression used to give advice or say what is preferable. Often followed by an infinitive (Il vaut mieux partir.) or by "que" + subjunctive (Il vaut mieux que je reste.).
target_language_example: Il vaut mieux que tu prennes un taxi.
native_language_example: You’d better take a taxi.

additional_notes: Used to recommend the best option or warn someone. It’s impersonal ("il" doesn’t refer to a person). It is usually followed by the subjunctive: « Il vaut mieux que tu restes ici. » / « Il vaut mieux que je vous parle franchement. » You can make it negative: « Il vaut mieux que tu ne le saches pas. »
target_language_example: Il vaut mieux que nous partions maintenant.
native_language_example: We’d better leave now.

additional_notes: "Il" = "he" and "veut" is the present tense of "vouloir" (to want). Often followed by an infinitive (Il veut devenir…, Il veut étudier…) or by "que" + a sentence (Il veut qu’on… = He wants us/people to…). The negative is "il ne veut pas" (he doesn’t want to).
target_language_example: Il veut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: He wants to leave now.

additional_notes: From the verb « venir » (to come). It can describe movement toward someone/something (« Il vient droit vers le pont. »). Very common patterns: « il vient de + place » = he comes from (« Il vient d'une ferme… »); « il vient de + infinitive » = he has just done something (« Il vient d'entrer… », « Il vient juste de te donner… »); « il vient voir + quelqu’un » = he comes to see someone (« Il vient me voir… »).
target_language_example: Il vient avec nous ce soir.
native_language_example: He’s coming with us tonight.

meaning: "he comes from" or "he has just (done something)".
additional_notes: 1) With a place/person/thing after it, it means origin: « Il vient de Gênes. » = he comes from Genoa. 2) With an infinitive (verb) after it, « venir de + infinitif » expresses the recent past: « Il vient de prier. » = he just prayed / he has just prayed. The subject can change (je/tu/il/elle/on/nous/vous/ils) but the structure stays the same.
target_language_example: Il vient de finir ses devoirs.
native_language_example: He has just finished his homework.

additional_notes: "Il" = "he" and "vit" is the present-tense form of "vivre" (to live). Used to say where someone lives (il vit en ville, il vit au coin), or who they live with (il vit avec ses parents). Note that "vit" is pronounced like "vee" (silent t).
target_language_example: Il vit à Paris depuis trois ans.
native_language_example: He has been living in Paris for three years.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (imparfait): it often describes an ongoing desire in the past, a repeated wish, or a background intention. Very common in questions like « Qu’est-ce qu’il voulait ? » (“What did he want?”) and « Qu’est-ce qu’il voulait dire ? » (“What did he mean?”). With « que + subjunctive »: « Il voulait que… » = “He wanted (that) …”.
target_language_example: Il voulait que je vienne avec lui.
native_language_example: He wanted me to come with him.

additional_notes: Impersonal structure with the verb falloir: "il faut" = "it is necessary". "Il vous faut + infinitive" means "you need/have to + verb" and addresses "vous" (you, formal or plural). In speech you may also hear "il vous faut + noun" (you need + a thing).
target_language_example: Il vous faut être patient pour apprendre le français.
native_language_example: You need to be patient to learn French.

additional_notes: Formal way to say something is necessary for “you” (vous). It’s built from falloir (“to be necessary”): il faut + indirect object (vous) + infinitive (être). Adjective agreement changes depending on who is “you” (ex: préparé/préparée/préparés). Less formal alternatives: « vous devez être… », « il faut que vous soyez… ».
target_language_example: Il vous faut être attentifs pendant la visite.
native_language_example: You need to be attentive during the visit.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal verb phrase "il faut" (= it is necessary). "Il vous faut" means "you need" (addressing one person with "vous" or multiple people). It’s followed by an infinitive: "être" (to be), then "davantage" (more), and typically an adjective that agrees with who you’re talking to (ex: organisé/organisée/organisés/organisées; patient/patiente/patients/patientes).
target_language_example: Il vous faut être davantage prudents sur la route.
native_language_example: You need to be more careful on the road.

additional_notes: Built with the impersonal verb « falloir »: « il faut » = “it is necessary / you must”. « Il vous faut… » is a polite/formal way to tell someone what they need to do. It’s typically followed by an infinitive (« être ») and then « plus » + an adjective. The adjective agrees with the person you’re talking to: organisée/patiente/polie (feminine singular), patient/poli (masculine singular), patientes/polies (feminine plural), patients (masculine plural or mixed group).
target_language_example: Pour ce travail, il vous faut être plus attentifs.
native_language_example: For this job, you need to be more attentive.

additional_notes: Impersonal structure with the verb falloir: "il faut" = "it is necessary". "Il vous faut + infinitive" means "you need/have to + verb" and addresses "vous" (you, formal or plural). In speech you may also hear "il vous faut + noun" (you need + a thing).
target_language_example: Il vous faut être patient pour apprendre le français.
native_language_example: You need to be patient to learn French.

additional_notes: Used when y replaces a place or something introduced with "à" (e.g., "à Paris" → "y"). It goes before the verb or auxiliary: "Il y est allé" = "He went there"; "Il y était" = "He was there". (Not to be confused with "il y a" = "there is/there are".)
target_language_example: Il y va demain.
native_language_example: He’s going there tomorrow.

additional_notes: Passé composé of the expression "il y a" ("there is/are"). Used to say that something existed or happened in the past, often to report an event: "Il y a eu un accident" (There was an accident). With plural nouns, English usually uses "there were" ("Il y a eu des problèmes" → There were problems). In questions you may hear "Il y a eu quoi ?" meaning "What happened?/What was there?" (quite conversational).
target_language_example: Il y a eu un problème hier soir.
native_language_example: There was a problem last night.

il y a eu beaucoup de

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a eu beaucoup de
meaning: “there were/there has been a lot of …”
additional_notes: Used to say that many people/things/events existed or happened. It’s the past form of “il y a” (there is/there are): present “il y a beaucoup de …” → past “il y a eu beaucoup de …”. “Eu” agrees with nothing here because “avoir” is used impersonally (the subject is “il”). Often followed by a plural noun, but it can also be used with uncountable nouns (e.g., “de la neige” → “beaucoup de neige”).
target_language_example: Il y a eu beaucoup de monde au concert hier soir.
native_language_example: There were a lot of people at the concert last night.
