additional_notes: Used to report that events, situations, or things occurred/existed in the past. It’s the past tense of "il y a" (there is/are) and is often followed by a plural noun: "Il y a eu des + nom(s)". Very common in news/reporting (e.g., changes, deaths, shootings, repercussions).
target_language_example: Il y a eu des problèmes pendant le vol.
native_language_example: There were some problems during the flight.

meaning: “there was a” / “there has been a” (something happened).
additional_notes: Used to say that an event occurred in the past. It’s the past tense of “il y a” (“there is/are”). Often followed by an event noun (un accident, un mariage, un scandale, un silence). With a specific time expression, it typically means simple past (“there was”); without one, it can translate as “there has been.”
target_language_example: Hier soir, il y a eu un accident sur l’autoroute.
native_language_example: Last night, there was an accident on the highway.

il y a eu un accident

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a eu un accident
additional_notes: Uses the past form of "il y a" ("there is/are") → "il y a eu" ("there was/were"). Very common for reporting an event that happened. You can add details with place/time: "devant la maison" (in front of the house), "ce matin" (this morning), "sur le bord de la route" (on the side of the road). You can also specify the type: "un accident de circulation" (a traffic accident).
target_language_example: Il y a eu un accident sur l'autoroute, alors on est en retard.
native_language_example: There was an accident on the highway, so we're late.

il y a eu un tremblement de terre

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a eu un tremblement de terre
additional_notes: Uses the past tense of « il y a » (il y a eu = “there was/there were”) to report that an event happened. « un tremblement de terre » means “an earthquake.” Often followed by a time (hier, ce matin) or a place (au Pérou).
target_language_example: Il y a eu un tremblement de terre cette nuit, mais personne n’a été blessé.
native_language_example: There was an earthquake last night, but nobody was hurt.

meaning: 'there was a' / 'there has been a' (something happened).
additional_notes: Past tense of "il y a" used to report that an event occurred. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (une enquête, une explosion). With a masculine noun, you’d use "il y a eu un". Common in news-style descriptions of events.
target_language_example: Il y a eu une panne de courant hier soir.
native_language_example: There was a power outage last night.

additional_notes: Used with "il y a" (= "there is/there are") to say there’s an additional thing, fact, or issue to mention or check. Often followed by "que..." to add details: "Il y a autre chose que tu devrais savoir." In a question ("Il y a autre chose ?"), it means “Is there anything else?”
target_language_example: Il y a autre chose dont je dois m'occuper ?
native_language_example: Is there anything else I need to take care of?

additional_notes: Used with a noun: « Il y a beaucoup de + nom » (Il y a beaucoup de travail.). It can also stand alone: « Il y a beaucoup en jeu » (“a lot is at stake”), or be followed by an infinitive with « à »: « Il y a beaucoup à faire » (“there’s a lot to do”).
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, il y a beaucoup de monde au musée.
native_language_example: Today, there are a lot of people at the museum.

additional_notes: Used to say that a large number/amount of something exists or is present. With a noun: « Il y a beaucoup de + nom » (e.g., beaucoup de touristes). With an uncountable idea like space, you can say « Il y a beaucoup de place » (“There is plenty of room”). After « beaucoup de », the noun is usually plural unless it’s uncountable.
target_language_example: Dans cette ville, il y a beaucoup de restaurants.
native_language_example: In this city, there are a lot of restaurants.

il y a beaucoup de choses

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a beaucoup de choses
meaning: “there are many things / a lot of things.”
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal expression “il y a” (“there is/are”) + “beaucoup de” (“a lot of”) + “choses” (“things”). Often followed by a relative clause with “qui/que/dont” to add details: “Il y a beaucoup de choses que…”, “Il y a beaucoup de choses dont…”. “Beaucoup de” stays the same for singular/plural nouns (unlike “many”).
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup de choses à apprendre quand on commence le français.
native_language_example: There are a lot of things to learn when you start French.

il y a beaucoup de choses que

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a beaucoup de choses que
additional_notes: Used to introduce a list or idea of many tasks, items, or questions that follow. It’s the pattern: il y a (there is/are) + beaucoup de choses (many things) + que + subject + verb. With "que", the next clause describes the things (e.g., things I need to do/buy/ask).
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup de choses que je dois finir avant demain.
native_language_example: There are many things that I need to finish before tomorrow.

il y a beaucoup de fleurs

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a beaucoup de fleurs
additional_notes: Uses the common structure “il y a” (“there is/there are”) + “beaucoup de” (“a lot of/many”) + a noun. You can swap in other nouns (Il y a beaucoup de monde = There are lots of people) or add adjectives after the noun (Il y a beaucoup de fleurs rouges = There are many red flowers).
target_language_example: Au printemps, il y a beaucoup de fleurs dans ce parc.
native_language_example: In spring, there are lots of flowers in this park.

il y a beaucoup de gens

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a beaucoup de gens
additional_notes: Used to say that many people are present somewhere. Often followed by a place: “Il y a beaucoup de gens + dans/à/sur…”. You can also use it by itself (“Il y a beaucoup de gens.”) to mean it’s crowded.
target_language_example: Le week-end, il y a beaucoup de gens au marché.
native_language_example: On weekends, there are a lot of people at the market.

additional_notes: Used to say that more alternatives exist. It’s typically followed by a plural noun: « Il y a d'autres options. » (There are other options.) You can also use it without a noun when it’s understood from context: « Il y en a d'autres. » (There are others.)
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : il y a d'autres possibilités.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there are other possibilities.

meaning: "there are / there is" + "some" (often before a noun, especially with an adjective).
additional_notes: Used to say that something exists/is present. With plural nouns, you often see "il y a des ..." (there are some ...), but it frequently becomes "il y a de + adjective + plural noun": "Il y a de jolies maisons". You also see it in common phrases like "Il y a de fortes/grandes chances" (= there’s a good chance / it’s quite likely). In "ce qu’il y a de mieux", it means “the best there is / the best possible.”
target_language_example: Il y a de bonnes raisons de partir tôt.
native_language_example: There are good reasons to leave early.

additional_notes: Used to state that water is present somewhere ("Il y a de l'eau ici / partout"). "De l'" is the partitive article meaning "some". In a question, intonation or "Est-ce qu'il y a de l'eau ?". In the negative, it usually becomes "Il n'y a pas d'eau."
target_language_example: Attention, il y a de l'eau par terre.
native_language_example: Careful, there’s water on the floor.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation still has a chance to improve or work out. You can add "pour + noun/pronoun" to mean "there is hope for ..." (e.g., "Il y a de l’espoir pour lui").
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il y a de l’espoir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there is hope.

additional_notes: Used to say that some amount of something exists or is present. It’s the “there is” structure (il y a) + a partitive article (de la) for feminine singular nouns that are treated as an uncountable substance or abstract idea: de la peinture, de la magie, de la force. With masculine singular it becomes "il y a du" (du feu), and with plural "il y a des".
target_language_example: Il y a de la neige sur la route.
native_language_example: There is some snow on the road.

additional_notes: Used to say that many things exist/are present. "De nombreuses" agrees with a feminine plural noun (e.g., chansons, explications, façons, rivières). With masculine plural nouns, use "il y a de nombreux" (e.g., de nombreux problèmes).
target_language_example: Il y a de nombreuses raisons de partir tôt.
native_language_example: There are many reasons to leave early.

additional_notes: Used to say that many of something exist or are present. It’s the phrase "il y a" (there is/are) + "de nombreux" (many) before a plural noun. "De nombreux" agrees with the noun: masculine plural "de nombreux" (parcs), feminine plural "de nombreuses" (animaux → masculine, but "de nombreuses choses").
target_language_example: Il y a de nombreux restaurants dans ce quartier.
native_language_example: There are many restaurants in this neighborhood.

meaning: “there’s enough / there’s something to …”; also “there’s reason to …”
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say there is enough of something or what’s needed to do it (Il y a de quoi manger = there’s something to eat / enough to eat). It can also mean there’s a good reason to feel a certain way (Il y a de quoi avoir peur / être fier = there’s reason to be scared / proud). On its own (Il y a de quoi.), it can mean “That’s true / fair enough” or “There’s plenty (of it),” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, il y a de quoi manger pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, there’s enough to eat for everyone.

additional_notes: Used to say that multiple things exist or are present. It’s the plural form of "il y a" + "des" (= "some" or plural "a/an"). Often followed by a plural noun: "Il y a des + noun". In negative sentences, "des" usually becomes "de": "Il n’y a pas de…".
target_language_example: Il y a des restaurants ouverts près d’ici.
native_language_example: There are some restaurants open near here.

meaning: years ago; a long time ago.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened several years in the past, often to emphasize that it was quite a long time ago. It can stand alone (Il y a des années !) or be followed by de cela / de ça (“ago / back then”).
target_language_example: On s’est rencontrés il y a des années, mais je me souviens encore de toi.
native_language_example: We met years ago, but I still remember you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or point out items, ideas, or facts in a general way. It’s often followed by an adjective (Il y a des choses importantes…), or by a relative clause with qui/que (Il y a des choses qui… / Il y a des choses que…).
target_language_example: Il y a des choses que je ne comprends pas.
native_language_example: There are things I don’t understand.

il y a des choses que

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a des choses que
additional_notes: Used to introduce an unspecified list of actions, facts, or information, followed by a relative clause with "que" (often with "je/tu/vous" + verb): "Il y a des choses que je dois faire" = "There are things I have to do." You can change the subject and verb after "que" depending on who is doing/knowing/wanting the things.
target_language_example: Il y a des choses que nous devons discuter.
native_language_example: There are things we need to discuss.

additional_notes: Built from il y a (“there is/there are”) + des gens (“people/some people”). Use it to say that people are present in a place (Il y a des gens à l’intérieur.) or to make a general statement about certain people (Il y a des gens qui… = “There are people who…”). Note: you usually don’t say *il y a les gens*; for “the people” you’d use other structures (e.g., Les gens sont…).
target_language_example: Il y a des gens qui parlent anglais ici ?
native_language_example: Are there people who speak English here?

il y a des gens qui

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a des gens qui
additional_notes: Used to introduce the idea that some people do a certain thing or have a certain belief. Very common for general statements; it’s followed by a verb clause (e.g., il y a des gens qui + verb). Often implies “some people” rather than all people.
target_language_example: Il y a des gens qui n’aiment pas le café.
native_language_example: Some people don’t like coffee.

additional_notes: With a time unit, it means “two [days/weeks/months/years] ago”: Il y a deux mois. With a noun, it means “there are two …”: Il y a deux voitures. Often followed by a plural noun or a time unit.
target_language_example: Je l’ai rencontré il y a deux ans.
native_language_example: I met him two years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It often comes at the beginning or end of a sentence. The full pattern is "il y a + duration" (e.g., il y a trois jours = three days ago).
target_language_example: J'ai commencé ce travail il y a deux ans.
native_language_example: I started this job two years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It can come at the end of the sentence (Elle a disparu il y a deux jours.) or at the beginning (Il y a deux jours, ...).
target_language_example: On s'est vus il y a deux jours.
native_language_example: We saw each other two days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It often comes at the end of the sentence (e.g., « Je suis parti il y a deux mois. ») but can also be placed earlier. « Il y a… » + a time period (un jour, une semaine, deux ans, etc.) means “... ago.”
target_language_example: On s'est rencontrés il y a deux mois.
native_language_example: We met two months ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long before now something happened. It often comes at the end of the sentence: « Je suis arrivé il y a deux semaines. ». More generally, « il y a + length of time » means “... ago” (il y a trois jours = three days ago).
target_language_example: On a déménagé il y a deux semaines.
native_language_example: We moved two weeks ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It’s built from "il y a" (there is/ago) + a time expression; you can swap in other times (il y a deux jours, il y a trois semaines, il y a un an). Often placed at the end of the sentence: "Je l’ai vu il y a dix ans."
target_language_example: J’ai commencé le français il y a dix ans.
native_language_example: I started French ten years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say that some amount of something is present. It’s the phrase “il y a” (“there is/are”) + the partitive article: du (masc. singular), de la (fem. singular), de l’ (before a vowel/h), or des (plural). Often used for things you can’t easily count (work, fog, noise, sun, frost, movement, etc.).
target_language_example: Aujourd’hui, il y a du vent.
native_language_example: Today, there is some wind.

additional_notes: Used to say something still exists/is present, or that there are additional things left. Often followed by a noun: "Il y a encore des problèmes" (There are still problems). In questions like "Qu'est-ce qu'il y a encore ?", it means "What is it now?/What else is there?" depending on context.
target_language_example: Il y a encore du travail à faire.
native_language_example: There’s still work to do.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate number, amount, distance, or time. With a quantity: « Il y a environ 30 personnes » = there are about 30 people. With a time expression: « Il y a environ une heure/un an » = about an hour/a year ago.
target_language_example: Il y a environ vingt minutes, j’ai envoyé un message.
native_language_example: About twenty minutes ago, I sent a message.

additional_notes: Used with a definite noun (le/la/les) to point out that something exists or to introduce an item in a list or sequence (often like “first, there’s…”). The article changes with gender/number: il y a le musée, il y a la facture, il y a les billets.
target_language_example: Dans ce prix, il y a le petit-déjeuner.
native_language_example: In this price, there’s breakfast included.

meaning: there is/are little; not much; not many.
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say a small quantity exists or is available. With countable nouns (plural): “not many” (Il y a peu de chiens). With uncountable nouns: “not much” (Il y a peu de lait). Often implies “fewer than expected,” but can be neutral.
target_language_example: Il y a peu de temps avant le départ.
native_language_example: There isn't much time before departure.

additional_notes: Used to suggest a possibility that something exists. "Il y a" means "there is/are"; adding "peut-être" softens it to an uncertain guess ("maybe"). Often followed by a noun phrase like "quelque chose", "une solution", "un meilleur moyen".
target_language_example: Il y a peut-être une erreur dans ce document.
native_language_example: There might be a mistake in this document.

meaning: 'there are lots of' / 'there is plenty of'.
additional_notes: Uses the structure "il y a" (there is/are) + "plein de" (lots of/plenty of) + noun. Very common in spoken French to mean "a lot of"; can sound a bit informal compared with "beaucoup de". The noun after "de" is usually plural ("plein de choses"), but you can also use it with an uncountable idea like "plein de place" (plenty of space).
target_language_example: Il y a plein de bons restaurants dans ce quartier.
native_language_example: There are lots of good restaurants in this neighborhood.

meaning: “more than … ago” or “there’s more / there are more.”
additional_notes:
Common uses:
1) Time: "il y a plus de + duration" = “more than + duration ago” (e.g., "il y a plus d’un mois").
2) Adding information or comparing: "Et il y a plus." = “And there’s more.” / "Il y a plus important / plus grave" = “There’s something more important / more serious.” In these comparisons, "plus" is usually followed by an adjective or idea that’s being emphasized.
target_language_example: Il y a plus de deux ans, j’habitais à Lyon, et il y a plus : j’y retourne bientôt.
native_language_example: More than two years ago, I lived in Lyon—and there’s more: I’m going back soon.

meaning: 'there are more than' / 'there is more than'.
additional_notes: Used to say a quantity is greater than another quantity ("plus de + noun") or greater than a number ("plus de + number"). Often followed by "que" for comparisons: "Il y a plus de X que de Y" (more X than Y).
target_language_example: Il y a plus de trente personnes dans la salle.
native_language_example: There are more than thirty people in the room.

additional_notes: Used to say that more than one thing exists or is available. Often followed by a plural noun ("Il y a plusieurs possibilités") or by a plural noun + relative clause ("Il y a plusieurs étoiles qui..."). Note: "Il y a plusieurs années" can mean "several years ago" (time ago), depending on context.
target_language_example: Il y a plusieurs restaurants près d'ici.
native_language_example: There are several restaurants near here.

meaning: "four ... ago" or "there are four" (depending on context).
additional_notes:
Two common patterns:
1) Time ago: « il y a + duration » = “... ago” (e.g., « il y a quatre jours » = “four days ago”).
2) Existence/quantity: « il y a + number + noun » = “there is/are ...” (e.g., « il y a quatre chaises » = “there are four chairs”). « Il y a » is used for both “there is” and “there are.”
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé à Paris il y a quatre jours.
native_language_example: I arrived in Paris four days ago.

additional_notes: Uses the common structure "il y a" (there is/there are) + "quelqu'un" (someone). In a question (often said like "Il y a quelqu’un ?"), it can mean "Is anyone there?" or "Is someone here?". You can add a place (là-bas, à l’intérieur) or a clause ("qui arrive" = "who is arriving").
target_language_example: Il y a quelqu’un à la porte.
native_language_example: There’s someone at the door.

il y a quelqu'un qui veut

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelqu'un qui veut
meaning: "Someone wants to…" / "There’s someone who wants to…"
additional_notes: Used to tell someone that another person is asking to speak to them or see them (often in a phone call, at the door, or at reception). Follow it with an infinitive like parler (to talk) or voir (to see), and add the person pronoun: te (you, informal), vous (you, formal/plural), lui (him/her).
target_language_example: Il y a quelqu'un qui veut vous parler à l'accueil.
native_language_example: Someone wants to speak to you at reception.

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present somewhere (often when you’re not sure what it is). Commonly followed by a place phrase like “là-haut” (up there), “par là” (around there), “ici” (here), “dans la pièce” (in the room), etc.
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose derrière la porte.
native_language_example: There’s something behind the door.

il y a quelque chose d'autre

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelque chose d'autre
additional_notes: Used to add an extra point or mention an additional item. Common in conversation when remembering something or continuing a list. You can also vary it: "Il y a autre chose" is a common shorter version.
target_language_example: Attends, il y a quelque chose d'autre que je dois te dire.
native_language_example: Wait, there’s something else I need to tell you.

il y a quelque chose que

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelque chose que
additional_notes: Used to introduce an unspecified “something” followed by a relative clause with que. Often followed by verbs like devoir/devrait (“must/should”) or pouvoir (“can”). In a question, it can mean “Is there something I can do?” (often implying “to help”).
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose que je dois te dire.
native_language_example: There’s something I have to tell you.

il y a quelque chose qui

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelque chose qui
additional_notes: Used to point out that an unspecified thing exists or is happening, and it is followed by a relative clause with qui + a verb (qui vit, qui pue, qui vient, etc.). In questions, it can mean “Is there something you’d like?” or “Is something wrong/that you want?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose qui ne va pas ?
native_language_example: Is something wrong?

il y a quelque chose qui cloche

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a quelque chose qui cloche
additional_notes: Used when you feel there’s a problem, inconsistency, or malfunction, even if you can’t identify it yet. Often followed by "avec" + thing/person: "Il y a quelque chose qui cloche avec cette télé."
target_language_example: Il y a quelque chose qui cloche avec ton histoire : ça ne tient pas debout.
native_language_example: Something’s off with your story: it doesn’t add up.

meaning: "a few ... ago" or "there are a few ..."
additional_notes: Two common uses: (1) with a time word (jours/semaines/mois/années): "il y a quelques + time" = "a few + time ago". (2) as "il y a" meaning "there is/there are": "il y a quelques + plural noun" = "there are a few + noun". "Quelques" is always followed by a plural noun.
target_language_example: Il y a quelques minutes, j'étais dans le métro.
native_language_example: A few minutes ago, I was on the subway.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It can come at the end of the sentence (Elle est partie il y a quelques années.) or at the beginning as a time marker (Il y a quelques années, ...). Built from il y a (“there is/there are”) + quelques (“a few”) + années (“years”).
target_language_example: J’ai commencé le français il y a quelques années.
native_language_example: I started French a few years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. Literally “there is a few days,” but in French it means “X time ago” (il y a + duration). Often used with the past tense: Je suis arrivé / J’ai perdu / J’ai commencé…
target_language_example: On s'est parlé il y a quelques jours.
native_language_example: We talked a few days ago.

additional_notes: Used to express a large quantity. With countable nouns, it usually means “so many” (Il y a tant de gens). With uncountable nouns, it can mean “so much” (Il y a tant de bruit). Often followed by a noun; you can also use “tant de + nom + à + infinitif” (Il y a tant de choses à faire).
target_language_example: Il y a tant de choses à apprendre en français !
native_language_example: There are so many things to learn in French!

additional_notes: Used with the expression "il y a" (there is/are) plus "toujours" (always) to say something is always present or always happens. The noun that follows determines whether English uses "is" or "are" (e.g., "de la place" → "there is"; "des armes" → "there are").
target_language_example: Il y a toujours une solution.
native_language_example: There is always a solution.

il y a toujours quelque chose

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a toujours quelque chose
additional_notes: Built on **il y a** (“there is/are”) + **toujours** (“always”) + **quelque chose** (“something”). It can be neutral/positive (“there’s always something to do/learn”) or complaining/annoyed, especially with **avec toi** (“there’s always something with you”).
target_language_example: Avec cette appli, il y a toujours quelque chose à apprendre.
native_language_example: With this app, there’s always something to learn.

meaning: "there is always a..." (with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Built from the common structure "il y a" = "there is/there are" + "toujours" = "always" + "une" = "a" (feminine). It’s often used to express a general truth or reassurance: "There’s always a solution/way out/possibility." Change "une" to "un" for masculine nouns ("il y a toujours un..."), or to "des" for plurals ("il y a toujours des...").
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : il y a toujours une solution.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there’s always a solution.

additional_notes: Used with a number to state how many things exist or are present: “il y a + number + (noun)”. It can refer to things in general (“There are three problems”) or in a specific place/situation (“There are three intelligent species on the planet”).
target_language_example: Dans cette ville, il y a trois musées.
native_language_example: In this city, there are three museums.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It’s built from "il y a" ("there is/are" but used for time = "ago") + a time expression ("trois ans"). Often placed at the end of the sentence: "Je suis arrivé il y a trois ans." You can also use it alone as a short answer to “When?”
target_language_example: J’ai commencé le français il y a trois ans.
native_language_example: I started French three years ago.

additional_notes: Used with a past event to say how long ago it happened. The pattern is: [past tense verb] + il y a + [time]. Example: « Je suis parti(e) il y a deux heures » = “I left two hours ago.”
target_language_example: J'ai commencé ce travail il y a trois jours.
native_language_example: I started this job three days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It typically goes after the verb (often in the past tense): « J’ai déménagé il y a trois mois. » You can swap the time amount: « il y a deux jours / une semaine / un an ».
target_language_example: J'ai commencé ce travail il y a trois mois.
native_language_example: I started this job three months ago.

meaning: there are too many / too much (of).
additional_notes: Used to say there is an excessive amount or number of something. Follow it with a noun: il y a trop de + nom. With plural countable nouns: « trop de + nom pluriel » (trop de villages). With uncountable nouns: « trop de + nom singulier » (trop de bruit). Often expresses complaint or frustration.
target_language_example: Il y a trop de monde dans le métro ce matin.
native_language_example: There are too many people on the subway this morning.

meaning: 'there is a' (used to say something exists or is located somewhere).
additional_notes: Very common way to point out the presence/existence of something. Often followed by a place phrase: « Il y a un arrêt de bus près d’ici. » In questions, use rising intonation or « Est-ce qu’il y a un… ? » For plural, you usually say « il y a des… » (there are…).
target_language_example: Il y a un café juste en face de la gare.
native_language_example: There’s a café right across from the train station.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. Very common with past tenses: « C’était il y a un an », « La maison a été construite il y a un an ». You can add precision with words like « environ » (about), or extend it: « il y a un an et demi » (a year and a half ago).
target_language_example: J’ai commencé ce travail il y a un an.
native_language_example: I started this job a year ago.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say that an additional/different one exists: "Il y a un autre chemin" (There’s another path). In questions, intonation or a question mark makes it "Is there another …?". Often followed by a noun (un autre chemin, un autre corps, un autre moyen, un autre type).
target_language_example: Il y a un autre endroit où on peut se rencontrer ?
native_language_example: Is there another place where we can meet?

il y a un besoin urgent de

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a un besoin urgent de
meaning: there is an urgent need for.
additional_notes: Used to say something is needed right away. It’s a formal, common structure: "il y a" (there is/are) + "un besoin urgent de" + noun (or "de" + infinitive if followed by a verb). Often followed by "davantage de" (more) or an uncountable noun: "de sang", "de logement", etc.
target_language_example: Il y a un besoin urgent de solutions concrètes.
native_language_example: There is an urgent need for practical solutions.

additional_notes: Uses the common structure “il y a …” to say that something exists or is present (“there is/are …”). You can add a place after it: “Il y a un chat dans la cuisine / sous la table / sur la table.” In speech, “Il y a” is often pronounced like “y a”.
target_language_example: Il y a un chat dehors.
native_language_example: There’s a cat outside.

meaning: “there is a big/large …” (introduces a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is located somewhere: **il y a** = “there is/there are”. **un grand** is the masculine singular form of “big/large”; it can also mean “tall” for people/things (e.g., a tall man, a tall tree). For a feminine noun, use **une grande** (e.g., *il y a une grande maison*).
target_language_example: Dans ce parc, il y a un grand arbre.
native_language_example: In this park, there is a big tree.

additional_notes: "Il y a" is the common way to say "there is/there are" in French. Add a place after it (e.g., "à la porte" = at the door, "dans le jardin" = in the garden, "ici" = here, "dehors" = outside). Often used to point out someone’s presence, sometimes with an adjective: "Il y a un homme bizarre…" = "There’s a strange man…".
target_language_example: Il y a un homme devant la maison.
native_language_example: There’s a man in front of the house.

additional_notes: Used to say that two people, things, or events are connected or related. Often followed by « entre … et … » (between … and …) or understood from context. « lien » can mean an emotional bond (between people) or a logical/causal connection (between ideas or events).
target_language_example: Je pense qu'il y a un lien entre ces deux histoires.
native_language_example: I think there is a connection between these two stories.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. The pattern is "il y a + time period" (e.g., il y a deux jours = two days ago). You can add "environ" to mean "about/roughly" (il y a un mois environ).
target_language_example: J'ai déménagé il y a un mois.
native_language_example: I moved a month ago.

meaning: a little while ago; it's been a while (since/that…).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened some time ago: « Il est parti il y a un moment. » = “He left a little while ago.” With « il y a un moment que + verb », it means “(someone) has been doing something for a while / it’s been a while since…”, often with an action still continuing now: « Il y a un moment qu'elle vous attend. » = “She’s been waiting for you for a while.”
target_language_example: J'ai envoyé le message il y a un moment.
native_language_example: I sent the message a little while ago.

meaning: "there is a small…" / "there is a little…"
additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present. It’s the phrase "il y a" (there is/there are) + an indefinite article (un/une/des) + the adjective "petit" (small/little). "Petit" must agree with the noun: un petit chien (masc.), une petite maison (fem.), des petits problèmes (plural). Often used to soften the idea of something negative: "un petit problème" = a minor problem.
target_language_example: Il y a un petit café au coin de la rue.
native_language_example: There’s a small café on the corner of the street.

additional_notes: Uses the common structure "il y a" (“there is/there are”) to point out that something is wrong. Often followed by "avec…" to specify what has an issue ("Il y a un problème avec les freins" = “There’s a problem with the brakes”). You can also say it on its own as a warning or to introduce bad news.
target_language_example: Il y a un problème avec la connexion internet.
native_language_example: There’s a problem with the internet connection.

meaning: “there is a” (introduces the existence/presence of a feminine singular thing).
additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present. It’s the feminine singular form of “il y a” + an indefinite article: “il y a un” (masculine) / “il y a une” (feminine). Very common for pointing things out (“Il y a une porte derrière.”) or introducing something new (“Il y a une dernière chose.”).
target_language_example: Il y a une erreur dans ce document.
native_language_example: There is a mistake in this document.

additional_notes: Used to say that another person/thing exists or is available. It must be followed by a noun (e.g., "Il y a une autre porte"). "Une autre" is feminine; for a masculine noun use "il y a un autre …" and for plural "il y a d’autres …".
target_language_example: Il y a une autre solution.
native_language_example: There is another solution.

meaning: “there is one thing…” / “one thing is…” (to introduce an important point).
additional_notes: Used to bring up a specific point, often followed by a relative clause: **il y a une chose que…** (“there’s one thing that…”), **il y a une chose dont…** (“there’s one thing about which… / that…”). Can also be said alone (**Il y a une chose.**) to create a pause before explaining.
target_language_example: Il y a une chose que je dois te dire.
native_language_example: There’s one thing I have to tell you.

il y a une chose que

target_language_multi_word_term: il y a une chose que
meaning: “There is one thing that …” / “There’s something that …”
additional_notes: Used to introduce a specific thing (often important) followed by a relative clause with que. Very common pattern: Il y a une chose que + subject + verb (e.g., je dois faire / tu dois savoir). You can swap une chose for quelque chose (“something”).
target_language_example: Il y a une chose que je veux te dire.
native_language_example: There’s one thing I want to tell you.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened (a point in the past). Often placed at the end of the sentence: «Tu as dit ça il y a une demi-heure.»
target_language_example: Je l’ai appelé il y a une demi-heure.
native_language_example: I called him half an hour ago.

additional_notes: Used to point out that two things are not the same. Very often followed by "entre X et Y" (between X and Y): "Il y a une différence entre toi et moi." You can add adjectives for emphasis (e.g., "une différence considérable / fondamentale").
target_language_example: Il y a une différence entre ce que tu dis et ce que tu fais.
native_language_example: There’s a difference between what you say and what you do.

additional_notes: Used to say an explanation exists (often implying there’s a reason behind something). It can be followed by an adjective (logique, simple, scientifique) or by “à + situation” (Il y a une explication à tout ça = There’s an explanation for all this). In careful writing you may add accents: “Il y a une explication scientifique à tout ça.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il y a une explication.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there’s an explanation.

additional_notes: Used to say how much time has passed since an event happened. The pattern is: [past tense] + il y a + duration (e.g., il y a deux minutes / trois jours). Note that "il y a" literally means "there is/are" but here it means "ago".
target_language_example: Je t’ai envoyé un message il y a une heure.
native_language_example: I sent you a message an hour ago.

meaning: “a week ago” (one week in the past).
additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It often comes at the end of the sentence: « Il est parti il y a une semaine. ». You can add « environ » to mean “about”: « il y a une semaine environ ».
target_language_example: On s’est vus il y a une semaine.
native_language_example: We saw each other a week ago.

meaning: "there will be" / "there is going to be".
additional_notes: Future tense of « il y a » (“there is/are”). Used to announce that something will exist or happen in the future. Very common with quantities and events: « Il y aura un contrôle demain » (There will be a test tomorrow), « Il y aura des problèmes » (There will be problems).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, il y aura assez de temps pour tout faire.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, there will be enough time to do everything.

meaning: “there was / there were” (past of “il y a”).
additional_notes: Used to say that something existed or was present at a certain time in the past. It’s the imperfect tense, often used for description/background (setting the scene): people/things/situations that were there. Plural in English depends on what follows (“il y avait une…” = there was; “il y avait des…” = there were).
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait beaucoup de monde.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there were lots of people.

additional_notes: Used to describe a large quantity in the past. "Il y avait" is the imperfect of "il y a" (there is/are). After "beaucoup de", the noun usually follows directly (no article: "beaucoup de jeunes", "beaucoup de neige").
target_language_example: Quand on est arrivés, il y avait beaucoup de monde.
native_language_example: When we arrived, there were a lot of people.

il y avait beaucoup de monde

target_language_multi_word_term: il y avait beaucoup de monde
meaning: there were a lot of people (it was crowded).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "il y a" ("il y avait") to describe a past situation/background: “there was/there were.” "Beaucoup de monde" literally means “a lot of people” (more like “a lot of folks/people around”) and is very commonly used to say a place was crowded. "Monde" here is singular but refers to people in general.
target_language_example: Hier soir, il y avait beaucoup de monde au restaurant, alors on a attendu dehors.
native_language_example: Last night, there were a lot of people at the restaurant, so we waited outside.

meaning: "there was some" / "there were (some)" (for an uncountable thing).
additional_notes: "Il y avait" is the imperfect of "il y a" (there is/are), used to describe what existed/was present in the past or to set a scene. "De la" is the partitive article (some) used with feminine singular uncountable nouns (e.g., brume, crème, peur, sueur). For masculine use "du" (il y avait du…), and for plural use "des" (il y avait des…).
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait de la musique dans la rue.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there was music in the street.

additional_notes: Used to say that several people/animals/things existed or were present in the past. It’s the imperfect tense of « il y a » and is followed by a plural noun: « Il y avait des + nom (pluriel) ».
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait des gens devant la porte.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there were people in front of the door.

additional_notes: Imperfect form of *il y a* (“there is/are”), used to describe what existed or what the situation/conditions were in the past (often background info): *Hier, il y avait du soleil / du brouillard.* The *du* is the partitive article (*de + le*) meaning “some” with uncountable or general quantities (fog, sun, broken glass, etc.). With feminine nouns you’ll see *de la*; with plural, *des*.
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait du monde devant le café.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there were people in front of the café.

additional_notes: Past-tense form of "il y a". Used to describe what existed or was present in a place or situation in the past. Often followed by a noun: "Il y avait un drapeau..." (= there was a flag), "Il y avait un hic" (= there was a problem/catch), "Il y avait un total de..." (= there was a total of...). You can change the article/number as needed (une / des) and it can also be negative: "il n’y avait pas de...".
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait un chat devant la porte.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there was a cat in front of the door.

additional_notes: Imperfect form of "il y a". Used to describe that something existed/was present at a place or at a time in the past, often as background description (people, things, events: "il y avait une vue", "il y avait une fête"). With plural: "il y avait des..."
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il y avait une longue file d’attente.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there was a long line.

additional_notes: Used in the pattern "il y en a" to say that some exist/are present/are available. "En" replaces something introduced with "de" (e.g., "des pommes" → "il y en a" = "there are some"). Often followed by a number or quantity: "il y en a trois" (there are three of them), "il y en a une centaine" (there are about a hundred).
target_language_example: Tu as des stylos ? Oui, il y en a dans le tiroir.
native_language_example: Do you have pens? Yes, there are some in the drawer.

additional_notes: Built on the common pattern "il y en a" (= "there are some"), where "en" replaces something already mentioned (often "some of it/them"). "d'autres" means "others/more". It can stand alone ("Il y en a d'autres.") or be followed by details like "comme toi" (like you) or a relative clause: "Il y en a d'autres qui arrivent" (others are arriving).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : il y en a d'autres qui peuvent t'aider.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there are others who can help you.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a lot of something exists. It’s typically followed by a number/quantity expression: des centaines (hundreds), des milliers (thousands), des tonnes/des tas (tons/loads). Built on "il y en a" = "there are some/there is some"; the extra "des" introduces the quantity phrase.
target_language_example: Des bons restaurants à Paris, il y en a des milliers.
native_language_example: There are thousands of good restaurants in Paris.

meaning: “There are still some (left)” / “There are more (of them).”
additional_notes: Uses **il y a** (“there is/are”) + **en** (“some/of it/of them,” referring to something already mentioned) + **encore** (“still/more”). Often used to say there is still some left, or that there are more remaining. You can add a quantity: **Il y en a encore un / beaucoup / plein**.
target_language_example: Tu veux un gâteau ? Il y en a encore.
native_language_example: Do you want a cake? There are still some left.

meaning: there are lots of them / there are plenty.
additional_notes: Uses the common pattern "il y a" (there is/are) + "en" (of them/of it) + "plein" (a lot). Often followed by "de" + noun: "Il y en a plein de..." = "There are lots of..." You can also say it alone as an excited emphasis: "Il y en a plein !"
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il y en a plein dans le magasin.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there are plenty in the store.

meaning: "there’s enough (of it) for…" / "it will last for…"
additional_notes: Used with a duration or a group to say how long something lasts or that there’s enough to cover someone/something. Common patterns: « Il y en a pour tout le monde » = there’s enough for everyone; « Il y en a pour une seconde / deux jours » = it lasts one second / two days (often about battery life, time, money, food, etc.). « en » refers to the thing you’re talking about (some of it), and « il y a » is an impersonal way to say “there is/are.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il y en a pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there’s enough for everyone.

additional_notes: Used to point out that among a group, some people/things do a certain action or have a certain quality. Very common in speech; often implies “some… (and others don’t)”. Built from: il y a = “there is/are” + en = “of them/some” + qui = “who/that”.
target_language_example: Il y en a qui préfèrent rester à la maison.
native_language_example: There are some people who prefer to stay at home.

additional_notes: Used to say that one exists or is available. Built on **il y a** (“there is/are”) + **en** (“some/any/of them,” replacing a noun mentioned or understood) + **un** (“one”). Often answers a question like *Tu en as un ?* (“Do you have one?”) → *Oui, il y en a un.*
target_language_example: Tu cherches un chargeur ? Il y en a un sur la table.
native_language_example: Are you looking for a charger? There’s one on the table.

meaning: "There is one" / "There’s one (of them)" (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used when you mean “one of it/them” and the thing has already been mentioned or is understood. « en » replaces “of it/them” (a previously mentioned noun), and « une » shows it’s ONE and feminine (for a masculine noun, you’d say « il y en a un »). Common in counts or comparisons: « Il y en a une de moins » = “There’s one less.”
target_language_example: Tu as des piles ? Oui, il y en a une dans le tiroir.
native_language_example: Do you have batteries? Yes, there’s one in the drawer.

meaning: “there will be some / there will be (some of it/them)” (in the future).
additional_notes: Future tense of the common structure **il y a** (“there is/are”) with **en** (“some / some of it/them”), used when the thing has already been mentioned or is understood. Often followed by a quantity or place: **Il y en aura trois** (“There will be three”), **Il y en aura partout** (“There will be some everywhere”), **Il y en aura pour tout le monde** (“There will be enough for everyone”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : il y en aura assez pour tout le monde.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there will be enough for everyone.

additional_notes: Imperfect past form of "il y en a". Used when "en" replaces a previously mentioned noun (meaning "some" or "(some) of it/them"): *Il y en avait beaucoup* = "There were a lot (of them)." You often add a quantity after it (beaucoup, un, deux, etc.).
target_language_example: Dans le frigo, il y en avait encore.
native_language_example: There were still some in the fridge.

additional_notes: Used to describe a past state, background situation, or ongoing action in the past (imparfait). Often sets the scene or explains what was happening when another event occurred (usually in the passé composé). Can also mean “he used to be” depending on context.
target_language_example: Il était malade, alors il est resté à la maison.
native_language_example: He was sick, so he stayed at home.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past tense (était) to describe an ongoing state in the past: where/ how someone was sitting, often as background description. Frequently followed by a place or position: "sur une chaise" (on a chair), "par terre" (on the floor), "entre X et Y" (between X and Y), "avec les bras/jambes croisés" (with arms/legs crossed).
target_language_example: Quand je suis entré, il était assis près de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: When I came in, he was sitting near the window.

meaning: 'he was in the process of' / 'he was (in the middle of) doing'.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that an action was ongoing at that moment in the past (like English "was doing"). It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « il était en train de + infinitif ». You can change the subject and tense: « je suis en train de… » (I’m doing…), « ils étaient en train de… » (they were doing…).
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, il était en train de préparer le dîner.
native_language_example: When I arrived, he was in the middle of making dinner.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (était) to describe an ongoing state, feeling, or characteristic in the past (background description). "Il" usually means "he," but it can also mean "it" (e.g., talking about a movie: "Il était très long"). Typically followed by an adjective: "Il était très content/fatigué."
target_language_example: Quand il était jeune, il était très timide.
native_language_example: When he was young, he was very shy.

meaning: "Once upon a time there was a..." (storybook opening).
additional_notes: Used at the start of fairy tales and stories to introduce a character. It’s the imperfect tense of être (il était = “he/it was”), followed by une fois (“once”), then un/une + noun. You can change un to une depending on the noun: « Il était une fois une princesse… »
target_language_example: Il était une fois un chat qui voulait devenir roi.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a cat who wanted to become king.

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine plural, or mixed group). "Aiment" is the present tense (3rd person plural) of "aimer". It can mean "to like" (Ils aiment ça. = They like that.) or "to love" (Ils aiment leurs enfants. = They love their children.). You can follow it with a noun (ils aiment leurs enfants), an infinitive (ils aiment se plaindre = they like to complain), or a pronoun like "ça" (they like that).
target_language_example: Ils aiment regarder des films le soir.
native_language_example: They like watching movies in the evening.

additional_notes: Used to describe an ongoing state, repeated situation, or background in the past (the imperfect). Common patterns: « ils avaient peur de… » = “they were afraid to/of…”, « ils avaient besoin de… » = “they needed…”. Often appears in reported speech after « ils ont dit que… » (they said that…).
target_language_example: Quand ils étaient jeunes, ils avaient toujours peur du noir.
native_language_example: When they were young, they were always afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: Present tense of **dire** (“to say/tell”) with **ils** (“they”). Often used to report what other people claim or announce, frequently followed by **que**: *Ils disent que…* In casual speech, negation may drop **ne**: *Ils disent pas…* (instead of *Ils ne disent pas…*).
target_language_example: Ils disent qu’ils vont arriver à 18 h.
native_language_example: They say they’re going to arrive at 6 p.m.

meaning: “they must / they have to” (they are required to).
additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (a group of males, or a mixed group). "Doivent" is the present tense of "devoir" (to have to / must). It’s used to express obligation or necessity, and is followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "ils doivent partir"). In the negative: "ils ne doivent pas..." = "they must not / they aren’t supposed to...".
target_language_example: Ils doivent partir maintenant.
native_language_example: They have to leave now.

meaning: 'they must be' / 'they have to be' (or 'they must be' = 'they’re probably…').
additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "Doivent" is the present tense of "devoir" (must/should/have to). With "être" it can express either (1) obligation/requirement: "They have to be replaced", or (2) a logical guess/probability: "They must be tired" (= they’re probably tired).
target_language_example: Ils doivent être en retard, il y a beaucoup de trafic.
native_language_example: They must be late; there’s a lot of traffic.

additional_notes: Present tense of the verb « faire » (to do/to make) with « ils » (they). Very common and used broadly: doing an action (« Ils font un test. »), making/producing something (« Ils font tout le nécessaire. »), or “doing” an activity (« Ils font ça depuis… »). In informal speech you may hear « Ils font pas… » (missing « ne ») instead of the more formal « Ils ne font pas… ».
target_language_example: Ils font ça tous les jours.
native_language_example: They do that every day.

meaning: "they have" + "it/him/her" (used to form the past tense: "they ...ed it/him/her").
additional_notes: “Ils” = “they.” “l’” is a direct object pronoun meaning “it,” “him,” or “her,” used before a verb that starts with a vowel (like “ont”). “ont” is the present of “avoir” (they have) and is used to build the passé composé: ils l’ont + past participle (fait, pris, emmené, etc.) → “they did it / they took him/her/it / they brought him/her, etc.” With “avoir,” the past participle can agree in gender/number when the direct object pronoun comes before it: “Ils l’ont pris” (masc. “him/it”), “Ils l’ont prise” (fem. “her/it”).
target_language_example: Ils l’ont trouvé hier soir.
native_language_example: They found it/him/her last night.

meaning: "they" + "to me" + "have" (used to form the past tense: "they ... to me").
additional_notes: Common start of a sentence in the passé composé: ils (they) + m’ (me, as an indirect object) + ont (have). It’s followed by a past participle: Ils m’ont dit (They told me), Ils m’ont donné (They gave me), Ils m’ont pris… (They took/caught me…). m’ is the shortened form of me before a vowel sound (ont). Meaning depends on the verb that follows (e.g., Ils m’ont eu = “They got me/fooled me”).
target_language_example: Ils m'ont envoyé un message hier.
native_language_example: They sent me a message yesterday.

meaning: 'they do not / they didn't' (start of a negation with 'ils').
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a negative sentence with the subject pronoun ils (“they”). In standard French, ne is paired with another negative word: pas (not), jamais (never), plus (no longer), rien (nothing), etc. In everyday spoken French, ne is often dropped (Ils savent pas).
target_language_example: Ils ne veulent pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: They don't want to come tonight.

additional_notes: From the verb *pouvoir* (“to be able to / can”) in the present tense: *ils peuvent* (“they can”). The standard French negation is *ne … pas*: *ils ne peuvent pas* (“they can’t”). In casual spoken French, *ne* is often dropped: *ils peuvent pas*.
target_language_example: Ils ne peuvent pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: They can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: This is the negative form of **ils sont** (“they are”) with **ne … pas** placed around the verb **être**: **ils ne sont pas + adjective / prepositional phrase / past participle**. In casual spoken French, **ne** is often dropped: **ils sont pas**.
target_language_example: Ils ne sont pas prêts pour le départ.
native_language_example: They aren’t ready to leave.

meaning: 'they have' / 'they did' (talking about what they did to us).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the passé composé: ils (they) + nous (to us) + ont (have). The object pronoun nous goes before the verb. In sentences like « Ils nous ont oubliés / saluées », the past participle can agree with nous (forgotten us / greeted us) in gender/number when nous refers to the direct object.
target_language_example: Ils nous ont aidés à trouver un hôtel.
native_language_example: They helped us find a hotel.

additional_notes: “Ils” = “they” + “ont” = the verb “avoir” (to have) in the present tense. Very commonly used to form the past tense (passé composé): ils ont + past participle (e.g., ils ont changé = they changed / they have changed). It can also mean possession: ils ont une voiture = they have a car.
target_language_example: Ils ont déjà fini leurs devoirs.
native_language_example: They have already finished their homework.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of *dire* with *ils* (they): *ils* + *ont* (have) + *dit* (said). Used for something they said in the past, often translated simply as “they said.” Common in reported speech: *Ils ont dit qu’ils…* (“They said that they…”).
target_language_example: Ils ont dit qu’ils viendraient demain.
native_language_example: They said they would come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past of devoir ("to have to" / "must"). It can express (1) obligation in the past: « Ils ont dû partir » = “They had to leave.” It can also express a deduction (very common): « Ils ont dû avoir un accident » = “They must have had an accident.” With deduction about a completed action, you’ll often see « ont dû » + infinitive (or + avoir/être + past participle).
target_language_example: Ils ont dû oublier l'adresse.
native_language_example: They must have forgotten the address.

additional_notes: "Ils ont eu" is the passé composé of avoir (ils + ont + eu) and talks about a completed past event. Depending on context, it can mean they possessed something (Ils ont eu plusieurs enfants = they had several children), they got/received something (Ils ont eu ce qu’ils voulaient = they got what they wanted), or they experienced something (Ils ont eu de la chance = they were lucky). In "ils ont eu raison", it’s part of the fixed phrase "avoir raison" = 'to be right'.
target_language_example: Ils ont eu beaucoup de succès cette année.
native_language_example: They had a lot of success this year.

additional_notes: This is the **passé composé** of *faire* for **ils** (“they”): *ils* + *ont* (have) + *fait* (done/made). It’s used for completed actions in the past. *Faire* can mean **do** or **make** depending on context: *Ils ont fait une pause* (“They took a break”), *Ils ont fait le tour du monde* (“They travelled around the world”), *Ils ont fait de leur mieux* (“They did their best”).
target_language_example: Ils ont fait la cuisine hier soir.
native_language_example: They cooked last night.

meaning: 'they put/placed' (past tense of mettre); also 'they took (time)' and in fixed phrases like 'they put an end (to)'
additional_notes: "Ils ont mis" is the passé composé of mettre (they put/placed). Common patterns: (1) mettre + object + place: « Ils ont mis mon nom dans la Coupe » = they put my name in the Goblet. (2) mettre + object (meaning install/add): « Ils ont mis un portail » = they installed/put in a gate. (3) mettre + duration + à + infinitive: « Ils ont mis deux ans à construire… » = it took them two years to build… (4) mettre fin à + noun: « Ils ont mis fin au… » = they put an end to…
target_language_example: Ils ont mis trois heures à arriver.
native_language_example: It took them three hours to arrive.

additional_notes: Passé composé of prendre (to take). Used for many common meanings: taking/grabbing something (Ils ont pris de la nourriture), having a meal/drink (Ils ont pris leur petit-déjeuner = they had breakfast), taking a risk (Ils ont pris un gros risque), taking someone away (can imply kidnapping depending on context), and choosing a route (Qu’est-ce qu’ils ont pris comme rues ? = Which streets did they take?).
target_language_example: Ils ont pris le bus pour aller au centre-ville.
native_language_example: They took the bus to go downtown.

meaning: “they all have” / “they have all” (all of them).
additional_notes: Used with the subject pronoun ils (“they”) + avoir (“have”), with tous emphasizing that every person in the group did the action. In the passé composé, tous is commonly placed between the auxiliary verb ont and the past participle: Ils ont tous changé (“They all changed”). Can also mean “they all have (something)” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ils ont tous compris la question.
native_language_example: They all understood the question.

meaning: “they were / they have been” (passé composé of être; often used to form the passive).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a past participle to make the passive voice: ils ont été + participe passé (e.g., attaqués, surpris). The past participle usually agrees with ils (masculine plural: -s).
target_language_example: Ils ont été invités à la fête, mais ils n’ont pas pu venir.
native_language_example: They were invited to the party, but they couldn’t come.

meaning: “they have” (present of avoir), used to form the past tense (passé composé): “they have/they did”.
additional_notes: “Ils” = “they” and “ont” is the 3rd person plural of “avoir” (to have). Most often, “ils ont + past participle” makes the passé composé: Ils ont changé = “They changed / They have changed.” In English you usually translate it as a simple past (“they did…”) or present perfect (“they have…”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ils ont perdu leurs clés.
native_language_example: They lost their keys.

additional_notes: “Avoir besoin de” means “to need.” After it, use a noun (Ils ont besoin de vacances) or an infinitive verb (Ils ont besoin de s’inspirer…). “De” may contract with articles: de + les → des, de + le → du, de + l’ stays de l’.
target_language_example: Ils ont besoin de temps pour réfléchir.
native_language_example: They need time to think.

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "ont" is the present tense of "avoir" (to have). "des" is the plural indefinite article meaning "some" (often not translated in English). Used to say that they possess or have something available: "Ils ont des armes" = "They have weapons"; "Ils ont des bonnes nouvelles ?" = "Do they have any good news?"; "Ils ont des jumelles" = "They have binoculars."
target_language_example: Ils ont des amis à Paris.
native_language_example: They have friends in Paris.

additional_notes: From the idiom **avoir l’air (de)** = “to seem / to look.” Often followed by **de + infinitive** (Ils ont l’air de s’amuser = They seem to be having fun) or by an **adjective** (Ils ont l’air heureux = They look happy). You can change the subject: *j’ai l’air, tu as l’air, il/elle a l’air, nous avons l’air, vous avez l’air, ils/elles ont l’air*.
target_language_example: Ils ont l’air fatigués aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: They look tired today.

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "Parlent" is the present tense of "parler". It can mean speaking a language (often with no preposition: "Ils parlent français") or talking about something (use "de": "Ils parlent de musique"), and it can also be used as a question: "Ils parlent ?" = "Are they speaking/talking?"
target_language_example: Ils parlent de toi en ce moment.
native_language_example: They’re talking about you right now.

meaning: “they can / they are able to” (sometimes “they may”).
additional_notes: "Ils" = “they” (masculine or mixed group). "Peuvent" is the present tense of "pouvoir" (to be able to / can). It’s used for ability (“They can speak French”), possibility (“They can maybe start…”), or permission depending on context. In questions, it often means “Can they…?” ("Ils peuvent faire ça ?").
target_language_example: S’ils veulent, ils peuvent venir demain.
native_language_example: If they want, they can come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Present tense of the verb **savoir** (to know a fact / to know that…). **Ils** = “they” (usually a group of men, or a mixed group). Often used before **que** (“that”): *Ils savent que…* In speech, **ils** is often not strongly pronounced, and there is a liaison: *ils savent* → sounds like **[il sav]**.
target_language_example: Ils savent que c’est important.
native_language_example: They know that it’s important.

meaning: "they" + "se" (themselves / each other) used with reflexive or reciprocal verbs.
additional_notes: Used before a verb in pronominal verbs (verbs that take a reflexive pronoun). Depending on context, it can mean they do something to themselves (reflexive) or to one another (reciprocal): Ils se battent = They’re fighting (each other). Ils se détendent = They relax. With another object it can be "to each other": Ils se disent la vérité = They tell each other the truth.
target_language_example: Ils se parlent tous les jours.
native_language_example: They talk to each other every day.

meaning: “they (have) …” in the past tense with a reflexive/pronominal verb.
additional_notes: Used to start the passé composé of pronominal (often reflexive) verbs: ils (they) + se (themselves/each other) + sont (are/have, using être). The past participle usually agrees with ils (masculine plural) when applicable: Ils se sont levés. In some verbs like se noyer (“to drown”), it means “they drowned.”
target_language_example: Ils se sont réveillés tôt.
native_language_example: They woke up early.

meaning: they got married / they married (each other).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb se marier (“to get married”). Used to say that a couple married at a specific time (often with il y a…, quand…, récemment, etc.).
target_language_example: Ils se sont mariés en juin.
native_language_example: They got married in June.

meaning: “they are” (for a group of males or a mixed group).
additional_notes: Used with the subject pronoun **ils** (they) + **sont** (are), the 3rd-person plural of **être**. Use **ils sont** for an all-male group or a mixed-gender group; use **elles sont** for an all-female group. Often followed by an adjective (Ils sont mignons.) or a place/state with **là / ici / dedans** (Ils sont là. / Ils sont là-dedans.).
target_language_example: Ils sont prêts à partir.
native_language_example: They are ready to leave.

meaning: “they went” / “they have gone” (masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of aller with être: ils (they) + sont (are) + allés (gone). Use for a group of males or a mixed group; for all-female, say « elles sont allées » (with -es). Often followed by a place with « à/dans/au/à la/aux » or an activity: « aller + infinitive » (e.g., « allés voir » = went to see).
target_language_example: Après le travail, ils sont allés au restaurant.
native_language_example: After work, they went to the restaurant.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of arriver with être: ils + sont + arrivé(s). The -s on arrivés agrees with ils (masculine plural; for an all-female group you’d write elles sont arrivées). Used for arriving at a place (à + city, en + country) and also figuratively in “arriver à la conclusion” = “to come to the conclusion.”
target_language_example: Ils sont arrivés à Paris hier soir.
native_language_example: They arrived in Paris last night.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of *arriver* with *être*: *ils sont arrivés* (“they arrived”), with agreement on *arrivés* (add -e / -es for feminine: *elles sont arrivées*). *Là-bas* means “over there / there (in that place)”. After *avant*, French typically uses a stressed pronoun: *avant elle / lui / nous / vous / eux / elles* (not *le/la/les*).
target_language_example: Ils sont arrivés là-bas avant moi.
native_language_example: They arrived there before me.

meaning: “they are in …” (in a place or in a state/situation).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **être** + **en** + a noun phrase to describe a location (**en classe** = in class) or a condition/situation (**en bon état** = in good condition; **en guerre (avec …)** = at war (with …); **en bons termes** = on good terms). You replace **ils** with another subject as needed (e.g., *je suis en…*, *elle est en…*).
target_language_example: Ils sont en vacances cette semaine.
native_language_example: They are on vacation this week.

meaning: they are (currently) / they are in the middle of (doing).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize an action happening right now (French version of the English present continuous). Structure: être (conjugated) + en train de + infinitive. Here: ils sont en train de + infinitive = “they are currently …”.
target_language_example: Ils sont en train de préparer le dîner.
native_language_example: They are preparing dinner (right now).

additional_notes: Used to point out that a group of males or a mixed group is present. Depending on context, “là” can mean either “here” (near the speaker) or “there” (at a specific place). Often said when noticing or locating someone/something: “Regarde, ils sont là.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, ils sont là pour t’aider.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, they’re here to help you.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *mourir* (to die) with the auxiliary *être*. *Ils sont morts* can describe (1) the event of dying (“they died”) or (2) the resulting state (“they’re dead”). In writing, you may also see it used in a time clause: *Quand ils sont morts, …* (“When they died, …”).
target_language_example: Ils sont morts il y a dix ans.
native_language_example: They died ten years ago.

additional_notes: Past tense with the verb "être" (passé composé) of "partir" = to leave/go away. "Ils" refers to a group of males or a mixed group. Often followed by time ("il y a une heure"), purpose/duration ("pour le week-end"), direction ("par là"), or a destination ("pour Paris").
target_language_example: Ils sont partis sans dire au revoir.
native_language_example: They left without saying goodbye.

additional_notes: Used to say that all the people/things in a group are present or in the same state. In questions, you’ll often see inversion: « Où sont-ils tous ? » (“Where are they all?”). « tous » here means “all (of them)” and typically comes after the verb.
target_language_example: Ils sont tous prêts.
native_language_example: They’re all ready.

meaning: 'they came' / 'they have come' (masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of venir with être: venir → ils sont venus. Used for arriving/coming to a place (chez moi, à mon appartement), coming from somewhere (depuis le Brésil), or coming at a time (la semaine passée, le lundi). Agreement: venus (masc. plural); if the group is all female: elles sont venues.
target_language_example: Ils sont venus tôt pour m’aider.
native_language_example: They came early to help me.

additional_notes: "Ils" = "they" (masculine plural, or mixed group). "Veulent" is the present tense of "vouloir" (to want). Often followed by an infinitive: "ils veulent apprendre" (they want to learn). It can also be followed by a noun: "ils veulent quelques heures de plus" (they want a few more hours), or by "que" + subjunctive to express what they want someone to do: "ils veulent que je vous parle" (they want me to talk to you).
target_language_example: Ils veulent partir maintenant.
native_language_example: They want to leave now.

additional_notes: Present tense of venir (to come) with ils (they). It can describe movement toward someone/somewhere (Ils viennent vers nous. = They’re coming toward us.) or be used in the near past with venir de + infinitive (Ils viennent juste de la sortir… = They just took her out…).
target_language_example: Ils viennent ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are they coming tonight?

meaning: "they go" / "they are going"; often used to form the near future ("they're going to...").
additional_notes: Subject pronoun "ils" (they, masculine or mixed group) + present tense of "aller" (to go). Very commonly followed by an infinitive to express the near future: "ils vont + infinitive" = "they are going to + verb".
target_language_example: Ils vont partir bientôt.
native_language_example: They’re going to leave soon.

meaning: “they’re going to … us” (near future with “nous” = us).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about something that’s about to happen: Ils vont + infinitive. The pronoun “nous” (us) is placed before the infinitive: « Ils vont nous voir » = “They’re going to see us.” Depending on the verb, “nous” can be a direct object (see us) or indirect object (talk to us).
target_language_example: Cache-toi : ils vont nous entendre !
native_language_example: Hide: they’re going to hear us!

additional_notes: “Ils” means “they” (for a group of men or a mixed group). “Étaient” is the imperfect past of “être” (to be). It’s used to describe a past situation, background, or ongoing state (where they were, how they were, what they were like), often setting the scene rather than focusing on a completed event.
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, ils étaient déjà fatigués.
native_language_example: When I arrived, they were already tired.

additional_notes: Used to say that every person in a group of males or mixed gender was in the same situation/state. "Ils" = they (masc./mixed), "étaient" = were (imperfect of être), and "tous" = all. "Tous" here is an adverb meaning “all (of them)” and typically goes right after the verb: « Ils étaient tous + adjective/past participle/noun phrase » (e.g., « en uniforme », « partis »).
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, ils étaient tous déjà là.
native_language_example: When I arrived, they were all already there.

additional_notes: Used on signs and in rules to say that smoking is not allowed. Often appears as « Il est interdit de fumer » or with emphasis: « strictement interdit » (= strictly forbidden). You can add a place: « ici », « dans le bâtiment », etc.
target_language_example: Il est interdit de fumer dans le train.
native_language_example: No smoking on the train.

additional_notes: Future tense of aller (to go) + bien (well). Used to reassure someone about a person or a situation: Il ira bien (He’ll be fine), Ça ira bien (It’ll be fine / It’ll work out). Often said as reassurance.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, ça ira bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’ll be fine.

additional_notes: From the verb adorer (to love/to adore). Used to express strong enthusiasm for something (a name, a person, a hobby, a place, etc.). More intense than "j'aime" (I like), but in everyday French it’s often used casually like “I love it!” You can follow it with a noun ("J'adore le théâtre"), a person ("J'adore ce type"), or an infinitive verb ("J'adore faire..."), and you can emphasize it with "J'adore ça !".
target_language_example: J'adore ce restaurant, on y mange très bien.
native_language_example: I love this restaurant; the food is really good there.

meaning: “I love this …” (referring to a singular feminine thing).
additional_notes: Used to express strong liking/love for something. It must be followed by a noun: **J’adore cette + noun**. **Cette** is the feminine singular form of “this,” used with feminine nouns (and also before a vowel sound/h mute: *cette amie*). For masculine nouns, use **ce/cet** (*J’adore ce film / cet endroit*).
target_language_example: J’adore cette chanson !
native_language_example: I love this song!

additional_notes: Contraction of "je" + "ai" (present tense of "avoir"). Used either as the main verb meaning "to have" (e.g., "j'ai un frère" = I have a brother) or very often as an auxiliary to form the past tense (passé composé): "j'ai + past participle" (e.g., "j'ai vécu" = I lived / I have lived). In negatives, it becomes "je n'ai pas".
target_language_example: J'ai fini mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I finished my homework.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of appeler: j’ + ai + appelé. Use it to say you called someone or called a place. With time expressions you can specify when: « J’ai appelé … il y a deux jours » = “I called … two days ago.”
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai appelé trop tard.
native_language_example: Sorry, I called too late.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *apprendre* with *je*: **j’ai appris**. It can mean (1) you learned something (knowledge/skill): *J’ai appris le français* (“I learned French”), or (2) you found out some news/information: *J’ai appris la nouvelle* (“I heard/found out the news”). It’s often followed by **que** (“that”) or **ce qui** (“what”): *J’ai appris que…*, *J’ai appris ce qui s’est passé*.
target_language_example: J’ai appris qu’il allait déménager.
native_language_example: I found out that he was going to move.

additional_notes: Past tense of attendre (“to wait”), using the passé composé: j’ + ai + attendu. Often followed by a duration (des heures, toute la journée, très longtemps) or by pour + infinitive (“in order to / to”): J’ai attendu toute ma vie pour le dire.
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai attendu longtemps, mais tu n'es pas venu.
native_language_example: Sorry, I waited a long time, but you didn’t come.

additional_notes: Past tense of comprendre (“to understand”), used to say you understood something just explained. In conversation it often means “Got it/OK, I understand,” and can sound firm depending on tone (e.g., "Ouais, j'ai compris" = “Yeah, I got it”).
target_language_example: D'accord, j'ai compris : on se retrouve à 18 h devant la gare.
native_language_example: Okay, I got it: we’re meeting at 6 p.m. in front of the station.

meaning: "I thought" / "I believed" (often: mistakenly, or for a moment).
additional_notes: Passé composé of « croire ». Very common with an infinitive (« j’ai cru entendre/voir… » = “I thought I heard/saw…”) or with « que » + a full clause (« j’ai cru qu’il allait… » = “I thought he was going to…”). It often suggests your impression wasn’t certain or turned out to be wrong.
target_language_example: J’ai cru que tu étais déjà parti.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense (passé composé of croire) to say you *thought* something was true, often later realizing it wasn’t or that you were mistaken. Very common in situations of surprise, fear, or misunderstanding: "J’ai cru que j’allais m’évanouir" (= I thought I was going to faint). It’s followed by a full clause with its own verb tense. (Also note: tu étais parti = speaking to a man; tu étais partie = speaking to a woman.)
target_language_example: Quand j’ai entendu le bruit, j’ai cru que quelqu’un était entré.
native_language_example: When I heard the noise, I thought someone had come in.

meaning: "I thought it was..." / "I believed it was..." (often a mistaken first impression).
additional_notes: Used to describe what you believed at first in the past. Very often it implies you were wrong or surprised afterward. Structure: « J'ai cru que + [imparfait] »; most commonly « c'était » = “it was”.
target_language_example: J'ai cru que c'était la bonne adresse, mais je me suis trompé.
native_language_example: I thought it was the right address, but I was mistaken.
