additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed in the past, often implying you later realized it wasn’t true. It’s followed by a verb phrase (e.g., future-in-the-past/conditional: *tu changerais…*; past perfect: *tu t’étais…*; or a negative: *tu ne… jamais*).
target_language_example: J'ai cru que tu étais déjà parti.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *dire* (“to say/tell”). Use it to report something you said in the past, including giving an instruction (often with *de* + infinitive: *J’ai dit de…* = “I told [someone] to…”).
target_language_example: Je t’ai dit de fermer la porte.
native_language_example: I told you to close the door.

additional_notes: Used to report what you previously said, followed by a full clause. The verb after « que » often shifts into the past: « J’ai dit que je le ferais » (“I said I would do it”). In casual speech you may also hear the future kept: « J’ai dit que je le ferai » (“I said I will do it”), though it’s less standard in careful French.
target_language_example: J’ai dit que je viendrais demain.
native_language_example: I said that I would come tomorrow.

meaning: “I said that I was going to …”
additional_notes: Used to report something you previously said you intended to do. After "j'ai dit que", French often uses the imperfect ("j'allais") for “was going to / intended to,” even if in English you might say “I said I would…”. The verb after "j'allais" stays in the infinitive (e.g., essayer, le faire, m'en occuper).
target_language_example: J'ai dit que j'allais t'appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I said I was going to call you tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you made a decision and are going to do something. It’s the passé composé of décider: "j’ai décidé" + "de" + infinitive (e.g., partir, revenir, profiter). The English meaning can be either simple past (I decided to) or present perfect (I've decided to), depending on context.
target_language_example: J'ai décidé de changer de travail.
native_language_example: I've decided to change jobs.

additional_notes: Used to say you did something before now. Very often followed by a past participle (passé composé): « J’ai déjà + appelé / commencé / entendu ». It can also mean “I have already (experienced/known)” depending on the verb (e.g., « J’ai déjà connu ça » = “I’ve been through that before”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, j’ai déjà réservé les billets.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I already booked the tickets.

additional_notes: Used to say you have previously seen something. Often followed by a direct object (e.g., « ce film ») or used with « ça » (“that/it”). « déjà » adds the idea of “already/before.”
target_language_example: J'ai déjà vu cette série, elle est super.
native_language_example: I've already seen this series; it's great.

meaning: "I had to" / "I needed to"; sometimes "I must have" (probably).
additional_notes: Passé composé of devoir (to have to). It often expresses a past obligation/necessity: « J'ai dû partir » = “I had to leave.” In some contexts it expresses a logical guess about the past: « J'ai dû m'évanouir » = “I must have fainted” (I probably fainted). The form « dû » (with the accent) can look like English “due” but it’s a different word.
target_language_example: J'ai dû annuler le rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I had to cancel the appointment.

additional_notes: Past tense of entendre (“to hear”). Used for something you heard at a specific time (J’ai entendu l’appel / à la radio) or for information/rumors you heard (J’ai entendu dire que…, J’ai entendu de bonnes choses sur…). Often translates as either “I heard” or “I’ve heard” depending on context.
target_language_example: J’ai entendu parler de ce restaurant, il paraît qu’il est excellent.
native_language_example: I’ve heard about that restaurant; apparently it’s excellent.

additional_notes: Past tense of « essayer » (to try): « j'ai essayé » uses the passé composé and is often followed by « de » + infinitive (e.g., « j'ai essayé de comprendre » = I tried to understand). It can also be used without an infinitive to mean you made an attempt (e.g., « J'ai essayé deux fois » = I tried twice). In context it often implies effort, even if it didn’t work: « J'ai essayé, mais… ».
target_language_example: J'ai essayé de t'appeler hier, mais tu ne répondais pas.
native_language_example: I tried to call you yesterday, but you weren’t answering.

additional_notes: Past tense of "essayer de" + infinitive. Used to say you made an effort to do something (often implying it didn’t work, or at least it took effort). In conversation it can be followed by an infinitive: "J'ai essayé de l'appeler" (I tried to call him).
target_language_example: J'ai essayé de te joindre, mais tu ne répondais pas.
native_language_example: I tried to reach you, but you weren't answering.

additional_notes: Used to say you made an effort to do something involving the person you’re speaking to. Structure: « j’ai essayé de + infinitive » (past tense, passé composé). « te » is the object pronoun meaning “you” (informal singular) and comes before the infinitive: « j’ai essayé de te contacter / te joindre / te le dire / te trouver ». Note: « essayer » looks like English “essay” but here it means “to try” (false friend).
target_language_example: J'ai essayé de te parler hier soir, mais tu ne répondais pas.
native_language_example: I tried to talk to you last night, but you weren’t answering.

additional_notes: Passé composé of avoir (je + ai + eu). Used for completed past events. Depending on the noun, it often translates as “I had” (j’ai eu une idée), “I got” (j’ai eu le boulot = I got the job), or “I received” (j’ai eu ton SMS = I got/received your text). Pronounced roughly like “zhay-oo” (two vowel sounds).
target_language_example: J'ai eu un problème avec ma carte.
native_language_example: I had a problem with my card.

meaning: I was lucky / I had good luck.
additional_notes: Literally “I had some luck.” Uses the past tense of avoir (j’ai eu) to talk about being lucky in a specific situation. Often followed by “de + infinitive” to say what you were lucky to do (e.g., de te rencontrer = to meet you).
target_language_example: J'ai eu de la chance de ne pas rater le train.
native_language_example: I was lucky not to miss the train.

meaning: “I got a …” / “I had a …” (past: I received or experienced something).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of avoir: "j’ai eu" = "I had". It’s commonly used with things you receive ("J’ai eu un appel" = I got a call) or sudden experiences/ideas ("J’ai eu un flash" = I had a flash / sudden inspiration). It must be followed by a masculine singular noun (un + noun); for feminine, use "j’ai eu une …".
target_language_example: J'ai eu un message de mon prof ce matin.
native_language_example: I got a message from my teacher this morning.

meaning: "I had a" / "I have had a" (past tense).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of avoir: « j’ » (I) + « ai » (have) + « eu » (had) + « une » (a, feminine). It’s used to say you had/experienced something in the past: « J’ai eu une liaison » (I had an affair), « J’ai eu une révélation » (I had a revelation). You use « une » because the following noun is feminine; with a masculine noun you’d say « j’ai eu un … ». In English it’s usually translated as simple past: “I had a …”.
target_language_example: J’ai eu une idée pendant le cours.
native_language_example: I had an idea during class.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: « j’ai failli + infinitif » = you came very close to doing something, but it didn’t happen (often a near miss). Despite looking like English “failed,” « faillir » means “to almost (do)” in this structure.
target_language_example: J’ai failli rater mon train.
native_language_example: I almost missed my train.

additional_notes: Used with the passé composé of faire (j’ + ai + fait). It can mean “I did” or “I have done,” depending on context. Common patterns: j’ai fait + [a thing/task] (“I did/made …”), j’ai fait + [activity] (“I did … / I went …,” e.g., j’ai fait l’armée = “I did military service”), j’ai fait + [distance/route] (“I covered …,” e.g., tout le chemin), j’ai fait de mon mieux (“I did my best”), j’ai fait n’importe quoi (“I did something stupid/whatever”).
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai fait une erreur.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a mistake.

additional_notes: Used to say you did the thing that followed (often something you thought was right/necessary, or what someone told/asked you to do). It’s commonly followed by another clause like "j’ai pu" (I could), "j’avais à faire" (I had to do), "tu as dit" (you said), or "vous avez demandé" (you asked).
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai fait ce que je pouvais.
native_language_example: Sorry, I did what I could.

meaning: “I did the …” / “I have done the …” (with faire + a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb faire in the passé composé: j’ai fait + le + noun. Common with things you “do” or “make,” like le boulot (the work/job), le maximum (the most you can), le nécessaire (what’s necessary), le test (the test), le tour (a trip/round): j’ai fait le tour du monde = “I traveled around the world.” Tense can mean either “I did” or “I have done” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, j’ai fait le nécessaire.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I did what was necessary.

meaning: "I did my…" / "I’ve done my…" (introduces something you did: my job, my choice, my best, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun after it: j’ai fait mon boulot (I did my job), j’ai fait mon choix (I made my choice), j’ai fait mon possible (I did my best). Note: in the idiom « faire son beurre », it means “to make money / profit” (e.g., « J’ai fait mon beurre avec… »).
target_language_example: J’ai fait mon devoir, je peux sortir ?
native_language_example: I did my homework; can I go out?

meaning: "I did everything that…" / "I did all that…"
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you did, followed by a clause (often in the passé composé): "…j’ai pu" (I could), "…tu as dit" (you said), "…vous avez demandé" (you asked for), "…vous vouliez" (you wanted). Can also imply “I did my best” when followed by "j’ai pu".
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai fait tout ce que je pouvais.
native_language_example: Sorry, I did everything I could.

additional_notes: Literally “I did/made a dream,” but in French you use faire (to do/make) + un rêve (a dream) to talk about dreaming. It’s typically used with a time expression like cette nuit / la nuit dernière (“last night”) and can be followed by an adjective (incroyable, merveilleux, etc.).
target_language_example: Cette nuit, j'ai fait un rêve très étrange.
native_language_example: Last night, I had a very strange dream.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "faire" with "avoir": j'ai fait = I did / I have done. Often used to say you did something (sometimes with emphasis or disbelief in questions: "J'ai fait ça, moi ?" = "I did that, me?"). "Ça" refers to something already mentioned or understood from context.
target_language_example: Non, je n'ai pas fait ça !
native_language_example: No, I didn’t do that!

additional_notes: With a direct object, it means you completed something: « J'ai fini mon service. » = “I finished my shift.” Used with a place (often with « ici », « au… », « dans… »), « finir » can mean “to end up”: « J'ai fini ici. » = “I ended up here.”
target_language_example: J'ai fini trop tard, alors j'ai pris un taxi.
native_language_example: I finished too late, so I took a taxi.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: people often drop "ne" in negatives. So "j'ai jamais" means the same as the standard written form "je n'ai jamais". Used with the past tense ("j'ai" / "je suis") to say you have never done/been something, or with "été aussi…" to mean "I’ve never been so…".
target_language_example: J'ai jamais vu un film aussi drôle.
native_language_example: I've never seen a movie that funny.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *lire* with *avoir*: **j'** (je) + **ai** (have) + **lu** (read). Used to say you read something (a file, report, article). Often translates to English simple past (“I read…”) or present perfect (“I have read…”), depending on context.
target_language_example: J'ai lu ton message ce matin.
native_language_example: I read your message this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense of oublier (“to forget”) using the passé composé: j’ai + oublié. Often used alone as an apology (“Sorry, I forgot.”) or followed by what was forgotten: j’ai oublié + noun (j’ai oublié les paroles) or j’ai oublié ce que… (“I forgot what…”).
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon mot de passe, je ne peux pas me connecter.
native_language_example: I forgot my password, I can’t log in.

additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t do an action because you forgot. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « j’ai oublié de + infinitive » (e.g., j’ai oublié de fermer la porte). Can also introduce something you forgot to mention: « Oh, j’ai oublié de te dire… ».
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai oublié de répondre à ton message.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot to reply to your message.

meaning: “I forgot my …” (talking about a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun after it (mon + masculine noun), e.g., mon livre, mon portable, mon portefeuille. In French, the past tense is built with avoir: j’ai oublié = “I forgot / I’ve forgotten.” If the noun is feminine, you usually say: j’ai oublié ma …
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon passeport à l'hôtel.
native_language_example: I forgot my passport at the hotel.

meaning: I spoke to / I talked to.
additional_notes: Used with the passé composé of parler (j'ai parlé) to say you spoke/talked to someone in the past. The preposition à introduces the person you spoke to (e.g., j'ai parlé à ma mère). In speech, you’ll often hear it shortened to "j’ai parlé à" → "j’ai parlé à" (same spelling, faster pronunciation).
target_language_example: J'ai parlé à ton professeur après le cours.
native_language_example: I spoke to your teacher after class.

meaning: “I haven’t / I didn’t / I don’t” (informal negative form of « j’ai »).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: it drops « ne » from the standard negative « je n’ai pas … ». Used before a past participle (« J’ai pas compris » = I didn’t understand / I haven’t understood) or before an infinitive in near future constructions (« J’ai pas décidé » = I haven’t decided). In careful writing or formal situations, use « je n’ai pas ».
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai pas le temps aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have time today.

meaning: “I spent” / “I had” (a time/day/evening) / “I made” (a call) / “I struck” (a deal).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé (past tense) of *passer* with *avoir*: **j’ai passé** = “I passed / I spent / I did,” depending on what follows. Common beginner patterns: **j’ai passé du temps** (I spent time), **j’ai passé la journée/la soirée** (I spent the day/evening), **j’ai passé un coup de fil** (I made a phone call), **j’ai passé un marché** (I made/struck a deal).
target_language_example: J’ai passé une bonne journée avec mes amis.
native_language_example: I had a good day with my friends.

meaning: “I had / I spent a …” (talking about time, like a day or an evening).
additional_notes: Used with a time period (une journée, une soirée, une semaine, etc.) to describe how your time was. It’s the passé composé of *passer*: *j’ai passé* + adjective + time word. Even though it looks like English “I passed,” here it usually means “I spent” or “I had.”
target_language_example: J'ai passé une semaine incroyable à Paris.
native_language_example: I had an incredible week in Paris.

additional_notes: Used to express a past thought or idea. Most often followed by **que** + a sentence: *J'ai pensé que...* (“I thought that...”). With **à** + a person/thing, it means “to think about (someone/something)”: *J'ai pensé à toi* (“I thought about you”).
target_language_example: J'ai pensé que tu avais raison.
native_language_example: I thought you were right.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed or assumed (often a reason or motivation for what you did). In French, after "penser que" you normally use the indicative (e.g., "j'ai pensé que tu voulais…"). In negative form, it often takes the subjunctive: "je n'ai pas pensé que tu viennes" (I didn’t think you would come).
target_language_example: J'ai pensé que tu étais déjà parti, alors je ne t'ai pas appelé.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left, so I didn’t call you.

additional_notes: Used to describe a past belief/opinion that may or may not still be true. "J'ai pensé" is the passé composé of *penser* (a completed thought in the past). "que" introduces what you thought, and "c'était" means "it was/that was" (from *ce + était*). Often followed by an adjective or a noun phrase: *important*, *une bonne idée*, *vous*, etc.
target_language_example: J'ai pensé que c'était trop tard.
native_language_example: I thought it was too late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed/assumed about someone (often as an explanation). It’s the passé composé of penser (j’ai pensé = “I thought”), followed by que + a clause starting with tu. What follows can be in the imperfect/conditional/etc. depending on the meaning: e.g., "J’ai pensé que tu aurais faim" = “I thought you would be hungry.”
target_language_example: J'ai pensé que tu étais déjà parti.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

additional_notes: Passé composé of "penser" + "à". Use "penser à" + noun/pronoun to say you had something in mind or considered something: "J'ai pensé à toi" (I thought of you), "J'ai pensé à ça" (I thought about that). Contrast: "penser que" is followed by a full clause/opinion ("Je pense que…" = I think that…).
target_language_example: Hier, j'ai pensé à toi.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I thought of you.

additional_notes: Passé composé of prendre (je prends → j’ai pris). Very common and flexible: it can mean you took/grabbed something (J’ai pris de quoi manger), took notes (J’ai pris des notes), had food/drinks (J’ai pris deux verres de vin), answered a call (J’ai pris l’appel), made a decision (J’ai pris ma décision), made an appointment (J’ai pris rendez-vous), or took care of someone (J’ai pris soin de toi). The exact English translation depends on the noun/phrase that follows.
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai pris le dernier billet.
native_language_example: Sorry, I took the last ticket.

meaning: 'I was able to' / 'I could' / 'I managed to' (in the past).
additional_notes: Past tense of "pouvoir" (passé composé). It often means you had the ability or the opportunity to do something and succeeded: "J'ai pu faire…" = "I was able to do…". In questions, it can express surprise/regret: "Comment j'ai pu… ?" = "How could I…?". Common with comparisons/time: "aussi vite que j'ai pu" (as fast as I could), "autant que j'ai pu" (as much as I could), "dès que j'ai pu" (as soon as I could).
target_language_example: Je suis parti dès que j'ai pu.
native_language_example: I left as soon as I could.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of recevoir. Used to say you received or got a message, letter, call, orders, etc. Often followed by a direct object: J'ai reçu ton message / un appel / une lettre. In formal contexts you may see: J'ai bien reçu… ("I have received…").
target_language_example: J'ai reçu ton e-mail ce matin.
native_language_example: I got your email this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of recevoir: « j’ai reçu » = I received / I’ve received. « une lettre » is a (paper) letter, not an email (use « un e-mail / un mail »). Often followed by « de » + person: « une lettre de mon père » (a letter from my father).
target_language_example: J'ai reçu une lettre de ma grand-mère hier.
native_language_example: I received a letter from my grandmother yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say something has been true for you for a long time (often up to the present). Common with past participles (j’ai toujours été…) or with verbs like rêver (j’ai toujours rêvé de…). In spoken French, "j’ai" is often pronounced like "j’ai"/"j’" before a vowel.
target_language_example: J’ai toujours voulu apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I've always wanted to learn French.

meaning: "I always knew that" (I’ve known all along that…).
additional_notes: Used to say you were certain about something from the start, often before it happened. It’s the passé composé of *savoir* (j’ai su = I found out / I came to know), but with *toujours* it typically means you had that knowledge all along. Commonly followed by a clause in the imperfect or conditional (e.g., *arriverait, pouvais, y arriverais, finirait*).
target_language_example: J’ai toujours su que tu réussirais.
native_language_example: I always knew you would succeed.

additional_notes: Literally "I have always wanted." Used to talk about a long-standing desire up to now. Often followed by an infinitive (j'ai toujours voulu + verb: "j'ai toujours voulu voyager") or by a noun ("j'ai toujours voulu un fils"). In more formal/written French, you may also see "j'ai toujours voulu dire" for "I've always wanted to say," but everyday speech often uses "j'ai toujours voulu te dire…".
target_language_example: J'ai toujours voulu apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I've always wanted to learn French.

additional_notes: Often used as the start of a sentence with a past participle (passé composé): **J’ai tout + past participle** = “I … everything” (e.g., *J’ai tout essayé* = “I tried everything”). On its own, **J’ai tout** can mean “I have everything / I’ve got everything,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : j’ai tout compris.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I understood everything.

additional_notes: Past tense of *trouver* with **avoir** (passé composé). Used when you located/discovered something (*J’ai trouvé une solution*), found/obtained something (*J’ai trouvé du travail*), or when you mean **“I thought / I found that…”** with **j’ai trouvé que + clause** (*J’ai trouvé que ça tout à fait normal*). It can also be used alone to mean “I’ve got it!” / “Found it!” (*Voilà, j’ai trouvé.*).
target_language_example: J’ai trouvé une bonne boulangerie près d’ici.
native_language_example: I found a good bakery near here.

additional_notes: Used to announce that you found something (an object, a place, a solution, etc.). Literally "I have found a" (passé composé of trouver). The noun that follows is masculine singular and usually begins with a consonant sound: un boulot, un travail, un gâteau, un point de vue. With a feminine noun, you’d say: j’ai trouvé une …
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé un bon restaurant près d'ici.
native_language_example: I found a good restaurant near here.

additional_notes: Used to say you discovered an object inside a place/container (a room, bag, pocket, someone’s things). Very common in conversation; you then add the location after "dans". In more formal writing you might also see "j’ai trouvé ceci dans…"
target_language_example: J’ai trouvé ça dans le tiroir du bureau.
native_language_example: I found this in the desk drawer.

additional_notes: Literally the passé composé of voir: "j'ai vu" = "I saw / I've seen." In conversation, especially in "C'est bon, j'ai vu", it can mean "OK, I understand" or "OK, I've got it" after someone explains or shows you something. It can also mean you noticed something ("I saw how you look at her") or discovered the truth about someone ("I saw his true face").
target_language_example: Pas besoin d'expliquer, j'ai vu.
native_language_example: No need to explain, I get it.

meaning: 'I saw the' / 'I've seen the' (feminine singular object).
additional_notes: "J'ai vu" is the passé composé of *voir* (to see): *j’* (I) + *ai* (have) + *vu* (seen). It’s followed by **la** when the thing you saw is feminine singular (*la photo*, *la Terre*). For masculine singular use **j’ai vu le…**, and for plural use **j’ai vu les…**. In speech, *j’ai* is often pronounced like “zhay”.
target_language_example: J’ai vu la voiture rouge devant l’école.
native_language_example: I saw the red car in front of the school.

additional_notes: Literally "I have seen that" (passé composé of voir). Used to say you saw something (on TV, in the news, online, etc.) or that you’ve already seen it before. In casual speech you may also hear just "Vu ça" or "J’ai déjà vu ça" (I’ve already seen that).
target_language_example: T'inquiète, j'ai vu ça sur Internet.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I saw that on the Internet.

additional_notes: Passé composé of être (je + ai + été). Often used (1) with an adjective to describe how you were/you felt: « J'ai été content/ravi. », and (2) to form the passive voice: « J'ai été acquitté » = “I was acquitted.” In many everyday contexts it translates to English simple past (“I was”), even though the literal form is “I have been.”
target_language_example: J'ai été très fatigué hier soir.
native_language_example: I was very tired last night.

additional_notes: Contraction of "je" + "ai" (present tense of "avoir"). Used either as the main verb meaning "to have" (e.g., "j'ai un frère" = I have a brother) or very often as an auxiliary to form the past tense (passé composé): "j'ai + past participle" (e.g., "j'ai vécu" = I lived / I have lived). In negatives, it becomes "je n'ai pas".
target_language_example: J'ai fini mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I finished my homework.

meaning: "I have something else" / "I have something else to do/say/ask".
additional_notes: Used to introduce an additional thing you want to say/ask, or to indicate you have other plans or something else on your mind (often implying you can’t do what was suggested). Frequently followed by: « de prévu » (planned), « en tête » (in mind), or « à + infinitive » (to do/say/ask).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j’ai autre chose de prévu.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come—I have other plans.

additional_notes:
Used to express necessity or a need. Most often followed by:
- "de" + noun/pronoun: "J'ai besoin de ça" (I need that), "J'ai besoin de temps" (I need time).
- "de" + infinitive: "J'ai besoin de me détendre" (I need to relax).
- "que" + subjunctive for a need involving someone else’s action: "J'ai besoin que vous m'écoutiez" (I need you to listen to me).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de ton aide.
native_language_example: I need your help.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something. The d' (de) links to what you need: j'ai besoin d'un/une + noun (j'ai besoin d'un café / d'une carte). With a verb, use de + infinitive: J'ai besoin d'y aller (“I need to go there”). The verb is avoir, so it can change: tu as besoin de…, il/elle a besoin de…, nous avons besoin de….
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un moment pour réfléchir.
native_language_example: I need a moment to think.

meaning: "I need a" (followed by a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you need something or someone. It’s the most common way to express need in French. Change the article depending on the noun: j’ai besoin d’une + feminine noun; j’ai besoin de + plural/uncountable (e.g., j’ai besoin de temps); j’ai besoin d’ + vowel sound (e.g., j’ai besoin d’un avocat).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un stylo, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I need a pen, please.

meaning: “I need a/an …” (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or requirement. "J’ai besoin de" = "I need"; it changes to "d’une" before a feminine singular noun (e.g., une autorisation, une signature). For a masculine noun, use "j’ai besoin d’un"; for a plural, "j’ai besoin de" + plural noun ("j’ai besoin de clés").
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’une minute, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: I need a minute, please.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity. Follow it with a noun (J’ai besoin de détails) or with an infinitive verb (J’ai besoin de partir). Before another verb, you usually keep "de" and use the infinitive: "J’ai besoin de te parler". In negatives: "Je n’ai pas besoin de...".
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de parler avec toi.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity/urgency to get information. Structure: « J’ai besoin de + infinitive » (here, « savoir »). Often followed by an indirect question: « pourquoi », « qui », « ce que », « où », etc. You can also say « J’ai besoin de savoir + nom/quelque chose » (e.g., « quelque chose », « la vérité »).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de savoir où tu étais hier soir.
native_language_example: I need to know where you were last night.

additional_notes: Used to say you need someone’s help, support, or presence. "J’ai besoin de" is followed by a person (toi/vous/lui/elle) or a thing (ex. "J’ai besoin d’aide" = I need help). You can add a place or time: "J’ai besoin de toi là-bas" (I need you there) or "quand j’ai besoin de toi" (when I need you).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de toi maintenant, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: I need you now, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something that belongs to or comes from the person you’re addressing. « votre » is the formal singular (“your” to one person politely) or plural (“your” to multiple people). It’s followed by a noun: « J’ai besoin de votre avis » (your opinion), « … de votre signature » (your signature).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, j’ai besoin de votre aide.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need your help.

additional_notes: Used to say you need someone's help/presence. "Vous" can mean one person you’re addressing formally, or multiple people ("you all"). You can add details like "ici" (here), "tout de suite" (right now), or "vous deux" (both of you).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, j'ai besoin de vous pour remplir ce formulaire.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need you to fill out this form.

meaning: "I need you to" (followed by a verb, usually in the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express a need or requirement that someone else does something. After "j'ai besoin que", French normally uses the subjunctive: "que tu croies", "que tu reviennes", "que tu signes", etc. In everyday speech you may also hear "J'ai besoin de toi pour..." (I need you to/for...) depending on the structure.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin que tu m'aides tout de suite.
native_language_example: I need you to help me right now.

meaning: I trust (in) / I have confidence in.
additional_notes: Used to say you trust a person or thing: "J'ai confiance en toi/elle/lui/vous" (I trust you/her/him/you [formal/plural]). You can also trust someone's ability or judgment: "J'ai confiance en ton jugement" (I trust your judgment). In negatives: "Je n'ai pas confiance en..." (I don't trust...).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, j'ai confiance en toi.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I trust you.

additional_notes: Used to say you have other things/people/plans besides the ones mentioned. It’s usually followed by a plural noun: j’ai d’autres projets / d’autres patients. The full pattern is: "j’ai" + "d’autres" + plural noun. Often implies “I have more/else to do.”
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas rester : j'ai d'autres choses à faire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't stay: I have other things to do.

meaning: "I have (some)" (used before a noun, often plural, especially when there’s an adjective).
additional_notes: It’s the start of "j’ai + [something]". In French, "des" often becomes "de" (or "d’") before a plural noun when an adjective comes before the noun: "J’ai de grands projets" (not *des grands projets* in standard French). You also see it in expressions like "de tout" (“everything / all kinds of things”) and in "ce que j’ai de mieux" (“the best I have”).
target_language_example: J’ai de bonnes idées pour ce projet.
native_language_example: I have some good ideas for this project.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel fortunate, often followed by de + infinitive to say what you’re lucky to do/have (e.g., j’ai de la chance de te connaître = I’m lucky to know you). Can also be said alone (J’ai de la chance.) or as a rhetorical question/tag (J’ai de la chance, hein ?). In phrases like Si j’ai de la chance ! it’s an emphatic way to say “Yes, I’m lucky!” (sometimes with irony depending on context).
target_language_example: J’ai de la chance d’avoir des amis comme toi.
native_language_example: I’m lucky to have friends like you.

additional_notes: Used to say you possess or have something in general, before a plural noun: j’ai + des + noun (e.g., des projets, des infos). "J’ai" is the contraction of "je ai". "Des" often means "some" or simply marks an unspecified plural in French.
target_language_example: J'ai des questions pour toi.
native_language_example: I have some questions for you.

meaning: “I have some …” (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: “Du” is the partitive article (de + le) meaning “some” or “(a bit) of.” Common with uncountable nouns (du boulot = some work, du respect = some respect) and certain fixed expressions like “du retard” (to be late / have a delay). Don’t confuse with “j’ai dû” (with an accent), which means “I had to.”
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai du retard.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m late.

meaning: "I have news" / "I have something new (to tell you)."
additional_notes: Used to announce you have new information or an update. Very common with "pour toi/vous" (for you) and in phrases like "dès que j'ai du nouveau" or "si j'ai du nouveau" meaning "as soon as I have any news" / "if I get any news." You can also say "du nouveau ?" to ask "Any news?"
target_language_example: Je te tiens au courant dès que j’ai du nouveau.
native_language_example: I’ll keep you posted as soon as I have any news.

additional_notes: Used to say you have some work/tasks, often implying you’re busy or have work waiting. You can add details: "en retard" (behind), "pour vous" (for you), "qui m’attend" (waiting for me). With this structure: "J’ai du + noun" = “I have some + noun” (an unspecified amount).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir ce soir : j’ai du travail.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come tonight: I have work to do.

meaning: "I still have" / "I have ... left" (also "I have more").
additional_notes: Used to say something remains to do/ask, time remains, or that you can add something else. Common patterns: "J'ai encore + noun" (J'ai encore du travail = I still have work), "J'ai encore + infinitive" (J'ai encore des choses à faire = I still have things to do), and "J'ai encore le temps" (I still have time). In "J'ai encore mieux", it means "I have something even better".
target_language_example: J’ai encore deux emails à envoyer avant de partir.
native_language_example: I still have two emails to send before leaving.

additional_notes: Literally “I have desire.” Most often followed by **de + infinitive**: *J’ai envie de parler* (I feel like talking). With a different subject or a full clause, you can use **avoir envie que + subjunctive**: *J’ai envie qu’elle soit heureuse* (I want her to be happy). In questions or negative/ironic contexts it can mean “Do you think I want to…?”
target_language_example: J’ai envie de prendre un café.
native_language_example: I feel like having a coffee.

meaning: "I feel like…" / "I want to…" (often: I’m in the mood to…).
additional_notes: "Avoir envie de" expresses a desire or urge. Use **j’ai envie de + infinitive**: *J’ai envie d’essayer* (I feel like trying). With a noun, use **j’ai envie de + noun** (or **d’** before a vowel): *J’ai envie d’une cigarette* (I feel like a cigarette). It’s generally a more “craving/feeling” want than **je veux** (which can sound more direct/demanding).
target_language_example: J’ai envie de sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: I feel like going out tonight.

additional_notes: Used to express a desire or urge. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « J’ai envie de + infinitive » (J’ai envie de sortir, de marcher). It can be a simple want (more like “I feel like…”) or a stronger desire depending on context. In a negative or rhetorical question, it often means “Do you think I WANT to…?” to show reluctance: « Tu crois que j’ai envie de faire ça ? ».
target_language_example: Là, j’ai envie de prendre un café.
native_language_example: Right now, I feel like having a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say you only need one thing (often to reassure, minimize, or explain). Follow with an infinitive verb after d’ (before a vowel): « J’ai juste besoin d’envoyer… ». With a noun, use de/d’ + article: « J’ai juste besoin d’un moment / d’un peu d’eau ».
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai juste besoin d'appeler ma sœur.
native_language_example: Sorry, I just need to call my sister.

additional_notes: Used to express a simple or immediate need. With an infinitive (verb) it means “I just need to…”: « J’ai juste besoin de parler / prendre l’air ». With a noun it means “I just need …”: « J’ai juste besoin de temps / de toi ». Often conveys “that’s all I need” or “for now,” and can soften a request or explanation.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, j’ai juste besoin de me reposer un peu.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I just need to rest a little.

additional_notes: “J’ai” means “I have.” The “l’” is the shortened form of “le” or “la” used before a word that starts with a vowel or silent h (h muet): j’ai l’adresse, j’ai l’intention, j’ai l’œil. Used to say you possess something (an address, authorization) or have something in/with you, depending on context.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, j’ai l’autorisation.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have the authorization.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **avoir l’air (de)** = “to look/seem (like/to)”. It describes appearance or the impression you give. Often followed by **de + noun** (J’ai l’air d’une banque.) or **de + infinitive** (J’ai l’air de faire quoi ?). In questions like **De quoi j’ai l’air ?**, it can mean “What do I look like?” or “What do you take me for?” depending on context/tone.
target_language_example: Tu crois que j’ai l’air fatigué ?
native_language_example: Do you think I look tired?

meaning: "I feel like…" / "I have the impression…" (I think/seems to me).
additional_notes: Used to express a subjective feeling or perception (not a certain fact). Common patterns: « J'ai l'impression de + infinitive » (I feel like doing / having done) and « J'ai l'impression que + clause » (I feel like / I get the sense that…). Often translates naturally as “I feel like…” or “It seems to me…”.
target_language_example: J'ai l'impression qu'il va pleuvoir.
native_language_example: I have a feeling it’s going to rain.

meaning: “I feel like…” / “I get the impression that…” (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to express a subjective feeling or perception about a situation. It’s typically followed by an infinitive: « j’ai l’impression de + infinitive » (e.g., « j’ai l’impression de rêver »). If you want to use a full clause with “that,” French often uses « j’ai l’impression que + (sentence) ».
target_language_example: J’ai l’impression de te connaître depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: I feel like I’ve known you for a long time.

meaning: "I feel/think that…" or "I get the impression that…"
additional_notes: Used to give your personal impression or a hunch (often not 100% certain). It’s commonly followed by the indicative: « J’ai l’impression que c’est lui. » You can also answer briefly: « J’ai l’impression que oui/non », and « …que si » to contradict a negative statement (roughly “actually, yes”).
target_language_example: J’ai l’impression que tu es fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I get the impression that you’re tired today.

meaning: "I have the…" / "I've got…" (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is a common starter for saying you have something (an object, a trait, or a condition): j’ai + feminine noun. It literally means “I have the…”, but in English you often translate it as “I have…” (without “the”) or sometimes “My … is …” (e.g., j’ai la peau sensible = “I have sensitive skin”). For masculine nouns, use "j'ai le"; for plural, "j'ai les"; and before a vowel sound, "j'ai l'".
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai la gorge sèche.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have a dry throat.

meaning: "I have the" (for a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: j’ai le + nom. Often expresses possession (j’ai le numéro), having something available/under control (j’ai le contrôle, j’ai le dossier), or having a condition involving a body part (j’ai le nez qui coule = my nose is running). If the noun is feminine, use « j’ai la »; plural: « j’ai les ». Before a vowel or silent h, « le/la » becomes « l’ » (j’ai l’adresse).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, j’ai le plan.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have the plan.

meaning: "I have the right to" / "I'm allowed to".
additional_notes: Used to state a right or permission to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., parler, me défendre, poser). You can change the subject: tu as le droit de… (you’re allowed to…), il/elle a le droit de… (he/she is allowed to…), on a le droit de…, nous avons le droit de…, vous avez le droit de…, ils/elles ont le droit de….
target_language_example: J'ai le droit de dire non.
native_language_example: I have the right to say no.

additional_notes: Used with plural nouns after "avoir" to talk about things you have. Very common with body parts ("J'ai les mains froides" = "My hands are cold") and it also appears in fixed expressions/idioms where the meaning isn’t literal (e.g., "J'ai les boules" = "I'm really annoyed/upset" (informal), "J'ai les crocs" = "I'm starving" (informal), "J'ai les moyens" = "I can afford it"). The adjective usually agrees in plural if you add one ("les mains froides").
target_language_example: J'ai les mains froides.
native_language_example: My hands are cold.

meaning: “I haven’t / I didn’t / I don’t” (informal negative form of « j’ai »).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: it drops « ne » from the standard negative « je n’ai pas … ». Used before a past participle (« J’ai pas compris » = I didn’t understand / I haven’t understood) or before an infinitive in near future constructions (« J’ai pas décidé » = I haven’t decided). In careful writing or formal situations, use « je n’ai pas ».
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai pas le temps aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have time today.

meaning: “I have someone …” (e.g., someone in mind / someone to see).
additional_notes: Used with a complement to express that there is a specific person involved. Common patterns: “J’ai quelqu’un en tête” = “I have someone in mind”; “J’ai quelqu’un à voir” = “I have someone to see / I need to see someone.” On its own (“J’ai quelqu’un.”) it usually just means “I have someone (with me/at home/etc.)” depending on context.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas rester : j’ai quelqu’un à voir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t stay: I have someone to see.

additional_notes: Used to say you have something (an object, a problem, or something intended for someone). Often followed by extra info: **dans** + body part (j’ai quelque chose dans l’œil = something is in my eye), **pour** + person (j’ai quelque chose pour lui = I have something for him), or a relative clause **qui…** (j’ai quelque chose qui t’est destiné = I have something meant for you).
target_language_example: J’ai quelque chose à te dire.
native_language_example: I have something to tell you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an important action you’re about to do or say. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., dire, faire, demander) and can take an indirect object: à te… (to you, informal) / à vous… (to you, formal or plural). You can also say: J'ai quelque chose d'important à dire. / J'ai quelque chose d'important à te dire.
target_language_example: J'ai quelque chose d'important à te dire avant de partir.
native_language_example: I have something important to tell you before leaving.

additional_notes: Used when you’re about to give someone something (a gift, a message, a surprise, an item you picked up). You can swap the person: « pour vous » (for you, formal/plural), « pour lui/elle » (for him/her).
target_language_example: J'ai quelque chose pour toi : je t'ai acheté un petit cadeau.
native_language_example: I have something for you: I bought you a small gift.

meaning: "I have something to …" (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an action you need/want to do (often something important to say, announce, show, fix, or deal with). It’s followed by the infinitive: « J'ai quelque chose à + verb » (à dire, à annoncer, à montrer, à régler, etc.).
target_language_example: Attends, j'ai quelque chose à te demander.
native_language_example: Wait, I have something to ask you.

j'ai quelque chose à te dire

target_language_multi_word_term: j'ai quelque chose à te dire
meaning: I have something to tell you.
additional_notes: Used to introduce news or a message you want to share. Often sounds a bit serious or important (it can create suspense), especially with openers like « Écoute » or « En fait ». You can change who you’re speaking to: « à vous dire » (to you, formal/plural), « à lui dire » (to tell him/her), « à leur dire » (to tell them).
target_language_example: Avant de partir, j'ai quelque chose à te dire.
native_language_example: Before leaving, I have something to tell you.

additional_notes: Literally “I have reason,” but it means “I’m right.” Often used in conversation to confirm you’re correct: “J’ai raison, pas vrai ?” (“I’m right, aren’t I?”). In the pattern “J’ai raison ou j’ai raison ?”, it’s a rhetorical way of saying “I’m right, obviously.”
target_language_example: Tu vois ? J'ai raison, pas vrai ?
native_language_example: See? I’m right, aren’t I?

additional_notes: Used to say you have a scheduled meeting with a specific person. Very common for medical, professional, or planned personal meetups. In speech it can also imply a date depending on context (e.g., "avec une fille").
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j'ai rendez-vous avec mon médecin.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have an appointment with my doctor.

additional_notes: Used to express that you have a lot to do or say. It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., dire, faire, raconter). You can add an object before the infinitive: à te/vous dire = “to tell you,” à te raconter = “to tell you (a story).”
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas sortir ce soir : j’ai tant de choses à faire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out tonight: I have so many things to do.

meaning: "I have a" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: From "je" + "ai" (present tense of avoir, “to have”). Used to say you have/possess something, or that you have something to do (e.g., "J'ai un truc à faire" = “I’ve got something to do”). Before a feminine singular noun, say "j'ai une".
target_language_example: Désolé, j'ai un rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have an appointment.

meaning: “I have a little …” / “I’ve got a small …” (introducing something small, often a gift or surprise).
additional_notes: Usually followed by a noun: j’ai un petit cadeau (a small gift), j’ai un petit quelque chose (a little something). “Petit” can sound modest/affectionate and is often used when you’re about to give or show something.
target_language_example: J’ai un petit souvenir pour toi.
native_language_example: I have a little souvenir for you.

meaning: "I have an appointment" / "I have a meeting".
additional_notes: Used to say you have a scheduled commitment at a specific time. "Un rendez-vous" can be a professional appointment (doctor, business, etc.) or sometimes a date (romantic context). Often followed by details like "chez le médecin" (at the doctor’s) or "à 15 h" (at 3 p.m.).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : j'ai un rendez-vous à 14 h.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have an appointment at 2 p.m.

additional_notes: Very common and informal: "truc" is a catch-all word for an unspecified object, plan, topic, problem, or secret. Often followed by details: "j’ai un truc à te dire" (something to tell you), "j’ai un truc de prévu" (something planned), "j’ai un truc pour toi" (something for you).
target_language_example: Attends, j’ai un truc important à te demander.
native_language_example: Wait, I have something important to ask you.

additional_notes: Uses "truc" (= a thing / something) as a very common, casual way to refer to an unspecified task, topic, or object. It’s followed by "à" + infinitive (e.g., régler, dire, montrer). In more formal French, you might say "j’ai quelque chose à…".
target_language_example: Désolé, je dois partir : j’ai un truc à faire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go: I’ve got something to do.

additional_notes: From the verb **avoir** (to have): **j'ai** = “I have.” It’s used to introduce something you possess or want to say, especially with announcements or information: **J’ai une annonce / une question / une idée.** The **j’** is a shortened form of **je** before a vowel sound. Use **un** instead of **une** with a masculine noun (**j’ai un problème**).
target_language_example: J'ai une question à te poser.
native_language_example: I have a question to ask you.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is feminine and is either mentioned just before or understood from context (e.g., une théorie, une faveur). If you say the noun, you can add it: « J’ai une autre théorie. » For a masculine noun, use « j’ai un autre … » (e.g., « J’ai un autre problème. »).
target_language_example: Attends, j’ai une autre question.
native_language_example: Wait, I have another question.

meaning: "I have a wife and…" (i.e., “I’m married and…”)
additional_notes: Used to introduce your family situation, often followed by children ("trois enfants", "un enfant"). French commonly uses "avoir" (“to have”) to talk about family relationships (wife/husband/children). Note: "une femme" can mean “a woman” or “a wife,” but in this pattern ("J’ai une femme…") it usually means “a wife.”
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir ce soir : j’ai une femme et deux enfants.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come tonight: I have a wife and two children.

meaning: "I have an idea." / "I’ve got an idea."
additional_notes: Used when you suddenly think of a solution or suggestion. Very common in conversation; it can stand alone or be introduced with fillers like "Oh" or "OK". Often followed by what the idea is (e.g., "J’ai une idée : on y va demain.").
target_language_example: J’ai une idée : on peut prendre le métro.
native_language_example: I’ve got an idea: we can take the subway.

additional_notes: From "je" (I) + "aime" (like/love). Use it with a noun ("J'aime le café."), with an infinitive verb to say you like doing something ("J'aime danser."), or with "ça" to mean "I like that/this" ("J'aime ça."). To say you don’t like something: "Je n'aime pas...".
target_language_example: J'aime apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I like learning French.

additional_notes: Common, everyday way to say you like something without it sounding as strong or intense as “j’adore” (I love it). Often used to express a positive opinion or preference: “J’aime bien ça” (I like that), “J’aime bien cet endroit” (I quite like this place). Can also be used on its own to mean “I like it” or “I’m fine with it”: “Moi, j’aime bien.”
target_language_example: J'aime bien ce film, surtout la musique.
native_language_example: I quite like this movie, especially the music.

meaning: 'I would like' / 'I'd like' (polite way to say what you want).
additional_notes: From the conditional of aimer (“to like/love”), used to make requests or wishes sound softer and more polite than je veux (“I want”). Often followed by an infinitive: j’aimerais aller…, j’aimerais te parler…. You can add bien (j’aimerais bien…) to mean “I’d really like to / I’d quite like to.”
target_language_example: J'aimerais un café, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a coffee, please.

meaning: “I was going” / “I was going to” (was about to).
additional_notes: Contraction of « je » + « allais » (imparfait of « aller »). Very common for the near future in the past: « j’allais + infinitive » = “I was going to / I was about to …” (often something planned or almost happening: « J’allais t’appeler. »). It can also mean simple past movement: “I was going (somewhere)”.
target_language_example: Je pensais que j’allais tomber.
native_language_example: I thought I was going to fall.

meaning: “I’m coming right away / I’ll be right there.”
additional_notes: Used to reply when someone is waiting for you or calling you; it means you’re on your way immediately (or very soon). In conversation it can also be used a bit loosely to mean “in a minute.” Often said with informal replies like “Ouais” or “Vas-y.”
target_language_example: Attends-moi devant l’entrée, j’arrive tout de suite.
native_language_example: Wait for me in front of the entrance; I’ll be right there.

additional_notes: *J'aurais* is the conditional of *j'ai* ("I have"). It’s used (1) with a past participle to talk about a hypothetical past or regret: *J'aurais compris* ("I would have understood"); (2) with certain past participles like *voulu* to express what you would have wanted to do: *J'aurais voulu parler…* ("I would have liked/wanted to talk…"); and (3) in questions about an unreal situation: *Qu'est-ce que j'aurais fait sans toi ?* ("What would I have done without you?").
target_language_example: J'aurais aimé venir, mais je travaillais.
native_language_example: I would have liked to come, but I was working.

additional_notes: This is the past conditional of "aimer" and is used to say you would have wanted something, but it didn’t happen (or you’re disappointed it didn’t). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive ("J’aurais aimé rester") or by "que" + subjunctive ("J’aurais aimé que tu m’en parles"). It can also sound like a gentle reproach: "I wish you had…".
target_language_example: J’aurais aimé te voir avant ton départ.
native_language_example: I would have liked to see you before you left.

meaning: "I should have" / "I ought to have" (regret about something not done).
additional_notes: Conditional perfect of devoir: j’ (je) + aurais (would have) + dû (had to/should). Used to say you did not do something in the past and you regret it or think it would have been better. Often followed by an infinitive: j’aurais dû venir (I should have come). Can also be used in questions: J’aurais dû dire quoi ? (What should I have said?).
target_language_example: J’aurais dû te prévenir plus tôt.
native_language_example: I should have warned you earlier.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional perfect of devoir ("aurais dû") to express regret or criticism about a past action that wasn’t done: you think it was the right thing to do earlier. Often followed by a time expression like "depuis longtemps" (for a long time), "il y a longtemps" (a long time ago), or "plus tôt" (earlier).
target_language_example: J'aurais dû le faire hier, mais j'ai oublié.
native_language_example: I should have done it yesterday, but I forgot.

meaning: "I should have (to you)" / "I ought to have (told you, believed you, etc.)."
additional_notes: Used to express regret about something you didn’t do in the past. It’s the past conditional of devoir: "j’aurais dû" + infinitive (e.g., "dire", "croire"). "Te" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to you" (informal singular). Often continues as "j’aurais dû te + [verb]" or "j’aurais dû te le + [verb]" ("I should have told it to you").
target_language_example: J'aurais dû te demander avant de partir.
native_language_example: I should have asked you before leaving.

meaning: “I could have” / “I would have been able to.”
additional_notes: This is the past conditional of pouvoir (“can/to be able to”): j’ (je) + aurais (would have) + pu (been able). It’s used for missed possibilities, regrets, or hypothetical past situations. It’s usually followed by an infinitive (e.g., j’aurais pu le faire = I could have done it), but it can also stand alone when the action is understood from context (J’aurais pu. = I could have.)
target_language_example: J’aurais pu venir, mais j’étais trop fatigué(e).
native_language_example: I could have come, but I was too tired.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you had in the past, or a past state/background situation (often translated as “I had/used to have” or sometimes “I was + adjective”). It’s also used as an auxiliary with a past participle to form the pluperfect (plus-que-parfait): « j'avais compris » = “I had understood.” In speech you’ll often hear « j'avais pas… » instead of « je n'avais pas… ».
target_language_example: J'avais déjà vu ce film quand j'étais petit.
native_language_example: I had already seen that movie when I was little.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you had in the past, or a past state/background situation (often translated as “I had/used to have” or sometimes “I was + adjective”). It’s also used as an auxiliary with a past participle to form the pluperfect (plus-que-parfait): « j'avais compris » = “I had understood.” In speech you’ll often hear « j'avais pas… » instead of « je n'avais pas… ».
target_language_example: J'avais déjà vu ce film quand j'étais petit.
native_language_example: I had already seen that movie when I was little.

meaning: "I needed" / "I was in need of" (imperfect past).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect (j'avais) to describe an ongoing need or a background situation in the past. It’s typically followed by de/d’ + noun or pronoun (de toi, d’elle, de ça), or by de + infinitive (e.g., j’avais besoin de partir = I needed to leave). In expressions like « Comme si j'avais besoin de ça », it’s often ironic: “as if I needed that (on top of everything).”
target_language_example: Hier, j'étais stressé : j'avais besoin d'une pause.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I was stressed: I needed a break.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of "avoir besoin de" (to need). Use it for ongoing/repeated needs in the past or to set background: "I needed...". Followed by a noun (besoin de compagnie), an infinitive (besoin de réfléchir), or a person/object + infinitive (besoin de te voir). In more formal French, say "j'avais besoin d'argent" instead of "de fric".
target_language_example: J'avais besoin de repos, alors je suis resté chez moi.
native_language_example: I needed some rest, so I stayed home.

meaning: “I … of it/of them” or “I … some (of it/them)” ("je" + the pronoun "en").
additional_notes: "En" replaces something introduced with "de" (de + noun) or an unspecified quantity. With "j'" it becomes "j'en". Common meanings: (1) “of it/of them” → "J’en prends la responsabilité" = “I take responsibility for it.” (2) “some (of it/them)” → "J’en veux" = “I want some.” (3) sometimes “from there/from it” depending on context. Placement: "en" usually goes before the verb ("j’en pense", "j’en prends").
target_language_example: J’en ai besoin.
native_language_example: I need it (I need some / I need it).

meaning: “I have some/any (of it/them)” / “I’ve had enough (of it)” (depending on context).
additional_notes: "En" replaces something introduced with "de" (or a quantity): e.g., "du pain" → "j'en ai" = "I have some (bread)." You often see it with a quantity or expression like "assez / trop / beaucoup" (j'en ai assez = I've had enough) and it can be followed by a past participle: "J'en ai assez entendu/vu" = "I've heard/seen enough (of it)."
target_language_example: J'en ai acheté deux, mais j'en ai déjà donné un.
native_language_example: I bought two, but I already gave one away.

meaning: I’ve heard about it / I’ve heard of it.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re familiar with something because you’ve heard people talk about it (but you may not know it well). The pronoun “en” replaces the thing you’re talking about (de + noun), like: « Tu connais ce film ? — Oui, j’en ai entendu parler. » (often said alone as a response).
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais visité ce musée, mais j’en ai entendu parler.
native_language_example: I’ve never visited that museum, but I’ve heard of it.

additional_notes: Past tense of **j’en ai** (“I have some/it”), using **avoir** in the passé composé: **j’ + en + ai + eu**. **En** replaces something introduced with **de / du / de la / des** (amount, number, or “some of it”). Often followed by a quantity or expression: **J’en ai eu deux** (“I had two (of them)”), **J’en ai eu assez / marre** (“I’ve had enough / I’m fed up”). On its own (**J’en ai eu.**), it means “I had some/it,” with the context understood.
target_language_example: Tu veux encore du gâteau ? — Non merci, j’en ai eu assez.
native_language_example: Do you want more cake? — No thanks, I’ve had enough.

additional_notes: Used to say you have completely ended something or want nothing more to do with it (a relationship, a situation, a task, even a person). **en** refers back to “it/that” (what you’re done with), and **avec** introduces the thing/person: *J’en ai fini avec lui / avec tout ça.* Often expresses strong finality or “I’ve had enough.”
target_language_example: Ça y est, j’en ai fini avec ce travail.
native_language_example: That’s it, I’m done with this job.

additional_notes: `en` replaces something previously mentioned (roughly “of it/of them”). It’s very common with quantities: **j’en ai vu beaucoup** (I saw a lot of them), **j’en ai vu un peu** (I saw a bit of it), **j’en ai vu assez** often means “I’ve had enough / I’ve seen enough.” Fixed expression: **j’en ai vu d’autres** = “I’ve seen worse / I’ve been through more than that” (said to show you’re not impressed or not shocked).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : j’en ai vu d’autres.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—I’ve seen worse than that.

meaning: “I have some/any (of it/them)” / “I’ve had enough (of it)” (depending on context).
additional_notes: "En" replaces something introduced with "de" (or a quantity): e.g., "du pain" → "j'en ai" = "I have some (bread)." You often see it with a quantity or expression like "assez / trop / beaucoup" (j'en ai assez = I've had enough) and it can be followed by a past participle: "J'en ai assez entendu/vu" = "I've heard/seen enough (of it)."
target_language_example: J'en ai acheté deux, mais j'en ai déjà donné un.
native_language_example: I bought two, but I already gave one away.

additional_notes: Very common way to say you’re tired of something or that you can’t take any more. Often followed by **de** + infinitive or noun: **J’en ai assez de + verb/noun** (e.g., *d’attendre*, *de ce bruit*). **en** refers to the thing you’re fed up with (sometimes implied). You can also say it alone: **J’en ai assez !**
target_language_example: J’en ai assez de ce bruit !
native_language_example: I’ve had enough of this noise!

meaning: "I'm fed up with" / "I've had enough of".
additional_notes: Used to say you’re tired of something and want it to stop. Pattern: « J’en ai assez de + noun/infinitive » (e.g., « J’en ai assez de ce bruit » / « J’en ai assez d’attendre »). « en » refers to the thing you’ve had enough of (roughly “of it/of that”). Often also said without « de » when the object is implied: « J’en ai assez ! » (“I’ve had enough!”).
target_language_example: J’en ai assez de travailler le week-end.
native_language_example: I’m fed up with working on the weekend.

additional_notes: From "avoir besoin de" (to need). "En" replaces something introduced with "de" (de ça, de lui/d’elle, du pain, etc.) and means “of it/of them/some.” Used when what you need is already known from context.
target_language_example: Je n'ai plus de café : j'en ai besoin pour rester éveillé.
native_language_example: I don't have any coffee left: I need it to stay awake.

meaning: "I feel like it" / "I want to (do it)".
additional_notes: From "avoir envie de…" (to feel like / want…). "En" replaces "de + something" already mentioned: e.g., "Tu veux du café ? — Oui, j'en ai envie." It can be a simple statement ("I feel like it"), an insistence ("But I want to"), or a rhetorical question ("Do you think I want to?").
target_language_example: Tu veux sortir ce soir ? Désolé, je suis fatigué : je n'en ai pas envie.
native_language_example: Do you want to go out tonight? Sorry, I'm tired: I don't feel like it.

meaning: "It’ll take me…" (a certain amount of time).
additional_notes: Used to say how long something will take you (often a task you’re doing right now). It’s part of the expression « en avoir pour + duration »: « J’en ai pour deux minutes » = “I’ll be two minutes.” To ask the time needed: « J’en ai pour combien de temps ? » (“How long will it take me?”).
target_language_example: Attends-moi, j’en ai pour cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Wait for me, it’ll take me five minutes.

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun "en" to mean "of it" / "of them" (replacing something introduced with de, du, de la, des, or a quantity). "Un" agrees with the item you mean: j'en ai un (masc.), j'en ai une (fem.), j'en ai deux/trois, etc. Often answers "Tu en as un ?" / "Vous en avez un ?"
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, j'en ai un de rechange.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have a spare one.

meaning: “I have one / I’ve got one (of it/them).”
additional_notes: Used with the pronoun **en** to mean “of it/of them” (it replaces **de + something**). **Une** stands in for a feminine noun already understood from context (e.g., **une idée**, **une blague**, **une nouvelle**). Common patterns: **J’en ai une bonne idée** = “I have a pretty good idea (of it)”; **J’en ai une nouvelle** = “I’ve got some news.”
target_language_example: Tu veux une autre suggestion ? J’en ai une.
native_language_example: Do you want another suggestion? I have one.

meaning: “I have one / I’ve got one (of it/them).”
additional_notes: Used with the pronoun **en** to mean “of it/of them” (it replaces **de + something**). **Une** stands in for a feminine noun already understood from context (e.g., **une idée**, **une blague**, **une nouvelle**). Common patterns: **J’en ai une bonne idée** = “I have a pretty good idea (of it)”; **J’en ai une nouvelle** = “I’ve got some news.”
target_language_example: Tu veux une autre suggestion ? J’en ai une.
native_language_example: Do you want another suggestion? I have one.

meaning: "I am (one)" / "I am (at that point)" / "I’m (almost) sure (of it)" (with *en* = “of it/of them”).
additional_notes: *En* replaces something introduced with **de** (of it/of them). So **j’en suis** often means “I’m one (of them)” or “I’m at that stage/point” depending on context. With adjectives like **sûr/sûre**, it commonly means **“I’m sure of it”**: *J’en suis presque sûr(e).*
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : j’en suis sûr.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’m sure of it.

additional_notes: Used to express hope or expectation. Often followed by "que" + a full sentence: "J’espère que…" (“I hope that…”). It can also be used on its own, like “I hope so / hopefully,” especially as a short reply: "Bien, j’espère" (“Fine, I hope”).
target_language_example: J’espère que tu vas mieux aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I hope you’re feeling better today.

additional_notes: Used before a clause (a full idea with a verb). The apostrophe is because "que" contracts to "qu'" before a vowel sound (e.g., "qu'il", "qu'on", "qu'un"). Note: "espérer" means "to hope", not "to expect".
target_language_example: J'espère qu'on se verra bientôt.
native_language_example: I hope we’ll see each other soon.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you hope is true about a man or boy. It’s the start of a longer sentence: J’espère (que) + clause. After que, il often becomes qu’il (elision). With espérer, French usually uses the indicative (e.g., j’espère qu’il sait…), not the subjunctive.
target_language_example: J’espère qu’il va bien.
native_language_example: I hope he’s doing well.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you hope will happen. "qu'on" is the contraction of "que" + "on" (que + on → qu’on). "On" often means "we" in everyday French (instead of "nous"), but it can also mean "people/one" depending on context.
target_language_example: J’espère qu’on va trouver une solution.
native_language_example: I hope we’ll find a solution.

additional_notes: Used to express hope or expectation about what follows. It introduces a clause with a subject and verb (often in the present or past): « J'espère que tu as raison. » In casual speech, « tu as » is often shortened to « t’as ».
target_language_example: J’espère que tu vas bien.
native_language_example: I hope you’re doing well.

meaning: "I hope you..." (speaking to one person you call "tu").
additional_notes: Used to express hope or a wish about what the other person will do or what will happen. It’s followed by a full clause (subject + verb), often in the future tense (e.g., tu viendras) or in the present (tu aimeras, tu peux/pourras). Switch to "j’espère que vous" when talking to someone you address as "vous" (formal or plural).
target_language_example: J’espère que tu vas bien.
native_language_example: I hope you’re doing well.

additional_notes: Used to express a hope about what the listener(s) will do, think, or feel. It’s followed by a full clause: "J’espère que vous + verb…". "Vous" can mean either "you" (formal) or "you all" (plural). After "j’espère que", French typically uses the indicative (e.g., présent, futur), not the subjunctive.
target_language_example: J’espère que vous pourrez venir demain.
native_language_example: I hope you can come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you’re hoping will happen. "Ça" is a very common pronoun meaning “it/that/this” (often referring to a situation or what was just mentioned). It’s usually followed by a verb: "J’espère que ça va" (I hope it’s going well), "J’espère que ça t’ira" (I hope it will suit you).
target_language_example: J’espère que ça ne te dérange pas.
native_language_example: I hope it doesn’t bother you.

meaning: "I was hoping you would…" / "I hoped you would…"
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect (j’espérais) to express an expectation or hope in the past. It’s usually followed by "que" + "tu" and then the subjunctive (e.g., "que tu sois", "que tu dises") or sometimes the conditional (e.g., "que tu me le dirais") depending on style and context.
target_language_example: J'espérais que tu viennes ce soir.
native_language_example: I was hoping you would come tonight.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb: j'essaie de + infinitive (e.g., j'essaie de comprendre). It expresses effort, not guaranteed success. The full form is "j'essaie de"; "j'" is short for "je" before a vowel sound (essaie).
target_language_example: J'essaie de parler français tous les jours.
native_language_example: I’m trying to speak French every day.

additional_notes: Used to express an assumption or a likely conclusion, often based on what you know (but not with complete certainty). Very common in conversation. In speech, it’s often followed by a clause with que: "J’imagine que tu as raison." You may also hear the more informal pronunciation/writing "J’imagine que t’as..." (= "tu as").
target_language_example: J’imagine que tu es fatigué après le voyage.
native_language_example: I guess you’re tired after the trip.

additional_notes: "y" replaces something introduced with "à" (e.g., penser à quelque chose → y penser = to think about it) or a place (aller à Paris → y aller = to go there). "j'" is just "je" shortened before a vowel sound (y, ai, etc.). Often translates as “it” in English when it stands for an idea/thing (J'y ai pensé = I thought about it), and as “there” when it stands for a place.
target_language_example: J'y vais demain.
native_language_example: I'm going there tomorrow.

additional_notes: This is a common chunk in the passé composé: j' (je) + y (pronoun meaning “there” or “to it/that”) + ai (have). Use y to replace something introduced with à (à Paris → j'y…, à ça → j'y…), or a place already known from context. It comes before the auxiliary: J'y ai pensé. (not *J'ai y pensé*).
target_language_example: J'y ai déjà été une fois.
native_language_example: I've already been there once.

additional_notes: “Y” replaces a place (there) or something introduced with à (to it/at it). In normal sentences, j’y suis often means “I’m there” (at that place) or “I’m on it / I’ve got it” depending on context. In the set expression “Va/Allez voir ailleurs si j’y suis”, it’s a dismissive, fairly informal way to say “Get lost / Go away.”
target_language_example: Tu me cherches ? Je suis dans le salon : j’y suis.
native_language_example: Are you looking for me? I’m in the living room: I’m there.

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun **y** to mean “there” (to a place already mentioned or understood). **J'y vais** can mean you’re going to that place (“I’m going there”) or that you’re leaving/heading out now (“Okay, I’m going”). Often appears with time or decision markers: *alors* (then), *de toute façon* (anyway), *il est tard* (it’s late), etc.
target_language_example: D'accord, j'y vais, on se voit demain.
native_language_example: Okay, I'm heading off—see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of être ("je" + "étais"). Used for background descriptions, ongoing situations, habits, or states in the past (where English often uses "was/were" or "used to"). Common in set phrases like "j'étais en train de…" (I was in the middle of…), "j'étais sur le point de…" (I was about to…), and "j'étais parti" (I had left / I was gone, depending on context).
target_language_example: Quand tu as appelé, j'étais au travail.
native_language_example: When you called, I was at work.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of « être » (j’étais) + « là » (“there”). Used to say you were present at some point in the past, often as background information or in explanations. Very common after « que » in reported speech: « Il savait que j’étais là » (“He knew I was there”).
target_language_example: Quand tu es arrivé, j’étais déjà là.
native_language_example: When you arrived, I was already there.

additional_notes: Used with "avoir" + past participle: « Je n’en ai jamais entendu parler. » It usually appears with negation (ne...jamais), though in casual speech the "ne" is often dropped (« J’en ai jamais entendu parler. »). Often followed by « de » + a person/thing: « Je n’ai jamais entendu parler de ce film. »
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais entendu parler de ce restaurant.
native_language_example: I’ve never heard of that restaurant.

additional_notes: In questions, **jamais** often means **“ever”** (not “never”). **Manger dans un restaurant** means “to eat at a restaurant.” You’ll often see it in questions like **As-tu/Avez-vous jamais mangé dans ce restaurant ?** = “Have you ever eaten at this restaurant?”
target_language_example: Tu as jamais mangé dans ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten at this restaurant?

additional_notes: Usually appears with **ne ... jamais ... rien** to mean someone **never says/does/understands anything**. Word order can change with pronouns: **Elle n’en a jamais rien dit** (“She never said anything about it”), **Vous ne me dites jamais rien** (“You never tell me anything”).
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais rien compris à ce jeu.
native_language_example: I never understood anything about this game.

additional_notes: Used with negation (often « ne ... jamais » and very commonly « ne ... plus jamais ») to say you don't want/expect to see the person again. « plus jamais » adds the idea of “not anymore, never again” (often emphatic). In full sentences you’ll usually see: « (Je) ne veux plus jamais te revoir » = “I never want to see you again.”
target_language_example: Désolé, mais je ne veux plus jamais te revoir.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I never want to see you again.

additional_notes: Used with a negative meaning to say something has not been seen at any time. Commonly appears in the passé composé with (ne) … jamais: « Je n’ai jamais vu ça. » In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped: « J’ai jamais vu ça. » It can also be used as a short standalone reaction: « Jamais vu ! » (= “Never seen it!”). With « encore », « n’ai encore jamais vu » means “have still never seen / have never yet seen.”
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais vu un film aussi long.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen such a long movie.

additional_notes: Used with the verb être in the passé composé: avoir + été. It usually appears in a negative sentence with ne…jamais (Je n’ai jamais été…), but in informal spoken French people often drop ne (J’ai jamais été…). It can refer to never having been somewhere (Je n’ai jamais été ici) or never having been a certain way (Il ne l’a jamais été = “He never was / He’s never been that”).
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais été aussi fatigué.
native_language_example: I’ve never been this tired.

additional_notes: Used with the verb être in the passé composé: avoir + été. It usually appears in a negative sentence with ne…jamais (Je n’ai jamais été…), but in informal spoken French people often drop ne (J’ai jamais été…). It can refer to never having been somewhere (Je n’ai jamais été ici) or never having been a certain way (Il ne l’a jamais été = “He never was / He’s never been that”).
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais été aussi fatigué.
native_language_example: I’ve never been this tired.

additional_notes: Used with a noun (Je cherche mon chat. = I’m looking for my cat) or with an idea/information (Je cherche quelle phrase écrire. = I’m trying to figure out what sentence to write). It can also mean “I’m trying to find (words)” as in Je cherche mes mots (I’m searching for the right words).
target_language_example: Je cherche une boulangerie près d'ici.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a bakery near here.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (verb in the “to ___” form): je commence à comprendre, je commence à m’y habituer. It expresses that something is beginning, often gradually. You can change the subject (tu commences à…, il/elle commence à…, etc.) and the tense (j’ai commencé à… = “I started to…”).
target_language_example: Je commence à parler français un peu mieux.
native_language_example: I’m starting to speak French a little better.

additional_notes: Used to say you understand an idea, a situation, someone’s feelings, a language, or what is happening. Often followed by a clause: « Je comprends que… » (“I understand that…”) or « Je comprends ce que… / ce qui… / comment… » (“I understand what… / what… / how…”). Can also be used alone as a reply: « Je comprends. »
target_language_example: Je comprends que tu sois fatigué, mais on doit partir maintenant.
