target_language_example: Attends deux minutes, je vais te donner mon numéro.
native_language_example: Wait two minutes, I’m going to give you my number.

meaning: "I'm going to make you…" / "I'm going to do … to/for you."
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to mean “I’m going to make you (do something)” (e.g., je vais te faire sortir = I’m going to make you go out). Used with a noun to mean “I’m going to make/prepare (something) for you” (je vais te faire des œufs). It can also be used as a threat: je vais te faire très mal = I’m going to hurt you badly. Word order changes with pronouns: je vais te le faire (I’m going to do it for you).
target_language_example: Attends, je vais te faire un café.
native_language_example: Wait, I'm going to make you a coffee.

meaning: "I'm going to ... it to you" / "I'll ... it for you".
additional_notes: A common sentence starter in the near future ("je vais" + infinitive). "te" is the indirect object pronoun (to you), and "le" is the direct object pronoun (it/him). In French, these pronouns come before the infinitive: "Je vais te le donner" (not *je vais donner te le*). "le" can change to "la" (it/her), "les" (them), or "l'" before a vowel ("Je vais te l'expliquer").
target_language_example: Je vais te le dire franchement.
native_language_example: I'm going to tell you honestly.

additional_notes: Common way to announce you’re about to share information. Breakdown: je vais + infinitive = near future (“I’m going to…”); te = “to you”; le = “it” (the thing you’ll say); dire = “to tell.” Often used with emphasis or tone: "Je vais te le dire exactement" (precisely), "Je vais te le dire, hein ?" (you know?/okay?), or in a rhetorical/defensive question: "Tu crois que je vais te le dire ?" (“Do you really think I’m going to tell you?”). In casual speech you may hear "Je vais te l’dire" or "J’vais te l’dire".
target_language_example: Attends deux secondes, je vais te le dire.
native_language_example: Wait two seconds, I'm going to tell you.

additional_notes: Common near-future structure: "je vais" + infinitive. "te" means "to you" (informal singular); with "vous" it becomes "je vais vous montrer". Can be used on its own as a promise/introduction before showing something ("Viens, je vais te montrer").
target_language_example: Attends une seconde, je vais te montrer comment ça marche.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m going to show you how it works.

additional_notes: A direct threat. Often used literally in serious contexts, but it can also be said jokingly/exaggeratedly (like “I’m gonna kill you!” in English) depending on tone and situation—still very aggressive, so avoid using it. Grammar: near future (aller + infinitive) = je vais + tuer; te = “you” (informal singular object pronoun).
target_language_example: Si tu touches à ma sœur, je vais te tuer.
native_language_example: If you touch my sister, I’m going to kill you.

meaning: "I'm going to (do) everything / I'm going to (do) it all" (before a verb).
additional_notes: Used with the near future ("aller" + infinitive): "je vais" + "tout" + verb (e.g., expliquer, dire, régler). "Tout" means "everything" and is placed before the infinitive verb. Often implies you will handle the whole situation: "Je vais tout régler" = "I’m going to take care of everything / fix everything."
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, je vais tout préparer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to prepare everything.

additional_notes: Uses the near future: "aller" (je vais) + infinitive (voir). Often means "I’ll check/find out" (je vais voir si/où/ce que…) and can also mean "I’m going to go see/visit" someone (je vais voir les autres). In contexts like "Je vais voir ce que ça donne", it’s like "we’ll see what happens / how it turns out."
target_language_example: Attends une seconde, je vais voir si c’est ouvert.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’ll check if it’s open.

meaning: "I’m going to … you" (using vous = formal singular or plural "you").
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to form the near future: je vais + infinitive. The pronoun vous comes before the infinitive (je vais vous aider / je vais vous appeler). Vous can mean one person (formal) or several people (plural).
target_language_example: Je vais vous appeler demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to call you tomorrow.

meaning: “I’m going to tell you” (to you, formal/plural).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you’re about to say. Literally “I go to tell you,” but in French it’s the common near-future form: aller (vais) + infinitive (dire). “Vous” can be formal (one person) or plural (several people). Often followed by a question word or clause: ce que/ce qui (what), où (where), pourquoi (why).
target_language_example: Je vais vous dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you the truth.

meaning: "I’m going to do/make (something) for you" / "I’m going to have you (do something)".
additional_notes:
Common with two patterns:
1) **je vais vous faire + noun** = “I’m going to make/do something for you” (e.g., *je vais vous faire à manger*, *je vais vous faire une faveur*, *je vais vous faire visiter* = “I’ll show you around”).
2) **je vais vous faire + infinitive** = “I’m going to make you / have you do something” (causative). It can also mean arranging for someone else to do it: *je vais vous faire chercher à la gare par ma sœur* = “I’ll have my sister pick you up at the station.”
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas, je vais vous faire un café.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to make you a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a demonstration or to guide someone to see something. It uses the near future: "je vais" + infinitive (montrer). "Vous" is used for one person formally or for multiple people; with one friend you’d usually say "je vais te montrer".
target_language_example: Attendez une seconde, je vais vous montrer comment ça marche.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m going to show you how it works.

additional_notes: Uses the near future: "je vais" + infinitive (aller) = "I’m going to go". "y" replaces a place or destination already understood ("there", "to it"). Often used to announce you’re leaving or deciding to go somewhere: "Alors/Dans ce cas, je vais y aller" = "Alright/In that case, I’ll go (then)."
target_language_example: Bon, je vais y aller : il est tard.
native_language_example: Alright, I'm going to go: it’s late.

meaning: “I’m going to be …” / “I will be …” (near future).
additional_notes: Built with aller (je vais) + infinitive (être). It’s used to talk about something that’s about to happen or a decision/intention: Je vais être clair/honnête/gentil (“I’m going to be clear/honest/nice”). With states/feelings it can also mean something is about to occur: Je sens que je vais être malade (“I feel like I’m going to be sick”).
target_language_example: Désolé, je vais être en retard.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to be late.

meaning: "I’m going to be late" / "I’ll be late."
additional_notes: Used to warn that you won’t arrive on time. The structure is: je vais + infinitive (near future: “I’m going to…”) + être en retard (“to be late”). You can specify where you’ll be late with en/à: en cours (“for class”), à l’audience (“to the hearing”).
target_language_example: Désolé, je vais être en retard au rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to be late for the appointment.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (je vais + verb) to say what you’re about to do or plan to do soon: je vais choisir, je vais partager, je vais prendre, je vais vous donner. Literally it’s “I go,” but in everyday French it very often means “I’m going to …” (similar to English).
target_language_example: Je vais appeler un taxi.
native_language_example: I’m going to call a taxi.

meaning: “I’m going to the …” (to a masculine singular place, or to a place name).
additional_notes: Used to say you are going somewhere. It’s the verb aller (to go) conjugated with je: je vais. The preposition au = à + le, used before masculine singular nouns (au bar, au labo, au stade) and some fixed expressions/places (au petit coin = to the restroom). With regions/directions you can also use au (au sud-ouest du village = to the southwest of the village). Contrast: je vais à la (feminine), je vais à l’ (before vowel), je vais aux (plural).
target_language_example: Je vais au supermarché après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m going to the supermarket after work.

additional_notes: Used to say you are heading to your workplace. Often followed by the mode of transport: en autobus/en train/en voiture (by bus/train/car) and à bicyclette/à pied (by bike/on foot). You can add time/frequency like tous les jours (“every day”).
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : je vais au travail.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I’m going to work.

additional_notes: Common reply to "Ça va ?" or "Comment ça va ?" It literally means "I’m going well," but it’s used to talk about your general state (health/mood). You can add emphasis like "Je vais très bien" (very well) or reassurance like "Je vais bien, je t’assure" (I’m fine, I promise).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je vais bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m fine.

additional_notes: Used to say you are going to a destination. “Je vais” = “I go / I’m going”, and “à” is used before places (cities, specific places): Je vais à Paris, je vais à l’école. With masculine countries you often use “au” instead (Je vais au Canada). With feminine countries you use “en” (Je vais en France).
target_language_example: Je vais à la gare.
native_language_example: I’m going to the train station.

meaning: “I’m going to the …” (to a feminine place/activity).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun: Je vais à la + [place/activity]. For masculine singular, use « je vais au »; for plural, « je vais aux ». Often refers to going somewhere or going to do an activity (e.g., à la pêche = going fishing).
target_language_example: Je vais à la bibliothèque après le travail.
native_language_example: I’m going to the library after work.

additional_notes: Used to express what you want or intend. Common patterns: (1) **je veux + infinitive**: *Je veux partir.* (I want to leave.) (2) **je veux + noun**: *Je veux une bière.* (I want a beer.) (3) **je veux que + subjunctive** to express what you want someone (or something) to do: *Je veux que tu viennes.* (I want you to come.) It can sound direct; **je voudrais** is a softer, more polite "I would like," especially when ordering or making requests.
target_language_example: Je veux un café, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: I want a coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to purchase something. Follow it with the item you want to buy (often with an article): du/de la/des for an unspecified amount (Je veux acheter du pain), or un/une/le/la/les for a specific item (Je veux acheter une maison / la robe).
target_language_example: Je veux acheter des billets pour le concert.
native_language_example: I want to buy tickets for the concert.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say you intend to purchase something. "Je veux" = "I want"; "acheter" = "to buy". "Une" is the feminine singular article (a/one), so it must match a feminine noun (une chemise, une montre). If the noun is masculine, use "je veux acheter un…" (un livre). You can also use it with quantity expressions that take "une" (une douzaine de…, une paire de…).
target_language_example: Je veux acheter une bouteille d’eau.
native_language_example: I want to buy a bottle of water.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to go somewhere or go do something. It’s often followed by a place (e.g., "dehors", "dans mon lit", "à Paris") or by an infinitive verb to express an activity ("aller dormir", "aller nager", "aller parler"). In speech you’ll also hear: "Je veux y aller" = "I want to go there."
target_language_example: Je veux aller au cinéma ce soir.
native_language_example: I want to go to the movies tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to learn something. Add what you want to learn after it: "Je veux apprendre le français / une nouvelle langue". You can also add an adverb like "plus vite" (faster).
target_language_example: Je veux apprendre le français cette année.
native_language_example: I want to learn French this year.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to learn how to do an action. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (apprendre à + verb), e.g., apprendre à nager, apprendre à parler. You can add details after the verb (like an object: apprendre à parler le français).
target_language_example: Je veux apprendre à cuisiner des plats français.
native_language_example: I want to learn to cook French dishes.

additional_notes: Used to say what you want to be in the future. Pattern: « Je veux devenir + (un/une) + noun » (Je veux devenir ingénieur / Je veux devenir un médecin). With roles/jobs, French often drops the article (ingénieur), but you may still hear it with some nouns (un médecin). It can also be followed by an adjective or phrase: « Je veux devenir riche » / « Je veux devenir amie avec… ».
target_language_example: Je veux devenir professeur de français.
native_language_example: I want to become a French teacher.

meaning: "I mean…" (to clarify, explain, or correct what you’re saying).
additional_notes: Literally "I want to say," but very often used in spoken French like English "I mean" as a filler before giving clarification, adding a detail, softening a statement, or correcting yourself: "Je veux dire, c’est quoi ça ?" It also appears in the fixed question "Tu comprends ce que je veux dire ?" = "Do you know what I mean?"
target_language_example: Je veux dire, ce n’est pas grave, mais préviens-moi la prochaine fois.
native_language_example: I mean, it’s not a big deal, but let me know next time.

je veux en savoir plus sur

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux en savoir plus sur
meaning: “I want to learn more about” / “I want to know more about”.
additional_notes: Used to say you want more information about someone or something. "En" refers back to the topic (roughly “about it/them”), and "sur" introduces what you’re asking about. You can change the subject and tense (e.g., "Tu veux en savoir plus sur…", "Nous voulons en savoir plus sur…").
target_language_example: Je veux en savoir plus sur ce projet.
native_language_example: I want to learn more about this project.

meaning: "I want to hear" (I want to listen to / be told).
additional_notes: Used to express that you want to hear something specific (the truth, someone’s opinion, news, etc.). It can also mean you want someone to say something out loud or tell you directly. Often followed by a noun or clause: « Je veux entendre la vérité » / « Je veux entendre ce que tu as à dire ».
target_language_example: Je veux entendre ce que tu as à dire.
native_language_example: I want to hear what you have to say.

meaning: "I want to do" / "I want to make."
additional_notes: Used to state your intention before an action. Follow it with an infinitive verb: je veux faire + (verb/noun phrase), e.g. "Je veux faire les courses" (I want to do the grocery shopping) or "Je veux faire du sport" (I want to exercise). In conversation you can also drop "faire" and say "Je veux + infinitive" (Je veux aller…, Je veux acheter…).
target_language_example: Je veux faire une pause.
native_language_example: I want to take a break.

additional_notes: Used to say you have the desire/intent to take action, either in general ("I want to do something") or with an added detail: *ce soir* (tonight), *dans ce monde* (in this world), *de ma vie* (with my life / make something of my life), *pour toi* (for you). You can replace **je** with another subject (e.g., *tu veux...*, *il/elle veut...*, *nous voulons...*).
target_language_example: Je veux faire quelque chose ce week-end.
native_language_example: I want to do something this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to soften or limit what you’re asking for or expressing ("only", "simply"). Very common before an infinitive (Je veux juste partir.) or before a que-clause (Je veux juste que tu saches…). Often implies “nothing more than that.”
target_language_example: Je veux juste te parler cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I just want to talk to you for five minutes.

je veux juste que tu sois

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux juste que tu sois
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or desire for someone’s state/behavior. It’s followed by the subjunctive: "tu sois" (from "être"). Often completed with an adjective or phrase: "en sécurité" (safe), "heureuse" (happy), "impliqué" (involved), "sûr" (sure/certain).
target_language_example: Je veux juste que tu sois là demain.
native_language_example: I just want you to be there tomorrow.

meaning: "I just want to... you" / "I only want to... you" (starting a sentence).
additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re about to say: *Je veux juste* = “I just/only want to…”. **Te** is an object pronoun meaning “to you” or “you” (direct object), placed before the verb it goes with: *te protéger* (protect you), *te remercier* (thank you), *te rendre la pareille* (return the favor), *te tenir dans mes bras* (hold you in my arms). Often followed by an infinitive.
target_language_example: Je veux juste te dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I just want to tell you the truth.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence before an infinitive to politely soften what you’re saying: « Je veux juste vous + infinitive… » (e.g., remercier, dire, demander, souhaiter). « vous » is the formal singular “you” (to a stranger/someone you don’t know well) or the plural “you” (to several people).
target_language_example: Je veux juste vous poser une question.
native_language_example: I just want to ask you a question.

additional_notes: "Je veux" means "I want." The pronoun "le" usually means "him" or "it" (masculine singular) and is placed before the verb it refers to: "Je veux le protéger" = "I want to protect him/it." With another verb in the infinitive, "le" typically goes before that infinitive (not after it).
target_language_example: Je veux le garder pour plus tard.
native_language_example: I want to keep it for later.

additional_notes: "Je veux" means “I want.” "Le" is a direct object pronoun meaning “him” or “it” (for a masculine noun). "Voir" is the infinitive “to see.” You can add time words like "maintenant" (now) or phrases like "de mes propres yeux" (with my own eyes). For a woman/ feminine noun, use "Je veux la voir"; for plural, "Je veux les voir."
target_language_example: Je veux le voir tout de suite.
native_language_example: I want to see him/it right away.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to eat (now or in general). Often followed by a food item or by something like “quelque chose de …” (something …): “Je veux manger quelque chose de salé.” You can also add “aussi” for “too”: “Moi aussi, je veux manger !”
target_language_example: J’ai faim : je veux manger maintenant.
native_language_example: I’m hungry: I want to eat now.

meaning: "I want to" + a reflexive verb ("I want to [do something] (to/for myself)").
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive with a reflexive pronoun (me = “myself/me”). Many French verbs are reflexive (e.g., se coucher = to go to bed, se débarrasser de = to get rid of, se joindre à = to join). In speech, “je” often becomes “j’” before a vowel sound: j’veux me… (informal pronunciation).
target_language_example: Je veux me reposer ce soir.
native_language_example: I want to rest tonight.

meaning: “I want to talk / I want to speak.”
additional_notes: Used with **de** to mean “to talk about” (**Je veux parler de…** = “I want to talk about…”), and with **à** to mean “to speak to” (**Je veux parler à…** = “I want to speak to…”). You’ll also see it in patterns like **C’est de ça que je veux parler** (“That’s what I want to talk about”) and **Tu sais de quoi je veux parler** (“You know what I’m talking about”).
target_language_example: Je veux parler de ce problème avec toi.
native_language_example: I want to talk about this problem with you.

meaning: "I want to speak to" / "I want to talk to".
additional_notes: Used to say you want to talk to someone. "Parler à" takes the preposition "à" before a person: parler à ma mère, parler à un avocat. In polite contexts (customer service, official situations), you may also hear "Je voudrais parler à..." (more polite).
target_language_example: Je veux parler à votre responsable, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I want to speak to your manager/person in charge, please.

additional_notes: Very common spoken/informal form of "je ne veux pas" (dropping "ne"). Used to refuse something or say you don’t want something to happen: "je veux pas + infinitive" (I don’t want to...), or "je veux pas que + subjunctive" (I don’t want [someone] to...).
target_language_example: Je veux pas sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: I don't want to go out tonight.

meaning: “I want us to…” / “I want people to…”
additional_notes: Used to express what you want to happen, followed by a verb in the subjunctive (je veux qu’on reste / qu’on soit / qu’on fasse…). “On” often means “we/us” in everyday French, but it can also mean “someone/people” (indefinite). If you want to be more explicit, you can say: « Je veux que nous… » (we) or « Je veux que tu… » (you).
target_language_example: Je veux qu’on parle calmement.
native_language_example: I want us to talk calmly.

meaning: "I want (that)…" (used to introduce what you want someone/something to do).
additional_notes: "Je veux que" is followed by the subjunctive to express a wish, demand, or requirement. Often used with another person as the subject after que: "Je veux que tu…" = "I want you to…". Common subjunctive patterns you’ll see: "que tu écoutes", "qu’il/elle aille", "qu’il/elle voie", "que ce soit".
target_language_example: Je veux que tu viennes demain.
native_language_example: I want you to come tomorrow.

meaning: "I want it to be…" / "I want (that) it be…"
additional_notes: Used to express what you want to happen or what you want something/someone to be. It introduces the subjunctive with être: « que ce soit » (not *que c’est*). You can follow it with a person/thing (« Je veux que ce soit toi. ») or with a past participle to mean “I want it done” (« Je veux que ce soit réparé. »).
target_language_example: Je veux que ce soit prêt avant demain.
native_language_example: I want it to be ready before tomorrow.

meaning: "I want you to…" (introduces what you want someone to do).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish, request, or demand directed at someone. It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., je veux que tu viennes / fasses / sois). In speech it can sound quite direct; to be more polite, you can use "j’aimerais que tu…" or "je voudrais que tu…".
target_language_example: Je veux que tu viennes avec moi.
native_language_example: I want you to come with me.

meaning: "I want you to go" / "I want you to (do something)".
additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to do. After "je veux que", French uses the subjunctive: "tu ailles" (from "aller", to go). It can be followed by a place ("à Boston", "au bureau de poste", "chez toi") or by other expressions like "mieux" ("I want you to get better").
target_language_example: Je veux que tu ailles te reposer.
native_language_example: I want you to go rest.

meaning: "I want you to do" (addressing one person).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone what you want them to do. It introduces the subjunctive: after "je veux que...", the next verb is in the subjunctive (here, "tu fasses" from "faire"). Often followed by an object or details: "quelque chose", "ça lundi", etc.
target_language_example: Je veux que tu fasses tes devoirs avant de sortir.
native_language_example: I want you to do your homework before going out.

meaning: "I want you to … (for me / to me)."
additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to do. After "je veux que tu…", French normally uses the subjunctive: "Je veux que tu me chantes / laisses / parles / rendes…". "me" is an object pronoun placed before the verb (it can mean "to me" or "me," depending on the verb).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu me montres tes photos.
native_language_example: I want you to show me your photos.

je veux que tu me dises

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux que tu me dises
additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone to tell you. It’s often followed by a question word (quoi/ce que/où/quand/comment/pourquoi) or by “tout” (everything). After “je veux que…”, French uses the subjunctive: “tu me dises” (not *tu me dis*).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu me dises la vérité.
native_language_example: I want you to tell me the truth.

meaning: “I want you to take …” (or “I want you to …”).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone what you want them to do. After "je veux que" (I want that…), French uses the subjunctive: "tu prennes" is the subjunctive form of "prendre" (to take). What follows can be an object ("ce médicament", "ça") or a verb phrase ("soin de …" in "prendre soin de" = to take care of).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu prennes ton parapluie avant de sortir.
native_language_example: I want you to take your umbrella before going out.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stay somewhere or with someone. After *je veux que…* (I want that…), French normally uses the subjunctive: *tu restes* (from *rester*, “to stay/remain”). Often followed by a place or person: *là* (there), *sur la plage* (on the beach), *avec Tom* (with Tom), *à distance* (at a distance).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu restes ici jusqu’à demain.
native_language_example: I want you to stay here until tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce important information you want the other person to be aware of. After it, French uses the subjunctive: savoir → que tu saches. You can follow it with que + a sentence (“…that…”) or with a question word like qui/ce qui (“…who/what…”).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu saches que je suis toujours là pour toi.
native_language_example: I want you to know that I’m always here for you.

meaning: "I want you to be…" (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone else to be/do. After « je veux que », French uses the subjunctive: « tu sois » (from « être », to be). You can follow it with an adjective (« heureux/heureuse », « silencieux/silencieuse ») or a prepositional phrase (« avec moi », « à mon côté »). Note agreement: adjectives change with the person’s gender (heureux/heureuse, fier/fière).
target_language_example: Je veux que tu sois prêt(e) à partir.
native_language_example: I want you to be ready to leave.

meaning: “I want you to …” (with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used before a reflexive verb (a verb that uses “se”), so you see “te” (yourself) because the subject is “tu.” After “je veux que…,” French normally uses the subjunctive: « Je veux que tu te sentes / concentres / souviennes… ».
target_language_example: Je veux que tu te reposes un peu.
native_language_example: I want you to rest a bit.

additional_notes: Used to say you want someone else to come/do something. After "je veux que..." (I want that...), French uses the subjunctive: "tu viennes" (not *tu viens*). You can add an action or destination after it: "Je veux que tu viennes avec nous / travailler ici / vivre avec moi."
target_language_example: Je veux que tu viennes à la réunion demain.
native_language_example: I want you to come to the meeting tomorrow.

meaning: “I want you (to…)” (formal/plural “you”), followed by the subjunctive.
additional_notes: Used to state what you want someone (one person formally, or several people) to do. After « je veux que vous », French normally uses the subjunctive: « vous ayez », « vous chantiez », « vous parliez », « vous sortiez ». Often sounds firm or like an order depending on context.
target_language_example: Je veux que vous m’appeliez demain matin.
native_language_example: I want you to call me tomorrow morning.

meaning: “I want you to go …” (to a group or to ‘you’ formal).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone what you want them to do, followed by a place or direction. After « je veux que », French uses the subjunctive, so « aller » becomes « vous alliez ». « vous » can mean either ‘you (plural)’ or ‘you (formal)’.
target_language_example: Je veux que vous alliez à l’accueil, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I want you to go to the reception desk, please.

meaning: "I want you to stop" (formal or plural "you").
additional_notes: Used to tell one person politely/formally (vous) or multiple people to stop doing something. It’s typically followed by either (1) a direct object: « Je veux que vous arrêtiez ceci » (“stop this”), or (2) « de » + infinitive: « Je veux que vous arrêtiez de faire ça » (“stop doing that”). Because it comes after « je veux que », the verb is in the subjunctive: « arrêtiez » (from « arrêter »). You may also see clarifiers like « tous les deux / toutes les deux » (“both of you”) placed in different spots for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je veux que vous arrêtiez de crier, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I want you to stop shouting, please.

additional_notes: Used to tell one person formally (vous) or several people (vous plural) to stop doing something. It’s followed by the subjunctive verb form "cessiez" because "je veux que…" expresses a desire/command. Very often you add "de" + infinitive: "Je veux que vous cessiez de me suivre" (…to stop following me). The extra phrases "tous les deux / toutes les deux" mean "both of you" (masc./mixed vs. fem.), and commas just add emphasis.
target_language_example: Je veux que vous cessiez de faire du bruit, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I want you to stop making noise, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a request or demand with a verb in the subjunctive after « je veux que ». « vous » is formal or plural “you,” and « me » means “to me / me” (e.g., je veux que vous me disiez…, je veux que vous me laissiez…).
target_language_example: Je veux que vous me répondiez aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I want you to answer me today.

je veux que vous me disiez

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux que vous me disiez
meaning: "I want you to tell me" (formal or plural "you").
additional_notes: Used to ask (often firmly) for information: je veux que + subject + verb in the subjunctive. Here, "vous" can mean either "you" (formal singular) or "you" (plural), and "disiez" is the subjunctive form of "dire" after "je veux que".
target_language_example: Je veux que vous me disiez ce qui s’est passé.
native_language_example: I want you to tell me what happened.

meaning: "I want you to know" (speaking to one or more people politely/formally).
additional_notes: Used to introduce important information, reassurance, or emphasis. It uses the subjunctive: « que vous sachiez » (from savoir, “to know”), because it follows « je veux que… ». Often continues with « que… » + a full idea: « Je veux que vous sachiez que… ».
target_language_example: Je veux que vous sachiez que je suis là pour vous aider.
native_language_example: I want you to know that I’m here to help you.

additional_notes: Used with **vouloir que** (“to want that…”), which is followed by the **subjunctive**: **vous soyez** (from *être*, “to be”). **Vous** can mean either **“you (plural)”** or **polite/formal “you” (singular)**. You can complete it with a noun/adjective (*je veux que vous soyez ma compagne* = “I want you to be my partner”) or with a past participle when using *être* (*je veux que vous soyez revenue* = “I want you to have come back / I want you back,” said to a woman).
target_language_example: Je veux que vous soyez à l’heure demain.
native_language_example: I want you to be on time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone ("vous" = you, formal or plural) to do. After "je veux que", French uses the subjunctive: "vous veniez" (from "venir"). You can add details like "avec moi" (with me), "ce soir" (tonight), or "seul(s)/seule(s)" (alone).
target_language_example: Je veux que vous veniez demain matin.
native_language_example: I want you to come tomorrow morning.

meaning: "I want you to…" (addressing you formally or as a group), before a reflexive verb.
additional_notes: Used to express a desire/command about what someone else should do: « je veux que + [subject] + verb (subjunctive) ». Here « vous vous » appears because the verb is reflexive (e.g., « vous vous rappeliez » = “you remember”; « vous vous y mettiez » = “you get to it”). Often sounds like a firm instruction in context.
target_language_example: Je veux que vous vous dépêchiez.
native_language_example: I want you to hurry up.

meaning: "I want something (that is)…" (followed by an adjective).
additional_notes: Used to ask for an unspecified thing with a certain quality. After "quelque chose", use "de" + adjective: "quelque chose de simple", "de doux", "de sucré". You can add an infinitive to specify the type: "quelque chose de sucré à manger" (something sweet to eat).
target_language_example: Je veux quelque chose de chaud à boire.
native_language_example: I want something hot to drink.

additional_notes: Used to express a desire to remain somewhere or not leave. It can be followed by a place (rester dans la maison = stay in the house) or by a person (rester avec lui = stay with him), or used alone (Je veux rester.)
target_language_example: Il pleut trop : je veux rester à la maison.
native_language_example: It’s raining too much: I want to stay at home.

meaning: "I want to know" / "I want to find out."
additional_notes: Used to express that you want information or an explanation. Often followed by a question word or clause: ce que (what), combien de temps (how long), comment (how), si (whether/if). In more formal or polite situations, you can soften it with: « Je voudrais savoir… » (I would like to know…).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir où tu as acheté ça.
native_language_example: I want to know where you bought that.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question where what is the direct object of the verb that follows: "Je veux savoir ce que tu fais" (what you’re doing). It’s often followed by a full clause (subject + verb). Compare: "ce qui" is used when what is the subject of the verb ("Je veux savoir ce qui se passe" = I want to know what’s happening).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: I want to know what you mean.

meaning: 'I want to know where…' (introduces an indirect question about location).
additional_notes: Used before a full clause to ask about the location of someone/something or where something happened: "Je veux savoir où + subject + verb". The "où" can mean "where" (place) or sometimes "to where" depending on the verb (e.g., where someone went).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir où tu vas ce soir.
native_language_example: I want to know where you're going tonight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question with **qui** (“who”). Typically followed by a verb clause: **Je veux savoir qui a fait ça** (“…who did that”) or **Je veux savoir qui sont vos amis** (“…who your friends are”). With **qui** as the subject, the verb comes right after (**qui a donné…**).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir qui a pris mes clés.
native_language_example: I want to know who took my keys.

je veux savoir qui vous a

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux savoir qui vous a
meaning: “I want to know who (has) … to you / who … you.”
additional_notes: Used to start a sentence where you’re asking for the identity of the person who did something to “vous” (you). It’s typically followed by a past participle: “Je veux savoir qui vous a dit ça” (who told you that), “qui vous a envoyé(e)(s)” (who sent you). With “envoyer” (to send), the past participle can agree with the direct object “vous” when “vous” refers to a woman or a group: envoyée (one woman), envoyées (women), envoyés (men/mixed).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir qui vous a donné cette information.
native_language_example: I want to know who gave you this information.

additional_notes: Used to express a simple or limited desire (often to soften what you’re asking for). Word order: "Je veux seulement + noun/infinitive". You can also say "Je veux juste..." (more common in speech).
target_language_example: Je veux seulement te poser une question.
native_language_example: I just want to ask you a question.

additional_notes: Used to soften or simplify what you’re asking for: you’re saying your desire is basic/only that. Often followed by an infinitive (je veux simplement partir) or by que + subjunctive (je veux simplement que tu sois heureuse).
target_language_example: Je veux simplement rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: I just want to go home.

meaning: "I just want (that)" + a clause in the subjunctive.
additional_notes: Used to express a simple wish/request about what you want to happen. It’s typically followed by a full clause with **que** and the **subjunctive** (e.g., *que tu reviennes*, *que les choses soient normales*). You can often translate it as “I just want you to…” or “All I want is for…”.
target_language_example: Je veux simplement que tu sois heureux.
native_language_example: I just want you to be happy.

meaning: "I just want you to..." / "All I want is for you to..."
additional_notes: Used to express a simple request or wish directed at one or more people (vous = "you" formal or plural). It is normally followed by the subjunctive because of the structure "je veux que...": e.g., "Je veux simplement que vous écoutiez" (not *écoutez*).
target_language_example: Je veux simplement que vous me disiez la vérité.
native_language_example: I just want you to tell me the truth.

meaning: “I just want to be …” / “I simply want to be …”
additional_notes: Used to express a simple wish about a state or identity. It’s followed by the infinitive être (“to be”) plus an adjective (différente, seul) or past participle used like an adjective (aimé = loved). Word order is fixed: Je veux simplement être + (adjective/description).
target_language_example: Je veux simplement être heureux.
native_language_example: I just want to be happy.

meaning: "I want to (do something) to/for you" or "I want you (to...)" (introduces an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb: **Je veux te + infinitif** (e.g., *je veux te croire / te présenter / te remercier*). **Te** is the unstressed object pronoun meaning “to you” (or “you” as the object). Before a vowel or silent *h*, **te** becomes **t’**: *Je veux t’aider.*
target_language_example: Je veux te parler demain.
native_language_example: I want to talk to you tomorrow.

je veux te montrer quelque chose

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux te montrer quelque chose
meaning: I want to show you something.
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you’re about to present, point out, or demonstrate. You can add a place with "dans + [place]" (e.g., "dans mon bureau" = in my office). Also common with "Viens" / "Viens ici" (“Come” / “Come here”) to invite someone to follow you.
target_language_example: Attends une seconde : je veux te montrer quelque chose.
native_language_example: Wait a second: I want to show you something.

additional_notes:
Often used to introduce a topic you want to discuss. It can sound serious or important depending on context. You can add details with:
- « au sujet de / à propos de + noun » = “about (a topic)”
- « de + noun » = “about”
You can also specify privacy: « Je veux te parler seule. » = “I want to talk to you alone / in private.”
target_language_example: Je veux te parler après le cours.
native_language_example: I want to talk to you after class.

meaning: "I want a" (followed by a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask for or say you want one item. The noun after "un" must be masculine and singular (e.g., "un bonbon"). For feminine singular, use "je veux une"; for plural, use "je veux des".
target_language_example: Je veux un café, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I want a coffee, please.

meaning: "I want a" (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you want something. It must be followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., une glace, une guitare). For masculine nouns, use "je veux un"; for plural, "je veux des". In polite requests, you’ll often hear "Je voudrais une…" (I’d like a…).
target_language_example: Je veux une place près de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: I want a seat near the window.

additional_notes: Used to express a desire or plan to live somewhere (je veux vivre en Italie / dans une ville / à la campagne) or to live in a certain way (je veux vivre en paix). With a direct object, vivre can also mean “to experience” (je veux vivre de beaux moments / une vie heureuse).
target_language_example: Je veux vivre près de la mer un jour.
native_language_example: I want to live near the sea one day.

meaning: "I want to see" / "I want to look at."
additional_notes: Used to express a desire or intention to see something (a person, an object, a place, information). Often followed by a noun (je veux voir ma famille) or by what you want to find out: "je veux voir ce que..." (= I want to see what...). "Je veux voir." can be used on its own as a short response meaning "I want to see (for myself)."
target_language_example: Je veux voir ce film ce soir.
native_language_example: I want to see this movie tonight.

meaning: “I want to … you” (used before an infinitive verb).
additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence pattern: **Je veux vous + infinitive** (e.g., *Je veux vous aider* = “I want to help you”). **Vous** is the polite/plural “you,” used with strangers, in formal situations, or when speaking to more than one person. On its own, **je veux vous** sounds incomplete—you normally need a verb after it.
target_language_example: Je veux vous aider à trouver votre chemin.
native_language_example: I want to help you find your way.

je veux vous montrer quelque chose

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux vous montrer quelque chose
additional_notes: Polite/formal way to address one or more people (vous). Used when you’re about to present, point out, or reveal something. In casual situations with one person you can say: « Je veux te montrer quelque chose. » You can add details with « dans + place » (location) or « de + adjective » (something very special/particular).
target_language_example: Je veux vous montrer quelque chose d’important.
native_language_example: I want to show you something important.

additional_notes: Uses **vous** (formal “you” to one person, or “you” to several people). Often followed by **de + noun** or **à propos de + noun** to say what you want to talk about (e.g., *Je veux vous parler de ce rapport*). You can add **seul(e)** to mean “in private/alone” (*Je veux vous parler seul*).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je veux vous parler un instant.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I want to talk to you for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a strong desire or intention. Often followed by an infinitive (je veux vraiment partir) or a direct object (je veux vraiment ça). Word order can vary for emphasis (Vraiment, je veux vraiment ça).
target_language_example: Je veux vraiment apprendre le français cette année.
native_language_example: I really want to learn French this year.

additional_notes: Used to express a desire to become something (a job/role, a quality, a better version of yourself) or to be in a certain state. Follow it with a noun (“Je veux être guitariste”), an adjective (“Je veux être intelligent”), or sometimes a past participle to mean “I want to be [invited/promoted]” (“Je veux être invitée/promu”). The form stays the same regardless of who is speaking; only the adjective/participle agrees with the speaker (e.g., invitée for a woman, invité for a man).
target_language_example: Je veux être plus patient.
native_language_example: I want to be more patient.

additional_notes: Future tense of venir (to come). Use it to say you’ll come somewhere in the future (often with time words like demain, plus tôt, vers six heures). It can also mean “I’ll come (to do something)” before an infinitive: Je viendrai te chercher = I’ll come pick you up.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je viendrai te voir ce week-end.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll come see you this weekend.

meaning: “I just (did something)” / “I’ve just (done something)” (very recent past).
additional_notes: Used as the near past: venir (present) + de + infinitive. It means the action happened moments ago. You can change the subject: « tu viens de… », « il/elle vient de… », « nous venons de… », etc. Common in everyday speech; neutral register (but it can introduce informal/vulgar verbs depending on what follows).
target_language_example: Je viens de rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: I just got home.

additional_notes: This uses the recent past construction: **venir de + infinitive** to say something happened a moment ago. Here it’s **je viens de** (I’ve just) + **faire** (do/make). If **faire** is followed by another verb (e.g., *faire nettoyer*, *faire peindre*), it often means **to have something done** (to get something cleaned/painted). You can change the subject: *tu viens de faire*, *il/elle vient de faire*, *nous venons de faire*, etc.
target_language_example: Je viens de faire mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I just did my homework.

additional_notes: Uses the recent past with venir de ("to have just") + an action. Structure: Je viens de finir de + infinitive (e.g., manger, lire). You can change the subject and tense: Tu viens de finir de…, Il/Elle vient de finir de…, Nous venons de finir de…. In casual speech, "de" before the second infinitive is often dropped: Je viens de finir (de) manger.
target_language_example: Je viens de finir de travailler, je rentre à la maison.
native_language_example: I just finished working; I'm going home.

meaning: “I just thought of …” / “It just occurred to me …”
additional_notes: Uses the recent past: "venir de" + infinitive = “to have just (done something).” Here, "penser à" means “to think of/about,” and it’s followed by "à" + a noun/idea/person. Common for a new thought that pops into your head; can also feel like “I just remembered …” depending on context.
target_language_example: Je viens de penser à une bonne solution.
native_language_example: I just thought of a good solution.

additional_notes: Uses the near-past structure: **venir de + infinitive** (“to have just done something”). Here, **je viens de recevoir** = “I just received.” You can replace **je** with other subjects: *tu viens de recevoir… / il vient de recevoir… / nous venons de recevoir…*. Very common in messages and conversation to emphasize something happened a moment ago.
target_language_example: Je viens de recevoir les résultats.
native_language_example: I just received the results.

additional_notes: Uses the recent past construction: venir de + infinitive. Here it’s conjugated as "je viens" + "de" + "voir" to say you saw something very recently. You can swap the subject and verb to fit the situation (e.g., "tu viens de voir…", "il/elle vient de voir…", "nous venons de voir…").
target_language_example: Je viens de voir une voiture passer très vite.
native_language_example: I just saw a car go by really fast.

additional_notes: Common patterns: **je viens de + infinitive** = "I just did" (recent past): *Je viens d'essayer.* **je viens de + place** = "I come from": *Je viens de loin.* **je viens (avec toi)** = "I’m coming (with you)"; adding **volontiers** means "gladly/willingly."
target_language_example: J'arrive dans cinq minutes : je viens !
native_language_example: I’ll be there in five minutes: I’m coming!

meaning: "I just had" / "I just got" (something just happened to me).
additional_notes: This is the pattern **venir de + infinitive** to express the **very recent past**: *je viens d’avoir…* = “I’ve just had/gotten…”. With **avoir**, it can mean “just had (on the phone)”, “just received (a message)”, or “just had (a baby/idea)”, depending on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Je viens d’avoir une super nouvelle.
native_language_example: I just got some great news.

meaning: “I just (did something)” / “I’ve just (done something)” (very recent past).
additional_notes: Used as the near past: venir (present) + de + infinitive. It means the action happened moments ago. You can change the subject: « tu viens de… », « il/elle vient de… », « nous venons de… », etc. Common in everyday speech; neutral register (but it can introduce informal/vulgar verbs depending on what follows).
target_language_example: Je viens de rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: I just got home.

meaning: “I just got …” / “I was just …” (something just happened to me).
additional_notes: Built on **venir de + infinitive** (“to have just done/just happened”) + **se faire + infinitive**. It often introduces an event that happened to you (often unpleasant): *Je viens de me faire renverser* (“I just got hit/knocked over”), *Je viens de me faire virer* (“I just got fired”). It can also mean you just had something done (a service): *Je viens de me faire faire un tatouage* (“I just got a tattoo”). With a bite: *Je viens de me faire mordre (par un moustique)* (“I just got bitten (by a mosquito)”).
target_language_example: Je viens de me faire voler mon sac dans le métro.
native_language_example: I just had my bag stolen on the subway.

meaning: "I just" / "I’ve just" (I did something very recently).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to express the very recent past: "venir de" = "to have just done"; adding "juste" emphasizes how recent it was. In speech it’s often shortened to "je viens de". Example pattern: "Je viens (juste) de + infinitive" (e.g., "Je viens juste de finir").
target_language_example: Je viens juste de prendre le bus.
native_language_example: I just took the bus.

additional_notes: Used to say where you live (je vis ici/là, je vis en Australie), who you live with (je vis avec ma mère), or more generally your current place/life situation. Not to be confused with je vois (“I see”).
target_language_example: Je vis à Paris depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Paris for two years.

additional_notes: Uses the verb *vivre* (“to live”). *À* is commonly used before cities (Je vis à Paris) and also some islands/places (Je vis à Tahiti, à Malte). For most countries you use **en** (en France) or **au/aux** (au Canada, aux États-Unis) instead of *à*.
target_language_example: Je vis à Lyon depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in Lyon for two years.

additional_notes: Used to say you notice or realize something based on what you observe or learn. Often followed by a full sentence with que.
target_language_example: Je vois que tu as compris.
native_language_example: I see that you understood.

meaning: “I would like” (polite way to say what you want).
additional_notes: Used to make polite requests or express what you’d like to do/have. It’s the conditional form of vouloir (“to want”), and sounds softer/more courteous than je veux (“I want”). Often followed by an infinitive (je voudrais parler… = “I’d like to talk…”) or a noun (je voudrais un café = “I’d like a coffee”).
target_language_example: Bonjour, je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Hello, I’d like a coffee, please.

meaning: 'I wanted' / 'I was wanting' (often: 'I wanted to…' as a polite way to say what you’d like).
additional_notes: "Je voulais" is the imperfect of "vouloir" (to want). It’s commonly used with an infinitive: "Je voulais + verb" (e.g., "je voulais réserver / je voulais prendre"). In conversation, it often sounds softer/more polite than "je veux" (I want), similar to "I wanted to ask/tell you…" in English.
target_language_example: Je voulais te demander un service.
native_language_example: I wanted to ask you a favor.

meaning: "I meant" / "what I was trying to say" (literally: "I wanted to say").
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of vouloir (voulais) to soften or qualify what you’re saying. Common when clarifying your meaning, correcting a misunderstanding, or adding precision: « Je voulais dire que… » = “I meant that…” / “What I was trying to say is…”.
target_language_example: Je voulais dire que je viendrai un peu plus tard.
native_language_example: I meant that I’ll come a little later.

additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re saying or to make your intention sound modest (often like an apology or reassurance). It uses the imperfect (voulais), which can sound more polite/less direct than "je veux". Usually followed by an infinitive: "Je voulais juste + verb".
target_language_example: Je voulais juste te demander un service.
native_language_example: I just wanted to ask you a favor.

meaning: "I just wanted to…" (said to someone informally as "you").
additional_notes: Used to introduce something small or polite you want to say/do (e.g., give a quick warning, thank someone, let them know something). It’s followed by an infinitive: « Je voulais juste te + infinitif » (prévenir, remercier, dire, faire savoir…). « te » is the informal object pronoun “to you.” For a formal version, use « je voulais juste vous… ».
target_language_example: Je voulais juste te dire merci pour ton aide.
native_language_example: I just wanted to say thank you for your help.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you’re about to say in a soft, polite way. Literally “I wanted just to tell you,” but in English it’s usually “I just wanted to tell you…”. Often followed by a noun/phrase (e.g., bonjour) or by “que + sentence” (e.g., que je t’aime).
target_language_example: Je voulais juste te dire merci pour ton aide.
native_language_example: I just wanted to tell you thank you for your help.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a polite remark or small request. It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., vous prévenir = to warn/inform you, vous souhaiter = to wish you, vous remonter le moral = to cheer you up). "Vous" is the formal/plural "you"; with one friend you’d usually say "je voulais juste te…".
target_language_example: Je voulais juste vous poser une question.
native_language_example: I just wanted to ask you a question.

meaning: “I wanted to apologize for …” / “I meant to apologize for …”.
additional_notes: Polite way to start an apology, often referring to a specific past moment or situation (hier, l’autre jour, l’autre soir, tout à l’heure). Uses the imperfect (je voulais) to sound softer/less direct than “je m’excuse pour …”. You can follow it with a noun or time expression: “je voulais m’excuser pour mon retard / pour ça / pour hier”.
target_language_example: Je voulais m'excuser pour mon retard.
native_language_example: I wanted to apologize for being late.

additional_notes: Used to express a past desire or wish. In French, after "vouloir que" you typically use the subjunctive (e.g., "Je voulais que Tom parte."). In English you often translate it as "I wanted [someone] to [do something]" rather than "I wanted that...".
target_language_example: Je voulais que tu viennes avec nous.
native_language_example: I wanted you to come with us.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb to introduce something you intended to do/say to someone ("te" = "to you"). Often sounds polite/soft when used to introduce a request or message (Je voulais te demander…, Je voulais te dire…). You typically follow it with an infinitive: demander, dire, souhaiter, prévenir/mette au courant, etc.
target_language_example: Je voulais te demander un service.
native_language_example: I wanted to ask you a favor.

meaning: “I wanted to ask you” (polite/soft way to ask).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect (voulais) to sound more tentative and polite than the direct present “je veux te demander” or “je te demande”. Often followed by: “si …” (to ask if), a direct question, or a noun (“quelque chose / une chose”). Can also stand alone as a lead-in before the question.
target_language_example: Je voulais te demander si tu as le temps ce soir.
native_language_example: I wanted to ask you if you have time tonight.

additional_notes: Common way to introduce what you’re about to say. Uses the imperfect (voulais), which often softens the statement (like “I just wanted to tell you…”). Follow it with a noun/phrase (Je voulais te dire bonjour.) or with “que” + a full clause (Je voulais te dire que je suis en retard.). You can also use it alone as a lead-in, sometimes implying “...something” or hesitating.
target_language_example: Je voulais te dire que je suis désolé.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell you that I’m sorry.

meaning: "I wanted to talk to you" / "I meant to talk to you."
additional_notes: Common opener to introduce a topic you want to discuss. Uses the imperfect (voulais) to express an intention or something you had in mind (often polite/soft). Often followed by a topic: « Je voulais te parler de… » (I wanted to talk to you about…).
target_language_example: Je voulais te parler de demain : tu es libre ?
native_language_example: I wanted to talk to you about tomorrow—are you free?

meaning: “I wanted to … (to/for you)” (polite way to introduce what you intended to do or say).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive with the object pronoun “vous” (you, formal or plural): je voulais vous + VERB (apporter, dire, donner, etc.). It often sounds softer/more polite than stating something directly. Don’t confuse it with “je vous voulais” (“I wanted you”), which is a different word order and meaning.
target_language_example: Je voulais vous demander un service.
native_language_example: I wanted to ask you a favor.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect (je voulais) to sound polite/less direct, often like “I wanted to speak with you / I meant to talk to you.” Common to introduce a topic: « je voulais vous parler de/au sujet de/à propos de … ». « vous » is the formal or plural “you”; with friends you’d often say « je voulais te parler ».
target_language_example: Bonjour, je voulais vous parler de mon dossier.
native_language_example: Hello, I wanted to talk to you about my file.

meaning: "I" + "you" (formal or plural), as an object pronoun before the verb.
additional_notes: Used when the speaker (je) does something to/for "vous". "Vous" can mean either (1) "you" to one person in a polite/formal way, or (2) "you" to several people. In French object pronouns like "vous" usually come before the verb: « Je vous assure… », « Je vous conseille… », « Je vous jure… ». By itself, « je vous » is incomplete—you need a verb after it.
target_language_example: Je vous remercie pour votre aide.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help.

meaning: “I have … you” / “I …ed you” (formal or plural “you”), used to start the past tense (passé composé).
additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir to form the passé composé: je + vous (you, formal singular or plural) + ai (have). It’s typically followed by a past participle (acheté, attendu, posé, sauvé, etc.). Depending on the verb, “vous” can mean “you” as a direct object (“I waited for you”) or “to you/for you” as an indirect object (“I asked you a question”).
target_language_example: Je vous ai envoyé un e-mail hier.
native_language_example: I emailed you yesterday.

meaning: I brought you (formal/plural) / I've brought you.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "apporter" (to bring) in the passé composé: "j'ai apporté" = I brought / I have brought. "Vous" can mean "you" (formal singular) or "you" (plural). Often followed by a direct object: "Je vous ai apporté de l'eau" (I brought you some water).
target_language_example: Je vous ai apporté votre commande.
native_language_example: I brought you your order.

meaning: “I told you” (to you, formal or plural).
additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of dire (“to tell/say”): je + vous (object pronoun “to you”) + ai dit. Commonly followed by **que** (I told you that…), **de + infinitive** (I told you to…), or **ce que** (what I told you). Can be used to remind someone or reproach them: *Qu’est-ce que je vous ai dit ?* (“What did I tell you?”).
target_language_example: Je vous ai dit de ne pas toucher à ça.
native_language_example: I told you not to touch that.

additional_notes: Used to remind or insist that you previously gave an instruction. "Vous" is either formal "you" (one person) or plural "you" (several people). It’s followed by an infinitive verb (de + infinitive): "Je vous ai dit de vous asseoir". In speech, the negative is: "Je ne vous ai pas dit de …".
target_language_example: Je vous ai dit de fermer la porte.
native_language_example: I told you to close the door.

je vous ai dit de ne pas

target_language_multi_word_term: je vous ai dit de ne pas
additional_notes: Used to remind or scold someone about a past instruction. "Je vous ai dit" is the past tense (passé composé) of *dire* (to tell). It’s followed by the infinitive: *Je vous ai dit de ne pas + verb* (e.g., *de ne pas fumer*, *de ne pas venir*). *Vous* can mean "you" (plural) or formal "you" (one person).
target_language_example: Je vous ai dit de ne pas toucher à ça.
native_language_example: I told you not to touch that.

meaning: "I made you / I had you" (do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive after it: « je vous ai fait + infinitif » expresses the causative idea of causing/forcing/arranging for someone to do something (e.g., « Je vous ai fait marcher… » = I made you walk). « vous » is the object pronoun (“you” formal/plural). In speech it can also imply “let you” depending on context.
target_language_example: Je vous ai fait attendre dix minutes, désolé.
native_language_example: I made you wait ten minutes, sorry.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of voir: « j’ai vu » (“I saw / I’ve seen”). « vous » is used for one person in a formal/polite situation or for more than one person (“you all”). « vu » can agree in gender/number in some cases (e.g., « Je vous ai vue » to a woman; « Je vous ai vus/vues » for several people), but « vu » is often seen as the default form.
target_language_example: Je vous ai vu à la réunion ce matin.
native_language_example: I saw you at the meeting this morning.

meaning: 'I saw you' / 'I’ve seen you' (addressing 'you' as a woman, or a group with at least one woman).
additional_notes: "Vous" is the formal 'you' (one person) or 'you all' (plural). In the passé composé, the past participle of "voir" is "vu". It becomes "vue" when the direct object pronoun (vous) comes before the verb and refers to a feminine person (or feminine/mixed plural). If you're addressing a man (singular), you would say: "Je vous ai vu."
target_language_example: Je vous ai vue hier au restaurant.
native_language_example: I saw you yesterday at the restaurant.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of voir: "j’ai vu" = "I saw / I have seen." "Vous" can mean "you" (formal singular) or "you" (plural). Because "vous" is the direct object and it comes before the verb, the past participle can agree: "vus" (masculine plural or mixed group) / "vues" (feminine plural). With one person (formal singular), you’ll often see "je vous ai vu" (to a man) or "je vous ai vue" (to a woman).
target_language_example: Je vous ai vus tous les deux à la sortie du cinéma.
native_language_example: I saw both of you when you came out of the movie theater.

additional_notes: Uses the pluperfect tense ("avais dit") to refer to an instruction given earlier than another past moment: "I had told you to…". It’s often used to remind someone of what you previously instructed them to do, sometimes with an implied reproach. Followed by an infinitive (e.g., "faire", "rester") or "ne pas" + infinitive for a negative instruction.
target_language_example: Je vous avais dit de fermer la porte avant de partir.
native_language_example: I had told you to close the door before leaving.

meaning: I advise you to / I recommend that you.
additional_notes: Polite/formal way to give advice to one or more people. Uses "vous" (formal singular or plural). Follow with an infinitive verb: « Je vous conseille de + infinitif » (e.g., partir, changer, prendre).
target_language_example: Je vous conseille de réserver à l'avance.
native_language_example: I advise you to book in advance.

additional_notes: Used to insist on what you’re saying or to introduce what comes next. The pronoun "vous" (to you) comes before the verb: "Je vous dis que..." (I’m telling you that...), "Je vous dis de..." (I’m telling you to...). It can also be used in set phrases like "Je vous dis au revoir" (I say goodbye to you).
target_language_example: Je vous dis la vérité.
native_language_example: I’m telling you the truth.

additional_notes: Used when you owe someone money (often said to a cashier/server: « Je vous dois combien ? » / « Combien je vous dois ? ») or when you owe something more figurative (an explanation, a favor, gratitude). It’s typically followed by an amount (« Je vous dois 12 euros ») or a noun (« Je vous dois une explication »).
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide, je vous dois une explication.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help, I owe you an explanation.

meaning: “I give you” / “I’m giving you” (formal or plural “you”).
additional_notes: Used when handing something to someone or granting something (e.g., permission). “Vous” is used for one person formally or for more than one person. In the past or future you’ll see the same pattern with other tenses: « Je vous ai donné… » (I gave you…), « Je vous donnerai… » (I will give you…).
target_language_example: Je vous donne ce document tout de suite.
native_language_example: I’m giving you this document right away.

meaning: “I … you … (of it / about it / for it / some).”
additional_notes: This is a common pronoun cluster: **je** (I) + **vous** (to you / you) + **en** (“some”, “any”, “of it/them”, “about it/them”, often replacing **de + noun** or a quantity). It appears right before the verb: **Je vous en parle** (I talk to you about it), **Je vous en donne deux** (I give you two of them), **Je vous en remercie** (I thank you for it). **En** can mean “some/any” with numbers and quantities (deux, un, quelques), or “about it/for it” with certain verbs (parler de, remercier de, etc.).
target_language_example: Je vous en enverrai demain.
native_language_example: I’ll send you some tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to politely beg someone not to do something, often in an emotional or urgent context. Common pattern: “Je vous en prie, ne + verb (imperative)” (e.g., ne partez pas). Also note: “Je vous en prie” alone can mean “You’re welcome,” but with “ne … (pas)” it means “Please, don’t…”.
target_language_example: Je vous en prie, ne dites rien à personne.
native_language_example: Please, don’t tell anyone.

additional_notes: Uses passé composé of *dire* (to say/tell): *j’ai dit*. *vous* is formal “you” or plural “you (all)”. *l’* (“it”) refers to what was said before (the thing you told them). Often used to insist or remind someone: “I told you (already) / I told you so.”
target_language_example: Je vous l’ai dit : je ne peux pas venir demain.
native_language_example: I told you: I can’t come tomorrow.

meaning: “I’ll leave you” / “I’ll let you …” / “I’ll leave (something) with you.”
additional_notes:
Common, polite phrase with several uses depending on what follows:
- To end a conversation: « Faut que je vous laisse. » = “I have to go / I’ll let you go.”
- To allow someone to do something: « Je vous laisse décider. » = “I’ll let you decide.”
- To leave something with someone: « Je vous laisse ma carte. » = “I’ll leave you my card.”
- To give time or privacy: « Je vous laisse un moment. » / « Je vous laisse seule. » = “I’ll leave you for a moment / I’ll leave you alone.”
target_language_example: Bon, je vous laisse. À tout à l’heure.
native_language_example: Well, I’ll let you go. See you later.

additional_notes: Used when two object pronouns come before the verb: "vous" = to you (polite singular or plural), and "le" = it (or him). Common with verbs like demander (ask), dire (tell), garantir (guarantee), promettre (promise), montrer (show). The verb comes after: Je vous le demande / Je vous le dis / Je vous le montre.
target_language_example: Je vous le répète : c'est important.
native_language_example: I'm telling you again: it's important.

additional_notes: Used to make a request or instruction more polite, often in formal or customer-service contexts. It can be placed at the end of the sentence (common in commands: « Restez assise, je vous prie. »). Similar in tone to « s’il vous plaît » or « veuillez… », and can sometimes sound quite formal/old-fashioned depending on context.
target_language_example: Entrez, je vous prie.
native_language_example: Come in, please.

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to make a request, often used in official speech, letters, announcements, or serious contexts. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « Je vous prie de + infinitive » (e.g., « Je vous prie de patienter »). In everyday conversation, people more often say « s’il vous plaît » or « je vous demande de ».
target_language_example: Je vous prie de bien vouloir fermer la porte.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

meaning: “I present to you / I offer you / let me introduce…” (formal).
additional_notes: Used in polite/formal situations with **vous**. Common patterns: **Je vous présente mes condoléances** (“Please accept my condolences”), **Je vous présente mes excuses** (“I apologize”), and **Je vous présente [quelqu’un]** (“Let me introduce [someone]”). You can also say **Permettez que je vous présente…** (“Allow me to introduce…”).
target_language_example: Je vous présente mon collègue, Paul.
native_language_example: Let me introduce my colleague, Paul.

additional_notes: A very formal, polite way to apologize, often used in emails, letters, announcements, or customer service. It can be followed by pour + noun/infinitive (“for …”), or à + person/group (“to …”). Can also be said alone as a complete apology.
target_language_example: Je vous présente mes excuses pour le retard.
native_language_example: I apologize for the delay.

additional_notes: Uses the formal/polite object pronoun vous (“you” singular formal or plural). Often followed by de + infinitive to thank someone for doing something (Je vous remercie d’être venu), or de/pour + noun to thank for something (Je vous remercie de votre aide / pour votre aide). Can be strengthened with Du fond du cœur (“from the bottom of my heart”) and can address a group (Je vous remercie tous).
target_language_example: Je vous remercie pour votre aide.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help.

additional_notes: Used in formal or polite situations. It’s followed by a noun (often with an adjective): votre aide, votre temps, votre accueil, votre attention, etc. « Je vous remercie » uses vous (formal ‘you’ or plural ‘you’). In more casual speech you can say « Merci pour … » or « Je te remercie pour … » (informal, singular).
target_language_example: Je vous remercie de votre aide précieuse.
native_language_example: Thank you for your valuable help.

additional_notes: Used to express good wishes to one or more people, or to someone you address formally (vous). It’s commonly followed by a noun phrase like bon voyage, bonne chance, une bonne journée/soirée, or something like tout le bonheur du monde. With an infinitive, it can also mean “I hope you will…” (e.g., Je vous souhaite de réussir).
target_language_example: Je vous souhaite un bon séjour en France.
native_language_example: I wish you a nice stay in France.

je vous suis reconnaissant pour votre

target_language_multi_word_term: je vous suis reconnaissant pour votre
meaning: I am grateful to you for your… / I appreciate your… (formal).
additional_notes: A polite, formal way to thank someone ("vous" = you, formal or plural). Use it before a noun like "aide/assistance" (help), "temps" (time), "travail" (work), etc. The adjective agrees with the speaker: "reconnaissant" (male) / "reconnaissante" (female). You can also say: "Je vous suis reconnaissant(e) de votre…".
target_language_example: Je vous suis reconnaissante pour votre aide et votre patience.
native_language_example: I’m grateful to you for your help and your patience.

meaning: to take/have a quick look (to glance).
additional_notes: Very common set phrase. It uses jeter (“to throw”) + coup d’œil (literally “blow of the eye”), but the meaning is simply “to glance / have a quick look.” You’ll also see similar patterns like jeter un regard (“to cast a look/glance”), often in negative form: sans même me jeter un regard (“without even giving me a look”).
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un coup d’œil à ce message ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at this message?

meaning: To take a quick look; to have a glance.
additional_notes: A very common, neutral expression for looking briefly at something (a document, a screen, an item in a store, etc.). Often used to ask permission politely: « Je peux jeter un coup d'œil ? » / « Vous voulez jeter un coup d'œil ? ». You can also say « jeter un coup d'œil à + noun » (e.g., « à ce dossier »).
target_language_example: Je peux jeter un coup d'œil à ton billet ?
native_language_example: Can I take a quick look at your ticket?

meaning: to take a look; to have a quick look.
additional_notes: Common, everyday expression meaning to look at something briefly (often as a favor or to check something). Usually used with "à": "jeter un œil à" + thing/person. Conjugates like "jeter" (je jette, tu jettes, il/elle jette).
target_language_example: Je peux jeter un œil à ton CV ce soir.
native_language_example: I can take a look at your résumé tonight.

additional_notes: From « jeter » (to throw) + « un coup d’œil » (a look/glance). It’s a common, casual way to ask someone to glance at something. Often used with « à » (Jette un coup d’œil à ça) or « sur » (Jette un coup d’œil sur le document). The « e » in « jette » is pronounced like “jet.”
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un coup d'œil à mon message avant que je l'envoie ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at my message before I send it?

additional_notes: Common, casual way to ask someone to look at something briefly (often as an imperative: « Jette un œil ! », « Jette un œil là-dessus. »). You can also use it to politely ask permission to look: « Ça vous dérange si je jette un œil ? ». Means a quick glance, not a long, careful examination.
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un œil à mon devoir avant que je l’envoie ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at my homework before I send it?

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: un jeu vidéo (a video game), des jeux vidéo (video games). Often used with jouer à: jouer à des jeux vidéo (to play video games).
target_language_example: On joue à des jeux vidéo ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we playing video games tonight?

additional_notes: An idiom used when someone has difficulty covering basic expenses with the money they have. Often used with “avoir du mal à…” (to have trouble) or “essayer de…” (to try).
target_language_example: Depuis qu'il a perdu son travail, il a du mal à joindre les deux bouts.
native_language_example: Since he lost his job, he’s having trouble making ends meet.

meaning: to join (a group) / to join someone (in doing something).
additional_notes: Most common in this meaning as **se joindre à** + person/group: **Je me joins à toi/nous** = “I join you/us.” It’s used to invite someone to join an activity (**se joindre à moi pour le déjeuner**) or to become part of a group/team (**se joindre à notre équipe**). Note: **joindre** without *à* can also mean “to reach/contact” someone (e.g., *joindre quelqu’un par téléphone*).
target_language_example: Je peux me joindre à vous pour le café ?
native_language_example: Can I join you for coffee?

additional_notes: Most often used as the reflexive verb: **se joindre à nous** (e.g., *te joindre à nous*, *se joindre à nous*). It means to come and participate with a group. Common in invitations: **Ça te dirait de te joindre à nous ?** (“Would you like to join us?”).
target_language_example: Tu veux te joindre à nous pour dîner ?
native_language_example: Do you want to join us for dinner?

additional_notes: A common compliment: "jolie" (pretty) + "fille" (girl). Usually used with an article, e.g. "une jolie fille" (a pretty girl) or "cette jolie fille" (that pretty girl). You can intensify it with words like "très" (very) or "vraiment" (really). Exclamation: "Quelle jolie fille !" = "What a pretty girl!"
target_language_example: C’est une jolie fille, et elle est très gentille.
native_language_example: She’s a pretty girl, and she’s very nice.

additional_notes: "jouait" is the imperfect tense of "jouer" (to play), used for background actions, ongoing situations, or habits in the past. With instruments, French uses "jouer de" + the instrument: "jouer du piano" (piano), "jouer de la guitare" (guitar).
target_language_example: Quand j'étais petit, je jouais du piano tous les jours.
native_language_example: When I was little, I used to play the piano every day.

additional_notes:
From the verb **jouer** (“to play”). **Il/elle joue au ...** is **jouer à + le** → **au** (used with masculine singular nouns): *jouer au rugby, au volley, au ballon*. With feminine nouns: **jouer à la ...**; with plural: **jouer aux ...**. 

For musical instruments, standard French is usually **jouer du/de la/des ...** (e.g., *jouer du piano*), though you may sometimes hear/see **jouer au piano** meaning “to play on the piano.”
target_language_example: Elle joue au tennis le samedi.
native_language_example: She plays tennis on Saturdays.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "jouer à" + a sport/game. With "golf" it becomes "jouer au golf" (à + le = au). Conjugation changes with the subject (e.g., je joue, tu joues, il/elle joue, nous jouons).
target_language_example: Le week-end, elle joue au golf avec ses amis.
native_language_example: On weekends, she plays golf with her friends.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **jouer à** + a sport/game. With **tennis** (masculine), it contracts to **au** (= à + le): **jouer au tennis**. Conjugation: **je joue**, **tu joues**, **il/elle joue**, **nous jouons**, **vous jouez**, **ils/elles jouent**.
target_language_example: Mon frère joue au tennis le week-end.
native_language_example: My brother plays tennis on the weekend.

additional_notes: From the verb jouer (to play). You use "jouer à" for games, and it becomes "jouer aux" before a plural noun: "aux jeux vidéo" (= "à + les jeux vidéo"). The subject changes the verb: "Je joue…" (I play), "il/elle joue…" (he/she plays).
target_language_example: Elle joue aux jeux vidéo tous les soirs.
native_language_example: She plays video games every evening.

additional_notes: Form of "jouer de" + definite article.
