Use it to say someone plays an instrument, especially instruments that take an article: "jouer de la" (feminine singular: la flûte, la basse), "jouer du" (masculine singular: du piano), "jouer de l'" (before a vowel: de l'orgue), "jouer des" (plural: des cymbales). Contrast: "jouer à" is used for playing games/sports ("jouer au foot").
target_language_example: Elle joue de la guitare depuis dix ans.
native_language_example: She has been playing the guitar for ten years.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **jouer de** + an instrument: *jouer de la guitare / du piano / du violon*. With a person, you conjugate **jouer**: *je joue, tu joues, il/elle joue, nous jouons...* To ask “Who plays the guitar?”, say: *Qui joue de la guitare ?*
target_language_example: Elle joue de la guitare tous les soirs.
native_language_example: She plays the guitar every evening.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "jouer" + "de" + an instrument: "jouer du piano" (piano), "jouer de la guitare" (guitar). The form "joue" is the present tense for il/elle/on; for "I play the piano" you say "je joue du piano".
target_language_example: Mon frère joue du piano depuis cinq ans.
native_language_example: My brother has been playing the piano for five years.

additional_notes: Used with musical instruments: **jouer de + instrument**. With masculine singular nouns it becomes **du** (de + le): *du piano*. With feminine: **de la** (*de la guitare*), before a vowel: **de l’** (*de l’accordéon*), plural: **des** (*des percussions*). You can change the adverb: *joue bien / très bien / vraiment bien*.
target_language_example: Il joue très bien du piano, mais il joue aussi de la guitare.
native_language_example: He plays the piano very well, but he also plays the guitar.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has a strong influence or is a significant factor in a situation or in someone’s life. The subject is the thing that influences (e.g., la chance, la télévision, le sport). Often followed by “la vie / la vie quotidienne / sa vie / notre vie / nos vies.”
target_language_example: L’éducation joue un rôle important dans la réussite.
native_language_example: Education plays an important role in success.

meaning: to play (a sport/game); to play in the (sunlight).
additional_notes: "Au" is the contraction of "à + le". Use "jouer à" with sports and games: "jouer au volley" (volleyball), "jouer au hockey" (hockey). With a feminine noun, use "jouer à la" (e.g., "jouer à la belote"); with plural, "jouer aux". In sentences like "jouer au soleil", it means to play in the sun/in the sunlight (not a sport).
target_language_example: On joue au foot après l'école.
native_language_example: We play soccer after school.

additional_notes: Used with the verb jouer + à + the sport: jouer au football, jouer au tennis, jouer au basket. In many French-speaking contexts, football means “soccer” (not American football).
target_language_example: On va jouer au football après l'école.
native_language_example: We’re going to play soccer after school.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the activity/sport. With sports and games in French, you usually say "jouer à" + the sport/game, which contracts to "jouer au" before a masculine singular noun like "tennis" (à + le = au).
target_language_example: On peut jouer au tennis après le travail ?
native_language_example: Can we play tennis after work?

additional_notes: Used to talk about playing card games in general (e.g., poker, bridge, etc.). With games you use "jouer à"; here it becomes "jouer aux" because "les cartes" is plural (à + les = aux).
target_language_example: On joue aux cartes après le dîner.
native_language_example: We play cards after dinner.

additional_notes: Used with "jouer à" + a game/sport. "Aux" = "à + les" because "échecs" is plural. You can say: "Je sais jouer aux échecs" (I know how to play chess) or "Je joue aux échecs" (I play chess / I’m playing chess).
target_language_example: On joue aux échecs après le dîner ?
native_language_example: Shall we play chess after dinner?

additional_notes: Used when you’re playing together with someone (jouer avec toi/nous/vous) or playing using/with an object or material (jouer avec la neige, jouer avec un ballon). In invitations, it can mean “come and play with us” = “join us (in the game/team).”
target_language_example: Tu veux jouer avec moi ?
native_language_example: Do you want to play with me?

additional_notes: Used to invite someone to play (a game, with toys, etc.). Depending on tone/context, it can also mean “Are you messing with me / kidding me?” especially in questions like « Tu es en train de jouer avec moi ? » or « Tu croyais jouer avec moi ? ». With a child or friendly situation, it’s usually literal.
target_language_example: Tu veux venir jouer avec moi après l’école ?
native_language_example: Do you want to come play with me after school?

additional_notes: Used with musical instruments: you say "jouer de" + the instrument (e.g., jouer du piano, jouer de la batterie). In questions, you can invert the verb: « Savez-vous jouer de la guitare ? »
target_language_example: Elle joue de la guitare tous les soirs.
native_language_example: She plays the guitar every evening.

additional_notes: Used with musical instruments: jouer + de/du/de la/de l’ + instrument. Here it’s "du" because "piano" is masculine singular (de + le = du). You can also use it after verbs like apprendre à ("learn to") or pouvoir ("can").
target_language_example: J'aime jouer du piano après le travail.
native_language_example: I like to play the piano after work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone who plays baseball; you can add adjectives like "professionnel" (professional) or "meilleur" (best). "Base-ball" is sometimes also written "baseball" in French.
target_language_example: Son frère est joueur de base-ball, et il s’entraîne tous les jours.
native_language_example: His brother is a baseball player, and he trains every day.

meaning: “day of” (a day for/with a specific purpose or characteristic).
additional_notes: Used in the pattern « un/le jour de + noun » to describe what kind of day it is: « un jour de fête » (a holiday/celebration day), « un jour de repos » (a day of rest). Also appears in the set phrase « (C’est) ton/mon/votre jour de chance » = “It’s your/my day/lucky day.”
target_language_example: Aujourd’hui, c’est un jour de repos pour moi.
native_language_example: Today is a day of rest for me.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a scheduled or taken day when you don’t work (your day off). Often used with a possessive: mon/ton/son jour de congé. Can also be plural: des jours de congé (days off).
target_language_example: J’ai pris un jour de congé vendredi.
native_language_example: I took a day off on Friday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about which weekday it is (lundi, mardi, mercredi, etc.) or to ask for it: « On est quel jour de la semaine ? ». You’ll often see it with numbers or order: « le premier/deuxième/troisième jour de la semaine ».
target_language_example: Je travaille tous les jours de la semaine, sauf le dimanche.
native_language_example: I work every day of the week except Sunday.

meaning: logbook; record of events/activities (often on a ship or plane).
additional_notes: Used for an official written record kept day by day (e.g., "journal de bord du capitaine" = the captain’s logbook). Can also be used more generally for a personal or project “log” where you note what happened and what you did.
target_language_example: Le capitaine a noté l’incident dans le journal de bord.
native_language_example: The captain noted the incident in the logbook.

additional_notes: A general term for juice made from fruit. Often used with partitive articles for an unspecified amount: boire du jus de fruit (“to drink some fruit juice”). You can also use it with specific amounts: un verre de jus de fruit (“a glass of fruit juice”), or ask what kind: Quel genre de jus de fruit as-tu ?
target_language_example: Je prends un jus de fruit au petit déjeuner.
native_language_example: I have fruit juice for breakfast.

additional_notes: Used to mark an end point in time (jusqu'à lundi, jusqu'à demain), or a limit/endpoint more generally (jusqu'à la fin). It can also mean “as far as” with places (jusqu'à Paris). Before a clause, it’s usually "jusqu'à ce que" + subjunctive: "jusqu'à ce qu'on vous relève" (“until someone relieves you”).
target_language_example: Attendez ici jusqu'à ce que je revienne.
native_language_example: Wait here until I come back.

additional_notes: Used to say an action continued late into the night. It commonly follows a verb (travailler, lire, discuter, débattre). You may also see the same idea as "tard dans la nuit" (late at night) or "jusqu'à tard dans la nuit".
target_language_example: On a parlé jusque tard dans la nuit.
native_language_example: We talked until late at night.

meaning: right at the right moment; just in time.
additional_notes: Used to say someone arrived exactly when they were needed or when something was happening. It can refer to a fortunate timing (often like “just in time”). Agreement notes from the examples: arrivé (he arrived), venue (you arrived, singular feminine), venues (you arrived, plural feminine).
target_language_example: On a fini de préparer le dîner et tu es arrivé juste au bon moment.
native_language_example: We just finished preparing dinner and you arrived right on time.

juste au coin de la rue

target_language_multi_word_term: juste au coin de la rue
additional_notes: Used to say something is very close, usually on the next corner. "Juste" here means "right/just" (emphasis on how close it is). You can also hear "au coin de la rue" alone for "at/on the street corner."
target_language_example: La boulangerie est juste au coin de la rue.
native_language_example: The bakery is right around the corner.

meaning: just need to / only need to.
additional_notes: Used to downplay or simplify what’s required (“nothing more than…”). Very common in spoken French. Structure: subject + avoir + juste besoin de + infinitive (e.g., J’ai juste besoin de dormir) or + noun (J’ai juste besoin de temps).
target_language_example: On a juste besoin de dix minutes.
native_language_example: We just need ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to point out a precise location. Often said while giving directions or showing where something/someone is. Can also imply someone was there a moment ago ("He was just there").
target_language_example: Mets ton sac juste là, près de la porte.
native_language_example: Put your bag right there, near the door.

meaning: “just a / only a” (to downplay or limit something).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (un + noun) to mean “just/only one” or “just/only a.” Often expresses “nothing more than,” like in “just a test.” With amounts, it’s commonly followed by “peu de …” (just a little …). Feminine form: “juste une.”
target_language_example: Je veux juste un café, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: I just want a coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used to soften a request (“just a little of…”, “just a bit closer”) or to downplay something (“it only hurts a little”, “probably just a bit younger”). Often placed before the thing being minimized (juste un peu de temps) or before a comparative (juste un peu plus…).
target_language_example: Je voudrais juste un peu d’eau, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like just a little water, please.

additional_notes: Used to minimize or downplay something, or to stress that there is only one. It must be followed by a feminine noun (e.g., "juste une fête", "juste une minute"). For masculine nouns, use "juste un".
target_language_example: Attends juste une minute, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Just wait a minute, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to wait briefly or to say you only need a very short amount of time. Common with wait/hold on verbs like « attends/attendez ». In questions like « Je peux te parler juste une seconde ? », it softens the request by suggesting it won’t take long (even if it might be a bit longer in practice).
target_language_example: Juste une seconde, je finis ce message.
native_language_example: Just a second, I’m finishing this message.

meaning: right next door; right beside (very close).
additional_notes: Means something/someone is very nearby. Often used alone to answer “Where is it?”: « C’est juste à côté. » You can add « de + noun/pronoun »: « juste à côté de chez nous » (right next to our place), « juste à côté de toi » (right next to you).
target_language_example: La pharmacie est juste à côté de la boulangerie.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is right next to the bakery.

meaning: “I have” (present of avoir), also used to form the past tense (“I have” + past participle = “I did / I have done”).
additional_notes: Contraction of « je » + « ai » (from « avoir »). Used literally to say you have something: « J’ai un sac. » Very often it’s the auxiliary for the passé composé (a common past tense): « J’ai attendu » = “I waited / I’ve waited”, « J’ai perdu » = “I lost / I’ve lost”, « J’ai vu » = “I saw / I’ve seen”. The “thing you did” usually comes right after: « J’ai + [past participle] ».
target_language_example: J’ai fini mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I finished my homework.

additional_notes: Past tense of *perdre* with *avoir* (passé composé). Used for losing a game (*j’ai perdu*), misplacing/losing an object (*j’ai perdu mon sac*), losing a body part or ability (*j’ai perdu la main*), and losing consciousness (*j’ai perdu connaissance*). If you say only *J’ai perdu.*, it usually means “I lost (the game / I failed).”
target_language_example: Désolé, j’ai perdu tes clés.
native_language_example: Sorry, I lost your keys.

meaning: 'I was' / 'I have been' (passé composé of être).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the passive voice, especially to say something happened to you: « J’ai été cambriolé / frappé / mordu » = “I was robbed/hit/bitten.” With the passive, the past participle usually agrees with the subject (e.g., « J’ai été cambriolé » masculine; « J’ai été cambriolée » feminine). It can also mean “I went” in some contexts (« J’ai été à Paris » = “I went to Paris”), but in these examples it’s passive “I was…”.
target_language_example: J’ai été blessé au bras.
native_language_example: I was injured in the arm.

meaning: “I have” (present of avoir), also used to form the past tense (“I have” + past participle = “I did / I have done”).
additional_notes: Contraction of « je » + « ai » (from « avoir »). Used literally to say you have something: « J’ai un sac. » Very often it’s the auxiliary for the passé composé (a common past tense): « J’ai attendu » = “I waited / I’ve waited”, « J’ai perdu » = “I lost / I’ve lost”, « J’ai vu » = “I saw / I’ve seen”. The “thing you did” usually comes right after: « J’ai + [past participle] ».
target_language_example: J’ai fini mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I finished my homework.

additional_notes: Used before a noun with de/d’: j’ai besoin de + noun (“I need …”). Use d’ before a vowel or silent h (d’un, d’une; d’aide, d’argent). For a verb, use j’ai besoin de + infinitive (“I need to …”).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’aide, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: I need help, please.

additional_notes: Used to express strong trust, belief, or confidence in someone or something (often with a serious or spiritual tone). The person/thing you believe in comes after en: j’ai foi en toi (you), en vous (you formal/plural), en lui/elle/eux/elles (him/her/them), en Dieu (God). You can also say: avoir foi en + [noun/pronoun].
target_language_example: Même quand c’est difficile, j’ai foi en toi.
native_language_example: Even when it’s hard, I have faith in you.

meaning: "I have a" / "I’ve got a" (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you possess something or you have a condition/issue. "J’ai" is the contracted form of "je ai" (I have). "Un" is the masculine singular article; use "j’ai une" with feminine nouns (e.g., "j’ai une idée").
target_language_example: J’ai un problème avec mon billet.
native_language_example: I have a problem with my ticket.

additional_notes: Used to say you have/experience something. Often used for health issues (J’ai une bronchite / une douleur), possessions or things you’ve got (J’ai une meilleure image), or a state/condition (J’ai une pêche d’enfer = “I feel great”). If the noun is masculine, use “j’ai un”.
target_language_example: J’ai une question.
native_language_example: I have a question.

additional_notes: From the verb aimer (“to like/love”) in the present tense: j’ + aime (je becomes j’ before a vowel). Use it to say you like something (J’aime le café.), love someone/something (Je t’aime.), or enjoy doing an activity with an infinitive (J’aime voyager.). Often strengthened with adverbs like bien (“quite/pretty much”) or vraiment (“really”).
target_language_example: J’aime bien ce film, mais je préfère le livre.
native_language_example: I quite like this movie, but I prefer the book.

additional_notes: Contraction of « je » + « étais » (imparfait of « être », “to be”). Used to describe a state in the past, background information, or something habitual (“used to”). Often sets the scene rather than describing a single completed action.
target_language_example: Quand j’étais petit, j’étais souvent malade.
native_language_example: When I was little, I was often sick.

meaning: the look/appearance (used in « avoir l’air » = to seem, look).
additional_notes: Most often used with « avoir l’air » to describe how someone/something seems: « Tu as l’air fatigué » (You look tired). With « en avoir l’air », it means “to seem so / to look like it,” referring back to something already mentioned: « Ça en avait tout l’air » = “It certainly looked like it.”
target_language_example: Il a l’air content aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: He looks happy today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **avoir**: **avoir l’air + adjective** (e.g., *Tu as l’air bien.*). It describes someone’s appearance or how they seem (health, mood, etc.), not literal “air.” In speech you often hear **t’as l’air bien** (= *tu as l’air bien*).
target_language_example: Tu as l’air bien aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You look well today.

meaning: to look/seem like; to appear to be.
additional_notes: Used with forms of "avoir" (j’ai / tu as / il a / vous avez l’air de...). It describes someone’s appearance or an impression. Common patterns: (1) "avoir l’air de" + infinitive: "Tu as l’air d’avoir faim" (You seem to be hungry). (2) "avoir l’air de" + noun: "Il a l’air d’un homme bien" (He looks like a good man). In questions it can sound slightly skeptical/ironic: "J’ai l’air de… ?" = "Do I look like…?"
target_language_example: On a l’air d’être perdus.
native_language_example: We look/seem lost.

meaning: to seem to be doing okay / to look like things are going fine.
additional_notes: Used with **avoir l'air de** (“to seem”) + **aller** (“to be doing/going”). Most often you’ll see it in **avoir l’air d’aller (mieux)** = “to seem to be doing (better)”. It can sound a bit vague/understated (things seem OK, nothing obviously wrong). Common in different tenses: **Elle a l’air d’aller** (present), **Ça avait l’air d’aller** (imperfect: “it seemed to be going fine”). In speech, **Tu as** often becomes **T’as**: **T’as l’air d’aller mieux.**
target_language_example: Après l’opération, il avait l’air d’aller mieux.
native_language_example: After the operation, he seemed to be doing better.

meaning: to seem/appear to be doing well (to look like you’re fine).
additional_notes: Used with the verb « avoir »: « avoir l’air de + infinitive » = “to seem/appear to…”. Here « aller bien » means “to be well / to be doing well.” Common in statements and questions: « J’ai l’air d’aller bien ? » = “Do I look okay?” « T’as l’air… » is an informal spoken contraction of « Tu as l’air… ».
target_language_example: Tu as l’air d’aller bien aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You look like you’re doing well today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir" (often in questions or with "tu as / j’ai") as in "avoir l’air d’un/une + noun" = "to look like / seem like a + noun." In speech, it often comes across as “Do I look like a…?” or “You look like a…”.
target_language_example: Tu as l’air d’un touriste avec cette carte.
native_language_example: You look like a tourist with that map.

meaning: to seem to; to look like (you’re) …
additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir: "avoir l’air de" + infinitive to say someone seems to be doing something (based on how it looks). Tenses change: "a l’air de" (seems), "avait l’air de" (seemed). Often used with "bien" (well): "avoir l’air de bien + infinitive".
target_language_example: Il a l’air de comprendre.
native_language_example: He seems to understand.

additional_notes: Used with "avoir l’air" to ask about someone’s appearance or how something will seem/come across: « J’ai l’air de quoi ? » = “What do I look like?” Often rhetorical and can sound annoyed or indignant, like “What do you take me for?” In the future: « Ça aura l’air de quoi ? » = “What will it look like?”
target_language_example: Avec cette coiffure, j’ai l’air de quoi ?
native_language_example: With this haircut, what do I look like?

meaning: to look well / to look in good shape.
additional_notes: Used with **avoir l’air** (“to seem/to look”): **Tu as l’air en forme** = “You look well/fit.” It comments on someone’s appearance/energy (not literally “air”). **En forme** is invariable (doesn’t change for gender/number).
target_language_example: Après tes vacances, tu as l’air en forme !
native_language_example: After your vacation, you look great!

meaning: to look/seem to be in great shape (very fit, full of energy).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir l’air" (= to look/seem): "Tu as l’air en pleine forme." Often said as a compliment or when someone seems energetic/healthy. "T’as" is the informal spoken contraction of "Tu as"; "Vous avez" is more formal or plural.
target_language_example: Après tes vacances, tu as l’air en pleine forme !
native_language_example: After your vacation, you look like you’re in great shape!

additional_notes: Definite form of "amour" (love), used for love in general or a specific love in context. Common in expressions like "de l'amour" (some love) and "Il y a de l'amour dans l'air" (There’s love in the air). Note: "faire l'amour" means "to make love" (to have sex).
target_language_example: Pour moi, l'amour, c'est du respect.
native_language_example: For me, love is respect.

additional_notes: A very strong, romantic expression for the person you love most (often your life partner). Use with the verb être: « Tu es l'amour de ma vie » (present) / « Tu étais l'amour de ma vie » (past, often implying the relationship is over or the person has died). Can also be used alone as an emotional phrase: « L'amour de ma vie. »
target_language_example: Je sais que tu es l'amour de ma vie.
native_language_example: I know you’re the love of my life.

additional_notes: Refers to the time from after lunch until evening. Often used with expressions like "cet après-midi" (this afternoon) or "tout l'après-midi" (all afternoon). It can also be used as a short question to confirm a time: "L'après-midi ?" (In the afternoon?).
target_language_example: On se voit l'après-midi ?
native_language_example: Shall we see each other in the afternoon?

additional_notes: “L’argent” is the general word for money in French (cash, funds, wealth). It often appears with the definite article “l’” because “argent” starts with a vowel sound. Common in phrases like “avoir besoin de l’argent” (to need money) and “prendre l’argent” (to take the money).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas assez d'argent pour acheter ce billet.
native_language_example: I don't have enough money to buy this ticket.

additional_notes: Used for the time when the sun is just rising. Common in set phrases like « jusqu'à l'aube » (“until dawn”). Figuratively, it can mean “the beginning” of something: « l'aube d'une ère nouvelle » (“the dawn of a new era”).
target_language_example: On partira à l'aube pour éviter la circulation.
native_language_example: We’ll leave at dawn to avoid traffic.

meaning: “the other” (the other person/thing), or “the other day/last time” in some time expressions.
additional_notes: Commonly used to point to an alternative or second item/person: « l’autre gars » = “the other guy,” « l’autre partie » = “the other part.” With time words like « l’autre fois / l’autre soir », it often means “the other day/night” or “last time/night” (a previous occasion). Can also appear in « dans l’autre sens » = “the other way/around.”
target_language_example: Tu peux prendre l’un, je prends l’autre.
native_language_example: You can take one, I'll take the other.

meaning: “the other” (the other person/thing), or “the other day/last time” in some time expressions.
additional_notes: Commonly used to point to an alternative or second item/person: « l’autre gars » = “the other guy,” « l’autre partie » = “the other part.” With time words like « l’autre fois / l’autre soir », it often means “the other day/night” or “last time/night” (a previous occasion). Can also appear in « dans l’autre sens » = “the other way/around.”
target_language_example: Tu peux prendre l’un, je prends l’autre.
native_language_example: You can take one, I'll take the other.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: "l'" is the shortened form of "la" used before a vowel sound (la eau → l'eau). Used for water in general or a specific body of water, depending on context (e.g., "L'eau est chaude" = the water is warm). Common in phrases like "sur l'eau" (on the water), "dans l'eau" (in the water), "de l'eau" (some water).
target_language_example: Je bois de l'eau, mais l'eau ici n'est pas très froide.
native_language_example: I drink water, but the water here isn’t very cold.

additional_notes: Often used for what you’re thinking about or what comes to you mentally: « venir à l’esprit » = “to come to mind”; « s’occuper l’esprit » = “to keep your mind busy / take your mind off things.” With « l’ » because « esprit » starts with a vowel sound.
target_language_example: Je n’arrive pas à me sortir ça de l’esprit.
native_language_example: I can’t get that out of my mind.

meaning: the time (on the clock); the hour.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what time it is or a specific time. Common in questions like « Quelle heure est-il ? » (What time is it?) and « Tu as l’heure ? » (Do you have the time?). « Oublier l’heure » means to lose track of time.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, vous avez l'heure ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have the time?

meaning: “the time for / the hour of” (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Used to say it’s time for something: commonly with meals (l’heure du déjeuner/dîner/thé), but also with events or moments (l’heure du changement, l’heure du couvre-feu). Often appears in phrases like C’est bientôt/presque l’heure du… (“It’s soon/almost time for…”) or À l’heure du… (“at … time”).
target_language_example: C'est l'heure du départ.
native_language_example: It's time to leave.

additional_notes: Used with the definite article (la → l’ before a vowel sound): l’histoire. In everyday conversation, it often means “the story” (what happened, the whole situation): Je connais toute l’histoire = “I know the whole story.” It can also mean “history” as a subject or the past in general: l’histoire de France = “the history of France.”
target_language_example: Tu peux me raconter l'histoire ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me the story?

additional_notes: "L'" is the shortened form of "le" before a vowel sound (homme starts with a silent h). It can refer to a specific man (e.g., "Est-ce l'homme que vous avez vu ?" = "Is he the man you saw?") or to humans in general in formal contexts (e.g., "la santé de l'homme" = "human health").
target_language_example: L'homme que j'ai rencontré hier est médecin.
native_language_example: The man I met yesterday is a doctor.

meaning: the right person for the job (in this situation).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is exactly the person needed to handle a particular situation or problem. It’s often a compliment about being capable, skilled, or dependable under pressure. Even though it uses the masculine word *homme*, it can be used generically; you may also hear *la femme de la situation* when talking about a woman.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : elle est l’homme de la situation.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: she’s the right person for the job.

additional_notes: “L’” is the shortened form of “le” before a vowel sound: l’hôpital. Often used with prepositions like “à l’hôpital” (at/in the hospital) or “de l’hôpital” (from the hospital).
target_language_example: Il est à l'hôpital depuis hier.
native_language_example: He has been in the hospital since yesterday.

additional_notes: "L'hôtel" is "le hôtel" shortened to avoid two vowel sounds in a row (le + hôtel → l'hôtel). Used to refer to a specific hotel already known in the conversation (e.g., asking about it: « Et l'hôtel ? » = « And the hotel? »). Often appears in phrases like « l'entrée de l'hôtel » (the hotel entrance) or « les employés de l'hôtel » (the hotel’s employees).
target_language_example: Où est l'hôtel ?
native_language_example: Where is the hotel?

additional_notes: Very often used in the set phrase **avoir l’impression (que + clause / de + infinitive)**: *J’ai l’impression que…* = “I have the impression that… / I feel like…”. With **en**: **J’en ai l’impression** (“That’s the impression I get / That’s what it seems like”), **Je n’en ai pas l’impression** (“I don’t get that impression / It doesn’t feel like that”). It can also mean “print/printing” in other contexts, but in these examples it means a subjective sense or perception.
target_language_example: J’ai l’impression qu’il va pleuvoir.
native_language_example: I have a feeling it’s going to rain.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like vivre, profiter de, or se concentrer sur to mean focusing on what’s happening now. Very common in the phrase « l’instant présent » (“the present moment / the here and now”).
target_language_example: Essaie de profiter de l'instant, sans penser au reste.
native_language_example: Try to enjoy the moment, without thinking about the rest.

additional_notes:
Often used with prepositions:
- « de l’intérieur » = from the inside (e.g., a door locked from inside)
- « à l’intérieur » = inside (location)
Can also be used more abstractly: « Ça vient de l’intérieur » = It comes from within (from inside you/the group/the system).
target_language_example: La porte est verrouillée de l’intérieur.
native_language_example: The door is locked from the inside.

additional_notes: Used for orderliness (organization, maintaining order) and for an order as a command. Common phrases: « donner l’ordre » = to give the order; « recevoir l’ordre » = to receive the order; « qui a donné l’ordre ? » = who gave the order? Often appears with other abstract nouns: « l’ordre et la paix » (order and peace).
target_language_example: Le capitaine a donné l’ordre de partir.
native_language_example: The captain gave the order to leave.

additional_notes: Contraction of **le + un**. Common in patterns like **l'un ou l'autre** (“one or the other”), **l'un des...** (“one of the...”), and **ni l'un ni l'autre** (“neither one nor the other”). Refers to one person/thing in a group, often contrasted with **l'autre** (“the other”).
target_language_example: L'un de mes amis parle anglais.
native_language_example: One of my friends speaks English.

meaning: "one of them" (referring to a masculine/mixed group).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is a member of a group previously mentioned. It agrees with the group: use "l'une d'entre elles" for a feminine group; "l'un(e) d'entre nous" = one of us; "l'un(e) d'entre vous" = one of you (plural/formal). Often follows "être": "Je suis l'un d'entre eux."
target_language_example: Je pense que Paul est l'un d'entre eux.
native_language_example: I think Paul is one of them.

meaning: one of them (one of those people/men).
additional_notes: Used to pick out a single person from a group. It agrees with the gender/number of the group: "l'un d'eux" = one of them (masculine or mixed group), "l'une d'elles" = one of them (feminine group). Common after "c'est", "je suis", "tu es" ("It's/I'm/you're one of them").
target_language_example: Je pense que l'un d'eux a menti.
native_language_example: I think one of them lied.

additional_notes: Used to single out one member of a group: l’un de nous (one of us), l’un de vos employés (one of your employees). It agrees with the noun: l’un de + plural group for masculine/mixed, and l’une de + plural group for feminine. Often followed by a plural noun or pronoun (nous, vous, eux/elles).
target_language_example: L’une de mes amies habite à Lyon.
native_language_example: One of my friends lives in Lyon.

additional_notes: Used when two (or more) people/things do something to/for one another. It often appears after verbs that require the preposition « de », like « prendre soin de » → « prendre soin l’un de l’autre » (“take care of each other”). With feminine subjects you may hear « l’une de l’autre ».
target_language_example: Ils se parlent rarement, mais ils ont besoin l’un de l’autre.
native_language_example: They rarely talk, but they need each other.

additional_notes: Refers to school as an institution or the place students go. Common in set phrases like "à l'école" (at school), "de l'école" (from school), "rentrer de l'école" (to come home from school), and in questions like "Et l'école ?" (How’s school?/And school?). Also used for school-related things: "le journal de l'école" (the school newspaper).
target_language_example: Je rentre de l'école à cinq heures.
native_language_example: I’m coming home from school at five o’clock.

meaning: “has/have him / her / it / them” (direct object pronoun + “a” = “has”).
additional_notes: Contraction of **le / la / les** → **l’** before a vowel, + **a** (from **avoir**) in the **passé composé**. It replaces a previously mentioned direct object: *Il a vu Marie → Il l’a vue.* With **avoir**, the past participle can agree with the direct object when it comes before the verb: *Il l’a vue* (Marie), *Il l’a aimé* (Pierre), *Il les a vues* (les filles).
target_language_example: Je l’ai déjà fait.
native_language_example: I’ve already done it.

meaning: “did he … it?” / “has he … it?” (question form with “he”).
additional_notes: Used in formal/written French question inversion: object pronoun **l’** (= **le** or **la**, “it/him/her”) + auxiliary **a** (“has”) + **-t-** (extra sound for pronunciation) + **il** (“he”). It’s followed by a past participle: **L’a-t-il fait ?** (“Did he do it?”). When **l’** stands for **la**, the past participle can agree: **Où l’a-t-il trouvée ?** (“Where did he find it/her?”).
target_language_example: Pourquoi l’a-t-il appelé ?
native_language_example: Why did he call him/her?

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of *dire* (“to say”) with a direct object pronoun. **l’** is the shortened form of **le** or **la** (it can mean “it,” “him,” “her,” or “that,” depending on context) and it comes before the auxiliary: **il/elle l’a dit** = “he/she said it.” Often used in phrases like **C’est lui qui l’a dit** (“He’s the one who said it”) or **Comme il l’a dit** (“As he said”).
target_language_example: Je te l’ai dit hier.
native_language_example: I told you yesterday.

additional_notes: Passé composé of faire with a direct object pronoun: l' = "it" (or "him" in other contexts), a = "has" (avoir), fait = "done/made". Used to say someone did something that’s already understood from context. With elle/il/on: « Elle l’a fait », « Il l’a fait », « On l’a fait ».
target_language_example: Tu pensais qu'il ne le ferait pas, mais il l'a fait.
native_language_example: You thought he wouldn’t do it, but he did it.

additional_notes: Very common spoken form of "ne ... pas": in casual speech, "ne" is often dropped ("Elle l'a pas dit" = "Elle ne l'a pas dit"). "l'" is the direct object pronoun "le" ("it") before "a". With an indirect object pronoun, you can say: "Elle me l'a pas dit" = "She didn't tell me (it)". In questions: "Il te l'a pas dit ?" = "He didn't tell you?".
target_language_example: Je te l'ai pas dit parce que j'ai oublié.
native_language_example: I didn’t tell you because I forgot.

additional_notes: This is the negative passé composé of faire with a direct object pronoun l’ (= le or la, “it/him/her”). It’s a very common spoken form where the first part of negation (ne) is dropped: Elle l’a pas fait = Elle ne l’a pas fait. In writing or formal speech, include ne: Il ne l’a pas fait.
target_language_example: Désolé, je l’ai pas fait hier.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t do it yesterday.

additional_notes: "l’" is the shortened form of "le" or "la" (it/him/her) placed before the verb. It’s used when the next word starts with a vowel sound, so "le/la ai" becomes "l’ai". Very common in the passé composé ("je l’ai vu" = I saw him/it; literally "I have seen him/it"). "l’" can refer to a person or a thing; the gender/meaning comes from context.
target_language_example: Je l’ai déjà fait.
native_language_example: I’ve already done it.

additional_notes: This is part of the past tense (passé composé) of **dire** (“to say/tell”) with a direct-object pronoun: **l’** = **le/la** (“it / him / her”) + **ai dit** (“said/told”). Most often you’ll see it with a subject, e.g. **je l’ai dit** (“I said it / I told him/her”), **tu l’as dit**, etc. **l’** is used before a vowel sound (instead of **le** or **la**).
target_language_example: Je l’ai dit hier à Marie.
native_language_example: I told Marie yesterday.

meaning: "I already said it" / "I’ve already said it."
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve already mentioned something and don’t want to repeat it. "l’" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (short for "le" or "la"), placed before the verb: "je l’ai dit" = "I said it." Often appears with context words like "Je te/vous l’ai déjà dit" (I already told you).
target_language_example: Je te l’ai déjà dit : je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I already told you: I can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: Passé composé of faire: j’ai fait = “I did/made.” The l’ is a direct-object pronoun meaning “it/him/her,” placed before the auxiliary verb (ai). Often used for emphasis with c’est moi qui…: C’est moi qui l’ai fait = “I’m the one who did it.”
target_language_example: Je suis désolé, je l’ai fait sans réfléchir.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I did it without thinking.

additional_notes: Common informal spoken form of **je ne l’ai pas** (the **ne** is often dropped in speech). **l’** is a direct-object pronoun meaning “it” (or “him”), used before the verb: **je l’ai pas vu** = “I didn’t see him/it.” With feminine objects/people you may see agreement on the past participle: **je l’ai pas vue** (“I didn’t see her”).
target_language_example: Désolé, je l’ai pas entendu.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t hear it.

additional_notes: Passé composé of trouver: « j’ai trouvé » = “I found / I’ve found.” « l’ » is a direct-object pronoun replacing something already mentioned (le/la), so it means “it” (or sometimes “him/her”). With a direct-object pronoun placed before the verb, the past participle can agree: « je l’ai trouvée » (for a feminine object).
target_language_example: Je l’ai trouvé dans mon sac.
native_language_example: I found it in my bag.

meaning: "(I) saw him/her/it" or "(I) have seen him/her/it."
additional_notes: This is part of the passé composé: **je + l’ (le/la) + ai + vu**. **l’** is a direct object pronoun meaning “him / her / it” (it replaces a noun mentioned earlier). It comes before the auxiliary verb **ai**. **Vu** agrees only if the direct object is **before** the verb and you can identify its gender/number (e.g., *Je l’ai vue* if it’s feminine).
target_language_example: Je l’ai vu hier au café.
native_language_example: I saw him/her/it yesterday at the café.

additional_notes: "l'" is a shortened form of "le" or "la" and means "him", "her", or "it". "aimais" is the imperfect (past) form of "aimer" for "tu". Often appears in reported speech with "que": "Elle a dit que tu l'aimais" = "She said that you loved/liked him/her."
target_language_example: Je pensais que tu l'aimais beaucoup.
native_language_example: I thought you liked/loved him/her a lot.

additional_notes: "l'" is the shortened form of "le" or "la" (him/her/it) used before a verb starting with a vowel sound, like "aime". The object pronoun comes before the verb in French: "Elle l'aime" = “She loves/likes him/her/it.” In negatives, "ne … pas" goes around the verb, while "l'" stays before it: "Elle ne l'aime pas".
target_language_example: Je l'aime beaucoup, mais je ne l'aime plus comme avant.
native_language_example: I like/love him/her/it a lot, but I don’t like/love him/her/it anymore like before.

meaning: likes him/her/it (has a positive feeling about).
additional_notes: “L’” is a direct object pronoun meaning “him / her / it” (it replaces the person or thing being liked). “Aimer bien” usually means “to like” (friendly/positive), not “to love” — “aimer” without “bien” can mean “to love.” Often used to soften the feeling: you like someone, you get along with them, you find them nice.
target_language_example: Je l’aime bien, mais je ne le connais pas très bien.
native_language_example: I like him/her, but I don’t know him/her very well.

additional_notes: Used with **tu**: **Tu l’aimes ?** = “Do you love/like him/her/it?” **l’** is the shortened form of **le / la** (direct object pronoun) before a vowel: **tu l’aimes**. In negatives, it becomes **tu ne l’aimes pas** (“you don’t like/love him/her/it”), and **plus** means “anymore” (**tu ne l’aimes plus ?**).
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu l’aimes autant ?
native_language_example: Why do you like/love him/her/it so much?

meaning: to call him/her/it; to name him/her/it.
additional_notes: "l'" is the direct object pronoun "le" (him/it) or "la" (her/it), shortened before a vowel or silent h. So "l'appeler" means "to call him/her/it" (e.g., on the phone) or "to call/name him/her/it" (i.e., what you will name something). The verb tense changes the meaning in time: "je dois l'appeler" (I have to call him/her), "je vais l'appeler" (I’m going to call him/her).
target_language_example: Je vais l'appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to call him/her tonight.

meaning: "you have it / you did it" ("l'" = it/him/her + "as" = you have).
additional_notes: Contraction of the direct object pronoun **l’** (short for **le/la**, meaning “it / him / her”) + **as** ("you have," from *avoir*). It’s very common in the **passé composé**: **tu l’as + past participle** (e.g., *Tu l’as dit* = “You said it”). The **l’** goes before the auxiliary verb (*as*).
target_language_example: Tu l'as déjà fait ?
native_language_example: Have you already done it?

additional_notes: Used in questions with inversion: object pronoun + verb + subject (… as-tu). Here, l’ is the shortened form of le or la (“it/him/her”) placed before the auxiliary avoir: l’as-tu fait ? = “Have you done it?”; l’as-tu vue ? = “Have you seen her/it?” (vue agrees with la).
target_language_example: L’as-tu déjà envoyé ?
native_language_example: Have you already sent it?

additional_notes: From dire (to say/tell): l' = “it” (direct object pronoun), as = “have” (tu form of avoir), dit = “said/told” (past participle). Used in phrases like « Tu me l'as dit » (You told me) or « Qui te l'a dit ? » (Who told you?). Agreement: with tu → « l'as », with il/elle/on → « l'a », with vous → « l'avez », etc.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, tu me l'as déjà dit.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you already told me.

meaning: "you did it" / "you made (him/her/it/them)" (passé composé of faire).
additional_notes: It’s made of the direct-object pronoun "le/la/les" → "l'" (it/him/her/them) + "as" (you have) + "fait" (done/made). The exact meaning depends on what "l'" refers to: "Tu l'as fait" = "You did it"; "Tu l'as fait venir ?" = "Did you have him/her come?"
target_language_example: Je sais que tu l'as fait exprès.
native_language_example: I know you did it on purpose.

additional_notes: Contraction of the direct object pronoun “le / la / l’” (“him / her / it”) + “avais” (imparfait of avoir: “I had”). Used when the thing/person is already known from context: e.g., “Je l’avais” = “I had it,” “Je ne l’avais jamais vu(e)” = “I had never seen him/her/it.” If the object is feminine and in front of the verb, the past participle agrees: “Je ne l’avais jamais vue” (I had never seen her/it [fem.]).
target_language_example: Je ne l’avais pas reconnu au début.
native_language_example: I hadn’t recognized him/her/it at first.

additional_notes: This is the past perfect (plus-que-parfait) of **dire** with **avoir**: **j’avais dit** = “I had said.” The **l’** is a direct object pronoun (short for **le / la**) meaning “it/that/him,” referring to something already known from context. Often used in phrases like **Je te l’avais dit ! / Je vous l’avais dit !** = “I told you so!” (i.e., I had said it before).
target_language_example: Je te l’avais dit : il allait être en retard.
native_language_example: I told you so: he was going to be late.

additional_notes: Contraction of **le/la** → **l’** ("it" / "him" / "her") + **avez** ("you have", **vous** form of *avoir*). Very common with the **passé composé**: *Vous l’avez vu* ("You saw it/him") and with a second pronoun: *Vous me l’avez dit* ("You told me"). The past participle may agree with **l’** when it stands for **la** (feminine): *Vous l’avez choisie*.
target_language_example: Vous l’avez déjà vu ?
native_language_example: Have you seen it/him already?

additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of "vous l'avez ..." (you have it/him/her ...). It combines: "l'" (short for "le" or "la" = him/it or her/it) + "avez" (you have) + "-vous" (you, formal/plural). Used with the passé composé: l' + avoir + past participle (e.g., "L'avez-vous vu ?" = Have you seen him/it?). The "l'" refers to something already known from context; for a person it matches their gender (le/la) and becomes l' before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: L'avez-vous déjà essayé ?
native_language_example: Have you tried it already?

additional_notes: Inversion question form: "Avez-vous vu…?" = "Have you seen…?" The "l'" is a direct-object pronoun meaning "him" or "it" (short for "le"), referring to a previously mentioned masculine noun/person; with a feminine referent you’d say "l’avez-vous vue ?" (from "la"). Common in formal speech/writing; in everyday conversation you often hear "Vous l’avez vu ?" or "Vous l’avez vu récemment ?"
target_language_example: Je cherche mon sac : l’avez-vous vu ?
native_language_example: I’m looking for my bag—have you seen it?

meaning: to take him/her to the hospital.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "emmener" (to take/bring someone along, usually by going somewhere with them) + "à l'hôpital" (to the hospital). "l'" is a direct object pronoun meaning "him" or "her" (instead of repeating a name). You can change it: "l'emmener" (him/her), "les emmener" (them), "m'emmener" (me), "t'emmener" (you).
target_language_example: Si elle ne va pas mieux, on va l'emmener à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: If she doesn’t get better, we’re going to take her to the hospital.

additional_notes: Used when you’re pleased/relieved to hear someone say something (often after waiting for them to admit or confirm it). The pronoun “l’” (= “it/that”) refers to what was just mentioned or is understood from context. Common with feelings + “de”: “Heureux/contente de vous/te l’entendre dire”, or with wanting emphasis: “Je veux te l’entendre dire” (= I want to hear you say it, personally).
target_language_example: Je suis soulagé de vous l’entendre dire.
native_language_example: I’m relieved to hear you say it.

additional_notes: “L’” is the shortened form of le or la ("him/it" or "her/it") placed before the verb. “Ont” is the 3rd person plural of avoir (“they have”) and is often used as the auxiliary in the passé composé: ils l’ont dit = “they said it.” With a direct object placed before the verb (like l’), the past participle may agree in gender/number: ils l’ont trouvée (found her/it [fem.]) vs ils l’ont trouvé (masc.).
target_language_example: Pourquoi ils ne l’ont pas fait ?
native_language_example: Why didn’t they do it?

meaning: “to be it/that” (to be so; to be in that state).
additional_notes: Used with the verb être when l’ replaces a previously mentioned adjective or description (often something like prêt, d’accord, occupé, content, etc.). It avoids repeating the adjective: « Tu es prêt ? — Oui, je vais l’être. »
target_language_example: Tu es prêt ? Oui, je vais l’être.
native_language_example: Are you ready? Yes, I’m going to be.

additional_notes: “La pêche” most often means the activity of fishing (especially in phrases like “aller à la pêche” = to go fishing). It can also mean the fruit “a peach” in food contexts. Context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Dimanche, on va à la pêche.
native_language_example: On Sunday, we're going fishing.

additional_notes: Refers to a female monarch (a queen regnant) or the wife of a king (queen consort). Often used with set phrases like « Vive la Reine ! » (“Long live the Queen!”) or « Que Dieu sauve/protège la Reine ! » (“God save/protect the Queen!”). Capitalizing « Reine » is common when talking about a specific queen as a title.
target_language_example: La Reine arrive au palais ce soir.
native_language_example: The Queen is arriving at the palace tonight.

meaning: “the Witch of the moors/heathland” (a name or nickname).
additional_notes: Used as a (usually capitalized) title/name for a specific witch character (“the Witch of the moors”), often in stories. You can exclaim it or say it as a question (like in the examples). "des landes" means “of the moors/heathland.”
target_language_example: On raconte que la Sorcière des landes apparaît quand il fait nuit.
native_language_example: They say the Witch of the moors appears when it’s night.

additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: in sports/play it’s a ball ("Lance la balle !"); with weapons/shooting it can mean a bullet ("La balle atteignit sa cible"). Often used as "une balle" (a ball / a bullet).
target_language_example: La balle a rebondi contre le mur.
native_language_example: The ball bounced off the wall.

additional_notes: Used for a place/company that handles money (accounts, loans, cash). In directions you might ask for it (la banque la plus proche). Not to be confused with other meanings of English “bank” (river bank, etc.).
target_language_example: Je dois aller à la banque pour retirer de l’argent.
native_language_example: I have to go to the bank to withdraw some money.

meaning: the battle; a fight (often a war battle).
additional_notes: Usually refers to a specific battle (often in war/history), but it can also be used more generally for a major fight or struggle. Common with verbs like gagner/perdre (to win/lose) and expressions like lors de la bataille (during the battle). In French you normally keep the article: la bataille.
target_language_example: Ils ont perdu la bataille, mais pas la guerre.
native_language_example: They lost the battle, but not the war.

additional_notes: A feminine noun used for a public or school library building or its collection of books. Don’t confuse with English “library” in the sense of a software library; in French that would usually be "une bibliothèque" only in a figurative sense, and in tech you’ll more often see "une librairie" or "une bibliothèque logicielle" depending on context.
target_language_example: Je vais à la bibliothèque pour emprunter un livre.
native_language_example: I'm going to the library to borrow a book.

additional_notes: A common drink noun; feminine singular (la), so you say: une bière (a beer), de la bière (some beer). In restaurants/bars you can order: « Une bière, s’il vous plaît. »
target_language_example: Je voudrais une bière, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a beer, please.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to mean “the right/correct” one: la bonne direction (the right direction), la bonne réponse (the correct answer), la bonne chose à faire (the right thing to do). It agrees with the noun’s gender/number: le bon (masc. sing.), la bonne (fem. sing.), les bons / les bonnes (plural).
target_language_example: Je crois que c’est la bonne solution.
native_language_example: I think it’s the right solution.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific piece of positive news. Very common with verbs like annoncer (to announce), dire (to tell), and apprendre (to learn/hear). Often followed by a clause introduced by que: « la bonne nouvelle, c’est que… ».
target_language_example: J’ai une bonne nouvelle : on part en vacances demain !
native_language_example: I have good news: we’re leaving on vacation tomorrow!

additional_notes: Used for the physical mouth (speaking, eating, kissing): « sur la bouche » = on the mouth/lips. Common expressions include « avoir la bouche sèche » (to have a dry mouth) and the idiom « Vous m’enlevez les mots de la bouche » (“You took the words right out of my mouth,” i.e., you said exactly what I was about to say).
target_language_example: Ouvre la bouche, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Open your mouth, please.

additional_notes: Refers to a bottle/container for liquids (milk, water, wine, etc.). In context, "cacher la bouteille" means to hide the bottle (often implying an alcoholic bottle). Plural: "les bouteilles".
target_language_example: Je vais acheter une bouteille d’eau.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy a bottle of water.

meaning: the box; the can; the container.
additional_notes: Common everyday noun for a physical box or container. It can also mean a tin/can (e.g., une boîte de conserve = a can of food). In other contexts, "la boîte" can mean "the company" (informal) or "a nightclub," but the examples here are the literal "box" sense.
target_language_example: J’ai mis les clés dans la boîte.
native_language_example: I put the keys in the box.

additional_notes: Used for the box where you put or receive mail. It can be a private mailbox at someone’s home or a public mailbox in the street. Often used with verbs like mettre/déposer une lettre (to put/drop a letter), relever/vider (to empty/collect), and with location questions: Où est la boîte aux lettres ?
target_language_example: J'ai mis la lettre dans la boîte aux lettres.
native_language_example: I put the letter in the mailbox.

additional_notes: La caisse can mean a physical container (a box/crate) that you can carry and put things in (e.g., books). In shops/supermarkets, la caisse is the checkout area/cash register, so faire la queue devant la caisse means “to line up at the checkout.” Context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la caisse, j’ai oublié mon porte-monnaie.
native_language_example: Meet me at the checkout; I forgot my wallet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about rural places (fields, villages, farms), often in contrast with the city (la ville). With prepositions you’ll often hear: « à la campagne » = in the countryside; « de la campagne » = from the countryside / rural.
target_language_example: Le week-end, on va souvent à la campagne pour se reposer.
native_language_example: On weekends, we often go to the countryside to rest.

additional_notes: Used for a device that records photos or video (a real camera, a phone camera, or a video/TV camera). Common with verbs like allumer/éteindre (turn on/off) or couper (cut/turn off), and in expressions like à travers la caméra (“through the camera”). Feminine noun: la caméra.
target_language_example: Tu peux allumer la caméra, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you turn on the camera, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the main city of a country or region (often where the government is). Common patterns: « la capitale de + [country/region] » and « aller/venir à la capitale ». The city may be clear from context (e.g., in France, « la capitale » usually means Paris).
target_language_example: Nous allons visiter la capitale demain.
native_language_example: We’re going to visit the capital tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to name the main city of a country/region. Structure: « la capitale de + [country/region] ». With a feminine country you usually get « de la » (la Finlande), with a masculine country « du » (le Japon), with a plural country « des » (les États-Unis), and with a vowel/h mute « de l’ » (l’Italie).
target_language_example: Lisbonne est la capitale du Portugal.
native_language_example: Lisbon is the capital of Portugal.

additional_notes: Used to name a capital city. "du" = "de + le" and is used before masculine singular nouns (often masculine country names like le Japon, le Sénégal, le Burundi). For feminine countries, use "la capitale de la" (ex: la capitale de la France). For plural names, use "la capitale des" (ex: les États-Unis).
target_language_example: La capitale du Canada est Ottawa.
native_language_example: The capital of Canada is Ottawa.

meaning: the card; the menu; the map.
additional_notes: The meaning depends on context. In shops/restaurants, "la carte" often means a payment card ("payer par carte", "accepter la carte"). In restaurants, "la carte" can also mean the menu; "la carte des vins" is the wine list. In other contexts, "la carte" can mean a map (e.g., "une carte routière").
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, on peut avoir la carte, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can we have the menu, please?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "avoir" (J'ai la chair de poule / J'en ai la chair de poule) or "donner" (Ça me donne la chair de poule / Tu me donnes la chair de poule) to express that something makes you get goosebumps.
target_language_example: Quand j'entends cette chanson, j'ai la chair de poule.
native_language_example: When I hear that song, I get goosebumps.

additional_notes: Common word for a (usually simple) chair. Used with prepositions like sur (on), sous (under), and sometimes dans (in) depending on context. Note: English "chaise" usually refers to a lounge chair (as in "chaise longue"), so it can be misleading—French "chaise" is typically just a regular chair.
target_language_example: Le sac est sur la chaise.
native_language_example: The bag is on the chair.

meaning: heat; warmth (from the weather, sun, or something hot).
additional_notes: Used to talk about physical heat in general (often the heat of the sun or hot weather): la chaleur du soleil, la chaleur de l’été. It can also describe the warmth given off by something (e.g., a fire) or the warmth of a place (la chaleur de la pièce).
target_language_example: Je n’aime pas trop la chaleur en été.
native_language_example: I don’t really like the heat in summer.

meaning: the bedroom; a room (e.g., in a house or hotel).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a bedroom in everyday French, but it can also refer to a room in general depending on context (especially in hotels: "une chambre" = a hotel room). Often used with prepositions like "dans la chambre" (in the room) and verbs like "donner sur" (to open onto/face).
target_language_example: J’ai réservé une chambre pour deux nuits.
native_language_example: I booked a room for two nights.

additional_notes: Used for luck in general (La chance est aveugle.) and for an opportunity (avoir la chance de + infinitive = 'to have the chance to…'). Common expressions: avoir de la chance ('to be lucky') and saisir la chance ('to seize the opportunity').
target_language_example: J’ai eu la chance de te rencontrer.
native_language_example: I was lucky to meet you.

meaning: the chance to; the luck to (be able to).
additional_notes: Used to talk about having an opportunity or being lucky enough to do something. Very common in the pattern "avoir la chance de + infinitive" (e.g., "J'ai eu la chance de…" = "I had the chance/luck to…"). It can also appear as "C'est la chance de…" meaning "It's the chance of…".
target_language_example: J'ai eu la chance de rencontrer le directeur.
native_language_example: I had the chance (was lucky enough) to meet the director.

additional_notes:
Used to form a superlative with a noun: 
- feminine singular: la chose la plus + adjective (la chose la plus importante)
- masculine singular: la chose la plus + adjective in masculine form (la chose la plus étrange)
Often followed by context like au monde (in the world) or de ma vie (of my life). In questions: Quelle est la chose la plus + adjective + que... ? (What is the most ... thing that...?).
target_language_example: C'est la chose la plus drôle que j'aie vue cette semaine.
native_language_example: It's the funniest thing I've seen this week.

additional_notes: Used for a physical target (shooting, archery, aiming at something) or a figurative one (the goal, or the intended audience in marketing: « la cible » = “target audience”). Often appears with verbs like « viser » (to aim at), « toucher » (to hit), « atteindre » (to reach).
target_language_example: Je n'arrive pas à viser la cible.
native_language_example: I can’t manage to aim at the target.

meaning: traffic; road traffic (the flow of vehicles).
additional_notes: Often refers to how heavy or light traffic is (Il y a de la circulation / la circulation est faible). Used in set phrases like accident de la circulation (traffic accident) and fermé/ouvert à la circulation (closed/open to traffic). Can also mean traffic rules: les règles de la circulation.
target_language_example: À cause de la circulation, on est arrivés en retard.
native_language_example: Because of the traffic, we arrived late.

meaning: the classroom; the class (group of students).
additional_notes: Usually refers either to the physical room where students learn ("dans la classe", "entrer dans la classe") or to the group of students as a whole ("toute la classe", "la classe a été divisée en groupes"). Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Toute la classe écoute le professeur.
native_language_example: The whole class is listening to the teacher.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a physical key (often used with "de": "la clé de la porte" = the key to/for the door). Figuratively, it can mean the key point, clue, or solution to a problem: "la clé de cette affaire" = the key to this case/matter.
target_language_example: Je n’ai plus la clé, je l’ai perdue.
native_language_example: I don’t have the key anymore; I lost it.

additional_notes: A feminine noun used for a natural rise in the land (smaller than a mountain). Common with verbs like monter (go up), descendre (go down), and grimper (climb): monter/descendre/grimper la colline. Plural: les collines.
target_language_example: Il y a une petite colline derrière la maison.
native_language_example: There’s a small hill behind the house.

additional_notes: Refers to a physical rope or cord. Used with common action verbs like couper (to cut), lâcher (to let go of), attraper/saisir (to grab/hold). Note: in some contexts, "corde" can also mean a string on a musical instrument, but the examples here are about a rope.
target_language_example: Tiens bien la corde !
native_language_example: Hold the rope tight!

meaning: the court (especially a court of law).
additional_notes: In legal contexts, "la cour" refers to the court/judges as an institution (similar to “the court” in English). Depending on context, "la cour" can also mean a courtyard (e.g., "la cour de l’école") or a royal court (historical).
target_language_example: La cour rendra sa décision demain.
native_language_example: The court will deliver its decision tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used for sporting competitions where people (or vehicles) race (running race, bike race, etc.). In everyday speech, it can also mean “the shopping/errands,” but in these examples it clearly means a race (e.g., win the race = remporter/gagner la course; start of the race = le départ de la course).
target_language_example: Elle s'entraîne tous les jours pour la course de dimanche.
native_language_example: She trains every day for Sunday’s race.

additional_notes: Most often means “the kitchen” (a room): Nettoie la cuisine. It can also mean “cooking” as an activity (faire la cuisine = to cook) and “cuisine/food style” in general (la cuisine française). In restaurants, fermer la cuisine means “to close the kitchen” (stop serving food).
target_language_example: Je suis dans la cuisine, je fais la cuisine.
native_language_example: I’m in the kitchen, I’m cooking.

meaning: the date (day/month/year); also a deadline or scheduled day for an event.
additional_notes: Used to talk about when something happens (la date du mariage, la date du voyage) or to ask/check the date (La date ? / Regarde la date.). Common with prepositions: la date de + noun (the date of...), à la date du… (on the date of…).
target_language_example: On doit choisir la date de la réunion.
native_language_example: We have to choose the date of the meeting.

additional_notes: Used for the last allowed day/time to do something (submit an application, pay, register, etc.). Common verbs with it: rater / manquer / louper la date limite = “to miss the deadline.”
target_language_example: La date limite pour s'inscrire, c'est vendredi à midi.
native_language_example: The deadline to sign up is Friday at noon.

additional_notes: Feminine form of « le/la dernier(ère) ». Used when the noun is feminine (or implied as feminine): « la dernière feuille », « la dernière ligne », « la dernière réunion ». It can mean the final one in a sequence (“the last”) or the most recent one (“the last/previous meeting”). Often used alone when the noun is understood from context: « C’était la dernière. » = “It was the last one.”
target_language_example: Ne prends pas celle-ci, prends la dernière.
native_language_example: Don’t take this one—take the last one.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the most recent previous time something happened. Often appears with past tenses (e.g., « j'ai… ») or in questions (« …la dernière fois ? »). In « c'est la dernière fois », it often means “this is the last time” (it won’t happen again).
target_language_example: Je ne l’ai pas vu depuis la dernière fois qu’on s’est parlé.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen him since the last time we talked.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the most recent occasion when something happened. Common patterns: "la dernière fois que + verb" (e.g., "la dernière fois que je l’ai vu"), and in questions: "C’était quand la dernière fois que… ?" (= "When was the last time…?"). In the past, French often uses the imperfect in the main clause to set the scene: "C’était la dernière fois que je le voyais."
target_language_example: La dernière fois que je suis venu ici, il pleuvait.
native_language_example: The last time I came here, it was raining.

meaning: the difference (a distinction; what is not the same).
additional_notes: Used to compare two or more things: “voir la différence” = to notice the difference; “Quelle est la différence ?” = What’s the difference? It can also mean a difference in amount (e.g., the price difference).
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas la différence entre ces deux mots.
native_language_example: I don’t know the difference between these two words.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things: « la différence entre A et B ». Common with verbs like « faire la différence entre » (to tell the difference between) or « expliquer la différence entre » (to explain the difference between).
target_language_example: Peux-tu m’expliquer la différence entre « depuis » et « pendant » ?
native_language_example: Can you explain the difference between “depuis” and “pendant”?

additional_notes: Used to compare two things, usually in the pattern: « la différence entre X et Y ». Common questions: « Quelle est la différence entre … ? » (“What’s the difference between …?”). You may also hear « faire la différence entre X et Y » meaning “to tell/distinguish the difference between X and Y.”
target_language_example: Quelle est la différence entre un chat et un tigre ?
native_language_example: What’s the difference between a cat and a tiger?

additional_notes: Most often refers to a feeling of pain or suffering. Common with verbs like "avoir" (to have): "J’ai une douleur au dos" (I have back pain), "ressentir" (to feel), "apparaître" (to appear), and "partir" (to go away). Can also mean emotional pain: "la douleur de la perte" (the pain of loss).
target_language_example: Après quelques jours, la douleur a diminué.
native_language_example: After a few days, the pain decreased.

meaning: drugs (illegal drugs); drugs as a substance.
additional_notes: Usually refers to illegal narcotics in everyday speech, especially in contexts like trafficking, possession, or addiction. In French, it’s often used as a mass noun ("la drogue"), even when English would say "drugs."
target_language_example: La police a trouvé de la drogue dans la voiture.
native_language_example: The police found drugs in the car.

additional_notes: Used to talk about relatives as a group (your family, their family, etc.). Often appears in phrases like « dans la famille » (“in the family” / among the family) or « aide à la famille » (“family assistance/support”). The singular « la famille » can refer to the whole household or family unit.
target_language_example: On va passer le week-end avec la famille.
native_language_example: We’re going to spend the weekend with the family.

additional_notes: Means “the woman” in general, but in context it can also mean “the wife” (e.g., “la femme de votre frère” = “your brother’s wife”). It’s feminine singular: une femme = a woman; la femme = the woman. “Femme” can also be used in some set phrases like “ma femme” = my wife (more common than “mon épouse” in everyday speech).
target_language_example: La femme au manteau rouge est médecin.
native_language_example: The woman in the red coat is a doctor.

additional_notes: Used for a physical window in a room/building. Common with verbs like ouvrir (to open), fermer (to close), nettoyer (to clean). You can also say à la fenêtre to mean “at/in the window” (e.g., someone appears at the window).
target_language_example: Il fait chaud : ouvre la fenêtre, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: It’s hot: open the window, please.

additional_notes: Literally “the open window,” but it’s often used after a verb like laisser (“to leave”) or dormir (“to sleep”) to mean someone left the window open while doing something: dormir la fenêtre ouverte = sleep with the window open. Agree with the noun: la fenêtre ouverte (fem.), la porte ouverte; les fenêtres ouvertes (plural).
target_language_example: Je dors souvent la fenêtre ouverte en été.
native_language_example: I often sleep with the window open in summer.

additional_notes: Depending on context, "la fille" can mean a female child/young person ("the girl") or someone’s female child ("the daughter"). It often appears in family relationships: "la fille de + person" = "the daughter of + person".
target_language_example: C'est la fille de mon voisin.
native_language_example: She’s my neighbor’s daughter.

additional_notes: Used for the end of something (a story, a line, an event, a period of time). Common patterns: « jusqu’à la fin » = “until the end / all the way to the end”; « la fin de + noun » = “the end of …”. In « Le meilleur pour la fin », it means “save the best for last.”
target_language_example: Je garde le dessert pour la fin.
native_language_example: I'm saving dessert for last.

meaning: 'the end of' (a period, event, or thing).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to mark the ending point of something: *la fin de la journée* (end of the day), *la fin de l'année* (end of the year). Often followed by an article: *la fin du* (de + le) and *la fin des* (de + les). Can also be used in a dramatic sense: *la fin de tout* (“the end of everything”).
target_language_example: On se voit à la fin de la semaine.
native_language_example: See you at the end of the week.

meaning: “the end of (the)” (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the ending point of an event, story, period, trip, etc. It must be followed by a masculine singular noun (la fin du film, la fin du voyage). With a feminine singular noun, use "la fin de la" (la fin de la journée), and with plural, "la fin des" (la fin des vacances).
target_language_example: On arrive à la fin du chapitre.
native_language_example: We’re getting to the end of the chapter.

meaning: “the end of the world.” (often: “it’s not the end of the world!” / “it’s a disaster!”)
additional_notes: Literal meaning: the apocalypse/end of the world. Very commonly used figuratively to exaggerate how bad a situation feels (“C’est la fin du monde !”), or in questions to downplay something (“Est-ce la fin du monde ?” = “Is it really that bad?”). You may also see it used literally in jokes or dramatic statements (“La fin du monde approche.”).
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas la fin du monde si on arrive en retard.
native_language_example: It’s not the end of the world if we arrive late.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like: **avoir la foi** (to have faith), **garder la foi** (to keep faith / keep believing), **perdre la foi** (to lose faith). It can refer to religious faith or more generally to trusting in something/someone.
target_language_example: Même quand c’est difficile, j’essaie de garder la foi.
native_language_example: Even when it’s hard, I try to keep the faith.

additional_notes: A feminine noun (la forêt). Used to talk about a wooded area in nature. Often appears with location words like derrière (behind), dans (in), or près de (near).
target_language_example: On se promène dans la forêt cet après-midi.
native_language_example: We’re going for a walk in the forest this afternoon.

meaning: the crowd; a mass of people.
additional_notes: Refers to a large group of people gathered in the same place (e.g., at a concert, in the street). It’s grammatically singular in French (la foule est…), even though it describes many people. Common verbs: applaudir (applaud), crier (shout), contrôler (control), se frayer un passage dans la foule (push through the crowd).
target_language_example: Il y avait tellement de monde que je me suis perdu dans la foule.
native_language_example: There were so many people that I got lost in the crowd.

additional_notes: Used for an official boundary between countries or regions. Common with verbs like "traverser" (to cross) and in phrases like "à la frontière" (at the border) and "la frontière entre X et Y" (the border between X and Y).
target_language_example: On a attendu une heure à la frontière.
native_language_example: We waited an hour at the border.

additional_notes: Used for a party or celebration (birthday, holiday, town festival, etc.). Common with verbs like « avoir lieu » (to take place) and « être terminée » (to be over). Also appears in set phrases like « faire la fête » (to party).
target_language_example: On fait une fête samedi soir pour son anniversaire.
native_language_example: We’re having a party Saturday night for his birthday.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a train station (gare SNCF). Common in directions with prepositions like près de (near), en face de (opposite/across from), à côté de (next to), and questions like Où se trouve… ?
target_language_example: Je vais à la gare pour prendre le train.
native_language_example: I'm going to the station to take the train.

additional_notes: “La glace” can mean frozen water (ice) or ice cream; context makes it clear. With verbs like “fondre” (to melt), “céder / se rompre” (to give way / break), it means ice. With flavors (“au chocolat”, “à la vanille”) or verbs like “aimer / manger”, it usually means ice cream. Related: “un glaçon” = an ice cube.
target_language_example: Attention, la glace est fine ici.
native_language_example: Careful, the ice is thin here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a war in general or a specific conflict understood from context. Often appears in set phrases like « commencer la guerre » (start the war), « mettre fin à la guerre » (end the war), and « la guerre est de retour » (war has returned).
target_language_example: Personne ne veut la guerre.
native_language_example: Nobody wants war.

meaning: 'the war is…' (used to describe the state or nature of the war).
additional_notes: "La guerre" means "the war" (feminine singular), and "est" is "is" (from *être*). You use it at the start of a sentence to add an adjective, location, or other description: *La guerre est finie* (the war is over), *inévitable* (inevitable), *partout* (everywhere), *sans fin* (endless).
target_language_example: La guerre est terrible pour les civils.
native_language_example: The war is terrible for civilians.

additional_notes: A feminine noun. Often used with verbs like jouer de la guitare (to play the guitar) or pratiquer la guitare (to practice the guitar). You can also say à la guitare to mean “on the guitar” (e.g., playing chords on guitar).
target_language_example: Elle joue de la guitare tous les soirs.
native_language_example: She plays the guitar every evening.

additional_notes: Refers to a person’s leg. Common with body-related phrases: « à la jambe » (in the leg, e.g., injured), « le long de la jambe » (along the leg), and in instructions like « Lève la jambe » (Lift your leg).
target_language_example: J’ai mal à la jambe depuis hier.
native_language_example: My leg has been hurting since yesterday.

additional_notes: Literally “the young girl.” Used for a girl/young woman (often a teenager). It can sound a bit formal or old-fashioned compared with "la fille" in everyday speech. Feminine singular: "la" + "jeune" + "fille".
target_language_example: La jeune fille attend le bus devant l'école.
native_language_example: The young girl is waiting for the bus in front of the school.

meaning: the day (as a span of time, often daytime).
additional_notes: Refers to the course of a day as a period of time (how the day went, how long it felt, what you did during it). Often contrasts with "la nuit" (night). Can also mean "during the day/daytime" in phrases like "pendant la journée" or "dans la journée".
target_language_example: On se voit dans la journée.
native_language_example: We'll see each other during the day.

additional_notes: Most often means “language” (e.g., la langue française). It can also mean the physical “tongue.” In the expression « tirer la langue », it means “to stick out your tongue” (often teasing or being silly).
target_language_example: J'apprends la langue française.
native_language_example: I'm learning the French language.

meaning: the letter (a written message sent by mail).
additional_notes: Used for a physical written message (a piece of paper) you send or receive in the mail.
