native_language_example: We took the train at 8 o’clock.

meaning: 'we all have' / 'all of us have' (often: 'we all + past participle').
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that every person in the group did/experienced something. Very common with the passé composé: « Nous avons tous + past participle » (e.g., nous avons tous réussi = we all succeeded). « Tous » can sometimes come after the past participle (« Nous avons réussi tous ensemble »), but the most typical pattern is right after « avons ».
target_language_example: Nous avons tous oublié nos clés.
native_language_example: We all forgot our keys.

additional_notes: Used when the subject is “we” and the whole group is female (or a feminine group grammatically). “toutes” agrees with the speaker group (feminine plural). In English you usually say “we all + verb” (“We all learned…”), while in French “toutes” often comes right after the conjugated verb: “Nous avons toutes + past participle.” For a mixed/masculine group, use “nous avons tous.”
target_language_example: Nous avons toutes réussi l'examen.
native_language_example: We all passed the exam.

additional_notes: Passé composé of trouver (to find). Used to say you discovered something in the past. Can be followed by a noun (nous avons trouvé des traces), or by a complement describing what you found (nous avons trouvé la porte verrouillée = we found the door locked; nous avons trouvé ce garçon plongé… = we found that boy deeply asleep).
target_language_example: Nous avons trouvé un bon restaurant près de la gare.
native_language_example: We found a good restaurant near the train station.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of « visiter »: « nous » + « avons » (have) + « visité » (visited). Used to talk about places you went to see (a city, museum, site, community) in the past. In everyday English, it often translates as “we visited” even though it’s literally “we have visited.”
target_language_example: Pendant nos vacances, nous avons visité trois châteaux.
native_language_example: During our vacation, we visited three castles.

meaning: "we saw" / "we have seen" (past tense of "to see").
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of voir: nous (we) + avons (have) + vu (seen). It’s used for a completed action in the past: seeing someone/something, watching a film or TV show, witnessing an event. In English it’s often translated as simple past (“we saw”), though it can also be “we have seen” depending on context. The past participle is always vu (not *vue*).
target_language_example: Nous avons vu Marie hier soir au cinéma.
native_language_example: We saw Marie last night at the movie theater.

meaning: "we saw a" / "we have seen a" (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of voir (to see): nous avons vu = “we saw / we have seen.” It’s followed by the indefinite article un before a masculine singular noun (un renard, un bateau, un inconnu). For a feminine noun, use une (nous avons vu une voiture).
target_language_example: Hier soir, nous avons vu un chat noir dans la rue.
native_language_example: Last night, we saw a black cat in the street.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of "être" for "nous". It’s used to talk about a past state or situation ("we were happy") and very often to form the passive voice: "nous avons été + past participle" = "we were + past participle" (e.g., "nous avons été pris" = "we were caught"). With "nous", past participles typically agree in number/gender when needed (e.g., "nous avons été satisfaits / satisfaites").
target_language_example: Nous avons été très contents de te voir.
native_language_example: We were very happy to see you.

nous avons été attaqués par des

target_language_multi_word_term: nous avons été attaqués par des
meaning: "we were attacked by" (followed by a plural noun).
additional_notes: This is the passive voice in the past: "nous" (we) + "avons été" (have been / were) + past participle "attaqués" (attacked). It usually introduces who did the attacking with "par" (by), and "des" is the plural "some" before a plural noun (des bandits, des pirates). The adjective agrees with the subject: with "nous" you commonly see "attaqués" (mixed/masculine group) or "attaquées" (all-female group).
target_language_example: Nous avons été attaqués par des chiens errants.
native_language_example: We were attacked by stray dogs.

meaning: 'we have' (present) or 'we have' used to form the past tense (passé composé).
additional_notes: "Nous" = we, "avons" is the form of "avoir" for "nous". In the passé composé, "nous avons" + past participle means "we did / we have done" (e.g., "nous avons choisi" = we chose; "nous avons vu" = we saw). "Nous avons" can also mean "we have" in the literal sense of possession (e.g., "Nous avons une voiture" = We have a car).
target_language_example: Nous avons réservé une table pour ce soir.
native_language_example: We booked a table for tonight.

additional_notes: Used with **de + noun** to mean “a lot of”: *Nous avons beaucoup de neige.* It can also be followed by **à + infinitive** to mean “we have a lot to …”: *Nous avons beaucoup à faire / à discuter.* Often appears in comparisons: **beaucoup plus** (“much more”) and **beaucoup mieux** (“much better”).
target_language_example: Nous avons beaucoup de travail aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: We have a lot of work today.

additional_notes: Used to say you (we) possess or have a large quantity/number of something. It’s followed by a noun; after beaucoup de, the noun usually comes without an article (e.g., beaucoup de nourriture, beaucoup de clients). With a verb infinitive, it often expresses “a lot of (something) to do” (e.g., beaucoup de devoirs à faire).
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, nous avons beaucoup de travail.
native_language_example: Today, we have a lot of work.

meaning: we need (we have a need for).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity: "nous avons besoin de + noun" (we need + a thing/person), and often "nous avons besoin de + infinitive" (we need to + verb). "Besoin" is a noun, so you literally say "we have need" in French. "De" changes to "du / de la / de l’ / des" depending on the noun (e.g., du soutien, de l’eau, des informations).
target_language_example: Nous avons besoin de parler maintenant.
native_language_example: We need to talk now.

additional_notes: Used to say that “we” need something (noun) or need to do something (verb). With a noun: nous avons besoin de + noun (often de + plural or de + un/une/ce/cet/cette/ces). With a verb: nous avons besoin de + infinitive (e.g., comprendre, nous protéger). In negative form: nous n’avons pas besoin de…
target_language_example: Nous avons besoin de parler maintenant.
native_language_example: We need to talk now.

nous avons besoin de plus de

target_language_multi_word_term: nous avons besoin de plus de
additional_notes: Used to say that you (as a group) need a larger amount of something. Follows with a noun: plus de + nom (often without an article): plus de glace, plus de données, plus de gens. In negative form it becomes: nous n’avons plus besoin de… (“we don’t need… anymore”).
target_language_example: Nous avons besoin de plus de temps pour finir ce projet.
native_language_example: We need more time to finish this project.

nous avons besoin de ton aide

target_language_multi_word_term: nous avons besoin de ton aide
additional_notes: Uses "avoir besoin de" (= to need). "Ton" is informal singular "your" (to one person you know). In formal situations or with someone you don’t know well, say: "Nous avons besoin de votre aide."
target_language_example: Nous avons besoin de ton aide pour terminer ce projet.
native_language_example: We need your help to finish this project.

additional_notes: Used to say that “we” possess or have something available/present. In French, the plural article **des** usually corresponds to **some** or **(a few)** in English, and it’s used before plural nouns: *Nous avons des bananes* (“We have (some) bananas”). It can also introduce abstract plural ideas: *des intérêts*, *des règles*, *des valeurs*.
target_language_example: Nous avons des questions pour vous.
native_language_example: We have some questions for you.

additional_notes: Used to state that “we” possess/have two of something. It’s followed by a plural noun: « Nous avons deux filles. » You can also use it for having two classes/subjects, two cars, etc. In casual speech, « on a deux… » is often used instead of « nous avons deux… ».
target_language_example: Nous avons deux billets pour le concert.
native_language_example: We have two tickets for the concert.

additional_notes: Used to say there is still time, something remaining, or something that continues to be true (e.g., more things to do, time left, options left, a long way to go). Word order stays: Nous avons encore + noun/quantity (+ à + infinitive).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, nous avons encore deux heures avant le départ.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we still have two hours before departure.

meaning: "we have a" (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir (to have) in the present tense: nous avons = we have. It’s typically followed by un + a masculine singular noun (un chien, un choix). For a feminine noun, use nous avons une; for plural, nous avons des.
target_language_example: Nous avons un appartement à Paris.
native_language_example: We have an apartment in Paris.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir" (to have): "nous" + "avons" (we have) + "une" (a/an for feminine singular nouns). It’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., une réunion, une réservation, une mission). Often used to state what you have scheduled or planned (a meeting, a reservation, a busy day, etc.).
target_language_example: Nous avons une visite à 10 heures.
native_language_example: We have a visit/appointment at 10 o’clock.

meaning: “we know” (we are familiar with / we know about).
additional_notes: Present tense of connaître (“to know/be familiar with” a person, place, or thing). Often used with a direct object: nous connaissons les règles (we know the rules). For people, it means “to know/know each other”: nous nous connaissons depuis longtemps (we’ve known each other for a long time). Contrast with savoir, used for facts/skills: nous savons la réponse (we know the answer).
target_language_example: Nous connaissons ce quartier, on peut t’aider.
native_language_example: We know this neighborhood; we can help you.

additional_notes: "Nous" = "we" and "devons" is the present tense of "devoir" ("to have to / must") for "we". Use it to express obligation, necessity, or something that should be done. Often followed by an infinitive: "nous devons + verb" (e.g., "nous devons partir").
target_language_example: Nous devons partir maintenant.
native_language_example: We have to leave now.

meaning: “we must / we have to do” (expressing obligation).
additional_notes: Built with **devoir + infinitive** to say what is necessary: *nous devons + faire...* (“we have to do...” ). **Faire** is very flexible: it can mean “do” (*faire de la publicité* = do advertising), “make” (*faire le meilleur usage* = make the best use), or be used in the **causative** pattern **faire + infinitive** meaning “have/get something done” (*faire tailler la haie* = have the hedge trimmed) or “make someone do” (*faire respecter la loi* = enforce the law / make the law be respected).
target_language_example: Nous devons faire attention à ce détail.
native_language_example: We have to pay attention to that detail.

meaning: “we must / we have to” + “ourselves / each other” (reflexive).
additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence pattern: **nous devons** (“we must”) + **nous** (a reflexive pronoun) + an infinitive. Use it when the action is done to/for **ourselves** or **each other**: *nous devons nous taire* (we must be quiet), *nous devons nous rencontrer* (we must meet), *nous devons nous entraider* (we must help each other). The reflexive pronoun **nous** comes before the verb in the infinitive.
target_language_example: Nous devons nous dépêcher si nous ne voulons pas être en retard.
native_language_example: We have to hurry if we don’t want to be late.

meaning: "we must/need to take" (or "we have to take").
additional_notes: Used to express obligation: "nous devons" = "we must/need to" + "prendre" = "to take". "Prendre" is very common and can mean taking transportation (prendre le bus), choosing a route (prendre les escaliers), accepting/assuming something (prendre un risque), or considering something (prendre ... en considération).
target_language_example: Nous devons prendre un taxi pour être à l’heure.
native_language_example: We need to take a taxi to be on time.

meaning: we must be / we have to be.
additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity about a state/quality for “we.” Followed by an adjective (prudentes, sûrs, forts), a phrase (prêts à...), or an infinitive phrase starting with an adjective (capables de + verb). The form changes with the subject (je dois être, tu dois être, il/elle doit être, vous devez être, ils/elles doivent être).
target_language_example: Nous devons être à l’heure pour le rendez-vous.
native_language_example: We have to be on time for the appointment.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of devoir ("to have to") to give advice, make a recommendation, or say what would be the right thing to do. Often followed by an infinitive: "Nous devrions partir" (We should leave). It can also stand alone to agree with a suggestion: "—On y va ? —Oui, nous devrions."
target_language_example: Nous devrions partir maintenant pour éviter les embouteillages.
native_language_example: We should leave now to avoid traffic jams.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of devoir (“should/ought to”) + an infinitive (faire). It’s commonly followed by a direct object (quelque chose, mieux, de notre mieux) or used in an embedded question after ce que (“what we should do”). Often expresses advice, a suggestion, or what seems like the right thing to do.
target_language_example: Nous devrions faire une pause avant de continuer.
native_language_example: We should take a break before continuing.

additional_notes: *Nous* is the object pronoun “to us / for us” (or part of “we” when the subject is *nous*). *En* replaces something introduced by **de** (“about it,” “from it,” “some of it/them,” “any,” a quantity). It’s very common with verbs like **parler de** (Nous en avons parlé = We talked about it), **avoir** with quantities (Il nous en reste = We have some left), **savoir** (Nous en savons plus = We know more), and **dire** (Nous en dire plus = tell us more about it). Pronouns go before the verb: *Il nous en reste…*, *Nous en avons…*, *Pouvez-vous nous en dire…*.
target_language_example: Vous pouvez nous en donner un peu ?
native_language_example: Can you give us some (of it)?

meaning: "we have some" / "we have it/them" (with "en" referring to a previously mentioned quantity).
additional_notes: “En” replaces something introduced with de (du, de la, des) or a quantity/amount: *des pommes → nous en avons* (“we have some [apples]”). It’s very common with quantities like **beaucoup**, **assez**, **plein**, **quelques-uns**, or with time/amount expressions like **en avoir pour un moment** (“to have [it] for a while / it’ll take a while”). Often you’ll add a quantity after it: *nous en avons beaucoup / assez / quelques-uns*. Without a quantity (*Nous en avons.*), it usually means “We have some.”
target_language_example: Tu veux des stylos ? Nous en avons quelques-uns.
native_language_example: Do you want pens? We have a few.

additional_notes:
"En" is a pronoun that usually means "about it/that" or "of it/that" and refers to something mentioned or understood. Common patterns:
- "Nous en sommes conscients / fiers / reconnaissants" = "We are aware of it / proud of it / grateful for it."
- "Nous en sommes à + noun/infinitive" = "We have reached the point of…" / "We are down to…" (a stage in a process).
- With a reflexive verb: "Nous nous en sommes amusés" = "We had fun with it / We were amused by it."
target_language_example: Nous en sommes à la dernière étape.
native_language_example: We’ve reached the last stage.

additional_notes: Present tense of the verb « faire » with « nous » (we). It’s used in many common expressions where English may not use “do/make,” e.g. « faire du sport » (to do/play sports), « faire des affaires » (to do business / get good deals), « faire une nuit blanche » (to pull an all-nighter). In « Ne nous faisons pas de faux espoirs », it means “let’s not get our hopes up” (literally “let’s not make ourselves false hopes”).
target_language_example: Aujourd’hui, nous faisons la cuisine ensemble.
native_language_example: Today, we’re cooking together.

additional_notes: This is the passé simple form of **nous sommes/avons été**. It’s mostly used in literature, historical writing, or storytelling—not in everyday conversation (where you’d usually say **nous avons été** or **on a été**). Often appears with a past participle to form a passive meaning: **Nous fûmes accueillis** = “We were welcomed.” The past participle may agree in gender/number (e.g., **accueillies**, **prises** for an all-female group).
target_language_example: Nous fûmes surpris par son silence.
native_language_example: We were surprised by his silence.

meaning: "we have" / "we've" + "them" (with "les" as the direct object pronoun).
additional_notes: Used in the passé composé with avoir when the direct object is "les" (= them) and it comes before the verb: "Nous les avons aidés" = "We helped them." With être/avoir participles, the past participle can agree in gender/number with a preceding direct object: "Nous les avons vues" (them = feminine plural), "Nous les avons vus" (them = masculine/mixed plural). Word order: subject (nous) + direct object pronoun (les) + auxiliary (avons) + past participle.
target_language_example: Nous les avons rencontrés hier soir.
native_language_example: We met them last night.

meaning: 'we do not' / 'we don't' (start of a negation with "nous").
additional_notes: "Nous" means "we" and "ne" is the first part of French negation. It’s usually completed by a second word (e.g., "ne... pas" = not, "ne... jamais" = never, "ne... plus" = no longer, "ne... rien" = nothing, "ne... que" = only). In speech, "ne" is often dropped ("Nous nageons jamais"), but in writing it’s typically kept.
target_language_example: Nous ne pouvons pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: We can't come tonight.

additional_notes: Used to express a strong obligation or rule in the negative. Formed from subject pronoun "nous" + negation "ne…pas" + "devons" (present tense of devoir, “must/should”). Often followed by an infinitive verb: "Nous ne devons pas + infinitive".
target_language_example: Nous ne devons pas oublier nos clés.
native_language_example: We must not forget our keys.

additional_notes: Common start of a negative sentence with pouvoir (“can / be able to”). It’s often followed by an infinitive: nous ne pouvons pas continuer (“we can’t continue”). Note: in formal writing/speech you may see the full negation with pas; without pas can sound more formal or literary depending on context.
target_language_example: Désolé, nous ne pouvons pas accepter cette offre.
native_language_example: Sorry, we can’t accept this offer.

additional_notes: Negative form of « nous pouvons » (“we can”). It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive: « nous ne pouvons pas aider / rester / vivre ». In everyday spoken French, « ne » is often dropped: « nous pouvons pas… » (or more commonly with « on »: « on ne peut pas… »).
target_language_example: Désolé, nous ne pouvons pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, we can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: Negative form of « nous sommes » (we are). It can be followed by an adjective (Nous ne sommes pas seuls), a noun with an article (Nous ne sommes pas des Américains / les bienvenus), or a past participle in the passé composé with être (Nous ne sommes pas partis = We didn’t leave). In everyday spoken French, « ne » is often dropped: « Nous sommes pas… ».
target_language_example: Désolés, nous ne sommes pas disponibles ce soir.
native_language_example: Sorry, we aren’t available tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say that “we” (a group including the speaker) are not members of a group or category described by a plural noun. Pattern: Nous ne sommes pas des + noun (often plural): « Nous ne sommes pas des étudiants. » If the noun is singular, use « nous ne sommes pas + un/une » (e.g., « nous ne sommes pas un couple »). In casual speech, « ne » is often dropped: « Nous sommes pas des… »
target_language_example: Nous ne sommes pas des touristes, on habite ici.
native_language_example: We’re not tourists; we live here.

additional_notes: Used with pronominal ("se") verbs. The first "nous" is the subject (we). The second "nous" is the reflexive/reciprocal object pronoun placed before the verb: reflexive = we do it to ourselves (Nous nous préparons.); reciprocal = we do it to each other (Nous nous aimons.). It also appears in verbs that are always used with "se", like "se souvenir" (Nous nous souvenons.) or "se rendre" meaning "to go" in literary style (Nous nous rendîmes...).
target_language_example: Nous nous appelons ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re calling each other tonight.

meaning: 'we ...' in the past tense (passé composé) with a reflexive verb; often 'we [did something] (to ourselves/to each other)'.
additional_notes: Used with reflexive/pronominal verbs in the passé composé: subject pronoun (nous) + reflexive pronoun (nous) + auxiliary être in the present (sommes) + past participle (e.g., Nous nous sommes disputés = We argued). The past participle often agrees with nous (plural), and can show gender in writing (e.g., amusées for an all-female group).
target_language_example: Nous nous sommes retrouvés devant la gare à 18 h.
native_language_example: We met up in front of the train station at 6 p.m.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *s’asseoir* (“to sit down”), used with *être* and a reflexive pronoun: *nous nous sommes assis* (masculine or mixed group) / *nous nous sommes assises* (all women). Often followed by a place: *devant la cheminée* (in front of the fireplace), *sur un banc* (on a bench), *en cercle* (in a circle).
target_language_example: Après le dîner, nous nous sommes assis dans le salon.
native_language_example: After dinner, we sat down in the living room.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "se rencontrer" = "to meet". "Nous" is "we" and the second "nous" is the reflexive pronoun meaning "each other." The ending -ées agrees with a female group speaking (all women). If the group is all men or mixed, you usually write "nous nous sommes rencontrés".
target_language_example: Nous nous sommes rencontrées à Paris pendant un voyage.
native_language_example: We met in Paris during a trip.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *se rencontrer* (“to meet”). It’s reflexive: *nous* (we) + *nous* (each other) + *sommes* (auxiliary *être*) + *rencontrés* (past participle). Used with a time or place: *dimanche*, *il y a quelques années*, *à Boston*. In mixed groups, agreement changes: *nous nous sommes rencontrées* if the group is all female; *rencontrés* if there’s at least one male.
target_language_example: Nous nous sommes rencontrés pendant un cours de français.
native_language_example: We met during a French class.

meaning: "to us" + "have" (they have … us), used to form the past tense with "avoir".
additional_notes: Used when "nous" is an object pronoun meaning “us” (often “to us”), followed by the auxiliary verb "ont" (= “have”, 3rd person plural: “they”). It comes before a past participle: "Ils nous ont aidés" (They helped us) / "Elles nous ont parlé" (They spoke to us). Agreement of the past participle depends on whether "nous" is a direct object (aidés) or indirect object (parlé stays the same).
target_language_example: Ils nous ont appelé hier soir.
native_language_example: They called us last night.

additional_notes: Present tense of *parler* with **nous** (“we”). Use it for languages (“we speak French”) or for discussing a topic (“we talk about the village”). Depending on context, it can mean either “we speak” (ability/habit) or “we’re talking” (right now).
target_language_example: Nous parlons de ça après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: We’ll talk about that after lunch.

additional_notes: Formed from "nous" (we) + the conditional of "pouvoir" (to be able to). Used to suggest an option politely ("We could wait"), to talk about a possible outcome ("We might all be dead tomorrow"), or to say you could use something/someone’s help ("We could use your help"). Often followed by an infinitive verb: "nous pourrions + infinitif".
target_language_example: Nous pourrions partir plus tôt si tu veux.
native_language_example: We could leave earlier if you want.

additional_notes: "Nous" = "we" and "pouvons" is the present tense of "pouvoir" (to be able to / can). It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "continuer", "discuter", "parler") to say what you can do. It can express ability, possibility, or permission depending on context, and it’s often used with adverbs like "peut-être" (maybe) or "encore" (still).
target_language_example: Nous pouvons commencer maintenant si tu veux.
native_language_example: We can start now if you want.

meaning: “we can do / we are able to do.”
additional_notes: "Nous" = we, "pouvons" is the present tense of "pouvoir" (can / to be able to), and "faire" = to do/to make. Often followed by an action ("Nous pouvons faire mieux" = We can do better) or used in patterns like "tout ce que nous pouvons faire, c’est…" (all we can do is…).
target_language_example: Désolé, c’est tout ce que nous pouvons faire pour l’instant.
native_language_example: Sorry, that’s all we can do for now.

additional_notes: Used with venir (or other movement verbs) to mean “to visit us.” The verb is rendre visite à + person (e.g., rendre visite à mes parents = to visit my parents). With an object pronoun: me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur rendre visite.
target_language_example: Tu peux venir nous rendre visite ce week-end ?
native_language_example: Can you come visit us this weekend?

additional_notes: Used to state that a group ("we") has knowledge or is aware of something. Often followed by a clause: "nous savons que…" (we know that…), a question word like "ce que"/"qui" (we know what/who…), or an object like "tout" (we know everything). In speech it can also be said emphatically: "Oh, nous savons !" = "Oh, we know!"
target_language_example: Nous savons que ce n’est pas facile.
native_language_example: We know that it’s not easy.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that two people ("you and I") share the same knowledge about something. It’s often followed by a clause with "que" (we both know that...) or a question word like "qui/ce que/ce qui" (we both know who/what...). You can also switch the pronoun: "vous savez tous les deux" (you both know), "ils/elles savent tous les deux/toutes les deux" (they both know).
target_language_example: Nous savons tous les deux que ce n’est pas vrai.
native_language_example: We both know that it isn’t true.

additional_notes: Used to say what "we" will be in the future (plans, predictions, or what day/date it will be). Often followed by a noun/adjective (nous serons votre hôte, nous serons heureux) or a place phrase (nous serons à Paris).
target_language_example: Dans une heure, nous serons prêts.
native_language_example: In an hour, we will be ready.

additional_notes: Used to describe who you are, what you are, or your state/condition: "nous sommes" + adjective (nous sommes riches), or + noun (nous sommes une famille de quatre), or + past participle/adjective (nous sommes obligés…). In everyday spoken French, people often use "on est" instead of "nous sommes."
target_language_example: Nous sommes prêts à partir.
native_language_example: We are ready to leave.

meaning: 'have we...?' (inverted yes/no question form, with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used to form a formal/written yes–no question in the passé composé when the verb takes être and is reflexive (nous + nous). The subject (nous) and auxiliary (sommes) are inverted and linked with a hyphen: « Nous sommes-nous … ? ». Often followed by a past participle: « Nous sommes-nous déjà rencontrés ? » (= Have we already met?). « pas » can be added for a negative question: « Ne nous sommes-nous pas… ? ». In everyday speech, people often prefer « Est-ce que nous nous sommes… ? » or just « On s’est… ? ».
target_language_example: Nous sommes-nous trompés d’adresse ?
native_language_example: Did we get the address wrong?

meaning: "we went" (past tense; said by a group of females).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of **aller** (to go), which uses **être** as the helping verb: *nous sommes allé(e)s*. With **être**, the past participle agrees with the subject: **allées** = feminine plural (a group of women/girls, or an all-female group). If the group is male or mixed, you usually write **nous sommes allés**.
target_language_example: Après le dîner, nous sommes allées au cinéma.
native_language_example: After dinner, we went to the movie theater.

meaning: 'we went' / 'we have gone' (past tense of aller).
additional_notes: Passé composé of aller with être: nous + sommes + allés (add -s because it's plural). Used to say where you went (Nous sommes allés au parc), that you went to do an activity (Nous sommes allés nager / faire des emplettes), or that you went around somewhere (Nous sommes allés autour du lac). In spoken English it’s often just “we went.”
target_language_example: Nous sommes allés au restaurant après le travail.
native_language_example: We went to the restaurant after work.

meaning: we went to the (masculine singular place/event).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "aller" with "être": "nous sommes allés" = "we went" / "we have gone." Use "au" (= à + le) before a masculine singular noun: au musée, au match, au café. For feminine singular, use "à la" (nous sommes allés à la plage). For plural, use "aux" (nous sommes allés aux États-Unis). The past participle agrees with "nous": allés (mixed/masculine group) or allées (all-female group).
target_language_example: Hier, nous sommes allés au restaurant après le travail.
native_language_example: Yesterday, we went to the restaurant after work.

additional_notes: Past tense of going somewhere (passé composé of aller) with "nous". Uses "être" as the helping verb: "nous sommes allés" (add -s because "nous" = plural). Use "à" before most cities and many places: "à Kyoto", "à Boston", "à la piscine", "à la montagne". For countries, you may use other prepositions (e.g., "au Canada", "en France").
target_language_example: Hier, nous sommes allés à la bibliothèque après l'école.
native_language_example: Yesterday, we went to the library after school.

additional_notes: Past tense of arriver (to arrive) with être in the passé composé. Used for completed arrival; often followed by a place with à (à la gare, au musée, à la maison) or by a time expression (il y a trois jours). Agreement: arrivés for a group including at least one male; arrivées if all are female.
target_language_example: Nous sommes arrivés à l'hôtel vers midi.
native_language_example: We arrived at the hotel around noon.

meaning: "we are faced with" / "we are confronted with" (a difficulty, problem, situation).
additional_notes: Used to say you (we) have to deal with a problem or difficult situation. It’s fairly formal and often followed by a noun phrase (des difficultés, des problèmes, une situation difficile). For other subjects: je suis confronté(e) à, tu es confronté(e) à, il/elle est confronté(e) à, ils/elles sont confronté(e)s à.
target_language_example: Nous sommes confrontés à une pénurie de personnel.
native_language_example: We’re faced with a staff shortage.

additional_notes: Used to state who/what “we” are by describing the group with a plural noun (often a job, identity, or category). Follow with a plural noun: Nous sommes des étudiants / des réfugiés. If the noun is singular, use “nous sommes un/une …” instead.
target_language_example: Nous sommes des touristes, nous cherchons le musée.
native_language_example: We’re tourists; we’re looking for the museum.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to describe what situation/state you’re currently in. Very common in set phrases like: « en accord » (in agreement), « en affaires » (in business), « en danger » (in danger), « en guerre » (at war), « en mission » (on a mission).
target_language_example: Nous sommes en retard.
native_language_example: We are late.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *rester* with *être* as the auxiliary. *Restés* agrees with *nous* (add -e for an all-female group: *restées*). Often followed by an expression like *en contact* (“in touch”).
target_language_example: Nous sommes restés à la maison toute la journée.
native_language_example: We stayed at home all day.

additional_notes: Used with a noun, adjective, or place/state to say that everyone in “we” shares the same situation. The word “tous” (all) typically comes right after the verb “sommes” (are): “Nous sommes tous prêts.” It can be followed by a noun (“… des animaux”), an adjective (“… prêts”), or another complement (“… là”).
target_language_example: Nous sommes tous contents de te voir.
native_language_example: We’re all happy to see you.

additional_notes: Present tense of "travailler" with "nous". It can describe a general routine (We work every day) or something happening now/these days (We are working on it). Often followed by time expressions (de... à..., de jour/la nuit), "ensemble" (together), "sur" (nous travaillons dessus/sur ce projet = we’re working on it/this project), or "pour" + infinitive to give a purpose (nous travaillons pour corriger... = we’re working to fix...).
target_language_example: Désolé, nous travaillons en ce moment : je te rappelle dans une heure.
native_language_example: Sorry, we’re working right now; I’ll call you back in an hour.

additional_notes: Present tense of vivre (“to live”). Used for where you live (Nous vivons chez eux / dans les mêmes dortoirs), and also more figuratively for experiencing something (Nous vivons des temps difficiles = “We’re going through difficult times”).
target_language_example: Nous vivons à Paris depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: We’ve been living in Paris for two years.

additional_notes: Present tense of vouloir (“to want”). Used to express what a group wants or intends to do. In polite requests, French often uses conditional instead: « nous voudrions… » (“we would like…”).
target_language_example: Nous voulons réserver une table pour ce soir.
native_language_example: We want to book a table for tonight.

additional_notes: Used to express what “we” want to happen. After « vouloir que », French normally uses the subjunctive: « Nous voulons que tu viennes. » Common patterns: « nous voulons que + person + verb » and « nous voulons que + thing + soit/soient + adjective/past participle » (e.g., « soit en sécurité », « soient punis »).
target_language_example: Nous voulons que tu restes avec nous ce soir.
native_language_example: We want you to stay with us tonight.

additional_notes: Used with the passé composé: "nous" = we, "vous" = you (formal singular or plural), "avons" = have. It’s followed by a past participle (appelé, cherché, vu, etc.). When "vous" is a direct object placed before the verb, the past participle may agree in gender/number: "Nous vous avons vu" (we saw you, to one man), "vus" (men/plural mixed), "vue" (one woman), "vues" (women).
target_language_example: Nous vous avons envoyé un message.
native_language_example: We sent you a message.

additional_notes: Used to describe an ongoing situation, background state, or repeated/habitual past (not a completed one-time event). Often followed by an adjective or a noun: Nous étions fatigués / Nous étions voisins. Adjective agreement: with a mixed group use fatigués/excités; with an all-female group use fatiguées/excitées (as in the examples).
target_language_example: Quand j’étais enfant, nous étions souvent chez mes grands-parents.
native_language_example: When I was a child, we were often at my grandparents’ place.

meaning: "we were (in the middle of) doing" (ongoing past action).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that an action was in progress in the past (like English “we were doing…”). It’s formed with the imperfect of être (nous étions) + en train de + infinitive: « nous étions en train de + verbe ». Often sets the background for another past event: « … quand / lorsque … ».
target_language_example: Nous étions en train de dîner quand tu as appelé.
native_language_example: We were in the middle of having dinner when you called.

meaning: 'we were all' (everyone in our group was).
additional_notes: "Nous étions" is the imperfect past of "être" (to be): "we were" (often describing a situation/background in the past). "Tous" means "all" and agrees with the group: it’s "tous" for a mixed/all-male group, and "toutes" for an all-female group ("nous étions toutes..."). Often followed by an adjective or a place: "nous étions tous fatigués" (we were all tired), "nous étions tous dans le bus" (we were all on the bus).
target_language_example: Après le voyage, nous étions tous épuisés.
native_language_example: After the trip, we were all exhausted.

additional_notes: Used when talking about exactly two people, and both are female (or the speaker is referring to two women/girls). It agrees in gender and number: you say "tous les deux" for two males or a mixed pair. Built with the imperfect of être ("nous étions" = "we were"), often for description/background (e.g., how you felt, where you were).
target_language_example: Nous étions toutes les deux surprises par la nouvelle.
native_language_example: We were both surprised by the news.

meaning: a new novel (newly written book of fiction).
additional_notes: Often refers to someone’s latest novel that is coming out soon or has just come out. In the examples, it’s used with possessives like ton/votre (your) and in questions about when it will be published (publié). Not to be confused with the literary movement called "le Nouveau Roman" (capitalized) in 1950s France.
target_language_example: J’ai acheté son nouveau roman hier.
native_language_example: I bought his/her new novel yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a house/home that is recently built or recently bought/moved into. Agreement: feminine singular → "une nouvelle maison"; plural → "de nouvelles maisons". Often appears with possessives: "ma/ta/votre/notre nouvelle maison".
target_language_example: On emménage dans notre nouvelle maison demain.
native_language_example: We’re moving into our new house tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a dress that is newly bought or new to the person. With feminine nouns like robe, nouveau becomes nouvelle. Often used with possessives: ma/ta/sa nouvelle robe.
target_language_example: J'ai acheté une nouvelle robe pour la fête.
native_language_example: I bought a new dress for the party.

additional_notes: Means a car that is new (either newly bought or recently acquired). Commonly used with a possessive (ma/ta/sa/notre/votre/leur nouvelle voiture) and can also refer to a replacement or upgraded car, not necessarily brand-new from the factory.
target_language_example: J'ai acheté une nouvelle voiture la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: I bought a new car last week.

additional_notes: Usually used with the definite article: « la nuit dernière ». It refers to the night immediately before today (often to talk about something that happened then). In everyday French, « hier soir » is also very common for “last night” (especially for the evening).
target_language_example: Je suis encore fatigué(e) à cause de la nuit dernière.
native_language_example: I’m still tired because of last night.

additional_notes: Used mainly in negative sentences with ne (often with another negative word like jamais, personne): Je ne vais nulle part. It can also mean “no... anywhere” / “not... anywhere” depending on the context: Tu ne vas nulle part = You’re not going anywhere. It can appear with ailleurs for emphasis: nulle part ailleurs = nowhere else.
target_language_example: Je n'ai trouvé mes clés nulle part.
native_language_example: I couldn't find my keys anywhere.

additional_notes: Used mainly in negative sentences with ne (often with another negative word like jamais, personne): Je ne vais nulle part. It can also mean “no... anywhere” / “not... anywhere” depending on the context: Tu ne vas nulle part = You’re not going anywhere. It can appear with ailleurs for emphasis: nulle part ailleurs = nowhere else.
target_language_example: Je n'ai trouvé mes clés nulle part.
native_language_example: I couldn't find my keys anywhere.

meaning: “right?” / “isn’t it?” (a tag question asking for confirmation).
additional_notes: Placed at the end of a statement to check that the listener agrees or to ask for confirmation. Common in both spoken and written French. It can follow different subjects/verbs (even with tu/vous), and often matches English tags like “right?”, “isn’t it?”, “don’t you?”, depending on context.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 18 h, n’est-ce pas ?
native_language_example: We’re meeting at 6 p.m., right?

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb être (“to be”) in the present tense: ne + être + pas. In everyday speech, ne is often dropped: « Cette maison est pas très grande. » In writing and more formal speech, keep « ne … pas ».
target_language_example: Ce n’est pas mon livre.
native_language_example: It’s not my book.

additional_notes: Used for personal possessions that are worth money or important (e.g., jewelry, passport, cash, phone). Common in hotels, airports, and safety/security instructions, often with a safe (un coffre) or a secure place (un endroit sûr).
target_language_example: Avant de partir, vérifie que tu as bien tous tes objets de valeur.
native_language_example: Before you leave, check that you have all your valuables.

additional_notes: Imperative form of s’occuper de (“to take care of / deal with”). It can be practical (“handle this person/thing”) or used as a sharp command meaning “mind your own business” (often with tes affaires / ce qui te regarde).
target_language_example: Occupe-toi de tes affaires, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Mind your own business, please.

meaning: to take care of; to deal with.
additional_notes: Usually used in the reflexive form: s’occuper de + noun/pronoun. It means handling a task/problem ("deal with") or looking after a person/thing ("take care of"). Often used with an imperative: « Occupe-toi de ça » (“Take care of that”).
target_language_example: Je m’occupe des enfants pendant que tu travailles.
native_language_example: I’m taking care of the kids while you work.

additional_notes: Uses the pattern **être occupé(e) à + infinitive** to say someone is busy doing something. **Occupée** is feminine singular (for *elle*, *maman*, *ma mère*); use **occupé** for a man (*il est occupé à…*) and **occupés/occupées** for plural.
target_language_example: Je suis occupée à préparer le dîner, je te rappelle après.
native_language_example: I’m busy preparing dinner; I’ll call you back later.

additional_notes: Used to react to something you notice or realize, often expressing surprise, recognition, or a quick comment. Very common before an adjective (Oh, c’est facile / sympa) or before identifying something/someone (Oh, c’est toi / ça). In speech, you’ll also hear it without the comma: « Oh c’est… ».
target_language_example: Oh, c'est incroyable !
native_language_example: Oh, it’s incredible!

meaning: “oh, my …” (an exclamation before a noun or term of address).
additional_notes: Used to express strong emotion (surprise, worry, affection, etc.) before a noun: "Oh, mon Dieu !" (Oh my God!), or affectionate terms like "Oh, mon amour" / "Oh, mon cœur." Note that "mon" is the masculine possessive adjective (“my”) used before masculine nouns (Dieu, amour, cœur).
target_language_example: Oh, mon ami, qu’est-ce qui se passe ?
native_language_example: Oh, my friend, what’s going on?

additional_notes: Used to react with surprise, annoyance, or strong curiosity before a question. It’s essentially “Oh” + “qu’est-ce que” (“what”), often followed by a verb: « Oh, qu’est-ce que tu fais ? » (“Oh, what are you doing?”). It can also be used with « c’est » / « c’était »: « Oh, qu’est-ce que c’est ? » (“Oh, what is it?”).
target_language_example: Oh, qu'est-ce que tu racontes ?
native_language_example: Oh, what are you talking about?

meaning: “we have” (very common in spoken French), sometimes “someone/people have”.
additional_notes: “On” literally means “one,” but in everyday French it often replaces “nous” (we). So “on a” is the spoken equivalent of “nous avons.” It’s followed by a past participle to form the passé composé: on a balayé (we swept), on a aperçu (we saw/caught sight of), on a entendu (we heard).
target_language_example: On a déjà mangé.
native_language_example: We already ate / We’ve already eaten.

additional_notes: “On” often means “we” in everyday French, or “people/they” in a general sense. “On a eu” is the passé composé of “avoir” (to have): it can mean having/receiving something (“On a eu notre journal.” = We got our newspaper) or experiencing something (“On a eu beaucoup de pluie.” = We had a lot of rain / There was a lot of rain). In questions, it can mean “Did we get/have…?”
target_language_example: On a eu un problème avec la réservation.
native_language_example: We had a problem with the reservation.

meaning: 'we did' / 'we have done' (past tense of faire).
additional_notes: Passé composé of faire with the subject pronoun on. In everyday French, on very often means “we” (instead of nous), especially in spoken French: On a fait le boulot = “We did the job.” It can also mean “someone/people did,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : on a fait de notre mieux.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we did our best.

additional_notes: Uses the indefinite subject pronoun "on" to mean "we" or "people/they/someone" when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or not specified. "a trouvé" is the passé composé of "trouver" (to find), so it refers to a completed finding in the past. Very common in reports/news: "On a trouvé son corps…" = "A body was found…".
target_language_example: On a trouvé une solution au problème.
native_language_example: We found a solution to the problem.

meaning: “we have” (very common in spoken French), sometimes “someone/people have”.
additional_notes: “On” literally means “one,” but in everyday French it often replaces “nous” (we). So “on a” is the spoken equivalent of “nous avons.” It’s followed by a past participle to form the passé composé: on a balayé (we swept), on a aperçu (we saw/caught sight of), on a entendu (we heard).
target_language_example: On a déjà mangé.
native_language_example: We already ate / We’ve already eaten.

additional_notes: Uses the subject pronoun "on" (often meaning “we” in everyday French, or “people/you” in a general sense) + "a besoin" from "avoir besoin" (“to need”). Common patterns: "On a besoin de + noun/infinitive" (On a besoin de plus d'hommes / On a besoin de parler), and "On a besoin que + subjunctive" for a clause (On a besoin que vous veniez…).
target_language_example: On a besoin de ton aide tout de suite.
native_language_example: We need your help right now.

additional_notes: Literally “one has need of.” Uses **avoir besoin de** (“to need”). After **de**, you can have a noun (often with **du/de la/des**: *on a besoin de calme / de la place / des preuves*) or an infinitive verb: *on a besoin de te parler* (“we need to talk to you”). **On** is flexible: it can mean “we,” “people in general,” or an informal “you.”
target_language_example: On a besoin de ton aide tout de suite.
native_language_example: We need your help right away.

additional_notes: Used to say that things are going well or that you hope they will. "On" often means "we" in everyday French, but it can also mean "people/you" in general (like "one"). Often used with adverbs like "parfois" (sometimes) or "de temps à autre" (from time to time), and in "si on a de la chance" = "if we’re lucky."
target_language_example: On a de la chance d’avoir trouvé une place.
native_language_example: We’re lucky to have found a spot.

additional_notes: "On" often means "we" in everyday French. With "avoir" + "des" (some), it says you have some things/people, or that some exist/are available (especially in questions). Used with plural nouns: On a des clients. / On a des projets. In a question: On a des pneus de rechange ? = Do we have any spare tires?
target_language_example: On a des problèmes, mais on va trouver une solution.
native_language_example: We have problems, but we’re going to find a solution.

meaning: "we have a" / "there's a" (used to report or announce something).
additional_notes: Literally "one has a," but in everyday French **on** often means **we** or is used impersonally (like "there is/there's"). Common in police/work situations to report a situation: *On a un intrus* = "We’ve got an intruder" / "There’s an intruder." Often followed by a noun (un problème, un mort, un intrus, etc.).
target_language_example: On a un problème ici.
native_language_example: We have a problem here.

additional_notes: "On" often means "we" in everyday French (instead of "nous"), though it can also mean "someone/people" in general. "On a" is the verb "avoir" (to have) in the present: "on a" = "we have" / "we’ve got". "Une" is the feminine form of "a/an"; use it before a feminine noun (e.g., une mission, une piste, une invitée). In context it can also be used like English "we’ve got" to introduce a task/problem/lead: "On a une affaire à régler".
target_language_example: On a une solution, je pense.
native_language_example: We have a solution, I think.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of devoir (devrait) with on (often meaning “we” in everyday French). It can express (1) a suggestion/advice: “we/you should…”, or (2) an expectation/probability: “it should…” / “we should have… (by then)”. Common in polite recommendations: On devrait + infinitive.
target_language_example: On devrait partir maintenant pour éviter les bouchons.
native_language_example: We should leave now to avoid traffic jams.

meaning: "we should do" / "we ought to do" (suggesting an action).
additional_notes: Uses "on" to mean "we" in everyday French. "devrait" is the conditional of "devoir" (must), used to make a suggestion or give advice more softly than "on doit faire" (we must do). Often followed by an infinitive or an object: "On devrait faire quelque chose", "On devrait faire ça".
target_language_example: On devrait faire une liste avant d'aller au supermarché.
native_language_example: We should make a list before going to the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to make a gentle suggestion. "On" here usually means “we” (people in general or you-and-me). "Devrait" is the conditional of "devoir" (should/ought to), which softens the tone, and "peut-être" adds uncertainty (“maybe”). Often followed by an infinitive verb: on devrait peut-être partir / faire / prendre / se séparer.
target_language_example: On devrait peut-être en parler demain.
native_language_example: Maybe we should talk about it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal subject pronoun "on" (often meaning "we" in everyday speech) + "devrait" (conditional of "devoir") to make a suggestion or recommendation. "Y" replaces a place already mentioned ("there"), and "aller" means "to go". You can add details after it (e.g., "en train", "ensemble").
target_language_example: Il est tard, on devrait y aller maintenant.
native_language_example: It’s late; we should go there now.

meaning: “it looks like / it sounds like …”; “you’d think …”
additional_notes: Literally “one would say” (conditional of dire). Used to make a guess based on appearance, sound, or impression: On dirait Jacquart ! = “It looks like Jacquart!” Can be followed by a noun (On dirait un fantôme), or by a full clause with que (On dirait que tu es fatigué).
target_language_example: On dirait qu’il va pleuvoir.
native_language_example: It looks like it’s going to rain.

meaning: “it looks like / it seems like / you’d think (that) …”
additional_notes: Used to express an impression or guess based on what you see/notice, not a confirmed fact. Often corresponds to English “looks like” or “sounds like.” You can also use it to comment on someone’s appearance: "On dirait que tu as…" = “It looks like you…”
target_language_example: On dirait que le bus a du retard.
native_language_example: It looks like the bus is late.

meaning: "it looks like you…" / "you seem to…" (based on what I’m noticing).
additional_notes: Used to express an impression or inference rather than a certain fact. Very common in spoken French: "On dirait que tu + verb" (= it seems like you’re…). It can also sound like a gentle comment or teasing observation, depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: On dirait que tu es fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: It looks like you’re tired today.

meaning: “It looks/sounds like a…” / “You’d think it’s a…”
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of dire (“would say”) to express an impression or comparison based on what you see/hear. Common with a noun: on dirait un ange (“looks like an angel”), on dirait un train (“sounds like a train”). You can also use other articles/genders: on dirait une…, on dirait des….
target_language_example: Avec ce bruit, on dirait un avion.
native_language_example: With that noise, it sounds like a plane.

meaning: “it looks like a…” / “it seems like a…” (talking about a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Commonly used to express an impression based on appearance or situation. It’s often followed by a noun: “On dirait une extraterrestre.” For a masculine noun, use “on dirait un…”.
target_language_example: Avec ce costume, on dirait une actrice de cinéma.
native_language_example: With that costume, she looks like a movie actress.

meaning: "they say that…" / "people say that…" (it is said that…).
additional_notes: Uses the indefinite subject "on" to report what people say in general (a rumor, hearsay, or commonly held opinion) without naming who said it. It’s followed by a full clause: "On dit que + subject + verb".
target_language_example: On dit que ce restaurant est très bon.
native_language_example: They say this restaurant is really good.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal subject pronoun "on" (often meaning "we" in everyday French) + "doit" ("must/has to"). It expresses obligation or necessity. Depending on context, English may translate it as "we have to" (group obligation) or "you have to" (general instruction).
target_language_example: On doit partir tout de suite.
native_language_example: We have to leave right away.

meaning: "we/you/people must" + a reflexive verb ("have to ... oneself/each other").
additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **on** (often means “we” in everyday French, but can also mean “you” in general or “people/one”) + **doit** ("must/has to", from *devoir*) + **se** (reflexive pronoun used before a reflexive infinitive like *se battre, se protéger, se débarrasser*). The exact meaning depends on the verb that follows: *On doit se battre* = “We have to fight”; *On doit se protéger* = “We have to protect ourselves.”
target_language_example: On doit se dépêcher.
native_language_example: We have to hurry.

meaning: 'We have to go' / 'We need to leave.'
additional_notes: Used to say it’s necessary to leave now. "On" often means "we" in everyday French. "doit" (from devoir) expresses obligation/necessity, and "y aller" means "to go there" or more generally "to go/leave" depending on context.
target_language_example: Désolé, on doit y aller : il est déjà tard.
native_language_example: Sorry, we have to go: it’s already late.

meaning: “we/people … some (of it) / about it,” with *en* replacing “de + something.”
additional_notes: *On* is an indefinite subject meaning “we,” “people,” or “you” (in general). *En* is a pronoun that usually replaces something introduced by **de** (or a quantity/partitive idea): **avoir besoin de** → *On en a besoin* (“We need it / we need some.”); **entendre parler de** → *On en a entendu parler* (“We heard about it.”). The exact English translation depends on the verb: *en* can mean “of it,” “some,” or “about it.”
target_language_example: On en parle demain.
native_language_example: We’ll talk about it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the pronouns **on** (often means “we” in everyday French, or “you/people” in general) and **en** (“some”, “some of it/them”, referring back to something already mentioned). Common with quantities: **on en a plein** (“we have lots”), **on n’en a plus** (“we don’t have any left”), **on en a la preuve** (“we have proof of it”).
target_language_example: Tu veux des biscuits ? On en a encore.
native_language_example: Do you want cookies? We still have some.

meaning: "we are" (very common in spoken French), or "one/people are."
additional_notes: "On" uses the verb form "est" (3rd person singular), but it often refers to "we" in everyday speech instead of "nous sommes": "On est fatigués" = "We’re tired." It can also mean people in general: "En France, on est souvent en retard" = "In France, people are often late." Adjectives usually match the real people being talked about (plural, masculine/feminine).
target_language_example: On est prêts à partir.
native_language_example: We’re ready to leave.

meaning: "we're in" / "it's" (used to locate yourself in a place, time period, or situation).
additional_notes: Common with months and seasons (on est en juin = it’s June), with many countries/regions that take "en" (on est en Amérique), and with states/situations (on est en liaison = we’re connected/linked; on est en république = we’re in a republic). For most masculine countries you usually use "au" instead (e.g., au Canada), but "on est en" stays the same when the country uses "en".
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas répondre : on est en réunion.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t answer: we’re in a meeting.

meaning: “we’re in the middle of … / we’re currently …”
additional_notes: Used to emphasize an action that is happening right now (ongoing). It’s followed by an infinitive verb: on est en train de + infinitive (e.g., on est en train de dîner). "On" often means “we” in everyday French, though it can also mean “someone/people” depending on context.
target_language_example: On est en train de travailler, je te rappelle plus tard.
native_language_example: We’re working right now; I’ll call you back later.

additional_notes: "On" often means "we" in everyday French. "On est" = "we are". Adding "tous" emphasizes that it’s true for all the people in the group (everyone), not just some.
target_language_example: On est tous prêts ?
native_language_example: Are we all ready?

additional_notes: "On" is very common in spoken French and often means "we" (instead of "nous"), but it can also be general/impersonal like "people" or "you". "Faire" can mean "to do" (an action/job) or "to make" (create/produce something): *On fait notre boulot* (we do our job), *On fait du pain* (we make bread).
target_language_example: Ce soir, on fait des pâtes.
native_language_example: Tonight, we're making pasta.

meaning: “So what do we do?” / “What do we do (now)?”
additional_notes: Very common spoken question to ask what the plan is or what to do next. Here, **on** usually means “we” (or “people in general”), and **faire** is “to do.” You can add **maintenant** (“now”) or **avec + noun/pronoun** to mean “What do we do with…?” (e.g., *On fait quoi avec ça ?*).
target_language_example: On fait quoi après le déjeuner ?
native_language_example: What do we do after lunch?

meaning: "we/people/one have/has it/him/her" (often in the passé composé: "we/they/people ... have done/seen/found it").
additional_notes: "On" can mean "we" (informal spoken French), "people/they" (general), or "one". "L'" is a shortened direct-object pronoun ("le" or "la") placed before the verb; it can refer to "it", "him", or "her" depending on context. "A" is the present of "avoir" used as the auxiliary in the passé composé (e.g., on l'a vu = we/they saw it).
target_language_example: On l'a déjà entendu, ce bruit.
native_language_example: We've already heard that noise.

additional_notes: "On" is a very common subject meaning "we" in everyday French, or more generally "people/they/one" (an unspecified subject). "Les" means "them" and comes before the verb (on les déteste = we hate them). It refers to people or things already known from context, and agrees in gender/number only in certain cases (e.g., past participle: on les a vus/vues).
target_language_example: On les voit tous les jours.
native_language_example: We see them every day.

meaning: 'someone (unspecified) has/have done [something] to him/her' (or 'someone gave/asked/taught him/her …').
additional_notes: "On" is an indefinite subject meaning "someone/people/they" (often used when you don’t know or don’t want to say who did it). "Lui" is the indirect object pronoun meaning "to him" or "to her". "A" is the auxiliary verb "avoir" in the passé composé, so this pattern is used to describe what was done to/for that person: On lui a + past participle (demandé, enseigné, volé, etc.).
target_language_example: On lui a expliqué le problème, mais il n’a pas compris.
native_language_example: They explained the problem to him, but he didn’t understand.

additional_notes: Very common pattern to talk about theft. "On" means “someone/they” (often unknown). "lui" = “to him/her.” Past tense: "a volé" (stole/has stolen). You then add the stolen item (masculine singular with "son"; for a feminine item you’d use "sa", and for plural "ses").
target_language_example: On lui a volé son sac dans le métro.
native_language_example: Someone stole his/her bag on the subway.

additional_notes: "On" is an impersonal subject meaning "someone/people/they" (or sometimes "we" in casual speech). "m'" = "me/to me" and "a" = "has" (from "avoir"). It’s very common when you don’t know or don’t want to say who did something: "On m’a dit…" = "I was told…" / "Someone told me…".
target_language_example: On m’a donné les mauvaises directions.
native_language_example: I was given the wrong directions.

additional_notes: Uses the indefinite subject "on" (someone/people/they) + "m'" (to me) + "a dit" (has said). Often introduces reported information: "On m'a dit de..." (I was told to...), or "On m'a dit que..." (I was told that...).
target_language_example: On m'a dit que le magasin fermait à 18h.
native_language_example: I was told that the store closes at 6 p.m.

on m'a dit que vous étiez

target_language_multi_word_term: on m'a dit que vous étiez
meaning: "I was told that you were…" / "They told me you were…"
additional_notes: "On" is an impersonal subject meaning "someone/people/they" (often you don’t know or don’t say who). "m’a dit" = "told me" (past). After "on m’a dit que", French uses the imperfect: "vous étiez" ("you were"). You typically follow it with a place (ici/là), a state (malade), or a situation (parti, proches).
target_language_example: On m’a dit que vous étiez en vacances.
native_language_example: I was told that you were on vacation.

meaning: "we/you/people" + "don’t / doesn’t" (start of a negative sentence with *on*).
additional_notes: *On* is a very common subject pronoun meaning “we” (often in spoken French), “people/one” (in general statements), or sometimes “you” (especially in instructions). *Ne* is the first part of negation (usually completed by *pas*, *jamais*, *plus*, *rien*, etc.). In informal speech, *ne* is often dropped (*On joue pas*), but it’s kept in more formal writing.
target_language_example: On ne comprend pas pourquoi il est parti.
native_language_example: We don’t understand why he left.

meaning: “one must not / you mustn’t / you shouldn’t” (it’s forbidden or not advisable).
additional_notes: Uses the subject pronoun "on" in a general sense (“people/one/you” in general). "devoir" ("doit") expresses obligation; in the negative ("ne ... pas"), it expresses prohibition or strong advice not to do something. Common for rules, laws, and social norms.
target_language_example: On ne doit pas fumer ici.
native_language_example: You mustn’t smoke here.

additional_notes: Uses the subject pronoun "on" (often meaning "we" in everyday French, or "people/one" in general statements) + the negative of "pouvoir" (to be able to). The negative word after "peut" can vary: "on ne peut pas" (can’t), "on ne peut jamais" (can never), "on ne peut aller nulle part" (can’t go anywhere). With "ne...que", it means "only": "On ne peut qu'espérer" = "We can only hope."
target_language_example: Désolé, on ne peut pas entrer ici.
native_language_example: Sorry, we can't go in here.

additional_notes: Common way to say something isn’t possible or can’t be done. Literally “one cannot,” but in everyday French it often means “we can’t,” “you can’t,” or “people can’t,” depending on context. Followed by an infinitive: on ne peut pas + verb (e.g., on ne peut pas ouvrir…).
target_language_example: Désolé, on ne peut pas entrer ici.
native_language_example: Sorry, you can’t come in here.

meaning: "you/we can’t do" / "it’s not possible to do".
additional_notes: "On" is an impersonal subject meaning "one/you/we/people (in general)" depending on context. This pattern is often followed by a noun or expression (e.g., "on ne peut pas faire grand-chose" = "you can’t do much"), or used with a general statement about what’s possible or impossible. In English it often becomes "you can’t…", "we can’t…", or "there’s no way to…".
target_language_example: On ne peut pas faire ça sans aide.
native_language_example: We can’t do that without help.

additional_notes: Common negative pattern: **ne ... rien** = “not ... anything.” **On** is an everyday subject meaning “one/people/we” depending on context. Often followed by an infinitive: **on ne peut rien faire / prouver / y faire** (“we can’t do anything / prove anything / do anything about it”).
target_language_example: Sans aide, on ne peut rien faire.
native_language_example: Without help, you can’t do anything.

additional_notes: Uses the indefinite subject "on" (meaning "we," "people," or "they" in general). It’s very often followed by "pas" (negation): "On ne sait pas…" = "We/People don’t know…" You can add words like "encore" (yet) or "toujours" (still): "On ne sait toujours pas…" = "It’s still not known…"
target_language_example: On ne sait pas pourquoi il est parti.
native_language_example: We don’t know why he left.

meaning: "we're not going to" / "we're not about to".
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about something that won’t happen (often a decision or strong refusal): « On ne va pas + infinitif ». « On » commonly means “we” or “people” in general. In speech, the « ne » is often dropped: « On va pas… ».
target_language_example: On ne va pas abandonner maintenant.
native_language_example: We’re not going to give up now.

meaning: "we talk / we’re talking" (or "people talk"), often introducing the topic being discussed.
additional_notes: "On" is a very common subject pronoun meaning "we" in everyday French (or sometimes "people/they/you" in a general sense). "On parle (de…)" means "we’re talking (about…)" / "we discuss (…)": *On parle d’autre chose ?* = "Can we talk about something else?". Without *de*, it can mean “we’re talking [topic/area]”: *On parle affaires.* = "We’re talking business.". With a language: *On parle italien.* = "We speak Italian."
target_language_example: On parle de ça demain ?
native_language_example: Shall we talk about that tomorrow?

additional_notes: "On" is a very common subject meaning "people in general" or informal "we" (instead of "nous"). "On peut" expresses ability/possibility/permission depending on context: stating what is possible or allowed (On peut boire cette eau…), making general statements (On peut pardonner…), or asking permission/making a suggestion as a question (On peut venir ? = Can we come?/May we come?).
target_language_example: On peut entrer ?
native_language_example: May we come in?

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is possible or allowed. "On" is an informal way to mean "we," but it can also mean "people in general" or "you" (like English "you can..."). Often followed by an infinitive or by "autre chose / autrement" to suggest alternatives. It can also introduce an offer: "On peut faire quelque chose pour toi ?" = "Can we do something for you?"
target_language_example: On peut faire une pause si tu veux.
native_language_example: We can take a break if you want.

meaning: we/you/people can do that; it’s possible to do that.
additional_notes: "On" is a very common subject meaning "we" in everyday French, but it can also mean "you" (in general) or "people/one." "Peut" is from "pouvoir" (can/to be able to). Used to ask permission or check if something is allowed/possible: "On peut faire ça ici ?" = "Can we do that here?"
target_language_example: D’accord, on peut faire ça demain.
native_language_example: Okay, we can do that tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common pattern with the indefinite subject pronoun on (“we/you/people/one”) + peut (“can”) + le (direct object pronoun meaning “it” for a masculine noun, or “him”). Often used to ask permission or possibility: On peut le garder ? (“Can we keep it?”). For a feminine noun, use on peut la; for plural, on peut les.
target_language_example: On peut le prendre avec nous ?
native_language_example: Can we take it with us?

meaning: “we/you/one can do it” / “it’s possible to do it.”
additional_notes: On is a very common subject in spoken French meaning “we” (often) or “you/people in general” depending on context. Peut is from pouvoir (“can/to be able to”), and le refers to “it” (a previously mentioned thing). Used to suggest a plan (On peut le faire ensemble.), encourage someone (On peut le faire !), or ask if something is possible (On peut le faire ?).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, on peut le faire demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we can do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to ask to have a conversation, often about something important or private. Literally “one/we can talk,” but in everyday speech it usually means “Can we talk?” You can add: “un peu” (for a bit), “quelque part” (somewhere/in private), or politeness like “s’il te plaît.”
target_language_example: On peut parler deux minutes, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can we talk for two minutes, please?

additional_notes: Very common spoken form of "on ne peut pas" (the "ne" is dropped in everyday speech). "On" often means "we" or "you" in a general sense, depending on context. Used to say something can’t be done or isn’t allowed.
target_language_example: On peut pas entrer ici sans billet.
native_language_example: We can’t go in here without a ticket.

additional_notes: Common pattern: "On peut se + verb ?" to suggest or ask if something is possible, especially with reciprocal/reflexive verbs (se voir = see each other, se revoir = see each other again, se cacher = hide, se débrouiller = manage). "On" often means "we" in everyday French (though it can also mean "one/people in general").
target_language_example: On peut se voir demain ?
native_language_example: Can we see each other tomorrow?

additional_notes: Literally "one can see." Very common with the impersonal subject "on" to mean "you" in general, "we," or "people." Often used to point out what is visible or noticeable: "On peut voir…" = "You can see…" / "You can notice…".
target_language_example: D'ici, on peut voir la mer.
native_language_example: From here, you can see the sea.

additional_notes: Literally “we can go there,” but very often used to suggest starting or leaving: “Ready? Let’s go.” It can also mean something is possible/allowed (“I think we can go.”). Variations: “On peut y aller ?” (Shall we go?), “On peut y aller doucement ?” (Can we go slowly / take it easy?), “On peut y aller à pied” (We can walk there).
target_language_example: Si tu es prêt(e), on peut y aller.
native_language_example: If you’re ready, we can go.

additional_notes: From the verb pouvoir (“can / to be able to”) in the conditional tense: on pourrait = “we/you/one could / might.” It’s commonly used to make a suggestion politely (On pourrait se voir bientôt. = “We could see each other soon.”) or to express a hypothetical possibility (On pourrait dire que… = “You could even say that…”). Here, on often means “we” in everyday French, but it can also mean “you” or “people in general,” depending on context.
target_language_example: On pourrait aller au cinéma ce soir, si tu veux.
native_language_example: We could go to the movies tonight, if you want.

meaning: we’re going home / let’s go home.
additional_notes: Uses "on" to mean "we" (common in spoken French). "Rentrer" means to go back/return (often home). Often used as an announcement or decision to leave and head home; can also sound like an instruction in context.
target_language_example: Il est tard, on rentre à la maison.
native_language_example: It’s late, we’re going home.

additional_notes: Used before a reflexive verb that starts with a vowel or silent h (so "se" becomes "s'": s'amuser, s'entendre, s'occuper). "On" often means "we" in everyday French, but it can also mean "people" or "you" in general. The exact English translation depends on the verb: e.g., "On s'amuse" = "We’re having fun", "On s'entend bien" = "We get along", "On s'occupe les uns des autres" = "We take care of each other".
target_language_example: On s'appelle demain.
native_language_example: We’ll call each other tomorrow.

meaning: “we/people + ourselves + of it/from it” (pronoun combo used with certain verbs).
additional_notes: This isn’t a standalone phrase with one fixed meaning: it’s the subject pronoun **on** (often meaning “we” in everyday French) + the reflexive pronoun **se** + **en** (“of it/from it/with it”). It appears in common verb phrases like **on s’en va / on s’en ira** (we’re leaving / we’ll leave), **on s’en sert** (we use it), **on s’en est sortis** (we got out of it / we managed), **on s’en charge** (we’ll take care of it), **on s’en passera** (we’ll do without it).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, on s’en occupe.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’ll take care of it.

meaning: “we/people/one have …” (passé composé with reflexive se, using être).
additional_notes: Used before a past participle: on (we/people/one) + s’ (se, “ourselves/each other”) + est (from être, the auxiliary used in reflexive verbs). Often means “we …” in everyday French: On s’est vus hier. = “We saw each other yesterday.” The past participle may agree with the subject (e.g., on s’est rencontrés / rencontrées) depending on who “on” refers to.
target_language_example: On s'est rencontrés au café.
native_language_example: We met at the café.

additional_notes: "On" is very common in spoken French and often means "we" (sometimes "they/people" in general). "S'occuper de" is followed by a person/thing: s'occuper de lui/d'elle/de toi/de vous/de ça/de tout. It can mean caring for someone (looking after) or dealing with something (taking care of a task/problem).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, on s'occupe de tout.
native_language_example: Don't worry, we'll take care of everything.

additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs (se + verb) to talk about what “we” do to ourselves or to each other: On se repose (we rest), on se calme (we calm down), on se rapproche (we get closer), on se renseigne (we get information). Very common for suggestions and inclusive instructions, like “Let’s …” or “We’re going to …”.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 18 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet up at 6 p.m.?

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb **se connaître** (“to know each other”). **On** often means “we” in everyday French (instead of **nous**). In a question (**Est-ce qu’on se connaît ?**), it can mean “Do we know each other?” or “Have we met before?”
target_language_example: Je suis sûre qu’on se connaît, on s’est déjà vus quelque part.
native_language_example: I’m sure we know each other; we’ve seen each other somewhere before.

additional_notes: Uses the verb *se connaître* (“to know each other”). *On* often means “we” in everyday spoken French. *Depuis* introduces either a starting point in time (*depuis l’enfance*, *depuis le lycée*) or a duration (*depuis dix ans* = “for ten years”).
target_language_example: On se connaît depuis trois ans.
native_language_example: We’ve known each other for three years.

additional_notes: Used to arrange a meeting point. Often followed by a location: "On se retrouve devant…" (Let’s meet in front of…), "On se retrouve dehors" (We’ll meet outside). "Où ?" means “Where?” In conversation it can also imply “See you there / we’ll meet there.”
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 18h devant le métro.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at 6 p.m. in front of the метро station.

meaning: “we’ll see each other again” / “we’ll meet again.”
additional_notes: A common way to say goodbye while implying you expect to meet again. Literally “one/people will see each other again,” but in everyday speech it often means “we’ll see each other again” (on = we). Can also sound emotional or dramatic depending on context (e.g., “de l’autre côté” can suggest the afterlife).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, on se reverra bientôt.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’ll see each other again soon.

meaning: “See you again” / “we’ll see each other again.”
additional_notes: Common goodbye phrase. "On" often means “we” (or a casual “you/we” depending on context), and "se" shows it’s reciprocal (“see each other”). Usually followed by a time expression: "On se revoit plus tard / demain / dans deux semaines."
target_language_example: D’accord, on se revoit demain matin !
native_language_example: Okay, see you again tomorrow morning!

additional_notes: Future tense of *se voir* (“to see each other”). *On* often means “we” in everyday French (instead of *nous*). It’s used to talk about a planned meeting (*On se verra tout à l’heure*), a vague future meeting (*On se verra un autre jour*), or sometimes as a warning/threat depending on context (*On se verra au tribunal*). The expression *On se verra quand on se verra* means “We’ll see when we see” (no specific plan).
target_language_example: T’inquiète, on se verra demain matin.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’ll see each other tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Literally “we see ourselves,” but it’s used to mean “we’ll see each other.” Common for making plans (“On se voit ce soir/dans une demi-heure”) or as a casual goodbye meaning “see you (soon).” It can also simply describe that you meet/see each other regularly (“On se voit presque tous les jours”).
target_language_example: D'accord, on se voit demain !
native_language_example: Okay, see you tomorrow!

meaning: "See you at the…" / "We’ll meet at the…"
