additional_notes: Used to demand that someone gives something back. Built from the imperative of **rendre** (to give back/return) + **moi** (to me) + **mon** (my, masculine singular; use **ma** for feminine, **mes** for plural). Often said in an annoyed or urgent tone: *Rends-moi mon peigne !*
target_language_example: Rends-moi mon téléphone, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me back my phone, please.

additional_notes: Usually used as the reflexive verb **se rendre compte (de + noun)** = “to realize/be aware of.” Very often you’ll see **s’en rendre compte** (“to realize it/that”), where **en** replaces something previously mentioned (e.g., a situation or fact). Example patterns: **Je me rends compte de votre situation** = “I realize your situation”; **Je m’en rends compte maintenant** = “I realize it now.”
target_language_example: Je ne m’en rendais pas compte avant.
native_language_example: I didn’t realize it before.

meaning: "visited" (someone) (past tense), as in "rendre visite à quelqu’un".
additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase **rendre visite à + person** = “to visit someone” (focuses on visiting a person, not a place). **Rendu** is the past participle of *rendre* and is used with **avoir**: *j’ai rendu visite à…* (I visited…).
target_language_example: J’ai rendu visite à ma grand-mère samedi.
native_language_example: I visited my grandmother on Saturday.

meaning: Go home. / Go back to your place.
additional_notes: Imperative (command) of "rentrer" + "chez toi" (to your home/your place), used when speaking to one person you address as "tu". For a more polite or plural version: "Rentrez chez vous." You can add "maintenant" for emphasis: "Rentre chez toi maintenant."
target_language_example: Il est tard, rentre chez toi.
native_language_example: It’s late, go home.

additional_notes: From the verb rentrer (“to return/get back”). With “à la maison” it means returning home. In context it can be an instruction (Rentre à la maison ! = Go home!) or describe someone’s return (Papa rentre à la maison demain. = Dad is coming home tomorrow).
target_language_example: Rentre à la maison avant la nuit.
native_language_example: Come home before nightfall.

meaning: to go back home / to return to (someone’s) place.
additional_notes: Used with a person after "chez": rentrer chez moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux/elles (“go back to my/your/his/her/our/your/their place”). It can also be used with a name: rentrer chez Marie (“go back to Marie’s place”). In everyday French, it often just means “to go home.”
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, je vais rentrer chez moi.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I’m going to go home.

meaning: to go back home; to return to my place.
additional_notes: Used when you’re away and want/need to return home. « rentrer » = to go back/come back (often to a usual place), and « chez moi » = at my place/home. You can swap the pronoun: rentrer chez toi (your place), rentrer chez lui/elle (his/her place), rentrer chez nous/vous/eux/elles.
target_language_example: Il est tard, je vais rentrer chez moi.
native_language_example: It’s late; I’m going to go back home.

meaning: to go back home (to your place).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "rentrer" (to go back/come back) + "chez" + a stressed pronoun. "chez toi" means “at your place / to your place” when used with a verb of movement. You can swap the pronoun: "rentrer chez moi" (my place), "chez lui/elle" (his/her place), "chez nous/vous/eux/elles". Often used to tell someone to go home: "Il est temps de rentrer chez toi."
target_language_example: Après le cours, je vais rentrer chez toi pour te rendre ton livre.
native_language_example: After the class, I'm going to go back to your place to return your book.

additional_notes: Used when addressing one person formally (vous) or multiple people. With verbs like "aller", "vouloir", "devoir", you often see the infinitive: "Vous devriez rentrer chez vous". "Rentrer" often implies returning home (going back), while "aller chez vous" is simply going to your place.
target_language_example: Après le travail, vous pouvez rentrer chez vous.
native_language_example: After work, you can go home.

meaning: to go home; to return home.
additional_notes: Used with the verb rentrer (“to go back/come back”) + à la maison (“home”). It means going back to where you live (or where you’re staying). Common with devoir (must/have to), vouloir (want), and aller (going to): « Je vais rentrer à la maison. »
target_language_example: On rentre à la maison après le travail.
native_language_example: We go home after work.

meaning: Go home / go back to your place.
additional_notes: Imperative of « rentrer » (to go back/return), used either for (1) one person with « vous » (polite/formal) or (2) several people. « chez vous » means “to your home/at your place.” Often used as an instruction/command.
target_language_example: Il est tard, rentrez chez vous maintenant.
native_language_example: It’s late—go home now.

meaning: went home; returned to his place.
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of "rentrer" with "être": "il est rentré chez lui" = "he went/returned home." "Chez lui" means "at his place/home" (for a man). You can change it: "chez elle" (her place), "chez moi" (my place), "chez toi" (your place, informal), "chez nous" (our place), "chez vous" (your place, formal/plural), "chez eux/elles" (their place).
target_language_example: Il est rentré chez lui vers minuit.
native_language_example: He went home around midnight.

additional_notes: Past participle of "rentrer" used with "être" in the passé composé: "être rentré(e) à la maison" = to have returned home. It agrees with the subject: rentré (m.), rentrée (f.), rentrés (m. pl.), rentrées (f. pl.). Often used with a time: "Je suis rentré(e) à la maison à 20h."
target_language_example: Je suis rentré à la maison après le travail.
native_language_example: I came back home after work.

additional_notes: An informal singular command (imperative) meaning “rest” or “get some rest,” addressed to one person you call tu. From the verb se reposer (“to rest”); it literally means “rest yourself.” You can add words like bien (well), un peu (a little), ici (here), pendant un moment (for a moment) to specify how/where/for how long.
target_language_example: Tu as l’air fatigué : repose-toi un peu.
native_language_example: You look tired: rest a little.

respecter le code de la route

target_language_multi_word_term: respecter le code de la route
meaning: to follow/obey the rules of the road (traffic laws).
additional_notes: Used when talking about driving and road safety. "Respecter" here means to obey or comply with rules. "Le code de la route" is the set of traffic laws (signs, speed limits, right of way, etc.).
target_language_example: Pour éviter une amende, il faut respecter le code de la route.
native_language_example: To avoid a fine, you have to follow the rules of the road.

additional_notes: Used to say you must comply with rules (laws, school rules, game rules). Very common with obligation expressions like « devoir » (must) and « devoir/ falloir » or « il est important de… ». You can specify which rules with « les règles de… » (e.g., « les règles de la circulation » = traffic rules).
target_language_example: Au travail, il faut respecter les règles de sécurité.
native_language_example: At work, you have to follow the safety rules.

additional_notes: Used to compare similarity in appearance or general resemblance: « X ressemble à Y ». You can use it for people, animals, objects, or even situations/ideas (« Ça ressemble à un plan » = “That looks like a plan”). Note the accent: « à ».
target_language_example: Tu ressembles à ta sœur.
native_language_example: You look like your sister.

additional_notes: From the verb **ressembler à** (“to look like / to resemble”). It’s followed by a person or thing: **Il/Elle ressemble à un/une…**. Use **à un** with masculine nouns and **à une** with feminine nouns (e.g., *Elle ressemble à une actrice*). Note: French uses **à**, even though English says “resemble” (no “to”).
target_language_example: Il ressemble à un professeur avec ces lunettes.
native_language_example: He looks like a teacher with those glasses.

additional_notes: From the verb **ressembler à** (“to look like / to resemble”). You use **ressembler à + noun** to compare appearance or impression. It agrees with the subject: **il ressemble à…**, **elle ressemble à…**, **ça/cela ressemble à…**. Use **à un** for masculine nouns and **à une** for feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Ce dessin ressemble à une photo.
native_language_example: This drawing looks like a photo.

additional_notes: General term for the fast-food industry/style of eating (burgers, fries, etc.). Often used with verbs like manger/consommer (to eat/consume) or with restaurant (un restaurant de restauration rapide).
target_language_example: On évite la restauration rapide pendant la semaine.
native_language_example: We avoid fast food during the week.

additional_notes: From **rester** (to remain) + **-t-** (linking sound) + **il** (he/it). Used in formal/written French to form questions like **Reste-t-il des billets ?** = “Are there any tickets left?” It often means “is there any … left?” or “do we have any … left?” depending on context. With time: **Combien de temps nous reste-t-il ?** = “How much time do we have left?”
target_language_example: Reste-t-il du café, ou faut-il en acheter ?
native_language_example: Is there any coffee left, or do we need to buy some?

additional_notes: Used when someone is sick, resting, or advised not to get up. Often appears with advice verbs like "devoir" (must) and "(re)commander / conseiller" (recommend/advise): « Tu devrais rester au lit. »
target_language_example: J'ai de la fièvre, donc je vais rester au lit aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I have a fever, so I'm going to stay in bed today.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone stays in the current place instead of leaving. Very common with modal verbs like devoir (must), pouvoir (can), and devoir/ falloir for obligation: « Je peux rester ici ? » / « Nous devons rester ici. ». You can change the place word: « rester là » (stay there), « rester chez moi » (stay at my place).
target_language_example: Je vais rester ici jusqu'à demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay here until tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that you want to extend your stay/time in a place. Very common with polite question forms like « Est-ce que je peux… ? », « Puis-je… ? » (formal), or « Pourrais-tu… ? » (to a friend), and with « Veuillez… » for polite instructions/requests.
target_language_example: Je peux rester un peu plus longtemps, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can I stay a little longer, please?

additional_notes: Used to say you will not go out and will remain at your home. Common with near-future plans: « Je vais rester… ». Also used for advice/instructions (e.g., from a doctor): « On te conseille de rester… ».
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, je reste à la maison parce qu'il pleut.
native_language_example: Today, I'm staying at home because it's raining.

meaning: back to square one; back to the starting point.
additional_notes: Used when a plan or process fails and you have to start over from the beginning. Often appears after verbs like « être » (être de retour à la case départ) or alone as a comment: « Retour à la case départ. » The image comes from board games: going back to the starting square.
target_language_example: On a perdu le dossier, alors c’est retour à la case départ.
native_language_example: We lost the file, so it’s back to square one.

meaning: to come back here next week.
additional_notes: Used to talk about returning to this place (“ici”) during the following week (“la semaine prochaine”). Often appears with the near future tense: « aller + infinitif » (e.g., « Tu vas revenir… » / « Vous allez revenir… »). In questions, you’ll see « tu » (informal singular) vs « vous » (formal singular or plural).
target_language_example: Je vais revenir ici la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: I'm going to come back here next week.

meaning: just for; only for (for the sole purpose/benefit).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize exclusivity: something is done only for a particular purpose ("rien que pour te voir" = just to see you) or reserved only for someone ("rien que pour elle" = just for her). You can also use "rien que" without "pour" to mean "just/only" ("rien que te parler" = just talking to you).
target_language_example: Je suis venu rien que pour te dire merci.
native_language_example: I came just to say thank you.

additional_notes: Means “nothing else” after a negative (often with ne…pas/plus, but in speech you may hear it without ne: « J’ai rien d’autre. »). In questions, it often means “anything else?”: « Vous n’avez rien d’autre ? » = “Don’t you have anything else?” / “Do you have anything else?” Can also follow a verb like penser à: « penser à rien d’autre » = “to think of nothing else.”
target_language_example: Je n'ai rien d'autre à ajouter.
native_language_example: I have nothing else to add.

additional_notes: Used to say you have no other tasks/activities planned (often implying you’re free or just killing time). Very common with the informal negation that drops "ne": "J’ai rien d’autre à faire"; in more formal French you may hear "Je n’ai rien d’autre à faire." It can also be a question: "Vous n’avez rien d’autre à faire ?" (often a slightly critical or surprised tone: “Don’t you have anything better to do?”).
target_language_example: On peut aller se promener : je n’ai rien d’autre à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: We can go for a walk: I have nothing else to do today.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to mean “nothing about” (rien de + noun): « Rien de nouveau » = “Nothing new.” With a past participle (rien de + past participle), it means “nothing (to be) … / nothing …ed planned, prepared, etc.”: « Rien de prévu » = “Nothing planned.” Often used with ne: « On ne sait rien de… » = “We don’t know anything about…”.
target_language_example: Je n’ai rien de spécial à dire.
native_language_example: I have nothing special to say.

meaning: nothing more; no more than that.
additional_notes: Used to limit or downplay what you just said: “that’s all.” Common after a statement (“Je veux juste être ton ami, rien de plus.”) or alone as a short reply (“Rien de plus, merci.”). With a negative it often means “I won’t say anything else” (“Je ne dirai rien de plus.”).
target_language_example: Je suis venu pour discuter, rien de plus.
native_language_example: I came to talk, nothing more.

meaning: to say nothing; not say anything.
additional_notes: Used with negation to mean “say nothing.” Common patterns: **sans rien dire** (“without saying anything”), **ne rien dire** (“to say nothing”), **je ne peux rien dire** (“I can’t say anything”), and in informal speech the **ne** is often dropped: **je peux rien dire**. Also **Ça ne veut rien dire** means “That doesn’t mean anything / That makes no sense.”
target_language_example: Il est resté silencieux sans rien dire.
native_language_example: He stayed quiet without saying anything.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the negation **ne … rien** with the verb **dire** in the past tense: **(ne) + avoir + rien + dit**. In everyday speech, **ne** is often dropped: **Elle t’a rien dit ?** = **Elle ne t’a rien dit ?**.
target_language_example: Je suis désolé, je ne t’ai rien dit parce que je ne savais pas.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I didn’t tell you anything because I didn’t know.

meaning: 'nothing' (as the subject of a negative verb).
additional_notes: Used when "rien" (= nothing) comes before the verb: "Rien ne + verbe...". In this structure, "ne" is used without "pas" (unlike most negations). Often followed by other words like pronouns or the verb: "Rien ne s'est passé" (Nothing happened), "Rien ne me retient" (Nothing is holding me back), "Rien ne vaut..." (Nothing is worth/equals...).
target_language_example: Rien ne m'empêchera d'essayer.
native_language_example: Nothing will stop me from trying.

rien ne me rendrait plus heureuse que de

target_language_multi_word_term: rien ne me rendrait plus heureuse que de
additional_notes: A strong way to say what would bring you the greatest happiness. Uses the conditional "rendrait" (“would make”) and a comparison "plus … que" (“more … than”). It’s followed by "de" + an infinitive (e.g., "de te voir" = “to see you”). You can change "heureuse" to match the speaker: "heureux" (male speaker), "heureuse" (female speaker).
target_language_example: Rien ne me rendrait plus heureuse que de passer la soirée avec toi.
native_language_example: Nothing would make me happier than spending the evening with you.

rien ne me rendrait plus heureux que de

target_language_multi_word_term: rien ne me rendrait plus heureux que de
additional_notes: A strong, heartfelt way to say that one thing is your greatest wish. Uses the conditional rendrait (“would make”), so it often sounds polite/romantic. After que, you usually use de + infinitive (de te voir…, de t’aider…, de passer du temps avec toi…). You can change heureux to match the speaker: heureux (male), heureuse (female), and change me to another person (te, le/la, nous, etc.).
target_language_example: Rien ne me rendrait plus heureux que de passer la journée avec toi.
native_language_example: Nothing would make me happier than spending the day with you.

meaning: 'nothing to' (followed by an infinitive) / 'nothing about' (with a noun phrase).
additional_notes: Commonly used in the pattern "(ne)... rien à + infinitive" to say there is nothing to do/offer/fear/etc.: "Je n’ai rien à dire". In informal speech, "ne" is often dropped: "J’ai rien à dire". With verbs like "piger/comprendre", "rien à + [noun clause]" means 'nothing (at all) about/ of what...': "Je ne comprends rien à ce que tu dis" = 'I don’t understand anything you’re saying.'
target_language_example: Je n’ai rien à ajouter.
native_language_example: I have nothing to add.

additional_notes: Used when talking about a car’s extra tire/wheel kept for emergencies (like a flat). Often found in the trunk (le coffre). In everyday speech you may also hear "roue de rechange".
target_language_example: On a crevé, mais heureusement on a une roue de secours.
native_language_example: We got a flat, but luckily we have a spare tire.

additional_notes: A common general term for tape that sticks (often like Scotch tape). Usually used with the partitive: du ruban adhésif (“some tape”). In everyday speech you may also hear simply du scotch (informal/brand-based).
target_language_example: Tu peux me passer du ruban adhésif, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you pass me some tape, please?

additional_notes: Job title for the person who leads the editorial team of a newspaper, magazine, or other publication and makes the final decisions on what gets published. Often used with "du/de la/des" (rédacteur en chef du journal) or "à" to indicate the publication (rédacteur en chef à Rolling Stone). Feminine form: "rédactrice en chef".
target_language_example: Elle est rédactrice en chef d'un magazine de mode.
native_language_example: She is the editor-in-chief of a fashion magazine.

additional_notes: “Répondre” is followed by “à” before the thing/person you answer (répondre à une question / à quelqu’un / à ça). In everyday French, you often use it with “ça” (“that”) to refuse or say you don’t have to answer.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas répondre à cette question maintenant.
native_language_example: I can’t answer this question right now.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "répondre" with the preposition "à" (répondre à + noun/pronoun). Very common in questions and negative statements: "Je ne peux pas répondre à cette question"; polite request: "Pouvez-vous répondre à cette question ?".
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne sais pas répondre à cette question.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't know how to answer this question.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "répondre" with the preposition "à" (répondre à + noun/pronoun). Common in formal contexts like interviews, court, or school; often appears with verbs like "refuser de" (to refuse to) or "pouvoir" (to be able to).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous répondre à la question, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you answer the question, please?

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *résoudre*: *j’ai résolu*, *tu as résolu*, *il/elle a résolu*. Uses *avoir* as the helping verb. *Résoudre* often translates to “to solve” in everyday contexts (a problem, an issue).
target_language_example: On a enfin résolu le problème.
native_language_example: We finally solved the problem.

additional_notes: Used to say you (or someone) will find a solution to a specific issue. Conjugate "résoudre" to match the subject (je dois résoudre…, nous devons résoudre…). Often used with can/can't, must/have to, need to: "Je peux / je ne peux pas", "Je dois", "Il faut".
target_language_example: On va résoudre ce problème ensemble.
native_language_example: We’re going to solve this problem together.

additional_notes: Used to talk about finding a solution to a difficulty or issue. Often appears with helper verbs like « pouvoir » (As-tu pu…? = Were you able to…?), « finir par » (ended up managing to…), and « parvenir à » (to manage to…). You can specify the type of problem with « le problème de/du… » (e.g., « le problème du logement » = the housing problem).
target_language_example: On doit résoudre le problème avant demain.
native_language_example: We have to solve the problem before tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb réussir + à + infinitive to say someone was able to do something (often after effort or difficulty). It’s usually in the past (a réussi à / as réussi à / j’ai réussi à), but can also be present (je réussis à…). Don’t confuse with réussir un examen (“to pass an exam”).
target_language_example: J’ai enfin réussi à finir mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I finally managed to finish my homework.

additional_notes: Imperative of "se réveiller" (to wake up). Used to tell one person to wake up; it uses "toi" because it’s addressed with "tu". For a more formal or plural version, use "réveillez-vous".
target_language_example: Réveille-toi, on est en retard !
native_language_example: Wake up, we’re late!

meaning: “it’s about / it’s a matter of” (used in: « il s’agit de… »).
additional_notes: Used almost always in the impersonal expression « il s’agit de + noun/infinitive », to clarify what something is about or what the issue is. Very common in negatives and questions: « il ne s’agit pas de… » (“it’s not about…”) and « s’il s’agit de… » (“if it’s a question of…”).
target_language_example: Il s’agit d’un malentendu.
native_language_example: It’s a misunderstanding.

meaning: to have fun; to enjoy oneself.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb (amuser = “to amuse,” s’amuser = “to amuse oneself” → “to have fun”). Very common with purpose: « pour s’amuser » (“for fun / just to have fun”). Also used to say people seem to be having fun: « Ils ont l’air de bien s’amuser » (“They seem to be having a good time”).
target_language_example: On va s'amuser ce soir !
native_language_example: We’re going to have fun tonight!

meaning: "is called" / "is named" (for a person or thing).
additional_notes: From the verb "s'appeler" (to be called), used to ask or say someone’s name. Common in questions like "Comment s'appelle-t-il ?" (What’s his name?) or statements like "Il s'appelle…" (His name is…).
target_language_example: Elle s'appelle Marie.
native_language_example: Her name is Marie.

meaning: to work things out; to come to an agreement; to sort itself out.
additional_notes: Used when you think a problem can be resolved or a compromise can be found (often in negotiations: price, schedule, plans). With a subject like « ça / tout », it means things will end up being okay: « Ça va s'arranger » = “It’ll work out.”
target_language_example: Pour l'heure, ne t'inquiète pas : ça va s'arranger.
native_language_example: For now, don’t worry: it’ll work out.

meaning: “(oneself) from it / away / out of it” (se + en, used with many verbs).
additional_notes:
“S’en” is the combination of the reflexive pronoun “se” (myself/yourself/himself…) + “en” (“of it/from it/some”). It appears in lots of common verb phrases, and the exact English translation depends on the verb:
- s’en aller = to go away/leave
- s’en sortir = to get out of it / get by / make it through
- s’en foutre (informal) = to not care at all
- s’en douter = to suspect it / to have guessed
In a sentence, “s’en” is placed before the verb (or before the auxiliary in compound tenses): Il s’en va, Il s’en est sorti.
target_language_example: Ne t'en fais pas, tu vas t'en sortir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you’ll get through it.

meaning: "gets by / manages / copes"; "makes it through" (a situation).
additional_notes: From the verb "s'en sortir". It’s used to talk about how someone is doing in a difficult situation (a problem, a challenge, financially, emotionally, etc.). Very common with adverbs like "bien" (well) or "mal" (badly): "Elle s'en sort bien." = “She’s managing well.” The "en" refers to “out of it/out of that situation” and doesn’t translate directly into English.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas comment il s'en sort avec tout ce travail.
native_language_example: I don’t know how he manages with all that work.

meaning: “(he/she/it) has” in the passé composé for reflexive/pronominal verbs (se + est).
additional_notes: Contraction of “se” (or “s’” before a vowel) + “est” (3rd person singular of “être”). Used to form the past tense of pronominal/reflexive verbs: e.g., “s’est passé” (happened / went), “s’est cassé” (broke). Often translates to English “has” or “got” depending on the verb and context, not literally “is itself.”
target_language_example: Il s'est réveillé très tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: He woke up very early this morning.

additional_notes: Used in formal-style questions with inversion: *s’est-il passé* = “did it happen” / “has it happened.” Very common in: *Que s’est-il passé ?* (“What happened?”). You can also ask *S’est-il passé quelque chose ?* (“Did anything happen?”). In everyday speech, people often use *Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?* instead of inversion.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qui s'est passé hier soir ?
native_language_example: What happened last night?

additional_notes: Past tense of **se passer** (“to happen/to go”), used with events or experiences (a flight, a trip, an exam, a meeting). It agrees with the subject: **Ça s’est bien passé** (It went well), **Le vol s’est bien passé** (The flight went well), **Tout s’est bien passé** (Everything went well). Often used in questions to check how something went: **Ça s’est bien passé ?**
target_language_example: L’entretien s’est bien passé, je suis soulagé(e).
native_language_example: The interview went well; I’m relieved.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of **se passer** = “to happen.” Used with an impersonal subject like **ça**, **quelque chose**, or **qu’est-ce qui**: **Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?** (“What happened?”). In questions, **qui** is usually correct (subject), not **que**. Although it looks like English “passed,” it usually does **not** mean “passed (an exam)” here.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce qui s'est passé hier soir.
native_language_example: I don't know what happened last night.

meaning: takes care of; looks after; handles.
additional_notes: From the verb "s’occuper de" (to take care of / deal with). It’s followed by a person or a thing: "s’occuper de moi" (take care of me) or "s’occuper de ces choses" (handle these things). Often used to mean caring for someone (emotionally/practically) or managing a task. The "s’" changes with the subject: je m’occupe de…, tu t’occupes de…, il/elle s’occupe de…, nous nous occupons de…, vous vous occupez de…, ils/elles s’occupent de….
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je m’occupe de tout.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of everything.

additional_notes: Past perfect form of **se mettre d’accord (avec quelqu’un / sur quelque chose)**. Used to say that an agreement had already been made before another past moment: *On s’était mis d’accord* = “We had agreed.” You’ll also see: **Je m’étais mis(e) d’accord**, **on s’était mis d’accord**, **ils/elles s’étaient mis(es) d’accord**.
target_language_example: On s’était mis d’accord sur l’heure, mais il est arrivé en retard.
native_language_example: We had agreed on the time, but he arrived late.

additional_notes: Elision: "si" becomes "s'" before a vowel sound ("il"), so "si il" → "s'il". Used with "il" meaning either "he" or impersonal "it" (e.g., "s'il y a..." = "if there is..."). Also common in "comme s'il..." = "as if...".
target_language_example: Dis-moi s'il vient ce soir.
native_language_example: Tell me if he's coming tonight.

meaning: "please, don’t…" (polite request to not do something).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone (tu) not to do/say something. It’s typically followed by a verb in the negative form: ne + verb + pas (or another negative word). Example pattern: « S’il te plaît, ne + verb + pas ».
target_language_example: S'il te plaît, ne parle pas si fort.
native_language_example: Please, don’t speak so loudly.

meaning: "Please don’t…" (polite request to not do something).
additional_notes: Used to start a polite negative request or instruction. It’s followed by a verb in the negative: “ne + verb + pas” (e.g., « S’il vous plaît, ne bougez pas. »). This is the formal/polite version (with « vous »).
target_language_example: S'il vous plaît, ne vous inquiétez pas.
native_language_example: Please, don’t worry.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to contact you if there is new information or a new development. Very common after a request like "Appellez-moi…" or "Je te/vous appelle…". Literally: "if there is something new."
target_language_example: Envoie-moi un message s'il y a du nouveau.
native_language_example: Send me a message if there’s any news.

additional_notes: Used to refer to or address a king, queen, emperor, etc. The possessive changes with the monarch’s gender: « Sa Majesté » for a woman (queen) and « Son Majesté » for a man (king). Often treated as a third-person noun in formal speech: « Sa Majesté attend. »
target_language_example: Sa Majesté recevra les invités à midi.
native_language_example: Her Majesty will receive the guests at noon.

additional_notes: Means “his/her credit card” depending on who owns it. Use **sa** with a feminine noun like **carte** (even if the owner is a man). In the examples, expressions like **exploser/épuiser sa carte de crédit** are figurative: to “max out” or “blow through” a credit card/credit limit (spend a lot).
target_language_example: Il a perdu sa carte de crédit et il a appelé la banque.
native_language_example: He lost his credit card and called the bank.

additional_notes: "Sa" means "his" or "her" depending on who owns the room (it agrees with the noun "chambre," which is feminine). Often used for someone’s bedroom, especially at home or in a hotel (e.g., "ramenez-la à sa chambre" = "take her back to her room").
target_language_example: Elle lit dans sa chambre tous les soirs.
native_language_example: She reads in her room every evening.

additional_notes: "Sa" means "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun "chemise," which is feminine, not with the owner). In context it often refers to someone taking off, tearing, ironing, hanging up, or tucking in their shirt. If the owner is a man, you still say "sa chemise" because "chemise" is feminine.
target_language_example: Il a enlevé sa chemise parce qu’il avait trop chaud.
native_language_example: He took off his shirt because he was too hot.

additional_notes: "Sa" is a possessive adjective that agrees with the noun "famille" (feminine singular), not with the owner. So it can mean either "his family" or "her family"—you know which from context. You can use it with verbs like parler de (talk about), connaître (know), manquer à (to be missed by), and soutenir (support).
target_language_example: Elle veut passer le week-end avec sa famille.
native_language_example: She wants to spend the weekend with her family.

meaning: his/her way of thinking; his/her mindset.
additional_notes: "Sa" means "his" or "her" depending on who you’re talking about (it agrees with the noun "façon"). You can swap the possessive: "ma/ta/notre/votre/leur façon de penser" (my/your/our/your/their way of thinking). Often used to comment on someone’s viewpoint or attitude: "Sa façon de penser est + adjective".
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas sa façon de penser.
native_language_example: I don’t understand his/her way of thinking.

meaning: his wife; her wife (rarely: its wife).
additional_notes: "Sa" means "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun that follows, not the owner). Since "femme" is feminine, you use "sa". Often the surrounding context tells you whether it means "his wife" or "her wife".
target_language_example: Elle a invité sa femme à dîner.
native_language_example: She invited her wife to dinner.

additional_notes: "Sa" is the feminine form of "his/her" and is used before feminine nouns like "femme" (wife). It can refer to a man’s or a woman’s spouse: French chooses "sa" based on the noun (femme), not on the owner. "Est" is the verb "to be" (il/elle est = he/she is).
target_language_example: Sa femme est médecin.
native_language_example: His wife is a doctor.

additional_notes: "Sa" is a possessive adjective meaning "his" or "her" (it depends on who the owner is). It agrees with the noun possessed: "fille" is feminine singular, so you use "sa". (For plural: "ses filles" = "his/her daughters".)
target_language_example: Sa fille a dix ans.
native_language_example: His/Her daughter is ten years old.

meaning: his/her youth; the time when he/she was young.
additional_notes: Refers to someone’s younger years. Use the possessive adjective to match the person: sa (his/her), ma (my), ta (your), notre (our), leur (their), etc. Often used to talk about memories, dreams, or to ask people to consider someone’s age/immaturity.
target_language_example: Il raconte souvent des histoires de sa jeunesse.
native_language_example: He often tells stories about his youth.

additional_notes: “Sa” is a possessive adjective meaning “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun’s gender, not the owner’s). “Main” is feminine, so it’s always “sa main” (= his hand / her hand). Common expression: “demander sa main” means “to ask for her hand (in marriage).” Note: French “main” means “hand” (false friend with English “main”).
target_language_example: Il a pris sa main et il lui a souri.
native_language_example: He took her hand and smiled at her.

additional_notes: "Sa" is the possessive adjective for a feminine singular noun (here, "maison"). It can mean "his" or "her" depending on who owns it (not the gender of the house). Use "son" instead before a vowel sound: "son ancienne maison".
target_language_example: Il cherche sa maison sur la carte.
native_language_example: He’s looking for his house on the map.

meaning: his/her illness (the illness of someone previously mentioned).
additional_notes: “Sa” means “his” or “her” depending on what is owned (here: “maladie” is feminine), not on the person’s gender. Common with verbs like “se remettre de” (to recover from), “guérir de” (to cure/be cured of), “récupérer de” (to recover from), and with adjectives like “grave” (serious).
target_language_example: Après sa maladie, il a dû reprendre le travail doucement.
native_language_example: After his illness, he had to go back to work gradually.

additional_notes: "Sa" can mean "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun "amie," which is feminine, not with the owner). "Meilleure" is the feminine form of "meilleur" (best). Used for someone’s closest friend who is a woman/girl; for a male best friend you’d say "son meilleur ami."
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec sa meilleure amie.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with his/her best friend.

additional_notes: "Sa" is the possessive adjective meaning "his" or "her" (it depends on who died, not on the speaker). It’s used to talk about someone’s death, often in time expressions like "avant sa mort" (before his/her death) or "après sa mort" (after his/her death).
target_language_example: Après sa mort, sa famille a déménagé.
native_language_example: After his/her death, his/her family moved.

meaning: his girlfriend (or her girlfriend, depending on context).
additional_notes: "Petite amie" means "girlfriend" (a romantic partner). "Sa" can mean "his" or "her" because it agrees with the noun "amie" (feminine), not with the owner. For a male partner, you say "son petit ami".
target_language_example: Il a invité sa petite amie à dîner.
native_language_example: He invited his girlfriend to dinner.

additional_notes: Literally “his/her place,” using the possessive adjective **sa** (feminine singular). It’s used for a physical place (a seat on a bus, a spot in a line, where something belongs: *Sa place est ici*) and also for someone’s role/position (*prendre sa place* = “take his/her place,” i.e., replace them). The possessive changes with the owner: **ma place** (my), **ta place** (your), **sa place** (his/her), **notre place**, **votre place**, **leur place**.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je crois que c’est sa place.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I think that’s his/her seat.

additional_notes: “Sa” is a possessive adjective meaning “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun: *poche* is feminine). You’ll often see it in literal contexts (*dans sa poche* = “in his/her pocket”, *de sa poche* = “from his/her pocket”). It also appears in the common idiom *connaître [un endroit] comme sa poche* = “to know [a place] like the back of one’s hand.”
target_language_example: Elle a sorti ses clés de sa poche.
native_language_example: She took her keys out of her pocket.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun to emphasize that something belongs uniquely to someone: "sa propre chambre" = "his/her own room". It agrees with the noun, not the owner: masculine singular = "son propre"; feminine plural = "ses propres"; masculine plural = "ses propres". Often adds emphasis/contrast (e.g., risking "sa propre vie" = "his/her own life").
target_language_example: Chacun a sa propre façon de faire les choses.
native_language_example: Everyone has their own way of doing things.

additional_notes: “Sa” means “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun, not the person). Since “santé” is feminine, you use “sa” even when talking about a man. Common in phrases like “s’inquiéter de sa santé” (to worry about his/her health), “préoccupé(e) par sa santé” (concerned about his/her health), “au prix de sa santé” (at the cost of his/her health), “sa santé a décliné” (his/her health declined), “sa santé est défaillante” (his/her health is failing).
target_language_example: Après l’opération, sa santé s’est améliorée.
native_language_example: After the operation, his/her health improved.

meaning: his/her sister (depending on who owns it).
additional_notes: "Sa" is a possessive adjective that agrees with the noun ("sœur" is feminine), not with the owner. So "sa sœur" can mean "his sister" or "her sister" (and sometimes "their sister" if referring to a singular group like a company/organization). For "your sister" use "ta sœur" (informal singular) or "votre sœur" (formal/plural).
target_language_example: Il vient avec sa sœur.
native_language_example: He’s coming with his sister.

meaning: "his/her head" (also used in expressions about being stubborn).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: someone’s head (sa = his/her/its, depending on who you’re talking about). Often appears in the expression « n’en faire qu’à sa tête », meaning “to do only what one wants” / “to be stubborn, not listen to others.”
target_language_example: Il n’en fait qu’à sa tête et refuse d’écouter les conseils.
native_language_example: He just does what he wants and refuses to listen to advice.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: **sa** can mean “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun *vie* (feminine), not with the person). Commonly seen in the expression **sa vie durant** = “all his/her life / throughout his/her life.”
target_language_example: Elle a vécu dans ce village toute sa vie.
native_language_example: She lived in this village her whole life.

meaning: his/her/its car (the car belonging to her/him/it).
additional_notes: "Sa" is a possessive adjective meaning "his" or "her" (or "its") and it agrees with the noun that follows. Since "voiture" is feminine, you use "sa" (not *son*), even if the owner is male. Context tells you whether it’s "his" or "her."
target_language_example: Elle a garé sa voiture devant la maison.
native_language_example: She parked her car in front of the house.

additional_notes: "Sa" means "his" or "her" depending on who owns the voice (it agrees with the feminine noun "voix," not with the speaker’s gender). Often used to describe the sound or tone of someone’s voice (e.g., "se fit douce" = "became soft/gentle"), or to express annoyance ("me court sur les nerfs" = "gets on my nerves").
target_language_example: J’ai reconnu sa voix tout de suite.
native_language_example: I recognized his/her voice right away.

additional_notes: Said about a woman or girl who got through something without harm. It agrees in gender and number: masculine singular is « sain et sauf », plural « sains et saufs » (mixed/masc) or « saines et sauves » (all female). Often used after danger, an accident, a trip, etc.
target_language_example: Après l’accident, elle est rentrée saine et sauve.
native_language_example: After the accident, she got home safe and sound.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like rentrer, revenir, arriver, s’en sortir to say someone made it back/through something without injury. It agrees with the people: sain et sauf (1 man), saine et sauve (1 woman), sains et saufs (men/mixed group), saines et sauves (women).
target_language_example: Après la tempête, tout le monde est rentré sain et sauf.
native_language_example: After the storm, everyone got home safe and sound.

additional_notes: Inversion of the verb "savoir" + "tu" to form a question, meaning “do you know…?” and often used like “can you…?” for skills/ability. Commonly followed by an infinitive: "Sais-tu nager ?" = “Can you swim?” More formal than "Tu sais… ?".
target_language_example: Sais-tu cuisiner ?
native_language_example: Can you cook?

additional_notes: Uses subject–verb inversion ("sais-tu") to form a question; it’s a fairly formal/standard way to ask if someone knows some information. Often followed by a verb clause (e.g., "…ce que ça signifie", "…ce que Tom fait"). A more neutral/common alternative is: "Est-ce que tu sais ce que…" or "Tu sais ce que… ?" in casual speech.
target_language_example: Sais-tu ce que ça veut dire ?
native_language_example: Do you know what that means?

meaning: “Do you know how…?” (asking if someone knows the method/way to do something).
additional_notes: Inversion question form of "Tu sais comment…?" (a bit more formal). Usually followed by an infinitive ("Sais-tu comment ouvrir…?") or a full clause ("Sais-tu comment elle se porte ?" = how she is doing).
target_language_example: Sais-tu comment arriver à la gare d’ici ?
native_language_example: Do you know how to get to the station from here?

meaning: "do you know where" (asking someone for the location of something/someone).
additional_notes: This is an inverted question form: "sais-tu" = "do you know" and "où" = "where". It’s used before a clause giving the thing you’re looking for: "Sais-tu où + subject + verb… ?" You may also see the more common non-inverted form in everyday speech: "Tu sais où… ?"
target_language_example: Sais-tu où se trouve la gare ?
native_language_example: Do you know where the train station is?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows a person’s identity. It’s a question form with inversion (verb + -tu): « sais-tu… ? ». It’s often followed by a clause like « sais-tu qui c’est ? » / « sais-tu qui il est ? ». You can also say the more neutral « Est-ce que tu sais qui… ? ».
target_language_example: Sais-tu qui a appelé tout à l’heure ?
native_language_example: Do you know who called earlier?

meaning: “Do you know who…?” (asking who did something).
additional_notes: "Sais-tu" is an inverted question form of "tu sais" (“you know”), used in more formal/neutral speech. "Qui a" introduces the person who performed an action in the past (passé composé), often followed by a past participle: "Sais-tu qui a écrit… ?" You can also use the more common spoken form "Tu sais qui a… ?"
target_language_example: Sais-tu qui a écrit cette chanson ?
native_language_example: Do you know who wrote this song?

additional_notes: Usually part of "je sais ce que..." to introduce a clause explaining what you know: "Je sais ce que j’ai vu" (I know what I saw). You’ll also often hear "Tu sais ce que je veux dire" = "You know what I mean." (With other subjects it changes: "tu sais ce que", "il/elle sait ce que", etc.)
target_language_example: Je sais ce que je dois faire.
native_language_example: I know what I have to do.

additional_notes: From the verb "savoir" (to know) + "où" (where). Often appears inside a longer sentence like "Je sais où il est" (I know where he is) or in a question like "Comment tu sais où… ?" (How do you know where…?). "Je sais" is the "I" form; other common forms: "tu sais où" (you know where), "il/elle sait où" (he/she knows where), "vous savez où" (you know where, formal/plural).
target_language_example: Je sais où tu travailles.
native_language_example: I know where you work.

additional_notes: "sais" is the present-tense form of the verb **savoir** (to know), used with **que** (that) to introduce a clause: **Je sais que…** = “I know that…”, **Tu sais que…** = “You know that…”. In questions you’ll often see **Tu sais que… ?** (“Do you know that…?”) or **Comment tu sais que… ?** (“How do you know that…?”).
target_language_example: Tu sais que je suis en retard ?
native_language_example: Do you know that I’m late?

meaning: 'know something' (have information); in "j’en sais quelque chose": 'I should know' (from experience).
additional_notes: Used with "savoir" to mean having information: "Si tu sais quelque chose, dis-le." Very common with the pronoun "en" (referring to what was just mentioned): "J’en sais quelque chose" / "Tu en sais quelque chose" = “I/you should know,” often implying personal experience or firsthand knowledge.
target_language_example: Il pense que c’est facile, mais j’en sais quelque chose.
native_language_example: He thinks it’s easy, but I should know (from experience).

meaning: (I) don’t know anything; I have no idea.
additional_notes: Often heard as part of the informal negative: «(Je) sais rien» = «Je ne sais rien». Very common with «en»: «J’en sais rien» = “I don’t know (about it/anything about it).” For emphasis you may also hear «Tu ne sais rien du tout» = “You don’t know anything at all.”
target_language_example: Désolé, j’en sais rien.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have no idea.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *savoir* (“to know”), in the 3rd person singular present (*il/elle/on sait* = “he/she/one/we know(s)”), followed by *ce que* (“what/that which”) to introduce what someone knows: *Il sait ce que tu veux* (“He knows what you want”). Often followed by another clause (sometimes with a different tense): *Je me demande s’il sait ce que Mary a fait* (“I wonder if he knows what Mary did”).
target_language_example: Elle sait ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: She knows what you mean.

additional_notes: "sait" is the 3rd-person singular present tense of *savoir* (to know), used with "que" to introduce a clause (a complete idea): *Il/Elle/On sait que + [subject + verb]*. For other subjects: *je sais que, tu sais que, nous savons que, vous savez que, ils/elles savent que*.
target_language_example: Elle sait que le train arrive à 18 h.
native_language_example: She knows that the train arrives at 6 p.m.

meaning: “(a) room for / (a) hall for” (used to name a type of room).
additional_notes: “Salle” means “room/hall.” “Salle de + noun” is used to specify the purpose: salle de sport (gym), salle de travail (work/study room), salle de conférence (conference room). In everyday speech you often say “la salle de sport” to mean “the gym,” and “être abonné à une salle de sport” means “to have a gym membership.”
target_language_example: La salle de conférence est au deuxième étage.
native_language_example: The conference room is on the second floor.

meaning: "Hi" + an affectionate "my …" (used before a term of endearment).
additional_notes: "Salut" is a casual greeting. "Mon" is the masculine form of "my" used before a noun of affection like "amour" (love) or "chou" (sweetie). You’ll also see "ma" (feminine) and "mes" (plural). In nicknames, French sometimes uses "mon" even when speaking to a woman (e.g., "mon amour").
target_language_example: Salut, mon amour, comment ça va ?
native_language_example: Hi, my love, how are you?

additional_notes: Used after a main verb to show someone did something and didn’t say goodbye (often implying it was abrupt or a bit rude). Structure: "sans" + infinitive (here: dire) + object (au revoir).
target_language_example: Je suis parti sans dire au revoir parce que j'étais pressé.
native_language_example: I left without saying goodbye because I was in a hurry.

meaning: safely; without incident; without any problems.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something arrived or happened with no trouble (no accidents, delays, or complications). Often goes with verbs like « arriver », « rentrer », « se passer », or « se dérouler ».
target_language_example: On est rentrés sans encombre après le concert.
native_language_example: We got home safely after the concert.

meaning: without leaving any trace; without a trace.
additional_notes: Used to describe disappearing or going somewhere so that nothing remains to show you were there (no evidence, no clues). Common with verbs like « disparaître » (to disappear), « partir » (to leave), « s’en aller » (to go away).
target_language_example: Il est parti sans laisser de traces.
native_language_example: He left without a trace.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone left abruptly or rudely, not doing the basic polite act of saying goodbye. Often follows verbs like partir, quitter, raccrocher (hang up). "même" adds emphasis (“even”).
target_language_example: Elle est sortie sans même dire au revoir à ses collègues.
native_language_example: She left without even saying goodbye to her coworkers.

meaning: "with all due respect" (polite way to disagree or criticize).
additional_notes: A very formal, old-fashioned set phrase used before (or sometimes alone as) a statement that may contradict, criticize, or correct the listener. It softens what follows and signals respect, especially when addressing someone in a higher position. Often followed by a comma: « Sauf votre respect, … ».
target_language_example: Sauf votre respect, je crois que vous vous trompez.
native_language_example: With all due respect, I think you're mistaken.

additional_notes: "Sauta" is the passé simple (literary past) of *sauter* (to jump). In everyday conversation you’ll usually hear *a sauté par-dessus* (passé composé). *Par-dessus* means “over (something),” often with an obstacle: *par-dessus la flaque/le mur/la clôture*.
target_language_example: Le chat sauta par-dessus la table.
native_language_example: The cat jumped over the table.

additional_notes: Past participle of « sauver » used in the common expression « sauver la vie (à quelqu’un) » = to save someone’s life. You can add « de + person » (e.g., « la vie de son ami ») or use an indirect object pronoun: « Tu m’as sauvé la vie » (You saved my life), « Il lui a sauvé la vie » (He saved his/her life).
target_language_example: Les pompiers lui ont sauvé la vie.
native_language_example: The firefighters saved his life.

additional_notes: "Savais-tu" is the informal (tu) past tense of "savoir" (to know): "did you know". It’s used to ask if someone already knew some information, often followed by "que" + a full clause. In more formal speech (vous), use "saviez-vous que".
target_language_example: Savais-tu que le musée est fermé le lundi ?
native_language_example: Did you know that the museum is closed on Mondays?

additional_notes: "Savais" is the imperfect tense of "savoir" (to know), used here with "que" (“that”) to introduce a clause: "Tu savais que…" = “You knew that…” or, as a question, “Did you know that…?”. Often used to talk about what someone knew at a certain time in the past, or to express surprise: "Tu savais que j'étais là ?"
target_language_example: Tu savais que le magasin était fermé aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Did you know that the store was closed today?

additional_notes: “Savait” is the imperfect past tense of “savoir” (to know). It’s used to describe knowledge someone had in the past (often as background information), and it’s followed by “que” + a clause.
target_language_example: Je savais que tu avais raison.
native_language_example: I knew that you were right.

additional_notes: This is the verb *savoir* (“to know how to”) in the *vous* form, with subject–verb inversion to ask a question. It’s often followed by an infinitive to ask about a skill: *Savez-vous nager ?* (“Do you know how to swim?”). More formal than *Vous savez… ?* and much more formal than *Tu sais… ?*.
target_language_example: Savez-vous parler anglais ?
native_language_example: Do you know how to speak English?

meaning: “Do you know how to speak (…)? / Can you speak (…)?”.
additional_notes: Polite/formal question using inversion (savez-vous…). Used to ask if someone speaks a specific language: savez-vous parler le japonais / le russe, etc. In everyday speech you’ll often hear: « Est-ce que vous savez parler… ? » or informal « Tu sais parler… ? ». Note: for some languages French doesn’t use « le » (e.g., « parler français », « parler anglais »).
target_language_example: Savez-vous parler le russe ?
native_language_example: Do you speak Russian?

additional_notes: This is the verb *savoir* (“to know how to”) in the *vous* form, with subject–verb inversion to ask a question. It’s often followed by an infinitive to ask about a skill: *Savez-vous nager ?* (“Do you know how to swim?”). More formal than *Vous savez… ?* and much more formal than *Tu sais… ?*.
target_language_example: Savez-vous parler anglais ?
native_language_example: Do you know how to speak English?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows a specific piece of information. It’s the polite/inverted form of the question (subject-verb inversion): savez-vous…? Often followed by a full clause: « Savez-vous ce que + subject + verb… ? » It can be followed by another verb directly: « Savez-vous ce que signifie ce symbole ? »
target_language_example: Savez-vous ce que vous cherchez exactement ?
native_language_example: Do you know what exactly you’re looking for?

additional_notes: Used to ask politely if someone knows the way to do something or how something works. It’s the inverted (more formal) form of “Vous savez comment… ?”. Often followed by an infinitive (“comment faire…”, “comment ouvrir…”) or a full clause (“comment ceci fonctionne”, “comment je peux y aller”).
target_language_example: Savez-vous comment changer la langue sur ce téléphone ?
native_language_example: Do you know how to change the language on this phone?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a location or destination. It’s an inverted question (verb before subject) and sounds polite/formal; in casual speech you often hear "Vous savez où…?" or "Tu sais où…?". It’s typically followed by a clause like "il est", "elle habite", "on peut le trouver", etc.
target_language_example: Savez-vous où se trouve la gare ?
native_language_example: Do you know where the train station is?

additional_notes: A polite/formal question using inversion (verb + subject): « savez-vous » = “do you know”. It’s usually followed by a clause with « qui » (“who”), e.g., « Savez-vous qui a fait ça ? » In casual speech, people often say « Vous savez qui… ? » or « Tu sais qui… ? »
target_language_example: Savez-vous qui a appelé ce matin ?
native_language_example: Do you know who called this morning?

meaning: “Do you know who…?” (asking who did something).
additional_notes: A polite/formal question using inversion ("savez-vous"). It’s followed by a relative clause with "qui" + a verb: "Savez-vous qui a dit ça ?" = "Do you know who said that?" In everyday speech you’ll often hear: "Vous savez qui a… ?"
target_language_example: Savez-vous qui a écrit cette lettre ?
native_language_example: Do you know who wrote this letter?

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of savoir (vous saviez) in a question to introduce information the speaker thinks may be new or surprising. Often used to start a fun fact or check someone’s knowledge. "Vous" can be formal singular or plural; informal would be "Savais-tu que…?".
target_language_example: Saviez-vous que le musée ferme à 18 h ?
native_language_example: Did you know that the museum closes at 6 p.m.?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the practical ability to do something well (skills gained from experience), or the technical expertise of a person, company, or craft. Often appears with avoir (“il a le savoir-faire…”) or as a general idea (“une question de savoir-faire”).
target_language_example: Elle a beaucoup de savoir-faire en cuisine.
native_language_example: She has a lot of know-how in the kitchen.

meaning: to know what / to find out what (…); to know what is happening (…); to know what/which (…)
additional_notes: Used with a following clause introduced by **ce que** (what + object) or **ce qui** (what + subject): **savoir ce qu’il faut faire** (to know what to do), **savoir ce qui se passe** (to know what’s happening). Very common in questions (**Comment savoir… ? / Je peux savoir… ?**) and in negatives (**Impossible de savoir… / Personne ne peut savoir…**).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce qu’il faut répondre.
native_language_example: I don’t know what to answer.

additional_notes: Used before a clause to introduce the thing someone knows or wants to know: «savoir ce que + subject + verb». Very common with expressions like «Je veux savoir ce que…» (I want to know what…), «Tu sais ce que… ?» (Do you know what…?), and «Fais-moi savoir ce que…» (Let me know what…).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce que tu en penses.
native_language_example: I want to know what you think about it.

meaning: to know what it is; to find out what it is.
additional_notes: Used when you want to identify or understand something (an object, situation, idea). Often appears with polite or rhetorical questions: « Je peux savoir ce que c’est ? » (“Can I know what it is?”) and « On peut savoir ce que c’est ? » (“So what is it, then?”—can sound slightly impatient depending on tone). Also common after verbs like « avoir besoin de », « croire », « vouloir »: « J’ai besoin de savoir… », « Je crois savoir… », « Tu veux savoir… ».
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce que c’est avant de décider.
native_language_example: I want to know what it is before deciding.

additional_notes: Used to say someone understands their actions/plan and is in control (“Tu es sûr de savoir ce que tu fais ?” = “Are you sure you know what you’re doing?”). In questions like “Je peux/On peut savoir ce que tu fais ?”, it often means “Can I/we know what you’re doing?” and can sound impatient, suspicious, or demanding depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Tu es sûr de savoir ce que tu fais ?
native_language_example: Are you sure you know what you’re doing?

meaning: to know (or find out) what happened.
additional_notes: Used when someone wants information about a past event. Often follows verbs like vouloir (Tu veux savoir…), aimerais (J’aimerais savoir…), pouvoir (Je peux savoir…?), or croire (Je crois savoir…). Inside the phrase, "ce qui" means "what" as the subject of the verb, and "s'est passé" is the past tense of "se passer" (to happen).
target_language_example: Je dois savoir ce qui s'est passé avant de décider.
native_language_example: I need to know what happened before deciding.

meaning: to know/find out what’s going on (what’s happening).
additional_notes: Used to ask for or request information about a situation. Often appears in questions: « On peut savoir ce qui se passe ? » (can sound impatient depending on tone) or more polite/formal: « Puis-je savoir ce qui se passe ? ». Literally “to know what is happening.”
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce qui se passe ici.
native_language_example: I want to know what’s going on here.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb (uses "se"). It can mean physically fighting ("Ils se battent") or fighting/struggling to achieve or defend something ("se battre pour ses droits"). Common pattern: "se battre contre" (fight against) and "se battre pour" (fight for).
target_language_example: Elle se bat pour ses droits.
native_language_example: She’s fighting for her rights.

additional_notes: From the verb "se cacher" (reflexive). It can mean someone/thing hides itself ("Il se cache") or something is hidden/contained in something else in a more abstract way ("Une possibilité se cache..."). In questions with inversion: "Se cache-t-il...?"
target_language_example: Une surprise se cache dans ce paquet.
native_language_example: A surprise is hidden in this package.

additional_notes: Used to describe what something includes as its parts or elements. The subject is usually a thing or group (family, year, minute), and what follows “de” is the list or number of components. Very common in factual descriptions and definitions.
target_language_example: Le menu se compose de trois plats.
native_language_example: The menu consists of three courses.

meaning: to go to bed; to lie down; (of the sun) to set.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb (je me couche, tu te couches, il/elle se couche, nous nous couchons, vous vous couchez, ils/elles se couchent). Commonly used with time: « Je vais me coucher. » / « C'est l'heure de se coucher. » Also used for the sun: « Le soleil se couche. »
target_language_example: Je me couche tôt parce que je travaille demain.
native_language_example: I go to bed early because I work tomorrow.

meaning: is heading toward; is going in the direction of.
additional_notes: From the verb *se diriger* (a reflexive verb) + *vers* (“toward”). Used for people or things moving toward a place/person/direction. Often translated as “to head for/toward” or “to make one’s way toward.”
target_language_example: On se dirige vers la gare à pied.
native_language_example: We’re heading toward the train station on foot.

meaning: moves; travels; shifts (from one place to another).
additional_notes: Form of the verb "se déplacer" (to move/to get around). Used for people, animals, vehicles, or anything that changes position (a target, a glacier, even pain). It often suggests movement from point A to point B, not just wiggling in place.
target_language_example: Je me déplace à vélo quand il fait beau.
native_language_example: I get around by bike when the weather is nice.

meaning: to get your hair cut (to have your hair cut).
additional_notes: Uses the pattern "se faire + infinitive" to mean having something done to/for yourself by someone else. Here, it implies going to a hairdresser/barber (not cutting your own hair). You can also specify who does it: "Je me fais couper les cheveux par le coiffeur."
target_language_example: Je vais me faire couper les cheveux demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to get my hair cut tomorrow.

meaning: to get up; to stand up; (for the sun) to rise.
additional_notes: Pronominal verb (uses a reflexive pronoun): je me lève, tu te lèves, il/elle se lève, nous nous levons, vous vous levez, ils/elles se lèvent. Commonly means getting out of bed (se lever tôt, se lever le matin) or standing up from a chair/table (se lever de son siège, se lever de table). It can also be used figuratively: une raison de se lever le matin (“a reason to get up in the morning”). With the sun: Le soleil se lève (“The sun rises”).
target_language_example: Je me lève à sept heures, mais le week-end je me lève plus tard.
native_language_example: I get up at seven o’clock, but on weekends I get up later.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb: "se lever" = "to get up" (literally "to raise oneself"). Conjugate with être and match agreement: "Je me suis levé(e) tôt." Often used with "avoir l’habitude de" (to be in the habit of) or to talk about routines and early mornings.
target_language_example: Je me lève tôt tous les jours pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: I get up early every day to go to work.

additional_notes: Form of the reflexive verb **se lever** (“to get up/stand up”). **se lève** is used with **il/elle/on** (and a name: *Tom se lève...*) in the present tense. Common with time expressions: *à sept heures*, *le matin*, *dès l’aube*.
target_language_example: Elle se lève tôt pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: She gets up early to go to work.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb « se lever » (to get up). « Se lève » is the present tense for il/elle/on (he/she/one). Often used with habits like « tous les matins » (every morning). It can also be used figuratively for a place or group (e.g., « Le village se lève tôt » = people in the village start their day early).
target_language_example: Je me lève tôt pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: I get up early to go to work.

meaning: “gets married” / “is getting married”; also “goes well with” (pairs well).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **se marier**. It most often means someone is getting married (e.g., *Ma cousine se marie demain*). It can also be used more figuratively for food, flavors, colors, etc. to mean they match well: *Le tofu se marie bien avec le saké* (“Tofu goes well with sake”).
target_language_example: Ce vin se marie bien avec le fromage.
native_language_example: This wine goes well with cheese.

meaning: to get married; to marry (each other).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb used for the act of marrying: « Ils se marient. » = “They’re getting married.” Often followed by « avec » for the person: « se marier avec quelqu’un ». Also used with « en » for the month/season: « se marier en juin ». Related noun: « un mariage » = a wedding/marriage.
target_language_example: Ils vont se marier l'année prochaine.
native_language_example: They’re going to get married next year.

additional_notes: "Se mirent" is the passé simple (literary past) of "se mettre" for "ils/elles". You’ll mostly see it in books and formal storytelling instead of the everyday spoken past "ils/elles se sont mis(es) à rire". The structure is "se mettre à + infinitive" to mean "to start/begin doing something".
target_language_example: En entendant la blague, elles se mirent à rire.
native_language_example: Hearing the joke, they started laughing.

additional_notes: Past simple of "se mettre à" ("to start/begin to"). Used in storytelling/written French to describe someone suddenly beginning an action; in everyday speech you more often see the passé composé: "s'est mis(e) à".
target_language_example: En entendant la blague, elle se mit à rire.
native_language_example: On hearing the joke, she started laughing.

additional_notes: This is the past historic (passé simple) form of "se mettre à + infinitive" (= to start doing something). You’ll mostly see it in novels and formal storytelling; in everyday speech French usually uses the passé composé: "il/elle s’est mis(e) à pleurer". Here, "pleurer" means "to cry".
target_language_example: En entendant la nouvelle, il se mit à pleurer.
native_language_example: On hearing the news, he started to cry.

additional_notes: From the verb *se passer* (“to happen; to take place”). Very common in expressions like **Tout se passe bien ?** (“Is everything going well?”) and **Ça se passe comment ?** (“How’s it going?”). You can also use it for events: **La réunion se passe à 14 h** (“The meeting takes place at 2 p.m.”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tout se passe bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is going well.

meaning: to go well; to happen smoothly.
additional_notes: Used with "ça" or "tout" to say that things are going well or that an event is unfolding without problems: "Tout se passe bien" = "Everything is going well". Often appears with "si" (if) and in wishes: "Que tout se passe bien !" = "May everything go well!".
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, tout se passe bien.
native_language_example: Don't worry, everything is going well.

additional_notes: Built on the verb **se passer** (= to happen, to take place). Often used in questions like **Qu’est-ce qu’il se passe ici ?** (“What’s going on here?”). Note: **se passer** does **not** mean “to pass” in the English sense (false friend).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce qui se passe ici.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what’s going on here.

additional_notes: Future tense of **se passer**. Used to talk about what will happen in the future, or how an event/situation will turn out: **ça se passera bien** = “it will go well.” Often appears in the structure **ce qui se passera** = “what will happen.”
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, tout se passera bien demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything will go well tomorrow.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "se plaindre" (to complain). It’s used with "de" + noun/phrase: "se plaindre de son salaire" (to complain about one’s salary). Common with frequency words like "toujours", "sans arrêt", "constamment". In the negative, "on ne se plaint pas" means “we can’t complain / we’re not complaining.”
target_language_example: Je ne me plains pas, mais je suis fatigué.
native_language_example: I’m not complaining, but I’m tired.

meaning: to happen; to occur (often for events, sometimes unexpected).
additional_notes: Used with things/events as the subject: « Un accident s’est produit. » In the past it commonly uses être: « s’est produit / s’est produite / se sont produits / se sont produites » (agree with the subject). Also used after verbs like « imaginer »: « imaginer cela se produire » = “imagine that happening.”
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce qui s’est produit hier soir.
native_language_example: I don’t know what happened last night.

additional_notes: From the verb « se produire » (often used like English “to happen”). Common patterns: « Ça/Cela se produit… » (It happens…), « Quand est-ce que cela se produit ? » (When does it happen?), « Si ça se produit… » (If it happens…). For a planned event, French often uses « avoir lieu » instead of « se produire ».
target_language_example: Si ça se produit encore, préviens-moi tout de suite.
native_language_example: If it happens again, let me know right away.

meaning: to rest; to take a break.
additional_notes: Reflexive verb used when someone rests or takes time to recover: « Je dois me reposer. » It often follows verbs like « conseiller de » (to advise to) or « laisser » (to let). Note: « se reposer sur + [person/thing] » means “to rely on” (e.g., « On ne doit pas se reposer sur le rapport. »).
target_language_example: Après le voyage, je vais me reposer un peu.
native_language_example: After the trip, I’m going to rest a little.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **se retrouver**. It’s used (1) when someone ends up in a situation or place (often unexpectedly): *Il se retrouve seul* (“He finds himself alone”), and (2) to talk about meeting up again: *On se retrouve à 18h ?* (“Shall we meet at 6?”). In questions like **Où se retrouve-t-on ?**, it means “Where are we meeting?”
target_language_example: Après le film, on se retrouve devant le cinéma.
native_language_example: After the movie, we’ll meet in front of the cinema.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb « se sentir » (to feel). It’s commonly followed by an adjective: « Il se sent bien / fatigué / blessé / exclu ». It can describe a person’s condition or mood, and can also be used for groups/countries (« La Chine se sent forte »). In questions: « Comment on se sent ? » = “How do we/you feel?”
target_language_example: Je me sens stressé aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I feel stressed today.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of the pronominal verb « se sentir » (to feel). Used to describe someone’s state/feelings over a period of time or as background in a story: « Il/elle se sentait + adjective » (he/she felt…). Can also be followed by « comme ça » (like that) or « différent(e) de… » (different from…).
target_language_example: Après l’examen, je me sentais soulagé(e).
native_language_example: After the exam, I felt relieved.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb ("sentir" + "se"). Used to describe someone’s state or feelings: se sentir bien/mieux/mal (to feel good/better/bad), se sentir seul(e) (to feel lonely), se sentir piégé(e) (to feel trapped), se sentir aimé(e) (to feel loved). Conjugates with être in compound tenses (e.g., je me suis senti(e)). Often followed by an adjective or comme ("se sentir comme..." = to feel like...).
target_language_example: Je me sens fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I feel tired today.

meaning: “is located” / “is situated” (to be found in a place; also: to rank/stand in a position).
additional_notes: Used mainly to give a location (physical place on a map): *se situer + sur/dans/à/en/au/aux* (e.g., *se situe au centre-ville*, *en Asie*). It can also be used figuratively for a ranking or position in a list/competition (e.g., *se situe au fond du panier* = “is at the bottom of the table”).
target_language_example: Le musée se situe près de la gare.
native_language_example: The museum is located near the train station.

meaning: "they (have)" in the past with a pronominal verb (passé composé).
additional_notes: Used with ils/elles in the passé composé for pronominal verbs (verbs with se): e.g. se sont assis (they sat down), se sont perdus (they got lost), se sont disputés (they argued). It’s made of se (themselves/each other) + sont (are/have, the verb être). In negatives: ne se sont pas…, and with time expressions you’ll see verbs like s’écouler: Trois ans se sont écoulés (Three years passed). Past participle agreement depends on the verb and what follows (e.g., Ils se sont parlé = no agreement; Ils se sont perdus = agreement with ils).
target_language_example: Ils se sont réveillés très tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: They woke up very early this morning.

meaning: “got married” / “were married” (said about two or more people).
additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb se marier (“to get married”). Used with plural subjects: Ils/Elles se sont mariés = “They got married.” With a mixed group or all men, use mariés; with all women, mariées. Often followed by a time expression (en secret, il y a quelques années, en octobre, le mois dernier).
target_language_example: Ils se sont mariés à Paris l'année dernière.
native_language_example: They got married in Paris last year.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of the reflexive verb "se moquer de" = to make fun of someone/something. Structure: "se moquer de + person/thing" (e.g., "se moquer de moi", "se moquer de sa tenue"). In other tenses you’ll see forms like "ils se moquent de..." (present) or "ils se moquaient de..." (imperfect).
target_language_example: Ils se sont moqués de son accent.
native_language_example: They made fun of his accent.

additional_notes: Passé composé of the reflexive verb **se rencontrer** (“to meet each other”). Used with **être**: *ils/elles se sont…* The past participle agrees with the subject: **rencontrés** (masc. plural), **rencontrées** (fem. plural). You’ll also see other forms: *je me suis rencontré(e), tu t’es rencontré(e), ils/elles se sont rencontrés/rencontrées*.
target_language_example: Ils se sont rencontrés à Paris en 2020.
native_language_example: They met in Paris in 2020.

additional_notes: From the verb "se soucier de" (a reflexive verb). It’s used to say someone cares/ worries about something or someone. Common pattern: "se soucier de + noun" (Elle se soucie de sa famille) or "se soucier de + question word" like "ce que / quand" (Qui se soucie de ce qu’ils pensent ?). Often used in the negative to mean "not to care": "Je ne m’en soucie pas" (= I don’t care about it).
target_language_example: Je me soucie de ton avis, même si je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: I care about your opinion, even if I don’t agree.

meaning: "was standing" / "was positioned" (past tense of se tenir).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something being in a certain posture or position at a given moment. Often followed by an adverb or place phrase: se tenir debout (to stand), se tenir sur une patte (to stand on one leg), se tenir au milieu de… (to be in the middle of…). It can refer to people, animals, or objects/vehicles.
target_language_example: Il se tenait près de la porte, sans rien dire.
native_language_example: He was standing near the door, without saying anything.

additional_notes: Form of the reflexive verb « se terminer » (to end/finish). Used to talk about how something ends (a story, a movie, a night, a situation). Often in questions like « Comment ça se termine ? » (“How does it end?”). Common pattern: « Ça se termine + bien/mal » (“It ends well/badly”).
target_language_example: Le film se termine à minuit.
native_language_example: The movie ends at midnight.

additional_notes: Imperfect (past) form of **se trouver**. Commonly used to say where someone/something **was** at a certain time: **Il se trouvait à Paris.** It can also mean “happened to be” (by chance): **Il se trouvait là au bon moment.** Often used with places (**où / là / ici / à bord / dans…**).
target_language_example: À ce moment-là, elle se trouvait dans sa chambre.
native_language_example: At that moment, she was in her room.

additional_notes: From the verb **se trouver**. Commonly used to say where something is situated (more neutral/formal than **être**). It often appears with place words like **ici, là, à…, devant, derrière, près de**, etc. In descriptions, French may invert the order: **Devant ma maison se trouve un lac** (= “In front of my house there is a lake”).
target_language_example: Le musée se trouve près de la gare.
native_language_example: The museum is located near the train station.

additional_notes: Question form (formal) of **il se trouve** from **se trouver** (“to be located / to be found”). The **-t-** is added for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel (e.g., *trouve-t-il*). Used to ask where something/someone is, or whether something is present/on a list: *Votre nom se trouve-t-il sur la liste ?* = “Is your name on the list?”
target_language_example: Où se trouve-t-il exactement ?
native_language_example: Where exactly is it located?

meaning: is located in downtown / in the city center.
