additional_notes: Used to give the location of a place. "se trouve" is a common, fairly formal way to say "is located / can be found" (often for buildings, offices, stations, etc.). "au centre-ville" means "in the city center" (literally: "in the town/city center").
target_language_example: L'hôtel se trouve au centre-ville, près de la gare.
native_language_example: The hotel is located downtown, near the train station.

meaning: “the … is located / is found / is (in a certain state)” (with *se trouver*).
additional_notes: Used with a noun after it (*se trouve le/la/les…*) to say where something is, where it sits within something, or what condition it’s in. Very common in questions: *Où se trouve le… ?* (Where is the…?), *Dans quelle direction se trouve le… ?* (In what direction is the…?), *En quel état se trouve le… ?* (What condition is the…?). Word order is inverted (verb before subject) in formal questions.
target_language_example: Où se trouve le musée, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Where is the museum, please?

additional_notes: Form of the verb "se trouver" (present tense, 3rd person plural). It’s commonly used to say where people or things are, often as a more neutral/formal alternative to "être" (to be): "Où se trouvent… ?" = "Where are…?"
target_language_example: Les toilettes se trouvent au fond du couloir.
native_language_example: The toilets are at the end of the hallway.

additional_notes: Most often used with an impersonal subject: « Ça se voit » = “It shows / You can tell.” Common in the negative too: « Ça ne se voit pas » = “You can’t tell / It doesn’t show.” Used to comment on something noticeable (feelings, changes, effort, etc.).
target_language_example: Tu as beaucoup travaillé : ça se voit.
native_language_example: You worked a lot—you can tell.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the week immediately before the current one. Often said as **la semaine dernière** (“last week”), especially after time expressions like **toute**: *toute la semaine dernière* = “all last week”. You can also use it with **de** to mean “from last week”: *les robes de la semaine dernière* = “the dresses from last week.”
target_language_example: On s’est vus la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: We saw each other last week.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the week after the current one. Often comes after a preposition like pour (for/by next week) or la (until next week): e.g., pour la semaine prochaine = for/by next week. You can also say la semaine prochaine to mean “next week.”
target_language_example: On se voit la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: See you next week.

additional_notes: Used almost always with **faire**: **faire semblant de ne pas + infinitive** = “to pretend not to …” (often meaning to ignore something on purpose). It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., *entendre, connaître, voir, remarquer*).
target_language_example: Elle a fait semblant de ne pas me voir.
native_language_example: She pretended not to see me.

meaning: “does it seem (to you)?” / “it seems” (in inverted question form).
additional_notes: Used mainly in formal/written French to form questions with inversion, often after a subject like cela/ça: « Cela vous semble-t-il juste ? » = “Does that seem fair to you?” It can also appear as a parenthetical comment (« …, semble-t-il, … ») meaning “so it seems / apparently.”
target_language_example: Cette décision vous semble-t-elle raisonnable ?
native_language_example: Does this decision seem reasonable to you?

additional_notes: Form of the verb « sembler » + « être » to express an impression/appearance (not certainty). Common patterns: « Ça/Cela semble être + noun/adjective » (“It seems to be…”). With a person: « Il/Elle semble être + adjective/noun » (“He/She seems to be…”). You can also say « Il me semble (que)… » = “It seems to me (that)…”.
target_language_example: D'après les indices, cela semble être la bonne solution.
native_language_example: Based on the clues, it seems to be the right solution.

additional_notes: Question form of the verb **sentir** ("to feel" or "to smell") with **inversion** (**sens + -tu**) for "do you…?". Used to ask if someone feels something physically (pain, a touch, a vibration) or notices a smell. (Different from **se sentir** = "to feel (well/bad)" about your general state.)
target_language_example: Sens-tu l’odeur de fumée ?
native_language_example: Can you smell the smell of smoke?

additional_notes: From the verb "sentir" (to smell). You use it to describe a nice odor: "X sent bon". (Opposite: "X sent mauvais" = smells bad.)
target_language_example: Ce gâteau sent bon !
native_language_example: This cake smells good!

meaning: "do you feel…?" / "can you smell…?" (formal or plural "you").
additional_notes: From the verb "sentir" in the present tense with inversion for a question ("sentez" + "vous"). It can mean either physical/emotional feeling ("Vous sentez-vous bien ?" = Do you feel well?) or smelling/perceiving an odor ("Sentez-vous la fumée ?" = Do you smell smoke?). With "en" ("Vous en sentez-vous à la hauteur ?"), it’s part of the expression "s’en sentir à la hauteur" = to feel up to it / capable of it.
target_language_example: Sentez-vous une odeur de gaz ?
native_language_example: Do you smell a gas smell?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of seven years ("depuis sept ans" = for seven years) or someone’s age ("Il a sept ans" = He is seven). Also appears in time expressions like "il y a sept ans" (seven years ago).
target_language_example: Elle a vécu ici pendant sept ans.
native_language_example: She lived here for seven years.

meaning: seven o’clock (7:00); also “seven hours” depending on context.
additional_notes: With a time of day, it usually means 7:00. Often used with prepositions like « à sept heures » (at seven) or « vers sept heures » (around seven). Without context, it can also literally mean a duration of seven hours.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à sept heures devant le café.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at seven o’clock in front of the café.

additional_notes: Question form (inversion) of the future tense of être: « il sera » → « sera-t-il ? ». « il » can mean “he” or “it,” depending on what you’re talking about. Often used with quand (“when”) to ask about timing (Quand sera-t-il prêt ?).
target_language_example: À quelle heure sera-t-il là ?
native_language_example: What time will he be there?

additional_notes: A formal question form in the future tense (inversion): sera (will be) + -t- (linking sound) + il (it/he) + publié (published). Used to ask when something (a book, magazine issue, etc.) will come out/be released. For “she,” use: sera-t-elle publié(e) (agreement often written: publiée for a feminine subject).
target_language_example: Quand sera-t-il publié ?
native_language_example: When will it be published?

additional_notes: Future tense of être ("sera" = "will be") + "bientôt" ("soon"). Used to say something will happen/arrive/be ready in the near future. Often followed by a time/event (Ce sera bientôt le Nouvel An.) or by an adjective (Ce sera bientôt prêt.)
target_language_example: Le repas sera bientôt prêt.
native_language_example: The meal will be ready soon.

meaning: “would you be…?” / “could you be…?” (polite, formal “vous” form).
additional_notes: This is the conditional of être (to be) with vous, used to ask a polite question or make a soft request. Often followed by an adjective or description: Seriez-vous intéressé(e)…? (“Would you be interested…?”), Seriez-vous prêt(e)(s)…? (“Would you be ready…?”). It can also be used to confirm someone’s identity: Seriez-vous Tim Norton ? (“Would you be Tim Norton?” = “Are you Tim Norton, by any chance?”). Agreement changes with who you’re addressing: intéressé (male singular), intéressée (female singular), intéressés/intéressées (plural).
target_language_example: Seriez-vous disponible demain matin ?
native_language_example: Would you be available tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: From the verb "se servir de" = "to use". "Sers-toi de ..." is the imperative for "tu" (telling one person you’re on first-name terms with to use something), often with body parts or tools: "Sers-toi de ta tête" = "Use your head." For a more formal/plural command, use "Servez-vous de ...". Not to confuse with "Servez-vous !" (without "de"), which often means "Help yourself!" (e.g., to food).
target_language_example: Sers-toi de ce couteau pour couper le pain.
native_language_example: Use this knife to cut the bread.

additional_notes: Used mainly in the negative: « ça ne sert à rien » = “it’s pointless / it’s no use.” You can also use it with an infinitive: « Ça ne sert à rien de + verb » (“There’s no point in doing …”). With « sinon »: « … sinon ça ne sert à rien » = “otherwise it’s pointless.”
target_language_example: Ça ne sert à rien de s'inquiéter maintenant.
native_language_example: There's no point in worrying now.

additional_notes: From the verb "servir" (to serve). "Servez-vous" can be (1) the present tense for "vous" meaning "you serve" (formal singular or plural): "Quels plats servez-vous ?" It can also be (2) an imperative meaning "Help yourself" / "Serve yourself" (often said when offering food): "Servez-vous une part de gâteau."
target_language_example: Servez-vous, il y a du pain sur la table.
native_language_example: Help yourself—there’s bread on the table.

additional_notes: “Ses” is the plural possessive adjective meaning “his/her” (it can refer to either a man or a woman). It’s used before a plural noun, like “amis” (friends), and the meaning is understood from context (who “ses” refers to).
target_language_example: Il parle souvent de ses amis d’enfance.
native_language_example: He often talks about his childhood friends.

additional_notes: "Ses" is a possessive adjective that means "his", "her", or "their" (plural owners), depending on context. It’s used with plural nouns like "chaussures" (shoes). For "his/her shoe" (singular), use "sa chaussure".
target_language_example: Il a oublié ses chaussures dans l’entrée.
native_language_example: He forgot his shoes in the entryway.

additional_notes: “Ses” means “his/her” (also “its” or “their” depending on context). With the plural noun “cheveux” (hair), French uses “ses” for both masculine and feminine owners: ses cheveux = his hair / her hair. Often used in descriptions (long/short, clean, gray) or with body-related verbs (se brosser les cheveux, se couper les cheveux).
target_language_example: Elle se brosse ses cheveux tous les soirs.
native_language_example: She brushes her hair every evening.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to describe hair color, texture, or length. "Ses" means "his" or "her" (it depends on who owns the hair, not on the gender of the person speaking). "Cheveux" is plural in French, so you usually use the plural verb form "sont" and plural adjectives: "Ses cheveux sont longs/gris."
target_language_example: Ses cheveux sont courts et bouclés.
native_language_example: His/Her hair is short and curly.

additional_notes: Used with a possessive adjective (ses = “his/her/their”) to talk about someone’s homework. Often used with the verb faire: faire ses devoirs = “to do one’s homework.”
target_language_example: Je dois finir mes devoirs avant de sortir.
native_language_example: I have to finish my homework before going out.

meaning: his/her fingers in his/her hair (often: to run fingers through one’s hair).
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like « passer » or « faire courir »: « passer/faire courir ses doigts dans ses cheveux » = to run your fingers through your hair (often from stress, thinking, or to fix your hair). The possessives change with the person: « mes doigts dans mes cheveux », « tes doigts dans tes cheveux », etc.
target_language_example: Je passe mes doigts dans mes cheveux quand je suis stressé.
native_language_example: I run my fingers through my hair when I'm stressed.

additional_notes: "Ses" is a possessive adjective meaning "his/her/their" (it agrees with the noun: enfants is plural, so ses). It can refer to one person’s children (his/her) or multiple people’s children (their); the context tells you which. Often appears with verbs like aimer (to love), penser à (to think about), léguer à (to leave/inherit to), choisir des noms pour (to choose names for).
target_language_example: Elle parle souvent de ses enfants.
native_language_example: She often talks about her children.

additional_notes: “Ses” is a possessive meaning “his” or “her” (it depends on who owns the glasses). “Lunettes” is plural in French, so you normally say it in the plural, like in English (“glasses”). Used for eyeglasses; for sunglasses you often say “ses lunettes de soleil.”
target_language_example: Elle ne peut pas lire sans ses lunettes.
native_language_example: She can’t read without her glasses.

additional_notes: "Ses" means "his/her" (or "their") depending on context; it agrees with the plural noun "lunettes" (glasses), not with the owner. Often used with verbs like "mettre" (put on), "enlever/ôter/retirer" (take off/remove), and "perdre" (lose).
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mes lunettes de soleil dans la voiture.
native_language_example: I forgot my sunglasses in the car.

additional_notes: "Ses" is a possessive determiner meaning "his", "her", or "its" (singular owner), and it agrees with the plural noun "mains". Used to talk about someone’s hands in general: "ses mains étaient…" (his/her hands were…), "il/elle a levé ses mains" (he/she raised his/her hands).
target_language_example: Elle s'est lavé les mains, puis elle a séché ses mains avec une serviette.
native_language_example: She washed her hands, then she dried her hands with a towel.

additional_notes: “Ses” is a possessive meaning “his/her” (or “its/their”) and agrees with the plural noun “parents” (not with the owner’s gender). So it can refer to either someone’s mom and dad, or more generally someone’s family/relatives depending on context.
target_language_example: Quand j’étais petit, je voyageais souvent avec ses parents.
native_language_example: When I was little, I often traveled with his/her parents.

meaning: 'his/her/its own' (emphasizing that they belong specifically to that person/thing).
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun: ses propres + nom (ex. ses propres vêtements, ses propres problèmes). It adds emphasis, like “their very own” or “their own (not someone else’s)”. The singular forms are: son propre (masc.), sa propre (fem.), ses propres (plural).
target_language_example: Elle veut avoir ses propres idées.
native_language_example: She wants to have her own ideas.

additional_notes: "Ses" is a possessive adjective meaning "his/her/its" (singular owner) or "their" (plural owners). It agrees with the noun "vêtements" (plural), not with the owner’s gender. Often used with verbs like ôter/retirer (to take off) or mettre (to put on).
target_language_example: Il a mis ses vêtements dans l’armoire.
native_language_example: He put his clothes in the closet.

additional_notes: "Ses" means "his" or "her" (you know which from context), and "yeux" is the plural of "œil" (eye). Often used literally (looking at someone’s eyes) or figuratively to talk about emotions you can see in someone’s gaze: "Je l’ai lu dans ses yeux" = "I could read it in his/her eyes."
target_language_example: On voyait la joie dans ses yeux.
native_language_example: You could see the joy in his/her eyes.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "ses" (his/her/their, plural) with "études" (studies). Often refers to someone’s period of education or academic program: "faire ses études" (to do/complete one’s studies), "finir ses études" (to finish), "pendant ses études" (during), "se concentrer sur ses études" (to focus on), "des difficultés dans ses études" (difficulties). The owner changes with context: ses = his or her or their.
target_language_example: Après ses études, elle a trouvé un travail à Paris.
native_language_example: After her studies, she found a job in Paris.

meaning: so long; for so long (so much time).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the duration of an action/state. Often comes after a verb: attendre si longtemps (wait so long), réfléchir si longtemps (think for so long). In questions like « Qu'est-ce qui prend si longtemps ? », it means “Why is it taking so long?”
target_language_example: Je ne t’ai pas vu depuis si longtemps.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen you in so long.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize how early something happens or is done. Often placed after the verb (e.g., se lever si tôt, rentrer si tôt). Don’t confuse with « aussitôt » (“as soon as / immediately”).
target_language_example: Pourquoi es-tu arrivé si tôt ?
native_language_example: Why did you arrive so early?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize speed, often in questions or statements of surprise. It can describe how fast something happens (Tout est allé si vite.) or how fast someone does something (Comment t'es arrivé si vite ?).
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu es parti si vite ?
native_language_example: Why did you leave so quickly?

si, pour une raison quelconque, cela

target_language_multi_word_term: si, pour une raison quelconque, cela
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical situation (“if…”) where the speaker doesn’t know or specify the cause (“pour une raison quelconque” = “for some reason”). It’s often followed by a verb describing what might happen: cela arrive / devait arriver / devait avoir lieu / devait survenir (“that happens / were to happen / were to take place / were to occur”).
target_language_example: Si, pour une raison quelconque, cela ne marche pas, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: If, for some reason, it doesn’t work, call me.

additional_notes:
Used to introduce a condition, often in set phrases like:
- « Si c’est ce que tu/vous crois/croyez » = “If that’s what you think.”
- « Si c’est ce que tu/vous veux/voulez » = “If that’s what you want.”
- « Si c’est comme ça » = “If that’s how it is / If that’s the way it is” (often sounds resigned or accepting).
target_language_example: Si c’est ce que tu préfères, on peut partir plus tôt.
native_language_example: If that’s what you prefer, we can leave earlier.

si c'est ce que tu veux

target_language_multi_word_term: si c'est ce que tu veux
additional_notes: Used to accept or go along with someone’s preference/decision. It can sound neutral or slightly resigned depending on tone and context. Often paired with “d’accord”, “très bien”, “OK”, etc.
target_language_example: On peut partir plus tôt, si c'est ce que tu veux.
native_language_example: We can leave earlier, if that’s what you want.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical or uncertain situation in the imperfect tense (condition). Often appears with the conditional: « Ce serait… si c’était… » (“It would be… if it were…”). Common in the set phrase « si c’était le cas » = “if that were the case,” and in « comme si c’était… » = “as if it were…”.
target_language_example: Je serais surpris si c’était possible.
native_language_example: I’d be surprised if it were possible.

meaning: "if it's not" / "if that isn't the case".
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition that something is not true, often in questions: « Si ce n’est pas Ian, qui est-ce ? » (“If it’s not Ian, who is it?”). With « le cas », it commonly means “if that’s not the case.” (Note: without « pas », « si ce n’est » can also mean “except (for),” but here the examples show the literal conditional use with « pas ».)
target_language_example: Si ce n’est pas aujourd’hui, on peut le faire demain.
native_language_example: If it’s not today, we can do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like demander, savoir, se demander to introduce an indirect yes/no question about a female subject (elle). Often followed by another verb: « si elle peut / si elle a / si elle veut ».
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas si elle vient ce soir.
native_language_example: I don’t know if she’s coming tonight.

additional_notes: Used after **si** (“if/whether”) with **elle était** (imparfait of *être*). Common in: (1) **indirect questions**: *Il a demandé si elle était…* = “He asked whether she was…”; (2) **comme si** (“as if”), often describing an unreal/imagined situation: *comme si elle était…* = “as if she were…”.
target_language_example: Je me demandais si elle était déjà partie.
native_language_example: I was wondering if she had already left.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition or hypothetical situation about yourself. Often followed by different tenses depending on meaning: present/future (Si je le revois...), imperfect for unreal or hypothetical present (Si je vous connaissais mieux...), and sometimes a polite expression like « si je peux me permettre » (“if I may”). Note: after « si », French does not use the conditional tense (you’ll typically see present/imperfect/plus-que-parfait instead).
target_language_example: Si je finis tôt, je passerai te voir.
native_language_example: If I finish early, I'll stop by to see you.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or ability, often when offering help or checking whether something is possible: "Je vais voir si je peux…" (I’ll see if I can…). It can stand alone at the end of a sentence to mean "if I can" (e.g., "Je m'en occupe, si je peux."). Also appears in stronger phrases like "Pas si je peux l'empêcher" = "Not if I can help it" (I’ll try to prevent it).
target_language_example: Je viendrai demain, si je peux.
native_language_example: I’ll come tomorrow, if I can.

meaning: 'if I … you' (introduces a condition with 'te' = 'you' as the object).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a conditional clause: **si** = “if”, **je** = “I”, **te** = “you” (informal singular object pronoun). **Te** comes before the verb: *si je te vois* (“if I see you”), *si je te quitte* (“if I leave you”). Often followed by another clause giving the result.
target_language_example: Si je te rappelle ce soir, réponds, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: If I call you back tonight, please answer.

additional_notes: Used to suggest an idea (often like an invitation): « Si on + imparfait ? » = “What if we + past tense” / “How about we…?” (e.g., « Si on changeait… ? »). It can also introduce a real condition: « Si on + présent…, (alors) … » = “If we…, then …” (general truths, plans, promises).
target_language_example: Si on allait prendre un café après le cours ?
native_language_example: What if we went to get a coffee after class?

meaning: “How about we…?” / “What if we went…?” (a suggestion).
additional_notes: Used to make a friendly suggestion for an activity, often as a question. It literally uses the imperfect of aller (“we were going”), but it functions like “shall we…?/how about…?”. Often appears with “Et” at the start: “Et si on allait… ?”.
target_language_example: Si on allait au cinéma ce soir ?
native_language_example: How about we go to the movies tonight?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition: if an event happens, if there’s a problem, or if anything changes. Very common with verbs like "arriver" (to happen), "survenir" (to occur), "clocher" (to be wrong). In spoken French, "Si quelque chose, ..." can be short for "If anything (happens/changes), ...".
target_language_example: Si quelque chose ne va pas, appelle-moi tout de suite.
native_language_example: If something isn’t right, call me right away.

additional_notes: Used to say “in case something happens/changes,” often in instructions or offers of help: « Appelle-moi si quoi que ce soit change/survient. » You can also use it in questions: « Si quoi que ce soit se produit, puis-je compter sur toi/vous ? » (toi = informal singular, vous = formal or plural).
target_language_example: Préviens-moi si quoi que ce soit arrive pendant mon absence.
native_language_example: Let me know if anything happens while I’m away.

additional_notes: Expresses a strong wish or regret about something that isn’t true right now (often something difficult or impossible). Typically followed by an infinitive (e.g., parler, voler, être). You can change the subject: si seulement tu pouvais… / si seulement on pouvait…
target_language_example: Si seulement je pouvais venir avec vous ce soir !
native_language_example: If only I could come with you tonight!

additional_notes: Used to start an "if" clause with "tu" (you, informal singular). It often sets a condition, possibility, or hypothesis: present (Si tu lis...), future/near future (Si tu as besoin...), imperfect for hypothetical situations (Si tu partais...), and past hypothetical with conditional (Si tu avais été..., tu aurais pu...). For formal "you," use "si vous."
target_language_example: Si tu veux, on peut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: If you want, we can leave now.

meaning: "if you have" (talking to one person informally).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition (something is true only if the other person has something: time, a moment, a question, hunger, etc.). "Tu" is informal singular (friends, family, kids). With a noun, it’s very common: "si tu as le temps" (if you have time), "si tu as une question" (if you have a question). Often followed by an instruction or suggestion.
target_language_example: Si tu as besoin d'aide, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: If you need help, call me.

additional_notes: Used to offer help or leave the door open for someone to ask for something later. You can follow it with a noun (si tu as besoin de quelque chose = if you need something) or an infinitive verb (si tu as besoin de parler = if you need to talk). Often used with an imperative or offer: Appelle… / Dis-moi… / Je suis là…
target_language_example: Si tu as besoin d'aide, je peux t'expliquer.
native_language_example: If you need help, I can explain it to you.

si tu as besoin de moi

target_language_multi_word_term: si tu as besoin de moi
additional_notes: A common conditional phrase to offer help or availability. Often paired with an imperative (Appelle…, Réveille-moi…) or a promise (Je serai là…). Word order can be either: “Appelle si tu as besoin de moi” or “Si tu as besoin de moi, appelle.” In everyday French you may also hear “si tu as besoin” (implied “of me”) or “si tu as besoin de quelque chose” (if you need something).
target_language_example: Je suis là si tu as besoin de moi.
native_language_example: I'm here if you need me.

si tu as quelque chose à dire

target_language_multi_word_term: si tu as quelque chose à dire
additional_notes: Used to challenge someone to speak up (often because they seem to be hinting, criticizing, or talking behind someone’s back). Commonly followed by an imperative like dis-le / dis-le-moi en face (“say it / say it to my face”). Can sound confrontational depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Si tu as quelque chose à dire, dis-le clairement.
native_language_example: If you have something to say, say it clearly.

meaning: "if you are" (used to start a condition).
additional_notes: "Si" introduces a condition, and "tu es" uses the informal singular "you" (tu) with the verb "être" (to be). It’s followed by a description/state: si tu es là (if you’re here), si tu es heureuse (if you’re happy), si tu es prête (if you’re ready). It can also be part of a longer form like "si tu es allé(e)..." = "if you went / have been...". Common pattern: "Si tu es…, (alors) …" = "If you’re…, (then) …".
target_language_example: Si tu es fatigué, on peut rentrer.
native_language_example: If you’re tired, we can go home.

additional_notes: Used to start a condition with si (“if”). tu = “you” (informal singular). le is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” (a masculine thing/idea) or “him” (a man/boy), and it goes before the verb: si tu le veux (“if you want it”), si tu le laisses (“if you leave it”), si tu le tues (“if you kill him/it”).
target_language_example: Si tu le finis aujourd’hui, on peut sortir demain.
native_language_example: If you finish it today, we can go out tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to start a conditional clause with a negative verb (si + tu + ne...). In everyday French, "ne" is often used with another negation word (e.g., "pas", "plus", "jamais"): "si tu ne viens pas" = "if you don't come". The result/main clause can come after or before it: "Si tu ne leur dis pas, je le ferai" / "Je le ferai si tu ne leur dis pas".
target_language_example: Si tu ne comprends pas, je peux répéter.
native_language_example: If you don't understand, I can repeat.

additional_notes: Often used to make a suggestion or invitation softer and more polite, implying it’s up to the other person. It can also be used like English “I mean / you know” (e.g., « Si tu veux, oui. » = “Yes, if you like / yes, I guess.”). In speech it’s sometimes shortened to « si tu veux » said quickly.
target_language_example: On peut se retrouver à 18h, si tu veux.
native_language_example: We can meet at 6 p.m., if you want.

additional_notes: Used with "si" + imparfait ("étais") to talk about unreal or unlikely situations. It’s often followed by the conditional to say what would happen: "Si tu étais…, tu ferais/tu serais…". Also common in "comme si tu étais…" = "as if you were…".
target_language_example: Si tu étais plus tôt, on pourrait partir maintenant.
native_language_example: If you were earlier, we could leave now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition: *si vous + verb*, meaning “if you…”. **Vous** is the formal singular (“you” to a stranger) or plural (“you all”), so *si vous* sounds polite or addresses more than one person. It can appear at the start of the sentence (*Si vous…*) or later (*… si vous …*).
target_language_example: Si vous avez des questions, n’hésitez pas à me demander.
native_language_example: If you have questions, don’t hesitate to ask me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition in polite/formal address (vous): "If you have X, then…" Common with besoin (need) or une question (a question): « si vous avez besoin… », « si vous avez une question… ». Often paired with a request or instruction in the next clause.
target_language_example: Si vous avez besoin d'aide, appelez-moi.
native_language_example: If you need help, call me.

si vous avez besoin de moi

target_language_multi_word_term: si vous avez besoin de moi
additional_notes: Used to offer help/availability politely (vous = formal or plural “you”). Often paired with a reassurance like “je suis là” (I’m here) or an instruction like “appelez-moi” (call me). You can also say “si tu as besoin de moi” to one person informally.
target_language_example: Je suis au bureau si vous avez besoin de moi.
native_language_example: I’m at the office if you need me.

additional_notes: A polite, formal/suggested default ("vous") used to invite questions. Often follows an offer of help or an instruction: "Contactez-moi / appelez-moi / venez me voir si vous avez des questions." You can add "des" (some/any) without changing the meaning much; in English it’s usually “any questions.”
target_language_example: Si vous avez des questions, n'hésitez pas à me contacter.
native_language_example: If you have any questions, don’t hesitate to contact me.

meaning: "if you (can/do) it" (starting a condition with polite/plural 'you' + 'it/him').
additional_notes: Used to begin an "if" clause (si...) where "vous" is the subject (polite or plural "you") and "le" is the direct object pronoun meaning "it" or "him." In French, object pronouns like "le" usually come before the verb: "si vous le pouvez" = "if you can (do) it," "si vous le trouvez" = "if you find it." The verb comes right after "le".
target_language_example: Si vous le voulez, on peut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: If you want, we can leave now.

additional_notes: Used to politely offer an option or to introduce a condition (often like “if you want” or “if you’d like”). It can sound like a softener meaning “if you prefer / it’s up to you,” as in offers and invitations: « Vous pouvez venir si vous voulez. »
target_language_example: On peut partir maintenant, si vous voulez.
native_language_example: We can leave now, if you’d like.

meaning: “if you don’t mind”; a polite “please” (asking someone to do something).
additional_notes: Used with "vous" to sound polite/formal when making a request or giving an instruction: "Si vous voulez bien + infinitive" (e.g., signer, venir, patienter). It can also be used alone as a courteous prompt ("Si vous voulez bien."). With emphatic punctuation ("Si vous voulez bien !"), it can sound impatient or like a firm "please!" depending on tone.
target_language_example: Si vous voulez bien patienter un instant, je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: If you don’t mind waiting a moment, I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition with the polite/formal or plural “you” (vous). Often followed by an adjective or noun: si vous êtes prêts (if you’re ready), si vous êtes étudiant (if you’re a student).
target_language_example: Si vous êtes fatigués, vous pouvez vous asseoir.
native_language_example: If you’re tired, you can sit down.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a conditional clause: si = “if” + ça = “that/it” (often referring to a situation or idea). Common in polite phrases like: « Si ça ne t'embête pas » (“If you don’t mind”), « Si ça t'intéresse » (“If you’re interested”), « Si ça vous va » (“If that works for you”).
target_language_example: Si ça marche, on part demain.
native_language_example: If it works, we’ll leave tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to state a length of time ("depuis six ans" = for six years; "pendant six ans" = for six years) or an age difference ("six ans plus âgé(e) que" = six years older than). "Six ans ?" can be used alone as a surprised question: “Six years?”
target_language_example: J'habite ici depuis six ans.
native_language_example: I've lived here for six years.

additional_notes: Means either a duration (six hours) or a time on the clock (six o’clock). Context usually makes it clear: with “par jour” or “plus de”, it’s a duration; with “vers” (around) or when talking about meeting/arriving, it’s a clock time. You can also say “à six heures” (at six o’clock).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à six heures devant le café.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at six o’clock in front of the café.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (pendant six mois, depuis six mois, ça fait six mois) or a point in the future/past (dans six mois, six mois plus tard). Often paired with time expressions like depuis (since/for), pendant (for/during), dans (in), environ (about), and plus tard (later).
target_language_example: Je reviens dans six mois.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in six months.

meaning: care of (used mainly in « prendre soin de » = “to take care of”).
additional_notes: Most common in the expression « prendre soin de + [person/thing] » meaning to look after someone/something or to be careful with it. You can use it for health (« Prenez soin de votre dos ») or for objects (« Il prend soin de sa voiture »).
target_language_example: Je prends soin de mes plantes tous les jours.
native_language_example: I take care of my plants every day.

meaning: 'care of him' (as in 'take care of him').
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb phrase **prendre soin de + person**: **prendre soin de lui** = “to take care of him / look after him.” Often appears in instructions or thanks: **Prends/Prenez (bien) soin de lui** (“Take (good) care of him”).
target_language_example: Pendant qu'il est malade, je vais prendre soin de lui.
native_language_example: While he's sick, I'm going to take care of him.

meaning: "care of you" / "care for you" (as in *prendre soin de toi* = "to take care of you").
additional_notes: Most commonly used with the verb *prendre*: *prendre soin de toi* = “to take care of you.” Very common as a friendly closing: *Prends soin de toi* / *Prenez soin de vous* (“Take care”). *bien* can add emphasis: *Prends bien soin de toi* (“Take good care of yourself”).
target_language_example: Je prendrai soin de toi pendant ton absence.
native_language_example: I’ll take care of you while you’re away.

additional_notes: Most often used in the expression « prendre soin de vous » (imperative: « Prenez soin de vous ! ») as a friendly way to say “Take care (of yourself)” when saying goodbye or wishing someone well. « vous » can be singular (formal “you”) or plural (“you all”).
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide — prenez soin de vous !
native_language_example: Thanks for your help—take care!

additional_notes: Used in a medical context to refer to the hospital unit where critically ill patients receive constant monitoring and specialized treatment. Common phrasing: « être en soins intensifs » = to be in intensive care.
target_language_example: Mon père est en soins intensifs depuis hier.
native_language_example: My father has been in intensive care since yesterday.

additional_notes: Imperative form (tu) of « être » + « gentil »: « sois gentil(le) avec + person » = telling someone to be kind to someone. Use « gentil » when speaking to a boy/man, « gentille » to a girl/woman (e.g., « Sois gentille avec ta sœur. »).
target_language_example: S'il te plaît, sois gentil avec moi.
native_language_example: Please, be nice to me.

additional_notes: "Sois" is the tu-form of être (to be). Used (1) as an imperative to tell someone to be present: "Sois là !" = "Be there!" and (2) after expressions like "je veux que...", "j'espère que..." to express a wish/requirement that someone be present (subjunctive): "Je veux que tu sois là" = "I want you to be there."
target_language_example: Je veux que tu sois là demain matin.
native_language_example: I want you to be there tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Literally “rising sun.” Can describe the sun in the morning (often in poetic/visual descriptions), and is also used in the fixed expression “le pays du soleil levant” to refer to Japan (“the Land of the Rising Sun”).
target_language_example: On a pris une photo du soleil levant depuis la plage.
native_language_example: We took a photo of the rising sun from the beach.

additional_notes: Used to ask questions by inverting the subject and the verb (être): "Nous sommes…" → "Sommes-nous… ?" Often followed by a place/state/time expression: "Sommes-nous dans… ?", "Sommes-nous en… ?" Can also appear in reflexive questions like "Nous sommes-nous déjà vus ?" (= Have we seen each other before?).
target_language_example: Sommes-nous prêts à partir ?
native_language_example: Are we ready to leave?

additional_notes: Used with “nous” to mean “we all …”. In compound tenses with être (especially reflexive verbs), “tous” often comes right after the auxiliary: “nous nous sommes tous + past participle” = “we all + verb” (e.g., we all sat down / we all fell asleep). It can also be in the present tense: “nous sommes tous …” = “we are all …” (e.g., “dans le même bateau” = “in the same boat”).
target_language_example: Nous nous sommes tous retrouvés au même endroit.
native_language_example: We all ended up in the same place.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun, not the owner). Use "son ami" for a male friend of either a man or a woman. (For a female friend: "son amie".) It can also mean "her boyfriend" in context.
target_language_example: Je l’ai vue au cinéma avec son ami.
native_language_example: I saw her at the movies with her friend (male)/boyfriend.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun: anniversaire is masculine). Most often, "son anniversaire" means someone’s birthday, but it can also mean the anniversary of an event (e.g., son anniversaire de mariage = his/her wedding anniversary).
target_language_example: On fait une fête pour son anniversaire.
native_language_example: We’re having a party for his/her birthday.

meaning: his money / her money / its money.
additional_notes: "Son" is the possessive adjective used with a masculine singular noun like "argent" (money), even if the owner is a woman: "Elle dépense son argent" = "She spends her money." For a plural owner, use "leur argent" (their money).
target_language_example: Il ne veut pas prêter son argent.
native_language_example: He doesn’t want to lend his money.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" depending on who you’re talking about (it agrees with the noun "bureau," which is masculine). "Bureau" can mean a workplace office (going to/leaving the office) or a desk (on the desk, at the desk), so the context tells you which.
target_language_example: Je t’appelle quand je suis de retour à son bureau.
native_language_example: I’ll call you when I’m back at his/her office.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" (not "its") depending on who owns the object; it’s used because "chapeau" is masculine singular. It can appear with verbs like mettre (put on), enlever/retirer/ôter (take off), or when something happens to the hat (e.g., the wind blows it away).
target_language_example: Elle cherche son chapeau partout.
native_language_example: She’s looking for her hat everywhere.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "son" + "chien" (dog). "Son" is used with masculine singular nouns like "chien" (even if the owner is a woman). In context, it can mean "his dog" or "her dog" depending on who you’re talking about.
target_language_example: Elle cherche son chien partout.
native_language_example: She’s looking for her dog everywhere.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" (or "its") depending on who owns the thing; it agrees with the noun that follows. Since "comportement" is masculine, you use "son" (not "sa"), even if it’s a woman’s behavior. Often used when judging or describing how someone acts.
target_language_example: Son comportement au travail est très professionnel.
native_language_example: His/Her behavior at work is very professional.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" depending on who you’re talking about; it matches the noun "corps" (masculine), not the person’s gender. In crime/accident contexts, "son corps" can imply a corpse; for a clear "dead body," French also says "son cadavre".
target_language_example: La police a retrouvé son corps près de la rivière.
native_language_example: The police found his/her body near the river.

additional_notes: “Son” is the possessive adjective used with the masculine singular noun “cœur” (heart). It can mean “his” or “her” depending on who owns the heart (e.g., *son cœur* = “his heart” or “her heart”). Often used figuratively for feelings and inner life: *dans son cœur* (“in his/her heart”), *rempli de joie* (“filled with joy”), *l’espoir a disparu de son cœur* (“hope disappeared from his/her heart”).
target_language_example: Elle garde toujours l’espoir dans son cœur.
native_language_example: She always keeps hope in her heart.

meaning: his/her speech; what he/she says (formal talk).
additional_notes: « Discours » is a (usually prepared) speech or formal talk, e.g., at an event or meeting. « Son » means “his” or “her” depending on who is being talked about (it agrees with the noun discours, masculine). You can also use it more broadly for someone’s “message” or “way of speaking” in a formal context.
target_language_example: Son discours a été très inspirant.
native_language_example: His/Her speech was very inspiring.

additional_notes: “Son” is a possessive adjective meaning “his/her/its” and it agrees with the noun that follows. Because “fils” is masculine singular, you use “son” even if the owner is a woman (e.g., “sa femme et son fils” = “his wife and his son”). The person who owns the son is understood from context (it can mean “her son” or “his son”).
target_language_example: J'ai parlé à son fils hier soir.
native_language_example: I spoke with his/her son last night.

additional_notes: Means “his/her brother,” depending on who owns the brother (son = his/her; frère = brother). You choose “son” (not “sa”) because frère is masculine. Used in many common structures: être fier de son frère (to be proud of his/her brother), prendre quelqu’un pour son frère (to mistake someone for his/her brother). In a question like « Son frère ? », it can mean “His/Her brother?” (surprise or clarification).
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma avec son frère ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with his/her brother tonight.

meaning: his/her/its story; his/her/its history (depending on context).
additional_notes: "Son" means “his/her/its” and agrees with the noun that follows, not the owner. Because "histoire" starts with a silent h (h muet), French uses "son" (not "sa") even if the owner is a woman: "son histoire" can mean “her story/history.” In personal contexts it often means “story” (account, explanation); in broader contexts (a country, an institution) it can mean “history.”
target_language_example: Elle dit que c'est son histoire, mais je ne suis pas sûr qu'elle soit vraie.
native_language_example: She says it's her story, but I'm not sure it's true.

additional_notes: "Son" is a possessive adjective meaning "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun, not the owner). Since "mari" is masculine singular, you use "son" (not *sa*), whether it’s her husband or his husband. For emphasis, you can say "le mari de + name": "le mari de Marie".
target_language_example: Je vais dîner avec son mari ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with her/his husband tonight.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" OR "her" (it agrees with the noun that follows). "Meilleur ami" is a male friend; for a female best friend, say "sa meilleure amie". Often used with "être" (to be) or "tomber amoureux/amoureuse de" (to fall in love with).
target_language_example: Je suis son meilleur ami depuis l'école primaire.
native_language_example: I've been his/her best friend since elementary school.

additional_notes: "Son" is a possessive adjective meaning "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun "nom," which is masculine, not with the person). Often used after verbs like connaître/savoir (to know) or prononcer (to say/pronounce) when talking about someone’s name.
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas son nom, mais je connais son visage.
native_language_example: I don’t know his/her name, but I know his/her face.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or mention a person’s surname. "son" agrees with the noun "nom" (masculine), so it can mean both "his" or "her" last name depending on context. Variants: "mon/ton/votre/leur nom de famille"; also commonly "son nom" in context.
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas son nom de famille, mais je connais son prénom.
native_language_example: I don’t know his/her last name, but I know his/her first name.

additional_notes: "Son" means “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun "roman" = masculine, not with the owner). Used to talk about a person’s latest book/novel; common with questions like "Que penses-tu de... ?" (What do you think of...?) and with publication verbs like "sortir" (to come out) or "être publié" (to be published).
target_language_example: J’ai adoré son nouveau roman, il est très bien écrit.
native_language_example: I loved his/her new novel; it’s very well written.

additional_notes: “Son” means “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun that follows, not the owner). Use it when referring to someone’s telephone number: donner son numéro de téléphone (to give your phone number), avoir son numéro (to have their number), connaître son numéro (to know their number).
target_language_example: J'ai son numéro de téléphone, je peux l'appeler.
native_language_example: I have his/her phone number, I can call him/her.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "laisser" to say someone left (forgot) their umbrella in/on the bus. "Son" means "his" or "her" depending on whose umbrella it is (it agrees with the noun "parapluie," which is masculine).
target_language_example: J’ai laissé mon parapluie dans le bus ce matin.
native_language_example: I left my umbrella on the bus this morning.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone likes doing in their free time. Usually followed by **de + infinitive** (Son passe-temps est de + verb) or by a **noun** (Son passe-temps est la peinture / la collection de timbres). For a female subject, you can also say **Son passe-temps est...** ("son" stays the same because *passe-temps* is masculine).
target_language_example: Son passe-temps est de jouer de la guitare.
native_language_example: His/Her hobby is playing the guitar.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "son" (his/its) + the noun "petit-déjeuner" (breakfast). It commonly appears after "prendre" (to have/eat), as in "prendre son petit-déjeuner" = "to have (his) breakfast".
target_language_example: Il prend son petit-déjeuner à 7 heures.
native_language_example: He has his breakfast at 7 o'clock.

meaning: her boyfriend / his boyfriend (depending on context).
additional_notes: Means “(someone’s) boyfriend.” In French, "son" is used (not "sa") before a feminine noun starting with a vowel sound, like "ami" (a-mi), to avoid two vowel sounds in a row. So "son petit ami" can refer to either “her boyfriend” or “his boyfriend”; the context tells you whose it is.
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas son petit ami, mais j’aimerais le rencontrer.
native_language_example: I don’t know her/his boyfriend, but I’d like to meet him.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective (son/sa/ses) + « point de vue » to talk about someone’s opinion or perspective on something. Often followed by « sur » + topic (e.g., « son point de vue sur ce sujet »).
target_language_example: J’aimerais connaître son point de vue sur la situation.
native_language_example: I’d like to know his/her point of view on the situation.

meaning: "his/its own" (emphasizes that something belongs specifically to him/it).
additional_notes: Used to stress that someone/something has a separate, personal version of something: son propre dîner (his own dinner), son propre monde (his own world). The possessive changes with the noun: sa propre maison, ses propres idées. "Propre" agrees with the thing owned (propre / propres), not with the owner.
target_language_example: Il a ses propres raisons.
native_language_example: He has his own reasons.

meaning: his father / her father / its father.
additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" depending on the noun that follows (here: "père" is masculine), not on who owns it. For emphasis or contrast, French often adds "à + stressed pronoun": "Son père à elle" = "Her father" (as opposed to someone else’s).
target_language_example: Son père travaille à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: Her/His father works at the hospital.

additional_notes: Used to state what someone’s father is like (nationality, job, situation, etc.). Note: **son** can mean **his** or **her**—it agrees with the noun (**père** is masculine), so it can refer to *her father* as well (e.g., *Sa mère est française et son père est russe*).
target_language_example: Son père est médecin.
native_language_example: His/Her father is a doctor.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the image of someone seen in a mirror. "Son" agrees with the noun "reflet" (masculine), not with the person—so it can mean "his" or "her" reflection depending on context.
target_language_example: Je me suis vu dans la glace et j'ai souri à mon reflet dans le miroir.
native_language_example: I saw myself in the mirror and smiled at my reflection.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun "sac," which is masculine, not with the owner). "Sac" can mean a bag in general (backpack, handbag, etc.); for a purse you may also hear "son sac à main."
target_language_example: J'ai oublié mon téléphone dans son sac.
native_language_example: I forgot my phone in his/her bag.

additional_notes: “Son” means “his” or “her” depending on who owns the thing (it agrees with the noun “travail,” which is masculine). “Son travail” can refer to someone’s job (what they do for a living) or to their work/effort on a specific project (e.g., school, research, writing).
target_language_example: Elle a fini son travail et elle rentre à la maison.
native_language_example: She finished her work and is going home.

additional_notes: "Son" means "his" or "her" (it agrees with the noun, not the person). Since "visage" is masculine, you use "son" even for a woman. Often used with verbs like "regarder" (to look at) or descriptions of facial color/expression ("rouge", "pâle").
target_language_example: Je reconnais son visage, mais j’ai oublié son nom.
native_language_example: I recognize his/her face, but I forgot his/her name.

additional_notes: Literally “his/her age.” Used with comparisons like « pour son âge » (“for his/her age”) to say someone seems young/old/tall/short/fit/etc. compared with what’s typical at that age. « C’est de son âge » means “It’s appropriate for his/her age / It’s typical for someone that age.”
target_language_example: Il est très mature pour son âge.
native_language_example: He’s very mature for his age.

additional_notes: Used in formal/standard questions with subject–verb inversion: verb + pronoun, linked with a hyphen ("sont-elles..."). It refers to "elles" (= they, feminine plural: a group of women/girls or feminine nouns). Common in writing and more formal speech; in conversation you’ll often hear "Est-ce qu’elles sont… ?" or "Elles sont… ?".
target_language_example: Sont-elles prêtes à partir ?
native_language_example: Are they ready to leave?

meaning: "are they?" (formal written question form of "ils sont").
additional_notes: Used to form an inverted question with "ils" (they) and the verb "être" (to be), mostly in formal speech and writing. It can be followed by an adjective or noun (Sont-ils prêts ?), a place/state (Sont-ils ici ?), or part of a larger question (Quand sont-ils partis ?). In everyday conversation, you often hear "Ils sont… ?" or "Est-ce qu’ils sont… ?" instead.
target_language_example: Sont-ils prêts à partir ?
native_language_example: Are they ready to leave?

additional_notes: Used in formal-style questions with subject–verb inversion: «sont-ils» = “are they” (masculine plural “they”), often after «Pourquoi… ?». «si» means “so” before an adjective/adverb: «si ennuyeux» = “so boring.” For feminine plural, use «sont-elles si… ?».
target_language_example: Pourquoi sont-ils si fatigués aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Why are they so tired today?

additional_notes: This is a formal question structure using inversion: verb + pronoun ("sont-ils" = "are they"). "tous" means "all" and refers to a group of people/things. It’s often followed by an adjective or past participle: "Sont-ils tous prêts ?" (Are they all ready?), "Sont-ils tous venus ?" (Did they all come?).
target_language_example: Sont-ils tous d’accord ?
native_language_example: Do they all agree?

additional_notes: Past tense of aller (to go) with être in the passé composé: ils/elles sont allés. It agrees with the subject: allés (masculine plural or mixed group), allées (feminine plural). Often used with a place (à, dans, chez) or an activity (e.g., sont allés voir...).
target_language_example: Ils sont allés au cinéma hier soir.
native_language_example: They went to the movie theater last night.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of *arriver* for **ils** (or a mixed group): **être** + past participle. *Arrivés* agrees in number/gender (e.g., **elles sont arrivées**). Often used with a place: **Ils sont arrivés à Boston** = “They arrived in Boston.” With **y**: **Ils y sont arrivés** = “They got there.” With **à** + noun it can mean “reached/came to” (e.g., a conclusion): **Ils sont arrivés à la même conclusion** = “They came to the same conclusion.”
target_language_example: Ils sont arrivés en retard, mais tout le monde était déjà là.
native_language_example: They arrived late, but everyone was already there.

meaning: "are those who" (used to introduce the people who...).
additional_notes: This is an inverted, more literary/formal word order: instead of "Ceux qui… sont…" (Those who… are…), French can say "… sont ceux qui…" (… are those who…). It’s often used with adjectives like "Heureux", "Nombreux", "Rares", "Peu nombreux", etc.: "Heureux sont ceux qui…" = "Happy are those who…"
target_language_example: Rares sont ceux qui savent rester calmes dans cette situation.
native_language_example: Few are those who know how to stay calm in this situation.

additional_notes: Used with a plural subject to identify/classify it: “X sont des Y” = “X are (some) Y.” Use “des” before a plural noun (often a category, job, religion, etc.). For adjectives, you don’t use “des”: “Ils sont gentils.”
target_language_example: Ces livres sont des romans policiers.
native_language_example: These books are detective novels.

additional_notes: Used with a plural subject to classify/describe what something is: "X sont des animaux ..." + adjective or noun phrase (dangereux, de compagnie, nocturnes, imaginaires). It’s the verb "être" (ils/elles sont) + "des" (plural “some”) + "animaux" (animals).
target_language_example: Les dauphins sont des animaux très intelligents.
native_language_example: Dolphins are very intelligent animals.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not easy to do: *sont difficiles à + verb* (e.g., *sont difficiles à comprendre*). It agrees with the subject: *est difficile à* (singular), *sont difficiles à* (plural); feminine forms are *difficile/difficiles*.
target_language_example: Ces exercices sont difficiles à faire sans aide.
native_language_example: These exercises are hard to do without help.

meaning: 'are in' (used with a noun to describe a state, condition, or location).
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase **être** (to be) in the **ils/elles** form (**sont**) + **en** + noun. It often describes a situation rather than a simple place: **en vente** = for sale, **en approche** = approaching, **en lambeaux** = in tatters, **en pleine floraison** = in full bloom, **en bas** = downstairs/down below. The exact English translation depends on the noun after **en**.
target_language_example: Les documents sont en cours de traduction.
native_language_example: The documents are being translated.

meaning: 'are (in the process of) / are currently' (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive (e.g., « sont en train de + infinitif ») to emphasize an action happening right now or in progress. It’s a form of the expression « être en train de »; « sont » is the 3rd-person plural (they/you plural) form of « être ». Often translates as “are currently …” or “are in the middle of …”.
target_language_example: Ils sont en train de préparer le dîner.
native_language_example: They are preparing dinner (right now).

additional_notes: Used with the verb être (to be) for a plural subject: (ils/elles) sont + les + plural noun. Common in definitions or identification: « X sont les Y ». Also appears in questions like « Qui sont les … ? » (Who are the …?).
target_language_example: Ce sont les voisins.
native_language_example: They are the neighbors.

additional_notes: Used with a plural subject: "ils/elles + sont" + "mes" + plural noun (or adjective + noun). "Mes" is the plural form of "mon/ma" and is used before both masculine and feminine plural nouns (e.g., mes amis, mes voisines). In questions, French often uses "Qui sont mes… ?" ("Who are my…?").
target_language_example: Ces clés sont mes clés de voiture.
native_language_example: These keys are my car keys.

additional_notes: "Sont morts" is the passé composé of *mourir* for plural subjects (ils/elles). It’s used to say that people/animals died or are dead. For a single person: *il/elle est mort(e)*; for plural females: *elles sont mortes*. Often followed by details like *à la guerre* (in the war), *dans une bataille* (in a battle), or *pour ça* (for that).
target_language_example: Beaucoup d’animaux sont morts pendant l’hiver.
native_language_example: Many animals died during the winter.

additional_notes: Passé composé of partir with être: used with plural subjects (ils/elles/les…) to say people/things have departed. The past participle agrees with the subject: partis (masc. plural) / parties (fem. plural). Often followed by a destination (vers…, pour…, à…).
target_language_example: Ils sont partis il y a dix minutes.
native_language_example: They left ten minutes ago.

additional_notes: Used with negation: standard French is « ne sont pas » (they are not). In casual spoken French, « ne » is often dropped, so you may hear « ils/elles sont pas » = « ils/elles ne sont pas ». You’ll also see it with other negative patterns like « ne … pas tous » (not all) and in compound tenses as « ne se sont pas + past participle » (did not / have not).
target_language_example: Ils sont pas prêts, donc on attend.
native_language_example: They aren’t ready, so we’re waiting.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives to make comparisons, often with "que" (than): "sont plus grandes que..." = "are taller than...". Many adjectives can be translated with “more + adjective” or with an “-er” form in English (plus grand = taller/bigger; plus petit = smaller). Watch out for "ne ... sont plus": with "ne ... plus", "plus" means "no longer" (e.g., "Ils ne sont plus en vie" = "They are no longer alive").
target_language_example: Ces exercices sont plus faciles que ceux d’hier.
native_language_example: These exercises are easier than yesterday’s.

meaning: are about to (do something); are on the verge of (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with a subject + form of "être" (here: "sont" = "are") + "sur le point de" + infinitive to say something is going to happen very soon. It often suggests imminence (sometimes with a dramatic tone): "Les choses sont sur le point de changer" = "Things are about to change."
target_language_example: Nous sommes sur le point de partir.
native_language_example: We’re about to leave.

additional_notes: Used when the subject is plural (or a singular group/person treated as plural with **ce sont**). **sont** = “are” (3rd person plural of *être*), and **tes** = “your” (informal singular “your,” used before a plural noun of any gender: *tes options, tes intentions, tes voisins*). Often appears in questions like **Quelles sont tes… ?** (“What are your…?”) or **Où sont tes… ?** (“Where are your…?”).
target_language_example: Où sont tes clés ?
native_language_example: Where are your keys?

additional_notes: Used with the verb être (sont = “are”) to say that all members of a plural group have the same quality or are in the same situation. Tous is usually placed right after the verb: « Ils sont tous… ». It refers to a masculine or mixed group; for an all-female group you often see « sont toutes ».
target_language_example: Ils sont tous prêts à partir.
native_language_example: They’re all ready to leave.

additional_notes: Used when you have two subjects (A et B) and want to say they share the same situation/quality. It commonly comes right after the verb: « Ils sont tous les deux… ». For feminine subjects, you usually say « sont toutes les deux ».
target_language_example: Mes parents sont tous les deux médecins.
native_language_example: My parents are both doctors.

additional_notes: Used with the verb être (“to be”) + the feminine plural form of tout (“all”). It agrees with what it refers to: use toutes for feminine plural nouns (batteries, réponses, affaires). Word order often matches English: noun + sont toutes + adjective/place (e.g., “are all correct / are all here”).
target_language_example: Ces feuilles sont toutes mouillées.
native_language_example: These sheets of paper are all wet.

additional_notes: “Sont” is the 3rd-person plural form of *être* (“to be”), used with plural subjects like *ils/elles*, *mes parents*, *les paysages*, *ces pommes*, etc. It’s commonly followed by an adjective: *sont très + adjectif*. Remember the adjective usually agrees with the subject in gender/number (e.g., *différents*, *strictes*, *sucrées*).
target_language_example: Ces exercices sont très faciles.
native_language_example: These exercises are very easy.

additional_notes: Past tense of venir for “they” (ils/elles): être (sont) + past participle (venus/venues). Means people arrived or came somewhere to do something (“sont venus étudier…”, “sont venus interroger…”). Agree the ending with the group: venus (masculine/mixed) vs venues (all feminine).
target_language_example: Ils sont venus trop tard pour le train.
native_language_example: They came too late for the train.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **être** (“to be”): **sont** = “are” (3rd person plural), **vos** = “your” (plural or formal singular). Often appears in questions like **Ce sont vos… ?** (“Are these your…?”) or with **De quelle couleur sont vos… ?** (“What color are your…?”).
target_language_example: Ce sont vos clés ?
native_language_example: Are these your keys?

meaning: “Get out of there.” / “Come out of there.”
additional_notes: Imperative (command) with **tu** of **sortir** (“to go out/to come out”). Used to tell someone to leave a place or come out from somewhere (e.g., a room, hiding place). It can also be used more figuratively to express disbelief or to tell someone to stop/leave with that idea (similar to “Get out of here!”). The formal/plural version is **sortez de là**. Related: **Je vous sors de là** = “I’ll get you out of there / out of this situation.”
target_language_example: Sors de là tout de suite !
native_language_example: Get out of there right now!

additional_notes: Used to indicate a type/category ("une sorte de + noun") or to soften what you’re saying, meaning “more or less / kind of.” It agrees with the article you use: "une sorte de" (most common), "un(e) sorte de" depending on what follows; in questions you often see "Quelle sorte de… ?" (“What kind of…?”). The noun after "de" is usually without an article: "une sorte de blague".
target_language_example: C’est une sorte de café, mais plus fort.
native_language_example: It’s a kind of coffee, but stronger.

additional_notes: Used after a quantity or adjective to talk about categories/varieties of something: «différentes sortes de + noun». «Sorte» is feminine, so you often see «une sorte de» (a kind of) or «des sortes de» (kinds of).
target_language_example: On vend plusieurs sortes de pain ici.
native_language_example: They sell several kinds of bread here.

meaning: to get out of here; to leave this place.
additional_notes: Literally “to go out from here.” Used when you want to leave the current place, often with a sense of urgency or escape. Conjugates with sortir: je sors d’ici, tu sors d’ici, il/elle sort d’ici, etc.
target_language_example: On doit sortir d'ici avant la nuit.
native_language_example: We have to get out of here before nightfall.

meaning: to get out of there; to get someone out of there (out of that situation).
additional_notes: Often used with an object pronoun (me/te/le/la/nous/vous/les): « me sortir de là » = “get me out of there.” Can refer to a physical place (get out of there) or a difficult situation (get out of this mess/problem).
target_language_example: Je vais essayer de te sortir de là.
native_language_example: I’m going to try to get you out of there.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object to say who you’re wishing luck to: « souhaiter bonne chance à quelqu’un » or, very commonly, « te/vous souhaiter bonne chance » (te = to you, informal singular; vous = to you, formal or plural). You can also just say « Bonne chance ! » as a standalone phrase.
target_language_example: Je te souhaite bonne chance pour ton examen.
native_language_example: I wish you good luck for your exam.

additional_notes: From the verb « souhaiter » (to wish, to want). Used in formal or polite questions (often customer service, invitations, offers). It’s the inverted form « souhaitez + vous » and is more formal than « vous voulez… ? ». It can be followed by an infinitive (« Souhaitez-vous y aller ? »), by « en » (« Souhaitez-vous en entendre plus ? »), or by « que + subjunctive » (« Souhaitez-vous que je vous laisse seule ? »).
target_language_example: Souhaitez-vous payer par carte ou en espèces ?
native_language_example: Would you like to pay by card or with cash?

additional_notes: Used to indicate position beneath something: « sous la chaise » (“under the chair”). Also used more abstractly for being affected by something (« sous la pression » = “under pressure”) or under authority (« sous la direction de… » = “under the direction of…”). Many set phrases use it (e.g., « sous la flèche verte » = “under the green arrow”; « sous la pédale » is idiomatic in « en avoir encore sous la pédale » meaning “to still have some power/energy left”).
target_language_example: Le sac est sous la table.
native_language_example: The bag is under the table.

additional_notes: Used mainly with "être" to say someone is currently taking a shower: "Il/Elle est sous la douche." It can also describe doing something while showering: "Je chante sous la douche."
target_language_example: Je suis sous la douche, je te rappelle après.
native_language_example: I’m in the shower; I’ll call you back later.

meaning: in the rain; out in the rain (being rained on).
additional_notes: Used for being outside while it’s raining, often implying you’re getting wet. Common with verbs like rester, marcher, chanter, danser, être pris (“to get caught”) sous la pluie.
target_language_example: On s’est promenés sous la pluie sans parapluie.
native_language_example: We went for a walk in the rain without an umbrella.

additional_notes: Literally means something is located beneath a table (or someone is hiding there). In other contexts, "sous la table" can also refer to something placed under the table (e.g., a hidden object).
target_language_example: Le chat dort sous la table.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping under the table.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically below/under a masculine singular noun: sous le bras (under the arm), sous le siège (under the seat), sous le sapin (under the tree). It can also mean “under the name of” in expressions like sous le nom de (“under the name of”). For feminine singular, use sous la; for plural, sous les.
target_language_example: Le chat dort sous le lit.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping under the bed.

additional_notes: "Sous" means "under"; "le lit" means "the bed." Used to say where something is located (or where to hide/put it). You can also use it as a short answer to "Où ?" ("Where?"): « Sous le lit. »
target_language_example: Mes chaussures sont sous le lit.
native_language_example: My shoes are under the bed.

additional_notes: Refers to the level of a building below ground level. Often used with prepositions like "au/du sous-sol" (in/from the basement) or "par le sous-sol" (through/by way of the basement).
target_language_example: On garde les vieilles affaires au sous-sol.
native_language_example: We keep the old stuff in the basement.

meaning: "remember" / "make sure to remember" (formal or plural command).
additional_notes: Imperative form of **se souvenir de** (“to remember”). Used to tell one person politely (**vous**) or multiple people to remember something. It is followed by **de + noun/pronoun** (Souvenez-vous de ça.) or **de + infinitive** (Souvenez-vous de ne le dire à personne !).
target_language_example: Souvenez-vous de prendre vos clés avant de partir.
native_language_example: Remember to take your keys before leaving.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun: souvent (often) + des (some/any). Des is the plural indefinite article (like “some”) and becomes de after negation: Je ne mange pas de pâtes. In questions, des often corresponds to “any”: Vous mangez souvent des champignons ? (“Do you often eat mushrooms?”).
target_language_example: Je prends souvent des photos quand je voyage.
native_language_example: I often take photos when I travel.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of "se souvenir" used to tell one person (tu) to remember something. Often followed by "de" + noun (Souviens-toi de ce nom) or "que" + clause (Souviens-toi que ton vote est secret).
target_language_example: Souviens-toi de prendre tes clés avant de partir.
native_language_example: Remember to take your keys before you leave.

additional_notes: Imperative form of **se souvenir de** (“to remember”). Used to remind one person you address as **tu**. It’s followed by **de** + a noun (Souviens-toi de ce nom) or **de ce que + clause** (Souviens-toi de ce que j’ai dit).
target_language_example: Souviens-toi de prendre tes clés avant de partir.
native_language_example: Remember to take your keys before leaving.

additional_notes: Common everyday term for a pen that uses a small rolling ball at the tip (ballpoint). Often used in instructions (e.g., on forms): « Écrivez avec un stylo à bille. »
target_language_example: Tu as un stylo à bille pour remplir ce formulaire ?
native_language_example: Do you have a ballpoint pen to fill out this form?

subvenir aux besoins de sa famille

target_language_multi_word_term: subvenir aux besoins de sa famille
meaning: to provide for/support one’s family (meet their needs).
additional_notes: Used to talk about earning enough money or having enough resources to cover a family’s basic needs (food, housing, bills, etc.). You can also say “subvenir aux besoins de + [person/group]” (e.g., subvenir aux besoins de ses enfants). Commonly used with “pouvoir/ne pas pouvoir” and “(trop) faible/insuffisant pour…”.
target_language_example: Avec ce travail, elle arrive enfin à subvenir aux besoins de sa famille.
native_language_example: With this job, she can finally provide for her family.

additional_notes: Used to ask a question with subject–verb inversion: "suis" (I am) + "je" (I). This is a more formal/literary way to say "Est-ce que je suis… ?" or, in speech, just "Je suis… ?" Often followed by an adjective or noun: "Suis-je prêt ?"
target_language_example: Suis-je en retard ?
native_language_example: Am I late?

meaning: "am I supposed to" / "am I meant/expected to".
additional_notes: Used to ask what you are expected or intended to do (often implying confusion, doubt, or mild protest). It’s the inversion question form of "je suis censé". Follow it with an infinitive: "Suis-je censé + infinitive ?" (e.g., faire, dormir, croire). Feminine speaker: "suis-je censée".
target_language_example: Suis-je censé attendre ici ?
native_language_example: Am I supposed to wait here?

meaning: "I went" / "I have gone" (past tense of aller, "to go").
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of aller with the auxiliary être: je suis allé(e). It often appears with y (“there”): J’y suis allé = “I went there / I’ve been there.” With être, the past participle agrees with the subject: allé (masc.), allée (fem.), allés/allées (plural).
target_language_example: Je suis allé au cinéma hier soir.
native_language_example: I went to the movie theater last night.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *arriver* with the auxiliary **être**: *je suis arrivé(e)* (add **-e** if the speaker is female). Used for physically arriving (*Quand je suis arrivé…*). With **y** (*J’y suis arrivé*), it often means “I managed it / I succeeded.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je suis arrivé à temps.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I arrived on time.

additional_notes: Past tense with être: "je suis arrivé(e)" (add -e if the speaker is female). Used with a time marker like "quand" (when) to describe what happened when you got to the train station. "À la gare" means "at/to the station" (the train station).
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé à la gare trop tard et j'ai raté le train.
native_language_example: I arrived at the station too late and I missed the train.

additional_notes: Most often used as **Je suis désolé(e)** to apologize or express regret. **Désolé** agrees with the speaker: **désolé** (male), **désolée** (female), **désolés / désolées** (plural). You can also say **J’en suis désolé** = “I’m sorry about that / I regret it.”
target_language_example: Je suis désolé, je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I can’t come tonight.

meaning: "I am in / on" (in a state, situation, or mode of transport).
additional_notes: This is the form of "être en" with "je" (je suis). It’s used before a noun (often without an article) to describe what state you’re in (je suis en service = I’m on duty; je suis en désaccord = I disagree / I’m in disagreement), where/situation you’re in (je suis en prison / en taule = I’m in prison), or how you’re traveling (je suis en hélico = I’m in a helicopter). The exact English translation depends on the noun after "en".
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas répondre : je suis en réunion.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t answer: I’m in a meeting.

additional_notes: From the verb **être** (to be): **je suis** = “I am” + **là** = “here/there.” In practice, **je suis là** usually means “I’m here” (present, available). It can also mean “I’m there” depending on context (location already mentioned). Common in phrases like **quand je suis là** (“when I’m here”) or **je ne suis là que pour...** (“I’m only here to/for...”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je suis là.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m here.

additional_notes: From the verb **naître** (to be born), used in the **passé composé** with **être**: *je suis né*. The past participle agrees with the subject: **je suis né** (male speaker) / **je suis née** (female speaker). Often followed by a place or date: *Je suis né à Paris / en 2001*.
target_language_example: Je suis né en France, mais j'ai grandi au Canada.
native_language_example: I was born in France, but I grew up in Canada.

meaning: "(I) am not" / "(I) have not" (informal: short for "(je) ne suis pas").
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: people often drop "ne" in negation. So "je suis pas" = "je ne suis pas" (I’m not). You’ll also see it in the passé composé with "être" as the helping verb, especially with reflexive verbs: "je me suis pas réveillé(e)" = "je ne me suis pas réveillé(e)" (I didn’t wake up). In "Tu ne me suis pas ?", "suis" is from "suivre" (to follow), so it means "You’re not following me?" (i.e., you don’t understand).
target_language_example: Je suis pas sûr de comprendre.
native_language_example: I’m not sure I understand.

meaning: "(I) am not yet" (informal for "je ne suis pas encore").
additional_notes: Common in spoken French: the negative "ne" is often dropped ("je suis pas" instead of "je ne suis pas"). Used with adjectives/past participles to say you haven’t reached a state yet: "(je) suis pas encore prêt(e)" (not ready yet), "(je) suis pas encore sûr(e)" (not sure yet), "(je) suis pas encore parti(e)" (haven’t left yet), "(je) m’en suis pas encore remis(e)" (I haven’t gotten over it yet). "Pas encore" = "not yet" (vs. "encore" alone can mean "still/again").
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis pas encore prêt.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m not ready yet.

meaning: "I'm not a…" (informal for « je ne suis pas un… »).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: « ne » is often dropped, so « je ne suis pas un… » becomes « je suis pas un… ». Used before a masculine singular noun (un). For a feminine noun, you’d say « je suis pas une… ».
target_language_example: T’inquiète, je suis pas un menteur.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m not a liar.
