meaning: "I'm not a…" (said by a woman or about something feminine).
additional_notes: This is a common spoken/informal shortening of the negative form **je ne suis pas une…** (“I am not a…”). It’s used before a **feminine singular noun** (une exception, une victime, etc.). In careful/formal French, keep **ne**: **je ne suis pas une…**. For masculine nouns, you’d say **je suis pas un…**.
target_language_example: T’inquiète, je suis pas une étrangère ici.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m not a stranger here.

additional_notes: Used to express gratitude: **(Je) suis reconnaissant(e) pour + noun/what someone did**. Add **-e** if the speaker is female: *Je suis reconnaissante pour…*. Often used with **vous/te**: *Je vous suis reconnaissant(e) pour votre aide.* In everyday speech you can also say *Merci pour…* (more common).
target_language_example: Je vous suis reconnaissant pour votre soutien.
native_language_example: I’m grateful to you for your support.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of rentrer with être: je suis rentré = “I came back/returned,” often implying “I came home.” It agrees with the subject: je suis rentrée (feminine). You’ll often see it after quand (when): Quand je suis rentré… = “When I got back…”
target_language_example: Je suis rentré tard hier soir.
native_language_example: I got home late last night.

additional_notes: Used after **je** to intensify an adjective: **je suis très + adjective** (“I am very + adjective”). Very common with feelings/opinions: **Je suis très content(e)** (very happy), **Je suis très fier/fière** (very proud). With **en** it means “about it/with it”: **J’en suis très content(e)** (“I’m very happy about it”). With an indirect object it can mean “I’m very grateful to you”: **Je vous suis très reconnaissant(e)**.
target_language_example: Je suis très heureux de te voir.
native_language_example: I’m very happy to see you.

meaning: 'am a' / 'am an' (used after je: 'je suis un...').
additional_notes: From the verb être (to be): je suis = I am. Use un before a masculine noun (je suis un scout, je suis un intrus). For feminine nouns, use une: je suis une étudiante. If the noun starts with a vowel sound, English may use 'an' but French still uses un/une (je suis un ingénieur / je suis une ingénieure).
target_language_example: Je suis un étudiant en français.
native_language_example: I am a French student.

meaning: 'I came' / 'I have come' (past tense of venir, masculine).
additional_notes: Passé composé of **venir** with **être**: **je suis venu** (masc.), **je suis venue** (fem.). With **être**, the past participle agrees in gender/number (ex. *nous sommes venus/venues*). Very often followed by an infinitive to say the purpose: *je suis venu te parler* (“I came to talk to you”).
target_language_example: Je suis venu te dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I came to tell you the truth.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of venir (to come) with être: je suis venu (masc.) / je suis venue (fem.). The past participle agrees with the subject (adds -e for feminine). Often used with an infinitive to mean "I came to + verb": je suis venue voir… = "I came to see…". Don’t confuse French venue here with the English noun “venue” (place).
target_language_example: Je suis venue te voir hier.
native_language_example: I came to see you yesterday.

additional_notes: Imperative of suivre (“to follow”) + moi (“me”). Uses the vous form: it can address one person politely or several people (e.g., a guide speaking to a group). For an informal singular command, you’d say: « Suis-moi. »
target_language_example: Suivez-moi, je vais vous montrer votre table.
native_language_example: Follow me, I’ll show you your table.

additional_notes: Refers to a (usually fictional) hero with extraordinary powers or abilities (e.g., Batman, Superman). Used with an article (un/une) and pluralizes as super-héros (same spelling in plural). The feminine form is often "super-héroïne".
target_language_example: Les super-héros protègent souvent la ville la nuit.
native_language_example: Superheroes often protect the city at night.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an assumption or probable idea. With "je suppose que", it often sounds like a cautious agreement or mild uncertainty ("I suppose/guess"). With "on suppose que", it means "it is assumed" (more impersonal, often in reports).
target_language_example: Je suppose que tu es déjà parti.
native_language_example: I guess you've already left.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific thing just mentioned or understood from context: sur ce point (on this point), sur ce coup (on that occasion), appuyez sur ce bouton (press this button). In speech, phrases like « Ne me lance pas sur ce… » mean “Don’t get me started on that…”.
target_language_example: Je suis d’accord sur ce point.
native_language_example: I agree on this point.

meaning: "on this" / "about this" (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns: sur cette + noun (e.g., sur cette carte = on this map). With some nouns it’s literal location (“on this…”), and with others it means the topic (“about this…”), e.g., des détails sur cette rencontre = details about this meeting/encounter.
target_language_example: Je n’ai rien écrit sur cette page.
native_language_example: I didn’t write anything on this page.

additional_notes: Used when talking about a phone call being played through the phone’s loudspeaker so other people in the room can hear. Common with verbs like « mettre » (Je te mets sur haut-parleur) or « être » (On est sur haut-parleur ?).
target_language_example: Tu peux répéter ? Je suis sur haut-parleur et ça grésille.
native_language_example: Can you repeat? I’m on speaker and it’s crackling.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun: sur + la. It often expresses position (on top of), direction/location (“on the right”), or being “on/along” something more abstract (e.g., sur la trace = on the trail/track of). Before a vowel or silent h, it becomes “sur l’” (sur l’autoroute).
target_language_example: Le livre est sur la table.
native_language_example: The book is on the table.

meaning: on the map (or on the menu).
additional_notes: “La carte” can mean a map, a menu, or a card. So “sur la carte” often means “on the map” (as in locating a place), but in a restaurant it commonly means “on the menu” (e.g., C’est sur la carte = It’s on the menu).
target_language_example: Je ne trouve pas ce village sur la carte.
native_language_example: I can’t find this village on the map.

meaning: on the hill; up on the hill.
additional_notes: Used to indicate location or movement involving a hill. With verbs of position (être, se tenir, se trouver, être situé), it means something is located on/up on the hill. With movement verbs like grimper/monter, it can describe going up onto the hill. Sometimes it implies a higher vantage point (up on the hill) rather than strictly “on top of” it.
target_language_example: On voit tout le village depuis la maison sur la colline.
native_language_example: You can see the whole village from the house on the hill.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located or happens (a kiss, a mark, lipstick). Often with verbs like embrasser/faire un bisou (to kiss) or avoir/mettre (to have/put).
target_language_example: Il m’a fait un bisou sur la joue.
native_language_example: He gave me a kiss on the cheek.

additional_notes: Used for names or items that are included on a list (guest list, waiting list, to-do list, etc.). Often appears with names: « Son/Votre nom est sur la liste. » It can also mean someone’s position in an order: « le prochain sur la liste » = the next one on the list.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas sur la liste, mais j’ai une réservation.
native_language_example: I’m not on the list, but I have a reservation.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located on the beach (sand/shore area). Often follows verbs like être (to be), aller (to go), jouer (to play), trouver (to find).
target_language_example: On se retrouve sur la plage à 16 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet on the beach at 4 p.m.?

meaning: on the road; on the way (traveling).
additional_notes: Used for being physically on a road while traveling (by car, etc.), or more generally being en route/in transit. In some contexts, "route" can also mean a route/sea lane ("route maritime"), so "sur la route" can mean "on the route" rather than literally on a roadway.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas répondre : je suis sur la route.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t reply: I’m on the road (traveling).

additional_notes: Used to say something is located/placed on top of a table. Common with verbs like "il y a" (there is/are), "mettre" (to put), and "poser" (to set/place).
target_language_example: J'ai laissé mes clés sur la table.
native_language_example: I left my keys on the table.

meaning: on the head; (figurative) are you crazy?!
additional_notes: Literal: describes something located or placed on someone’s head (une bosse sur la tête, un chapeau sur la tête). Figurative in the expression « Tu es tombé(e) sur la tête ? » meaning “Have you lost your mind?” / “Are you crazy?” Also appears in oaths like « Sur la tête de ma mère ! » (“On my mother’s life!”) to swear you’re telling the truth.
target_language_example: Mais tu es tombé sur la tête ou quoi ?
native_language_example: Are you crazy or what?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: sur le + noun (e.g., sur le canapé). With feminine singular you use sur la; with plural, sur les. Before a vowel or silent h: sur l’ (e.g., sur l’écran).
target_language_example: Le livre est sur le bureau.
native_language_example: The book is on the desk.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is positioned on a bench (a seat in a park, street, etc.). With verbs like s’asseoir (to sit down), être assis (to be seated), or dormir (to sleep).
target_language_example: Ils attendent sur le banc devant la gare.
native_language_example: They’re waiting on the bench in front of the train station.

meaning: on the button (the one you press/click).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like appuyer sur (press) and cliquer sur (click). The preposition sur means “on/onto,” and le bouton is “the button,” often in physical devices or on-screen interfaces (e.g., “OK”).
target_language_example: Appuie sur le bouton pour démarrer.
native_language_example: Press the button to start.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or placed on top of a desk/office desk. Common with verbs like être (to be), il y a (there is), poser/mettre (to put/place). In answers, it can be shortened to just the location: « Sur le bureau. »
target_language_example: J’ai laissé mon téléphone sur le bureau.
native_language_example: I left my phone on the desk.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located or lying/sitting on the couch. Often with verbs like être (to be), s'asseoir (to sit), s'étendre (to lie down), dormir (to sleep). Also common with a possessor: sur le canapé du salon (on the living-room couch), sur mon/ton/son canapé (on my/your/his couch).
target_language_example: Je suis resté sur le canapé toute la soirée.
native_language_example: I stayed on the couch all evening.

meaning: on the way; along the path/route.
additional_notes: Used for location or events happening during a trip or journey ("on the way"). It can also mean something is physically in the way/blocking the path (especially with objects: « Les chaises sont sur le chemin. »). Related: « en chemin » = on the way (often about being in transit), « sur le chemin de + lieu » = on the way to + place.
target_language_example: Je suis sur le chemin, j'arrive dans dix minutes.
native_language_example: I'm on the way; I'll be there in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens while returning to where you came from. Often followed by a destination: sur le chemin du retour à la maison (on the way back home), sur le chemin du retour pour Boston (on the way back to Boston). You can also use it alone: Nous sommes sur le chemin du retour. (We’re on our way back.)
target_language_example: On s’est arrêtés prendre un café sur le chemin du retour.
native_language_example: We stopped to get a coffee on the way back.

meaning: on the side; to/on one side.
additional_notes: Used for location or orientation: something is on the side of an object (une entaille sur le côté), someone is lying on their side (dormir sur le côté), or something is located on a particular side (sur le côté droit / ouest). Often followed by a detail like droit/gauche, orest/est, etc.
target_language_example: Mets le sac sur le côté, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Put the bag to the side, please.

meaning: on the back; on one’s back.
additional_notes: Used literally for position (lying on your back: « être/allongé/étendu sur le dos »). It can also mean carrying something on your back (« porter [qqch] sur le dos »).
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, je me suis allongé sur le dos pour me reposer.
native_language_example: After the hike, I lay on my back to rest.

meaning: 'on the bed' (on top of the bed).
additional_notes: Uses sur (“on”) + le lit (“the bed”) to say someone/something is on the bed (sitting, lying, jumping). Contrast: dans le lit = “in bed” (under the covers/asleep).
target_language_example: Le chat dort sur le lit.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping on the bed.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located, drawn, written, or mounted on a wall. Often follows a verb like "être", "avoir", "dessiner", "accrocher" (e.g., "Il y a … sur le mur").
target_language_example: J'ai accroché une photo sur le mur.
native_language_example: I hung a photo on the wall.

meaning: about to start; just about to begin.
additional_notes: Used to say something is imminent (it will happen very soon). It’s built from the common pattern “être sur le point de + infinitive” = “to be about to + verb.” Change “être” to match the subject: je suis / tu es / il est / ils sont, etc.
target_language_example: Nous sommes sur le point de commencer le cours.
native_language_example: We’re about to start the class.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something is going to happen very soon: « être sur le point de + infinitif ». The « le » is an object pronoun meaning “it” (or “him”), referring to something already mentioned: « sur le point de le découvrir » = “about to discover it.”
target_language_example: Je suis sur le point de le terminer.
native_language_example: I’m about to finish it.

meaning: to be about to leave / to be just about to depart.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is very close to leaving (imminent). It often follows a form of "être" (je suis, il est, ils étaient) + "sur le point de" + infinitive. You can add a destination with "pour" (for) or "à" (to), or use "partir de" for leaving from a place.
target_language_example: Je suis sur le point de partir, mais j’attends encore cinq minutes.
native_language_example: I'm about to leave, but I'm waiting five more minutes.

meaning: on the floor; on the ground.
additional_notes: Used to say something or someone is directly on the floor/ground (not on a chair, bed, table, etc.). Often with verbs like être (to be), s’asseoir (to sit down), mettre/poser (to put/place), tomber (to fall).
target_language_example: Il y a des chaussures sur le sol.
native_language_example: There are shoes on the floor.

meaning: on the roof; onto the roof.
additional_notes: Used with "sur" to indicate location (being on top of the roof) or movement/destination (going up onto the roof), depending on the verb (e.g., "être/se trouver" vs. "monter/arriver"). Often used when pointing something out: "Regardez … sur le toit !"
target_language_example: Les enfants sont montés sur le toit pour récupérer le ballon.
native_language_example: The kids climbed onto the roof to get the ball back.

additional_notes: Means something is located or happening on the sidewalk. Often used with verbs like être/avoir (Il y a…), faire, marcher, tomber. In many places, you’re not supposed to ride a bike on the sidewalk: « On ne doit pas faire du vélo sur le trottoir. »
target_language_example: Attends-moi sur le trottoir, près de l’entrée.
native_language_example: Wait for me on the sidewalk, near the entrance.

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun: sur + les (the plural "the"). Most commonly means location ("on top of the"): *sur les tables* = "on the tables". With some verbs (e.g., *parler sur...*, *un livre sur...*), it can mean "about". Note: *sur* can look like English "sure" but it means "on/onto/about".
target_language_example: Le livre est sur les tables.
native_language_example: The book is on the tables.

additional_notes: Used mainly in police/news contexts to mean the physical place where the crime happened. Often appears with verbs like arriver (to arrive), être (to be), retrouver/trouver (to find), and with passive voice: « a été retrouvé sur les lieux du crime » (“was found at the crime scene”).
target_language_example: La police a trouvé des empreintes sur les lieux du crime.
native_language_example: The police found fingerprints at the crime scene.

additional_notes: Commonly used in expressions like « Ça/Il me tape sur les nerfs » (= “It/He gets on my nerves”) and similar verbs: « porter sur les nerfs », « courir sur les nerfs ». With « être »: « Je suis sur les nerfs » means “I’m really nervous / on edge / stressed out.” This is fairly informal/colloquial.
target_language_example: Après une journée comme ça, je suis sur les nerfs.
native_language_example: After a day like that, I’m really on edge.

meaning: 'about him' or 'on/at him,' depending on the verb.
additional_notes: With verbs like savoir / connaître / dire, it usually means “about him” (information): « Qu’est-ce que tu sais sur lui ? » = “What do you know about him?” With verbs involving position/aim (pointer, garder, rester), it can mean “on him/at him” (directed toward him): « Pointe ça sur lui. » = “Point that at him.” The meaning is often clear from context and the verb.
target_language_example: Je n’en sais pas beaucoup sur lui.
native_language_example: I don’t know much about him.

meaning: (in « prendre sur moi ») to hold back / put up with it; to force myself to stay calm.
additional_notes: Most often heard inside the expression « prendre sur soi » (or « prendre sur moi/toi/lui… »), meaning to control your feelings, be patient, or endure something even if it’s difficult. It does not literally mean “on me” here.
target_language_example: Je prends sur moi, mais ça m’énerve vraiment.
native_language_example: I’m holding it in, but it’s really annoying me.

additional_notes: Used to say where to put or leave something (often with verbs like laisser, mettre, poser, placer). In French, "sur" means "on" (on top of a surface), and "bureau" means "desk" (also "office" depending on context; here it’s clearly "desk").
target_language_example: Tu peux le déposer sur mon bureau, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you put it on my desk, please?

meaning: on my account; charged to me / blamed on me.
additional_notes: Literal sense: something is recorded “to my account” (e.g., charge it to my account/tab, bill it to me, put it on my bill). Figurative sense: something is attributed to you—either people are talking about you (“sur mon compte” = about me) or someone blames you (“mettre ça sur mon compte” = put the blame on me).
target_language_example: Vous pouvez mettre ça sur mon compte, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you put that on my account/tab, please?

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically on top of, supported by, or leaning against something that belongs to someone. "ses" is the possessive adjective for "his/her" with plural nouns (e.g., sur ses jambes, sur ses genoux). It can also be used figuratively in set expressions like "sur ses traces" (on his/her tracks = following closely).
target_language_example: Il a posé son sac sur ses épaules.
native_language_example: He put his bag on his shoulders.

additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns (son = his/her/its). With "sur", it can mean physical position ("on") as in sur son dos / sur son vélo, or topic/reference ("about") as in sceptique sur son succès / quelque chose sur son identité. The possessive changes with the noun: sur sa (feminine singular), sur ses (plural).
target_language_example: Il a posé son sac sur son lit.
native_language_example: He put his bag on his bed.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically on a person’s face (cream, lipstick, a smile, an expression). The possessive changes with the person: sur mon visage (my), sur ton visage (your), sur son visage (his/her), sur notre/votre/leur visage (our/your/their).
target_language_example: Il avait de la peinture sur son visage.
native_language_example: He had paint on his face.

additional_notes: Used with a possessive (sur mon/ton/son/notre/votre/leur épaule) to say something is resting against or placed on someone’s shoulder. Common with verbs like poser (to place), mettre (to put), reposer (to rest), s’endormir (to fall asleep).
target_language_example: Elle a appuyé sa tête sur mon épaule.
native_language_example: She rested her head on my shoulder.

meaning: 'on you'; also used after some verbs to mean 'rely on you' or 'look after you'.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'on you' (location/contact), e.g. *Mets ça sur toi* = 'Put that on you / put it on'. With certain verbs, *sur toi* is part of a common expression: *compter sur toi* = 'count on you / rely on you'; *veiller sur toi* = 'watch over you / look after you'.
target_language_example: Je peux compter sur toi ce soir ?
native_language_example: Can I count on you tonight?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is sitting or placed on a (public) bench, often in a park or on the street. Common with the verb "(s')asseoir" (to sit down): "s'asseoir sur un banc".
target_language_example: On s'est assis sur un banc pour manger une glace.
native_language_example: We sat on a bench to eat an ice cream.

additional_notes: A noun for the electric device used to dry hair. Often used with an article: un/mon/le sèche-cheveux. It’s invariable in the plural in writing: des sèche-cheveux.
target_language_example: Tu peux me passer le sèche-cheveux, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the hair dryer, please?

additional_notes: Past participle of « séjourner » used with « avoir » to form the passé composé: « j’ai séjourné / tu as séjourné / il a séjourné / nous avons séjourné… ». Means to stay somewhere temporarily (often for travel). Commonly followed by « dans un hôtel » plus details like « bon marché », « de luxe », or a star rating (« trois/cinq étoiles »).
target_language_example: On a séjourné dans un hôtel près de la gare.
native_language_example: We stayed in a hotel near the train station.

meaning: "sure you want to" / "certain you want to".
additional_notes: Used (often in a question) to double-check someone’s decision or warn that something might be a bad idea. It follows the pattern: être sûr/sûre de + infinitive. Agreement: sûr (masc.), sûre (fem.). Example: Tu es sûr de vouloir... / Vous êtes sûrs de vouloir... (plural).
target_language_example: Tu es sûr de vouloir partir maintenant ?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to leave now?

additional_notes: Used with expressions like "être sûr(e) que..." (to be sure that...) or "c'est sûr que..." (it’s certain that...). "qu'il" is the contraction of "que" + "il". In questions, it often checks or challenges certainty: "Tu es sûr qu'il... ?" / "Vous êtes sûr qu'il... ?". Note agreement: sûr (m.), sûre (f.), sûrs/sûres (plural).
target_language_example: Je suis sûr qu'il va venir ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m sure he’s going to come tonight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause (often with the subj./indicative depending on context, but usually indicative) stating what you’re sure about. Very common in questions like « T’es sûr(e) que… ? » / « Vous êtes sûr(e) que… ? » and statements like « Je suis sûr(e) que… ». Agree « sûr » with the subject: sûr (m.), sûre (f.), sûrs/sûres (pl.).
target_language_example: Je suis sûr que tu vas y arriver.
native_language_example: I’m sure you’ll manage to do it.

meaning: "sure you want to" / "certain you want to" (addressing a woman).
additional_notes:
Used to check or challenge someone’s decision: « Tu es sûre de vouloir… ? » = “Are you sure you want to…?” 
Agreement changes with the person: masculine « sûr » (Tu es sûr de vouloir…?), plural « sûrs / sûres », and formal « vous »: « Êtes-vous sûr(e) de vouloir… ? ». Often followed by an infinitive verb (faire, y aller, vous y rendre).
target_language_example: Tu es sûre de vouloir partir maintenant ?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to leave now?

additional_notes: Used to ask or state certainty about something that follows (often in questions to double-check). It agrees with the person: masculine is “sûr que”, feminine is “sûre que”. Often appears after “Tu es… ? / T’es… ?”
target_language_example: Tu es sûre que tu as bien fermé la porte ?
native_language_example: Are you sure you closed the door properly?

meaning: “has/have” (with reflexive/pronominal verbs in the passé composé).
additional_notes: Contraction of **se** + **est** (3rd person singular of *être*). Used to form the past tense of reflexive/pronominal verbs: **il/elle/on s’est + past participle** (e.g., *il s’est lavé*, *qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?*). With reflexive verbs, the past participle often agrees with the subject when the reflexive pronoun is the direct object: *elle s’est blessée*.
target_language_example: Elle s’est réveillée très tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: She woke up very early this morning.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition with "il" as the subject. Common in conditional sentences (often with imperfect + conditional past: « S’il avait…, il aurait… ») and in simple conditions: « S’il vient, … ». It can mean “if he” (a male person) or “if it” (impersonal "il", e.g., about weather or a situation).
target_language_example: S’il est en retard, on commencera sans lui.
native_language_example: If he’s late, we’ll start without him.

meaning: "please" (said to one person you address as tu).
additional_notes: Used to make a request more polite. You can place it at the end (Aide-moi…, s’il te plaît.) or at the beginning for emphasis (S’il te plaît, pardonne-moi !). Literally means “if it pleases you.” For someone you address as vous, use “s’il vous plaît.”
target_language_example: Tu peux répéter, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you repeat, please?

additional_notes: Used to make a request more polite, especially with strangers or in formal situations. It can go at the end of the sentence (most common) or at the beginning for emphasis. Literally means “if it pleases you.”
target_language_example: Pourriez-vous parler plus lentement, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you speak more slowly, please?

meaning: Question inversion meaning “does she…?/is she…?/will she…?” after a verb.
additional_notes: Used in formal/written French questions with inversion: verb + “-t-” + elle (e.g., "Parle-t-elle ?"). The extra “-t-” is added for pronunciation when the verb in 3rd person singular ends in a vowel sound (often written with a final -a, -e, or -i), like "mènera-t-elle" or "dérange-t-elle". You don’t use it after verbs that already end in a pronounced consonant (e.g., "prend-elle" is wrong; you’d say "prend-elle" is not used—rather "prend-elle" would normally be "prend-elle" without -t-, but in practice you’d write "prend-elle ?").
target_language_example: Viendra-t-elle demain ?
native_language_example: Will she come tomorrow?

meaning: “does he/it…?” in formal question word order (verb–t–il).
additional_notes: Used in written/formal French to form a question by inverting the subject pronoun il (“he/it”) after the verb: verb + -t- + il. The -t- is added only for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel sound (e.g., brille-t-il, joue-t-il, pleuvra-t-il). It doesn’t change the meaning; it just links the sounds. (With verbs ending in a consonant sound, you usually get verb + il without -t-, e.g., prend-il.)
target_language_example: Parle-t-il français ?
native_language_example: Does he speak French?

additional_notes: Used in questions with subject–verb inversion. The pattern is: verb + “-t-” + “il/elle/on” + “encore”. The “-t-” is just for pronunciation (it appears when the verb ends in a vowel, e.g., « joue-t-il », « neige-t-il »). With « encore », the meaning is usually “still” (continuing), and sometimes “again” depending on context.
target_language_example: Travaille-t-il encore à Paris ?
native_language_example: Does he still work in Paris?

meaning: "ever" in an inverted question: "will he ever…? / does he ever…?"
additional_notes: Used with subject–verb inversion when the subject is "il" (he/it): verb + "-t-" + "il" + "jamais". The "-t-" is only there for pronunciation (e.g., "pardonnera-t-il"). Although "jamais" usually means "never" with "ne" ("il ne vient jamais" = he never comes), in questions it often means "ever" and can sound rhetorical or express doubt/surprise: "Reviendra-t-il jamais ?" = Will he ever come back?
target_language_example: Comprendra-t-il jamais ce que tu essaies de dire ?
native_language_example: Will he ever understand what you’re trying to say?

additional_notes: Used in formal written French to form a yes/no question by inversion: verb + “-t-” + il + un/une. The “-t-” is inserted when the verb ends in a vowel sound (e.g., existe-t-il, présente-t-il, faudra-t-il, pratique-t-il) to make pronunciation smoother. “Il” can mean “he” or “it” depending on the verb (often “it” with expressions like existe-t-il…). In everyday speech, people often prefer “Est-ce qu’il y a… ?” or intonation instead of inversion.
target_language_example: Y a-t-il un problème ?
native_language_example: Is there a problem?

additional_notes: Used in yes/no questions with inversion: verb + “-t-” + “il” + “vraiment”. The “-t-” is just a linking sound added when the verb ends in a vowel (e.g., « importe-t-il », « intéresse-t-il »). “Il” can mean “he” or “it” depending on what it refers to (often “it” with « cela », « ce médicament », etc.).
target_language_example: Ça vaut-t-il vraiment le coup ?
native_language_example: Is it really worth it?

meaning: Question inversion: “does he/it … to …?” (adds a linking -t- before il).
additional_notes: Used in more formal/written French to form questions with inversion when a verb ends in a vowel sound and is followed by il/elle/on. You insert -t- between the verb and the pronoun for pronunciation: aide-t-il… ?, cherche-t-il… ?, arrivera-t-il… ?. The "à" belongs to the following infinitive/place phrase (e.g., aider à faire, arriver à Boston), not to the -t-il itself.
target_language_example: Cette méthode fonctionne-t-elle à long terme ?
native_language_example: Does this method work in the long term?

meaning: “does one / do people…?” (formal question form with on).
additional_notes: Used in questions with inversion: verb + “-t-” + on (e.g., appelle-t-on). The “-t-” is added only for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel (a/e/i/o/u) in the 3rd person singular (like appelle, accuse, cherche). It often has an impersonal meaning (“one/people”), common in formal or written French.
target_language_example: Où va-t-on maintenant ?
native_language_example: Where are we/people going now?

meaning: “to you” + “has” (te + a), as in “he/she/it has [done something] to you” or “has [told/given...] you.”
additional_notes: Contraction of **te** (indirect/direct object pronoun “you”) + **a** (3rd person singular of **avoir**, “has”), used before a verb in the past tense: **Il t'a dit** (He told you), **Ça t'a fait du bien ?** (Did that do you good?). It only appears before a word starting with a vowel sound, so **te a → t’a**. Don’t confuse it with **ta** (= “your” feminine singular), e.g., **ta voiture**.
target_language_example: Il t'a envoyé un message ce matin.
native_language_example: He sent you a message this morning.

additional_notes: Contraction of "t'" (= "te", meaning "to you") + "a dit" (passé composé of "dire"). Used when someone told you something in the past: "Qu'est-ce qu'il t'a dit ?" = "What did he tell you?" The full form is "il/elle t'a dit" (he/she told you).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'elle t'a dit exactement ?
native_language_example: What exactly did she tell you?

additional_notes: Contraction of **te + a fait** (“to you” + “has done/made”), used in the **passé composé** of *faire*. Common patterns: **Qu’est-ce qu’il/elle t’a fait ?** = “What did he/she do to you?” (something done to you). **Qu’est-ce qu’il t’a fait faire ?** = “What did he make you do?” (the *faire faire* causative: made you do something). **Qu’est-ce que ça t’a fait ?** can mean “What did it do to you?” or more naturally “How did it affect you / How did it make you feel?”
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce qu’il t’a fait faire ?
native_language_example: What did he make you do?

meaning: “I have … you” / “I … you” (te + ai), used with the passé composé.
additional_notes: Contraction of **te** (“to you” or “you” as an object pronoun) + **ai** (1st person singular of **avoir**, used to form the **passé composé**). It comes **before** the past participle: **Je t’ai vu** = “I saw you.” Also used in negatives: **Je ne t’ai pas vu**.
target_language_example: Je t’ai appelé hier soir.
native_language_example: I called you last night.

additional_notes: Contraction of "te" (you, object pronoun) + "aime" (loves). Used with different subjects depending on context: "je t'aime" = I love you; "il/elle t'aime" = he/she loves you. In writing, the apostrophe is used because "te" comes before a vowel sound (aime).
target_language_example: Je t'aime beaucoup.
native_language_example: I love you a lot.

additional_notes: From "aimer" (to like/love) + "bien" (well). "Aimer bien" usually means "to like" or "to be fond of" someone/something. It’s weaker than "je t’aime" (I love you) and often avoids sounding romantic. "t'" is the shortened form of "te" (= you) used before a vowel: "je t’aime bien".
target_language_example: Je t'aime bien, mais je ne veux pas sortir avec toi.
native_language_example: I like you, but I don’t want to go out with you.

meaning: Informal contraction of "tu as" (“you have” / “have you”).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French. It’s the casual form of "tu as" (2nd person singular of "avoir"). Used in statements ("T'as raison" = "You’re right") and in questions ("T'as compris ?" = "Did you understand?"). In writing, prefer "tu as" unless you’re reproducing dialogue or an informal tone.
target_language_example: T'as déjà mangé ?
native_language_example: Have you eaten already?

meaning: "you said" / "you told (someone)" (spoken form of "tu as dit").
additional_notes: Very common in casual spoken French. It’s a contraction of "tu as dit" (passé composé of "dire"). Often used to refer back to what someone said: "C’est ce que t’as dit" (“That’s what you said”). With an object, it can mean “told”: "Qu’est-ce qu’il t’a dit ?" (“What did he tell you?”). In writing, the apostrophe shows dropped letters: "t’" + "as".
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu changes d’avis ? C’est pas ce que t’as dit hier.
native_language_example: Why are you changing your mind? That’s not what you said yesterday.

meaning: informal: “you heard / have you heard?”; sometimes “listen!”
additional_notes:
Contraction of « tu as entendu ». Used a lot in spoken French.
- In questions, it means “did you hear…?” or “where did you hear that?”
- Said on its own or followed by a comma, it can mean “Did you hear me?” / “Listen, …” to insist that someone pays attention.
target_language_example: T'as entendu ? On part dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Did you hear? We’re leaving in five minutes.

meaning: “you had” / “you got” (informal for « tu as eu »).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French. It’s the passé composé of « avoir »: « tu as eu ». Depending on context, it can mean you received something (« Où est-ce que t’as eu ça ? » = where did you get that?), you experienced something (« Qu’est-ce que t’as eu ? » = what happened to you / what did you have?), or you obtained a result/amount (« T’as eu combien ? » = how much did you get?).
target_language_example: Alors, t’as eu quoi comme note ?
native_language_example: So, what grade did you get?

additional_notes: Very common spoken contraction of "tu as fait" (passé composé of faire). Used to ask what someone did ("Qu’est-ce que t’as fait ?") or to comment on what they’ve done ("T’as fait de ton mieux" = you did your best). In writing or more formal speech, use "tu as fait".
target_language_example: Pourquoi t'as fait ça ?
native_language_example: Why did you do that?

meaning: “you haven’t / you didn’t / you don’t have” (informal spoken French).
additional_notes: Contraction of « tu as » + « pas ». In everyday speech, « ne » is often dropped, so « tu n’as pas… » becomes « t’as pas… ». Meaning depends on context: it can be a negative of avoir (possession: “you don’t have…”) or a negative in the passé composé (with « avoir » as auxiliary): “you didn’t / haven’t …” (e.g., « t’as pas compris ? » = “you didn’t understand?”).
target_language_example: T’as pas vu mes clés ?
native_language_example: You haven’t seen my keys?

additional_notes: Very common informal spoken contraction of « tu as vu ». Used to ask if someone saw something (« T'as vu ce qu'ils m'ont fait ? ») or to point something out / get agreement, like “see?” (“Look, he totally turned red, you see?”).
target_language_example: T'as vu comme il pleut aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: Did you see how much it’s raining today?

meaning: Informal contraction of "tu as" (“you have” / “have you”).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French. It’s the casual form of "tu as" (2nd person singular of "avoir"). Used in statements ("T'as raison" = "You’re right") and in questions ("T'as compris ?" = "Did you understand?"). In writing, prefer "tu as" unless you’re reproducing dialogue or an informal tone.
target_language_example: T'as déjà mangé ?
native_language_example: Have you eaten already?

additional_notes: Contraction of “tu as l’air”. Used to comment on someone’s appearance or mood. Common patterns: **t’as l’air + adjective** (T’as l’air heureux), **t’as l’air de + noun** (T’as l’air d’un idiot), or **t’as l’air de + infinitive** (T’as l’air de plaisanter = You seem to be joking).
target_language_example: T’as l’air fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You look tired today.

meaning: “you haven’t / you didn’t / you don’t have” (informal spoken French).
additional_notes: Contraction of « tu as » + « pas ». In everyday speech, « ne » is often dropped, so « tu n’as pas… » becomes « t’as pas… ». Meaning depends on context: it can be a negative of avoir (possession: “you don’t have…”) or a negative in the passé composé (with « avoir » as auxiliary): “you didn’t / haven’t …” (e.g., « t’as pas compris ? » = “you didn’t understand?”).
target_language_example: T’as pas vu mes clés ?
native_language_example: You haven’t seen my keys?

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French. It’s a contraction of "tu as raison" (literally, “you have reason”). Often used to agree, sometimes reluctantly: "OK, t’as raison." You can also say "Ouais, t’as raison" for a casual “yeah, you’re right.”
target_language_example: Bon, t’as raison : on devrait partir maintenant.
native_language_example: Alright, you’re right: we should leave now.

meaning: Informal spoken form of « tu as un… »: “you have a…” / “do you have a…?”
additional_notes: Very common in casual speech. « t’ » is the shortened « tu », and « as » is the verb *avoir* (“to have”). Used in statements (*T’as un micro.*) and in questions just by intonation (*T’as un conseil à me donner ?*). In more formal French, use « tu as un… » or « est-ce que tu as un… ? ».
target_language_example: T’as un stylo, s’il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Do you have a pen, please?

additional_notes: Contraction of "tu as une" in casual spoken French. Used to ask if someone has something (often with the noun omitted if it’s obvious: "T’as une ?"). Can also be used with a noun to mean “you have a...” in statements (e.g., "T’as une mine superbe" = “You look great” / “You’ve got a great look”).
target_language_example: T’as une minute ?
native_language_example: Do you have a minute?

additional_notes: Spoken/informal contraction of « tu aurais dû » (conditional past of devoir). Used to say someone should have done something in the past, often implying criticism or regret: « T'aurais dû appeler » = “You should have called.” In more formal writing, use « tu aurais dû ».
target_language_example: T'aurais dû me prévenir avant de venir.
native_language_example: You should have warned me before coming.

meaning: "to have you" (t’ = te = "you" + avoir = "to have"), often used to form the past infinitive like "to have met/seen/known you".
additional_notes: T’ is the shortened form of te before a vowel or silent h: te + avoir → t’avoir. Very common in structures like "ravi/heureux de" + past infinitive: "Ravi de t’avoir connu" = "Glad to have known/met you". Often followed by a past participle: t’avoir vu(e), t’avoir rencontré(e), t’avoir revu(e), etc. The ending may agree with a woman when written (vu/vue, rencontré/rencontrée) in some contexts.
target_language_example: Je suis content de t’avoir aidé.
native_language_example: I’m glad to have helped you.

meaning: contraction of “te” + “en”: “to you (about it / of it / some)”, or in “t’en vas” = “you go away” (tu t’en vas).
additional_notes: “T’en” is very common in spoken French. It combines the indirect object pronoun “te” (to you) with “en” (about it / of it / some / from there). It often appears with verbs that use “de” (e.g., parler de, penser de): “t’en parler” = talk to you about it, “t’en penser” = think about it. In “tu t’en vas” (from s’en aller = to leave/go away), “t’” is the reflexive pronoun and “en” is part of the verb; “Ne t’en va pas !” = “Don’t go!”
target_language_example: Je t’en parle demain.
native_language_example: I’ll talk to you about it tomorrow.

meaning: informal contraction of « tu en as » (“you have some / you’ve got some of it”).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French. « t’ » = « tu » and « en » replaces something introduced with de (or a quantity/“some”). Often appears inside verb phrases, e.g. « Qu’est-ce que t’en as pensé ? » = “What did you think of it?” and « T’en as assez fait » = “You’ve done enough (of that).”
target_language_example: T'en as besoin ?
native_language_example: Do you need some?

meaning: informal contraction of « tu en as » (“you have some / you’ve got some of it”).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French. « t’ » = « tu » and « en » replaces something introduced with de (or a quantity/“some”). Often appears inside verb phrases, e.g. « Qu’est-ce que t’en as pensé ? » = “What did you think of it?” and « T’en as assez fait » = “You’ve done enough (of that).”
target_language_example: T'en as besoin ?
native_language_example: Do you need some?

meaning: Spoken contraction of « tu en es »: “you are / you are (of it)”—often used like “are you sure (about that)?”
additional_notes: « En » refers back to something already mentioned (“about it/that”, “of it/them”). Very common in speech before an adjective: « Pourquoi t’en es si sûr ? » = “Why are you so sure (about it)?” / « T’en es capable ? » = “Are you capable of it?” Alone as a question (« T’en es ? »), it can mean “Are you in?/Are you one (of them)?” depending on context. Don’t confuse with « tu t’en es… » in verbs like « s’en tirer » (“to get out of it / to manage”), e.g. « Tu t’en es bien tiré. »
target_language_example: T’en es certain ?
native_language_example: Are you sure about that?

additional_notes: Often appears as **je t'en prie** (to one person you say *tu* to). In requests, it means “please” with insistence or politeness: *Dis-le-moi, je t’en prie.* It can also be used to reply to thanks meaning “you’re welcome” (similar to *de rien*), or to politely insist/allow something: *Mais je t’en prie !* = “Please, go ahead / Not at all!”
target_language_example: Viens avec nous, je t'en prie.
native_language_example: Please come with us.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French and casual writing (texts, chats). It’s formed by dropping the vowel in "tu" before a vowel sound: tu es → t’es. In more formal contexts, prefer "tu es" (or "vous êtes" depending on who you’re speaking to).
target_language_example: T’es prêt(e) ?
native_language_example: Are you ready?

additional_notes: Informal spoken form of « tu es sûr que c’est… ». Used to check or challenge someone’s certainty about a place, direction, or thing. Add what you’re asking about after « c’est » (e.g., ici/là/par là/le tien). Can also be said with « sûre » if speaking to a woman: « T’es sûre que c’est… ? »
target_language_example: T’es sûr que c’est la bonne adresse ?
native_language_example: Are you sure it’s the right address?

meaning: “you’re a …” (spoken form of « tu es un … »).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French: « tu » becomes « t’ » before a vowel, and « es » is often reduced so « tu es » → « t’es ». It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (or adjective used like a noun): « t’es un ange », « t’es un flic ? ». Depending on the word after it, it can be a compliment or an insult. For a feminine noun, you’d use « t’es une … ». In writing, « tu es un … » is more formal.
target_language_example: T’es un vrai ami.
native_language_example: You’re a real friend.

meaning: your room / your bedroom (addressing one person with tu).
additional_notes: “Ta” is the feminine singular form of “your” used with tu (informal singular). It agrees with the noun: chambre is feminine, so you say ta chambre (not *ton*). In polite speech (vous), use “votre chambre.”
target_language_example: Tu peux ranger ta chambre, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you tidy your room, please?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person you call "tu" (friend, child, someone your age, etc.). It agrees with the feminine noun "famille," so it’s always "ta" (not "ton"). With "vous" it becomes "votre famille".
target_language_example: Tu vas voir ta famille ce week-end ?
native_language_example: Are you going to see your family this weekend?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to a man about his spouse. In French, "femme" can mean "woman" in general, but with a possessive (ma/ta/sa femme) it usually means "wife". Agree with the person being addressed: "ta" is for "tu" (informal singular).
target_language_example: Tu as parlé à ta femme de ce projet ?
native_language_example: Did you talk to your wife about this project?

meaning: your daughter (or your girl, in some contexts).
additional_notes: "Ta" is the informal singular form of "your" (used with someone you address as "tu"). "Fille" most commonly means "daughter" in this possessive pattern (ma/ta/sa fille), but it can also mean "girl" depending on context. For "your girlfriend," French usually says "ta copine" / "ta petite amie".
target_language_example: Ta fille a quel âge ?
native_language_example: How old is your daughter?

additional_notes: Used when talking about someone’s hand (often in a caring/medical context: “And your hand?”) or when asking someone to put out/give their hand. It’s the informal singular possessive (ta), used with someone you address as tu. (Formal: votre main.)
target_language_example: Donne-moi ta main, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Give me your hand, please.

additional_notes: Used to describe your (the person you’re speaking to) mother with an adjective or location/state: *Ta mère est vieille / vivante ? / à la maison ?* The determiner **ta** is the familiar form of “your” (used with friends, family, kids). In more formal situations you’d usually say **votre mère est…**
target_language_example: Ta mère est gentille ?
native_language_example: Is your mother nice?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the part that belongs to you (your portion of food/money/treasure) or the part you are responsible for (your share of the work). You can also hear it alone when giving someone their portion: « Voilà ta part. »
target_language_example: Je vais faire ma part, et toi tu fais ta part.
native_language_example: I’ll do my part, and you do your part.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person you know well (informal singular “tu”). Literally “your (female) little friend,” but in modern French it usually means “girlfriend” (a romantic partner). More formal/polite: “votre petite amie.”
target_language_example: Tu viens avec ta petite amie ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you coming with your girlfriend tonight?

additional_notes: Used literally for a physical spot (your seat, your space) or figuratively for someone’s proper role/position (“where you belong”). Often appears with location phrases like “Ta place est ici” (Your place is here) or “Ta place est à mes côtés” (Your place is by my side).
target_language_example: Non, c’est ma place — ta place est là-bas.
native_language_example: No, that’s my seat—your place is over there.

additional_notes: “Ta” means “your” when speaking to one person (tu) and when the noun is feminine singular. With “sœur” (feminine), you use “ta”: ta sœur. For “your sister” in formal/plural “you” (vous), use “votre sœur.”
target_language_example: Est-ce que ta sœur vient ce soir ?
native_language_example: Is your sister coming tonight?

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s head (body part): « Mets ta tête en arrière. » It can also be used figuratively to mean “your brain/mind,” especially in commands like « Utilise ta tête ! » (“Use your head!”). In casual speech, « ta tête ! » can be a blunt retort meaning “Your head/Your face!” depending on context.
target_language_example: J’ai mal à ta tête ? Non, j’ai mal à la tête.
native_language_example: Do I have a headache in your head? No, I have a headache (literally: in the head).

additional_notes: "Ta" is the informal singular possessive ('your') used with a feminine noun like "vie". It’s used literally (danger, survival: "Ta vie pourrait en dépendre") and also in common expressions like "gagner ta vie" = "to earn a living" (make money to live), and "toute ta vie" = "all your life".
target_language_example: Fais attention : ta vie est importante.
native_language_example: Be careful: your life is important.

meaning: 'your car' (to one person you address informally).
additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person with tu (a friend, family member, child). Ta is the feminine singular form of 'your' before a feminine noun like voiture. For a more formal or plural 'your', use votre voiture. Before a vowel sound, ta becomes ton (e.g., ton auto).
target_language_example: Où as-tu garé ta voiture ?
native_language_example: Where did you park your car?

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to the dashboard inside a car (where the speedometer, screens, and controls are). By extension, it can also mean a “dashboard” in software or a control panel showing key information (a set of indicators). You’ll often hear: « sur le tableau de bord » (“on the dashboard”).
target_language_example: J’ai laissé mes lunettes sur le tableau de bord.
native_language_example: I left my glasses on the dashboard.

additional_notes: Imperative form of *se taire* (“to be quiet”), addressed to one person (*tu*). Often sounds harsh/impolite, especially with an exclamation mark or insults. For a softer option: *Chut !* (“Shh!”), *Silence, s’il te plaît.* or *Tais-toi, s’il te plaît.*
target_language_example: Tais-toi un instant, j’essaie d’écouter.
native_language_example: Be quiet for a moment, I’m trying to listen.

additional_notes: "Tais-toi" is the tu-form command of *se taire* (to be quiet). It’s often blunt and can sound rude/angry, especially as "shut up"; in more polite situations, prefer "Taisez-vous et…" (formal/plural) or softer options like "Chut, et…" / "Silence, s’il te plaît." Used to tell someone to stop talking and then do something else.
target_language_example: Tais-toi et écoute ce que je te dis.
native_language_example: Shut up and listen to what I’m telling you.

additional_notes: Imperative of *se taire* (“to be quiet”), addressed to **vous** (either several people, or one person in a formal/polite way). Often sounds like an order; depending on tone/context it can be quite harsh (close to “shut up”), especially with "Ça suffit" (“That’s enough”).
target_language_example: S'il vous plaît, taisez-vous pendant le film.
native_language_example: Please be quiet during the movie.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to express a large quantity: **tant de + noun** (tant de fruits, tant de travail). It can convey surprise, regret, or emphasis depending on context (e.g., *Pourquoi tant de… ?*, *Tant de… pour ça !*).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas pourquoi il y a tant de bruit ce soir.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why there’s so much noise tonight.

meaning: "so many things to" (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive after "à" to say there are many things that need to be done/said, etc.: "tant de choses à faire / à dire / à apprendre". Often expresses that there’s a lot to do or talk about (sometimes with an emotional tone).
target_language_example: On a tant de choses à préparer avant le départ.
native_language_example: We have so many things to prepare before leaving.

meaning: "as long as you" / "while you" (introduces a condition).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition that must be true for something else to happen: « Tant que tu + verb…, (alors) … ». It’s often followed by the present tense even when talking about the future. With « pas », it can mean “not as long as you… / not while you…”, often in a firm refusal (« Pas tant que tu vivras sous mon toit ! »).
target_language_example: Tant que tu es ici, tu peux me poser des questions.
native_language_example: As long as you’re here, you can ask me questions.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/lui/nous/vous/leur): « Il me tape sur les nerfs » = “He gets on my nerves.” You can also use it with « ça » or « quelque chose » as the subject: « Ça me tape sur les nerfs » / « Quelque chose lui tape sur les nerfs ».
target_language_example: Le bruit des travaux me tape sur les nerfs.
native_language_example: The construction noise is getting on my nerves.

additional_notes: A common dessert. The pattern “tarte aux + [ingredient]” means a tart/pie made with that ingredient (e.g., tarte aux fraises = strawberry tart). Often used with “de la” when offering or talking about an unspecified amount: « Tu veux de la tarte aux pommes ? »
target_language_example: On prend une part de tarte aux pommes ?
native_language_example: Shall we have a slice of apple pie?

meaning: a pile of; lots of (a bunch of).
additional_notes: Literally means “pile of.” Used with a noun: *un tas de bois* (“a pile of wood”) or figuratively *un tas de choses* (“lots of things”). With insults like *tas de merde*, it means “piece of shit” (very rude; *putain de* adds emphasis).
target_language_example: J'ai un tas de travail aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I have lots of work today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a serving of coffee in a cup. Often with an article: « une tasse de café » (a cup of coffee), « ma tasse de café » (my cup of coffee). Note: « tasse » is feminine, so it’s « une autre tasse » (not « un autre »).
target_language_example: Je voudrais une tasse de café, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a cup of coffee, please.

meaning: to come get you / pick you up; to look for you.
additional_notes: Often used with aller/venir: « Je vais/viens te chercher » = “I’m going to come get you / pick you up.” Can also mean “to look for you” depending on context. With an object, it can mean “to get/fetch something for you”: « Je vais te chercher de l’eau » = “I’ll get you some water.”
target_language_example: Je passe te chercher à 8 heures.
native_language_example: I’ll pick you up at 8 o’clock.

meaning: 'to go to bed' (you, informal singular) / 'to lie down'.
additional_notes: Form of the reflexive verb **se coucher** used with **tu** (informal 'you'). Common in commands and routines: **Va te coucher !** ('Go to bed!'). In questions it can sound like surprise or checking: **Te coucher ?** ('Go to bed?').
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué(e) : je vais me coucher.
native_language_example: I’m tired: I’m going to bed.

meaning: to ask you (for something / to do something).
additional_notes: “Demander” means “to ask” or “to request.” In “te demander,” **te** = “to you” (indirect object), so it’s often used like: **te demander un service** (ask you a favor), **te demander une chose/une question** (ask you something), or **te demander de + infinitive** (ask you to do something). Note: it can look like English “demand,” but it’s usually much softer than “to demand.”
target_language_example: Je voulais te demander si tu pouvais m’aider demain.
native_language_example: I wanted to ask you if you could help me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when you want to ask someone a question or make a request. Very common with polite starters like « Est-ce que je peux te demander quelque chose ? » (Can I ask you something?) or « Laisse-moi te demander quelque chose » (Let me ask you something). « te » is the informal “to you” (tu); with a formal or plural “you,” it becomes « vous demander quelque chose ».
target_language_example: Excuse-moi, je peux te demander quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask you something?

additional_notes: Very common casual way to introduce a question. "un truc" literally means “a thing” but in everyday French it often just means “something” (like “a thing” in casual English). Uses "te" (to you) for someone you’re on first-name terms with; for a more formal/polite version, say "vous demander quelque chose" or "Je peux vous poser une question ?"
target_language_example: Je peux te demander un truc avant qu’on y aille ?
native_language_example: Can I ask you something before we go?

additional_notes: Used to politely introduce a request. Often said with "Est-ce que je peux… ?", "Je voudrais…" (more formal), or "Pourrais-je… ?" (more formal). "Te" is the informal (tu) object pronoun; with someone you address as "vous", say "vous demander une faveur".
target_language_example: Excuse-moi, je peux te demander une faveur ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask you a favor?

additional_notes: Made of the indirect object pronoun "te" (to you, informal singular) + the verb "dire" (to say/tell). Often appears after another verb in the infinitive: "je peux te dire" (I can tell you), "je viens te dire" (I’m coming to tell you). In speech you may also hear it in set phrases like "Laisse-moi te dire…" (Let me tell you…).
target_language_example: Je dois te dire quelque chose.
native_language_example: I have to tell you something.

additional_notes: Used when you’re leaving and want to say goodbye directly to someone. Structure: dire au revoir à + person → “to say goodbye to + person”; with “te” (to you) it becomes “te dire au revoir.” Often follows verbs like venir/venir juste (“to come/just come”) or venir/aller in the future (“I’ll come to say goodbye to you”).
target_language_example: Je passe te dire au revoir avant de partir.
native_language_example: I’m stopping by to say goodbye to you before leaving.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker wants to bring up a topic or share information with “you” (informal singular). It commonly follows verbs like avoir besoin de (need to), devoir (must/have to), vouloir (want to), or vouloir + conditional (je voudrais… = I’d like to…). You can swap “te” for other object pronouns: vous dire (tell you, formal/plural), lui dire (tell him/her), leur dire (tell them).
target_language_example: Je peux te dire quelque chose en privé ?
native_language_example: Can I tell you something in private?

additional_notes: Very common spoken phrase to introduce a point or confession. "un truc" literally means “a thing,” but in everyday French it often means “something” / “stuff” in a casual way. Often used with verbs like "je dois / je vais / je veux" and sometimes preceded by "Écoute" (Listen).
target_language_example: Je dois te dire un truc : je pars demain.
native_language_example: I have to tell you something: I’m leaving tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information you’re about to say to someone (often something important, serious, or emphatic). The pronoun changes with the person: je dois te dire… (to you, informal singular), je dois vous dire… (to you, formal or plural). Common with verbs like devoir/aller: Je dois/Je vais te dire une chose…
target_language_example: Je vais te dire une chose : tu as raison.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you something: you’re right.

meaning: “tell you” or (with a reflexive verb) “tell yourself.”
additional_notes: “Te” is the object pronoun “you” (singular, informal). With dire: “Je te dis…” = “I’m telling you…”. With the reflexive verb se dire: “Tu te dis…” = “you tell yourself… / you think to yourself…”. The meaning depends on whether it’s “je te dis” (I tell you) or “tu te dis” (you tell yourself).
target_language_example: Je te dis la vérité.
native_language_example: I’m telling you the truth.

meaning: “I owe you” (money/a favor); sometimes “I must” (depending on context).
additional_notes: From the verb **devoir**. With an indirect object pronoun like **te** (= “to you”), **je te dois…** usually means **“I owe you…”**: *Je te dois 10 euros.* In questions you may see inversion: **Combien te dois-je ?** = “How much do I owe you?” Note: **tu te dois de + infinitive** is a different pattern (reflexive **se devoir de**) meaning **“you owe it to yourself to / you should / you must.”**
target_language_example: Je te dois 5 euros.
native_language_example: I owe you 5 euros.

additional_notes: “Te” is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to you” (informal singular). It goes before the verb: « Je peux te donner… ». Before a vowel or silent h, it becomes « t’ »: « Je peux t’en donner. ». Often used with things like money, time, help, advice, work, etc. Note: « donner » can look like English “donate,” but it usually just means “give” in general (not necessarily a donation).
target_language_example: Je peux te donner un coup de main demain.
native_language_example: I can give you a hand tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the informal "tu" form: "te" means "to you" (singular, informal). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun or something treated as masculine: "te donner un conseil" (give you advice), "te donner un indice" (give you a hint), "te donner un travail" (give you an assignment/job). For a feminine noun, use "te donner une…"
target_language_example: Je peux te donner un conseil ?
native_language_example: Can I give you some advice?

meaning: “I will give you” (future tense of donner with “te” = “to you”).
additional_notes: Used when the speaker is talking about giving something to “you” in the future: Je te donnerai + noun/pronoun (Je te donnerai mon numéro. / Je te donnerai ça.). In negatives, you often see ne...pas in writing (Je ne te donnerai pas...), but in casual speech the ne is frequently dropped (Je te donnerai pas...). It can also be used more broadly for “I will grant you” or “I won’t give in to you” depending on context (e.g., refusing to give something or to give someone what they want).
target_language_example: Je te donnerai une réponse demain.
native_language_example: I’ll give you an answer tomorrow.

additional_notes: From the verb "déranger" (to bother/to disturb). Used mostly in questions or with "si" to politely check if something is okay for the other person: "Ça te dérange pas ?" / "Ça ne te dérange pas ?" = "Do you mind?" You can also say "Je ne te dérange pas ?" meaning "Am I bothering you?" (often when you’re about to ask for something).
target_language_example: Si ça te dérange pas, je vais ouvrir la fenêtre.
native_language_example: If you don't mind, I'm going to open the window.

meaning: "make yourself" / "get (something) done to you" (with *faire* in the reflexive).
additional_notes: This is *se faire* with **te** ("yourself" / "to you") used with *tu*. Common patterns: **te faire des amis** = "make friends"; **ne pas te faire de mal** = "don’t hurt yourself"; **te faire comprendre** = "make yourself understood"; **te faire rire** = "make you laugh"; **te faire examiner (par un médecin)** = "get examined (by a doctor)". The exact English translation often changes depending on what follows (*des amis*, *mal*, a verb like *comprendre*, *rire*, *examiner*).
target_language_example: Je peux te faire un café si tu veux.
native_language_example: I can make you a coffee if you want.

additional_notes: Used to say or ask whether you trust someone. Structure: faire confiance à + person → "Je te fais confiance" (I trust you), "Je ne te fais pas confiance" (I don’t trust you). With a verb like pouvoir: "Je peux te faire confiance ?" (Can I trust you?). "Te" is the object pronoun for "you" (informal singular); for someone you address as "vous": "vous faire confiance".
target_language_example: Je te fais confiance, mais dis-moi la vérité.
native_language_example: I trust you, but tell me the truth.

meaning: to get your hair cut (to have your hair cut).
additional_notes: Uses the structure "se faire" + infinitive to mean having something done to you/by someone else (typically a service). Here, it implies going to a hairdresser/barber rather than cutting your own hair. You can swap the pronoun depending on the person: me faire, te faire, se faire, nous faire, vous faire, se faire couper les cheveux.
target_language_example: Je vais me faire couper les cheveux demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to get my hair cut tomorrow.

meaning: "you make yourself" / "you get" (in reflexive uses of faire).
additional_notes: This is the 2nd-person singular form of the reflexive verb construction **se faire**: **tu te fais**. Common patterns: **se faire + noun** (often with **du/de la/des**) to mean you bring something on yourself or you end up doing it a lot (e.g., *se faire du souci* = to worry). And **se faire + infinitive** to mean something happens to you (often negative or passive-like): *tu te fais tuer* = you get yourself killed / you get killed. With negation: **Ne te fais pas...**
target_language_example: Fais attention : tu te fais du mal.
native_language_example: Be careful: you’re hurting yourself.

additional_notes:
From the verb **falloir** (“to be necessary”), which is used in the impersonal form **il faut**. **Te faut-il** is a more formal/literary question form (inversion) of **il te faut**. 
- **Que te faut-il ?** = “What do you need?” 
- **Te faut-il + noun ?** = “Do you need + noun?” 
- **Te faut-il + infinitive ?** = “Do you have to + verb?”
target_language_example: Te faut-il de l’aide pour finir ?
native_language_example: Do you need help to finish?

meaning: will do you good; will make you feel better.
additional_notes: From the expression « faire du bien à quelqu’un » (= to do someone good / help them feel better), often used for health, rest, comfort, or something beneficial. « te » is the indirect object pronoun “to you” (informal singular). You can change it depending on the person: « me fera du bien » (will do me good), « lui fera du bien » (will do him/her good), « vous fera du bien » (will do you good, formal/plural). « fera » is the future tense of « faire » (will do/make).
target_language_example: Prendre l’air frais te fera du bien.
native_language_example: Getting some fresh air will do you good.

meaning: to join us (come with us / be part of our group).
additional_notes: Uses the verb **se joindre à** = “to join (a person/group).” Here it’s in the **tu** form with the reflexive pronoun **te** (“you join yourself to us”). Often used to invite someone or ask them to participate: **Tu veux/Veux-tu te joindre à nous ?** (“Do you want to join us?”). Similar to **venir avec nous** (“come with us”).
target_language_example: On va dîner au restaurant ; tu veux te joindre à nous ?
native_language_example: We’re going to have dinner at the restaurant; do you want to join us?

additional_notes: This is the combination of two object pronouns: **te** (to you) + **le/la** (it/him/her), with **l'** used before a vowel or silent H (e.g., *te l'ai dit*). It appears before the verb: *Je te l’ai dit* (“I told you (it)”). Common with verbs like *dire*, *demander*, *donner*, etc.
target_language_example: Je te l’envoie ce soir.
native_language_example: I'll send it to you tonight.

additional_notes: A common spoken form of "(il/elle/on) te l'a dit" = "(he/she/they/one) told you it". "te" = "to you" (informal singular object pronoun), "l'" = "it" (le/la shortened before a vowel), and "a dit" is the passé composé of "dire" ("to say/tell"). Used in questions and confirmations like "Elle te l'a dit ?" (Did she tell you?).
target_language_example: Je te l'ai dit hier.
native_language_example: I told you yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone that you already said something. It’s part of the verb phrase in the passé composé: "je t’ai dit" = "I told you". "te" = "to you" and "l’" = "it/that" (short for "le"), both pronouns come before the auxiliary: "Je te l’ai dit." Often heard in casual speech as "J’te l’ai dit."
target_language_example: Je te l’ai dit hier : je ne peux pas venir.
native_language_example: I told you yesterday: I can’t come.

additional_notes: A formal/inverted question using the reflexive verb « se laver » (to wash oneself): « tu te laves les mains » = “you wash your hands.” In questions, French can invert the subject and verb: « te laves-tu… ? ». « les mains » is definite (“the hands”) even though English usually says “your hands.” More common in everyday speech: « Tu te laves les mains ? »
target_language_example: Te laves-tu les mains avant de cuisiner ?
native_language_example: Do you wash your hands before cooking?

meaning: “to you it” (object pronouns: te = to you, le = it/him).
additional_notes: Used when a verb takes two object pronouns: an indirect object (te = “to you”) + a direct object (le = “it” / “him”). It usually comes before the verb: « Je te le dis. » With an infinitive, it goes before the infinitive: « Je vais te le dire. » (In your examples: dire, demander, promettre, rendre, permettre.) The phrase itself is neutral, but it can appear in rude expressions like « Tu peux te le mettre où je pense. »
target_language_example: Je vais te le donner demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to give it to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Made of object pronouns + infinitive: **te** = “to you” and **le** = “it” (a masculine thing/idea). These pronouns come **before** the infinitive **dire**. Very common in sentences like **« Combien de fois faut-il te le dire ? »** = “How many times do I have to tell you?”
target_language_example: Je vais te le dire après le cours.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you after class.

additional_notes: From the verb *dire* (“to say/tell”) with two pronouns: *te* = “to you” and *le* = “it/so.” Most often heard as **je te le dis** (“I’m telling you”) to insist or emphasize what you’re saying. It can also appear in set, conversational phrases like **Si je te le dis !** (“You have no idea!”) or **Voyons si je te le dis !** (“As if I’d tell you!”).
target_language_example: Je te le dis, ça va marcher.
native_language_example: I’m telling you, it’s going to work.

additional_notes: Used with an object: te montrer + quelque chose ("to show you something") or te montrer + comment + verb ("to show you how to..."). In a different structure, se montrer means "to show oneself / to appear" (e.g., "Comment oses-tu te montrer ici ?" = "How dare you show your face here?").
target_language_example: Je vais te montrer où c’est.
native_language_example: I’m going to show you where it is.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "montrer" (to show) with the indirect object pronoun "te" = "to you" (informal singular). You can swap "te" for "vous" for formal/plural ("vous montrer quelque chose"). Often used to invite someone to look at or see something: "Viens, je veux te montrer quelque chose."
target_language_example: Attends une seconde, je vais te montrer quelque chose.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m going to show you something.

meaning: "Don’t get involved in / don’t meddle in" (someone else’s business).
additional_notes: This is the negative informal imperative of *se mêler de* (“to get involved in, to meddle in”). It’s used to tell someone to stay out of something: *Te mêle pas de ça/de ma vie.* More formal/polite: *Ne te mêle pas de…* or *Ne vous mêlez pas de…* (to one or more people).
target_language_example: Te mêle pas de cette affaire, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Don’t get involved in this matter, please.

meaning: 'to talk to you' / 'to speak to you'.
additional_notes: "Te" is the object pronoun used with "tu" (informal 'you'). So "te parler" is used when speaking to someone you address as "tu" (a friend, family member, child, etc.). With formal/plural "vous", you would say "vous parler".
target_language_example: Je peux te parler un instant ?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you for a moment?

meaning: to talk to you about something.
additional_notes: Used when you want to bring up a topic with someone you address as “tu” (te = “to you”). It often introduces something important or personal. Common with verbs like avoir besoin de / devoir / pouvoir / vouloir / vouloir (conditional: je voudrais) + te parler de…
target_language_example: Est-ce que je peux te parler de quelque chose après le cours ?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you about something after class?

meaning: to talk to you in private (one-on-one).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a confidential conversation away from other people. Often phrased politely as a question (e.g., « Est-ce que je peux… ? », « Puis-je… ? ») or to express preference/need (« J’ai besoin de… », « Je préférerais… »). The « te » is the informal object pronoun “to you” (use « vous parler en privé » for a formal or plural “you”).
target_language_example: Après la réunion, je dois te parler en privé.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I need to talk to you in private.

additional_notes: Used with the verb plaire: "(something) te plaît" literally means "(something) pleases you," and in natural English it’s usually "you like (something)." The thing you like is the grammatical subject: "Cette veste te plaît ?" = "Do you like this jacket?" Negative: "Ça ne te plaît pas ?" You can also ask "Qu’est-ce qui te plaît ?" (What do you like/what appeals to you?).
target_language_example: Ce restaurant te plaît ?
native_language_example: Do you like this restaurant?

meaning: to ask you a few questions.
additional_notes: Literally “to put/place a few questions to you,” but it’s the normal way to say “ask you a few questions.” Used with permission/softening phrases like « Je peux… ? », « Je veux juste… », « Je veux seulement… ». You can swap « te » (to you, informal singular) for « vous » (to you, formal or plural): « Je peux vous poser quelques questions ? ».
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je peux te poser quelques questions ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask you a few questions?

additional_notes: Very common way to say “to ask (someone) a question.” Literally “to pose you a question.” Here, te = “to you” (informal singular). With a more formal or plural “you,” use vous: Je dois vous poser une question. Often used with polite starters like Je voudrais / Je voulais / Laisse-moi…
target_language_example: Excuse-moi, je peux te poser une question ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask you a question?

meaning: (I) ask/beg you; used to mean “please” (more insistent).
additional_notes: Most often used as **je te prie (de...)**. It can soften a request (**Parle-moi, je te prie.**) or make it sound more urgent/insistent (**Je te prie de le faire.** = “I’m asking/begging you to do it.”). **Te** is the informal “you” (tu). With **vous**, it becomes **je vous prie (de...)** (more formal).
target_language_example: Je te prie de m’écouter un instant.
native_language_example: Please listen to me for a moment.

additional_notes: "Te" is the direct object pronoun meaning "you" (informal singular) and it comes before the verb: je vais te protéger (I’m going to protect you). In negatives, it still stays before the verb: nous ne pouvons pas te protéger (we can’t protect you). The verb is "protéger" (to protect); you may also see "toi-même" added for emphasis/reflexive meaning: te protéger toi-même (protect yourself).
target_language_example: Je suis là pour te protéger.
native_language_example: I’m here to protect you.

meaning: to introduce you; to run (as a candidate).
additional_notes:
Two common patterns:
1) présenter qqn à qqn = “to introduce someone to someone” (Je veux te présenter un ami = I want to introduce a friend to you).
2) se présenter à une élection = “to run/stand for election” (Tu devrais te présenter aux élections = You should run in the elections).
target_language_example: Laisse-moi te présenter ma sœur.
native_language_example: Let me introduce you to my sister.

meaning: to take you home; to give you a ride home.
additional_notes: Used when offering to escort someone back to their place (often by car, but not necessarily). Literally “to bring you back to your home.” The pronoun changes with the person: me ramener chez moi (take me home), le/la ramener chez lui/elle (take him/her home), nous ramener chez nous (take us home), vous ramener chez vous (take you home, formal/plural).
target_language_example: Si tu es fatigué, je peux te ramener chez toi après le dîner.
native_language_example: If you’re tired, I can take you home after dinner.

meaning: to take/bring you back home; to drive you home.
additional_notes: Used when someone escorts you home (often by car, but it can be any way). It literally means “to bring you back to the house/home.” You can swap the object pronoun: me/nous/le/la/les ramener à la maison (e.g., "Je vais la ramener à la maison.").
target_language_example: Il est tard, je te ramène à la maison.
native_language_example: It’s late—I’ll take you home.

meaning: "take you home" / "drive you back to your place."
additional_notes: From the verb *ramener* (“to bring back”). This phrase is used when someone offers to accompany you back to where you live—often by car, but it can also just mean walking you home. The pronoun *te* is informal “you” (to a friend, family, child). More formal: *je vous ramène chez vous*.
target_language_example: Si tu veux, je te ramène chez toi après le dîner.
native_language_example: If you want, I’ll take you home after dinner.

additional_notes: From the verb "se rappeler" (to remember). It’s used with the reflexive pronoun "te" for "tu": "Tu te rappelles… ?" = "Do you remember…?" In negatives, French uses "ne … pas": "Tu ne te rappelles pas" = "You don’t remember."
