You’ll often also see "(se) rappeler de" before a noun or person: "Tu ne te rappelles pas de moi ?" = "You don’t remember me?"
target_language_example: Tu te rappelles de son nom ?
native_language_example: Do you remember his name?

additional_notes: From se rappeler (“to remember”), in the inverted question form. Used to ask if someone remembers a thing (Te rappelles-tu ce que…?), a person/event (Te rappelles-tu du…?), or a time/situation (Te rappelles-tu quand/lorsque…?, Te rappelles-tu comment…?). In everyday speech, people also often say: “Tu te rappelles… ?”.
target_language_example: Te rappelles-tu où on a garé la voiture ?
native_language_example: Do you remember where we parked the car?

meaning: to cheer you up; to lift your spirits.
additional_notes: Used when someone is sad, discouraged, or having a hard time. The base expression is « remonter le moral (à quelqu’un) » = to boost someone’s morale/spirits. The object pronoun changes depending on who you’re cheering up: me remonter le moral (cheer me up), lui remonter le moral (cheer him/her up), nous remonter le moral (cheer us up), etc.
target_language_example: Après cette mauvaise journée, un message de toi m’a vraiment remonté le moral.
native_language_example: After that bad day, a message from you really cheered me up.

additional_notes: "Te" is the object pronoun (you, informal singular) placed before the infinitive "rencontrer". Used when talking about meeting someone (first time or not), e.g. "Content(e) de te rencontrer" (“Nice to meet you”) or "Ils aimeraient te rencontrer" (“They’d like to meet you”).
target_language_example: Je suis ravi de te rencontrer enfin.
native_language_example: I’m delighted to finally meet you.

meaning: (1) “make you” (+ adjective); (2) “surrender” (in “te rendre” = “give yourself up”); (3) “go to” (in “te rendre à” = “go/arrive at”).
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- rendre + someone + adjective: “to make someone [adjective]” (Te rendre fière = make you proud).
- se rendre: “to surrender / give yourself up” (Tu devrais te rendre = You should surrender).
- se rendre à + place: “to go to / head to” (Te rendre au Palais = go to the Palace).
Note: “rendre” often does NOT mean English “to render.”
target_language_example: Je veux te rendre heureux.
native_language_example: I want to make you happy.

additional_notes: Reflexive form of *se reposer* used with **tu**. Often follows verbs like **aller** (*aller te reposer* = go rest) or **devoir** (*tu devrais te reposer* = you should rest). Can also mean to take it easy or recover (e.g., after being tired or sick).
target_language_example: Après le travail, tu peux te reposer un peu.
native_language_example: After work, you can rest a bit.

additional_notes: Used with the infinitive revoir (“to see again”) plus the direct object pronoun te (“you”). Often follows verbs like vouloir (to want), espérer (to hope), penser (to think), e.g., Je veux / J’espère / Je ne pensais plus te revoir.
target_language_example: J’espère te revoir bientôt.
native_language_example: I hope to see you again soon.

additional_notes: Usually comes from **se sentir** (reflexive): **tu te sens…** = “you feel …” (often about health or mood: *Tu te sens bien / mieux ?*). Without the reflexive meaning, **je te sens** literally means “I feel/sense you,” and in conversation it can mean “I get you / I feel you,” which is informal.
target_language_example: Tu te sens mieux aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Do you feel better today?

meaning: “do you feel…?” (talking to one person, informal “you”).
additional_notes: Inversion form of *tu te sens…* used to ask a question. It’s the verb *se sentir* (“to feel”), with the reflexive pronoun *te*. Often followed by an adjective (bien, malade, chanceux) or by *de* + infinitive to ask if someone feels up to doing something (*Te sens-tu de… ?*).
target_language_example: Te sens-tu prêt à partir ?
native_language_example: Do you feel ready to leave?

meaning: to hug you (to hold you in my arms).
additional_notes: Literally “to hold you tight in my arms.” Used to express affection, comfort, or reassurance. You can change the pronoun and possessor: « le/la serrer dans mes bras » (hug him/her), « te serrer dans mes bras » (hug you), « te serrer dans ses bras » (hug you in his/her arms).
target_language_example: Viens ici, je veux te serrer dans mes bras.
native_language_example: Come here, I want to hug you.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **se souvenir (de)** = “to remember.” **Tu te souviens (de + noun)** = “You remember (…)
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de son nom ?
native_language_example: Do you remember his name?

additional_notes: This is the inverted-question form of « se souvenir de » (to remember): « Tu te souviens de… ? » is the more common spoken word order, while « Te souviens-tu de… ? » sounds more formal/literary. It’s followed by « de » + a noun (« de ce jour-là ») or « de » + an indirect question (« de quoi », « de la ville où… »).
target_language_example: Te souviens-tu de l’adresse du restaurant ?
native_language_example: Do you remember the restaurant’s address?

meaning: "looks good on you" / "suits you" (said about clothes or colors).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "aller à" meaning "to suit" (not "to go"). Used to compliment how something looks on someone: "Ça te va bien" = "That suits you / looks good on you." It can refer to an item of clothing (un pull, une chemise) or a color (Le noir te va bien).
target_language_example: Cette veste te va bien !
native_language_example: That jacket looks good on you!

meaning: "looks really good on you" / "suits you very well."
additional_notes: Used to compliment someone on how an item of clothing, jewelry, a hairstyle, a color, etc. suits them. Built from aller (va) + indirect object pronoun te (“to you”) + très bien (“very well”). You can change the pronoun: me va très bien (suits me very well), lui va très bien (suits him/her very well), vous va très bien (suits you—formal/plural).
target_language_example: Cette couleur te va très bien !
native_language_example: That color looks really good on you!

additional_notes: "Te" is the direct-object pronoun for talking to one person you address with "tu". It’s used before the verb: "Je veux te voir" (I want to see you). In polite/formal or plural situations, use "vous voir" instead.
target_language_example: Je suis content de te voir !
native_language_example: I’m happy to see you!

additional_notes: This is a fragment of the verb phrase **(je) te vois**: **te** is the direct object pronoun meaning “you” (singular, informal), placed before the verb. It’s commonly used after **je** (“I”) and can appear in clauses like **si je te vois…** (“if I see you…”).
target_language_example: Si je te vois demain, je te dirai bonjour.
native_language_example: If I see you tomorrow, I’ll say hello.

meaning: “in time for” (usually: « à temps pour », often with « juste » = “just in time for”).
additional_notes: In this pattern you typically say « (juste) à temps pour + noun/event » to mean you arrive/return before something starts (e.g., a holiday, a meeting). « temps pour » by itself is uncommon; it’s normally part of « à temps pour ».
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé juste à temps pour le début du film.
native_language_example: I arrived just in time for the start of the movie.

meaning: to tend to; to be prone to.
additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir: "avoir tendance à" + infinitive to describe a usual habit or typical behavior (often something you do without meaning to). You can also use it for general tendencies: "Les gens ont tendance à…".
target_language_example: J’ai tendance à oublier mes clés quand je suis pressé.
native_language_example: I tend to forget my keys when I’m in a hurry.

meaning: “hold/keep (yourself/yourselves)” (polite or plural “you”), used for commands and instructions.
additional_notes: Form of the verb *tenir* addressed to **vous** (either one person formally or several people). Common in imperatives like: *tenez-vous prêt* (get ready), *tenez-vous tranquille* (keep still/quiet), *tenez-vous à distance* (keep your distance), *tenez-vous la main* (hold hands). In questions like *D’où tenez-vous cette information ?*, it means “Where did you get/obtain that information?” (with *vous* as “you,” not reflexive).
target_language_example: Tenez-vous à l’écart, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please stand back / keep away.

meaning: to keep quiet; to hold your tongue.
additional_notes: Means not saying something (often a secret) or stopping yourself from speaking. The possessive changes with the subject: tenir ta langue (you, informal), tenir votre langue (you, formal/plural), tenir sa langue (his/her/one’s), tenir leur langue (their). Often used after a request/order: « Tiens ta langue ! »
target_language_example: J’ai promis de tenir ma langue.
native_language_example: I promised to keep quiet.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone (informal singular "tu") to get their stuff together or take their belongings. "Affaires" is plural and can mean personal items (bags, clothes, etc.) or, more generally, one’s business/concerns depending on context.
target_language_example: N'oublie pas tes affaires avant de partir.
native_language_example: Don’t forget your things before leaving.

additional_notes: "Tes" is the informal singular possessive adjective meaning "your" (used when talking to one person you address as "tu"). It agrees with the noun: use "tes" before a plural noun ("amis" = friends). For "your friend" (singular), say "ton ami" (male friend) or "ton amie" (female friend).
target_language_example: Je vais sortir avec tes amis ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going out with your friends tonight.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to someone you address as tu. Note the plural form: cheveux is almost always plural in French even when referring to all the hair on someone’s head. It often comes up in compliments (Tes cheveux sont beaux.) or asking about a new haircut/style (Tu as fait quelque chose à tes cheveux ?).
target_language_example: J’adore tes cheveux, tu as changé de coupe ?
native_language_example: I love your hair—did you change your haircut?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person you address as "tu" (informal singular). Often appears with verbs like "faire" or "finir": « faire tes devoirs » = to do your homework. With « toi-même / par toi-même », it means doing it yourself (without help).
target_language_example: Tu peux sortir après avoir fait tes devoirs.
native_language_example: You can go out after doing your homework.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase used when speaking to one person (tu). “Tes” is used before a plural noun starting with a consonant sound (enfants). With a vowel sound, use “tes” as well (e.g., tes amis). In formal/polite speech (vous), use “vos enfants”.
target_language_example: Tes enfants aiment l’école ?
native_language_example: Do your children like school?

meaning: your hands (addressing one person with tu).
additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive (tes). With a noun like mains (plural), tes is used (not ton/ta). Common in commands or instructions: « Laisse tes mains… » / « Mets tes mains… »
target_language_example: Garde tes mains sur la table, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Keep your hands on the table, please.

additional_notes: Used with the informal singular "tu" to talk to one person about their mother and father. "Tes" is the possessive adjective for "tu"; it changes with the noun: "ton père" (your father), "ta mère" (your mother), "tes parents" (your parents).
target_language_example: Tes parents viennent te chercher à quelle heure ?
native_language_example: What time are your parents coming to pick you up?

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s parents or ask where/what condition they are in. It’s the informal singular “tes” (not polite/plural “vos”). Often followed by an adjective (sympas, riches), a place (à la maison), or a situation/state (en route, en vie).
target_language_example: Tes parents sont au courant ?
native_language_example: Do your parents know?

additional_notes: Used when speaking informally to one person ("tu"). It’s the possessive adjective "tes" + plural noun "yeux" (eye/eyes). Common in instructions or advice: "Ferme tes yeux" (Close your eyes), "Protège tes yeux" (Protect your eyes).
target_language_example: Regarde-moi dans tes yeux.
native_language_example: Look me in the eyes.

meaning: “hold on / stay / keep yourself (in a position).”
additional_notes: Imperative ("tu" form) of **se tenir** (“to hold oneself / to stay / to stand”). It’s often followed by an adverb or a phrase: **Tiens-toi bien** (“Hold on tight / Brace yourself”), **Tiens-toi à distance de…** (“Keep your distance from…”).
target_language_example: Tiens-toi tranquille, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Stay still/quiet, please.

meaning: Hang in there; hold on (don’t give up).
additional_notes: Imperative form (spoken to one person) of "tenir bon". Used to encourage someone to endure, keep going, or stay strong through a difficult moment; can also imply “hold on” a little longer (e.g., until someone returns). You can also hear it with "Tiens bon !" or "Tiens bon, encore un peu."
target_language_example: Je sais que c’est dur, mais tiens bon : on y est presque.
native_language_example: I know it’s hard, but hang in there: we’re almost there.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "tirer sur" (to shoot at). "Tirer dessus" is used with an object pronoun (me/you/him/her/us/them): "Il m’a tiré dessus" = "He shot at me." In these examples, "tiré" is the past participle (passé composé: "a tiré"). It usually implies using a gun (or weapon) and does not necessarily mean the person was hit.
target_language_example: On m’a tiré dessus, mais je n’ai pas été blessé.
native_language_example: They shot at me, but I wasn’t hurt.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **tirer sur + [person/thing]**. In crime/violence contexts it means to use a gun and shoot at someone (whether or not you hit them). In other contexts, **tirer sur** can also mean “to pull on” (e.g., *tirer sur la porte* = pull on the door), but with a person (*sur lui / sur elle / sur quelqu’un*) it usually means “shoot at.”
target_language_example: La police dit qu’il a tiré sur un passant.
native_language_example: The police say he shot at a passerby.

meaning: “you” with emphasis (like “you, you…” / “you’re the one who…”).
additional_notes: Uses dislocation for emphasis: "toi" is placed first to highlight or contrast the person, and the sentence continues with the normal subject pronoun "tu". Often used to stress a difference from others ("You, on the other hand...") or to insist on a quality ("You really are..."). Common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Toi, tu comprends toujours tout très vite.
native_language_example: You, you always understand everything really fast.

additional_notes: Used to put strong emphasis on the person you’re talking to (often to praise, tease, accuse, or express surprise). It’s a common French structure where the stressed pronoun (toi) is repeated with the normal subject pronoun (tu). Because it uses tu/toi, it’s in the informal/familiar register (with "vous" you’d say: « Vous, vous êtes… »).
target_language_example: Toi, tu es vraiment sympa !
native_language_example: You, you’re really nice!

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the subject is doing something personally (often like “do it yourself”). It can also mean “as yourself,” as in comparisons ("comme toi-même" = “like yourself”). Related forms: moi-même (myself), lui-même/elle-même (himself/herself), nous-mêmes (ourselves), vous-mêmes (yourselves), eux-mêmes/elles-mêmes (themselves).
target_language_example: Tu peux le faire toi-même.
native_language_example: You can do it yourself.

additional_notes: Used to include the person you’re speaking to in something that also applies to someone else. Often comes after a statement ("Il a peur, et toi aussi") or after a wish/greeting ("Bonne chance à toi aussi !"). It can also be used alone as a short reply meaning "you too" ("Ouais, toi aussi.").
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué, et toi aussi.
native_language_example: I’m tired, and you are too.

meaning: 'you too' (with emphasis), introducing what also applies to you.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the same thing is true for the listener as well. Common in spoken French to repeat the subject for emphasis: “Toi aussi, tu…” (= “You too, you…” / “You also…”). The comma is optional; you may also hear “Toi aussi tu…”.
target_language_example: Toi aussi, tu peux venir avec nous.
native_language_example: You can come with us too.

additional_notes: Uses the stressed pronoun toi (“you”, informal) + et (“and”) to highlight the person you’re speaking to: “you and X…”. Often followed by a noun or another pronoun (toi et moi, toi et ta sœur). When it’s the subject, French commonly uses a plural verb, often with vous to match the addressee: “Toi et Paul, vous venez ?”.
target_language_example: Toi et moi, on part maintenant.
native_language_example: You and I are leaving now.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that it’s only the two of you (often like “just you and me”), or to highlight a bond/comparison (“you and me are the same”). In standard written French, you may also see the more formal subject form “toi et moi, nous…”.
target_language_example: Ce soir, c’est toi et moi : on va régler ça ensemble.
native_language_example: Tonight, it’s you and me: we’re going to sort this out together.

meaning: 'you and me, we…' (to emphasize the two of us as a pair).
additional_notes: Common spoken pattern used to spotlight the relationship or situation between you and the other person: “You and me, we need to talk / we can do this.” The subject pronoun is usually “on” (very common in speech) even though it means “we” here; you could also say “toi et moi, nous…”. It often introduces something personal, serious, or uniting (or sometimes a subtle warning: “Toi et moi, on va parler.”).
target_language_example: Toi et moi, on va trouver une solution.
native_language_example: You and me, we’re going to find a solution.

meaning: “you and I, we’re …” (introduces what you two are/have in common).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a comparison or relationship between two people: *Toi et moi, on est pareil* (“You and I, we’re the same”). **On est** is common spoken French for **nous sommes** (“we are”). Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (*pareil*, *des amis*, *faits/faites du même bois*). Agreement can change in expressions like *faits/faites* depending on gender/people referred to.
target_language_example: Toi et moi, on est dans la même équipe.
native_language_example: You and I, we’re on the same team.

meaning: “you and I are …” (talking about you and me together).
additional_notes: Uses the stressed pronouns toi and moi as a combined subject, followed by the 1st-person plural of être (sommes). In everyday French, you’ll also often hear: “Toi et moi, on est …” or “Toi et moi, nous sommes …”.
target_language_example: Toi et moi sommes dans la même équipe.
native_language_example: You and I are on the same team.

meaning: 'you who' / 'you (the one) who…' (to emphasize who did something).
additional_notes: Used to single out or emphasize the person being talked to as the one who did/does something. Very common in cleft sentences like « C’est toi qui + verbe » (“It’s you who…”). After « toi qui », the verb is usually in the same person as « tu » (e.g., « toi qui as… », « toi qui es… »).
target_language_example: Toi qui as appelé, tu peux rappeler plus tard ?
native_language_example: You who called—can you call back later?

meaning: “yourself a bit” (used after an imperative with a reflexive verb: “... a little / ... a bit”).
additional_notes: This is not usually used alone. It appears in commands with -toi (imperative + reflexive pronoun), e.g. « Approche-toi un peu » (“Come a bit closer”). « un peu » softens the command (like “a bit / a little”), and can suggest a small adjustment or “for a moment,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Calme-toi un peu.
native_language_example: Calm down a bit.

additional_notes: Common way to say someone fell in love. It uses the past tense (passé composé) with être: « il/elle est tombé(e) amoureux/amoureuse de … ». The adjective agrees with the subject: tombé amoureux (male), tombée amoureuse (female), tombés/tombées (plural). You can also use the infinitive: « tomber amoureux/amoureuse de … ».
target_language_example: Elle est tombée amoureuse de son collègue.
native_language_example: She fell in love with her coworker.

additional_notes: Used with the verb « tomber amoureux/amoureuse de » = “to fall in love with.” Agreement changes with the speaker: « tombé amoureux de » (man), « tombée amoureuse de » (woman). In the present tense: « je suis amoureux/amoureuse de… » = “I’m in love with…”. Followed by a person/thing you love (often with a name or pronoun like « toi », « lui », « elle »).
target_language_example: Elle est tombée amoureuse de lui pendant le voyage.
native_language_example: She fell in love with him during the trip.

additional_notes: "Ton" means "your" when talking to one person you address with "tu" (informal singular). "Aide" is a feminine noun, but it still takes "ton" (not *ta*) because it starts with a vowel sound: *ton aide*. Common in phrases like *sans ton aide* (without your help), *merci pour ton aide* (thanks for your help), and *j’ai besoin de ton aide* (I need your help).
target_language_example: J’ai besoin de ton aide pour porter ces cartons.
native_language_example: I need your help to carry these boxes.

additional_notes: Used to talk to one person (tu) about their (male) friend. It also appears before a masculine singular noun starting with a vowel sound: ton amie (your (female) friend), ton école (your school). For a plural group: tes amis (your friends).
target_language_example: J'ai vu ton ami hier au café.
native_language_example: I saw your friend yesterday at the café.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to someone’s opinion. Often appears with verbs like « demander » (to ask for) and « donner » (to give): « On t’a demandé ton avis ? » / « Peux-tu donner ton avis ? ». « avis » is masculine, so it takes « ton » (not « ta »). You can swap the possessive: « mon avis », « son avis », « votre avis », etc.
target_language_example: J'aimerais connaître ton avis sur ce restaurant.
native_language_example: I'd like to know your opinion about this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used when speaking informally to one person you call “tu.” The noun “chien” is masculine, so it takes “ton” even if the dog is female. For “your dog” when addressing someone with “vous,” use “votre chien.”
target_language_example: Ton chien est très gentil, il adore jouer.
native_language_example: Your dog is very nice; he loves to play.

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive adjective "ton" (used with someone you call "tu"). "Fils" means "son". In more formal or plural situations, you’d use "votre fils". "Ton" is used before a masculine singular noun like "fils".
target_language_example: Comment va ton fils ?
native_language_example: How is your son?

meaning: your brother (addressing one person you’re speaking to).
additional_notes: "Ton" is the possessive adjective meaning "your" used with a singular masculine noun (like "frère") and also before a vowel sound. It’s used when you’re talking to one person (tu). For more formal/polite speech to one person, use "votre frère".
target_language_example: Parle à ton frère, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Talk to your brother, please.

additional_notes: “Ton” is the possessive adjective meaning “your” when talking to one person informally (tu) and before a masculine singular noun like “manteau.” For a woman’s coat you’d still say “ton manteau” because “manteau” is masculine. In polite speech (vous), use “votre manteau.”
target_language_example: Mets ton manteau, il fait froid dehors.
native_language_example: Put on your coat, it’s cold outside.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person you address with "tu" (a friend, child, someone your age in an informal context). For a formal/polite situation or someone you address with "vous," use "votre nom." Often appears in questions like "C'est quoi ton nom ?" or prompts like "Écris ton nom."
target_language_example: Excuse-moi, c’est quoi ton nom ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s your name?

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive “ton” (to one person you address as “tu”). For polite/formal or plural “your,” use “votre numéro de téléphone.” Often used when asking for someone’s contact info: “Donne-moi…” (more direct) or “Est-ce que je pourrais avoir…” (more polite).
target_language_example: Tu peux me donner ton numéro de téléphone ?
native_language_example: Can you give me your phone number?

meaning: your point of view; your opinion.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s perspective or opinion (often in discussions). You can swap the possessive to match the person: mon/ton/son/notre/votre/leur point de vue. It’s neutral and common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je respecte ton point de vue, mais je ne suis pas d’accord.
native_language_example: I respect your point of view, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person you address as « tu ». It agrees with the masculine noun « père » (so it’s « ton », not « ta »). In questions it often means “your father” in the family sense (not slang here).
target_language_example: Tu peux demander à ton père de venir te chercher ?
native_language_example: Can you ask your dad to come pick you up?

additional_notes: Used to describe your father’s state, location, or situation. Often followed by an adjective (en vie), a place/status (au front), or a phrase like "au courant" (aware/informed). In questions it may appear after "Est-ce que…" (e.g., "Est-ce que ton père est… ?").
target_language_example: Je crois que ton père est déjà parti.
native_language_example: I think your father has already left.

additional_notes: "Ton" is the possessive adjective for "your" used before a masculine singular noun (sac). In context it can be a handbag, backpack, or any bag. You may also see it in expressions like "Vide ton sac !" which literally means "Empty your bag!" but often means "Say what you really think" / "Spit it out."
target_language_example: N'oublie pas ton sac avant de partir.
native_language_example: Don’t forget your bag before you leave.

additional_notes: "Ton" is the informal singular "your" (used with "tu"). "Travail" can mean your place of employment (job/work) or the tasks you have to do. Common with verbs like "faire" (to do) and "quitter" (to leave).
target_language_example: Je finis ton travail et ensuite on sort.
native_language_example: I’ll finish your work and then we’ll go out.

additional_notes: “Ton” is the possessive adjective meaning “your” when speaking to one person (tu) and the noun is masculine singular (“téléphone”). It’s used for a phone/telephone (often a cellphone in everyday speech). For a female noun you’d use “ta …” (ta voiture), and for plural “tes …” (tes clés).
target_language_example: Où est ton téléphone ?
native_language_example: Where is your phone?

additional_notes: "Ton" is the informal singular "your" (used with friends, family, kids, etc.). "Visage" means "face" (often a bit more neutral/polite than "gueule"). It’s common in expressions like "Je peux le voir sur ton visage" (“I can see it on your face”). In some contexts (e.g., with "Dégage !"), talking about someone’s face can sound rude or insulting.
target_language_example: Je vois la fatigue sur ton visage.
native_language_example: I can see the tiredness on your face.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or confirm someone’s actual/legal name, especially if they use a nickname, username, or false name. Literally “your true name” (ton = your, vrai = real/true, nom = name).
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas ton vrai nom, seulement ton pseudo.
native_language_example: I don’t know your real name, only your username/nickname.

additional_notes: Short for “Ne touche pas.” Often used as a warning or when telling someone to stop touching something. You can add “à + [thing]” to say what not to touch: “Touche pas à mon sac.”
target_language_example: Touche pas à ça, c’est fragile.
native_language_example: Don’t touch that, it’s fragile.

meaning: "still in" / "always" + en (in, while, in the process of).
additional_notes: “Toujours” can mean “always” or “still,” depending on context. When followed by “en,” it often introduces (1) a place: “toujours en Australie” = “still in Australia,” (2) a state/condition: “toujours en retard” = “always/still late,” or (3) an action with “en + gerund”: “toujours en travaillant” = “always while working.” The exact English translation depends on what comes after “en.”
target_language_example: Elle est toujours en train de parler.
native_language_example: She’s always talking.

additional_notes: Used to complain or comment that someone is late every time (or very often). Common with "être" (Tu es toujours en retard) or "arriver" (Elle arrive toujours en retard). Can also be said alone as a remark: "Toujours en retard."
target_language_example: Mon frère est toujours en retard le matin.
native_language_example: My brother is always late in the morning.

meaning: 'is/was always (in the middle of) doing' (constantly doing).
additional_notes: Used with être (est/était/etc.) + toujours en train de + infinitive to say someone is constantly doing something, often with an annoyed or critical tone. It can describe something happening repeatedly or as a habitual behavior, not just right this second.
target_language_example: Tu es toujours en train de regarder ton téléphone !
native_language_example: You're always looking at your phone!

additional_notes: Used to say someone hasn’t died (often when their status is uncertain or you’re checking if someone is alive). It’s commonly used with the verb « être »: « Il/Elle est toujours en vie. »
target_language_example: Il est blessé, mais il est toujours en vie.
native_language_example: He’s injured, but he’s still alive.

additional_notes: Used to complain or comment that a person, expression, story, answer, technique, etc. never changes. It can stand alone like a short remark (“Toujours la même !”), but it often appears with a noun: “toujours la même histoire / réponse / technique.” Gender changes with what it refers to: masculine “toujours le même” or plural “toujours les mêmes.”
target_language_example: Tu dis toujours la même chose !
native_language_example: You always say the same thing!

additional_notes: Used with the verb vouloir (to want) in the past: most often with avoir + voulu, e.g. j’ai toujours voulu… (I’ve always wanted…), il a toujours voulu… (he has always wanted…), il avait toujours voulu… (he had always wanted…). It expresses a long-standing desire up to that point in time.
target_language_example: J’ai toujours voulu apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I’ve always wanted to learn French.

additional_notes: Used with a form of avoir (j'ai/tu as/il a/nous avons, etc.) + été (past participle of être) to say something has always been the case or someone has always been a certain way: « Ça a toujours été comme ça. » / « Il a toujours été gentil. »
target_language_example: Elle a toujours été très patiente.
native_language_example: She has always been very patient.

additional_notes: Used with a form of avoir (j'ai/tu as/il a/nous avons, etc.) + été (past participle of être) to say something has always been the case or someone has always been a certain way: « Ça a toujours été comme ça. » / « Il a toujours été gentil. »
target_language_example: Elle a toujours été très patiente.
native_language_example: She has always been very patient.

meaning: 'have always been like that / this way.'
additional_notes: Used with the verb "être" in the past tense to say someone has been a certain way for as long as you can remember. It’s most commonly heard as part of a full sentence like "Il a toujours été comme ça" or a question like "Tu as toujours été comme ça ?". "Comme ça" means "like that/like this" (often referring to someone’s personality, habits, or behavior).
target_language_example: Elle a toujours été comme ça : très timide.
native_language_example: She’s always been like that: very shy.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to refer to a whole group of things/people close to the situation or already known from context: tous ces cris (all these screams), tous ces problèmes (all these problems). For feminine plural, use "toutes ces" (e.g., toutes ces idées).
target_language_example: Pourquoi il y a tous ces gens devant la porte ?
native_language_example: Why are there all these people in front of the door?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific group of people you can see/identify in the situation. "Tous" = all, "ces" = these (plural), "gens" = people. Often used in questions or complaints: "Que font tous ces gens ici ?"
target_language_example: Pourquoi tous ces gens attendent devant la porte ?
native_language_example: Why are all these people waiting in front of the door?

additional_notes: "Tous" means “all,” "ces" means “these,” and "livres" means “books.” Used to refer to a specific set of books that are present or already known in the context. It can be the subject (Tous ces livres sont à toi.) or an object after de (se débarrasser de tous ces livres).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas porter tous ces livres en même temps.
native_language_example: I can’t carry all these books at the same time.

additional_notes: "Truc" is a very common, informal word meaning "thing/stuff" (often when you don’t know the exact name or it’s not important). "Tous ces trucs" refers to a group of items (physical or abstract: facts, tips, etc.). Often used in questions like "C'est quoi tous ces trucs ?" (What’s all this stuff?).
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu gardes tous ces trucs dans ton sac ?
native_language_example: Why do you keep all this stuff in your bag?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people defined by what follows in the relative clause with « qui » (e.g., « …qui parlent anglais »). « Ceux » is masculine plural; for feminine use « toutes celles qui ». You can also use « tous ceux qui » as the subject of a sentence.
target_language_example: Tous ceux qui veulent venir doivent s'inscrire.
native_language_example: All those who want to come must register.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “all the” (the whole group) or “every” in the sense of “each” when talking about repeated occasions (e.g., tous les jours = every day). It agrees with the noun: tous les (masc. plural) / toutes les (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Tous les étudiants doivent montrer leur carte.
native_language_example: All the students have to show their ID card.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens annually or regularly each year. It’s interchangeable with "tous les ans" / "toutes les années" in many contexts; you can place it at the beginning or end of the sentence: "Tous les ans, ..." or "..., tous les ans."
target_language_example: Tous les ans, je prends une semaine de vacances en août.
native_language_example: Every year, I take a week of vacation in August.

meaning: every two days; every other day.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a regular frequency. It literally means “all the two days,” but in practice it means something happens once every two days (often the same as “every other day”).
target_language_example: Je fais du sport tous les deux jours.
native_language_example: I work out every other day.

additional_notes: Used to express a habitual action that happens on Sundays. Often goes with the imperfect for past habits (e.g., « Elle jouait… ») or with the present for current routines.
target_language_example: On déjeune chez mes grands-parents tous les dimanches.
native_language_example: We have lunch at my grandparents' every Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or confirm complete information about something. Usually appears with verbs like donner / dire / raconter / savoir / avoir: « Donne-moi tous les détails. » The form stays the same in most contexts (tous = masculine plural; détails is plural).
target_language_example: Raconte-moi tous les détails de ton voyage.
native_language_example: Tell me all the details about your trip.

additional_notes: Uses "tous" (all) + "les" (the) + "enfants" (children) to talk about every child in a group in a general way. It’s often followed by a verb in the plural: "Tous les enfants dorment."
target_language_example: Tous les enfants de la classe sont là aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: All the children in the class are here today.

additional_notes: Literally “all the men.” It can mean “all men/mankind” in a general sense. Watch out for the pattern “Tous les hommes ne … (pas)”: it usually means “Not all men …” (e.g., “Tous les hommes ne sont pas comme toi” = “Not all men are like you”).
target_language_example: Tous les hommes ont besoin de respect.
native_language_example: All people need respect.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about men as a group. In French it often implies a broad generalization (like “All men are the same”). Grammatically: *tous* (plural “all”) + *les hommes* (“men”) + *sont* (“are”, 3rd person plural of *être*). If you mean “all humans/people,” French more commonly uses *tous les êtres humains* or *tout le monde* rather than *tous les hommes*.
target_language_example: Tous les hommes sont différents, mais chacun mérite du respect.
native_language_example: All men are different, but everyone deserves respect.

additional_notes: A general statement about equality, often used with contexts like "devant la loi" (before the law) or "devant Dieu" (before God). Note: in French, "les hommes" can mean “men” specifically, but it is also often used in older/formal contexts to mean “human beings / people.”
target_language_example: Dans une démocratie, tous les hommes sont égaux en droits.
native_language_example: In a democracy, all people are equal in rights.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens regularly each morning (a routine/habit). Often placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also go near the verb for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je bois du café tous les matins avant de partir.
native_language_example: I drink coffee every morning before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens monthly (a repeated schedule, payment, subscription, etc.). You can place it at the end of the sentence or after the verb: « Je suis payé tous les mois. »
target_language_example: Je paie mon loyer tous les mois.
native_language_example: I pay my rent every month.

meaning: all the means; every possible way (to do something).
additional_notes: Refers to using every method or resource available to reach a goal. Common patterns: « tous les moyens possibles » (“every possible means”) and « se donner tous les moyens de + infinitive » (“to give oneself all the means to…”). In « Tous les moyens sont bons », it often implies “anything goes” / “any means are acceptable,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Pour finir le projet à temps, on va essayer tous les moyens.
native_language_example: To finish the project on time, we’re going to try every possible way.

meaning: all the same; all alike (usually said critically).
additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people/things have no real differences: “They’re all the same.” Often sounds dismissive or complaining (e.g., “Les hommes sont tous les mêmes.” = “Men are all the same.”). It agrees with gender/number: tous (masc. plural) / toutes (fem. plural) + les mêmes. You’ll often see it with a pronoun or subject: “Ils sont tous les mêmes”, “Vous êtes tous les mêmes”.
target_language_example: Ils promettent beaucoup, mais au final, ils sont tous les mêmes.
native_language_example: They promise a lot, but in the end, they’re all the same.

additional_notes: Means something happens each evening (as a routine). Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence: « Tous les soirs, ... » / « ... tous les soirs. ». Note: in French, « soir » is evening; « nuit » is night (as in nighttime).
target_language_example: Je fais mes devoirs tous les soirs.
native_language_example: I do my homework every evening.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of exactly three people (or things) together. Often placed after the subject or object it refers to: « Je vous reconnais tous les trois » (I recognize all three of you). You can also say « nous trois / vous trois / eux trois » in similar contexts.
target_language_example: On va y aller tous les trois après le déjeuner.
native_language_example: The three of us are going to go there after lunch.

additional_notes: Means the entire group of students. Often used as a subject: « Tous les étudiants sont… » (“All the students are…”). You can also modify it with words like « presque »: « presque tous les étudiants » = “almost all the students.”
target_language_example: Tous les étudiants doivent arriver à l’heure.
native_language_example: All the students must arrive on time.

additional_notes: Means the entire human race, without exception. Often used in general statements (science, ethics, rights). You’ll also see the singular: "tout être humain" = "every human being."
target_language_example: Tous les êtres humains ont besoin de dormir.
native_language_example: All human beings need to sleep.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun (or a mixed-gender plural group): tous mes fichiers, tous mes frères. For feminine plural, use "toutes mes" (e.g., toutes mes affaires). Before a singular noun, use "tout mon" (m.) or "toute ma" (f.).
target_language_example: Tous mes amis habitent loin d'ici.
native_language_example: All my friends live far from here.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: "tous" (all) + "mes" (my, plural) + "amis" (friends). You can swap in other possessives (e.g., "tous tes amis" = all your friends) or other nouns (e.g., "tous mes voisins" = all my neighbors). Also note: "tous" is pronounced like /tu/ (the final -s is silent).
target_language_example: Tous mes amis habitent près d’ici.
native_language_example: All my friends live near here.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “all our …”. It agrees with the noun: feminine plural is « toutes nos » (ex. toutes nos affaires). In speech and writing it often appears with a noun right after it: « tous nos objectifs », « tous nos livres ».
target_language_example: On doit ranger tous nos vêtements avant de partir.
native_language_example: We have to put away all our clothes before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has or affects every one of their items/people/things: « tous ses doigts » (all his fingers), « tous ses caprices » (all his whims). « ses » can mean his, her, or its (it agrees with the plural noun that follows). With a feminine plural noun, use « toutes ses » (e.g., « toutes ses idées »).
target_language_example: Elle connaît tous ses voisins.
native_language_example: She knows all her neighbors.

meaning: exactly like (someone); the spitting image of.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is a perfect copy of someone else, especially in looks or personality. Very common patterns: « C'est toi tout craché » (You're exactly like yourself/your past self) and « Son père tout craché » (His/Her father, exactly). You may also hear « du X tout craché » meaning “pure X / typical X” (e.g., « Du Bobby tout craché »). It’s informal and « tout craché » stays invariable (no agreement).
target_language_example: Avec sa manière de parler, c'est sa mère tout craché.
native_language_example: The way he talks, he's the spitting image of his mother.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize proximity (stronger than just près). Often appears on its own ("Tout près.") as a short answer, or with de/d’ici: "tout près d’ici" (very close to here).
target_language_example: La station de métro est tout près d'ici.
native_language_example: The subway station is very close to here.

additional_notes: Used to make something sound straightforward or obvious (“just do it”). It can also emphasize inability or refusal: “ne pas pouvoir tout simplement…” = “simply couldn’t…”. With adjectives, it often acts as an intensifier meaning “simply/absolutely”: “tout simplement génial” = “simply brilliant.”
target_language_example: Je n'ai tout simplement pas le temps aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I just don’t have time today.

meaning: completely/entirely; (with a person) entirely yours / at your service.
additional_notes: Common patterns: **tout à fait** = “completely,” “absolutely,” “quite” (strong agreement: *Vous avez tout à fait raison.*). With a person/pronoun (**tout à toi / tout à vous**), it means “entirely yours” or “at your disposal/at your service” (often used politely: *Je suis tout à vous.*).
target_language_example: Je suis tout à vous si vous avez des questions.
native_language_example: I’m at your service / I’m here for you if you have questions.

meaning: 'completely / entirely' or 'quite'; also 'exactly' in agreement ("Yes, exactly").
additional_notes: An intensifier placed before an adjective/adverb: «tout à fait normal» (quite/completely normal), «tout à fait choqué» (completely shocked), «tout à fait bien» (completely fine). In replies it can mean strong agreement: «Tout à fait.» = “Exactly / Absolutely.”
target_language_example: — Tu es d’accord ? — Tout à fait.
native_language_example: — Do you agree? — Absolutely.

meaning: 'completely / entirely' or 'quite'; also 'exactly' in agreement ("Yes, exactly").
additional_notes: An intensifier placed before an adjective/adverb: «tout à fait normal» (quite/completely normal), «tout à fait choqué» (completely shocked), «tout à fait bien» (completely fine). In replies it can mean strong agreement: «Tout à fait.» = “Exactly / Absolutely.”
target_language_example: — Tu es d’accord ? — Tout à fait.
native_language_example: — Do you agree? — Absolutely.

meaning: all that time; the whole time.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a duration that has just been mentioned or is understood from context, often implying “during that entire period.” Common with questions like Où étais-tu tout ce temps ? and with pendant: pendant tout ce temps (“during all that time”).
target_language_example: Je t’ai attendu tout ce temps.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for you all this time.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the totality of something, usually followed by a relative pronoun: **tout ce qui** + verb (everything that + subject), **tout ce que** + subject + verb (everything that + object), or **tout ce dont** + verb (everything that + "about/that you need"). Often corresponds to English “everything that…” or “all that…”.
target_language_example: Je veux tout ce que tu as écrit.
native_language_example: I want everything you wrote.

additional_notes: Used before a relative clause with verbs/adjectives that normally take **de** (e.g., **avoir besoin de** = “to need”, **parler de** = “to talk about”). **dont** replaces **de + which/that**. So **tout ce dont il a besoin** = “everything he needs.”
target_language_example: J'ai tout ce dont j'ai besoin pour le voyage.
native_language_example: I have everything I need for the trip.

tout ce dont nous avons besoin

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce dont nous avons besoin
additional_notes: Uses the structure **tout ce dont + (subject) + avoir besoin** to mean “everything that (someone) needs.” **dont** replaces **de + something** because **avoir besoin** is followed by **de** (avoir besoin de…). You can change the subject: *tout ce dont j’ai besoin* (everything I need), *tout ce dont tu as besoin*, etc.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : on a tout ce dont nous avons besoin pour le voyage.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we have everything we need for the trip.

tout ce dont vous avez besoin

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce dont vous avez besoin
additional_notes: Used to say someone has all the necessary things (objects, information, help, etc.). The structure "tout ce dont" means "everything that" with "de" ("dont") because French uses "avoir besoin de" = "to need" + "of". You’ll often see it in questions (Avez-vous… ?) and instructions (Prenez…).
target_language_example: Voici tout ce dont vous avez besoin pour commencer.
native_language_example: Here is everything you need to get started.

additional_notes: Used before a clause starting with a vowel sound (so you see elision: ce que → ce qu’). It introduces a relative clause meaning “everything that,” often followed by a subject + verb (e.g., tout ce qu’il veut = everything he wants). Can also mean “all I have/need/left,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Je te donnerai tout ce qu’on a trouvé.
native_language_example: I’ll give you everything we found.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing what a man has done/knows/touches, etc. It’s the structure: tout (everything) + ce que (what/that which) + il (he). The "e" in "que" drops before a vowel: que + il → qu'il. Often followed by a verb: « tout ce qu'il a fait » (everything he did), « tout ce qu'il touche » (everything he touches), « tout ce qu'il faudra » (everything that will be necessary).
target_language_example: Je comprends tout ce qu'il dit.
native_language_example: I understand everything he says.

additional_notes: Used to say you have (or there is) everything necessary for a task or situation. Very common with avoir/il y a: « J’ai tout ce qu’il faut » (I’ve got everything we need), « Il y a tout ce qu’il faut ici » (There’s everything we need here). Can also imply “don’t worry, we’re prepared.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, j’ai tout ce qu’il faut pour le dîner.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ve got everything we need for dinner.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause meaning “everything that…” with the subject on. In everyday French, on often means “we” (instead of nous), but it can also mean “people/you in general.” Very common in phrases like tout ce qu’on peut (“everything we can”) and tout ce qu’on a fait (“everything we did / have done”).
target_language_example: Je te remercie pour tout ce qu’on a fait pour moi.
native_language_example: Thank you for everything you (all) did for me.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the complete set of things in a clause: "tout ce que" + subject + verb. Often followed by a verb in the passé composé or present (e.g., "tout ce que j'ai voulu", "tout ce que tu dis"). For people, you usually use "tout le monde" instead of *tout ce que*.
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit tout ce que je savais.
native_language_example: I told you everything I knew.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to all the things you previously said. Common in phrases like "C'est tout ce que j'ai dit" (that's all I said), "Je retire tout ce que j'ai dit" (I take back everything I said), and in questions like "Tu as entendu tout ce que j'ai dit ?" (Did you hear everything I said?).
target_language_example: Désolé, je retire tout ce que j'ai dit.
native_language_example: Sorry, I take back everything I said.

additional_notes: A relative clause meaning “everything that I did.” Often used after another phrase, e.g. C’est… (“That’s…”), Pour… (“For…”), Avec… (“With…”), to refer back to all your actions/efforts. Can be adapted: tout ce que tu as fait (everything you did), tout ce qu’il/elle a fait, etc.
target_language_example: Je suis désolé pour tout ce que j'ai fait.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for everything I've done.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone/something is your only possession or your entire amount of something. Often follows a form of "être" (Ils sont tout ce que j’ai. = They’re all I have.) or "donner" (Je te donne tout ce que j’ai. = I’m giving you everything I have.).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas beaucoup d'argent, mais je te donne tout ce que j'ai.
native_language_example: I don’t have much money, but I’m giving you all I have.

additional_notes: Used to talk about everything someone possessed/owned or had available at a time in the past. Often appears in sentences like: “C’est tout ce que j’avais (à dire)” = “That’s all I had (to say).” You can also use it alone as an incomplete sentence for emphasis (“Tout ce que j’avais.” = “Everything I had.”). Grammar note: j’avais is the imperfect of avoir, describing a past state (what you had at that time).
target_language_example: J'ai perdu tout ce que j'avais pendant le voyage.
native_language_example: I lost everything I had during the trip.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing everything you do, say, can do, etc. It’s often followed by a verb: « tout ce que je peux » (all I can), « tout ce que je sais » (all I know), « tout ce que je veux » (all I want).
target_language_example: Je te dirai tout ce que je sais.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you everything I know.

additional_notes: Used to refer to all the things you say (often as the object of a verb like croire, critiquer, répéter, etc.). Common in emphasis or complaints: «Il critique tout ce que je dis» (he criticizes everything I say), «Vous retournez tout ce que je dis contre moi» (you use everything I say against me). Often seen in the pattern «tout ce que + subject + verb» = “everything that …”.
target_language_example: Elle note tout ce que je dis pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: She writes down everything I say during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or promise a full account of your knowledge about something (often with verbs like dire/t'expliquer: « Je vais te dire tout ce que je sais. »). It can also be said alone as a sentence fragment (« Tout ce que je sais. ») meaning “That’s all I know.”
target_language_example: Je vais te raconter tout ce que je sais sur cette histoire.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you everything I know about this story.

additional_notes: Used to talk about having/getting/doing whatever you want. Often comes after verbs like avoir (to have), faire (to do/make), offrir (to offer), or être (to be): «J’ai… tout ce que je veux», «Je peux… tout ce que je veux». In «Je lui fais faire tout ce que je veux», it means “I make him/her do whatever I want” (faire faire = to make someone do). In «Tu es tout ce que je veux», it means “You’re everything I want” (romantic/strong emphasis).
target_language_example: Avec ce travail, je peux acheter tout ce que je veux.
native_language_example: With this job, I can buy everything I want.

tout ce que je veux, c'est

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce que je veux, c'est
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that this is your only/main desire or request. The structure is: "Tout ce que je veux, c'est + noun/infinitive/clause". It’s often followed by a noun (un baiser), a person (toi), or an infinitive (être libre). In speech you may also hear: "Tout ce que je veux, c’est que + subject + verb" (All I want is for…).
target_language_example: Tout ce que je veux, c'est un peu de temps.
native_language_example: All I want is a little time.

additional_notes: Built with **tout ce que** (“everything that / all that”) + **je voulais** (“I wanted”). It refers to a complete set of things (or sometimes even a person) that matched what the speaker wanted. You can extend it with another verb: **tout ce que je voulais voir/faire/dire** (“everything I wanted to see/do/say”).
target_language_example: Ce voyage était tout ce que je voulais.
native_language_example: That trip was everything I wanted.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing the totality of things “we” do, say, see, ask for, can, etc. It’s often followed by a verb: « tout ce que nous demandons / disons / voyons / pouvons ». Don’t confuse it with « tout ce que nous avons » (“everything that we have”).
target_language_example: Tout ce que nous voulons, c’est un peu de temps.
native_language_example: All we want is a little time.

meaning: 'everything that you' / 'all that you' (introduces a clause about what you do, say, have, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the totality of things connected to the listener ("tu") and is followed by a verb: tout ce que tu possèdes (everything you own), tout ce que tu diras (everything you say), tout ce que tu demandes (everything you ask for). Often appears in promises or conditions (Je ferai tout ce que tu veux/diras).
target_language_example: Je comprends tout ce que tu dis.
native_language_example: I understand everything you’re saying.

tout ce que tu as dit

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce que tu as dit
additional_notes: Used to refer to the complete set of things someone said. Structure: "tout" (everything) + "ce que" (what/that which) + subject + past tense ("tu as dit" = you said). Can be the object of a verb (Je me rappelle…) or the subject of a sentence (Tout ce que tu as dit était vrai).
target_language_example: J'ai noté tout ce que tu as dit pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: I wrote down everything you said during the meeting.

tout ce que tu as fait

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce que tu as fait
additional_notes: Built on the structure **tout ce que + subject + verb** (“everything that…”). Here it uses the **passé composé** (**tu as fait**) to talk about completed actions. It’s common in emotional contexts, especially **gratitude** (Merci pour tout ce que tu as fait…) or **reproach/shock** (Après tout ce que tu as fait ?).
target_language_example: Je n’oublierai jamais tout ce que tu as fait pour nous.
native_language_example: I’ll never forget everything you did for us.

additional_notes: Often used to refer to everything someone has (money, items, resources) or everything they can offer in the moment (effort, arguments, things to say). In questions like « C’est tout ce que tu as ? », it can mean “Is that all you’ve got?” (sometimes challenging or disappointed). In « tout ce que tu as à dire », it means “all you have to say.”
target_language_example: Donne-moi tout ce que tu as.
native_language_example: Give me everything you’ve got.

tout ce que tu as à faire est

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce que tu as à faire est
meaning: 'all you have to do is' (followed by de + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to say the solution is simple: “all you need to do is…”. It’s followed by **de** + an infinitive (verb in the “to…” form): *Tout ce que tu as à faire est de demander.* You can change **tu** to **vous** for a more formal/polite version: *Tout ce que vous avez à faire, c’est de…* (very common in speech).
target_language_example: Tout ce que tu as à faire est de cliquer sur ce bouton.
native_language_example: All you have to do is click that button.

additional_notes: Built with the very common structure **tout ce que + subject + verb** = “everything that/what + …”. Here, **ce que** introduces a relative clause (“that/what you say”). In questions like **C’est tout ce que tu dis ?**, it can sound like “Is that all you have to say?” depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Je crois tout ce que tu dis.
native_language_example: I believe everything you say.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to share all the information they have about a person/thing/topic. It often follows verbs like dire (tell), savoir (know), expliquer (explain): « Dis-moi tout ce que tu sais sur… » / « Je veux savoir tout ce que tu sais. ». The structure is compositional: tout (everything) + ce que (what/that which) + tu sais (you know).
target_language_example: Explique-moi tout ce que tu sais sur cette affaire.
native_language_example: Explain to me everything you know about this case.

additional_notes: Literally “all that you want.” Used with verbs like fournir (provide), manger (eat), avoir (have), faire (do) to say there are no limits: “as much as you want / whatever you want.” In some contexts (e.g., "Tu peux me faire tout ce que tu veux"), it can mean “You can do whatever you want to me,” which may sound strong depending on the situation.
target_language_example: Prends tout ce que tu veux dans le frigo.
native_language_example: Take anything you want from the fridge.

additional_notes: Uses the structure **tout ce que + subject + verb** = “everything that …”. Here **tu voulais** is the imperfect of *vouloir* (“you wanted”). You can swap the person/tense: *tout ce que je veux* (everything I want), *tout ce qu’il voulait* (everything he wanted), etc. Often used as an object: *J’ai fait tout ce que tu voulais.*
target_language_example: J’ai acheté tout ce que tu voulais au supermarché.
native_language_example: I bought everything you wanted at the supermarket.

meaning: "everything that you" / "all that you" (formal or plural "you").
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause meaning "everything that you ...". It’s followed by a verb: "tout ce que vous voulez" (everything you want), "tout ce que vous pouvez" (everything you can). Here, "vous" is either polite singular (to one person) or plural (to several people).
target_language_example: Je ferai tout ce que vous me demanderez.
native_language_example: I will do everything you ask me.

meaning: "everything that you have" / "all that you have".
additional_notes: Built on the very common pattern **tout ce que + subject + verb** (“everything/all that …”). **Vous avez** is the formal/plural “you have,” so it can address one person politely or several people. Depending on context, it can mean “all you bought/wrote/went through” or, in a question, “is that all you have?” (implying “is there anything else?”).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir si c’est tout ce que vous avez préparé.
native_language_example: I want to know if that’s everything you prepared.

meaning: "everything that you have" / "all that you have".
additional_notes: Built on the very common pattern **tout ce que + subject + verb** (“everything/all that …”). **Vous avez** is the formal/plural “you have,” so it can address one person politely or several people. Depending on context, it can mean “all you bought/wrote/went through” or, in a question, “is that all you have?” (implying “is there anything else?”).
target_language_example: Je veux savoir si c’est tout ce que vous avez préparé.
native_language_example: I want to know if that’s everything you prepared.

tout ce que vous avez à faire est

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce que vous avez à faire est
additional_notes: Used to say something is the only requirement or the simplest step to achieve a result. It’s followed by either “de + infinitive” (Tout ce que vous avez à faire est de demander.) or “c’est de + infinitive” in a very common variant (Tout ce que vous avez à faire, c’est de demander.). “Vous” is the formal/plural “you”; with “tu” you get “tout ce que tu as à faire, c’est de …”.
target_language_example: Tout ce que vous avez à faire est de remplir ce formulaire.
native_language_example: All you have to do is fill out this form.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (politely/formally, with "vous") to share all the information they have about something. Often appears after verbs like "dire" (to tell) or "me dire" (tell me). "Tout ce que" means "everything that/which," and "vous savez" means "you know."
target_language_example: Dites-moi tout ce que vous savez sur cet incident.
native_language_example: Tell me everything you know about this incident.

additional_notes: Means “everything that you want.” Used after verbs like dire (say), donner (give), prendre (take), demander (ask), avoir (have), être (be): e.g., “Dites… / Prenez… / Demandez…”. Uses the formal/polite “vous”; with friends you’d usually say “tout ce que tu veux”.
target_language_example: Choisissez tout ce que vous voulez.
native_language_example: Choose anything you want.

meaning: "everything that is" / "everything that's …" (i.e., all that exists or all things of a kind).
additional_notes: Used to refer broadly to all things that match a description or category. It’s often followed by an adjective or noun phrase: « tout ce qui est nécessaire » (everything that’s necessary), « tout ce qui est romantique » (everything that’s romantic). In some contexts it can mean “everything around/in/near …” when followed by a place phrase (e.g., « tout ce qui est autour de lui »).
target_language_example: J’ai rangé tout ce qui est sur la table.
native_language_example: I put away everything that’s on the table.

tout ce qui est en mon pouvoir

target_language_multi_word_term: tout ce qui est en mon pouvoir
meaning: everything I can (do); everything in my power.
additional_notes: A fairly formal set phrase used to promise you’ll do your best or take all possible action. Often followed by an infinitive with pour: « …pour aider / pour vous aider » (…to help / …to help you). You can also use other possessives: « tout ce qui est en ton/son/notre/votre/leur pouvoir ».
target_language_example: Je ferai tout ce qui est en mon pouvoir pour résoudre ce problème.
native_language_example: I will do everything I can to solve this problem.

meaning: everything that happened; all that happened.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a whole sequence of events in the past (often something important, surprising, or upsetting). It can follow prepositions like après (“after”), pour (“for/about”), or be the object of verbs like voir (“to see”) and savoir (“to know”).
target_language_example: On devrait parler de tout ce qui s'est passé hier soir.
native_language_example: We should talk about everything that happened last night.

additional_notes: Refers to the whole situation, set of things, or information being talked about, usually close in the conversation/context. Often points back to what was just mentioned (events, actions, details). You can also say “tout ça” in a more casual style.
target_language_example: Tout ceci est très compliqué à expliquer.
native_language_example: All of this is very complicated to explain.

meaning: "all that" / "all of that" (everything being talked about).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to information, events, or details already mentioned or understood from context. Often appears in questions like « Qu’est-ce que tout cela veut dire ? » (= “What does all of this mean?”).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas tout cela.
native_language_example: I don't understand all of this.

additional_notes: Means a large amount of money being talked about in the situation. Uses "tout" (all) + "cet" (this/that, masculine singular before a vowel sound) + "argent" (money). You’ll often see it in questions about spending, owning, finding, or receiving money.
target_language_example: Tu vas faire quoi avec tout cet argent ?
native_language_example: What are you going to do with all that money?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to mean the entire thing/time period ("tout le trajet" = the whole trip) or all of something ("tout le truc" = all the stuff/thing). It agrees with the noun: "toute la" (fem. sing.), "tous les" (masc. plur.), "toutes les" (fem. plur.).
target_language_example: J’ai passé tout le week-end à étudier.
native_language_example: I spent the whole weekend studying.

meaning: 'everyone has' / 'everyone did' (with a verb in the past).
additional_notes: "Tout le monde" means "everyone." When it’s followed by "a" + past participle, it forms the passé composé (past tense) for an action that everyone did (e.g., "Tout le monde a crié" = "Everyone shouted"). You’ll often see it introducing a group reaction or action.
target_language_example: Tout le monde a ri quand il a raconté cette blague.
native_language_example: Everyone laughed when he told that joke.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of rire (a ri = laughed). Often followed by "de + person/thing" to mean "to laugh at": "Tout le monde a ri de moi" (Everyone laughed at me). You can also add an exception with "sauf": "Tout le monde a ri, sauf Tom" (Everyone laughed except Tom).
target_language_example: Tout le monde a ri de lui pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: Everyone laughed at him during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used with the passé composé of être (a été) to describe how everyone was at a past moment or over a past period. Even though it refers to many people, "tout le monde" is grammatically singular, so adjectives often stay singular masculine by default: « Tout le monde a été gentil. » (You may also hear plural agreement in informal speech, but singular is the standard.)
target_language_example: Tout le monde a été très patient pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: Everyone was very patient during the meeting.

meaning: 'everyone has' / 'everyone did' (with a verb in the past).
additional_notes: "Tout le monde" means "everyone." When it’s followed by "a" + past participle, it forms the passé composé (past tense) for an action that everyone did (e.g., "Tout le monde a crié" = "Everyone shouted"). You’ll often see it introducing a group reaction or action.
target_language_example: Tout le monde a ri quand il a raconté cette blague.
native_language_example: Everyone laughed when he told that joke.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about people in general. It’s typically followed by a plural noun (des + noun): Tout le monde a des défauts. (Note: literally “all the world has…”, but it means “everyone has…”.)
target_language_example: Tout le monde a des qualités et des défauts.
native_language_example: Everyone has strengths and weaknesses.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement about people. It’s made of: tout le monde (everyone) + a (has) + un/une (a). Choose un for masculine nouns and une for feminine nouns: « tout le monde a un frère » / « tout le monde a une histoire ». Even though « tout le monde » refers to many people, the verb stays singular (a).
target_language_example: Tout le monde a un endroit préféré.
native_language_example: Everyone has a favorite place.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about what people like. Literally "all the world likes," but in everyday French it means "everyone" (people in general). You can follow it with a noun (Tout le monde aime le pain.) or with an object pronoun (Tout le monde l’aime. = Everyone likes it/him/her.).
target_language_example: Dans cette ville, tout le monde aime le marché du samedi.
native_language_example: In this town, everyone likes the Saturday market.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about what people like. Here, **les** is the plural definite article (“the” / “some”), so it’s followed by a plural noun: *les chips, les frites, les glaces*. You can also change **les** to **le/la/l’** for singular: *Tout le monde aime le chocolat.*
target_language_example: Tout le monde aime les bons desserts.
native_language_example: Everyone likes good desserts.

additional_notes: Used to say that a person, thing, law, story, etc. is widely known. "Tout le monde" = "everyone" (singular idea), and "connaît" is the present tense of "connaître" (to know/be familiar with). Often followed by a direct object (e.g., son nom, la loi).
target_language_example: Dans ce quartier, tout le monde connaît le boulanger.
native_language_example: In this neighborhood, everyone knows the baker.

additional_notes: Used to make a general recommendation, opinion, or (sometimes strong) instruction about what all people should do. "Tout le monde" = everyone; "devrait" is the conditional of "devoir" (to have to / should), making it sound like advice rather than a strict obligation ("tout le monde doit"). Often followed by an infinitive: "Tout le monde devrait + verbe".
target_language_example: Tout le monde devrait respecter les règles.
native_language_example: Everyone should respect the rules.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation that applies to all people (“tout le monde” = everyone; “doit” is the 3rd person singular of “devoir,” meaning “must / have to”). It’s typically followed by a verb in the infinitive: “tout le monde doit + infinitive” (e.g., payer, participer).
target_language_example: Ici, tout le monde doit montrer une pièce d’identité.
native_language_example: Here, everyone must show an ID.

additional_notes: “Tout le monde” means “everyone/everybody” and it takes a singular verb: tout le monde est / a / fait. It’s often followed by an adjective (Tout le monde est prêt.), a place (Tout le monde est ici.), or a phrase like “au courant” (aware) or “en retard” (late).
target_language_example: Tout le monde est prêt à partir.
native_language_example: Everyone is ready to leave.

additional_notes: This is the formal French question structure using inversion: subject + verb + -il/-elle. Here, the subject is “tout le monde” (“everyone”), and “est-il” means “is (he/it)?” even though it refers to a group of people. It’s common in writing and formal speech. In everyday conversation you’ll often hear: “Est-ce que tout le monde est … ?” or simply “Tout le monde est … ?”.
target_language_example: Tout le monde est-il prêt à partir ?
native_language_example: Is everyone ready to leave?

additional_notes: "Tout le monde" means "everyone." "Fut" is the passé simple (simple past) of "être" (to be), mostly used in literature and formal storytelling; in everyday speech you usually say "tout le monde était" (everyone was) or sometimes "tout le monde a été" (everyone has been/was). Often followed by an adjective: "Tout le monde fut surpris" (Everyone was surprised).
target_language_example: Pendant l'annonce, tout le monde fut choqué.
native_language_example: During the announcement, everyone was shocked.

additional_notes: Used to talk about all the people in the place you’re in. Often followed by a verb in the 3rd person singular (e.g., « Tout le monde ici comprend… »).
target_language_example: Tout le monde ici est très gentil.
native_language_example: Everyone here is very nice.

additional_notes: “Tout le monde” means “everyone” (literally “all the world”). The “l’” is the shortened form of “le” or “la” (him/it or her/it) and comes before a verb starting with a vowel or silent h: l’attend, l’a vu, l’adore. It refers to a person or thing already known from context.
target_language_example: Tout le monde l’aime.
native_language_example: Everyone loves him/her/it.

additional_notes: **Tout le monde** means “everyone.” The **le** is a direct-object pronoun placed **before** the verb and usually refers to a masculine singular person or thing (“him” or “it”). Pattern: **Tout le monde + le + verb** (e.g., *Tout le monde le sait* = “Everyone knows it”).
target_language_example: Tout le monde le sait.
native_language_example: Everyone knows it.

additional_notes: Used to say that a fact is common knowledge. "le" is an object pronoun meaning "it" (the thing being talked about). Often used for emphasis (sometimes with words like "évidemment"). Can be used as a statement or in a question: "Est-ce que tout le monde le sait ?" = "Does everyone know?"
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : tout le monde le sait déjà.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everyone already knows it.

meaning: “everyone … to me / … me” (everyone + “me” as the object).
additional_notes: Used to say that everybody does something to you, or feels something about you. **Tout le monde** = “everyone.” **Me** is an object pronoun meaning “me/to me,” placed **before** the verb: *Tout le monde me connaît* (“Everyone knows me”). With **connaître** (to know a person), the 3rd person singular is often written **connaît** (with a circumflex).
target_language_example: Tout le monde me regarde.
native_language_example: Everyone is looking at me.

tout le monde ne peut pas être

target_language_multi_word_term: tout le monde ne peut pas être
additional_notes: Used to say that a quality, role, or achievement isn’t possible for all people. In standard French, this often implies "not everybody" rather than "nobody". You typically complete it with a noun or adjective: « Tout le monde ne peut pas être + adjectif/nom ».
target_language_example: Tout le monde ne peut pas être médecin.
native_language_example: Not everyone can be a doctor.

additional_notes: "Tout le monde" means "everyone" (literally "all the world"). It’s followed by the 3rd-person singular form of the verb: "tout le monde peut" (not *peuvent*). It’s usually followed by an infinitive: "Tout le monde peut apprendre…" = "Anyone can learn…"
target_language_example: Avec un peu de pratique, tout le monde peut y arriver.
native_language_example: With a bit of practice, anyone can do it.

additional_notes: Used to say something is common knowledge (known by all people in a group, or by people in general). Often followed by a clause with que/ce que/qui/ce qui: « Tout le monde sait que… » (Everyone knows that…), « Tout le monde sait qui… » (Everyone knows who…), « Tout le monde sait ce qui… » (Everyone knows what…).
target_language_example: Tout le monde sait que ce restaurant est très bon.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that this restaurant is very good.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement presented as common knowledge. The verb is usually present tense (sait), even when what follows is about the past: « Tout le monde sait que je l'ai pris. » Can also be used ironically or sarcastically to mean “as if everyone knows.”
target_language_example: Tout le monde sait que c'est difficile.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that it’s difficult.

additional_notes: "Tout le monde" means "everyone." "Savait" is the imperfect past of "savoir" (to know), often used for a general state or background information in the past. You’ll often see it with "que" + a clause ("Tout le monde savait que...") or with a direct object ("Tout le monde savait la chanson").
target_language_example: Quand il est arrivé, tout le monde savait déjà la nouvelle.
native_language_example: When he arrived, everyone already knew the news.

additional_notes: Used before a reflexive verb (or a verb used reflexively). With "tout le monde" (singular in French), you still use "se". Depending on the verb, it can mean everyone does something to themselves (e.g., "tout le monde se calme" = everyone calms down) or to each other (e.g., "tout le monde se connaît" = everyone knows each other).
target_language_example: Après la réunion, tout le monde se dépêche de rentrer chez soi.
native_language_example: After the meeting, everyone hurries to go home.

tout le monde se mit à

target_language_multi_word_term: tout le monde se mit à
additional_notes: Past simple (literary) of "tout le monde s’est mis à". Used in stories and written narration to show that everyone began doing something at the same time. It’s followed by an infinitive: "se mit à + infinitive" (e.g., applaudir, rire, parler).
target_language_example: Quand il est entré, tout le monde se mit à crier.
native_language_example: When he came in, everyone started shouting.

additional_notes: "Tout le monde" means "everyone" (literally "all the world"). "Sera" is the future tense of "être" (to be): it’s used to talk about how everyone will be later (e.g., happy, tired, there, at home, aware).
