Often followed by an adjective (fatigué, heureux) or a place/state (là, à la maison, au courant).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : tout le monde sera prêt à temps.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everyone will be ready on time.

meaning: "everyone is going to" (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Used with the near future (futur proche): **tout le monde va + infinitive**. It means that everyone will do something soon or is expected to do it. The verb **va** is from **aller** (to go) and stays **va** because **tout le monde** is grammatically singular even though it means many people.
target_language_example: Tout le monde va comprendre bientôt.
native_language_example: Everyone is going to understand soon.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about people in general. "Tout le monde" = "everyone" (literally "all the world"), and "veut" is the present tense of "vouloir" (to want). Often followed by an infinitive: "tout le monde veut + verb" (e.g., "tout le monde veut réussir").
target_language_example: Tout le monde veut avoir du temps libre.
native_language_example: Everybody wants to have free time.

additional_notes: Used to describe a state or situation that applied to everyone at a particular time in the past. It’s the phrase "tout le monde" (everyone) + the imperfect of "être" (was/were), often followed by an adjective or description: "tout le monde était fatigué" (everyone was tired).
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, tout le monde était prêt.
native_language_example: When I arrived, everyone was ready.

additional_notes: Used to refer to everything remaining besides what was just mentioned. Common in comparisons (e.g., “more important than everything else”) and when talking about what’s left over (e.g., food, items, tasks).
target_language_example: Je m’occupe du dossier, et tu fais tout le reste.
native_language_example: I’ll take care of the file, and you do everything else.

additional_notes: Means the entire amount of money someone has. The possessive changes with the owner: tout mon argent (all my money), tout ton argent (all your money), tout leur argent (all their money). Often used with verbs like dépenser (to spend), perdre (to lose), voler (to steal).
target_language_example: J’ai dépensé tout mon argent pendant les soldes.
native_language_example: I spent all my money during the sales.

additional_notes: Used to sum up a situation (“tout ça” = “all that / all of this”) and then explain the reason, purpose, or responsibility. Very common with: « grâce à … » (thanks to), « à cause de … » (because of, usually negative), and « pour … » (for). The comma is optional in writing; in speech there’s often a short pause: « Tout ça c’est… ».
target_language_example: Tout ça, c'est grâce à toi.
native_language_example: All of that is thanks to you.

additional_notes:
Built on the common expression **avoir l’air** (= to seem/to look). You can follow it with:
- an adjective: **Tout a l’air normal / en ordre / bon.**
- **de + infinitive**: **Tout a l’air de bien se passer.** (= Everything seems to be going well.)
Note: In correct French spelling, it’s **Tout a l’air** (with an apostrophe), not *a l'air*.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : tout a l’air sous contrôle.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything seems to be under control.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about the whole situation or all items. It’s often followed by an adjective (Tout est différent), or by a set phrase like "tout est en place" (everything is in place) or "tout est en règle" (everything is in order).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tout est prêt.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is ready.

meaning: “That’s all there is to say.” / “Everything has been said.”
additional_notes: Used to conclude a discussion or signal that no more explanation is needed (often meaning “case closed” or “nothing more to add”). It can be a full standalone sentence: « Tout est dit. » Similar idea to « Voilà, c’est tout. »
target_language_example: Je t’ai expliqué la situation : tout est dit.
native_language_example: I’ve explained the situation—that’s all there is to say.

meaning: to mess everything up; to ruin everything.
additional_notes: Very informal and can sound crude because of “foutre” (roughly like “to fuck up”). Used when someone is about to spoil a plan/situation completely. You can change the tense/person: je vais/tu vas/il va tout foutre en l’air, etc.
target_language_example: Fais attention : tu vas tout foutre en l'air !
native_language_example: Be careful: you're going to mess everything up!

meaning: “everything will be fine / all will be well.”
additional_notes: A reassuring phrase used to comfort someone or express hope about the future. Literally “everything will go well” (future tense of aller: ira). Often said on its own or with a softener like « Ne t’inquiète pas, tout ira bien. »
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : tout ira bien demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything will be fine tomorrow.

meaning: “everything will go well / everything will be fine.”
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or express optimism about how a situation will turn out. Built from: tout (“everything”) + se passera (future of se passer, “to happen/go”) + bien (“well”). Often follows verbs like espérer (to hope), parier (to bet), être sûr (to be sure), or is said on its own as encouragement.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : tout se passera bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything will be fine.

meaning: Everything is fine / all is well.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or to check if everything is OK. Common in questions like « Est-ce que tout va bien ? » (“Is everything OK?”). « Tout va bien maintenant » means “Everything is fine now.” « Pour l’instant, tout va bien » = “So far, everything is fine.”
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, tout va bien.
native_language_example: Don't worry, everything is fine.

meaning: "Everything will be fine" / "It will all work out."
additional_notes: A very common reassurance when someone is worried or scared. Uses the near-future idea with "aller" (va) + infinitive: "se passer" = "to happen". Often said on its own, or followed by something comforting: "Tout va bien se passer, je te le promets." You may also hear the shorter version: "Ça va bien se passer."
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : tout va bien se passer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything will be fine.

meaning: Everything is fine / all is well.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or to check if everything is OK. Common in questions like « Est-ce que tout va bien ? » (“Is everything OK?”). « Tout va bien maintenant » means “Everything is fine now.” « Pour l’instant, tout va bien » = “So far, everything is fine.”
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, tout va bien.
native_language_example: Don't worry, everything is fine.

meaning: earlier (today) / just now; or later (in a little while).
additional_notes: Time expression whose meaning depends on context: with apologies/thanks ("Désolé/Merci pour tout à l'heure") it usually means "earlier" or "just now"; with a future action ("Je passerai/repasserai tout à l'heure") it usually means "later" or "in a little while." It refers to the same day (not yesterday or tomorrow).
target_language_example: Je te rappelle tout à l'heure.
native_language_example: I’ll call you back later.

additional_notes: Feminine form of "tout seul". Used to say someone did something without help ("by herself") or that she is alone ("on her own"). Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence: "Elle l’a fait toute seule."
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas : tu n'es pas toute seule.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’re not alone.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to mean the entire thing or every part of it: « toute la région », « toute la maison », « toute la famille ». It agrees in gender/number (compare: « tout le » masculine singular, « toute l’ » before a vowel/h, « tous les / toutes les » plural).
target_language_example: J’ai passé toute la journée à travailler.
native_language_example: I spent the whole day working.

additional_notes: Means something lasts for the entire day. Often used with a verb in the past or present: « J’ai travaillé toute la journée » (I worked all day). With « Ça a pris / ça prendrait toute la journée », it means “it took/would take all day.”
target_language_example: On a attendu toute la journée.
native_language_example: We waited all day.

additional_notes: Means “throughout the morning” (from morning until around noon). Often used with the passé composé or imparfait to show a duration: « J’ai attendu toute la matinée » / « Il pleuvait toute la matinée ». Feminine agreement: toute + la matinée.
target_language_example: J'ai travaillé toute la matinée, puis je suis allé déjeuner.
native_language_example: I worked all morning, then I went to have lunch.

additional_notes: Means “throughout the whole night,” often to say something lasted from evening until morning. It can describe an activity (danser, parler), a feeling/state (pleurer), or staying awake (veiller) for the entire night.
target_language_example: On a travaillé toute la nuit pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: We worked all night to finish the project.

additional_notes: Means the entire duration of the week. Often used with or without "pendant" ("pendant toute la semaine" = "for the whole week"). Agreement: "tout" matches the feminine noun "semaine" → "toute".
target_language_example: Je travaille de nuit toute la semaine.
native_language_example: I work nights all week.

additional_notes: Used to mean something lasts for the entire evening (from the start of the evening until it ends). Often placed after the verb: « Il sera là toute la soirée. »
target_language_example: On a regardé des films toute la soirée.
native_language_example: We watched movies all evening.

meaning: "your whole life ahead of you" (plenty of time; you’re still young).
additional_notes: Used with a person/object pronoun to say someone has lots of time ahead (often because they’re young): « toute la vie devant + elle/lui/moi/toi/nous/vous/eux ». Commonly appears as « avoir toute la vie devant soi » (generic “oneself”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tu as toute la vie devant toi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you have your whole life ahead of you.

meaning: the whole city / everyone in the city.
additional_notes: Can mean (1) physically all over the city (as in « J’ai fait toute la ville » = I went all around the city), or (2) all the people in the city (as in « Toute la ville en parle » = everyone is talking about it). « Toute » agrees with « ville » (feminine singular).
target_language_example: Après la rumeur, toute la ville le sait.
native_language_example: After the rumor, the whole city knows it.

additional_notes: Means “for my entire life” (duration up to now) or “in my entire life” (often after a superlative: *le plus… de toute ma vie* = “the most… in my whole life”). It can also be used emotionally to mean “it’s my whole life” (*C’est toute ma vie.*)
target_language_example: Je rêve d’habiter à Paris toute ma vie.
native_language_example: I dream of living in Paris all my life.

meaning: his/her entire life; all their life.
additional_notes: Means from birth until now (or until death). It agrees with the person: toute ma vie (my whole life), toute ta vie (your whole life), toute sa vie (his/her whole life), toute notre/votre/leur vie. Often placed after the verb to show something lasted a lifetime.
target_language_example: J'ai habité ici toute ma vie.
native_language_example: I've lived here my whole life.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean “all these / all those,” often with emphasis (e.g., time: toutes ces années; things: toutes ces provisions; questions: toutes ces questions). It agrees with the noun: masculine plural is tous ces (tous ces livres).
target_language_example: Je n’arrive pas à croire que tu aies gardé toutes ces lettres.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you kept all these letters.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a set of specific things already known or visible in context. Often implies “all this stuff” (information, objects, details). Agreement: feminine plural (toutes) + demonstrative (ces) + plural noun (choses).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas parler de toutes ces choses maintenant.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about all these things right now.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean “all the.” It agrees with the noun: masculine plural is “tous les” (Tous les jours), feminine plural is “toutes les” (Toutes les routes). Often used for general statements or proverbs.
target_language_example: Toutes les questions sont importantes.
native_language_example: All the questions are important.

meaning: both (of them), when referring to two females.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the statement applies to the two people/things together. It agrees in gender and number: masculine mixed group = « tous les deux », feminine = « toutes les deux ». It can be placed after the subject or after the verb: « Elles sont toutes les deux… », « Elles ont toutes les deux… ».
target_language_example: Vous pouvez venir toutes les deux si vous voulez.
native_language_example: You can both come if you want.

additional_notes: "Toutes" is the feminine plural of "tout" (= all). Used with a plural feminine noun: "toutes les + noun". Be careful with negation: "Toutes les filles ne sont pas ainsi" often means "Not all girls are like that" (it doesn’t necessarily mean that none are like that).
target_language_example: Toutes les filles de la classe sont arrivées en avance.
native_language_example: All the girls in the class arrived early.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens each night (a repeated routine or habit). Often placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also appear at the beginning for emphasis.
target_language_example: Je prends une tisane toutes les nuits avant de dormir.
native_language_example: I have an herbal tea every night before going to sleep.

additional_notes: "Toutes" agrees with the feminine plural noun "portes". Common in home/security contexts with verbs like "verrouiller" (to lock) and "fermer" (to close/shut). You can also specify a place: "toutes les portes de la maison" (all the doors in the house).
target_language_example: Avant de partir, vérifie que toutes les portes sont bien verrouillées.
native_language_example: Before leaving, check that all the doors are properly locked.

additional_notes: Means the complete set of answers (e.g., to a question, quiz, or problem). Often used with verbs like connaître/avoir (“to know/have all the answers”) and can be followed by “à + [question]” (e.g., “toutes les réponses à cette question”).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas toutes les réponses, mais je peux essayer de t'aider.
native_language_example: I don't have all the answers, but I can try to help you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about everything you own/do in a feminine plural category: toutes mes recettes, toutes mes plantes, etc. It’s the feminine plural form of "tout" and must agree with the noun that follows. For masculine plural nouns, use "tous mes" (e.g., tous mes livres).
target_language_example: J’ai perdu toutes mes clés.
native_language_example: I lost all my keys.

additional_notes: Used before a plural feminine noun: toutes ses + noun (e.g., toutes ses erreurs = all his/her mistakes). It refers to everything belonging to one person. The possessor can be "his" or "her"—French uses "ses" based on the noun being possessed (plural), not on the owner’s gender. With masculine plural nouns, use "tous ses".
target_language_example: Elle a oublié toutes ses affaires à la maison.
native_language_example: She forgot all her things at home.

meaning: all one’s strength; with all one’s might.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize maximum physical or mental effort. Often appears in phrases like « de toutes ses forces » (“with all his/her strength”) or with verbs like « épuiser » (to use up/exhaust) and « concentrer » (to focus). The possessive changes with the person: « toutes mes forces », « toutes tes forces », « toutes leurs forces », etc.
target_language_example: Elle a poussé la porte de toutes ses forces.
native_language_example: She pushed the door with all her strength.

meaning: all kinds of; all sorts of.
additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean a wide variety. It agrees with the feminine plural "sortes" (so it stays "toutes sortes de"), and the noun that follows is usually plural but can be singular depending on meaning (e.g., "toutes sortes de choses"). Often implies diversity rather than an exact list.
target_language_example: On y trouve toutes sortes de restaurants, du plus simple au plus chic.
native_language_example: You can find all kinds of restaurants there, from the simplest to the fanciest.

meaning: all kinds of things; all sorts of things.
additional_notes: Used to say there is a wide variety of items/ideas/activities (often without listing them). You can also use the same pattern with a noun: “toutes sortes de livres” (all kinds of books).
target_language_example: On peut faire toutes sortes de choses ici.
native_language_example: You can do all kinds of things here.

additional_notes: Used with "de" to identify a particular train by where it comes from (train de Paris = train from Paris), sometimes by its schedule (le train de huit heures = the 8 o’clock train). In everyday speech you may also hear "le train pour Paris" for “the train to Paris.”
target_language_example: Le train de Lyon arrive à 18 h 20.
native_language_example: The train from Lyon arrives at 6:20 p.m.

meaning: in the middle of reading / currently reading.
additional_notes: Usually used as part of the structure « être en train de + infinitive » to emphasize an action that is happening right now (more explicit than the simple present). Tense changes with « être »: « je suis en train de lire » (I’m reading right now), « j’étais en train de lire » (I was reading).
target_language_example: Je suis en train de lire un livre, je te rappelle après.
native_language_example: I’m in the middle of reading a book; I’ll call you back later.

additional_notes: Usually used in the structure « être en train de + infinitive » to emphasize that something is happening right now/in progress: « Il/elle est en train de mourir » = “He/She is dying.” You conjugate « être » (suis, es, est, était, etc.) and keep « mourir » in the infinitive.
target_language_example: Vite, appelle une ambulance : il est en train de mourir !
native_language_example: Quick, call an ambulance: he’s dying!

meaning: in the middle of watching; currently watching.
additional_notes: Used in the structure « être en train de + infinitive » to emphasize an action happening right now. Here the infinitive is « regarder » (to watch/look at). Often translates as “(be) watching” or “(be) in the middle of watching.”
target_language_example: Je suis en train de regarder une vidéo, je te rappelle après.
native_language_example: I’m watching a video right now; I’ll call you back later.

additional_notes: Used to describe what a job mainly involves. Pattern: (Mon/Son/Leur) travail consiste à + infinitive. You can also use it more generally: Une partie de ton travail consiste à… (= Part of your job is to…).
target_language_example: Mon travail consiste à aider les clients par téléphone.
native_language_example: My job consists of helping customers over the phone.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done together as a team (not by one person). Often appears with “C’est…” or “Ce n’est pas…” (e.g., “C’est un travail d’équipe.”). You may also see it alone as a label or slogan (e.g., on a slide or poster).
target_language_example: On a réussi grâce au travail d'équipe.
native_language_example: We succeeded thanks to teamwork.

meaning: work to do; a task/job to get done.
additional_notes: Often used with avoir: "J'ai du travail à faire" (I have some work to do) or "J'ai un travail à faire" (I have a specific task/assignment to do). "On a du travail à faire" can mean "we" or "people/you" have work to do, depending on context.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas sortir ce soir : j'ai du travail à faire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't go out tonight: I have work to do.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone’s job/role is: subject + travailler + comme + profession/role (usually without an article): « Je travaille comme professeur. » You can change the verb form: « Il travaille comme… », « Nous travaillons comme… ».
target_language_example: Elle travaille comme infirmière à l’hôpital.
native_language_example: She works as a nurse at the hospital.

meaning: “works in a” (works at/in a place or organization).
additional_notes: Used with a singular feminine noun for the workplace or field (une banque, une école, une ferme). For masculine nouns, use « travaille dans un » (dans un hôpital). You can also use « travaille à » with specific workplaces (Je travaille à la banque) but « dans » emphasizes the type of place/sector.
target_language_example: Ma sœur travaille dans une entreprise internationale.
native_language_example: My sister works at/in an international company.

additional_notes: Means putting in a lot of effort, often to reach a goal (réussir, atteindre ses objectifs, rattraper le temps perdu). It can be used with devoir/pouvoir/prêt à to talk about necessity or willingness: « tu dois travailler dur », « il faut travailler dur », « être prêt à travailler dur ».
target_language_example: Si on veut finir à temps, il faut travailler dur.
native_language_example: If we want to finish on time, we have to work hard.

additional_notes: Means putting in a lot of effort in order to achieve success. Often used with necessity verbs like "il faut" (it’s necessary), "on doit" (we/you/people must), or "devoir" (must/have to): e.g., "Il faut travailler dur pour réussir."
target_language_example: Je travaille dur pour réussir à l'école.
native_language_example: I work hard to succeed at school.

additional_notes: Used to encourage or express the need to put in more effort. You can also say "travailler plus fort" (common in Canada). In speech, "dur" is pronounced like "deur".
target_language_example: Si tu veux réussir, il faut travailler plus dur.
native_language_example: If you want to succeed, you have to work harder.

additional_notes: A neutral/formal, respectful term. It’s feminine; the masculine is "travailleur du sexe". Often used with "être" (to be): "Elle est une travailleuse du sexe."
target_language_example: Elle a dit qu’elle était travailleuse du sexe.
native_language_example: She said she was a sex worker.

additional_notes: Formal question form of the verb travailler ('to work') using inversion (verb + -vous). Used to ask if someone has a job, whether they’re working on a certain day, or what/who they’re working on/for (e.g., Pour qui travaillez-vous ? Sur quoi travaillez-vous ? Travaillez-vous lundi ?). In everyday speech, people often say Vous travaillez ? instead.
target_language_example: Travaillez-vous demain matin ?
native_language_example: Are you working tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: Used to say someone worked throughout the entire night. It commonly appears with the passé composé: « avoir » + « travaillé » (e.g., j’ai/tu as/il a/nous avons travaillé toute la nuit). You can add a reason with « pour/afin de » + infinitive (e.g., afin de finir…).
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis fatigué : j’ai travaillé toute la nuit.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm tired: I worked all night.

additional_notes: Uses the verb « traverser » + a direct object (no preposition): « traverser la rivière », « traverser la rue ». Often used when talking about how to get to the other side (by a bridge, boat, etc.).
target_language_example: On peut traverser la rivière par le pont.
native_language_example: We can cross the river via the bridge.

traverser la rivière à la nage

target_language_multi_word_term: traverser la rivière à la nage
additional_notes: Used with "traverser" (to cross) + "la rivière" (the river) + "à la nage" (by swimming). You can swap in another place: "traverser le lac à la nage" (swim across the lake). Often used with ability/success verbs like "pouvoir" (can), "réussir à" (manage to), and "être en mesure de" (be able to).
target_language_example: On ne peut pas traverser la rivière à la nage aujourd'hui : le courant est trop fort.
native_language_example: We can’t swim across the river today: the current is too strong.

additional_notes: Used for going from one side of a street/road to the other. Very common in everyday instructions and safety contexts (e.g., at a crosswalk: « Pour traverser la rue, appuyez sur ce bouton. »). « Traverser » can also be used with other places: traverser la ville (cross the city), traverser le pont (cross the bridge).
target_language_example: Avant de traverser la rue, regarde à gauche et à droite.
native_language_example: Before crossing the street, look left and right.

additional_notes: Past form of **traverser la rue** (“to cross the street”), usually used with **avoir**: *j’ai traversé la rue*, *ils ont traversé la rue*. It means going from one side of the street to the other.
target_language_example: J’ai traversé la rue pour aller à la boulangerie.
native_language_example: I crossed the street to go to the bakery.

additional_notes: Common plural noun phrase for earthquakes (though the singular exists: « un tremblement de terre »). Often used with quantities and frequency: « beaucoup de / de nombreux tremblements de terre », « la fréquence des tremblements de terre ».
target_language_example: Après les tremblements de terre, plusieurs routes étaient fermées.
native_language_example: After the earthquakes, several roads were closed.

additional_notes: Used either to express a duration of 30 years (pendant trente ans = for thirty years) or an age (avoir trente ans / un homme de trente ans = to be thirty / a thirty-year-old man).
target_language_example: Elle a trente ans, et elle habite à Paris depuis trente ans.
native_language_example: She is thirty years old, and she has lived in Paris for thirty years.

additional_notes: Used to state a duration (pendant trente minutes = for thirty minutes) or a delay/offset (en retard de trente minutes = thirty minutes late).
target_language_example: Je reviens dans trente minutes.
native_language_example: I'll be back in thirty minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (depuis trois ans = for three years), a time interval (Trois ans se sont écoulés = Three years have passed), or someone’s age (quand elle avait trois ans = when she was three). Often appears in time expressions like « Ça fait trois ans que… » (“It’s been three years since…” / “For three years now…”).
target_language_example: J’habite ici depuis trois ans.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for three years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the length of time someone spent incarcerated, often with verbs like « passer » (to spend) or « faire » (to serve): « Il a passé/fait trois ans en prison. » You can swap « trois » for other numbers (deux, cinq, etc.) and « ans » for other time units (mois, semaines).
target_language_example: Il a fait trois ans en prison pour fraude.
native_language_example: He served three years in prison for fraud.

additional_notes: Used to state an amount of money. In French, you usually pronounce the final -s in "trois" before a consonant ("trois cents..."). "Cent" takes an -s ("cents") when it’s multiplied and not followed by another number (300 = "trois cents"), but it loses the -s if another number follows (301 = "trois cent un").
target_language_example: Ça fait trois cents dollars, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: That comes to three hundred dollars, please.

additional_notes: Used to state the number of children someone has. Often after verbs like "avoir" (to have): « J’ai trois enfants. » or in phrases like « père/mère de trois enfants » (father/mother of three children).
target_language_example: Elle a trois enfants et un chien.
native_language_example: She has three children and a dog.

additional_notes: Used with comparatives like "plus" or "moins" to express a multiple: "trois fois plus" = three times more, "trois fois moins" = three times less. It can refer to quantity ("trois fois plus de livres") or degree ("trois fois plus cher").
target_language_example: Cette voiture est trois fois plus chère que la mienne.
native_language_example: This car is three times more expensive than mine.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how often something happens daily (a frequency), especially for routines or instructions (e.g., meals, medicine). You can swap the number: une/deux/quatre fois par jour = once/twice/four times a day.
target_language_example: Je dois prendre ce comprimé trois fois par jour.
native_language_example: I have to take this pill three times a day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency. You can swap out the number: « une fois / deux fois / quatre fois… par semaine ». Similar patterns: « par jour » (per day), « par mois » (per month).
target_language_example: Je fais du sport trois fois par semaine.
native_language_example: I work out three times a week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (how long something takes: «Ça a pris trois heures»), frequency/amount of time («trois heures par semaine»), time ago («il y a trois heures»), or a time difference early/late («trois heures en avance / trop tôt»). After a number, «heure» is plural: «trois heures».
target_language_example: On a attendu trois heures avant de partir.
native_language_example: We waited three hours before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to state a duration (pendant/durant trois jours = for three days) or a point in time relative to something else (trois jours après = three days after). It can also be said alone as a short answer (“Trois jours.” = “Three days.”).
target_language_example: Je reste à Paris pendant trois jours.
native_language_example: I'm staying in Paris for three days.

additional_notes:
Used to talk about a duration or a point in time.
- With **depuis trois mois**: “for three months” (something started three months ago and is still true now).
- With **dans trois mois**: “in three months” (three months from now).
- With **en trois mois**: “in three months” meaning “within three months” (time needed to do something).
Also appears with verbs like **s’écouler** (“to pass”): *Trois mois se sont écoulés.*
target_language_example: J'apprends le français depuis trois mois.
native_language_example: I've been learning French for three months.

additional_notes: A time duration or a point in time relative to now. Common patterns: "pendant/durant trois semaines" = for three weeks; "depuis trois semaines" = for the past three weeks (still continuing); "il y a trois semaines" = three weeks ago; "Ça fait trois semaines" = it’s been three weeks.
target_language_example: Je serai en vacances pendant trois semaines.
native_language_example: I’ll be on vacation for three weeks.

additional_notes: Used with the verb « prendre » to mean “to take (something) too seriously.” Very common with the reflexive form « se prendre trop au sérieux » = “to take yourself/oneself too seriously.” It can also refer to taking situations, jokes, rules, etc. too seriously: « prendre tout trop au sérieux ».
target_language_example: Ne te prends pas trop au sérieux !
native_language_example: Don’t take yourself too seriously!

additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t have enough energy to do the action that follows. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: « trop fatigué(e) pour + infinitif ». Agree « fatigué » with the person: fatigué (masc.), fatiguée (fem.), fatigués/fatiguées (plural).
target_language_example: Je suis trop fatiguée pour sortir ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm too tired to go out tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say someone isn’t old/mature enough for an action. Pattern: "être trop jeune pour" + infinitive (e.g., "trop jeune pour sortir"). You can change the adjective for gender/number: "trop jeune" (m./f. singular), "trop jeunes" (plural). Often implies a rule (age limit) or judgment about readiness.
target_language_example: Il est trop jeune pour conduire.
native_language_example: He’s too young to drive.

meaning: too far; too much (gone too far).
additional_notes: Literally “too far.” Used both for physical distance (“Is it too far to walk?”) and figuratively to mean someone has exceeded acceptable limits (e.g., with words, behavior, or criticism): “Tu es allé trop loin.” Often used with forms of aller (aller trop loin = to go too far).
target_language_example: Désolé, je crois que je suis allé trop loin avec ma blague.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think I went too far with my joke.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has crossed a line (with words or actions) and it’s not acceptable. Often said in a reproachful tone: « Tu es allé(e) trop loin, cette fois. » (past tense of aller + trop loin).
target_language_example: Je plaisantais, mais là tu es allé trop loin, cette fois.
native_language_example: I was joking, but you went too far this time.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens after the right/expected time (often implying it’s missed or no longer possible). Can refer to being late for an event (“arriver trop tard”) or doing something very late at night (“trop tard la nuit”). Often used with "c'est" to reassure: « Ce n'est pas trop tard » = “It’s not too late.”
target_language_example: Dépêche-toi, sinon il sera trop tard !
native_language_example: Hurry up, otherwise it’ll be too late!

additional_notes: Used to say something happens earlier than it should. It often follows the verb ("arriver trop tôt") and can be strengthened with a time amount: "trois heures trop tôt" = "three hours too early". It can also be said on its own as a response or comment: "Trop tôt."
target_language_example: On est partis trop tôt, alors on a attendu dehors.
native_language_example: We left too early, so we waited outside.

meaning: too old to (do something); too old for (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not the right age for an activity or situation. Pattern: « être trop vieux/vieille pour + infinitive » (too old to do) or « être trop vieux/vieille pour + noun/pronoun » (too old for that/for me). Negative/contrast is common: « On n’est jamais trop vieux pour apprendre » (“You’re never too old to learn”). Switch to feminine with a woman: « trop vieille pour ».
target_language_example: Je suis trop vieux pour rester debout toute la journée.
native_language_example: I'm too old to stand all day.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens faster than is appropriate, safe, or desired. Common with verbs like conduire (to drive), parler (to speak), or passer (to pass/go by, for time). It can also be used alone as a short comment or warning: « Trop vite ! ».
target_language_example: Tu marches trop vite pour moi.
native_language_example: You’re walking too fast for me.

additional_notes: A medical/psychological diagnosis, often shortened to « TSPT » in French (equivalent to English “PTSD”). Commonly used with verbs like « souffrir de » (to suffer from) or « avoir » (to have): « Je souffre d’un trouble de stress post-traumatique / Je souffre de trouble de stress post-traumatique / J’ai un trouble de stress post-traumatique ».
target_language_example: Après l’accident, on lui a diagnostiqué un trouble de stress post-traumatique.
native_language_example: After the accident, he was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder.

meaning: to find something; to come up with something (a solution/idea).
additional_notes: Used for physically finding an object (e.g., “find something in a bag”) and very often for finding/choosing something suitable (“find you something to do”) or for coming up with an idea or solution (“we’ll find something”). It’s common with an infinitive: “trouver quelque chose à + verb” (to find something to do).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, on va trouver quelque chose.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we’ll figure something out.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: « trouver un travail » (find a job), « trouver un moyen » (find a way). With a reflexive pronoun (« se trouver un… » / « te trouver un… »), it often means “to get yourself a…” or “to find yourself a…”, as in « Tu devrais te trouver un passe-temps. »
target_language_example: Je dois trouver un appartement rapidement.
native_language_example: I need to find an apartment quickly.

additional_notes: Used when talking about solving a problem by identifying an answer or approach. Very common in everyday speech and in formal contexts (work, school). Often followed by “à” for what you’re solving: “trouver une solution à ce problème.”
target_language_example: On va trouver une solution à ce problème ensemble.
native_language_example: We’re going to find a solution to this problem together.

meaning: "do you find…?" / "what do you think…?" (asking for an opinion).
additional_notes: This is the verb "trouver" (to find/think) with subject–verb inversion used in questions: "Tu trouves…" → "Trouves-tu…?" It’s very common for asking how someone feels about something: "Comment trouves-tu Kyoto ?" = "What do you think of Kyoto?" You can also use it with adjectives: "Trouves-tu ce travail trop dur ?" = "Do you find this job too hard?"
target_language_example: Trouves-tu ce film intéressant ?
native_language_example: Do you find this movie interesting?

meaning: "do you find…?" / "what do you think of…?"
additional_notes: This is the verb *trouver* (to find) with **inversion** for questions: *vous trouvez* → *trouvez-vous ?* It’s used both for literally finding something (*Trouvez-vous une place ?* = “Are you finding a seat/spot?”) and very often for giving an opinion: *Comment le/la trouvez-vous ?* = “How do you find him/her/it?” = “What do you think of him/her/it?” (Note the object pronoun can be *le/la/les*.)
target_language_example: Comment trouvez-vous ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: What do you think of this restaurant?

additional_notes: Past participle of *trouver* (“to find”) used with *avoir*: *j’ai trouvé quelque chose* = “I found something / I’ve found something.” In questions, it often means “Did you find anything?”: *T’as trouvé quelque chose ?* You may also hear the shortened question *Trouvé quelque chose ?* (missing *tu as*), which is informal.
target_language_example: J’ai trouvé quelque chose qui pourrait nous aider.
native_language_example: I found something that could help us.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir in the passé composé: « j’ai / tu as / il a / on a trouvé un… » = “I/you/he/we found a…”. « un » is the masculine singular article and can change to « une » (feminine) or « des » (plural) depending on the noun: « trouvé une solution », « trouvé des clés ».
target_language_example: J’ai trouvé un bon restaurant près d’ici.
native_language_example: I found a good restaurant near here.

additional_notes: Used to compliment a person, object, artwork, name, or place (“C’est très beau !”), and also to describe nice weather with faire (“Il fait très beau” = “The weather is really nice/beautiful”). It agrees in gender and number: très belle (f.), très beaux (m. pl.), très belles (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Ta robe est très belle !
native_language_example: Your dress is very beautiful!

additional_notes: Used to describe a feminine noun (une ville, une femme) as “very beautiful.” It’s très (very) + belle (beautiful, feminine singular). For a masculine noun/person, use “très beau” (un très beau bâtiment). You can intensify it further with “vraiment”: “vraiment très belle.”
target_language_example: Cette robe est très belle.
native_language_example: This dress is very beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to say something is of high quality, enjoyable, or that someone is very skilled. It agrees with the noun/person described: très bonne (feminine), très bons / très bonnes (plural). With senses: Ça a très bon goût = “It tastes really good”; Ça sent très bon = “It smells really good.”
target_language_example: Ton idée est très bonne.
native_language_example: Your idea is very good.

additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s work: « Tu as fait un très bon travail. » It can also describe a job/position someone has: « Tom a un très bon travail. » By itself (« Très bon travail. »), it’s a short compliment meaning “Great job.”
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide : tu as fait un très bon travail !
native_language_example: Thanks for your help: you did a great job!

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun (e.g., une très bonne idée) or after the verb être to describe a feminine person/thing (e.g., Elle est très bonne en maths). For masculine nouns/people, use très bon; for plural, très bons / très bonnes.
target_language_example: C'est une très bonne question.
native_language_example: That’s a very good question.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is hard (a task, language, exam, situation). It agrees in gender/number with the noun: très difficile (m./f. singular), très difficiles (plural).
target_language_example: Cet exercice est très difficile, mais je vais essayer.
native_language_example: This exercise is very difficult, but I’m going to try.

additional_notes: Used with a person or thing you feel proud about: « être très fier/fière de + noun/pronoun ». Agree the adjective with the subject: fier (masc.), fière (fem.). Common with pronouns: « fier de lui/d’elle » (proud of him/her), « fier de toi/de vous » (proud of you), « fier de moi » (proud of me).
target_language_example: Je suis très fier de toi !
native_language_example: I'm very proud of you!

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s behavior or attitude. Often said as a complete sentence: « Très gentil. » You can also use it in the polite phrase « C’est/C’était très gentil de votre part » (“That’s/That was very kind of you”). Note agreement: gentil (masc.), gentille (fem.); in plural: gentils / gentilles.
target_language_example: Merci pour votre aide, c’est très gentil de votre part.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help, that’s very kind of you.

additional_notes:
Used to express a strong level of happiness. 
- Agreement: heureux (masc. singular), heureuse (fem. singular), heureux (masc. plural), heureuses (fem. plural).
- Common with être: Il/Elle est très heureux/heureuse.
- Can also be used in polite wishes/commands: Soyez très heureux.
target_language_example: Je suis très heureux de te voir.
native_language_example: I’m very happy to see you.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something matters a lot. It can describe a thing (un dossier très important), an idea (c'est très important), or what you’re about to say (quelque chose de très important). Word order: très comes right before the adjective important.
target_language_example: C'est très important de lire les instructions.
native_language_example: It's very important to read the instructions.

additional_notes: Used to strongly express that something is interesting. It agrees in gender and number with the noun: très intéressant (masc. sing.), très intéressante (fem. sing.), très intéressants / très intéressantes (plural). Often used to react to information or describe a topic.
target_language_example: Ton projet a l'air très intéressant !
native_language_example: Your project looks very interesting!

additional_notes: Used to describe a feminine noun (or a woman/girl) as “very pretty.” Because "jolie" is feminine, the masculine form is "très joli" (e.g., "un très joli appartement"). Often placed before the noun in compliments ("Très jolie robe !") or after "être" ("Elle est très jolie").
target_language_example: Cette photo est très jolie.
native_language_example: This photo is very pretty.

additional_notes: Used to describe that someone has little free time. It agrees with the person described: très occupé (masc. sing.), très occupée (fem. sing.), très occupés (masc. pl.), très occupées (fem. pl.). Often used politely as a guess about someone’s schedule (e.g., Vous devez être très occupé).
target_language_example: Désolé, je suis très occupé cette semaine.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m very busy this week.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say there is a small quantity/number. With countable nouns it means “very few” (très peu de gratte-ciel). With uncountable nouns it means “very little” (très peu de temps). Often used with “choses” (“very little/few things”) and with “sur” or “de” to mean you don’t know much about someone/something (très peu de choses sur lui / de lui).
target_language_example: J’ai très peu de temps aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I have very little time today.

additional_notes: An adverb phrase used to describe how an action is done (how fast). It commonly follows the verb: « marcher/parler/courir très vite ». You can also use it with « aller »: « On va très vite. »
target_language_example: Tu écris très vite !
native_language_example: You write very fast!

additional_notes: "Tu" is the informal singular “you” (used with friends, family, kids). "Aimes" is from "aimer" (“to like/love”). With a question mark or rising intonation, it becomes a question: "Tu aimes… ?" = “Do you like…?” You can also use it to check/confirm: "Tu aimes ça, non ?" = “You like that, right?”
target_language_example: Tu aimes ce film ?
native_language_example: Do you like this movie?

additional_notes: Used to ask a friend or someone you address with tu if they like something masculine singular with le (e.g., le jazz, le bowling). For feminine nouns, use tu aimes la…; for plural, tu aimes les…; if the noun starts with a vowel or silent h, use tu aimes l’… (e.g., l’ananas).
target_language_example: Tu aimes le fromage ?
native_language_example: Do you like cheese?

meaning: “do you like the…?” / “you like the…” (talking about things in general).
additional_notes: Used with "les" + plural noun to talk about things in general (surprises, fruits, etc.). It can be a statement (Tu aimes les fruits.) or a question (Tu aimes les sushis ?).
target_language_example: Tu aimes les jeux vidéo ?
native_language_example: Do you like video games?

additional_notes: Used to show possession (Tu as une voiture. = You have a car.) and very commonly as the auxiliary in the passé composé: tu as + past participle (Tu as couru. = You ran / You have run). In casual speech it’s often pronounced/written “t’as”.
target_language_example: Tu as déjà mangé ?
native_language_example: Have you eaten already?

additional_notes: Passé composé of acheter (to buy). Used to talk about a completed purchase in the past. It’s made of tu (you, informal singular) + as (have) + acheté (bought). Often followed by what was bought: « Tu as acheté le billet ? »
target_language_example: Tu as acheté du pain ce matin ?
native_language_example: Did you buy bread this morning?

meaning: you did (it) well; you really/indeed have (done) ...
additional_notes: "Bien" often adds emphasis or means "properly". With a past tense like "tu as bien fait", it commonly means "you did the right thing" / "good job". In questions ("Tu as bien dormi ?"), it usually means "Did you sleep well?" With other verbs ("tu as bien maigri"), it can mean "you've really" + verb (e.g., "you've lost a lot of weight").
target_language_example: Tu as bien fait de venir tout de suite.
native_language_example: You did the right thing by coming right away.

additional_notes: Past tense of "dire" (passé composé): "tu" + "as" + "dit". Used to report or remind someone of their words. Often followed by a clause with "que" ("Tu as dit que...") or by a direct quote ("Tu as dit non").
target_language_example: Tu as dit que tu viendrais demain.
native_language_example: You said you would come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report or remind someone of what they previously said. The verb tense is passé composé (tu as dit), followed by que to introduce the clause. In the reported clause, French often shifts the tense (e.g., tu as dit que tu avais faim = you said you were hungry).
target_language_example: Tu as dit que tu pouvais venir demain, non ?
native_language_example: You said you could come tomorrow, right?

additional_notes: Used to report or remind someone of what they previously said, introducing a clause about them. It uses the informal “tu” (you, singular), so it’s for friends, family, kids, etc. In more formal situations, use “vous avez dit que vous…”. Tense in the second part can change: e.g., “tu as dit que tu allais… / que tu avais… / que tu le ferais…”.
target_language_example: Tu as dit que tu viendrais ce soir.
native_language_example: You said you would come tonight.

tu as dit que tu voulais

target_language_multi_word_term: tu as dit que tu voulais
additional_notes: Used to remind someone of what they previously said they wanted. "Tu as dit" is in the passé composé (you said), and "que" introduces the reported clause. After "tu as dit que…", French often uses the imperfect ("tu voulais") to report what someone wanted at that time (sequence of tenses). You can follow it with a noun or an infinitive: "tu as dit que tu voulais une voiture" / "tu as dit que tu voulais partir".
target_language_example: Tu as dit que tu voulais changer de travail.
native_language_example: You said you wanted to change jobs.

meaning: "you have already" / "have you already…?" (and often "have you ever…?" in questions).
additional_notes: Made of "tu as" (you have) + "déjà" (already). Very common in spoken questions: "Tu as déjà fini ?" = "Are you done already?" When used with an action in the past (often with a past participle: "tu as déjà + fini/trouvé/visité…"), it can also mean "have you ever…?" depending on context: "Tu as déjà visité Paris ?" = "Have you ever visited Paris?"
target_language_example: Tu as déjà mangé des escargots ?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten snails?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has seen something before at any time up to now. Built with the past tense (tu as vu = “you saw/you have seen”) plus déjà (“already/ever” in questions). In more formal speech, use “vous avez déjà vu… ?”.
target_language_example: Tu as déjà vu un film aussi long ?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a movie that long?

meaning: you must have / you probably had to (past inference or obligation).
additional_notes: Formed with **avoir** in the present + **dû** (past participle of *devoir*) + an infinitive: **tu as dû + infinitif**. It often expresses a logical conclusion about the past (**You must have... / You probably...**) rather than a certain fact. It can also mean past necessity (**you had to...**) depending on context. For feminine/masculine plural objects with *avoir*, *dû* usually stays **dû** (no agreement) because it’s followed by an infinitive.
target_language_example: Avec tout ce travail, tu as dû finir très tard.
native_language_example: With all that work, you must have finished very late.

additional_notes: Passé composé of *entendre* (to hear): **tu as entendu** = “you heard” or, in context, “have you heard?”. Often followed by **ce que + clause** (“what…”) or used alone to confirm someone heard: **Tu as entendu.** = “You heard (it).” Common pattern: **tu as entendu dire (que…)** = “you heard (people) say / you heard about (that…).” Note: *entendre* can sometimes mean “to understand” (e.g., **Tu entends ?**), but **tu as entendu** usually focuses on hearing.
target_language_example: Tu as entendu ce qu’ils ont dit ?
native_language_example: Did you hear what they said?

meaning: 'you had' / 'you got' / 'you have had' (past: you experienced/received).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of avoir (tu as + eu). It’s used to talk about something that happened in the past: having something (tu as eu une voiture), experiencing something (tu as eu un accident / des difficultés), or receiving news (Tu as eu de ses nouvelles ? = Did you hear from them?). Often translated as “you had” or “you got,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu as eu le temps de manger ?
native_language_example: Did you have time to eat?

tu as eu de la chance

target_language_multi_word_term: tu as eu de la chance
meaning: you were lucky / you got lucky.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone that something good happened to them (often by chance). Past tense of « avoir de la chance » (“to be lucky”). You can add « de + infinitive » to say what they were lucky to do: « Tu as eu de la chance de le voir ! »
target_language_example: Tu as eu de la chance de trouver un taxi si vite.
native_language_example: You were lucky to find a taxi so quickly.

meaning: "you did" / "you have done" (past tense of faire).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of faire with tu: tu (you) + as (have) + fait (done/made). It’s used to talk about something you did in the past, often with an object (tu as fait ton travail = you did your work). It can also appear in questions: Tu as fait bon voyage ? (Did you have a good trip?).
target_language_example: Tu as fait quoi hier soir ?
native_language_example: What did you do last night?

tu as fait ce que tu

target_language_multi_word_term: tu as fait ce que tu
meaning: "you did what you..." (often followed by *devais* = "had to/should" or *pouvais* = "could").
additional_notes: This is the start of a common reassuring/approving phrase: *Tu as fait ce que tu devais (faire)* (“You did what you had to / what you should have done”) or *Tu as fait ce que tu pouvais* (“You did what you could”). It uses *ce que* (“what/that which”) + *tu* and is typically followed by a verb in the imperfect (*devais, pouvais*) to describe what was expected or possible in that situation.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : tu as fait ce que tu pouvais.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you did what you could.

meaning: 'you did' / 'you have done' (used before a noun or activity).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of *faire* with **tu** (you, informal singular): **tu as fait** + **du** (= *de + le*, often like “some”). It’s used with a following noun/activity: **faire du sport** = “to do sport/exercise,” **faire du beau travail / du bon boulot** = “to do good work,” **faire du mieux (que tu as pu)** = “to do your best (that you could).”
target_language_example: Tu as fait du bon travail aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You did good work today.

additional_notes: Addressed to one person (tu). Uses the past tense (passé composé) of faire: tu + as + fait. Often used in questions to ask for the reason or method: Pourquoi tu as fait ça ? (Why did you do that?) / Comment tu as fait ça ? (How did you do that?) / Tu as fait ça pour moi ? (Did you do that for me?).
target_language_example: Je n'arrive pas à croire que tu as fait ça.
native_language_example: I can't believe you did that.

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of **laisser** (“to leave; to let”), used with **tu** (“you” informal singular). It’s often followed by an infinitive: **tu as laissé + verb** = “you let + verb” (e.g., **tu as laissé passer ta chance** = “you let your chance pass / you missed your chance”).
target_language_example: Tu as laissé la porte ouverte.
native_language_example: You left the door open.

additional_notes: "Tu as lu" is the passé composé of "lire" with "tu" (informal singular "you"). It can be a statement ("Tu as lu mon livre." = you read my book) or a question ("Tu as lu les règles ?" = have you read the rules?). It’s also used figuratively in "Tu as lu dans mes pensées" meaning "You read my mind."
target_language_example: Tu as lu ce message ?
native_language_example: Did you read this message?

additional_notes: This is the passé composé of *mettre* with **tu**: *tu as mis* + something. It’s used for putting/placing something (*Tu as mis la clé sur la table*), putting on clothing (*Tu as mis ton manteau ?*), applying something (*Tu as mis de la crème solaire ?*), and sometimes for time: *Tu as mis le temps* = “You took a long time.”
target_language_example: Tu as mis ton pull ?
native_language_example: Did you put on your sweater?

additional_notes: Informal singular ("tu") form of the passé composé of *oublier* (to forget): *tu as oublié* + a thing (*tu as oublié ton manteau*) or + *de* + verb (*tu as oublié de verrouiller la porte*). It can be a neutral statement or a reproach depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Tu as oublié de m’appeler ce matin.
native_language_example: You forgot to call me this morning.

meaning: "did you talk to" / "have you spoken to" (someone).
additional_notes: Used to ask if the person you’re speaking to has talked to someone else. It’s the past tense of "parler à" (to talk to) with "tu" (you, informal singular). The person you spoke to comes after "à": "Tu as parlé à Tania ?". Can also mean "Did you tell (someone)?" depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu as parlé à Marc de la réunion ?
native_language_example: Did you talk to Marc about the meeting?

additional_notes: "Tu as perdu" is the passé composé of perdre (to lose). Use it for losing a game/battle (Tu as perdu !), losing something abstract (du temps = time; espoir = hope; la mémoire = memory), or for having misplaced an object (Tu as perdu ton sac ?). In questions, it often means "Have you lost…?".
target_language_example: Tu as perdu tes clés ?
native_language_example: Did you lose your keys?

meaning: “you took” / “did you take?” (past tense of prendre).
additional_notes: Used with many everyday meanings of prendre in the passé composé: taking/grabbing something (Tu as pris tes clés ?), taking photos (Tu as pris ces photos ?), having/eating/drinking something (Tu as pris ton petit déj ?), and in some fixed expressions like prendre son pied (“to have a great time,” informal). Often used in questions like “Tu as pris… ?” = “Did you take/have…?”
target_language_example: Tu as pris mon stylo par erreur ?
native_language_example: Did you take my pen by mistake?

additional_notes: Used with the passé composé (tu as + past participle) to say someone has always done something up to now, or that something has consistently been true in the past. In English it often translates as “you’ve always…” or sometimes “you always…” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu as toujours dit la vérité.
native_language_example: You’ve always told the truth.

meaning: you have always been (you’ve always been).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s consistent state/quality over time. Often followed by an adjective or noun ("tu as toujours été un rêveur"), or by "là" / "à mes côtés" to emphasize someone was always there for you. This is the "passé composé" of "être" with "toujours".
target_language_example: Tu as toujours été gentil avec moi.
native_language_example: You have always been kind to me.

meaning: "you have everything" / "you did everything" (with a past participle).
additional_notes: Used with the verb avoir. By itself, it can mean “you have everything.” Very often it’s followed by a past participle (passé composé), where tout means “everything” as the object: tu as tout trouvé = “you found everything,” tu as tout oublié = “you forgot everything,” etc.
target_language_example: Tu as tout compris.
native_language_example: You understood everything.

additional_notes: Uses the passé composé of *trouver* (“to find”) with **tu** (informal “you” to one person). It’s common in questions: **Tu as trouvé la sortie ?** (“Did you find the exit?”). With **où**, it means “Where did you find it?”: **Tu as trouvé ça où ?**. If addressing someone formally or more than one person, use **vous avez trouvé**.
target_language_example: Tu as trouvé ce que tu cherchais ?
native_language_example: Did you find what you were looking for?

additional_notes: Passé composé of *tuer* (to kill): **tu** (you, informal singular) + **as** (have) + **tué** (killed). Used to state a completed action in the past; in English it’s often translated as simple past ("you killed"). It normally takes a direct object: *Tu as tué mon père.*
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu as tué cet homme ?
native_language_example: Why did you kill that man?

meaning: "did you see" / "have you seen" (sometimes: "you know/you saw, right?")
additional_notes: Literally "you have seen" (passé composé of voir). Used to ask what someone saw/has seen: « Tu as vu X ? ». It can also introduce a remark to point something out or check agreement, like "Did you see how…?" / "You saw that…, right?".
target_language_example: Tu as vu comme il fait froid aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Did you see how cold it is today?

additional_notes: Literally “you have seen the…”. It’s the passé composé of voir (to see) with tu. Often used as a question in speech (“Tu as vu le… ?”) or as an exclamation to point something out (“Tu as vu le… !”). You’ll usually follow it with a noun: tu as vu le vélo ?, tu as vu le client ?, etc.
target_language_example: Tu as vu le nouveau film ?
native_language_example: Did you see the new movie?

meaning: “you were / you have been” (past of “to be,” addressed to one person informally).
additional_notes: Past tense of être with tu (informal singular “you”) in the passé composé. Used for states/qualities (Tu as été super / courageuse), roles (Tu as été mon ami), and in the passive voice with a past participle (Tu as été embauchée = “You were hired”; Tu as été retiré = “You were removed”; Tu as été suivi ? = “Were you followed?”). Agree the following adjective/participle for gender/number (e.g., courageuse, embauchée).
target_language_example: Tu as été très patient pendant l’attente.
native_language_example: You were very patient during the wait.

additional_notes: Used to show possession (Tu as une voiture. = You have a car.) and very commonly as the auxiliary in the passé composé: tu as + past participle (Tu as couru. = You ran / You have run). In casual speech it’s often pronounced/written “t’as”.
target_language_example: Tu as déjà mangé ?
native_language_example: Have you eaten already?

additional_notes: Used to say someone needs something. Most often followed by **de + noun/infinitive**: *Tu as besoin de + nom* (“You need a …”), *Tu as besoin de + verbe* (“You need to …”).
target_language_example: Tu as besoin de repos.
native_language_example: You need rest.

additional_notes: Literally “you have need of.” Used to say someone needs something, or to ask if they need something. The thing you need can be a noun (Tu as besoin de gants.) or an infinitive verb (Tu as besoin de parler…). In questions, intonation often makes it a yes/no question.
target_language_example: Tu as besoin de dormir un peu.
native_language_example: You need to sleep a little.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone needs your help, presence, or support. Often appears in questions ("Est-ce que tu as besoin de moi ?" = "Do you need me?") or with an added place/time ("ici" = "here"). "avoir besoin de" is the common way to say "to need" in French.
target_language_example: Si tu as besoin de moi, je suis là.
native_language_example: If you need me, I’m here.

meaning: “you have …” (used in the pattern **tu as de + adjective + plural noun**).
additional_notes: In compliments, French often uses **de** (instead of **des**) before an adjective + plural noun: **Tu as de beaux yeux.** = “You have beautiful eyes.” This is the same grammar as **des beaux yeux** → **de beaux yeux**. With **si/tellement** (“so”), it’s still **de**: **Tu as de si beaux yeux.**
target_language_example: Tu as de très beaux cheveux.
native_language_example: You have very beautiful hair.

meaning: “you have some …” (used before a feminine singular, uncountable noun).
additional_notes: This is **tu as** (“you have”) + the **partitive article** **de la** (“some”). It’s used for things you can’t normally count as individual units (e.g., *de la fièvre* “a fever/some fever”, *de la monnaie* “some change”, *de la crasse* “some dirt”). With nouns starting with a vowel or silent h, it becomes **de l’** (*tu as de l’argent ?*). With masculine uncountable nouns: **du** (*tu as du temps*). With plural nouns: **des** (*tu as des amis*). In *Tu as de la visite*, it means “You have visitors / You have company.”
target_language_example: Tu as de la monnaie pour le parking ?
native_language_example: Do you have some change for the parking meter?

additional_notes: Literally “you have (some) luck.” Used to tell someone they’re fortunate, often followed by **de + infinitive** to say why: *Tu as de la chance de…* (“You’re lucky to…”). Can be sincere or teasing depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Tu as de la chance d’avoir des amis comme ça.
native_language_example: You’re lucky to have friends like that.

meaning: 'do you have any…?' / 'have you got any…?' (informal 'you' singular).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has some things (plural) in a casual conversation. It’s the question form of "tu as" (= "you have") + "des" (= "some" for plural nouns). With uncountable nouns, French often uses "du / de la" instead of "des" (e.g., "Tu as du temps ?").
target_language_example: Tu as des questions ?
native_language_example: Do you have any questions?

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say someone has some amount of something. **Du** is the partitive article (**de + le**), often meaning “some” (often not translated in English). Common with abstract nouns (Tu as du potentiel ! = “You have potential!”) and with set expressions like **avoir du retard** (“to be late / to be behind schedule”). It can also describe something on you: Tu as du rouge-à-lèvres sur la joue. (“You have lipstick on your cheek.”).
target_language_example: Tu as du café sur ton t-shirt.
native_language_example: You’ve got coffee on your T-shirt.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *avoir* to say someone still has something (time, a chance, a need) or still feels something: *Tu as encore sommeil ?* = “Are you still sleepy?” It can also introduce encouragement: *Tu as encore toute la vie devant toi !* = “You still have your whole life ahead of you!” Note: *encore* can also mean “again” in other contexts, but with *tu as...* it often means “still.”
target_language_example: Tu as encore besoin de moi ?
native_language_example: Do you still need me?

meaning: you feel like (doing); you want to (do).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a desire or urge, often in the moment (what you feel like doing). It can be a question (Tu as envie de… ? = Do you feel like…?) or a statement. Followed by an infinitive: tu as envie de + verb (tu as envie de sortir). With a noun, use "tu as envie de + noun" (tu as envie de pizza) or "tu as envie de quoi ?" (what do you feel like?).
target_language_example: Tu as envie de sortir ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you feel like going out tonight?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **avoir l’air** (“to seem/appear”). It’s most often followed by an adjective: **Tu as l’air fatigué(e)** (“You look tired”). You can also use **avoir l’air de + infinitive**: **Tu as l’air de comprendre** (“You seem to understand”). Agreement: add **-e** if talking to a woman (**Tu as l’air fatiguée**).
target_language_example: Tu as l’air un peu stressé aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You look a little stressed today.

meaning: “you have the …” (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **tu as** (“you have”) + **le** (“the”, for a masculine singular noun). It’s often followed by a noun or set expression: **tu as le mal de mer** (“you’re seasick / you have seasickness”), **tu as le cœur dur** (“you have a hard heart / you’re hard-hearted”), **tu as le jeu en main** (“you have the upper hand / you’re in control”). For feminine nouns, you’d use **tu as la…**; for plural, **tu as les…**.
target_language_example: Tu as le temps ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you have time tonight?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "avoir" (to have) + "peur" (fear): "avoir peur" = to be afraid. Common patterns: "Tu as peur de + noun" (Tu as peur des chiens.) and "Tu as peur que + clause" (Tu as peur qu’il pleuve ?). Often said as a question: "Tu as peur ?"
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu as peur de rentrer seul ?
native_language_example: Why are you scared to go home alone?

additional_notes: Literally “you have something.” Very common in questions to suggest something is on someone’s mind or that they’re involved: « Tu as quelque chose en tête ? » (Do you have something in mind?), « Tu as quelque chose à voir là-dedans ? » (Do you have anything to do with it?). It can also point out something physically on someone: « Tu as quelque chose dans le cou. »
target_language_example: Tu as quelque chose sur le visage.
native_language_example: You have something on your face.

meaning: 'do you have something to…?' / 'do you have anything to…?'
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to ask if someone has anything to add, say, ask, do, etc.: « Tu as quelque chose à ajouter ? » = “Anything to add?” It can also introduce a more specific idea like « à protéger » (“to protect”) or be followed by a longer expression (e.g., « à voir avec… » / « à faire avec… » = “to do with…”).
target_language_example: Tu as quelque chose à déclarer ?
native_language_example: Do you have anything to declare?

additional_notes: Used to agree with someone or confirm that what they said is correct. It literally means “you have reason,” but in everyday French it’s the standard way to say “you’re right.” You can use it on its own or at the start of a sentence (e.g., “Tu as raison, mais…”).
target_language_example: Tu as raison, ce n’est pas une bonne idée.
native_language_example: You’re right, it’s not a good idea.

additional_notes: Used with “tu” (you, informal singular) + “as” (have) + “un” (a, masculine singular). It’s followed by a masculine noun (“un client”) or can be used before an adjective + noun (“un si grand potentiel”). For feminine nouns, use “tu as une …”. For formal/plural “you,” use “vous avez un/une …”.
target_language_example: Tu as un rendez-vous demain.
native_language_example: You have an appointment tomorrow.

meaning: "you have a" (talking to one person; before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir" (to have) in the present tense: "tu as" = "you have" (informal singular "you"). "Une" is the feminine form of "a/an" and goes before a feminine noun (e.g., "une mère", "une idée"). For a masculine noun, use "tu as un".
target_language_example: Tu as une idée ?
native_language_example: Do you have an idea?

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to talk about what you would have done in another situation (often with regret, criticism, or advice after the fact). Very common in phrases like "Tu aurais dû..." / "Tu aurais mieux fait de..." meaning "You should have...".
target_language_example: Tu aurais pu me prévenir avant de partir.
native_language_example: You could have warned me before leaving.

meaning: “you should have” (you didn’t, and it would have been better).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional perfect of devoir ("aurais dû" + infinitive) to talk about a past action that was advisable but didn’t happen. It often expresses regret or mild reproach: “You should have refused,” “You should have been there.”
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû me prévenir plus tôt.
native_language_example: You should have told me earlier.

meaning: "you should have (to) me…" (you didn’t, and I regret it / I’m reproaching you).
additional_notes: This uses the past conditional of *devoir* (*aurais dû*) to talk about something that was the right thing to do in the past, but didn’t happen. It’s often used to express criticism or frustration: *Tu aurais dû me le dire plus tôt* (“You should have told me earlier”). It’s normally followed by an infinitive: *tu aurais dû me + dire / consulter / parler…*
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû me prévenir avant de partir.
native_language_example: You should have warned me before leaving.

meaning: "you should have seen…" (you missed it; often said for emphasis).
additional_notes: Uses the past conditional of devoir ("aurais dû") + infinitive to talk about something in the past that would have been good/important/impressive to see, but didn’t happen (or the listener wasn’t there). Very common to introduce an emphatic comment: "Tu aurais dû voir sa tête !" = "You should’ve seen his face!"
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû voir le monde qu’il y avait au concert !
native_language_example: You should have seen how many people were at the concert!

meaning: 'you could have' (you had the opportunity/ability, but didn’t).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional perfect: "tu" + "aurais" (avoir, conditional) + past participle (here "pu", from "pouvoir"). Often expresses regret, reproach, or a missed possibility: "Tu aurais pu m'appeler" = you could have called me (but you didn’t).
target_language_example: Tu aurais pu me prévenir plus tôt.
native_language_example: You could have warned me earlier.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone will have in the future, often after a condition or in instructions (e.g., “when/if you… you will have…”). It can also express necessity: “tu auras besoin de…” = “you will need…”. In the fixed pattern “tu auras beau + infinitive”, it means “you may try as much as you want / even if you…”, with the idea that it won’t change the outcome.
target_language_example: Si tu travailles bien, tu auras plus de temps libre.
native_language_example: If you work well, you’ll have more free time.

meaning: 'you had' / 'you used to have' (imparfait of avoir).
additional_notes: Used to describe a past state, habit, or ongoing situation (imparfait). Common patterns: *tu avais + noun* (you had), *tu avais + adjective* (you were/ felt: e.g., *tu avais chaud* = you were hot), and in conditional sentences with *si* to express an unreal/imagined situation (*si tu avais...*).
target_language_example: Quand tu avais dix ans, tu avais déjà une grande collection de livres.
native_language_example: When you were ten, you already had a big collection of books.

additional_notes: Literally 'you had reason.' Used to tell someone that their earlier opinion or prediction was correct. It's in the imperfect tense (avais), often referring to something you thought or said before; in the present you'd say 'tu as raison' ('you are right').
target_language_example: Tu avais raison : il pleut aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: You were right: it's raining today.

additional_notes: From the verb *chercher* (“to look for / to search for”) with *tu* (“you”, informal singular). It can be a simple statement (*Tu cherches un appartement.*) or a question (*Tu cherches qui ?*). In some contexts it can be confrontational and mean “are you looking for trouble?” (e.g., *Tu cherches des histoires ?* / *Tu cherches la merde ?*).
target_language_example: Tu cherches quelque chose en particulier ?
native_language_example: Are you looking for anything in particular?

additional_notes: Literally "you understand." Used either as a normal statement ("you understand") or as a check that the other person is following (often like "you know?" / "you see?"). In speech it can be said with rising intonation to mean a question: "Tu comprends ?" It can also appear in a tag question: "Tu comprends, n'est-ce pas ?"
target_language_example: On part à huit heures, tu comprends ?
native_language_example: We’re leaving at eight, you understand?

additional_notes: From the verb connaître (“to know/be familiar with” a person, place, thing, or a fact you’ve learned). Used to ask if someone knows someone/something (Tu connais Tom ?), check familiarity (Tu connais ce nom ?), or in a casual tone meaning “you know/you’ve seen this before” (Ça, tu connais ?). With information or an answer, it means you already know it (Tu connais déjà la réponse).
target_language_example: Tu connais ce restaurant ?
native_language_example: Do you know this restaurant?

additional_notes: From the verb *croire* (“to believe/think”). Often used to ask someone’s opinion or challenge what they’re saying: *Tu crois que… ?* (“Do you think that…?”). It can also sound skeptical or confrontational depending on tone/context, especially in *Tu crois… ?* or *À qui tu crois parler ?* (“Who do you think you’re talking to?”).
target_language_example: Tu crois qu'il va pleuvoir demain ?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s going to rain tomorrow?

additional_notes: Very common in spoken French to ask for someone’s opinion or guess. It’s the informal “tu” form; in formal situations you’d use “vous croyez que… ?”. The apostrophe (qu’) is used because the next word starts with a vowel sound (e.g., qu’il, qu’ils).
target_language_example: Tu crois qu’on a le temps avant le train ?
native_language_example: Do you think we have time before the train?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or expectation about what a man will do. Often introduces the subj./future/conditional in the rest of the sentence. In conversation it can also sound doubtful or incredulous, like “You really think he’ll…?”
target_language_example: Tu crois qu'il va accepter ?
native_language_example: Do you think he’s going to accept?

additional_notes: Used to ask (sometimes rhetorically) what the other person thinks or believes. "Tu crois" uses the informal "tu" (to one person you’re on first-name terms with). "On" often means "we" in everyday French, but it can also mean "someone/people" in general, depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu crois qu'on peut partir maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do you think we can leave now?

additional_notes: Literally “you believe/think that.” Used to ask for someone’s opinion or guess: « Tu crois que ça va marcher ? » (“Do you think it’ll work?”). Very often used as a rhetorical or challenging question in conversation: « Tu crois que je l’ai pas vu ? » (“You think I didn’t see it?”). Uses « tu », so it’s for informal situations (friends, peers, family).
target_language_example: Tu crois que je peux venir avec vous ?
native_language_example: Do you think I can come with you?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or to challenge what they think (often a bit skeptical or rhetorical). It uses the informal "tu" form; in more formal situations you’d use "Vous croyez que c’est…?". Very commonly followed by an adjective or noun: "…facile ?", "…grave ?", "…elle ?".
target_language_example: Tu crois que c’est une bonne idée ?
native_language_example: Do you think it's a good idea?

meaning: “Do you think I have…?” / “You think I…?” (often rhetorical).
additional_notes: Used to question or challenge what someone assumes about you, often with a tone of disbelief or annoyance. It’s commonly followed by a noun (“…le choix ?”), “besoin de…” (“…besoin de ça ?”), or an expression like “que ça à faire” (“nothing better to do”). In everyday speech, “croire” here often means “think,” not “believe” in a religious sense.
target_language_example: Tu crois que j'ai du temps à perdre ?
native_language_example: Do you think I have time to waste?

meaning: “Do you think I…?” / “You think I…?” (often rhetorical).
