additional_notes: Literally "you know" (from savoir). Often used informally with "tu". With an infinitive, "tu sais + verb" means "you know how to + verb" (ability). It can also be a filler like English "you know" to introduce or emphasize something.
target_language_example: Tu sais nager ?
native_language_example: Do you know how to swim?

meaning: "you can do" / "you know how to do".
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s ability or skill. Often followed by an infinitive: « Tu sais faire du vélo ? » (“Can you ride a bike?”). In « ce que tu sais faire », it means “what you can do” (your skills). Common in questions like « Tu sais faire quoi ? » / « Qu’est-ce que tu sais faire ? ».
target_language_example: Tu sais faire la cuisine ?
native_language_example: Can you cook?

meaning: 'you know what…' (introduces a question or something you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Used in informal speech with "tu" to ask about or introduce information: "Tu sais ce qu’il a dit ?" = "Do you know what he said?" The apostrophe (qu’) is used before a vowel sound: qu’il, qu’on, qu’était, etc. In more formal situations, you’d use "vous savez ce que…".
target_language_example: Tu sais ce qu’on fait ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you know what we're doing tonight?

meaning: "Do you know what he…?" / "You know what he…" (lead-in before a clause).
additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize information about what a man did/said/what will happen, often as a question: “Tu sais ce qu’il a fait ?” = “Do you know what he did?” It’s commonly followed by a verb phrase (a fait, a dit, va se passer, etc.). In speech, it can also be rhetorical, like “You know what he did?!”
target_language_example: Tu sais ce qu'il a dit au prof ?
native_language_example: Do you know what he said to the teacher?

meaning: "you know what…" (introduces what I'm about to say/ask).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to lead into a statement or a question, often to get the listener’s attention or to set up something (sometimes rhetorical): “Tu sais ce que je pense ?” / “Tu sais ce que je vais faire ?”. Can also be said with a pause: “Tu sais ce que…”.
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que je veux manger ce soir ?
native_language_example: You know what I want to eat tonight?

meaning: "do you know what it is?" / "do you know what it’s like?"
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone understands something (an experience, situation, or concept). Often rhetorical or challenging, like “You know what it’s like…?” You’ll also see: "Tu sais ce que c’est, X ?" and "Tu sais ce que c’est que X ?" (both mean “Do you know what X is?”).
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que c’est de travailler de nuit ?
native_language_example: Do you know what it’s like to work nights?

meaning: “You know what I’ve…?” / “Guess what I…?” (to introduce something you did/decided/realized, etc.).
additional_notes: Used as a lead-in to announce something (often with a bit of suspense or emphasis). It’s usually followed by a past participle because "j’ai" is the helper verb for the passé composé: "Tu sais ce que j’ai fait/décidé/découvert… ?" It can be a real question or a rhetorical way to get someone’s attention.
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que j’ai préparé pour ce soir ?
native_language_example: You know what I’ve prepared for tonight?

tu sais ce que j'ai fait

target_language_multi_word_term: tu sais ce que j'ai fait
meaning: "Do you know what I did?" / "You know what I did?"
additional_notes: Used to introduce a story or reveal something you did. Often said as a rhetorical question to build suspense or to emphasize a point (sometimes with a reproachful tone, e.g., reminding someone of what you did for them). In casual speech it’s common without inversion: "Tu sais…?"
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que j'ai fait hier soir ? J'ai appelé le restaurant pour réserver.
native_language_example: Do you know what I did last night? I called the restaurant to book a table.

meaning: "you know what I…" (often used to introduce a question or suggestion).
additional_notes: Common in spoken French to set up what you’re about to say: a question (Tu sais ce que je regarde ?), advice (Tu sais ce que je ferais à ta place ?), or what you should do (Tu sais ce que je devrais faire ?). It’s often rhetorical—more like “You know what?” than checking if the person really knows. You can also use the formal version: « vous savez ce que je… ».
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que je pense ? On devrait partir plus tôt.
native_language_example: You know what I think? We should leave earlier.

tu sais ce que je pense

target_language_multi_word_term: tu sais ce que je pense
additional_notes: A direct statement meaning the other person already knows your opinion. Often used to introduce or emphasize an opinion, and it can sound a bit confrontational depending on tone. You’ll often hear it followed by **de + [person/thing]** (“about”): *Tu sais ce que je pense de lui/d’elle/de ça.* It can also be used as a rhetorical question: *Tu sais ce que je pense ?*
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que je pense : ce n’est pas une bonne idée.
native_language_example: You know what I think: it’s not a good idea.

tu sais ce que je veux

target_language_multi_word_term: tu sais ce que je veux
additional_notes: Often used as a lead-in to emphasize a desire or to set up a question (sometimes rhetorical): "Tu sais ce que je veux ?" It can sound insistent or a bit confrontational depending on tone, like reminding someone they already know.
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que je veux : qu’on se parle franchement.
native_language_example: You know what I want: for us to speak honestly.

meaning: "Do you know what you…?" (often: "Do you realize what you…?")
additional_notes: Used with "tu" (informal ‘you’) to start a question about the other person’s actions/words/plans: "Tu sais ce que tu fais/dis/vas faire…?" Very often it’s rhetorical and expresses surprise, annoyance, or a warning (similar to “Do you realize what you just said/did?”).
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que tu viens de promettre ?
native_language_example: Do you realize what you just promised?

meaning: “Do you know what that…?” / “Do you realize what that…?”
additional_notes: Used in speech to introduce a question about the meaning, cost, effect, or consequences of something: « Tu sais ce que ça coûte / implique / représente / veut dire ? ». Often used rhetorically to emphasize a point (similar to “Do you realize…?”), not just to ask for information.
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que ça change si on part plus tôt ?
native_language_example: Do you know what it changes (what difference it makes) if we leave earlier?

additional_notes: Conversational lead-in before a question, suggestion, or remark, often rhetorical: "Tu sais ce qui est le plus... ?" It uses "tu" (informal); the formal version is "vous savez ce qui". Often followed by a verb: "tu sais ce qui m’énerve ?"
target_language_example: Tu sais ce qui serait génial ? On partirait plus tôt.
native_language_example: You know what would be great? We’d leave earlier.

meaning: "do you know how/what…?" or "you know what … is/are like."
additional_notes: Literally “you know how.” Used either (1) as a question asking for information (“Do you know how/what…?”), often followed by a full clause (e.g., *Tu sais comment il s’appelle ?*), or (2) to refer to shared experience: “You know what they’re like” (*Tu sais comment ils sont*). In the second use, *comment* is closer to “what … are like” than to “how.”
target_language_example: Tu sais comment on dit ça en français ?
native_language_example: Do you know how to say that in French?

meaning: “you know what (I mean / I’m talking about).”
additional_notes: Used in conversation to refer to something understood from context. It often introduces an explanation or a (sometimes slightly teasing) rhetorical question: “Tu sais de quoi j’ai envie ?” = “Guess what I feel like / You know what I’m craving?” You’ll also hear it continued with “je veux parler” (“I want to talk about”).
target_language_example: Tu sais de quoi je parle : de ce problème au travail.
native_language_example: You know what I’m talking about: that problem at work.

additional_notes: Used to ask or state whether someone knows the location of a person/thing, or where someone is going. Often followed by a clause (où + subject + verb): « Tu sais où il est ? » You can also use it on its own (« Tu sais où ? ») meaning “Do you know where?” in context. Informal alternative: « Tu sais où c’est ? » = “Do you know where it is?”
target_language_example: Tu sais où on peut se garer ?
native_language_example: Do you know where we can park?

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of something they already know, or to emphasize what you’re about to say. It’s very common in conversation and is followed by a full clause (subject + verb): “Tu sais que + …”.
target_language_example: Tu sais que j’ai cours demain matin.
native_language_example: You know that I have class tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of a fact about you, or to emphasize what you’re about to say. Very common in conversation; it can sound a bit insistent depending on tone. Often followed by a verb phrase (e.g., "tu sais que je cherche...", "tu sais que je dis...").
target_language_example: Tu sais que je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: You know that I can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: A direct, personal sentence using **tu** (informal “you”), said to a friend/partner/close family member. Often used to reassure someone, remind them of your feelings, or introduce emphasis (sometimes followed by **pas vrai ?** = “right?”).
target_language_example: Tu sais que je t'aime, même quand on se dispute.
native_language_example: You know I love you, even when we argue.

additional_notes: Used to say (or suspect) someone has information about a topic, often implying there may be a secret or important detail. Very common in questions with a topic marker: « Tu sais quelque chose sur… ? / à propos de… ? / là-dessus ? »
target_language_example: Tu sais quelque chose sur cette histoire ?
native_language_example: Do you know anything about this story?

meaning: "you know who" (referring to a person you both know, often without naming them).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to hint at someone without saying their name (for secrecy, suspense, or because it’s obvious). It can introduce an indirect question ("Tu sais qui j’ai vu ?" = "Do you know who I saw?") or be said alone to mean "you-know-who."
target_language_example: Je l’ai croisé hier… tu sais qui.
native_language_example: I ran into him yesterday… you-know-who.

additional_notes: Literally “you knew that…”. Uses the imperfect (savais) to ask about someone’s prior knowledge. Often used as a surprised or accusatory question, and it can be followed by “non ?” to mean “right?” / “didn’t you?”.
target_language_example: Tu savais que je venais aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Did you know I was coming today?

additional_notes: Used to say how someone appears based on what you observe (their behavior, tone, or expression). Often followed by an infinitive (tu sembles comprendre) or an adjective (tu sembles surpris). Less direct than stating something as a fact; it expresses an impression.
target_language_example: Tu sembles fatigué aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You seem tired today.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone will be like or where they will be in the future, often to reassure or make a promise (Tu seras bien.) or in time clauses with quand/lorsque (“when”), e.g., quand tu seras grand (“when you’re grown up”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : tu seras prêt demain.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’ll be ready tomorrow.

additional_notes: “Tu sois” is the subjunctive present of “être” with “tu.” It usually appears after “que” in sentences that express necessity, doubt, emotion, or purpose (e.g., « Il faut que tu sois… », « pour que tu sois… »). You also see it in set patterns like « où que tu sois » = “wherever you are / may be.”
target_language_example: Je veux que tu sois prêt à huit heures.
native_language_example: I want you to be ready at eight o’clock.

meaning: "your name is" / "you're called" (used to ask someone's name).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb s'appeler (“to be called”). It’s the informal singular “you” (tu). Often used in questions like « Tu t'appelles comment ? » or « Comment tu t'appelles ? ». A more formal/polite version is « Vous vous appelez comment ? » / « Comment vous vous appelez ? ». You can answer with « Je m'appelle … ».
target_language_example: Salut ! Tu t'appelles comment ?
native_language_example: Hi! What's your name?

meaning: "you ... about it / of it" (a pronoun combo used before a verb).
additional_notes:
This is not a fixed expression by itself: it’s the subject pronoun "tu" + the reflexive pronoun "te" (contracted to "t'" before a vowel) + the pronoun "en". "En" usually replaces something introduced by "de" ("about it", "of it", "some"), and the exact meaning depends on the verb: 
- "Tu t’en occupes" = you take care of it.
- "Tu t’en rends compte" = you realize it / you’re aware of it.
- "Tu t’en souviens" = you remember it.
Very common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Tu t’en souviens ?
native_language_example: Do you remember it?

meaning: "you" + "have" (passé composé) for reflexive verbs; used to say what "you" did (to yourself).
additional_notes: This is the passé composé of reflexive verbs: "tu" + "te" → "t'" + "es" (from "être"). It’s followed by a past participle: "Tu t'es levé(e)", "Tu t'es lavé(e)". With reflexive verbs, French uses "être" as the helping verb, and the past participle often agrees with the person (levé / levée) depending on gender and sentence structure.
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu t'es arrêté si vite ?
native_language_example: Why did you stop so quickly?

additional_notes: This is the passé composé form of **se faire** with **tu**. It’s commonly used in two patterns: (1) **tu t’es fait + infinitive** = “you had/got something done” (often something you arranged): *Tu t’es fait couper les cheveux ?* (“Did you get your hair cut?”). (2) **tu t’es fait + past participle / expression** = “you got …” in a passive sense, often something unpleasant or accidental: *tu t’es fait sortir* (“you got kicked out”), *tu t’es fait prendre* (“you got caught”), *tu t’es fait avoir* (“you got tricked”). It can also mean “you made” in the sense of forming relationships: *Tu t’es fait des amis ?* (“Did you make friends?”).
target_language_example: Tu t'es fait voler ton vélo ?
native_language_example: Did your bike get stolen?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to one person with the informal “tu.” “Te” is the reflexive pronoun that goes with “tu,” common in pronominal verbs: tu te dépêches (you hurry up), tu te moques (you make fun), tu te crois… (you think you are…). In English it’s often not translated word-for-word (it may disappear or become “yourself,” depending on the verb).
target_language_example: Tu te lèves tôt ?
native_language_example: Do you get up early?

meaning: "you think you are…" / "who do you think you are…?"
additional_notes: From the verb *se croire* (“to think of oneself as / to imagine oneself”). It’s often used as a reproach or challenge, especially in questions: *Tu te crois où ?* (“Where do you think you are?”), *Tu te crois malin ?* (“You think you’re smart?”). It’s typically followed by an adjective (*malin*), a place (*au cinéma*, *sur Facebook*), or a comparison (*au-dessus de tout*, *mieux que moi*).
target_language_example: Tu te crois chez toi ici ?
native_language_example: Do you think you’re at home here?

tu te fous de ma gueule

target_language_multi_word_term: tu te fous de ma gueule
meaning: "Are you kidding me?" / "Are you messing with me?" / "Are you making fun of me?" (very rude).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used when you feel someone is mocking you, lying to you, or treating you like an idiot. Often said angrily as a confrontation (similar tone to “Are you fucking kidding me?”). "se foutre de" = to mess with / make fun of; "gueule" is a crude word for “mouth/face,” so the whole expression is aggressive.
target_language_example: Tu te fous de ma gueule ? Tu savais très bien que c’était interdit.
native_language_example: Are you kidding me? You knew perfectly well that it was forbidden.

meaning: “Are you kidding?” / “You’re making fun of me.”
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "se moquer de" = "to make fun of" / "to mock". In questions ("Tu te moques de moi ?"), it often means “Are you kidding (me)?” said in disbelief or annoyance. It can also be literal: someone is laughing at you, possibly "dans mon dos" (“behind my back”).
target_language_example: Tu te moques de moi ? Je viens de te le dire !
native_language_example: Are you kidding me? I just told you!

meaning: "Who do you think you are?" / "You think you're…?" (accusing someone of acting like they are someone else).
additional_notes: Built on "se prendre pour + noun" = to take yourself for / to think you are (often said sarcastically or angrily). Used to challenge someone who is acting bossy, important, tough, heroic, etc.: "Tu te prends pour ma mère ?" = "Who do you think you are, my mother?"
target_language_example: Tu te prends pour le chef ou quoi ?
native_language_example: Who do you think you are, the boss or what?

additional_notes: Spoken, informal/neutral way to ask someone if they remember. Often used as a tag question at the end of a sentence to remind someone: « …, tu te rappelles ? ». You can follow it with a direct object (« Tu te rappelles ce que je t’ai dit ? ») or with « de » + person/thing (« Tu te rappelles de lui / de moi / de son nom ? »).
target_language_example: Tu te rappelles où on s’est rencontrés ?
native_language_example: Do you remember where we met?

additional_notes: Used to ask or state that someone remembers something. It comes from the verb "se rappeler" (to remember). It’s commonly followed by "de" + a noun ("Tu te rappelles de son nom ?") or "de ce que" + a clause ("Tu te rappelles de ce que nous avons dit ?"). In everyday French, you may also hear "Tu te rappelles …" without "de".
target_language_example: Tu te rappelles de notre première rencontre ?
native_language_example: Do you remember our first meeting?

additional_notes: Very common spoken expression used to make someone notice the importance of something, often with surprise or disbelief. It’s frequently rhetorical (you don’t necessarily expect an answer). More formal: « Vous vous rendez compte ? »
target_language_example: Tu te rends compte ? On a oublié les billets à la maison !
native_language_example: Can you believe it? We forgot the tickets at home!

additional_notes: From the verb **se sentir** (“to feel”), used with reflexive pronouns: *je me sens, tu te sens, il/elle se sent*, etc. It’s commonly followed by an adjective (*tu te sens triste* = “you feel sad”) or an expression like *mieux* (“better”). In questions it can mean “Do you feel…?” or “Are you feeling up to it?” (*Tu te sens d’attaque ?*).
target_language_example: Tu te sens mieux aujourd’hui ?
native_language_example: Do you feel better today?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "se souvenir de" (to remember). It can be a statement ("Tu te souviens de ta promesse." = You remember your promise.) or a question ("Tu te souviens ?" = Do you remember?). With what you remember, it’s usually followed by "de" + noun ("Tu te souviens de ta promesse ?"), "de" + pronoun ("Tu te souviens de quoi ?"), or sometimes a full clause without "de" ("Tu te souviens combien tu as payé ?").
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de son prénom ?
native_language_example: Do you remember his first name?

meaning: “do you remember … ?” / “you remember …” (talking to one person).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **se souvenir de** (“to remember”). **Tu** addresses one person informally. It’s usually followed by a noun (**Tu te souviens de nous ?**) or **de + ce que/quoi** (**Tu te souviens de ce que tu as fait ?**). In speech, you may hear **t’as** (= **tu as**) in the past: **Tu te souviens de ce que t’as fait ?**
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de la première fois qu’on s’est rencontrés ?
native_language_example: Do you remember the first time we met?

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase **se souvenir de** (“to remember”). It’s built like: **Tu te souviens de + noun**. When the noun has an article/possessive, French keeps **de**: **Tu te souviens de notre ami ?** (“Do you remember our friend?”). **Tu** is used with friends/family (informal/familiar); with someone you don’t know well, you’d say **Vous vous souvenez de notre … ?**. **Notre** stays the same for masculine and feminine singular nouns (ami, lune), and becomes **nos** for plural.
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de notre professeur de français ?
native_language_example: Do you remember our French teacher?

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **se tromper** (“to be mistaken”). It’s commonly used to correct someone: **Tu te trompes.** = “You’re mistaken.” Note: **tromper** (without *se*) usually means “to deceive” or “to cheat on (someone),” so the meaning changes with the reflexive pronoun.
target_language_example: Tu te trompes : le rendez-vous est demain, pas aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: You’re mistaken: the appointment is tomorrow, not today.

additional_notes: Uses the informal subject pronoun tu (to one person you’re on familiar terms with). In the present tense, it can describe a habit (“you work [in general]”) or something happening now (“you’re working [right now]”), depending on context. Often followed by details like avec (“with”), trop (“too much”), le soir (“in the evening”), etc.
target_language_example: Tu travailles aujourd’hui ou tu es en congé ?
native_language_example: Are you working today, or are you off?

meaning: 'you’re going to' / 'you will' (near future, with a verb).
additional_notes: "Tu vas" is the present tense of "aller" (to go) for "tu". It’s most often used in the near future tense: "tu vas" + infinitive (e.g., "tu vas voir", "tu vas faire"). In questions, it commonly means "Are you going to…?" ("Tu vas le faire ?"). On its own it literally means "you go", but in everyday French it’s usually followed by another verb.
target_language_example: Tu vas comprendre dans une minute.
native_language_example: You’ll understand in a minute.

meaning: “you’re going to have to” (you will need to; obligation).
additional_notes: Uses the near future: tu vas + infinitive. Here the infinitive is devoir (“to have to”), which is followed by another verb in the infinitive: tu vas devoir + VERB. It’s a common way to tell someone they’ll be required to do something soon or inevitably.
target_language_example: Tu vas devoir partir maintenant.
native_language_example: You’re going to have to leave now.

meaning: "you’re going to do" / "what are you going to do" (near future).
additional_notes: Formed with the near-future tense: aller (tu vas) + infinitive (faire). Used to talk about what someone is going to do soon, or to ask about their plans: « Tu vas faire quoi ? » = “What are you going to do?” Can take an object: « tu vas faire un prêt » (“you’re going to take out a loan”). Often appears in questions with « qu’est-ce que… » or informally with « quoi ».
target_language_example: Tu vas faire quoi ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are you going to do tonight?

meaning: “you’re going to … it/him” (near future with the direct object pronoun *le*).
additional_notes: Used with *aller* + infinitive (the “near future”): *tu vas le + verbe* = “you’re going to + verb + it/him.” *Le* replaces a masculine singular direct object (a thing, an idea, or a man/boy). Common in threats: *Tu vas le regretter !* (“You’ll regret it!”), *Tu vas le payer !* (“You’ll pay for it!”). If the object is feminine, use *la*; plural: *les*.
target_language_example: Tu vas le faire maintenant ?
native_language_example: Are you going to do it now?

meaning: “you’re going to … me” / “you’re going to … to me” (near future).
additional_notes: Used with the near-future tense: **tu vas** + infinitive. **me** is the object pronoun (“me/to me”) and usually goes right before the infinitive: *Tu vas me faire mal* (“You’re going to hurt me”). Often used as a warning about what someone is about to do.
target_language_example: Attention, tu vas me faire tomber !
native_language_example: Careful, you’re going to make me fall!

meaning: "you’re going to" (followed by a reflexive verb: "you’re going to [do something to yourself]").
additional_notes: This is the near future: **aller (tu vas)** + infinitive. The **te** is a reflexive pronoun used with reflexive verbs (e.g., *te détendre, te taire, te rétablir, te débarrasser de…*). In speech, it can sound like a prediction (*tu vas te rétablir* = “you’ll recover”) or a strong warning/order depending on tone (*tu vas te taire ?*).
target_language_example: Tu vas te souvenir de mon nom.
native_language_example: You’re going to remember my name.

meaning: "you’ll see" / "wait and see"; or "are you going to see (someone)?"
additional_notes: Literally "you’re going to see" (aller + infinitive), often used to mean “you’ll see” as a promise, reassurance, warning, or to build suspense: « Attends, tu vas voir. » It can also be a real question about visiting/meeting someone when followed by a person: « Tu vas voir tonton Jay ? » (= “Are you going to see/visit Uncle Jay?”).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tu vas voir, ça va bien se passer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you’ll see, it’ll go well.

additional_notes: Used to warn someone that, if they don’t hurry/change something, they will arrive late. Very common with places/events: « en retard au boulot/en cours » (late for work/class) and « en retard pour l’école/pour ta partie » (late for school/your game/match).
target_language_example: Si tu ne pars pas maintenant, tu vas être en retard.
native_language_example: If you don’t leave now, you’re going to be late.

meaning: 'you’re going to' / 'you will' (near future, with a verb).
additional_notes: "Tu vas" is the present tense of "aller" (to go) for "tu". It’s most often used in the near future tense: "tu vas" + infinitive (e.g., "tu vas voir", "tu vas faire"). In questions, it commonly means "Are you going to…?" ("Tu vas le faire ?"). On its own it literally means "you go", but in everyday French it’s usually followed by another verb.
target_language_example: Tu vas comprendre dans une minute.
native_language_example: You’ll understand in a minute.

additional_notes: Literally 'you go well,' but used to ask or state how someone is doing. Most often a question: "Tu vas bien ?" (neutral, common). With emphasis (e.g., "Mais tu vas bien ?") it can also mean "Are you okay?!" or "What’s wrong with you?" depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Après l'accident, tu vas bien ?
native_language_example: After the accident, are you okay?

additional_notes: Common in spoken French with normal word order (subject + verb + question word at the end). More neutral/formal options are "Tu vas où ?" with a polite tone, or "Où vas-tu ?" (more formal/literary). Often used when someone is leaving or heading somewhere, sometimes with surprise or annoyance depending on tone.
target_language_example: Hé, tu vas où comme ça ?
native_language_example: Hey, where are you going like that?

additional_notes: Literally the future of "voir" with "tu". Used both for simple future meaning (you will see/notice something) and as a set phrase meaning “you’ll see” (= wait and you’ll find out / it will become clear).
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tu verras, tout ira bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you’ll see, everything will be fine.

additional_notes: Common way to ask a question in everyday French without inversion (instead of “veux-tu…?”). Often followed by an infinitive (“Tu veux venir ?” = Do you want to come?) or a noun (“Tu veux un café ?” = Do you want a coffee?). Also appears in set patterns like “Tu veux dire… ?” (= What do you mean…? / You mean…?).
target_language_example: Tu veux un café ?
native_language_example: Do you want a coffee?

meaning: “do you want to go” / “you want to go.”
additional_notes: Literally “you want to go.” Used to ask someone if they want to go somewhere or go do an activity. Often followed by an infinitive (aller manger, aller nager, aller voir un film) or a place with à (aller à la plage).
target_language_example: Tu veux aller au café avec moi ?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to the café with me?

additional_notes: Literally “you want (to)?” but used to soften a request, often placed at the end like a tag question: « …, tu veux bien ? ». Can also start a request: « Tu veux bien + infinitive… ? ». Tone depends on context: it can sound friendly, insistent, or even irritated (e.g., « Tu veux bien te taire ? »).
target_language_example: Tu veux bien m’aider deux minutes ?
native_language_example: Could you help me for two minutes?

meaning: "you mean" / "do you mean …?" (asking or clarifying meaning).
additional_notes: Used to check you understood correctly, to clarify what someone intended, or to introduce what you think the other person is saying: « Tu veux dire que… ? » = “You mean that…?” In a statement, it can also mean “I know what you mean”: « Je vois ce que tu veux dire. »
target_language_example: Tu veux dire qu’on part à huit heures ?
native_language_example: You mean we’re leaving at eight o’clock?

meaning: "do you want to do" / "you want to do".
additional_notes: Common in questions to ask what someone wants to do: « Qu’est-ce que tu veux faire ? » or « Tu veux faire quoi ? ». Uses informal « tu » (to one person you’re on familiar terms with). « faire » is very flexible: it can mean to do, to make, or to have/play (e.g., « faire un bonhomme de neige » = make a snowman; « faire une partie de billard » = play a game of pool).
target_language_example: Tu veux faire un tour avec moi ?
native_language_example: Do you want to go for a walk with me?

meaning: “do you want to … me?” / “would you like to … for me?”
additional_notes: Used to start a question with vouloir (to want) + an infinitive verb: **Tu veux me + [infinitive]?** The **me** is an object pronoun meaning “to me / me,” and it comes **before** the infinitive: *Tu veux me parler ?* (“Do you want to talk to me?”), *Tu veux me raconter… ?* (“Do you want to tell me…?”).
target_language_example: Tu veux me montrer comment ça marche ?
native_language_example: Do you want to show me how it works?

additional_notes: Spoken shortcut of **tu ne veux pas** (the **ne** is dropped). Often used to make a suggestion or invitation in a casual way: **Tu veux pas + infinitive ?** It can also mean “you don’t want to…” in statements.
target_language_example: Tu veux pas venir avec nous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Why don’t you come with us tonight?

meaning: "Do you want us to…?" / "Do you want to… (together)?"
additional_notes: Used to suggest or propose doing something together. It’s formed with "tu veux" (you want) + "qu’on" (= "que" + "on", meaning “that we”). The verb after "qu’on" is typically in the subjunctive: "Tu veux qu’on aille… ?", "Tu veux qu’on prenne… ?" In casual speech, people sometimes drop the "ne" in negatives ("Tu veux qu’on s’en aille ?").
target_language_example: Tu veux qu’on se retrouve à 19 h ?
native_language_example: Do you want us to meet up at 7 p.m.?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone if they want you to do something. After "vouloir que", French normally uses the subjunctive: "Tu veux que je conduise ?" (not *"je conduis"). More formal: "Vous voulez que je… ?"
target_language_example: Tu veux que je t’aide avec tes devoirs ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you with your homework?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants you to do. It uses the pattern **vouloir que + subjunctive**: *Tu veux que je fasse…* (literally “you want that I do…”). Often followed by a specific task: *Tu veux que je fasse quoi ?* / *Tu veux que je fasse ça maintenant ?*
target_language_example: Tu veux que je fasse la vaisselle ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to do the dishes tonight?

meaning: "do you want me to (for you / to you) …?"
additional_notes: Used to offer or propose doing something, or to check what the other person wants. Pattern: « Tu veux que je te + verbe (subjonctif) … ? » (e.g., je te laisse, je te lise, je te montre). « te » is an indirect/direct object pronoun meaning “to you” or “you,” depending on the verb. Often comes as a question; without « est-ce que », it can sound more direct.
target_language_example: Tu veux que je te montre où c'est ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to show you where it is?

tu veux que je te dise

target_language_multi_word_term: tu veux que je te dise
meaning: "Do you want me to tell you…?" (often: “What do you expect me to say?”)
additional_notes: Literally “you want that I tell you.” Used to introduce what you’re about to say (Tu veux que je te dise un truc ?), or—especially with Qu’est-ce que…?—to show you don’t know what to answer / you’re frustrated or resigned (Qu’est-ce que tu veux que je te dise ? = “What do you want me to say?”). In speech you may hear the shorter form without « que »: « Qu’est-ce tu veux… ».
target_language_example: Qu’est-ce que tu veux que je te dise ? Je n’y peux rien.
native_language_example: What do you want me to say? I can’t do anything about it.

additional_notes: Informal expression used to show disbelief, annoyance, or sarcasm at what someone just said or did. Literally it means “you want to laugh,” but in real use it’s like saying someone’s claim is ridiculous. Often said with a rising intonation as a question: « Tu veux rire ? »
target_language_example: —Je vais finir ce projet en une heure. —Tu veux rire ?
native_language_example: “I’m going to finish this project in an hour.” “Are you kidding?”

meaning: "do you want to know" / "you want to know".
additional_notes: Common way to introduce an explanation or reveal information, often leading into a question: « Tu veux savoir pourquoi ? » (= “Do you want to know why?”). Uses informal « tu » (said to one person you’re on familiar terms with). You can follow it with a question word (pourquoi, comment) or with « ce que… » (“what…”).
target_language_example: Tu veux savoir la vérité ?
native_language_example: Do you want to know the truth?

meaning: “Do you want to…?” (informal), introducing a verb that uses “te” (you/yourself).
additional_notes: Used with the informal subject pronoun “tu” to ask (or challenge) someone: “Tu veux te + infinitive… ?” The “te” is an object/reflexive pronoun needed by certain verbs (e.g., se battre = to fight, se lever = to get up, se joindre à = to join, se fondre = to blend in). In English, you usually just say “Do you want to + verb…?” without translating “te” as “yourself.”
target_language_example: Tu veux te reposer un peu ?
native_language_example: Do you want to rest a bit?

meaning: “Do you want a…?” (asking if someone wants a masculine noun item).
additional_notes: Common informal question to offer someone something. Used with a masculine singular noun: tu veux un beignet ? For a feminine noun, use “tu veux une… ?”. In more polite/formal situations, use “Vous voulez… ?”.
target_language_example: Tu veux un café ?
native_language_example: Do you want a coffee?

meaning: “Do you want a…?” (to a friend/one person).
additional_notes: Used to offer something singular and feminine (une + a feminine noun): Tu veux une salade ? / une tisane ? In more formal or polite situations, use « Vous voulez une… ? ».
target_language_example: Tu veux une bière ?
native_language_example: Do you want a beer?

additional_notes: Used to offer or suggest showing something to someone. Often followed by a noun (“tu veux voir ma collection… ?”) or “un truc + adjective” (“tu veux voir un truc cool ?”). It’s conversational and direct; you can add “Est-ce que” for a more neutral tone (“Est-ce que tu veux voir… ?”).
target_language_example: Tu veux voir la photo que j’ai prise ?
native_language_example: Do you want to see the photo I took?

meaning: “do you really want (to)…?” / “do you really mean it?”
additional_notes: Used to express surprise, doubt, or to double-check what the other person wants. It’s often followed by an infinitive (tu veux vraiment y aller ?) or by “que” + subjunctive (tu veux vraiment que je parte ?). Tone depends on context: it can be neutral (just confirming) or slightly challenging (are you sure?).
target_language_example: Tu veux vraiment commander ça ?
native_language_example: Do you really want to order that?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (one person you address as tu) if they want to become or be something. It’s followed by a noun or adjective (e.g., chef, amie) or by a past participle/adjective like payé(e) (“paid”). For formal or plural, use vous voulez être.
target_language_example: Tu veux être médecin plus tard ?
native_language_example: Do you want to be a doctor later?

additional_notes: From the verb *venir* (to come), used with *tu* (informal 'you'). Very common as a question to invite or check if someone is coming: *Tu viens ?* It can also be part of other structures like *Tu viens de + infinitive* = 'you just did (something)' (e.g., *Tu viens de dire quoi ?*).
target_language_example: On part maintenant — tu viens ?
native_language_example: We’re leaving now—are you coming?

meaning: "Are you coming with me?" / "You’re coming with me."
additional_notes: Literally “you come with me.” Often used either as a question (with rising intonation) to invite someone to come along, or as a firm statement/command meaning “You’re coming with me,” especially in contexts like “Ça suffit, tu viens avec moi.” You can soften it with “Tu veux venir avec moi ?” or “Viens avec moi.”
target_language_example: Tu viens avec moi au café ?
native_language_example: Are you coming with me to the café?

meaning: “you see” / “you know” (used to point something out or explain).
additional_notes: Literally means “you see” (from voir = to see). Often used in spoken French to check that someone understands or to introduce an explanation: “Tu vois, …” ≈ “See/you know, …”. In negative form: “Tu vois pas …” = “You don’t see … / you don’t realize …”.
target_language_example: Tu vois, il suffit de cliquer ici.
native_language_example: You see, you just have to click here.

meaning: "you see what…" / "you know what…" (to point something out or check understanding).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to introduce an explanation, highlight a consequence, or make sure the other person understands (often like English “you see…/you know…”). It’s usually followed by a clause: « tu vois ce que je veux dire ? » = “you know what I mean?”
target_language_example: Tu vois ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: You know what I mean?

tu vois ce que je veux dire

target_language_multi_word_term: tu vois ce que je veux dire
additional_notes: Used to check that the other person understands what you’re saying, often at the end of a sentence. Literally “you see what I want to say,” but it’s the common French way to say “you know what I mean.” You can add a tag like “non ?” to seek agreement.
target_language_example: Il faut partir tôt pour éviter les embouteillages, tu vois ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: We need to leave early to avoid traffic, you know what I mean?

additional_notes: “Tu” is the informal singular “you” (used with friends, family, kids). “Voulait” is the imperfect past tense of “vouloir,” often used for (1) an ongoing or repeated desire in the past (“you wanted to…”) or (2) a softer, polite-sounding question like “Did you want something?” In questions it can imply “Were you trying to…?” or “Were you planning to…?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu voulais un café ou un thé ?
native_language_example: Did you want a coffee or a tea?

meaning: “you wanted to … me / you were going to … to me”.
additional_notes: Used when addressing someone informally (tu). It’s the imperfect of vouloir (“to want”), often used to refer to an intention or request in the past (“you wanted to talk to me / tell me / show me…”). Typically followed by an infinitive (parler, dire, montrer, etc.).
target_language_example: Tu voulais me demander quelque chose ?
native_language_example: Did you want to ask me something?

additional_notes: Used to ask or confirm what someone had intended to say. The imperfect (voulais) often makes it sound a bit softer or like “you were going to tell me / you meant to tell me,” especially when returning to an earlier topic: « Alors, qu’est-ce que tu voulais me dire ? ».
target_language_example: Tu voulais me dire quelque chose d’important ?
native_language_example: Did you want to tell me something important?

meaning: “you wanted to talk to me” / “did you want to talk to me?”
additional_notes: Literally “you wanted to speak to me.” Often used to check why someone contacted you or to bring up a topic: “Tu voulais me parler de … ?” Uses the imperfect (voulais), which commonly sounds like “were you wanting to…” / “did you want to… (earlier)?” and can feel slightly softer than “tu veux.”
target_language_example: Tu voulais me parler de quoi ?
native_language_example: What did you want to talk to me about?

additional_notes: “Y” is a pronoun that usually replaces a place (“there”) or something you’re involved in. So **tu y es** can be literal (you’re there: *Tu y es en sécurité* = you’re safe there) or idiomatic to encourage/correct someone: **Tu y es presque** (“You’re almost there”), **Tu y es !** (“That’s it!/You got it!”). As a question (**Tu y es ?**), it can mean “Are you there?” or “Do you get it?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu y es presque, ne lâche pas !
native_language_example: You’re almost there—don’t give up!

additional_notes: Means being at your house/home. Very common with verbs of going/returning: "rentrer à la maison" (to go/come home), "revenir à la maison" (to come back home), "venir à la maison" (to come to my/your house). In your examples, the "-tu" is just question word order (inversion): "Quand rentres-tu…?" = "When are you coming home?"
target_language_example: Je reste à la maison ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm staying home tonight.

additional_notes: Used to describe what someone’s state, condition, or situation was in the past, often as background information (not a completed action). Common after "que" in reported thoughts/speech: "J’ai cru que tu étais…" / "J’ai entendu dire que tu étais…".
target_language_example: Je pensais que tu étais fatigué.
native_language_example: I thought you were tired.

meaning: a private one-on-one conversation/meeting (just the two of you).
additional_notes: Used for situations where two people talk or meet alone, often privately (e.g., to discuss something personal or important). You can say “en tête-à-tête” (= one-on-one) or “un tête-à-tête” (= a one-on-one chat/meeting). It can be plural: “des tête-à-tête”.
target_language_example: Après la réunion, j’aimerais te parler en tête-à-tête.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I’d like to talk to you one-on-one.

meaning: a scatterbrain; an airhead (a forgetful person).
additional_notes: An informal, often teasing (but still insulting) expression said about someone who is very absent-minded or forgets things easily. Used as an exclamation ("Tête de linotte !") or with "être/avoir" ("Tu es / Tu as une tête de linotte").
target_language_example: J’ai encore oublié mes clés : quelle tête de linotte !
native_language_example: I forgot my keys again: what a scatterbrain!

additional_notes: Used to say something happened earlier today in the morning (often earlier than expected). It commonly comes after the verb: « Il a appelé tôt ce matin. » You can intensify it with « très »: « très tôt ce matin ». It can also be used alone as a short time answer: « — Quand ? — Tôt ce matin. »
target_language_example: J'ai reçu un message tôt ce matin.
native_language_example: I got a message early this morning.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens early during the morning (often soon after waking up). You can make it stronger with "très" ("très tôt le matin" = "very early in the morning").
target_language_example: On se retrouve tôt le matin, vers 7 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet early in the morning, around 7 a.m.?

additional_notes: Very common spoken contraction of « tu es ». Used with adjectives or nouns: « T’es fatigué(e) », « T’es une bête ». Mostly appears in informal writing (texts, dialogue) to reflect speech.
target_language_example: T’es prêt(e) ?
native_language_example: Are you ready?

additional_notes: A common loanword in French for a short-sleeved casual shirt. The plural is usually written "des T-shirts" (often with a hyphen). Used after clothing verbs like "porter" (to wear).
target_language_example: J’ai acheté un T-shirt pour le match.
native_language_example: I bought a T-shirt for the game.

additional_notes: Used for an unplanned event, often something that causes damage or injury (e.g., a car crash or a household mishap). In French, you commonly say "avoir un accident" (to have an accident) or "un accident de voiture" (a car accident).
target_language_example: Il a eu un accident de voiture hier soir.
native_language_example: He had a car accident last night.

meaning: a road traffic accident (a car crash).
additional_notes: Used to talk generally about an accident involving vehicles on the road. Common in news/police/insurance contexts. You can also hear/see: "accident de voiture" (car accident), and "accident de la circulation" (traffic accident, more formal).
target_language_example: Nous avons appelé les secours après un accident de la route.
native_language_example: We called emergency services after a road traffic accident.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an accident involving a car. You’ll often hear it with verbs like « avoir » (to have/be in) or « faire » (to have/cause): « avoir un accident de voiture », « faire un accident de voiture ». You can add an adjective like « grave » (serious): « un accident de voiture grave ».
target_language_example: Heureusement, personne n’a été blessé dans l’accident de voiture.
native_language_example: Fortunately, nobody was hurt in the car accident.

additional_notes: Used to talk about one friend (male) or a friend in general. Often followed by details like "de mon père" (my father’s friend) or "à moi" (a friend of mine). For a female friend, use "une amie". In "Juste un ami", it often means “just a friend” (not a romantic partner).
target_language_example: C'est un ami à moi, il s'appelle Julien.
native_language_example: He's a friend of mine; his name is Julien.

additional_notes: Used to indicate who the friend is connected to; the person comes after "de" (often with a possessive like "mon/ma/mes" or a name): "un ami de mon père", "un ami de Marie". In the plural: "des amis de ...".
target_language_example: C'est une amie de ma sœur.
native_language_example: She's a friend of my sister.

meaning: a friend of mine (one of my friends).
additional_notes: Uses the pattern "un/une + noun + à moi/toi/lui/elle/nous/vous/eux" to mean “one of my/your/his/her/our/your/their …”. It often introduces someone without specifying which one. Very close in meaning to "un de mes amis" (= one of my friends). Feminine: "une amie à moi".
target_language_example: Un ami à moi vient dîner ce soir.
native_language_example: A friend of mine is coming over for dinner tonight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for one year) or a point in time relative to now/another moment. Often appears after time expressions like « il y a » (ago) and « depuis » (for/since): « Il y a plus d’un an » = more than a year ago; « depuis plus d’un an » = for more than a year. Liaison is common: « un an » sounds like /ɛ̃ nɑ̃/.
target_language_example: J’ai travaillé à Paris pendant un an.
native_language_example: I worked in Paris for one year.

meaning: an angel; (figuratively) a very kind, sweet, or patient person.
additional_notes: Used literally for an angel (religious/mythical being) or as a compliment: "Tu/T’es un ange" = “You’re an angel” (thanks for being helpful, patient, etc.). Also appears in comparisons like "dormir comme un ange" (sleep very peacefully) or "ressembler à un ange" (look like an angel).
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide, tu es un ange.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help, you’re an angel.

meaning: an animal; (figurative) a brutal or wild person.
additional_notes: Usually means a literal animal. In comparisons with "comme" ("comme un animal") or with adjectives like "enragé" (rabid), it can be figurative and negative, suggesting someone is behaving in a savage, cruel, or uncontrolled way. In questions like "Est-ce un animal ?", "un" is used because the noun starts with a vowel sound (linking: "un_nanimal").
target_language_example: Il a traité les gens comme des animaux.
native_language_example: He treated people like animals.

additional_notes: A common way to say “camera” in French (literally “photo device”). Often used with the verb prendre: prendre des photos = to take pictures.
target_language_example: J’ai oublié mon appareil photo à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot my camera at home.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used for a place to live, usually one unit in a larger building. Common with verbs like trouver (to find), louer (to rent), habiter/vivre (to live), and with descriptions like de luxe (luxury) or très joli (very nice).
target_language_example: Nous cherchons un appartement près du métro.
native_language_example: We’re looking for an apartment near the метро/subway.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a telephone call in everyday French. Often used with verbs like recevoir (to receive/get a call) and attendre (to be expecting a call). You can specify who it’s for with pour: « Un appel pour le Colonel. »
target_language_example: J'attends un appel de mon médecin.
native_language_example: I'm expecting a call from my doctor.

additional_notes: A common noun for a tree in general. Used with many verbs: abattre un arbre (to cut down a tree), être contre un arbre (to lean/stand against a tree), derrière un arbre (behind a tree), dans un arbre (in a tree), percuter un arbre (to hit a tree with a vehicle). In figurative or poetic contexts, it can describe someone as being like a tree (strong, rooted, etc.).
target_language_example: Il y a un grand arbre devant la maison.
native_language_example: There is a big tree in front of the house.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used for the natural phenomenon (often after rain). Plural: des arcs-en-ciel (often invariable in everyday use).
target_language_example: Après la pluie, on a vu un arc-en-ciel au-dessus de la ville.
native_language_example: After the rain, we saw a rainbow over the city.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an alternative way of doing something or an alternative solution. Often followed by "de" + infinitive ("un autre moyen de sortir" = another way to get out) or by "par lequel" to specify the means ("un autre moyen par lequel je puisse te payer" = another way I can pay you).
target_language_example: On peut essayer un autre moyen si ça ne marche pas.
native_language_example: We can try another way if it doesn’t work.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a refill or an additional drink. Often followed by “de + drink” (un autre verre de bière / de vin). In a restaurant/bar it’s a polite request with verbs like « pouvoir »: « Puis-je / Pourrais-je avoir un autre verre ? » It can also literally mean a different physical glass, but most often it means another serving to drink.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je peux avoir un autre verre de vin, s’il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have another glass of wine, please?

additional_notes: Used when asking for or offering a refill (one more glass). You can say it as a request (Puis-je avoir… ?) or an offer (Tu veux… ?). Also works with other drinks: un autre verre d’eau, un autre verre de bière.
target_language_example: Je prendrai un autre verre de vin, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’ll have another glass of wine, please.

additional_notes: Most often means an aircraft you travel in: «monter dans un avion» = to board/get on a plane. It can also refer to other types of aircraft (e.g., military) and to «un avion en papier» (a paper airplane).
target_language_example: On prend un avion demain matin.
native_language_example: We’re taking a plane tomorrow morning.

meaning: a lawyer (also: an avocado, depending on context).
additional_notes: Most often means “a lawyer” in legal contexts (e.g., “Avez-vous un avocat ?” = “Do you have a lawyer?”). In food/shopping contexts, it can mean “an avocado” (e.g., “Prends un avocat.”). Not a close cognate of “lawyer”; it can look like English “advocate,” but in everyday French it usually refers to a lawyer.
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’un avocat.
native_language_example: I need a lawyer.

additional_notes: Means a bath (the act of bathing in a bathtub) and can also refer to the bathwater. Most commonly used with the verb "prendre" (to take): "prendre un bain" = "to take a bath". Often contrasted with "une douche" (a shower).
target_language_example: Après le sport, je prends un bain chaud.
native_language_example: After working out, I take a hot bath.

meaning: "a beautiful / nice" (masculine singular), used before a noun.
additional_notes: Beau is an adjective meaning “beautiful / handsome / nice.” With a masculine singular noun you often see it as “un beau + noun” (e.g., un beau pays, un beau sourire). It can also be used ironically in some set expressions to mean “a fine…” in a negative sense (e.g., être dans un beau pétrin = “to be in a fine mess”).
target_language_example: C'est un beau moment à partager.
native_language_example: It’s a beautiful moment to share.

additional_notes: Used to say something is needed quickly or is very important. Often followed by a noun (or noun phrase): « un besoin urgent de volontaires / de vacances ». You can change the subject: « J’ai / Tu as / On a un besoin urgent de… ».
target_language_example: Nous avons un besoin urgent de soutien.
native_language_example: We have an urgent need for support.

meaning: "a good" (masculine singular), used before a noun.
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: un bon + noun (e.g., un bon groupe). With a feminine noun, you use "une bonne" (une bonne idée). In some contexts it can mean “a good pick/bet” (e.g., un bon ticket).
target_language_example: C'est un bon plan pour économiser de l'argent.
native_language_example: It's a good way to save money.

additional_notes: Used to describe a friend you appreciate or trust. The adjective usually comes before the noun here: un bon ami (masculine). Feminine: une bonne amie. You can add à moi / à toi / à lui, etc. to mean “a friend of mine/yours/his…”.
target_language_example: Julie est une bonne amie ; elle m'aide toujours quand j'en ai besoin.
native_language_example: Julie is a good friend; she always helps me when I need it.

meaning: a good boy; a good lad / a good guy (male).
additional_notes: Literally “a good boy.” Used to praise a male (often a child, but it can also be said to an adult in a friendly or slightly patronizing way). In the imperative, it’s used as a request/command: « Sois un bon garçon » = “Be a good boy.” For a girl: « une bonne fille » (or more commonly for children: « une bonne petite fille »).
target_language_example: Allez, sois un bon garçon et écoute le professeur.
native_language_example: Come on, be a good boy and listen to the teacher.

meaning: a good time; a good moment (to do something).
additional_notes: Common in expressions like « passer un bon moment » (“to have a good time”) and questions like « Quand est-ce un bon moment pour toi/vous ? » (“When is a good time for you?”). In « depuis un bon moment », it means “for a long time / in quite a while,” not “since a good moment.”
target_language_example: On peut se parler plus tard ? Ce soir, c’est un bon moment pour toi ?
native_language_example: Can we talk later? Is tonight a good time for you?

additional_notes: Used in greetings and small talk. With "passer" it means "to have/spend a good weekend" (e.g., "Tu as passé un bon week-end ?"). With "souhaiter" or "passer" in the imperative, it’s a common way to say "Have a good weekend!" (formal: "Passez un bon week-end" / "Je vous souhaite un bon week-end"; informal: "Passe un bon week-end").
target_language_example: Bon, je te laisse : passe un bon week-end !
native_language_example: Alright, I’ll let you go: have a good weekend!

additional_notes: Used with faire or construire: faire/construire un bonhomme de neige = “to make/build a snowman.” Literally “a little man of snow.”
target_language_example: Les enfants font un bonhomme de neige dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The kids are making a snowman in the garden.

meaning: a bit of; a piece of; (with time) a while.
additional_notes: Literally “an end of,” but in everyday French it commonly means “a bit/piece of” something (often food: un bout de gâteau) or “a while/quite some time” with time expressions (un bout de temps, Ça fait un bout de temps). With time, it often suggests a fairly long time in a casual way.
target_language_example: On va marcher un bout de chemin, puis on prendra le bus.
native_language_example: We’ll walk part of the way, then we’ll take the bus.

additional_notes: Used for any small sheet of paper, often something informal (to write a note, a phone number, etc.). In phrases like « C’est juste / Ce n’est qu’un bout de papier », it can also mean “just a piece of paper” to downplay the importance of a document.
target_language_example: Tu as un bout de papier pour que je note l’adresse ?
native_language_example: Do you have a piece of paper so I can write down the address?

additional_notes: Means a very young child. Common in family contexts: « avoir un bébé » = to have a baby (give birth / become a parent), « attendre un bébé » = to be expecting a baby. Can also be used in comparisons like « comme un bébé » (e.g., to fall/cry/sleep like a baby).
target_language_example: Ils ont eu un bébé l'année dernière.
native_language_example: They had a baby last year.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning something you give to someone (often for a birthday, holiday, or to thank them). Used with verbs like offrir (to give) and faire (to make/give): offrir un cadeau à quelqu’un, faire un cadeau à quelqu’un. You can specify who it’s from with de la part de: un cadeau de la part de Marie.
target_language_example: J’ai un petit cadeau pour toi.
native_language_example: I have a small gift for you.

additional_notes: Used to say who gave the gift: « un cadeau de + person » (a gift from + person). For the occasion, use « un cadeau de Noël / d’anniversaire » (“a Christmas/birthday gift”). To say who it’s for, add « pour + person »: « un cadeau de Noël pour toi ».
target_language_example: C'est un cadeau de mes parents.
native_language_example: It's a gift from my parents.

additional_notes: Used to say a present is intended for a particular person. Structure: (avoir/acheter) + un cadeau pour + [person]. With a noun: « pour Sandrine / pour ma petite amie ». With a pronoun: « pour elle / pour lui ».
target_language_example: J'ai un cadeau pour toi.
native_language_example: I have a gift for you.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or offering coffee, or suggesting a casual coffee meet-up (prendre un café = to have a coffee). Also note the spelling: un café (coffee / a café) vs un caffe (not French).
target_language_example: On se retrouve pour un café après le travail ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet up for a coffee after work?

additional_notes: A masculine noun for a large vehicle used to carry goods (e.g., un camion de livraison = a delivery truck). Used with common verbs like conduire (to drive), percuter (to hit/collide with), and monter dans (to get into).
target_language_example: Il y a un camion garé devant la maison.
native_language_example: There’s a truck parked in front of the house.

additional_notes: Used to mean an unspecified amount of time (not exact), often suggesting it may take longer than expected. Common with verbs like prendre (to take) and with pendant to mean “for a while.”
target_language_example: Je vais rester ici un certain temps avant de rentrer.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for a while before going home.

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article meaning "a" or "an." "Un chat" refers to one cat in general (not a specific cat). The plural is "des chats" (some cats).
target_language_example: J'ai un chat noir à la maison.
native_language_example: I have a black cat at home.

additional_notes: A common, basic noun: "un cheval" (a horse), "le cheval" (the horse). Used literally (an animal) and in common expressions, e.g. "fort comme un cheval" (as strong as a horse) or "Je pourrais manger un cheval" (I’m so hungry I could eat a horse). Plural: "des chevaux".
target_language_example: Dans ce parc, on peut voir un cheval et des poneys.
native_language_example: In this park, you can see a horse and ponies.

additional_notes: A friendly compliment meaning someone is a good person. In this expression, "chic" means "nice/kind" (not "stylish"), and "type" means "guy". Often used with emphasis: "vraiment un chic type" = "really a great guy." Mostly informal/colloquial.
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide : tu es vraiment un chic type !
native_language_example: Thanks for your help: you’re really a great guy!

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "un" = "a" (masculine singular) + "chien" = "dog". The plural is "des chiens" (some dogs).
target_language_example: J’ai un chien à la maison.
native_language_example: I have a dog at home.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb jeter: « jeter un coup d'œil (à) » = “to take/have a quick look (at).” With y (« Jetez-y un coup d'œil »), it means “have a quick look at it/there.”
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un coup d'œil à mon email ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at my email?

additional_notes: Often used with the verb « jeter »: « jeter un coup d'œil (à…) » = to take a quick look (at…). « Jetez-y un coup d'œil » means “take a quick look at it,” where « y » replaces what you’re looking at. Common in everyday speech and can be a polite suggestion (« Ça mérite un coup d'œil » = it’s worth a look).
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un coup d'œil à mon email avant que je l’envoie ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at my email before I send it?

meaning: a quick/sudden burst of (something); a quick swipe/strike of (something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to describe a brief action or sudden event: *un coup de chiffon* (a quick wipe with a cloth), *un coup de vent* (a gust of wind). It also appears in common expressions like *prendre un coup de vieux* (“to suddenly feel/look older”). The word *coup* can also mean “blow/strike,” depending on the context.
target_language_example: Je donne un coup de fil et j’arrive.
native_language_example: I’ll make a quick phone call and I’ll come right away.

meaning: a gunshot (a shot fired from a gun).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the sound/event of a firearm being fired (often heard: *entendre un coup de feu*, *un coup de feu retentit*). It can refer to one single shot; plural: *des coups de feu* (“gunshots”).
target_language_example: On a entendu un coup de feu près du parc.
native_language_example: We heard a gunshot near the park.

additional_notes: Common, everyday way to talk about a phone call. Used with verbs like donner/passer: « passer un coup de fil » = to make/place a call; « donner un coup de fil » = to give someone a call. Often means a quick call.
target_language_example: Je te donne un coup de fil ce soir.
native_language_example: I’ll give you a call tonight.

meaning: a hand; a bit of help.
additional_notes: Used to ask for or offer help with a task. Very common in spoken French with verbs like donner/avoir/fil(er) un coup de main (to give/get/lend a hand).
target_language_example: Tu peux me donner un coup de main pour porter ces cartons ?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand carrying these boxes?

meaning: a kick (a blow with the foot).
additional_notes: Literally “a blow of foot.” Often used with the verb donner: donner un coup de pied à [person/thing] = to kick [someone/something]. You can also say donner un coup de pied dans [something] (to kick something) or donner un coup de pied pour [verb] to show purpose (e.g., to boost yourself up).
target_language_example: Il m’a donné un coup de pied dans la jambe.
native_language_example: He kicked me in the leg.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb phrase « jeter un coup d’œil (à …) » = “to take/have a quick look (at …)”. Very common for asking permission or offering to check something briefly: « Je peux jeter un coup d’œil ? » / « Je vais jeter un coup d’œil à … ».
target_language_example: Tu peux jeter un coup d’œil à mon email avant que je l’envoie ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at my email before I send it?

additional_notes: A masculine noun (un couteau / le couteau). Used for everyday table settings (fork and knife) and also in more serious contexts like crime reports. Plural: des couteaux.
target_language_example: Peux-tu me passer un couteau, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you pass me a knife, please?

meaning: a dead end (street); a dead end (situation).
additional_notes: Used literally for a street that does not continue (no through road). Figuratively, it means an impasse or situation with no way forward. Masculine noun: un cul-de-sac; plural: des culs-de-sac.
target_language_example: On s'est trompés de route : c'est un cul-de-sac.
native_language_example: We took the wrong road: it’s a dead end.

additional_notes: Refers to a detective hired by a private person (not the police) to investigate or follow someone. Often used with verbs like engager or employer (to hire). You can also say une détective privée for a woman.
target_language_example: Ils ont engagé un détective privé pour retrouver leur chien.
native_language_example: They hired a private investigator to find their dog.

additional_notes: Most often means a paid job position (similar to “un boulot,” but more neutral/formal). Common with verbs like trouver (to find), chercher (to look for), avoir (to have), and expressions like un emploi à temps partiel (a part-time job) or un emploi près de chez moi (a job near my home).
target_language_example: Elle a enfin trouvé un emploi dans une petite entreprise.
native_language_example: She finally found a job at a small company.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a place in a general way (often with an adjective: un endroit charmant/sûr/dangereux). It can be a real location (un musée) or a more abstract one (le monde est un endroit dangereux). Often interchangeable with « un lieu », but « endroit » feels more everyday.
target_language_example: On cherche un endroit tranquille pour déjeuner.
native_language_example: We're looking for a quiet place to have lunch.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with a location. It’s usually followed by a verb (e.g., vivre, rester, travailler) to describe what you can do in that place.
target_language_example: Je cherche un endroit où je peux étudier au calme.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a place where I can study quietly.

additional_notes: Means “a child” in general. It can be literal (someone’s son/daughter) or used figuratively to say someone is being childish (e.g., “me prendre pour un enfant” = “treat me like a child”).
target_language_example: Ils ont deux enfants.
native_language_example: They have two children.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: un excellent boulot / un excellent travail / un excellent cadeau. With a feminine noun, use **une excellente** (e.g., une excellente idée). In the plural: **d’excellents / d’excellentes**.
target_language_example: C’est un excellent restaurant.
native_language_example: It’s an excellent restaurant.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or offering an illustration to clarify an explanation or point: « donner un exemple » = “to give an example.” Often appears in questions like « Vous voulez un exemple ? » or « Tu peux me donner un exemple ? ». With pronouns: « m'en donner un » = “give me one (example).”
target_language_example: J’ai besoin d’un exemple pour comprendre.
native_language_example: I need an example to understand.

additional_notes: Means a movie in general. Often used with common verbs like voir/regarder un film (to see/watch a movie), aller voir un film (to go see a movie), and tourner un film (to shoot/make a film). You can specify the type with de + genre, e.g., un film de Noël (a Christmas movie).
target_language_example: On va regarder un film ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we going to watch a movie tonight?

additional_notes: Common informal word for a police officer. Often sounds casual or slightly pejorative depending on tone/context; in polite situations, prefer "un policier / une policière" or "un agent de police".
target_language_example: Il a dit qu'il était un flic, mais je ne l'ai pas cru.
native_language_example: He said he was a cop, but I didn’t believe him.

additional_notes: Means “a boy” (male child) or more generally “a young man/guy,” depending on context. It can also be used about someone’s child (“un garçon ou une fille ?” = “a boy or a girl?”). In some contexts, “garçon” can mean “waiter,” but that meaning usually appears when addressing staff (e.g., « Garçon ! ») or in restaurant context.
target_language_example: Il y a un garçon dans la classe.
native_language_example: There’s a boy in the class.

meaning: "a big/large" or "a great" (before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine noun to describe size (grand hôpital = large hospital; grand garçon = tall/big boy) or importance/degree (un grand sens des responsabilités = a strong/great sense of responsibility). Feminine form: "une grande"; plural: "des grands / des grandes". Often placed before the noun.
target_language_example: C'est un grand problème pour nous.
native_language_example: It's a big problem for us.

additional_notes: A warm, emphatic way to thank someone. Often used alone (spoken or written) or followed by “pour…” + noun/infinitive: “Un grand merci pour votre aide.” In writing you may also see “Un grand merci à tous !” (thanks to everyone).
target_language_example: Un grand merci pour ton message !
native_language_example: A big thank you for your message!

additional_notes: "Gros" is an adjective meaning "big/large" (size or importance) and it agrees with the noun: un gros risque (a big risk), un gros tube (a large tube), un gros problème (a big problem). With a person ("un gros type"), it often means "a big/heavy guy" and can sound rude or insensitive depending on context. For a woman, you’d say "une grosse" (e.g., une grosse erreur).
target_language_example: On a eu un gros problème hier soir.
native_language_example: We had a big problem last night.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone extremely intelligent or exceptionally talented (often in science, art, music, etc.). It can also be used more casually as a compliment for someone who found a clever solution: « Tu es un génie ! »
target_language_example: Tu es un génie : tu as trouvé la solution en deux minutes !
native_language_example: You’re a genius—you found the solution in two minutes!

additional_notes: Literally “a man.” Used to refer to a man in general or an unknown man (“un homme est venu…” = “a man came…”). In expressions like « devenir un homme » / « faire de lui un homme », it can mean “to become/make him a (grown) man,” implying adulthood or maturity depending on context.
target_language_example: C'est un homme très gentil.
native_language_example: He's a very kind man.

meaning: a good, decent man (a respectable person).
additional_notes: "Bien" here describes someone’s character, not that he is physically "well". You can also say "C’est quelqu’un de bien" (“He/She is a good person”).
target_language_example: Tout le monde dit que c’est un homme bien.
native_language_example: Everyone says he’s a good, decent man.

meaning: "a man who" (introduces a description about a man).
additional_notes: Used to start a relative clause describing a man: "un homme" + "qui" + verb. "Qui" refers back to "un homme" and is the subject of the following verb (e.g., "un homme qui travaille"). Often used with "connaître" (to know) or "être" (to be).
target_language_example: C'est un homme qui comprend vite.
native_language_example: He's a man who understands quickly.

additional_notes: “Riche” means “rich/wealthy” and agrees with the noun: “un homme riche” (a rich man). You can use the same pattern with other nouns (e.g., “une femme riche” = a rich woman).
target_language_example: C'est un homme riche, mais il est très simple.
native_language_example: He’s a rich man, but he’s very down-to-earth.

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article un (“a”). In conversation, you’ll often hear it when asking if there’s a hotel nearby: « Y a-t-il un hôtel… ? » or « Où il y a un hôtel ? ». « Tenir un hôtel » means “to run/own a hotel.”
target_language_example: Nous cherchons un hôtel pas trop cher.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a hotel that isn’t too expensive.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used to call someone stupid or to say someone seems stupid ("passer pour un idiot" = "to look like an idiot"; "prendre quelqu’un pour un idiot" = "to take someone for an idiot"). Strong and rude in many contexts; in formal situations avoid it. Feminine: "une idiote".
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas un idiot : je comprends très bien.
native_language_example: I'm not an idiot: I understand perfectly well.

meaning: a moment; a second (a very short time).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to wait briefly (often with verbs like « excuse-moi » or « attends »), or to say something will happen very soon (« dans un instant » = “in a moment”).
target_language_example: Attends un instant, j'arrive.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, I'm coming.

meaning: a game; (sometimes) play/just a game (not serious).
additional_notes: Usually means a game (a pastime, board game, video game, etc.). In expressions like « C’est (comme) un jeu » or « Tu crois que c’est un jeu ? », it can imply “this is just a game / you’re not taking it seriously” (often said to criticize or warn). With « jouer à », it names the game or activity: « jouer à un jeu ».
target_language_example: Pour lui, tout est un jeu, mais pour moi c’est sérieux.
native_language_example: For him, everything is a game, but for me it’s serious.

meaning: "one day, he..." (introducing a moment in a story; sometimes "someday, he...")
additional_notes: Used to set the scene and start a new event in a narrative: *Un jour, il + verb...* (= “One day, he + verb...”). Depending on context, *un jour* can mean a specific day in the past (“one day”) or an unspecified day in the future (“someday”), especially with future forms like *il faudra*.
target_language_example: Un jour, il a décidé de tout changer.
native_language_example: One day, he decided to change everything.

additional_notes: Used for time off from work or school (vacation/leave). Common with the verb « prendre »: « prendre un jour de congé » = to take a day off. You can also say « demander un jour de congé » (to request a day off).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un jour de congé demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to take a day off tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or estimate a short amount of time, often meaning “about a couple of days” rather than exactly 48 hours. Can be used with verbs like donner (give), rester (stay), or in time estimates with dans (in): « dans un jour ou deux » = “in a day or two.”
target_language_example: Je reviens dans un jour ou deux.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in a day or two.

additional_notes: A common Christmas greeting. Often used with souhaiter (“to wish”): « Je te/vous souhaite un joyeux Noël. » You can also say it by itself (« Un joyeux Noël ! ») or with « à + person » (“to”): « Un joyeux Noël à vous tous/toutes. »
target_language_example: Je te souhaite un joyeux Noël et une bonne année !
native_language_example: I wish you a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year!

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine indefinite article (“a/an”). The plural is "des livres" (“some books”). Don’t confuse "un livre" (a book) with "une livre" (a pound, a unit of weight).
target_language_example: J’ai acheté un livre en français.
native_language_example: I bought a book in French.

additional_notes: Used with avoir: "avoir mal à la tête" = to have a headache, and "avoir un mal de tête" is also common. You can add adjectives: "un gros mal de tête" (a bad headache).
target_language_example: J’ai un gros mal de tête, je vais me coucher tôt.
native_language_example: I have a bad headache, I'm going to bed early.

additional_notes: In France, "football" usually means soccer. If you mean American football, you often specify "football américain" (as in "un match de football américain"). "Match" is commonly used for sports games, especially team sports.
target_language_example: On va au stade pour voir un match de football ce soir.
native_language_example: We’re going to the stadium to watch a soccer match tonight.

meaning: a good guy; a decent guy.
additional_notes: “Mec” is informal for “guy” (like “dude”). Adding “bien” means the person is kind/reliable/respectable (“a good one”), not “good-looking.” You can say it directly to someone: « T’es un mec bien. »
target_language_example: Il m’a aidé sans rien demander : c’est vraiment un mec bien.
native_language_example: He helped me without asking for anything: he’s really a good guy.

additional_notes: Used for a note someone sends or leaves for you. With verbs like envoyer (send) and laisser (leave). You can also hear it as a notification: « Vous avez un message. »
target_language_example: Je t’envoie un message ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m sending you a message tonight.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun: un million de prisonniers (“a million prisoners”), un million de façons (“a million ways”). Very often it’s an exaggeration meaning “loads/so many,” especially in phrases like un million de fois (“a million times”) or un million de questions (“a million questions”).
target_language_example: J’ai un million de choses à faire aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: I have a million things to do today.

additional_notes: A literal amount of money. Often used in the idiom « la question à un million de dollars » (“the million-dollar question”), meaning a very important or hard question; « à un million de dollars » can also mean “worth a million dollars.”
target_language_example: Si je gagnais un million de dollars, je partirais faire le tour du monde.
