meaning: a second chance (another opportunity to try again).
additional_notes: Used when asking for or giving someone another opportunity after a mistake or failure. Very common with the verb donner: « Donner une seconde chance à quelqu’un » (to give someone a second chance).
target_language_example: Je te donne une seconde chance, mais ne recommence pas.
native_language_example: I'm giving you a second chance, but don't do it again.

additional_notes: Literally “one second,” but very often used loosely to mean “just a moment” in everyday requests: Donnez-moi une seconde. / Excusez-moi une seconde. You can also use it to mean “not even a second” with negation: Pas une seconde. / Je n’en ai que pour une seconde (“It’ll only take a second”). In some contexts it can be brusque (e.g., Fermez-la… une seconde = “Shut up for a second”).
target_language_example: Attends une seconde, j’arrive.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m coming.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for a week) or a time frame from now (in about a week). Often appears with prepositions like "dans" (in), "pendant" (for/during), and "en" (in, meaning the time it took to do something).
target_language_example: On part en voyage pour une semaine.
native_language_example: We’re going on a trip for a week.

meaning: a towel; also a napkin (at the table).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “towel” (bath towel, hand towel, etc.), especially with adjectives like humide (“wet”) or materials like coton (“cotton”). In restaurants it can also mean a “napkin” (serviette de table). The word is feminine: une serviette.
target_language_example: Après la douche, prends une serviette propre.
native_language_example: After the shower, take a clean towel.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is just one of something. It agrees with the noun: feminine singular noun → « une seule + noun » (une seule question). For masculine, use « un seul » (un seul problème). Often used in expressions like « une seule chose » (only one thing) or « une seule fois » (only once).
target_language_example: Je veux une seule réponse, pas dix excuses.
native_language_example: I want only one answer, not ten excuses.

meaning: a solution; an answer (to a problem).
additional_notes: Used when talking about solving a problem or finding a way out of a difficult situation. Often appears with verbs like "avoir" (to have), "trouver" (to find), and expressions like "il doit y avoir" / "il y aura" (there must be / there will be).
target_language_example: On va trouver une solution ensemble.
native_language_example: We'll find a solution together.

meaning: a kind of; sort of; a type of.
additional_notes: Used to describe something approximately, not exactly (often like “sort of” in English). It can also mean a category/type (“a kind/type of”). In speech you may also hear the shortened form “une sorte d’…” before a vowel.
target_language_example: C’est une sorte de problème, mais je ne sais pas comment l’expliquer.
native_language_example: It’s sort of a problem, but I don’t know how to explain it.

additional_notes: Used for an unexpected event/thing (“a surprise”) or for something meant to be kept secret until the reveal (“It was supposed to be a surprise”). Often with verbs like faire (to make/plan) and être (to be).
target_language_example: Ne lui dis rien : c'est une surprise !
native_language_example: Don't tell him anything: it's a surprise!

additional_notes: A common dessert. You’ll often see it with verbs like faire (to make) or confectionner (to make/prepare) and faire cuire (to bake/cook). Note: In French, faire une tarte aux pommes à quelqu’un can mean “to make an apple pie for someone.”
target_language_example: On prend une tarte aux pommes en dessert ?
native_language_example: Shall we have an apple pie for dessert?

meaning: “a cup of” (used to measure a drink).
additional_notes: Used before a drink or other liquid/food served in a cup (e.g., une tasse de café, de thé, de lait, de chocolat). The word after de often appears without an article: une tasse de café (not *une tasse du café*).
target_language_example: Je voudrais une tasse de thé, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a cup of tea, please.

additional_notes: Used to order or offer coffee. You can change the quantity word: « un café » (a coffee/espresso), « une tasse de thé » (a cup of tea). In questions/offers, it often appears with « vous voulez… ? » or « voudriez-vous… ? ».
target_language_example: J’aimerais une tasse de café, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I’d like a cup of coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used when offering or asking for tea. Very common in polite offers with "Voulez-vous… ?" or "Puis-je vous servir… ?". You can swap the drink: "une tasse de café" (a cup of coffee).
target_language_example: Je prends une tasse de thé, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have a cup of tea, please.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to emphasize degree or type: une telle opération (such an operation), une telle erreur (such a mistake). It agrees with the noun: un tel (masc. sing.), une telle (fem. sing.), de tels / de telles (plural). Often used for strong reactions (surprise, admiration, regret).
target_language_example: Je n’ai jamais vu une telle situation.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen such a situation.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an action or event (often shocking, surprising, or hard to believe) without naming it directly. It agrees in gender and number: une telle chose (feminine singular), un tel geste (masculine singular), de telles choses (plural).
target_language_example: Je n’arrive pas à croire qu’il ait dit une telle chose.
native_language_example: I can’t believe he said such a thing.

meaning: "a very beautiful" (feminine), before a feminine noun.
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun that follows (or is understood from context). Example: « une très belle semaine » = “a very beautiful week.” Masculine would be « un très beau … » (e.g., « un très beau jour »).
target_language_example: J'ai passé une très belle journée.
native_language_example: I had a very beautiful day / I had a wonderful day.

meaning: “a very good …” (feminine), or “a very good one.”
additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun: une très bonne chose (a very good thing), une très bonne question (a very good question). In context, it can also stand alone to mean “a very good one” when the noun is understood. Agreement matters: masculine would be « un très bon ».
target_language_example: Cette idée ? C’est une très bonne !
native_language_example: That idea? It’s a very good one!

additional_notes: Used to strongly approve a suggestion or plan. Often comes after "C’est..." ("It’s...") to evaluate something: "C’est une très bonne idée." You can also say someone "a une très bonne idée" to mean they came up with a very good idea.
target_language_example: Aller plus tôt, c’est une très bonne idée.
native_language_example: Going earlier is a very good idea.

additional_notes: Refers to someone’s life in general (their existence, experiences, lifestyle). Very common with adjectives or descriptions: une vie stressante (a stressful life), une vie tranquille (a quiet life), une vie meilleure (a better life), vivre/mener une vie… (to live/lead a … life). Can also refer to a single human life when something is at stake: Une vie est en jeu. (“A life is at risk.”).
target_language_example: Elle veut mener une vie simple et heureuse.
native_language_example: She wants to lead a simple and happy life.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s life as generally happy or satisfying, often with verbs like vivre (to live) or avoir (to have): vivre une vie heureuse, avoir une vie heureuse. It’s a neutral, common phrase.
target_language_example: Elle espère mener une vie heureuse en France.
native_language_example: She hopes to live a happy life in France.

meaning: an old woman (can sound rude); also “an old …” before a feminine noun.
additional_notes: As an adjective, vieille agrees with feminine nouns: une vieille photo, une vieille voiture. Before a vowel sound it becomes vieil(le) amie → une vieille amie (same spelling, pronounced with a linking sound). Used alone as a noun (une vieille) often feels informal or dismissive; une vieille femme is more neutral/polite.
target_language_example: Une vieille femme a besoin d’aide pour traverser la rue.
native_language_example: An elderly woman needs help crossing the street.

additional_notes: "Une" is the feminine form of "a/an." "Voiture" is a common word for a (passenger) car. Often used with location phrases like "dans l'allée" (in the driveway) or with verbs of movement like "passer" (to go by/pass).
target_language_example: J'ai une voiture, mais je vais au travail en bus.
native_language_example: I have a car, but I go to work by bus.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to emphasize that something is genuine or the "real deal": une vraie lettre (a real letter), une vraie amie (a true friend), une vraie beauté (a real beauty). It’s the feminine form of the adjective vrai/vraie; use un vrai before a masculine noun (un vrai ami). Sometimes it can also be used for strong emphasis or (depending on tone) irony.
target_language_example: C'est une vraie surprise !
native_language_example: It's a real surprise!

additional_notes: Used for the streak of light you see when a small space rock burns up in the atmosphere. In French, you often say "voir une étoile filante" (to see a shooting star) and "faire un vœu" when you see one.
target_language_example: J’ai vu une étoile filante hier soir.
native_language_example: I saw a shooting star last night.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is unlike any other (often in a positive, admiring way). You can use it as a full sentence for emphasis: « Unique en son genre. »
target_language_example: Ce restaurant est unique en son genre dans la ville.
native_language_example: This restaurant is one of a kind in the city.

additional_notes: Inversion of the verb and subject pronoun for asking a question in formal French ("vous"). Used when speaking politely to one person or to several people. With "utiliser" it asks about using something, or using something as something else ("Utilisez-vous cette cabane comme maison ?").
target_language_example: Utilisez-vous cette application tous les jours ?
native_language_example: Do you use this app every day?

meaning: “is she going to…?” / “will it…?” (formal question with *elle*).
additional_notes: This is question inversion with the verb *aller* (used for the near future: *aller + infinitive*). *Elle* can mean “she” or “it” (referring to a feminine noun like *la tempête*, *la pluie*). The *-t-* is added only for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel: *va-t-elle…?*
target_language_example: À quelle heure va-t-elle arriver ?
native_language_example: What time is she going to arrive?

additional_notes: Question form with inversion of the verb aller: "il va" → "va-t-il". Used to ask about what a man/it (il) is going to do, or about the future in general (often translated as "will it…?"). The -t- is added only for pronunciation when a verb ending in a vowel is followed by "il" (or "elle", "on").
target_language_example: Va-t-il venir ce soir ?
native_language_example: Is he going to come tonight?

additional_notes: This is the inverted question form of the near future (aller + infinitive): "on va + infinitive" → "va-t-on + infinitive ?". "On" often means “we” in everyday French, but it can also mean “people/one” in a more general sense depending on context. The -t- is inserted for pronunciation between two vowels: "va-t-on".
target_language_example: Va-t-on trouver une solution rapidement ?
native_language_example: Are we going to find a solution quickly?

meaning: 'is going to go' / 'will go'; also 'will be okay' (in expressions like « ça va aller »).
additional_notes: « va » is the present tense of aller (to go) for il/elle/on, so « il/elle/on va aller… » often expresses the near future (like “is going to…”). It can be followed by: an adverb (« Il va aller plus lentement. » = “He’ll go more slowly.”), a place with « à » (« Il va aller à Boston. »), or a state (« Il va aller mieux. » = “He’ll get better.”). In « Tout/Ça va aller (bien) », it means “Everything/It will be OK.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tout va aller bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything will be fine.

meaning: "is going to happen/occur" or "is going to arrive".
additional_notes: "Va" is the present tense of aller (to go) used for the near future: aller + infinitive = "going to". With arriver, it often means either (1) an event will happen (Quelque chose va arriver.), or (2) someone/something will arrive (Il va arriver d'une minute à l'autre.). Context usually makes it clear.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, tout va arriver en son temps.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything will happen in its own time.

additional_notes: From the verb *aller* (to go). Used to talk about how someone is doing (health, mood, situation): *il/elle va bien* = “he/she is doing well.” You can also say *ça va bien* (“it’s going well / I’m fine”).
target_language_example: Après l'accident, il va bien.
native_language_example: After the accident, he’s doing well.

meaning: “is going to … soon” (something will happen soon).
additional_notes: Used with the near-future construction **aller + infinitive**: **il/elle/on va bientôt + infinitive** (or **je vais bientôt**, **nous allons bientôt**, etc.). **Bientôt** usually goes between the form of **aller** and the infinitive. Often translated as “soon” / “before long.”
target_language_example: Je vais bientôt partir.
native_language_example: I’m going to leave soon.

meaning: 'is going to have to' (will need to; will be obliged to).
additional_notes: Formed with aller (va) + devoir + infinitive: it expresses a near-future necessity/obligation. You’ll also see other subject forms: je vais devoir, tu vas devoir, on va devoir, ils vont devoir, etc.
target_language_example: Je vais devoir partir tôt demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to have to leave early tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Va" is the present tense of aller used to form the near future: aller + infinitive. "Va durer" is used to say something will continue for a certain length of time, often with a duration (deux heures) or with words like "longtemps" (a long time) and "un moment" (a while).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, ça ne va pas durer longtemps.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s not going to last long.

meaning: “is going to do / will do” (near future); sometimes “will make”.
additional_notes: This is the near-future construction: **aller (va)** + **infinitive (faire)**. It’s used to say what someone is about to do soon: *Qu’est-ce qu’elle va faire ?* = “What is she going to do?” With **ça**, it can mean “it will make/produce” or “it will look/seem”: *Ça va faire vrai* = “It’s going to look real.”
target_language_example: Je vais faire les courses ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to do the grocery shopping tonight.

meaning: "will have to" / "it’s going to be necessary".
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "il va falloir" (impersonal: "it will be necessary"). In speech, people often drop "il" and just say "va falloir". Common patterns: "va falloir + infinitive" (Va falloir être patient.) and "va falloir que + subject + subjunctive" (Va falloir que tu ranges.). Often implies obligation or necessity, like "we’ll have to".
target_language_example: Va falloir qu’on parte maintenant.
native_language_example: We’ll have to leave now.

meaning: “is going to work” / “will work” (also literally: “is going to walk”).
additional_notes: Most often used with "ça" or "cela" to mean something will work out or function: "Ça va marcher ?" = "Will it work?". Literally, "marcher" means "to walk", so in context (especially with a person/animal as the subject) it can mean "is going to walk".
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, ça va marcher.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’ll work.

additional_notes: This is the near future ("aller" + infinitive): "ça va prendre..." = "it’s going to take..." (often about time). In the imperative, "Va prendre..." tells someone to go do something: "Va prendre ton bain" (go take your bath), "Va prendre l’air" (go get some fresh air). You’ll also see it inside common expressions like "prendre une raclée" (to get a beating).
target_language_example: Ça va prendre cinq minutes.
native_language_example: It’s going to take five minutes.

meaning: 'is going to' + a reflexive verb (near future), like 'is going to get/handle/improve'.
additional_notes: This is the start of the near-future tense: **aller (va)** + infinitive. Here it’s followed by a reflexive verb starting with a vowel, so **se** becomes **s'** (e.g., *va s'en remettre*, *va s'en occuper*, *va s'améliorer*). The full pattern is **il/elle/on va + s' + infinitive** (or **je vais / tu vas / nous allons / vous allez / ils vont**).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, ça va s'arranger.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s going to work itself out.

meaning: 'it'll work out' / 'it'll be okay' (things will get better or be resolved).
additional_notes: From the verb "s'arranger" (to work out / to get sorted out). Very common with "ça" or "tout": "Ça va s'arranger" / "Tout va s'arranger" to reassure someone after a problem. Also used about situations resolving themselves (a conflict, a mistake, a delay, etc.).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, ça va s'arranger.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’ll work out.

additional_notes: Used in the near future tense: **aller (present)** + **se + infinitive**. It means someone/something is about to do an action to itself or that will happen "by itself" (common with things breaking, expanding, etc.). Changes with the subject: **je vais me… / tu vas te… / il/elle/on va se… / nous allons nous… / vous allez vous… / ils/elles vont se…**.
target_language_example: Attention, ça va se renverser !
native_language_example: Careful, it’s going to tip over!

additional_notes: From the verb phrase « se passer » (“to happen,” “to take place”). « va se passer » is the near future: « aller » (va) + infinitive (se passer). Often used in questions like « Qu’est-ce qu’il va se passer ? » (“What’s going to happen?”). Not the same as English “to pass.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas : rien ne va se passer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: nothing is going to happen.

additional_notes: This is the start of the near-future tense: **aller (va)** + infinitive. **Te** is the unstressed object pronoun (“you” as the object) and it comes **before** the infinitive: *Il va te chercher* (“He’s going to look for you / pick you up”). You’ll often see it in patterns like **ça va te plaire** (“you’re going to like it”), **personne ne va te remarquer** (“no one will notice you”).
target_language_example: Je vais te rappeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to call you back tonight.

additional_notes: Uses aller (va) + infinitive (être) to talk about what will happen soon or what you expect will be the case. Changes with the subject: je vais être, tu vas être, il/elle/on va être, nous allons être, vous allez être, ils/elles vont être.
target_language_example: Demain, ça va être compliqué.
native_language_example: Tomorrow, it’s going to be complicated.

meaning: Extra “-t-” used in questions after a verb ending in a vowel (e.g., va-t-il? = does he go?/is it going?).
additional_notes: This “-t-” is added for pronunciation (a liaison sound) in subject–verb inversion, mainly before il/elle/on: va-t-il, va-t-elle, va-t-on. It has no meaning by itself; the meaning comes from the verb (aller: va… = goes/is going; aller can also mean “to suit/fit” as in Ça me va). You don’t use it if the verb already ends in -t or -d (e.g., part-il ?).
target_language_example: Comment va-t-on y aller ?
native_language_example: How are we going to get there?

additional_notes: Imperative ("tu" form) of the verb phrase "s’en aller" (to leave/go away). Often used as an order and can sound rude or angry, especially with "Laisse-moi tranquille !" You’ll also see it written "va-t’en" (with an apostrophe).
target_language_example: Va-t’en, je suis occupé.
native_language_example: Go away, I’m busy.

additional_notes: Question form with inversion of the verb aller: "il va" → "va-t-il". Used to ask about what a man/it (il) is going to do, or about the future in general (often translated as "will it…?"). The -t- is added only for pronunciation when a verb ending in a vowel is followed by "il" (or "elle", "on").
target_language_example: Va-t-il venir ce soir ?
native_language_example: Is he going to come tonight?

additional_notes: From the verb *aller* (to go). Used to talk about how someone is doing (health, mood, situation): *il/elle va bien* = “he/she is doing well.” You can also say *ça va bien* (“it’s going well / I’m fine”).
target_language_example: Après l'accident, il va bien.
native_language_example: After the accident, he’s doing well.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "aller" to say something (often clothes, but also a job/role/mission) fits someone extremely well. Pattern: "Ça/Cette robe/ce travail + me/te/lui/vous + va comme un gant." Similar idea to English "fits like a glove."
target_language_example: Ce costume me va comme un gant.
native_language_example: This suit fits me perfectly.

additional_notes: From the verb aller (to go). In full standard French you usually say ne va pas (he/she/it doesn’t go) or n’y va pas (don’t go there). In everyday speech, ne is often dropped: Ça va pas = “It’s not OK / It’s not going well.” With reflexive/en: ne t’en va pas = “don’t leave / don’t go away.”
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas venir : ça va pas aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I’m not doing well today.

meaning: “go and get …” (often used as a rude insult, like “go fuck yourself”).
additional_notes: Literally “go (and) make yourself …”, but it’s normally followed by another verb/phrase (e.g., va te faire foutre / va te faire voir / va te faire niquer). In practice it’s frequently used as an aggressive, very vulgar way to tell someone off, especially with niquer.
target_language_example: Va te faire voir !
native_language_example: Get lost!

additional_notes: Very vulgar and aggressive. Used to tell someone to go away or express strong anger/contempt. Avoid in polite conversation; it can easily start a fight. Common variants: "Va te faire voir !" (less vulgar), "Va te faire foutre !" is among the strongest.
target_language_example: Si tu continues à m’insulter, je te bloque—alors va te faire foutre.
native_language_example: If you keep insulting me, I’m blocking you—so fuck off.

meaning: fits you very well / suits you very well; (also) is doing very well.
additional_notes: From the verb "aller". With clothing/colors, "(ça) va très bien (à + someone)" means it looks good on someone: "Ce manteau vous va très bien" = "That coat suits you very well." With people/things, it means someone/something is doing fine/very well: "Elle va très bien" / "Sa famille va très bien." You can also use it as an answer about how things are going: "Oui, ça va très bien."
target_language_example: Cette couleur te va très bien.
native_language_example: That color suits you very well.

meaning: "goes to the" / "go to the" (with a feminine destination).
additional_notes: Form of the verb aller (to go) + à la (“to the” before a feminine singular noun). It can describe someone going somewhere (Elle/Il va à la…) or be an instruction (Va à la… = “Go to the…”). Common with places and activities: à la librairie (to the bookstore), à la messe (to Mass).
target_language_example: Elle va à la bibliothèque après l’école.
native_language_example: She goes to the library after school.

additional_notes: "Vais-je" is the 1st person singular of aller (je vais) used in inversion to form a formal/literary question: "Vais-je + infinitive ?" = "Am I going to + verb?" In everyday speech, people more often say "Est-ce que je vais... ?" or "Je vais... ?".
target_language_example: Vais-je devoir payer maintenant ?
native_language_example: Am I going to have to pay now?

meaning: “I’m going to (do) it / (do) it to him/it.”
additional_notes: Used with the near-future tense: **je vais + infinitive** (“I’m going to + verb”). **Le** is a direct object pronoun placed **before** the infinitive: *Je vais le prendre* (“I’m going to take it”). What **le** refers to depends on context (often “it”; sometimes “him”). It can also change to **la** (her/it-feminine) or **les** (them): *Je vais la prendre / Je vais les prendre.*
target_language_example: Pas maintenant : je vais le faire après.
native_language_example: Not now: I’m going to do it later.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the full sentence "Je vais le faire" (near-future tense: aller + infinitive) to express an intention or something you’re about to do. "Le" means "it" (a previously mentioned thing). You can emphasize who will do it with "C’est moi qui vais le faire" ("I’m the one who’s going to do it").
target_language_example: T’inquiète, je vais le faire ce soir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to do it tonight.

meaning: 'I’m going to take' / 'I’m going to have'.
additional_notes: Used with the near future tense: **je vais + infinitive**. **Prendre** is very common and can mean 'take' (a bus/taxi), 'take' (medicine), or 'have' (food/drink): *Je vais prendre le bus / un taxi / mes médocs / un café*.
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un café avant de partir.
native_language_example: I’m going to have a coffee before leaving.

meaning: "I’m going to (do something) to/for you" (je vais + te…).
additional_notes: Used with "je vais" to talk about the near future: "Je vais te + verb" = "I’m going to + verb + you". "Te" is an object pronoun meaning "to you" or "you" (depending on the verb) and it comes before the verb: "Je vais te dire" (I’m going to tell you), "Je vais te laisser" (I’m going to leave you/let you). Often followed by another pronoun: "Je vais te le dire" (I’m going to tell it to you).
target_language_example: Je vais te montrer comment ça marche.
native_language_example: I’m going to show you how it works.

meaning: “I’m going to see…” / “I’ll go see…” (near future of *voir*).
additional_notes: Formed with *aller* (present) + infinitive: *je vais voir* + person/thing. It can mean “go visit/see someone” (*je vais voir Patsy*), or “go check/find out” (*je vais voir ce que je peux faire* = “I’ll see what I can do”).
target_language_example: Attends une minute, je vais voir si le magasin est encore ouvert.
native_language_example: Wait a minute, I’m going to see if the store is still open.

additional_notes: Used with the subject “je” as “je vais bien” to say you’re fine or doing well, often as an answer to “Ça va ?” or “Comment ça va ?”. It can also reassure someone (like “I’m okay, really”). In speech, it’s often shortened to “ça va” or “je vais bien, merci.”
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, je vais bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m fine.

meaning: was worth it / was worth the effort.
additional_notes: From "valoir la peine" = "to be worth it" (literally, "to be worth the trouble/effort"). Used to say something was worthwhile after doing it. Often appears as "Ça valait la peine de + infinitive" (Ça valait la peine d'attendre = It was worth waiting) or "en valoir la peine" (le voyage en valait la peine = the trip was worth it). Tense changes: "vaut la peine" (present), "valait la peine" (imperfect/past).
target_language_example: Même s’il faisait froid, la promenade valait la peine.
native_language_example: Even though it was cold, the walk was worth it.

meaning: "are you going to…?" / "do you go…?" (question form of *tu vas*).
additional_notes: *Vas-tu* is the inverted (more formal) way to ask a question with *tu vas* (from *aller*, “to go”). It’s used (1) with another verb to talk about the near future: *Vas-tu rester ?* (“Are you going to stay?”), and (2) by itself or with a place to ask if someone is going somewhere: *Vas-tu à la réunion ?* (“Are you going to the meeting?”). In casual speech, you’ll often hear *Tu vas… ?* instead of *Vas-tu… ?*.
target_language_example: Vas-tu venir avec nous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you going to come with us tonight?

additional_notes: Used with "tu" to form the near future: "tu vas faire ..." = "you’re going to do ...". Very common in questions like "Tu vas faire quoi ?" (What are you going to do?) and "Comment tu vas faire ?" (How are you going to do it?/How will you manage?).
target_language_example: Tu vas faire quoi ce soir ?
native_language_example: What are you going to do tonight?

meaning: "are you going to…?" / "do you go…?" (question form of *tu vas*).
additional_notes: *Vas-tu* is the inverted (more formal) way to ask a question with *tu vas* (from *aller*, “to go”). It’s used (1) with another verb to talk about the near future: *Vas-tu rester ?* (“Are you going to stay?”), and (2) by itself or with a place to ask if someone is going somewhere: *Vas-tu à la réunion ?* (“Are you going to the meeting?”). In casual speech, you’ll often hear *Tu vas… ?* instead of *Vas-tu… ?*.
target_language_example: Vas-tu venir avec nous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you going to come with us tonight?

meaning: "Go ahead, go ahead" / "Come on, come on" (urging or encouraging someone).
additional_notes: Repeated for emphasis. Used a lot in spoken French to push someone to act, to give permission ("go ahead"), or to show impatience/pressure ("come on!"). Very common and informal; tone depends on context and can sound supportive or annoyed.
target_language_example: Vas-y, vas-y, dis-lui la vérité !
native_language_example: Come on, come on, tell him the truth!

meaning: is worth it; is worth the effort.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something is worth doing: « Ça vaut la peine de + infinitive » (e.g., « Ça vaut la peine d’essayer. »). You can also use it to say something is worth it in general: « Ça vaut la peine. »
target_language_example: Ce film vaut la peine d’être vu.
native_language_example: This movie is worth seeing.

meaning: is worth it / is worth doing.
additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort, time, money, or trouble. Often followed by "de" + infinitive: "Ça vaut le coup de + verb" (It’s worth + -ing). Can also be used on its own: "Ça vaut le coup" (It’s worth it).
target_language_example: Ça vaut le coup d'essayer une fois.
native_language_example: It’s worth trying once.

additional_notes: From the verb *valoir* (“to be worth”). Often used in the full form **il vaut mieux + infinitive** (“it’s better to…”): *Il vaut mieux partir tôt.* In speech, **il** is often dropped: *Vaut mieux partir.* You can also use **vaut mieux que + subjunctive** (“it’s better that…”): *Vaut mieux que je parte / que tu répondes.* The short form **Vaut mieux pas** is a very common, informal-sounding way to say “Better not.”
target_language_example: Vaut mieux qu’on rentre maintenant, il se fait tard.
native_language_example: We’d better go home now; it’s getting late.

additional_notes: From the verb *valoir* (“to be worth”). Used to compare two options: **X vaut mieux que Y** (“X is better than Y”). Very common in proverbs and general statements. You can use nouns (**La santé vaut mieux que la richesse**) or infinitives (**Prévenir vaut mieux que guérir**). The plural is **valent mieux que** (e.g., *Ces solutions valent mieux que celles-là*).
target_language_example: Dans ce cas, il vaut mieux que tu partes tôt.
native_language_example: In that case, it’s better that you leave early.

additional_notes: "vend" is the present tense of "vendre" (to sell) for il/elle/on (he/she/one). "des" usually means "some" or "(plural) a/an" before a plural noun (des légumes = some vegetables). Used to say what someone sells.
target_language_example: Elle vend des livres au marché.
native_language_example: She sells books at the market.

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans or availability on Friday evening. In French, "soir" is the evening/night period; depending on context, it often matches English "Friday night" (e.g., going out) or "Friday evening" (e.g., dinner).
target_language_example: On se voit vendredi soir ?
native_language_example: Are we seeing each other Friday night?

meaning: "do you come" / "are you coming"? (formal or plural "you").
additional_notes: Inversion of the verb and subject pronoun to form a question: "venez" (you come/are coming) + "vous". Used for formal "you" (one person) or plural "you". Often appears in questions about where someone comes from ("Venez-vous de… ?" = "Are you from…?") or whether they’re coming ("Venez-vous ou non ?").
target_language_example: Venez-vous avec nous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you coming with us tonight?

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) addressed to “vous” (one person formally or several people). Used to ask/tell someone to accompany you; can be followed by a destination: « Venez avec moi à… ».
target_language_example: Venez avec moi au bureau, s’il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Come with me to the office, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that you will accompany someone. Very common in questions like « Je peux venir avec toi/vous ? » (“Can I come with you?”). Object pronouns (toi, vous, lui, eux, etc.) usually follow « avec ».
target_language_example: Tu veux que je vienne avec toi au supermarché ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to come with you to the supermarket?

additional_notes: Used to invite, ask, or tell someone to accompany you. Very common with questions or polite requests like « Tu pourrais venir avec moi ? » and « Tu veux bien venir avec moi ? ». You can swap the pronoun: « venir avec toi » (with you), « venir avec lui/elle » (with him/her), « venir avec nous/vous/eux/elles » (with us/you/them).
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu peux venir avec moi au magasin ?
native_language_example: Can you come with me to the store?

additional_notes: Used to invite someone to join your group. "Venir" is "to come" (toward the speaker), and "avec nous" means "with us." Often used in questions or polite invitations: "Peux-tu venir avec nous ?" / "Voudriez-vous venir avec nous… ?"
target_language_example: Si tu veux, tu peux venir avec nous au cinéma.
native_language_example: If you want, you can come with us to the movie theater.

additional_notes: Used to talk about moving toward the speaker’s location (“here”). Often follows verbs like aimer/pouvoir/devoir: « Tu veux venir ici ? »
target_language_example: Tu peux venir ici, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you come here, please?

meaning: to come see me; to come visit me.
additional_notes: Used to invite or request that someone come to your place (or come to meet you) for a visit. The pronoun changes with the person: venir te voir (come see you), venir le/la voir (come see him/her), venir nous voir (come see us), venir vous voir (come see you/formal or plural), venir les voir (come see them). Often follows another verb: pouvoir venir me voir (can come see me), devoir venir me voir (should come see me), demander de venir me voir (ask to come see me).
target_language_example: Tu veux venir me voir ce week-end ?
native_language_example: Do you want to come see me this weekend?

additional_notes: Past participle of venir (“to come”) + ici (“here”), used with être in the passé composé: je suis venu(e) ici, tu es venu(e) ici, il est venu ici, elle est venue ici, etc. Means someone came to this place (often “here,” where the speaker is).
target_language_example: Je suis venu ici pour te voir.
native_language_example: I came here to see you.

meaning: "came here to" / "came here in order to" (to express purpose).
additional_notes:
Used with a subject + venir (conjugated) + ici + pour + infinitive to say why someone came. 
- Agreement with the subject: venu (m. sg.), venue (f. sg.), venus (m. pl.), venues (f. pl.).
- Often interchangeable with « venir ici afin de… » (more formal) or « venir ici pour + noun » (e.g., « pour le travail »).
- « ici » can be replaced by « là » depending on context.
target_language_example: Je suis venue ici pour apprendre le français.
native_language_example: I came here to learn French.

meaning: came to see me; came to visit me.
additional_notes: Past tense of « venir me voir » (“to come see/visit me”). Uses « être » in the passé composé: « il/tu est(es) venu(e) me voir ». The past participle can agree with the subject (venu/venue/venus/venues). The object pronoun « me » goes before the infinitive « voir ».
target_language_example: Elle est venue me voir après le travail.
native_language_example: She came to see me after work.

verrais-tu un inconvénient à ce que

target_language_multi_word_term: verrais-tu un inconvénient à ce que
meaning: 'Would you mind if…?' / 'Would it be a problem if…?'
additional_notes: A polite way to ask permission or check if something would bother someone. Uses the conditional of voir (verrais-tu = would you see) to soften the request. The verb after « à ce que » is in the subjunctive: « …à ce que je fasse / jette / parte / rentre ». You can also use « verriez-vous… » for formal situations.
target_language_example: Verrais-tu un inconvénient à ce que j'ouvre la fenêtre ?
native_language_example: Would you mind if I opened the window?

verriez-vous un inconvénient à ce que

target_language_multi_word_term: verriez-vous un inconvénient à ce que
meaning: “Would you mind if…?” / “Would you have any objection to…?”
additional_notes: Very polite, formal way to ask permission. It’s built on the conditional of voir (“verriez-vous…”) and is typically followed by “à ce que” + a verb in the subjunctive: “Verriez-vous un inconvénient à ce que je parte… ?” (literally, “Would you see a drawback if I…?”).
target_language_example: Verriez-vous un inconvénient à ce que j’ouvre la fenêtre ?
native_language_example: Would you mind if I opened the window?

meaning: "toward the" (in the direction of a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement toward something: a place (vers la ville), a side (vers la gauche), etc. It’s made of vers (“toward”) + la (“the” for feminine singular nouns). Compare: vers le (masculine singular) and vers les (plural).
target_language_example: On va vers la gare.
native_language_example: We’re going toward the train station.

meaning: "toward the" / "in the direction of the" (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun to show direction or movement toward something: vers le haut (upwards), vers le plafond (toward the ceiling), vers le Nord (toward the North). You can use it after verbs like aller (to go), regarder (to look), partir (to leave), lever (to raise). Note: unlike à + le → au, there is no contraction here—it's always vers le.
target_language_example: On marche vers le centre-ville.
native_language_example: We’re walking toward downtown.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction (where someone/something is heading), often with verbs like se diriger (to head), aller/partir (to go/leave), or filer (to dash off). You can also say it alone on a map or as a short instruction: « Vers le nord. »
target_language_example: On marche vers le nord pour rejoindre le village.
native_language_example: We’re walking toward the north to reach the village.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement in the direction of the south. Common with movement verbs like aller, marcher, voler, se diriger. You can also say simply "au sud" for a location (in the south), but "vers le sud" emphasizes heading that way.
target_language_example: Nous allons vers le sud pour les vacances.
native_language_example: We're going south for vacation.

meaning: 'does he want' / 'does he really want it?' (question form).
additional_notes: This is the verb–subject inversion used to form a question in more formal French: "veut" (wants) + "-il" (he) with a hyphen. It’s equivalent to "Est-ce qu’il veut… ?" or the informal spoken order "Il veut… ?". Used with a following infinitive or object: "Où veut-il aller ?" (Where does he want to go?), "Le veut-il ?" (Does he want it?).
target_language_example: Veut-il venir avec nous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Does he want to come with us tonight?

additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning of a word, phrase, sign, or situation. Often appears in questions: « Qu’est-ce que ça veut dire ? » (What does that mean?) and « Que veut dire… ? » (What does … mean?). « Ce qui veut dire… » means “which means… / that is to say…”.
target_language_example: Ça veut dire quoi, « rendez-vous » ?
native_language_example: What does “rendez-vous” mean?

additional_notes: Used in spoken French to ask for the meaning of a word/phrase: "Ça veut dire quoi ?" (very common). More formal/neutral equivalents are "Qu’est-ce que ça veut dire ?" or "Que veut dire … ?" You can replace "quoi" with the word you’re asking about: "Ziri, ça veut dire quoi ?"
target_language_example: « Bizarre », ça veut dire quoi ?
native_language_example: What does “bizarre” mean?

meaning: 'wants to see you' (wants to meet/speak with you).
additional_notes: Used when someone is asking to meet you or talk to you. Often sounds like a summons when the subject is an authority figure (le directeur, le patron, etc.). You can add details like where/when: « Il/Elle veut te voir en bas / maintenant ». Adding « toi » emphasizes *you* specifically: « Il veut te voir toi, pas moi ».
target_language_example: Le médecin veut te voir tout de suite.
native_language_example: The doctor wants to see you right away.

additional_notes: "Veux-tu" is the inverted question form of "tu veux" (from "vouloir", to want). It’s used to ask if someone wants something or wants to do something: "Veux-tu un café ?" / "Veux-tu venir ?". With object pronouns it often becomes "Veux-tu le/la/les… ?" (= Do you want it/him/her/them?). In everyday speech, people often prefer "Tu veux… ?" or the more polite "Voulez-vous… ?".
target_language_example: Veux-tu venir avec nous ce soir ?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with us tonight?

additional_notes: Formed with **vouloir** (veux) + **tu** + **aller**. The **-tu** is an **inversion** used to ask a question (a slightly more formal/neutral way than *Tu veux aller… ?*). Often followed by a place (*Où veux-tu aller ?*) or an infinitive to say “go do something” (*Veux-tu aller prendre un verre ?*).
target_language_example: Veux-tu aller au café après le travail ?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to the café after work?

additional_notes: A common way to offer something. It uses inversion for questions: *veux-tu* = “do you want?”. *Du* is the partitive article (*de + le*) meaning “some” (typically with masculine singular or uncountable nouns): *du beurre, du ketchup, du citron*. For feminine nouns you’d use *de la* (*veux-tu de la salade ?*), and before a vowel/h mute *de l’* (*veux-tu de l’eau ?*).
target_language_example: Veux-tu du café ?
native_language_example: Do you want some coffee?

meaning: "do you want to do" (asking what someone wants to do/make).
additional_notes: Formed with the verb *vouloir* (to want) + inversion (*veux-tu* = “do you want?”) + an infinitive. Very common in questions about plans/choices: *Que veux-tu faire ?* (“What do you want to do?”). It can also be used before a noun phrase where *faire* means “to do” or “to make”: *faire la liste* (“make the list”), *faire des études* (“do studies / study”).
target_language_example: Que veux-tu faire ce week-end ?
native_language_example: What do you want to do this weekend?

additional_notes: A common, polite/informal question using inversion (verb + -tu) with "tu". Often followed by: "avec" + person (Veux-tu jouer avec moi ?), "en ligne" (online), or "à" + game/activity (jouer à cache-cache, jouer à un jeu).
target_language_example: Veux-tu jouer avec moi après l'école ?
native_language_example: Do you want to play with me after school?

additional_notes: Question formed with inversion: « veux-tu… ? » = “do you want…?” and « manger » = “to eat.” Often used on its own (« Veux-tu manger ? ») or with what to eat: « Veux-tu manger un morceau / un bout ? » = “Do you want to eat a piece / have a bite?” You can also add timing: « Quand veux-tu manger ? » = “When do you want to eat?”
target_language_example: Tu veux manger maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do you want to eat now?

meaning: "Do you want to… (with me as the object)?"
additional_notes: This is the verb "vouloir" (to want) in a yes/no question using inversion: "veux-tu…?" = "do you want…?" It’s usually followed by an infinitive, and "me" means "me" (the person receiving the action): "Veux-tu me parler ?" (Do you want to talk to me?), "Veux-tu me rencontrer ?" (Do you want to meet me?). In everyday speech you’ll also often hear "Tu veux…?" instead of the more formal-sounding inversion.
target_language_example: Veux-tu me dire la vérité ?
native_language_example: Do you want to tell me the truth?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants to happen or what they want someone else to do. It’s the inverted question form of "tu veux que…" and it’s normally followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "Veux-tu que je vienne ?").
target_language_example: Veux-tu que je t’aide avec tes devoirs ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you with your homework?

additional_notes: Used to offer to do something (or ask for instructions). It’s the inverted-question form of "Tu veux que je…" and is followed by a verb in the subjunctive: "Veux-tu que je demande / garde / laisse / prévienne / recommence / rentre / répète / traite… ?" In more formal/polite speech you can also say: "Voulez-vous que je… ?"
target_language_example: Veux-tu que je t’aide avec ça ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you with that?

meaning: "do you want me to be" (asking what role/state someone wants you to have).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants or expects you to be (a person, role, or condition). It uses inversion for a question (veux-tu = "do you want") and the subjunctive after "vouloir que" (que je sois, from être). You can change "sois" to match the subject: que tu sois, qu’il/elle soit, que nous soyons, etc.
target_language_example: Veux-tu que je sois plus discret(e) ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to be more discreet?

meaning: "Do you want me to (do something) for you?"
additional_notes: Used to offer to do something for someone or ask for their preference. Literally "do you want that I to you..."; it’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., je te montre, je te prenne, je te réveille). "Te" means "to you" or "you" as an object, depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Veux-tu que je te prépare un café ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to make you a coffee?

additional_notes: Question form with inversion: "veux" (you want) + "tu" (you) + "savoir" (to know). Often followed by a question word or clause: "Veux-tu savoir pourquoi…?" (why), "qui…?" (who), or "ce que…" (what). More formal/neutral than "Tu veux savoir… ?"
target_language_example: Veux-tu savoir ce qui s'est passé ?
native_language_example: Do you want to know what happened?

meaning: "Do you want a…?" (asking if someone wants one item).
additional_notes: Uses inversion for a question: "Veux-tu…?" = "Do you want…?". "Un" is the masculine singular article (a/an/one). Before a feminine noun, use "veux-tu une…?".
target_language_example: Veux-tu un café ?
native_language_example: Do you want a coffee?

meaning: "do you really want to...?" (emphasizes doubt or surprise).
additional_notes: Formed with verb–subject inversion (veux + tu) to ask a question. Commonly followed by an infinitive: "Veux-tu vraiment faire/voir/savoir... ?" You can make it more neutral/less direct with: "Est-ce que tu veux vraiment... ?"
target_language_example: Veux-tu vraiment partir maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do you really want to leave now?

meaning: “(you) mean”; “to mean” (as in: what do you mean?).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "vouloir dire" (literally “to want to say”), used to ask for clarification or to check understanding: "Qu’est-ce que tu veux dire ?" = “What do you mean?” / "Tu vois ce que je veux dire ?" = “You see what I mean?” Often appears inside "ce que ... veut dire" (“what ... means”). In fast speech you may hear contractions like "c’que j’veux dire".
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you mean.

additional_notes: From the verb "vouloir" (to want): "tu veux faire + infinitive" is a very common way to say what someone wants to do. It’s often used in questions like "Qu’est-ce que tu veux faire ?" (What do you want to do?) and can also express refusal or preference: "C’est la dernière chose que je veux faire" (That’s the last thing I want to do). You’ll frequently add another verb after it: "Tu veux faire quoi ?" / "Tu veux faire ça ?"
target_language_example: Tu veux faire quoi ce soir ?
native_language_example: What do you want to do tonight?

additional_notes: Very common spoken form of « (ne) veux pas », where « ne » is dropped in casual speech: « j’en veux pas » = « je n’en veux pas ». Often used with object pronouns like « en » (some/any of it) or « le/la/les » (it/them): « Tu n’en veux pas ? » = “You don’t want any?”
target_language_example: Merci, j’en veux pas.
native_language_example: Thanks, I don’t want any.

meaning: "you want (that)…" (used to introduce what you want to happen).
additional_notes: This is the 2nd-person singular of *vouloir* (*tu veux*) + *que*. It often introduces a clause with the subjunctive: *Tu veux que je vienne ?* = “Do you want me to come?” In English, it’s usually translated as “Do you want (someone/something) to…?” rather than “want that…”. Often used in questions that sound surprised, annoyed, or challenging.
target_language_example: Tu veux que je t’aide maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do you want me to help you now?

additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase « vouloir savoir » (“to want to know”), used with « tu »: « tu veux savoir… ? » = “do you want to know…?”. Often followed by a direct question (« Qu’est-ce que tu veux savoir ? ») or by « ce que » (“what/that which”): « tout ce que tu veux savoir » = “everything you want to know”. You can also see it in « Si tu veux savoir, … » = “If you want to know, …”.
target_language_example: Tu veux savoir pourquoi je suis en retard ?
native_language_example: Do you want to know why I'm late?

additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **[person] + vouloir (veux/veux/voulez/veut…) + savoir + comment + clause**. It’s used to ask about the way something happens or is done. For “I want to know how…”, use **je veux savoir comment…**.
target_language_example: Tu veux savoir comment ça marche ?
native_language_example: Do you want to know how it works?

meaning: 'want to see' (you want to look at something).
additional_notes: Formed with "vouloir" (to want) + "voir" (to see). Used to offer/show something or ask if someone wants to see it: "Tu veux voir… ?" = "Do you want to see…?" In questions it’s often spoken casually; you can add "Est-ce que" for a more neutral tone ("Est-ce que tu veux voir… ?").
target_language_example: Tu veux voir les photos de mon voyage ?
native_language_example: Do you want to see the photos from my trip?

additional_notes: From vouloir (to want) + vraiment (really). Used to emphasize that the desire is genuine or strong, often in questions to confirm or challenge someone: « Tu veux vraiment… ? » You can change the subject: « je veux vraiment… », « il/elle veut vraiment… ». In statements it often means “I truly/really want to…”.
target_language_example: Tu veux vraiment partir maintenant ?
native_language_example: Do you really want to leave now?

additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern **vouloir + infinitive**. **Veux** is the present-tense form of *vouloir* for **tu** (“you want”): *tu veux être…* (“you want to be…”). With **je**, it becomes *je veux être…* and is often spoken/written informally as **j’veux être…**.
target_language_example: Tu veux être médecin plus tard ?
native_language_example: Do you want to be a doctor later?

additional_notes: Made of **vie** (“life”) + **est** (“is”). It often appears after a possessive adjective: **ma/ta/sa/notre/votre/leur vie est…** (“my/your/his/her/our/your/their life is…”). Also common in fixed expressions like **(ta/votre) vie est en jeu** (“your life is at stake”).
target_language_example: Ma vie est différente maintenant.
native_language_example: My life is different now.

meaning: real life; reality (as opposed to fiction, dreams, or online life).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens in the real world (everyday reality), often in contrast with a movie/story, a dream, imagination, or the internet. Often appears with articles: « la vie réelle » (“real life”). You can also say « dans la vie réelle » (“in real life”).
target_language_example: Dans la vie réelle, je suis beaucoup plus timide.
native_language_example: In real life, I’m much more shy.

additional_notes: "Vieil" is the form of "vieux" used before a masculine singular noun that starts with a vowel sound (e.g., ami, homme). It usually means you’ve known the person for a long time (a longtime friend), not necessarily that they are elderly. Often used with possessives: "mon/ton/son vieil ami".
target_language_example: Je vais dîner avec un vieil ami ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m having dinner with an old friend tonight.

additional_notes: "Vieil" is the masculine form of "vieux" used before a singular masculine noun that starts with a vowel sound (often a vowel or silent h): vieil homme, vieil ami. Use "vieux" before a consonant (un vieux monsieur) and "vieux" after the noun (un homme vieux).
target_language_example: Ce vieil homme habite ici depuis trente ans.
native_language_example: This old man has lived here for thirty years.

meaning: an old lady; an elderly woman.
additional_notes: A generally polite/neutral way to refer to an older woman (often more respectful than just saying « une vieille »). It can also be used figuratively to personify something (e.g., « la lune, une vieille dame… »).
target_language_example: J’ai aidé une vieille dame à porter ses sacs.
native_language_example: I helped an old lady carry her bags.

meaning: “spinster / old maid” (an unmarried woman, often said in a judgmental way).
additional_notes: An old-fashioned, often pejorative label for a woman who never married (or is still unmarried at an older age). Commonly used after verbs like "rester" or "finir" (rester/finir vieille fille = to remain/end up a spinster). Be careful: it can sound rude or sexist; in neutral speech you can say "une femme célibataire" (a single woman).
target_language_example: Dans ce village, certaines personnes la traitaient de vieille fille, ce qu’elle détestait.
native_language_example: In that village, some people called her an old maid, which she hated.

meaning: “Will he come?” / “Is he coming?” (future, with formal question inversion).
additional_notes: This is the future tense of **venir** (“to come”) with **inversion** to form a question: **viendra** (he will come) + **-t-** (a linking sound) + **il** (he). It’s a fairly formal/literary way to ask; in everyday speech you often hear **Est-ce qu’il viendra ?** or **Il viendra ?**.
target_language_example: Viendra-t-il nous voir ce soir ?
native_language_example: Will he come see us tonight?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "venir" + "de" + infinitive to express the recent past: something happened a moment ago. The form changes with the subject (je viens de…, tu viens de…, il/elle vient de…, etc.). Example: "Tu viens de le dire" = "You just said it."
target_language_example: Je viens de finir mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I just finished my homework.

additional_notes: Used to invite someone to come with you or closer (“Viens”) and then say what you’re about to do using the near future: “je vais + infinitive” (I’m going to + verb). “Te” is the informal object pronoun meaning “to you/for you” (e.g., je vais te montrer = I’m going to show you). For a more formal version, use “Venez, je vais vous…”.
target_language_example: Viens, je vais te montrer où c’est.
native_language_example: Come, I’m going to show you where it is.

meaning: "are you coming?" / "do you come?" (inversion question form of "tu viens").
additional_notes: Used to ask a question with the verb first + subject pronoun after it (inversion), common in more formal written/spoken French. In everyday conversation, you often hear "Tu viens ?" instead. Can refer to coming somewhere ("Viens-tu avec moi ?" = Are you coming with me?) or to the "venir de" construction ("Que viens-tu de faire ?" = What did you just do?).
target_language_example: Viens-tu demain soir ?
native_language_example: Are you coming tomorrow evening?

additional_notes: Used to invite or ask someone to accompany you. It’s the imperative (command/request) form of *venir* addressed to one person you speak to as **tu**. It can sound like a firm command or a polite request depending on tone and words like **s’il te plaît**. Often followed by a destination: **Viens avec moi à la gare** (“Come with me to the station”).
target_language_example: Viens avec moi au café, s’il te plaît.
native_language_example: Come with me to the café, please.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "venir" + "de" + infinitive to express the recent past: something happened a moment ago. The form changes with the subject (je viens de…, tu viens de…, il/elle vient de…, etc.). Example: "Tu viens de le dire" = "You just said it."
target_language_example: Je viens de finir mes devoirs.
native_language_example: I just finished my homework.

additional_notes: This is the near past (passé récent): **venir de + infinitive**. Here **tu viens de dire** = “you just said.” It’s used for something that happened moments ago. You can change the subject and tense: *je viens de dire* (I just said), *il vient de dire* (he just said), *je venais de dire* (I had just said / I had only just said). Often followed by **que** to introduce what was said: *Tu viens de dire que…*.
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu es fâché ? Je viens de dire la vérité.
native_language_example: Why are you upset? I just told the truth.

additional_notes: From the verb *venir* (to come) + *ici* (here). **Viens** is the informal singular command (or present tense for "I come" in context, e.g., *je viens ici* = "I come here"). Often used as an instruction: *Viens ici !* (Come here!), *Viens ici tout de suite* (Come here right away).
target_language_example: Viens ici, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Come here, please.

additional_notes: Imperative form of venir (“to come”) + me voir (“to see me”). Used to invite someone to come to you, either to visit you or to come watch you do something (e.g., jouer = “play/perform”). Often followed by a time (demain, tout de suite) or a condition (si tu es libre).
target_language_example: Viens me voir après le travail.
native_language_example: Come see me after work.

additional_notes: Commonly used as an imperative to call someone over and draw their attention to something (often like “come look!”). It can stand alone (“Viens voir !”) or be followed by what you want them to notice (“Viens voir, il y a…”). It’s built from the verb venir (to come) + voir (to see).
target_language_example: Viens voir, j’ai trouvé tes clés !
native_language_example: Come look, I found your keys!

additional_notes: 1) **venir de + infinitive** expresses the recent past: *Il/Elle vient de partir* = “He/She just left.” 2) **venir de + place/thing** indicates origin or source: *Elle vient de Russie* = “She comes from Russia”; *Ça vient de l’ambassade* = “It comes from the embassy.”
target_language_example: Il vient de rentrer à la maison.
native_language_example: He just got home.

additional_notes: Form of the near-future/near-past structure **venir de + infinitive**. With **il/elle/on** in the present: **vient (juste) de + infinitive** = “(he/she/one) just did …”. **Juste** adds emphasis (“just now”). Example: *Il vient de partir* / *Il vient juste de partir* = “He just left.”
target_language_example: Elle vient juste de finir son travail.
native_language_example: She just finished her work.

meaning: 'lives are at stake' / 'lives are on the line'.
additional_notes: Used to stress that a situation is very serious and that people could die (or be seriously harmed). Often appears with numbers (des centaines/milliers/millions de vies) or possessives (nos vies). You can also say: « Une vie est en jeu » (one life is at stake).
target_language_example: Si on tarde à évacuer, des vies sont en jeu.
native_language_example: If we delay evacuating, lives are at stake.

additional_notes: Used for counting (vingt-six ans), giving dates (le vingt-six octobre = October 26th), or answering a question with just the number.
target_language_example: J’ai vingt-six ans.
native_language_example: I’m twenty-six years old.

additional_notes: Used with "avoir" to give someone’s age: "avoir vingt ans" = "to be twenty (years old)." "ans" is used for ages and years (not "années" in this context).
target_language_example: J'ai vingt ans aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I’m twenty years old today.

additional_notes: French uses “et” (and) only with numbers ending in 1 for 21, 31, 41, 51, 61, and 71 (e.g., “vingt et un”). For 81 and 91, it’s “quatre-vingt-un” and “quatre-vingt-onze” (no “et”). You’ll hear it as a short standalone answer when giving a number, and rising intonation (“Vingt et un ?”) can show confirmation/surprise (“Twenty-one?”).
target_language_example: J’ai vingt et un ans.
native_language_example: I am twenty-one years old.

meaning: visit from time to time; visit occasionally.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the common verb phrase **rendre visite à quelqu’un** (“to visit someone”): *Elle me rend visite de temps en temps.* The key time expression here is **de temps en temps** = “from time to time / occasionally.”
target_language_example: Je rends visite à mes grands-parents de temps en temps.
native_language_example: I visit my grandparents from time to time.

meaning: 'a visit to' (as in "rendre visite à" = "to visit").
additional_notes: Usually used in the expression "rendre visite à + person" to mean "to visit (someone)". In French, you don’t typically say *visiter quelqu’un* for people; *visiter* is more for places (e.g., *visiter Paris*).
target_language_example: Je vais rendre visite à mes grands-parents ce week-end.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my grandparents this weekend.

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask (1) where someone went/visited and (2) the duration of their stay. You’ll usually see it in the pattern: « Quel pays/État as-tu (ou avez-vous) visité, et combien de temps es-tu/êtes-vous resté(e) ? ». Note: « visité » is the past participle used with « avoir » (as-tu visité), while « resté/restée » uses « être » and agrees with the subject (resté = masculine, restée = feminine).
target_language_example: Tu as visité quelle ville, et combien de temps es-tu resté(e) ?
native_language_example: Which city did you visit, and how long did you stay?

meaning: "lives in" (he/she lives in; also used figuratively).
additional_notes: "Vit" is the 3rd-person singular present of "vivre" (to live). It’s followed by a place or a figurative “world/reality”: "Il/Elle vit dans + noun" (e.g., "sa propre réalité", "son propre monde").
target_language_example: Elle vit dans un petit appartement à Paris.
native_language_example: She lives in a small apartment in Paris.

meaning: "lives in this house" / "is living in this house."
additional_notes: "Vit" is the 3rd-person singular present of **vivre** (to live). It’s commonly used after **qui** in questions: **Qui vit dans cette maison ?** (= Who lives in this house?). In negatives you often see **Personne ne vit...** (= Nobody lives...).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas qui vit dans cette maison.
native_language_example: I don't know who lives in this house.

meaning: '(he/she) lives in a' / '(he/she) is living in a'.
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun after it (un + noun): "Elle/Il vit dans un ...". "vit" is the present tense (3rd person singular) of "vivre" (to live), and "dans" means "in". For a feminine noun, use "vit dans une".
target_language_example: Il vit dans un petit appartement près du centre-ville.
native_language_example: He lives in a small apartment near downtown.

meaning: “lives in a” (she/he lives in a + feminine noun).
additional_notes: Form of the verb vivre: "il/elle vit" = "he/she lives" (present tense). Used to say where someone lives, followed by "dans" + an indefinite article ("une" for feminine nouns; "un" for masculine: "il vit dans un appartement").
target_language_example: Elle vit dans une petite maison près de la mer.
native_language_example: She lives in a small house near the sea.

meaning: “faster than” (used in comparisons, usually with plus/aussi/moins).
additional_notes: You’ll almost always see it as part of a comparison: **plus vite que** (faster than), **moins vite que** (less fast/slower than), **aussi vite que** (as fast as). The word **que** introduces what you’re comparing to (a person, thing, or clause).
target_language_example: Peux-tu marcher plus vite que ça ?
native_language_example: Can you walk faster than that?

additional_notes: Form of the verb vivre (to live): ils/elles vivent = “they live.” Used with dans + a place (city, house, neighborhood, etc.) to say where people live. For one person: il/elle vit dans.
target_language_example: Mes voisins vivent dans un petit appartement.
native_language_example: My neighbors live in a small apartment.

meaning: “Do you live…?” / “Are you living…?” (formal or plural “you”).
additional_notes: This is the present tense of **vivre** (“to live”) with **inversion** for a question: **vivez + -vous**. Used when speaking to **one person formally (vous)** or to **multiple people**. It’s typically followed by a place or a time phrase: *Vivez-vous à Paris ?* / *Depuis quand vivez-vous ici ?*
target_language_example: Vivez-vous près d’ici ?
native_language_example: Do you live near here?

additional_notes: Used with the infinitive vivre (“to live”) + dans une (“in a”) before a feminine singular place or setting: une ville, une communauté, une commune, une caverne, etc. For masculine nouns, you’d use vivre dans un (ex: dans un appartement).
target_language_example: Elle veut vivre dans une grande ville.
native_language_example: She wants to live in a big city.

meaning: “There you go, it’s…” / “Right, it’s…” (to confirm or conclude).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to present the result or to wrap things up, often after doing or saying something. Common with past participles or evaluations: « Voilà, c’est fait » (done), « Voilà, c’est dit » (said), « Voilà, c’est bon/mieux » (it’s good/better).
target_language_example: Voilà, c'est terminé.
native_language_example: There you go, it’s finished.

additional_notes: Most often used as **voilà ce que…** (“here’s what… / that’s what…”) to introduce an explanation, plan, or the thing you found/need/said. It can point forward to what comes next in the sentence, or refer back to something just mentioned (like “That’s what you said…”).
target_language_example: Voilà ce que je propose : on se retrouve à 18 h.
native_language_example: Here’s what I propose: we meet at 6 p.m.

meaning: “here’s/that’s what he/it …” (introducing an explanation or the key point).
additional_notes: Used to present or point to what follows (often the explanation, result, or important detail). It’s very common before a verb phrase: « Voilà ce qu’il a dit » (“That’s what he said”), « Voilà ce qu’il me faut » (“Here’s what I need”), « Voilà ce qu’il se passe » (“That’s what’s happening”). In speech it often summarizes: “So, this is what he does/did…”.
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas discuter : voilà ce qu’il faut faire.
native_language_example: I don’t want to argue: here’s what needs to be done.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a plan or the next steps, often after getting someone’s attention or agreement (e.g., “Alors…”, “Ok…”, “Très bien…”, “Écoute…”). “Voilà” means “here/there you go,” “ce qu’on” = “what we,” and “va faire” is the near future (“is going to do”).
target_language_example: Bon, voilà ce qu'on va faire : tu appelles le client et je prépare le dossier.
native_language_example: Alright, here’s what we’re going to do: you call the client and I’ll prepare the file.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or point to the information that follows (an explanation, a fact, an opinion, etc.). Often followed by a verb clause: "Voilà ce que je pense..." = "Here’s what I think..."
target_language_example: Voilà ce que je veux dire : on doit partir maintenant.
native_language_example: Here’s what I mean: we have to leave now.

meaning: to see what… (to find out what…).
additional_notes: Used before a clause with a verb: « voir ce que + subject + verb ». Often means “to find out/observe what will happen or what someone can do.” In some contexts it can sound like a warning/threat: « Tu vas voir ce que tu vas prendre » (“You’ll see what you’re going to get”).
target_language_example: Attends un peu, on va voir ce que ça donne.
native_language_example: Wait a bit, we’ll see how it turns out.

voir ce que je peux faire

target_language_multi_word_term: voir ce que je peux faire
meaning: “see what I can do” / “see what I can do about it.”
additional_notes: Used to say you’ll try to help or find a solution, without promising a specific result. Very common in polite replies (e.g., after a request or problem): “Let me see what I can do.” You’ll often hear it as: « Je vais voir ce que je peux faire » or « Laisse(z)-moi voir ce que je peux faire (à ce sujet) » (informal vs. formal/plural).
target_language_example: Je ne peux rien garantir, mais je vais voir ce que je peux faire.
native_language_example: I can’t promise anything, but I’ll see what I can do.

meaning: to see/find out what’s going on (what’s happening).
additional_notes: Used when you go check a situation to understand what is happening (often because you heard something, there’s confusion, or you’re curious). Common with aller/va/allons/je vais: « Va/Allons voir ce qui se passe. »
target_language_example: J'entends du bruit dehors : je vais voir ce qui se passe.
native_language_example: I hear noise outside—I’m going to see what’s going on.

meaning: to see (meet with) [someone] in my office.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to come to your office for a quick meeting or talk. Common with te/vous: « Je peux te/vous voir dans mon bureau ? » (Can I see you in my office?). It can sound a bit formal or authoritative depending on tone/context (e.g., a boss calling an employee). Often paired with a time: « dans une minute / dans une heure ».
target_language_example: Je peux vous voir dans mon bureau après le déjeuner ?
native_language_example: Can I see you in my office after lunch?

meaning: to see something; to take a look at something.
additional_notes: Used when you want to look at or check something (often because it’s important, suspicious, or you want someone’s opinion). It can be a literal “see with your eyes” or a general “come look.” In questions, it can also mean “can you see anything?” (e.g., Peux-tu voir quelque chose ?).
target_language_example: Viens voir quelque chose : il y a un problème avec la porte.
native_language_example: Come take a look at something: there’s a problem with the door.

meaning: to see/watch a movie (go to the movies).
additional_notes: Means either watching a movie in general or going out to a cinema to watch one—often used with "aller" (aller voir un film) to emphasize going to see it. "Film" can mean a movie (and also a film/movie in a broader sense).
target_language_example: On va voir un film ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we going to see a movie tonight?

meaning: to see a doctor (to consult a doctor).
additional_notes: Common way to say you’re going to consult a doctor (not just ‘see’ visually). Often used with devoir/pouvoir: « Je dois voir un médecin » (I need to see a doctor). You can also say « aller voir un médecin » for emphasis on going to the appointment; with advice: « Tu devrais voir un médecin ».
target_language_example: Si ça ne va pas mieux demain, je vais voir un médecin.
native_language_example: If it’s not better tomorrow, I’m going to see a doctor.

meaning: to see that; to check it out ("see what's going on").
additional_notes: Used to draw attention to something (often something interesting, surprising, or important) or to suggest going to look at it more closely. Very common in spoken French in phrases like "Attends de voir ça" (just wait and see) and "Allons voir ça" (let’s go take a look).
target_language_example: Viens voir ça, c'est incroyable !
native_language_example: Come check this out, it’s incredible!

vois-tu un inconvénient à ce que

target_language_multi_word_term: vois-tu un inconvénient à ce que
meaning: "Do you mind if…?" / "Would it bother you if…?"
additional_notes: A polite way to ask permission or check whether something would be a problem. It’s often followed by the subjunctive: « Vois-tu un inconvénient à ce que je + subjunctive… ? » (e.g., « …à ce que nous entrions ? »). You can also use it in a more formal register with « voyez-vous ».
target_language_example: Vois-tu un inconvénient à ce que j’ouvre la fenêtre ?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I open the window?

meaning: "see what" / "look at what" (often: "see what you can…").
additional_notes: Uses the imperative of voir ("vois" = "(you) see/look") + ce que ("what/that which"). Common in instructions or suggestions: "Vois ce que tu peux…" = "See what you can…" It can also be used to point out consequences: "Vois ce que tu lui as causé !" = "Look what you did to him!"
target_language_example: Vois ce que tu peux faire pour l’aider.
native_language_example: See what you can do to help him/her.

additional_notes: This is the informal spoken form of negation where "ne" is dropped: "je (ne) vois pas", "tu (ne) vois pas". It can be literal (not seeing with your eyes) or figurative (not noticing, not understanding: "Tu ne vois pas ce qui se passe ?"). In formal writing, include "ne": "je ne vois pas".
target_language_example: Je vois pas pourquoi tu es fâché.
native_language_example: I don’t see why you’re upset.

additional_notes: This is the noun "voiture" (car) followed by the verb "est" (is), used to describe a car with an adjective or to give its status/location (e.g., "Ma voiture est neuve" = My car is new; "Votre voiture est prête" = Your car is ready). In real sentences, "voiture" is usually preceded by an article or possessive (ma/ta/notre/votre).
target_language_example: Ma voiture est en panne.
native_language_example: My car is broken down.

additional_notes: Refers to thieves who steal from people’s pockets or bags (often in crowds, public transport, or tourist areas). Common in warnings like « Soyez attentif/attentive/attentifs aux voleurs à la tire » (“Watch out for pickpockets”).
target_language_example: Dans le métro, fais attention aux voleurs à la tire.
native_language_example: On the metro, watch out for pickpockets.

meaning: “your friends” (addressing more than one person, or speaking formally to one person).
additional_notes: “Vos” is the possessive adjective for “your” used with *vous* (formal singular or plural). With *amis* (masculine plural), it can refer to a mixed group of friends (men and women) or all men; for all women, you can say “vos amies.” Often used in questions like “Qui sont vos amis ?” (“Who are your friends?”) or to refer to people waiting/located somewhere (“Vos amis vous attendent.”).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous appeler vos amis ?
native_language_example: Can you call your friends?

additional_notes: "Vos" is the possessive for "your" (used with plural nouns, and also as a polite/formal "your"). "Armes" means weapons (guns, swords, etc.). Often used in commands in a military/police/action context: *Baissez vos armes* (Lower your weapons), *Rendez vos armes* (Surrender your weapons).
target_language_example: Veuillez déposer vos armes au contrôle de sécurité.
native_language_example: Please leave your weapons at the security checkpoint.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective “vos” with the plural noun “enfants.” It can mean “your” when speaking to more than one person (informal plural) or to one person in a polite/formal way (vous). Often used in questions like « Et vos enfants ? » (“And your kids/children?”).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous garder vos enfants avec vous, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you keep your children with you, please?

meaning: your hands (to multiple people, or politely to one person).
additional_notes: Used with commands/instructions addressing a group (or using polite vous to one person): Donnez-moi vos mains (Give me your hands), Montrez-moi vos mains (Show me your hands). Contrast: tes mains = your hands (informal, one person).
target_language_example: Lavez vos mains avant de manger.
native_language_example: Wash your hands before eating.

meaning: "your parents" (speaking to more than one person, or formally).
additional_notes: Uses the possessive determiner "vos" with the plural noun "parents". "Vos" is used with vous (either plural "you" or formal singular "you"). For one person informally, you’d usually say "tes parents"; for one person formally, "vos parents" is also possible. Common with verbs like "obéir à" (to obey), "manquer à" (to miss someone), and "être proche de" (to be close to).
target_language_example: Vos parents sont très gentils.
native_language_example: Your parents are very nice.

additional_notes: "Vos" is the possessive used with "vous" (either talking to more than one person, or to one person in a polite/formal way). It can be literal (someone’s eyes) or figurative in common expressions like "à vos yeux" = "in your eyes / in your view".
target_language_example: Je peux lire la vérité dans vos yeux.
native_language_example: I can read the truth in your eyes.

additional_notes: A very formal title used when addressing a prince/princess or other high-ranking royal. It’s used as a direct form of address (often with a comma), and it takes the polite pronoun “vous” when speaking to the person.
target_language_example: Votre Altesse, puis-je vous accompagner ?
native_language_example: Your Highness, may I accompany you?

meaning: Your Majesty (formal way to address a king or queen).
additional_notes: A very formal, respectful form of address used when speaking to a monarch. It can be used on its own as a direct address (“Votre Majesté !”) or within a sentence as the subject (“Votre Majesté comprend…”). The noun is capitalized (Majesté), and in speech it’s usually paired with very formal language.
target_language_example: Votre Majesté, puis-je vous poser une question ?
native_language_example: Your Majesty, may I ask you a question?
