additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens (a specific point in time). It’s common with verbs like arriver (to arrive), venir (to come), rentrer (to come back/go home), être (to be). In schedules you often see: « de neuf heures à cinq heures » = “from nine to five.” You can add precision: « à cinq heures précises » (at exactly five) or « au plus tard à cinq heures » (by five at the latest).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à cinq heures devant la gare.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at five o’clock in front of the station.

meaning: at five o’clock in the morning (at 5 a.m.).
additional_notes: Used to say the exact time when something happens. "du matin" specifies morning (A.M.); without it ("à cinq heures"), the time could be unclear (5 a.m. or 5 p.m.). You can replace "cinq" with any number: "à six heures du matin", etc.
target_language_example: On part à cinq heures du matin pour éviter la circulation.
native_language_example: We’re leaving at 5 a.m. to avoid traffic.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something is right next to something else (location/position). It’s the feminine singular form of "à côté de" + "la" (e.g., à côté de la porte, à côté de la voiture). For masculine: "à côté du"; for plural: "à côté des"; before a vowel/h mute: "à côté de l’".
target_language_example: Le café est à côté de la gare.
native_language_example: The café is next to the train station.

meaning: completely off the mark; totally wrong (missing the point).
additional_notes: An idiomatic, fairly informal expression used to say someone’s idea, guess, or understanding is way off. Often intensified with "complètement" (completely). You can use it about a person ("Tu es à côté de la plaque") or about what they said/thought ("Ton hypothèse est à côté de la plaque").
target_language_example: Non, tu es à côté de la plaque : ce n’est pas lui le responsable.
native_language_example: No, you’re completely off the mark: he isn’t the one responsible.

additional_notes: Literally “at the side of him.” Used for physical position (sitting/standing next to a man). It can also be used figuratively to mean “compared to him” (e.g., someone seems small à côté de lui).
target_language_example: Je suis resté à côté de lui pendant le concert.
native_language_example: I stayed next to him during the concert.

additional_notes:
Used after certain verbs to introduce what is to be said. Very common with:
- « avoir … à dire » = “to have … to say / something to say” (C’est tout ce que tu as à dire ? / J’ai un truc à dire.)
- « hésiter à dire » = “to hesitate to say”.
- « (avoir) son mot à dire » = “to have a say (in something)” (often about decisions).
target_language_example: Si tu as quelque chose à dire, dis-le maintenant.
native_language_example: If you have something to say, say it now.

meaning: to do; that needs to be done.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it must be done (e.g., des choses à faire = things to do), or after avoir to express an obligation or task (e.g., j’ai un truc à faire = I’ve got something to do). Often implies a remaining task on a list ("to-do").
target_language_example: J’ai encore deux appels à faire ce soir.
native_language_example: I still have two calls to make tonight.

additional_notes: Used as “à” + infinitive (“faire”) + “ça” (“that/this”) after many verbs and expressions. Common patterns: “arriver à faire ça” (manage to do that), “passer du temps à faire ça” (spend time doing that), “forcer quelqu’un à faire ça” (force someone to do that), “avoir intérêt à faire ça (bien)” (had better do that (well)). “Ça” can mean “that” or “this” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tu n’es pas obligé(e) à faire ça.
native_language_example: You don’t have to do that.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like « approcher » or « arriver » to say an event/date is coming soon, as if it were taking “big steps” toward you: « Noël approche à grands pas. » It’s a common, neutral expression.
target_language_example: Les vacances arrivent à grands pas.
native_language_example: The holidays are coming up fast.

additional_notes: Used with "à" to give a specific time on the clock for an event (meeting, departure, waking up, etc.). You can swap in other times: à sept heures, à huit heures et demie (8:30), à huit heures du matin (8 a.m.), à huit heures du soir (8 p.m.).
target_language_example: Le train part à huit heures.
native_language_example: The train leaves at eight o’clock.

additional_notes: Used before a vowel sound or silent “h” word that is masculine singular (le): à + le → à l’ (e.g., à l’aéroport, à l’université). It can mark direction (go to), location (be at), time in set expressions (à l’aube = at dawn), or what something relates to (rien à l’art = nothing about art).
target_language_example: Je vais à l’université demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to the university tomorrow.

meaning: in the back; at the rear.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a position behind something (the back of a room, a line, a building, etc.). Very common for vehicles: à l'arrière = in the back seat/in the back. Often contrasts with à l'avant (“in the front”).
target_language_example: Les enfants sont assis à l'arrière de la voiture.
native_language_example: The kids are sitting in the back of the car.

meaning: at the airport; to the airport.
additional_notes: Uses « à » with a place. It can mean being located there (« Je suis à l'aéroport. » = I’m at the airport) or going there with a verb of movement like « aller » (« aller à l'aéroport » = to go to the airport). « l’ » is « le » shortened before a vowel: « le aéroport » → « l’aéroport ».
target_language_example: On se retrouve à l'aéroport à 8h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the airport at 8.

meaning: to the hospital; at/in the hospital.
additional_notes: Used with motion verbs (aller, conduire, emmener) to mean “to the hospital.” With a state (être), it means someone is “in/at the hospital” (usually as a patient or because they’re hospitalized).
target_language_example: Après l'accident, elle est restée à l'hôpital pendant deux jours.
native_language_example: After the accident, she stayed in the hospital for two days.

meaning: at the hotel; to the hotel.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of location (être, rester) to mean “at the hotel,” and with verbs of movement (aller, retourner) to mean “to the hotel.” Often refers to the hotel you’re staying at or meeting at.
target_language_example: On se voit à l'hôtel à 18 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the hotel at 6 p.m.?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically at school or is attending school. With verbs of movement it can mean “to school” (Je vais à l’école = I’m going to school). With a person (envoyer quelqu’un à l’école), it means “to send someone to school.”
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, les enfants sont à l'école.
native_language_example: Today, the kids are at school.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is listening attentively or ready to receive information. Common in radio/TV: « Restez à l’écoute » = “Stay tuned.” With « être à l’écoute de + [source/person] » it means “to be listening to” or “to be attentive to” (e.g., a station, a person).
target_language_example: Restez à l’écoute, on revient après la pub.
native_language_example: Stay tuned, we’ll be back after the ads.

meaning: at the bank; to the bank.
additional_notes: “À” can indicate location (“at”) or destination (“to”), depending on the verb/context: Je suis à la banque (I’m at the bank) vs. se rendre/aller à la banque (to go to the bank). It can also be used as a short answer to say where you’re going: « À la banque. »
target_language_example: Je dois aller à la banque cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I have to go to the bank this afternoon.

meaning: at the library; to the library.
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "à" with the definite article "la" to mean being at a place or going to a place. With verbs of movement like "aller" or "se rendre", it often means "to the library"; with verbs describing location or activity like "étudier" or "travailler", it often means "at the library".
target_language_example: Je vais à la bibliothèque après le cours.
native_language_example: I'm going to the library after class.

meaning: in the countryside; in a rural area.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like vivre, habiter, aller, passer des vacances to say someone is in (or going to) the countryside. Opposite idea: à la ville (in the city).
target_language_example: On va passer le week-end à la campagne.
native_language_example: We're going to spend the weekend in the countryside.

meaning: in the cellar / in the basement; (going) down to the basement.
additional_notes: Used to say something is located in the cellar/basement (e.g., wine storage), or as a short answer to indicate where something/someone is. It can also be used jokingly/figuratively to mean putting someone “out of the way” or hidden/neglected (e.g., « On va quand même pas mettre maman à la cave ! »).
target_language_example: Les valises sont à la cave.
native_language_example: The suitcases are in the basement.

additional_notes: "Fac" is short for "la faculté" and is common in everyday speech. Used with verbs like "aller" (to go), "être" (to be), "étudier" (to study) to talk about being at or going to university (often implying a university campus or studies).
target_language_example: Je suis à la fac aujourd'hui, mais je rentre tôt.
native_language_example: I'm at university today, but I'm coming home early.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the ending point of something masculine/singular: à la fin du dîner / du livre / du concert / du discours / du document. With a feminine noun, use « à la fin de la » (à la fin de la journée). If the noun starts with a vowel sound, use « à la fin de l’ » (à la fin de l’année).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la fin du cours.
native_language_example: We'll meet up at the end of the class.

meaning: at the end of the month.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the last days of a month. It can mean the end of the current month (from context), or you can specify which month: « à la fin du mois de novembre » (at the end of November). Often used with deadlines or planned events.
target_language_example: Je te paierai à la fin du mois.
native_language_example: I’ll pay you at the end of the month.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like être/aller/rester/venir to say someone is/was/went/stayed/came at a party or celebration. Not to confuse with « la fête » meaning “a holiday/celebration” in general; « à la fête » is the location/context (at the party/event).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la fête vers huit heures.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the party around eight o’clock.

meaning: at the train station; to the train station.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of location (être, attendre, travailler) to mean “at the station,” and with verbs of movement (aller, arriver, conduire, déposer, se rendre) to mean “to the station.” “La gare” usually means the train station (not the bus station).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la gare à 9 h.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the train station at 9 o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to locate an event in the context of a war or military conflict (e.g., being injured, dying, taking risks). With verbs of going (aller), it can mean “to go to war.” In games, jouer à la guerre means “to play war” (play at war/war games).
target_language_example: Mon grand-père a été prisonnier à la guerre.
native_language_example: My grandfather was a prisoner in the war.

à la hauteur de la tâche

target_language_multi_word_term: à la hauteur de la tâche
meaning: up to the task; capable of doing the job.
additional_notes: Used to say whether someone has the ability, skill, or confidence needed to succeed at a particular task or challenge. Often used with the verb "être" (to be): "Je suis / je ne suis pas à la hauteur de la tâche". You can also say "à la hauteur" on its own when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, tu es à la hauteur de la tâche.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, you’re up to the task.

à la maison plutôt que de sortir

target_language_multi_word_term: à la maison plutôt que de sortir
meaning: at home rather than going out.
additional_notes: Used to express a preference or choice: staying at home instead of going out. Often follows verbs like « préférer » (to prefer) or « rester » (to stay): « Je préfère rester à la maison plutôt que de sortir. » « Plutôt que (de) + infinitive » means “rather than (doing)”.
target_language_example: Ce soir, je reste à la maison plutôt que de sortir.
native_language_example: Tonight, I'm staying at home rather than going out.

meaning: 'at home for' (a purpose, a deadline time, or an event).
additional_notes: Used with (1) an infinitive to express purpose: « à la maison pour me reposer » (“at home to rest”); (2) a time/deadline: « à la maison pour minuit » (“home by midnight”); or (3) an occasion: « à la maison pour Noël » (“home for Christmas”). With verbs like « rentrer », it often means “go/come back home for…”.
target_language_example: Je suis à la maison pour travailler au calme.
native_language_example: I'm at home to work in peace.

à la maison toute la journée

target_language_multi_word_term: à la maison toute la journée
additional_notes: Used to say someone stays/spends the entire day at home. Common with verbs like « rester » (to stay) or « être » (to be): « rester à la maison toute la journée », « être à la maison toute la journée ». « Toute la journée » means “the whole day / all day long.”
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, je suis à la maison toute la journée.
native_language_example: Today, I'm at home all day.

meaning: to the sea; at/by the seaside.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of going or staying (aller/rester/passer des vacances) to mean spending time at the seaside. In some contexts it can be literal (“into the sea”), especially with verbs like jeter (“throw”).
target_language_example: Dimanche, on va à la mer si le temps est beau.
native_language_example: On Sunday, we’re going to the seaside if the weather is nice.

additional_notes: Used to say that you cross or travel through water by swimming (e.g., traverser un lac/une rivière/la Manche à la nage). Often follows verbs like "traverser" (to cross).
target_language_example: On peut rejoindre l’île à la nage si la mer est calme.
native_language_example: You can reach the island by swimming if the sea is calm.

meaning: to the beach; at the beach.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (aller, se rendre) to mean “to the beach,” and with activities/being somewhere to mean “at the beach.” The preposition “à” commonly indicates a destination or location.
target_language_example: On va à la plage cet après-midi.
native_language_example: We're going to the beach this afternoon.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like dire (to tell), avouer (to confess), rapporter (to report), remettre (to hand over) to indicate the police are the recipient. "Police" is feminine singular in French, so you say "la police" (not *le police*).
target_language_example: On a signalé le vol à la police.
native_language_example: They reported the theft to the police.

meaning: at the door; (be) at the door/entrance.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like être/se tenir (to be/stand) to say someone is at the door, and with frapper to mean knocking at the door. Often refers to the entrance of a room/house.
target_language_example: Il y a quelqu’un à la porte.
native_language_example: There’s someone at the door.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like aller/partir (“to go/leave”) to talk about the activity of fishing: aller à la pêche = “to go fishing.” It’s also used in expressions like être à la pêche (“to be out fishing”).
target_language_example: On va à la pêche demain matin ?
native_language_example: Are we going fishing tomorrow morning?

meaning: 'to the question' (used with verbs like répondre / answer).
additional_notes: Often used after verbs that take the preposition "à", especially "répondre à" (to answer) and in phrases like "la réponse à la question" (the answer to the question). In French you say "répondre à une question" (literally, respond to a question), not *répondre une question*.
target_language_example: Je vais répondre à la question maintenant.
native_language_example: I’m going to answer the question now.

meaning: on the radio; on/through the radio (broadcast).
additional_notes: Used to say something is heard, said, or broadcast via radio. Common with verbs like entendre (to hear), écouter (to listen to), passer (to be played/air), parler (to talk about). With people or programs it often means “on air” (e.g., Je vous ai entendu à la radio = I heard you on the radio). Not the same as "dans la radio".
target_language_example: J'ai appris la nouvelle à la radio en allant au travail.
native_language_example: I heard the news on the radio on my way to work.

additional_notes: Used with the verb être (Je suis à la recherche de…) to mean you are looking for something, or with verbs of movement/action (partir, aller, retourner…) to mean going in search of something. Usually followed by a noun or pronoun (de + le/la/les → du/de la/des).
target_language_example: Je suis à la recherche d'un appartement près du métro.
native_language_example: I'm looking for an apartment near the метро.

meaning: at the meeting; to the meeting.
additional_notes: Means being present at a meeting ("at") or going/heading there ("to"), depending on the verb: être/absent à la réunion (to be at/absent from the meeting), aller/se rendre/assister à la réunion (to go to/attend the meeting).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la réunion à 14 h.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the meeting at 2 p.m.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement like "aller" to mean going to the gym ("aller à la salle de sport"). It can also describe location (being at the gym) depending on the verb and context. "Salle de sport" is feminine, so it takes "la"; with "à" it becomes "à la".
target_language_example: Ce soir, je vais à la salle de sport après le travail.
native_language_example: Tonight, I'm going to the gym after work.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition « à » + « la » (often contracted to « au » with masculine nouns). With « être/rester », it usually means being at the event (location/time): « rester à la soirée » = to stay at the party. With verbs like « inviter », « aller », « participer », it often means going/being invited/participating in the event: « inviter quelqu’un à la soirée » = to invite someone to the party.
target_language_example: Je vais aller à la soirée avec des amis.
native_language_example: I’m going to the party with some friends.

meaning: at the station; to the station.
additional_notes: Means being located at a station (at the station) or going there (to the station), depending on the verb and context. Often used for meeting points (se rencontrer à la station) or drop-offs (me déposer à la station). Can be followed by a type or name: à la station de métro / à la station Ueno.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à la station à 18 h ?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the station at 6 p.m.?

meaning: to temptation (in phrases like “resist/give in to temptation”).
additional_notes: Used after verbs that take the preposition à, especially: résister à la tentation (to resist temptation) and céder à la tentation (to give in to temptation). Also appears in the biblical phrase: « Ne nous conduis pas à la tentation » (“Lead us not into temptation”).
target_language_example: J’ai réussi à résister à la tentation d’acheter quelque chose.
native_language_example: I managed to resist the temptation to buy something.

additional_notes: Used to say something is broadcast or seen on television. Very common in speech; “télé” is short for “télévision.” Often with verbs like voir (to see), regarder (to watch), passer (to be shown/broadcast).
target_language_example: On a regardé le match à la télé hier soir.
native_language_example: We watched the game on TV last night.

additional_notes: Used to say something is broadcast or watched via television. Common with verbs like parler (to speak), voir/regarder (to see/watch), passer (to be shown/appear), and with nouns like une émission (a show) or un match (a game).
target_language_example: On regarde les infos à la télévision tous les soirs.
native_language_example: We watch the news on TV every evening.

meaning: to/on the head; at the head (of), in charge.
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to the body part: *blessé à la tête* (injured in the head), *un coup à la tête* (a blow to the head), *des pieds à la tête* (from head to toe), *monter à la tête* (go to your head, e.g., alcohol). With **être à la tête (de)** it means being the leader/in charge of something (*à la tête de l’entreprise*).
target_language_example: Elle est à la tête de l’équipe depuis 2023.
native_language_example: She has been in charge of the team since 2023.

additional_notes: Used in set expressions like « revenir à la vie » / « ramener quelqu’un à la vie » (“to come back to life” / “to bring someone back to life”). Also appears after adjectives like « nécessaire/indispensable à la vie » (“necessary/essential for life”), often with a qualifier: « à la vie moderne » (“for modern life”).
target_language_example: Après l’accident, il est revenu à la vie.
native_language_example: After the accident, he came back to life.

meaning: "to do it" (after a verb that takes "à").
additional_notes: Used when a verb is followed by "à" + infinitive, and "le" stands for “it” (a thing/action already mentioned). Common patterns include: "forcer quelqu’un à le faire" (force someone to do it), "hésiter à le faire" (hesitate to do it), and "avoir à le faire" (have to do it).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas le faire, mais je vais devoir à le faire.
native_language_example: I don’t want to do it, but I’m going to have to do it.

additional_notes: Most commonly used in two ways: (1) after an adjective, it means “to read / readable” (e.g., facile à lire = easy to read). (2) after a noun/quantity, it means “(something) to read” or “left to read” (e.g., trois pages à lire = three pages to read). Not to confuse with the verb phrase “arriver/parvenir à lire” = “manage to read.”
target_language_example: J'ai un article à lire ce soir.
native_language_example: I have an article to read tonight.

meaning: “to the” / “at the” (contraction of « à + le » before a vowel sound).
additional_notes: « à l’ » is used before a masculine singular noun that starts with a vowel or silent h: « à l’intérieur », « à l’horizon », « à l’ère ». It can express location (at), direction (to), or more abstract links like giving priority: « donner la priorité à l’engagement ». (Feminine « à la » does not contract.)
target_language_example: On se retrouve à l’entrée du musée.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the entrance of the museum.

meaning: "to my" / "in my" (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Made of the preposition « à » + the possessive « ma » (my, feminine singular). It shows a relationship like “to my…” (e.g., « réfléchir à ma proposition » = to think about my proposal) or “in my…” in fixed expressions like « à ma façon » (in my way) and « à ma surprise » (to my surprise). Used only with feminine singular nouns; compare « à mon » (masculine) and « à mes » (plural).
target_language_example: Je préfère le faire à ma manière.
native_language_example: I prefer to do it my way.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take an indirect object introduced by « à » (e.g., parler à, expliquer à, promettre à, demander à). It marks the person you’re speaking to or doing something for: « à ma femme » = “to my wife.”
target_language_example: Je vais téléphoner à ma femme ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to call my wife tonight.

meaning: "to my mother" / "for my mother"; with "être à": "(belonging) to my mother."
additional_notes: Most often used after a verb like parler à (talk to), demander à (ask), donner à (give). With the structure "être à + person", it means something belongs to that person: « Il est à ma mère » = « It belongs to my mother ».
target_language_example: J’ai donné les clés à ma mère.
native_language_example: I gave the keys to my mother.

meaning: in my place; if you were me.
additional_notes: Used either literally (returning to your seat/spot) or figuratively (put yourself in my situation, do something instead of me). Often appears with verbs like « se mettre à ma place » (put yourself in my shoes) and in questions like « Qu’est-ce que tu ferais à ma place ? » (What would you do if you were me?). You can change the possessive: « à ta place » (in your place), « à sa place » (in his/her place), « à notre/votre/leur place ».
target_language_example: Si j’étais à ta place, je lui parlerais tout de suite.
native_language_example: If I were you, I would talk to him right away.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like répondre (to answer), usually in répondre à + [question]. In French you answer *to* a question (répondre à une question), not “answer a question” directly.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous répondre à ma question, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you answer my question, please?

additional_notes: Uses the preposition « à » with an indirect object (often after verbs like « parler à » = to talk to). It can also mark a relationship or link to someone, as in « fiancé à ma sœur » (engaged to my sister). « Ma sœur » means “my sister” (feminine singular).
target_language_example: J’ai envoyé un message à ma sœur.
native_language_example: I sent a message to my sister.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like donner/apporter/acheter to mean “(something) to eat” (food). With donner à manger à + person/animal = “to give (someone/animal) something to eat / to feed.”
target_language_example: Tu as quelque chose à manger ?
native_language_example: Do you have something to eat?

meaning: to tell me; to say to me.
additional_notes: Often used after **avoir ... à + infinitive** to mean “to have something to do/say.” In questions like **Qu’as-tu à me dire ?**, it means “What do you have to tell me?” (i.e., what is it you want/need to tell me?). With **autre chose**, it means “anything else”: **Tu as autre chose à me dire ?** = “Do you have anything else to tell me?”
target_language_example: J'ai quelque chose d'important à te dire.
native_language_example: I have something important to tell you.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at 12:00 in the daytime. In everyday speech, especially in France, "à midi" can also mean "at lunchtime" (the midday meal), depending on context.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à midi devant le café.
native_language_example: Let's meet at noon in front of the café.

meaning: "to my" / "at my" (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate direction/recipient ("to") or location/time in relation to you ("at"). It’s followed by a noun: à mon cours (to my class), à mon tour (my turn), à mon appartement (to my apartment), à mon rythme (at my pace), à mon avocat (to my lawyer). With feminine singular nouns use « à ma », and with plural use « à mes ». Note: « à mon » is also used before a feminine noun starting with a vowel/silent h (e.g., « à mon amie »).
target_language_example: Tu peux venir à mon bureau après le cours.
native_language_example: You can come to my office after class.

meaning: "to my brother" / "for my brother" (and in some contexts: "like my brother").
additional_notes: Used after the preposition "à". Common uses: (1) possession: "C'est à mon frère" = "It’s my brother’s"; "Ça appartient à mon frère" = "That belongs to my brother." (2) indirect object (giving/buying/saying): "J’ai acheté un cadeau à mon frère" = "I bought a gift for my brother." (3) resemblance: "Il ressemble à mon frère" = "He looks like my brother."
target_language_example: Je vais téléphoner à mon frère ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to call my brother tonight.

meaning: to my father; (with “c’est / appartenir”) my father’s.
additional_notes: Most often means “to my father” (an indirect object): « Dis-le à mon père » = “Tell it to my father.” In possession sentences, « c’est à mon père » means “It’s my father’s” (literally “it’s to my father”), similar to « appartenir à » = “to belong to.” Also used after « penser à »: « je pense à mon père » = “I’m thinking about my father.”
target_language_example: Je vais parler à mon père ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk to my father tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It can refer to 9:00 in the morning or at night; add context or clarify with "du matin" (in the morning) / "du soir" (in the evening) if needed. You can also emphasize exact time with "à neuf heures précises" (at exactly nine o’clock).
target_language_example: On se retrouve à neuf heures devant le café.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at nine o’clock in front of the café.

additional_notes: Used before a singular masculine noun to mean “to/at our” (e.g., à notre fête, à notre hôtel). Before a vowel or silent h, it becomes “à notre” + noun (e.g., à notre hôtel). Common in the set phrase “À notre + adjective + noun,” meaning “much to our…” (e.g., À notre grand mécontentement… = “Much to our great displeasure…”).
target_language_example: La clé est à notre réception.
native_language_example: The key is at our front desk.

à partager votre code avec moi

target_language_multi_word_term: à partager votre code avec moi
meaning: to share your code with me.
additional_notes: Used after expressions like « être disposé(e)(s) à… » (“to be willing to…”) + infinitive. « votre » is the formal/plural “your”; in informal singular you’d usually say « à partager ton code avec moi ».
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas disposé à partager votre code avec moi sans votre autorisation.
native_language_example: I’m not willing to share your code with me without your permission.

meaning: to leave; (in “à partir de”) from / starting from.
additional_notes: Used with the verb partir (“to leave”): être prêt(e) à partir (to be ready to leave), penser à partir (to be thinking of leaving), le premier/le dernier à partir (the first/last to leave). Very commonly extended as “à partir de + [noun/time]” meaning “from” or “starting from,” and in recipes/materials to mean “made from” (fait à partir de…).
target_language_example: On est prêts à partir, mais à partir de demain je travaille à la maison.
native_language_example: We’re ready to leave, but starting tomorrow I’m working from home.

additional_notes: Used to indicate an origin, starting point, or source material. Common in passive constructions like « être fait/fabriqué à partir de + [ingredient/material] » (“to be made from”). Note: the base phrase is « à partir de »; it becomes « à partir du » before a masculine singular noun (de + le → du).
target_language_example: Le jus d’orange est fait à partir d’oranges fraîches.
native_language_example: Orange juice is made from fresh oranges.

meaning: to nobody / to anyone (in a negative sentence).
additional_notes: Used with verbs that take an indirect object (often with « à »), especially in negatives with « ne … personne »: « parler à personne » (talk to nobody), « faire de mal à personne » (harm nobody), « dire à personne » (tell nobody), « se fier à personne » (trust nobody). Without « ne » (or another negative word), « personne » usually means “a person/someone,” which can be confusing.
target_language_example: Je n’ai donné mon adresse à personne.
native_language_example: I didn’t give my address to anyone.

meaning: to rain (used after a verb like “commencer/se mettre” to mean “to start raining”).
additional_notes: Usually appears in patterns like « commencer à pleuvoir » (to start raining) and « se mettre à pleuvoir » (to start raining, often suddenly). « Il » is an impersonal subject here (like English “it” in “it’s raining”). You can add intensity: « à torrents » / « très fort » = “very heavily.”
target_language_example: On allait sortir, mais il s'est mis à pleuvoir.
native_language_example: We were about to go out, but it started raining.

à propos de ce qui a eu lieu

target_language_multi_word_term: à propos de ce qui a eu lieu
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a past event or situation that already took place. Often follows a feeling or reaction (e.g., être contrarié(e), être inquiet/inquiète, être en colère) to say what it’s about.
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas parler à propos de ce qui a eu lieu hier.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re talking/thinking/asking about. Very common after verbs like parler de (to talk about), discuter de (to discuss), or être en colère à propos de (to be angry about). Often shortened to just à propos de + noun/pronoun: « à propos de ce problème », « à propos de ça ». Note: « à propos de » is similar to « au sujet de » (about).
target_language_example: Je dois te parler à propos de quelque chose d’important.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you about something important.

additional_notes: Used to ask what the topic/subject is. It often comes after a noun or a whole situation: « C’est à propos de quoi ? » (= What is this about?). You’ll also see « à propos de + noun » (about + noun), and « à propos, … » meaning “by the way,” (different use).
target_language_example: On se réunit demain, mais à propos de quoi exactement ?
native_language_example: We’re meeting tomorrow, but what exactly is it about?

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a topic or situation already mentioned. Common after verbs like parler (to talk), savoir (to know), faire une vidéo (to make a video), or être désolé (to be sorry): « Je suis désolé à propos de ça. ». Often interchangeable with « au sujet de ça » or, in casual speech, « là-dessus ».
target_language_example: On peut parler à propos de ça plus tard ?
native_language_example: Can we talk about that later?

à proximité du bord de la falaise

target_language_multi_word_term: à proximité du bord de la falaise
meaning: near the edge of the cliff.
additional_notes: Used to warn or describe being close to a dangerous drop. « à proximité de » means “near/close to,” and « le bord » is “the edge/rim.” You can swap in another place: « à proximité du bord de la route » (near the edge of the road).
target_language_example: Ne t'approche pas trop à proximité du bord de la falaise.
native_language_example: Don’t get too close to the edge of the cliff.

meaning: “when was the last time…?” / “how far back does … date?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about the date/time of the last occurrence of something. It’s a fairly formal phrasing (common in interviews, medical/dental checkups, questionnaires). Grammar tip: it’s built on *remonter à* (“to date back to”), so it’s often followed by something like *la dernière fois*, *vos dernières vacances*, *votre dernière visite*, etc.
target_language_example: À quand remonte votre dernière vaccination ?
native_language_example: When was your last vaccination?

à quand remonte la dernière fois que

target_language_multi_word_term: à quand remonte la dernière fois que
additional_notes: Used to ask how long ago something last happened. Literally “to when does the last time that… date back?”, but in natural English it’s “When was the last time (that)…?” Often followed by a verb in the past tense (e.g., tu as…, vous avez…).
target_language_example: À quand remonte la dernière fois que tu as voyagé à l’étranger ?
native_language_example: When was the last time you traveled abroad?

additional_notes: Used to ask which floor of a building someone lives on or where something is located. Often part of a longer question (e.g., « À quel étage êtes-vous ? » / « À quel étage se trouve… ? ») or said alone as a short follow-up question.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, à quel étage est la salle 204 ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, on what floor is room 204?

additional_notes: Used in questions with a feminine singular noun after it (e.g., à quelle vitesse, à quelle hauteur, à quelle porte). It’s the feminine form of "à quel" (masc.) and "à quels/à quelles" (plural). Often translates as "at what" or "to which" depending on the noun and context.
target_language_example: À quelle heure commence le cours ?
native_language_example: What time does the class start?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the distance to a place or thing. It’s a formal/neutral phrasing (common in writing, signs, or careful speech). You can also ask the same idea more casually with “C’est à quelle distance ?” or “C’est loin ?”.
target_language_example: À quelle distance se trouve l'hôtel le plus proche ?
native_language_example: How far away is the nearest hotel?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the frequency of an action (how many times per day/week/month, etc.). It’s commonly followed by a verb: « À quelle fréquence + verbe… ? »
target_language_example: À quelle fréquence vas-tu au cinéma ?
native_language_example: How often do you go to the movies?

meaning: "at what time" (asking the time something happens).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a specific time on the clock. Often comes at the beginning of a question: « À quelle heure pars-tu ? » It can also introduce an embedded question: « Décide à quelle heure tu veux te réveiller. »
target_language_example: À quelle heure commence le cours ?
native_language_example: What time does the class start?

additional_notes: Used to ask what time someone closed a shop/business (or ended an activity). It uses the passé composé: « as fermé » = “you closed / you have closed.” « As-tu » is the inverted (question) form of « tu as » and is informal/singular (talking to one person you address as tu). Often followed by what was closed: « la boutique / le magasin ».
target_language_example: À quelle heure as-tu fermé le restaurant hier ?
native_language_example: What time did you close the restaurant yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a specific time in the past. It uses the formal/plural subject “vous” and inversion (“avez-vous”) in a question. It’s typically followed by a past participle to form the passé composé: « À quelle heure avez-vous fermé… ? »
target_language_example: À quelle heure avez-vous commencé le travail hier ?
native_language_example: What time did you start work yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the start time of an event. Follow with a masculine noun like le concert / le film / le test. For feminine nouns, use: « À quelle heure commence la … ? » (e.g., la réunion).
target_language_example: À quelle heure commence le match ?
native_language_example: What time does the game start?

additional_notes: Used to ask at what time you are expected to arrive. Often followed by an extra detail, e.g. à quelle heure dois-je venir te chercher ? (“What time should I come pick you up?”). Note: the inversion dois-je is a more formal/question style; in everyday speech you also hear À quelle heure est-ce que je dois venir ? or Je dois venir à quelle heure ?
target_language_example: À quelle heure dois-je venir demain ?
native_language_example: What time should I come tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to ask the scheduled time of an event or service. It’s usually followed by a noun (le concert, le dîner, le prochain train…). For services/meals you can also use the passive form: « À quelle heure est servi le petit déjeuner ? » (“What time is breakfast served?”).
target_language_example: À quelle heure est la réunion ?
native_language_example: What time is the meeting?

meaning: “What time does the … leave/depart?” (asking about a schedule).
additional_notes: Used to ask the departure time of a means of transport. You can replace **le** depending on the noun: **le** bus / train, **la** navette (“shuttle”), **l’** avion, **les** trains. Often followed by the destination: **… pour Paris** (“to Paris”). You can add **prochain** (“next”): **À quelle heure part le prochain train ?**
target_language_example: À quelle heure part le prochain bus pour le centre-ville ?
native_language_example: What time does the next bus to downtown leave?

additional_notes: Used to ask what time something happened, followed by a verb (often a reflexive verb in the passé composé): « À quelle heure vous êtes-vous couché(e)(s) ? » / « … levé(e)(s) ? » / « … réveillé(e)(s) ? ». This is the formal/plural form with inversion (« êtes-vous »). The past participle may agree in gender/number with the subject (couchée, levés, réveillées, etc.).
target_language_example: À quelle heure vous êtes-vous endormi(e)(s) ?
native_language_example: What time did you fall asleep?

additional_notes: Used to ask the time when someone did something, typically followed by a past participle (passé composé): « À quelle heure êtes-vous arrivé(e) ? ». Agree the past participle with the person being addressed: arrivé (male), arrivée (female), and add -s for plural (arrivés/arrivées). Very formal/polite; in everyday speech you’ll often hear « À quelle heure tu es… ? » or « Vous êtes… à quelle heure ? ».
target_language_example: À quelle heure êtes-vous parti(e) ce matin ?
native_language_example: What time did you leave this morning?

meaning: to someone; from/for someone (depending on the verb).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect object (a person affected by the action). Common with verbs like parler à quelqu’un (talk to), dire à quelqu’un (tell), donner à quelqu’un (give to), arriver à quelqu’un (happen to), devoir quelque chose à quelqu’un (owe someone).
target_language_example: Je vais en parler à quelqu’un demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk about it to someone tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used after verbs that take the preposition à (e.g., donner à…, envoyer à…, penser à…). It can mean the recipient (“Give it to someone else”) or who you’re thinking/expecting (“I was thinking of someone else”). In “C’est à quelqu’un d’autre”, it often means “It belongs to someone else.”
target_language_example: Désolé, ce message est à quelqu’un d’autre.
native_language_example: Sorry, this message is for someone else.

additional_notes: Used after many verbs/adjectives that require the preposition « à » before an indirect object, e.g. « penser à quelque chose » (to think about something), « être allergique à quelque chose » (to be allergic to something), « servir à quelque chose » (to be useful for something), « s’accrocher à quelque chose » (to hold on to something). « Quelque chose » means “something” (an unspecified thing).
target_language_example: Je suis allergique à quelque chose dans ce plat.
native_language_example: I’m allergic to something in this dish.

meaning: 'to whom' / 'who' (as the indirect object, after à).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the person receiving an action (the indirect object), typically with verbs that take à: parler à (talk to), donner à (give to), téléphoner à (call). Often appears in questions: « À qui est-ce que… ? », « À qui… ? ». Can also be used in fixed expressions like « À qui le tour ? » (“Whose turn is it?”).
target_language_example: À qui as-tu donné les clés ?
native_language_example: Who did you give the keys to?

additional_notes: Used to ask who is the owner of something. It’s a question structure: À qui (to whom) + appartient (belongs). Often followed by a noun with a determiner (ce livre, cette voiture, la valise). You can also use it inside a longer sentence: Je me demande à qui appartient…
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, à qui appartient ce sac ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, who does this bag belong to?

meaning: "who does this belong to?" (asking who owns something).
additional_notes: Used to ask about ownership. Structure: "À qui" = "to whom" + "appartient" (from "appartenir", to belong) + "cette" (this, feminine singular) + the noun. Use "ce" before a masculine noun starting with a consonant ("À qui appartient ce sac ?") and "cet" before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or silent h ("À qui appartient cet ordinateur ?").
target_language_example: À qui appartient cette clé ?
native_language_example: Who does this key belong to?

meaning: 'Whose is this?' / 'Who does this belong to?'
additional_notes: A question used to ask who the owner is. It’s usually written and pronounced as the more natural form: « À qui est ce bébé ? » often becomes « À qui est ce bébé ? » or « C’est à qui ? » in everyday speech. Agreement depends on the noun: « À qui est ce… ? » (masc. singular), « À qui est cette… ? » (fem. singular), « À qui sont ces… ? » (plural).
target_language_example: À qui est cette valise ?
native_language_example: Whose suitcase is this?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that it could be any person, often in questions or negative statements (like “to anyone at all”). Similar idea: “à personne” = “to nobody,” while “à qui que ce soit” keeps it open but stresses “anyone.”
target_language_example: Ne raconte ça à qui que ce soit.
native_language_example: Don’t tell that to anyone.

meaning: "to what?" / "what ... about?" (used after a verb that takes "à").
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to the object of a verb that is followed by "à" (e.g., penser à = to think about, rêver à = to dream about, ressembler à = to look like). Often appears in questions: "À quoi penses-tu ?" = "What are you thinking about?" It can also introduce a clause: "Je sais à quoi ça ressemble" = "I know what it looks like."
target_language_example: À quoi tu penses en ce moment ?
native_language_example: What are you thinking about right now?

additional_notes: It’s the preposition « à » (“to/at”) + the possessive adjective « sa » (“his/her/its” for a feminine singular thing). The possessive agrees with the thing owned (the noun that follows), not the owner: « à sa mère » can mean “to his mother” or “to her mother.” Note: before a feminine singular noun starting with a vowel or silent h, French usually uses « son » instead of « sa » (e.g., « à son amie »).
target_language_example: J’ai parlé à sa sœur après le cours.
native_language_example: I spoke to his/her sister after class.

additional_notes: Used after many verbs to indicate direction/recipient (e.g., écrire à sa mère = write to his/her mother; demander à sa mère = ask his/her mother; présenter quelqu’un à sa mère = introduce someone to his/her mother). “Sa” can mean “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun mère, not the person who owns it).
target_language_example: Il téléphone souvent à sa mère le dimanche.
native_language_example: He often calls his mother on Sundays.

meaning: 'in its/his/her place'; 'instead of him/her' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like remettre / mettre to mean putting something back where it belongs: « Remets ça à sa place. » It can also mean taking someone’s place (replacing them): « Prends-moi à sa place. » With a person as the object (e.g., « Remets-le à sa place ! »), it can be figurative: telling someone off / putting them in their place.
target_language_example: Après avoir nettoyé la cuisine, j’ai remis chaque chose à sa place.
native_language_example: After cleaning the kitchen, I put everything back in its place.

additional_notes: Used to give a specific time when something happens. With clock times, French uses “à” (at): à 7 heures, à 7h, à 19 heures. Minutes can be added (e.g., à sept heures et quart).
target_language_example: Le train part à sept heures.
native_language_example: The train leaves at seven o’clock.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take the preposition **à** before an indirect object (e.g., **écrire à**, **parler à**, **mentir à**, **obéir à**, **faire plaisir à**). **Ses** means “his/her/their” depending on context, but **parents** here usually means “parents” (mother and father).
target_language_example: Je téléphone à ses parents ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm calling his/her parents tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say the time something happens. With clock times, French uses « à » (at): « à six heures » (at six). For “in the morning,” add « du matin »; for “in the evening/night,” « du soir » / « de la nuit ». You can also specify the day part: « à six heures le matin » is common in speech.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à six heures devant la gare.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at six o’clock in front of the station.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. With times in French, you often use « à » to mean “at” (e.g., « à six heures », « à six heures et demie »). « et demie » means “and a half” (half past the hour).
target_language_example: Le train part à six heures et demie.
native_language_example: The train leaves at six thirty.

meaning: to his / at his / with his (depending on the verb).
additional_notes: Made of **à** (“to/at”) + **son** (“his” or “its” before a masculine singular noun). The exact English preposition depends on the verb: **ajouter à son...** (“add to his…”), **rire à son...** (“laugh at his…”), **échouer à son examen** (“fail his exam”), **aller à son cabinet** (“go to his office”). Note the common fixed phrase **être à son compte** = “to be self-employed.”
target_language_example: Je vais parler à son professeur après le cours.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk to his teacher after class.

meaning: at his/her office; at his/her desk.
additional_notes: Uses the preposition « à » to show location. « son bureau » can mean someone’s office (the workplace/room) or their desk (the piece of furniture), depending on context. « son » is used for both masculine and feminine owners when the noun is masculine (« bureau » is masculine): « Il est à son bureau » / « Elle est à son bureau ».
target_language_example: Je suis à son bureau, je t’appelle plus tard.
native_language_example: I’m at his/her office; I’ll call you later.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to show the recipient/indirect object (often with verbs like donner, transmettre, raconter, léguer, remettre). It means something is given/told/passed on to the speaker’s or subject’s son.
target_language_example: Je vais expliquer la règle à son fils.
native_language_example: I’m going to explain the rule to his son.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic of a person/thing already known in context. It often follows verbs like savoir (to know), dire (to say/tell), apprendre (to learn), or expressions like se faire du souci (to worry). The pronoun can change: à mon sujet (about me), à ton sujet (about you), à leur sujet (about them).
target_language_example: Je n'ai rien entendu à son sujet depuis des semaines.
native_language_example: I haven't heard anything about him/her in weeks.

additional_notes: Built from the preposition « à » (to/at) + the possessive adjective « ta » (your, feminine singular). It’s used before a feminine singular noun: « à ta voix », « à ta question ». Note: before a vowel sound, French usually uses « ton » instead of « ta » even for feminine nouns (e.g., « à ton amie »).
target_language_example: Je l’ai envoyé à ta sœur.
native_language_example: I sent it to your sister.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **à** to mark the person you are speaking to, writing to, giving something to, or saying/telling something to. **ta** means “your” (informal singular ‘you’) before a feminine singular noun like **mère**.
target_language_example: Tu peux téléphoner à ta mère ce soir ?
native_language_example: Can you call your mother tonight?

meaning: "to your place/seat" or "in your position (if I were you)".
additional_notes: Used literally to mean going back to where you’re supposed to be (your seat, spot, position): « Retourne à ta place. » It’s also common in advice to mean “if I were you / in your situation”: « À ta place, je ferais… ». Note: it does NOT usually mean “at your place” (at your home); that’s « chez toi ».
target_language_example: À ta place, je n'accepterais pas cette offre.
native_language_example: If I were you, I wouldn’t accept that offer.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “to ask you (something)”: *J’ai une chose à te demander* = “I have something to ask you.” It also appears after verbs like *continuer* to mean “keep asking you”: *continuer à te demander…*. Note: *demander* usually means “to ask/request,” not “to demand” (false friend).
target_language_example: J’ai une question à te demander avant de partir.
native_language_example: I have a question to ask you before leaving.

meaning: 'to tell you' (as in 'I have something to tell you').
additional_notes: Used after a noun to show what you need to say to someone: "J’ai [quelque chose / un secret / un mot] à te dire." Literally it’s "to say to you," but in natural English it’s usually "to tell you." Uses the informal object pronoun "te" (to you); the formal version is "à vous dire."
target_language_example: J’ai quelque chose à te dire ce soir.
native_language_example: I have something to tell you tonight.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to indicate the person you’re addressing or directing something to (here, your parents). It’s the preposition à + tes (your, plural/informal 'tu') + parents. Common with verbs like demander (ask), dire (say), passer (pass on): « Demande … à tes parents », « Dis bonjour à tes parents », « Passe le bonjour à tes parents ».
target_language_example: Je vais écrire à tes parents ce soir.
native_language_example: I’m going to write to your parents tonight.

additional_notes: Used when addressing someone informally (tu) and referring to something that belongs to them or is connected to them. It’s the preposition « à » (to/at) + the possessive determiner « ton » used before a masculine singular noun (or a vowel sound): « à ton père », « à ton ami ». For feminine nouns, use « à ta »; for plural, « à tes ».
target_language_example: Je vais parler à ton professeur demain.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk to your teacher tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "à" to mark the person something is told/given to (an indirect object). "Ton" means "your" (informal singular).
target_language_example: Je vais parler à ton père ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to talk to your father tonight.

meaning: to both of you; to the two of you.
additional_notes: Used to address two people (often as part of wishes, congratulations, or statements that apply to both). Typically follows verbs like féliciter, souhaiter, arriver à, dire à, etc. Variants: « à toutes les deux » when the two people are female; « à tous les trois » for three people, etc.
target_language_example: Merci à tous les deux pour votre aide !
native_language_example: Thank you both for your help!

additional_notes: Used to address or refer to the whole group. Common in greetings and thanks (e.g., « Salut à tous ! », « Merci à tous »), and in general statements like « ouvert à tous » (“open to everyone”). Often follows nouns like « merci », « bon travail », « bonne chance ». Can refer to mixed-gender groups; for an all-female group you may see « à toutes ».
target_language_example: Bonne journée à tous !
native_language_example: Have a nice day, everyone!

additional_notes: Used with verbs like dire/annoncer/montrer to indicate the recipient is the whole group (everyone), not a specific person. Often contrasts with à quelqu’un (to someone).
target_language_example: Je vais envoyer le message à tout le monde.
native_language_example: I’m going to send the message to everyone.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something moving extremely quickly (running, driving, passing by). Often with verbs like courir (to run), rouler/conduire (to drive), passer (to go by).
target_language_example: Le train est parti à toute allure.
native_language_example: The train left at full speed.

meaning: to work; working (in the pattern: verb + à + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used when a first verb is followed by an action introduced by “à”. Common with verbs like autoriser (to allow), continuer (to continue), apprendre (to teach/learn), être disposé (to be willing), refuser (to refuse): e.g., “continuer à travailler” = “to keep working.” Here “à” doesn’t mean “to/at” as a place; it links to the infinitive.
target_language_example: Je commence à travailler demain.
native_language_example: I start working tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common preposition used for moving from one side to the other (à travers la rue = across the street; à travers la forêt = through the forest). It can also be figurative: à travers le monde = throughout/around the world; à travers les âges = through the ages.
target_language_example: On marche à travers le parc pour aller au musée.
native_language_example: We walk through the park to go to the museum.

additional_notes: Used to express movement or passage from one side/area to another within or across a place. Comes before a feminine singular noun (à travers la vallée, la France). For masculine singular use “à travers le”, for plural “à travers les”.
target_language_example: Nous avons marché à travers la forêt pour rentrer.
native_language_example: We walked through the forest to get back.

additional_notes: Used to describe movement or a line of sight passing through a place/material (a forest, a desert, fog) or looking through an instrument/opening (e.g., a telescope). It’s the masculine singular form: à travers le + masculine noun; also common are à travers la, à travers les, and à travers l’.
target_language_example: On a marché à travers le parc pour rentrer plus vite.
native_language_example: We walked through the park to get home faster.

additional_notes: Used to show movement or passage from one side to the other, or within/among a place: light through curtains, a path through marshes, blood through veins, looking through binoculars, a stream across fields. It can also be figurative: being led through hardships/trials. Often followed by a plural noun with the article “les”.
target_language_example: Nous avons marché à travers les bois pour rentrer.
native_language_example: We walked through the woods to get back home.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like « arriver à » or « parvenir à » to mean “to reach/come to a conclusion.” « si + adjective » means “so (adjective).” Agreement: « conclusion » is feminine, so « intéressante » is feminine singular to match it.
target_language_example: Nous sommes arrivés à une conclusion si intéressante après la réunion.
native_language_example: We came to such an interesting conclusion after the meeting.

meaning: to have to do with; to be related to.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avoir": "avoir (quelque chose / beaucoup / rien) à voir avec" + noun/pronoun. Common in questions like "Qu'est-ce que ça a à voir avec… ?" (= "What does that have to do with…?"). Often implies a connection or relevance.
target_language_example: Ça n'a rien à voir avec toi.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with you.

meaning: to have to do with this; to be involved in it.
additional_notes: Used with "avoir" (e.g., "Qu’est-ce que X a à voir là-dedans ?") to ask what someone/something has to do with a situation, often implying they shouldn’t be involved or it’s not their business. "Là-dedans" means "in all this / in this matter."
target_language_example: Je n’ai rien à voir là-dedans.
native_language_example: I have nothing to do with this.

meaning: "to your" (addressing multiple people or using formal "you").
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun with "vos" (= your, plural/formal): "à vos prières" (to your prayers). Very common in instructions/commands: "Retournez à vos places" (Back to your seats), "À vos postes !" (To your stations/posts!), "À vos marques" (On your marks). Also appears in warnings like "Gare à vos doigts !" (Watch your fingers!).
target_language_example: À vos téléphones, tout le monde !
native_language_example: Phones out, everyone!

additional_notes: Used with the formal/plural possessive "votre" after "à". It appears in many fixed expressions, e.g. "à votre disposition" (at your disposal), "à votre sujet / à votre propos" (about you), "à votre bord" (on your boat/vehicle), "à votre tour" (your turn). For one person you know well, you’d often use "à ton / à ta" instead.
target_language_example: Je reste à votre disposition si vous avez des questions.
native_language_example: I remain at your disposal if you have any questions.

meaning: (1) in your place/seat; (2) if I were you; (3) in your place (instead of you).
additional_notes: Used both literally (go/stay in your seat: « Allez/Restez à votre place. ») and figuratively. With the conditional, it often means “if I were you” to give advice: « Je ne ferais pas ça à votre place. » It can also mean doing something instead of someone: « Laissez-moi le faire à votre place. » (« votre » is formal/plural “your”; informal singular is « à ta place ».)
target_language_example: À votre place, je demanderais au professeur de répéter.
native_language_example: If I were you, I'd ask the teacher to repeat.

meaning: "to go there" / "to go (to it)" (often: "ready to go").
additional_notes: Used after expressions like « être prêt(e) à… » or « se préparer à… » to mean being ready/preparing to leave and go to a place. « y » replaces a place or destination already known from context (e.g., à Paris → y).
target_language_example: On est prêts à y aller ?
native_language_example: Are we ready to go?

additional_notes: Used with **à + infinitive** to describe an activity someone spends time on or starts doing: *passer du temps à écrire* (spend time writing), *se mettre à écrire* (start writing). It also appears in set phrases where **à + infinitive** means “for (doing)”: *une machine à écrire* = “a typewriter” (a machine for writing).
target_language_example: Je me suis mis à écrire un email.
native_language_example: I started writing an email.

additional_notes: This is an "à + infinitive" phrase used after certain verbs/expressions to say what someone is doing or spending time doing. Common patterns: « continuer à + infinitif » (to keep doing), « passer du temps à + infinitif » (to spend time doing), and « être à + infinitif » (to be in the middle of doing). Here, it means “(to be) studying French.”
target_language_example: Elle passe ses soirées à étudier le français.
native_language_example: She spends her evenings studying French.

additional_notes: Used to introduce, identify, or highlight something: “And this/that is…”, “That’s …”, “Now THAT is …”. Often said while pointing at something or reacting to it. Common with nouns/adjectives: “Ça, c’est une bonne idée.” / “Ça, c’est moi.”
target_language_example: Ça, c’est mon téléphone.
native_language_example: That’s my phone.

meaning: “..., right?” / “..., isn’t that so?” (a tag question).
additional_notes: Used at the end of a sentence to check that the other person agrees or to confirm something you believe is true. It’s neutral/polite and works in many situations (with tu or vous). The “ça,” in front just refers back to “that/it” and is often optional depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: On se retrouve à 18 h, n'est-ce pas ?
native_language_example: We’re meeting at 6 p.m., right?

additional_notes: Used to guess or infer something about the past based on evidence: **devoir (au passé composé) + infinitif**. It expresses strong likelihood, not certainty. Often followed by an adjective or noun: *Ça a dû être difficile/cher/une bataille…*
target_language_example: Tu avais l'air épuisé hier : ça a dû être une longue journée.
native_language_example: You looked exhausted yesterday: it must have been a long day.

additional_notes: Past tense (passé composé) of « ça marche » (“it works”). Used to say something succeeded or the method/plan functioned. Very common in spoken French: « Ça a marché ! » = “It worked!”; in questions: « Tu crois que ça a marché ? » = “Do you think it worked?”
target_language_example: J’ai redémarré l’ordinateur et ça a marché.
native_language_example: I restarted the computer and it worked.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about how something went or what something was like in the past. Often followed by an adjective or a noun phrase: “Ça a été merveilleux / amusant / une bonne journée.” Also used in passive constructions: “Ça a été diffusé” = “It was broadcast.”
target_language_example: Ça a été difficile au début, mais après ça allait mieux.
native_language_example: It was hard at first, but after that it got better.

meaning: 'It was a' / 'It has been a' (talking about something in the past).
additional_notes: Used to describe what something turned out to be after it happened (experience, event, result). It uses the past tense of « être » (passé composé): « ça » = it/that, « a été » = was/has been, followed by a masculine noun with « un » (e.g., « un succès », « un échec »). With a feminine noun, you use « ça a été une … ».
target_language_example: Ça a été un moment inoubliable.
native_language_example: It was an unforgettable moment.

meaning: “it was a …” / “that was a …” (describing something in the past).
additional_notes: Used to describe how an event/experience/period of time turned out. Very common in spoken French, where ça (“that/it”) refers to something understood from context. Often followed by a noun phrase: ça a été une fête, une expérience, une nuit, etc. In more formal writing you may also see/choose: « ce fut une… » or « cela a été une… ».
target_language_example: Ça a été une journée difficile, mais on s’en est sortis.
native_language_example: It was a difficult day, but we got through it.

additional_notes: Used to say how something appears or seems. Common patterns: **ça a l’air + adjective** (Ça a l’air bon. = It looks good.) and **ça a l’air de + infinitive** (Ça a l’air de te surprendre. = It seems to surprise you / You seem surprised).
target_language_example: Ça a l’air compliqué, mais on va y arriver.
native_language_example: It looks complicated, but we’ll manage.

additional_notes: Used to say something occurs (often unexpectedly) or to reassure someone that it’s normal. It can refer to an event (“Je ne voulais pas que ça arrive” = “I didn’t want that to happen”) or to a situation happening frequently (“Ça arrive souvent/tout le temps” = “It happens often/all the time”).
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, ça arrive à tout le monde.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it happens to everyone.

meaning: "just like that" / "offhand" (often to soften or downplay what you’re saying).
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like dire: « Je te dis ça comme ça » = “I’m just saying” (no big deal, no strong intention). In the negative (« Ne dis pas ça comme ça »), it can mean “don’t say it like that” (your wording/tone sounds harsh or wrong). « Si on peut appeler ça comme ça » means “if you can even call it that,” implying doubt about whether the label fits.
target_language_example: Je ne critique pas, je dis ça comme ça.
native_language_example: I’m not criticizing, I’m just saying.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of devoir (devrait) to express what is expected, likely, or considered normal/recommended. Common with adjectives: « Ça devrait être facile/clair/prêt. »
target_language_example: Ne t’inquiète pas, ça devrait être facile.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it should be easy.

meaning: 'it must be' / 'it should be' (a guess or logical conclusion).
additional_notes: Used to make an assumption based on clues or what seems likely. Literally “that/it must be,” with "devoir" + infinitive ("être"). Often translates as “must be” (strong probability) rather than obligation. Can also mean “should be” when pointing out what’s probably true (e.g., location: "Ça doit être là" = “It should be there”).
target_language_example: Il n'est pas encore là : ça doit être le trafic.
native_language_example: He’s not here yet: it must be traffic.

additional_notes: Used to say the effort, cost, or trouble was justified in the end. "valait" is the imperfect of "valoir" (to be worth), and "en" refers back to what you did or went through (the effort/sacrifice). Often used after finishing something difficult: "Finalement, ça en valait la peine."
target_language_example: Le trajet était long, mais ça en valait la peine.
native_language_example: The trip was long, but it was worth it.

additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort, time, money, or trouble. The pronoun “en” refers to what you’re talking about (the situation/effort/cost), and “valoir la peine” literally means “to be worth the trouble.” Often used on its own for emphasis: « Ça en vaut la peine ! »
target_language_example: Le trajet est long, mais ça en vaut la peine.
native_language_example: The trip is long, but it’s worth it.

meaning: 'that makes/does'; also 'it's been (a length of time)'.
additional_notes:
Very common with several patterns:
- Time: « Ça fait deux ans » = “It’s been two years.” / « Ça fait une heure que… » = “I’ve been … for an hour.”
- Result/total: « Ça fait deux » = “That makes two.”
- Effect/impact: « Qu’est-ce que ça fait ? » = “What does it do?/What difference does it make?” and « Je sais l’effet que ça fait » = “I know what it feels like.”
target_language_example: Ça fait trois jours que je suis malade.
native_language_example: I’ve been sick for three days.

ça fait combien de temps que

target_language_multi_word_term: ça fait combien de temps que
meaning: “how long has it been since…?” / “how long have you been…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about duration up to now. It’s followed by a clause (often in the present tense for ongoing situations: « Ça fait combien de temps que tu travailles ici ? » = “How long have you been working here?”). With a completed past event, French may still use the present-perfect/past: « Ça fait combien de temps que vous avez déménagé ici ? » = “How long ago did you move here?” Often spoken as « Ça fait combien de temps que t’es… ? » (t’es = tu es).
target_language_example: Ça fait combien de temps que tu apprends le français ?
native_language_example: How long have you been learning French?

additional_notes: Used to express relief, comfort, or something that’s good for you (physically or emotionally). Very common with an infinitive: “Ça fait du bien de + infinitive” = “It feels good to…” / “It’s good to…”. You can also add an indirect object: “Ça me/te/lui fait du bien” = “It does me/you/him/her good.”
target_language_example: Après une longue journée, ça fait du bien de se reposer un peu.
native_language_example: After a long day, it feels good to rest a bit.

additional_notes: Used to say something is pleasant, relieving, or comforting. Literally it’s like “that does good,” but the natural English is “it feels good (to…).” It’s often followed by an infinitive (de + verb): « Ça fait du bien de + infinitif ». You can also specify who benefits with « faire du bien à quelqu’un » (e.g., « Ça me fait du bien de… » = “It does me good to…”).
target_language_example: Après une longue journée, ça fait du bien de se reposer.
native_language_example: After a long day, it feels good to rest.

additional_notes: Used to say something is painful (physically or emotionally). Very common in questions like « Est-ce que ça fait mal ? » (“Does it hurt?”). « Ça » can refer to what’s happening (an injection, touching something, the truth, etc.), and « faire mal » literally means “to do/make pain.”
target_language_example: Arrête, ça fait mal !
native_language_example: Stop, that hurts!

meaning: "it’s part of the" (that’s included in it / comes with it).
additional_notes: Used to say something is a normal or expected element of an activity, job, experience, etc. It’s a common, neutral expression. Often followed by a noun: du métier (the job), du travail (the work), du spectacle (the show). You can also say: ça fait partie de + noun (when there’s no “le”): Ça fait partie de la vie.
target_language_example: Les retards, ça fait partie du voyage.
native_language_example: Delays are part of the trip.

meaning: “It’s been a long time” / “long time no see.”
additional_notes: Very common in spoken French to say it’s been a long time since you saw someone or since something happened. Often followed by **que +** a clause: **Ça fait un bail qu’on ne s’est pas vus** (“It’s been a while since we saw each other”).
target_language_example: Ça fait un bail qu’on ne s’est pas parlé !
native_language_example: We haven’t talked in a long time!

meaning: "it will be better" / "things will get better."
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or express hope that a situation (health, mood, problems) will improve in the future. Often paired with a time phrase like demain, bientôt, dans un jour ou deux, la prochaine fois. Literally it’s "that will go better," but in English you usually say "it'll be better" or "you'll feel better."
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, ça ira mieux après un peu de repos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’ll be better after a bit of rest.

meaning: 'that/it has' + 'me' (used to talk about what something did to you in the past).
additional_notes: Common spoken pattern: **ça** (“that/it”) + **m’** (“to me”) + **a** (“has”) + past participle or expression. It’s often followed by something like **changé** (“changed”), **aidé** (“helped”), **fait peur** (“scared me”), or a time expression like **pris des années** (“took me years”). In more formal writing, you may see **cela m’a** instead of **ça m’a**.
target_language_example: Ça m'a beaucoup aidé.
native_language_example: That really helped me.

meaning: "I was happy/glad to…" / "It was a pleasure to…"
additional_notes: Used to express pleasure about something you just did (often at the end of a conversation or meeting). The verb is in the past: *ça m’a fait plaisir de + infinitive* (to talk, to meet, to see). With people you’re being formal/polite with, use **vous** in the rest of the sentence; with friends, use **te**. You can also say **ça m’a fait plaisir** on its own (“It was a pleasure”).
target_language_example: Ça m’a fait plaisir de vous aider.
native_language_example: I was happy to help you.

additional_notes: Used to give your impression or opinion based on what you see/know. Often followed by an adjective (Ça m'a l'air bien / délicieux) or by "de" + noun (Ça m'a l'air d'une bonne idée).
target_language_example: Ça m'a l'air compliqué, mais je vais essayer.
native_language_example: It seems complicated to me, but I’m going to try.

meaning: "that/it" + "to me" (used before a verb: “it ___ to me”).
additional_notes: Common in fixed patterns like “ça me convient / ça me va” (“that works for me / suits me”) and with feelings or effects: “ça me rendrait heureuse” (“that would make me happy”). “Ça” is the subject (“that/it”), and “me” is an indirect object pronoun (“to me”) placed before the verb.
target_language_example: Ça me fait peur.
native_language_example: That scares me.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive (ça me fait penser, ça me fait rire) or a noun phrase (ça me fait plaisir). Often expresses a reaction; in negative or rhetorical questions it can mean “Do you think I enjoy that?” In fixed expressions it can show strong emotion: ça me fait bouillir le sang (“it makes my blood boil”), ça me fait gerber (“it makes me sick” — vulgar/very informal).
target_language_example: Quand tu dis ça, ça me fait rire.
native_language_example: When you say that, it makes me laugh.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something (an idea, a plan, a thing). In French, the thing you like is the subject (ça) and the person is an indirect object (me): "Ça me plaît" = "It pleases me". Common with emphasis: "Ça, ça me plaît." For negation you’ll often hear informal spoken French without "ne": "Ça me plaît pas" (more formal: "Ça ne me plaît pas").
target_language_example: Ce film ? Oui, ça me plaît beaucoup.
native_language_example: This movie? Yes, I like it a lot.

meaning: "it makes me" (it drives me / it causes me to become).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to say something causes a change in your mood or state: « Ça me rend + adjective ». Common with feelings like « fou/folle » (crazy), « dingue » (mad/crazy), « nerveux/nerveuse » (nervous), « cinglé(e) » (crazy—quite strong). You can switch the pronoun: « ça te rend… » (it makes you…), « ça le/la rend… » (it makes him/her…).
target_language_example: Le bruit constant, ça me rend nerveux.
native_language_example: The constant noise makes me nervous.

meaning: “it seems to me” / “it strikes me as.”
additional_notes: Used to give your personal impression or opinion about something. Common patterns: « Ça me semble + adjective » (bon, correct, étrange) and « Ça ne me semble pas + adjective/infinitive » (faisable). Similar in meaning to « il me semble que… » but followed directly by an adjective (or sometimes an infinitive).
target_language_example: Ça me semble trop cher pour ce que c'est.
native_language_example: It seems too expensive to me for what it is.

meaning: “It’s biting!” / “It bites.” (often: the fish are biting).
additional_notes: Literally “that/it bites.” Very common when fishing: « Alors, ça mord ? » = “Any bites?” / “Are they biting?” and « Ça mord pas » = “Nothing’s biting.” It can also be used as a warning about an animal: « Attention, ça mord ! » = “Careful, it bites!”
target_language_example: On change d’endroit : ici, ça mord pas.
native_language_example: Let’s move spots: nothing’s biting here.

meaning: "it/that doesn't…" (start of a negative sentence with ne…).
additional_notes: “Ça” means “it/that,” and “ne” is the first part of French negation. It’s almost always completed by another word later in the sentence: ne…pas (not), ne…jamais (never), ne…plus (no longer), ne…rien (nothing), ne…que (only), etc. Examples: « Ça ne marche pas » (It doesn’t work), « Ça ne doit jamais se produire » (That must never happen), « Ça ne marche que sous Windows » (It only works on Windows).
target_language_example: Ça ne va pas aujourd’hui.
native_language_example: It’s not going well today.

additional_notes: Used when something isn’t functioning (a device, plan, method) or isn’t effective with someone: « Ça ne marche pas avec moi » = “That doesn’t work on/with me.” Can also mean “That’s not how it works”: « Ça ne marche pas comme ça ».
target_language_example: J’ai essayé de redémarrer l’ordinateur, mais ça ne marche pas.
native_language_example: I tried restarting the computer, but it doesn’t work.

meaning: "it can't / that can't" (it is not possible).
additional_notes: Made of "ça" (it/that) + "ne… pas" (not) + "peut" (can, from "pouvoir"). It’s typically followed by an infinitive: "Ça ne peut pas attendre" (It can’t wait), "Ça ne peut pas continuer" (It can’t continue). It can express impossibility or that something is not feasible/acceptable, and also appears in set ideas like "Ça ne peut pas faire de mal" (It can’t hurt). In casual speech, "ne" is often dropped: "Ça peut pas…"
target_language_example: Désolé, ça ne peut pas attendre.
native_language_example: Sorry, it can't wait.

additional_notes: Used to say something is urgent and must be done now. Often appears as a question ("Ça ne peut pas attendre ?") meaning "Can’t it wait?" or with a time word like "demain"/"demain matin". In casual speech, "ça" can refer to a call, a task, or any situation.
